I have either too many or not enough words to describe this game. I will permit that I have followed Mr. Schafer since I was about 7 or 8 after playing Day of the Tentacle, and despite some of his games not being considered runaway successes, I find magic in every one he has a part in. This game grabs me in a special place that wrenches me back to 1995 and MS-DOS, and the sense of wonder is the same. If nothing else, he's captured the essence of what made point-and-click adventures so special to me.
Technically, the game is pleasant to look at despite a few graphical glitches here and there, the sound is a brilliant score and mix of audio, and the voice acting is superb. The puzzles may seem easy but revisiting DOTT after growng up proved that the puzzles just took some abstract thinking versus genius-level leaps of logic- in that respect I find it slightly disappointing, but then again, I'm here for the story.
Speaking of the story, it's pretty enticing. How exactly will Shay plan his mutiny? How does Vella slay the beast, or can she? It's a great hook into a more in-depth game. Granted, Act I is 'short', about 3-4 hours if you're really combing through everything, but then again most adventure games could have been clocked in under about 4 hours. The length is not so much of an issue when the game is quality.
The game's not perfect, but it satisfies many of my adventure game needs and more and for that it deserves a hearty pat on the back and a 'well done'.

Hotline miami is one of the most fun and most annoying games I have ever played. The immense pain when ,you were one guy away from finishing a level, and you die. The huge satisfaction when you finally complete a level after hours of trial and error. All of thease things make up one of the best games I have ever played.
So if we go onto the store page for hotline miami and look at the reveiws. You can see that this game is rediculosly popular with its players and the only negative reveiws about this game was the fact it was too hard for them. So what makes up this game? What makes it so good? Thease are the questions im hoping to awnser in this video.
Lets start with the basics. Every good game has sound right? Well have you ever heard the music in this game? Its absolutly amazing and I have even searched up the music on youtube and have enjoyed listening to it even outside the game. I love how when you meet the charactors the music is very lound and threatning almost as if your about to get a loud jumpscare. I love the music so much that I bought the hotline miami cs go music kit, and I enjoy imagining the cs go maps as top down rage makers.
So what else is there in a good game? a good game needs to be chalenging. An easy game is no fun, and this game went up to the line between easy and hard and strapped itself to a suicidal rocket heading to Mount Impossible. Im not saying Hotline is impossible, but it certainly gets near it towards the higher chapters.
Now another thing a good game needs is a good storyline. Hotline Miami has one but I find it confusing and hard to follow. Which hopfully is on purpose as im not very far into the game and I hope as it progresses it gets more clear. To be honest I think its mostly my fault that I dont know the storyline as I skip most of the talking and most of the awnser phone messages.
Another thing that makes a good game is good combat (only in shooting and fighting games). Hotline manages to combine stratgy of which room to hit first with the one hit kill from enimies to make a challenging yet fun game. In this game to do well you need to organise an order of how and when to do things, you have to try and pick of induviduals or attack two and try and dodge bullets. I love the way you can time your entrance so that you can take out one person before you get in and i love the way that if your out of ammo you can throw your can at them and finish them off.
Over all I think this is a well rounded and great game that you should defiatly buy if you havent got it. Its impressive how they managed to balace difficult with fun and I think this is one of those games that will come round once a decade.

(Keep in mind that this is for act one only, so story elements aren't complete, and probably shouldn't be judged unless there are glaring inconsistencies, of which, I found none)
-The Characters are fun and enjoyable. A good amount of actors from Psychonauts return as minor characters, which may make some people happy. The addition of Backer voices doesn't deter from any gameplay or story and is just a much a part of the story as every other character.
-The puzzles aren't too difficult (more on this later). Feels like a casual, story-driven experience that isn't meant to test your brain too hard.
-The soundtrack is pretty good. It isn't overwhelming, but makes its presence known during major points in both parts of the act(which is by no means a bad thing).
- I'm indifferent about Ellijah Wood as Shay. I'm not entirely convinced this has to do with how Shay's situation is at the beginning of his story, but I could be wrong. (Let me make a disclaimer here, Shay's voice could be FAR worse)
- The way the puzzles were designed seem like they were meant to invoke a more casual, story-based experience. This may deter who actually like difficult gameplay.
- Backers get spoiled kinda early if they recognize a key piece of music from the game's documentary and, specifically, how its referred as. Took the joy of revealing the Act One climax right out from under me.
TL:DR: Overall, its a good start to a game that was kickstarted. It is well made and, at an assumed six to eight hours of gameplay (if act two is the same length as act one) for twenty dollars, I'd recommend it to anyone who is a fan of adventure games, and most definately recommend it if it ever goes on sale (which it inevitable since its on steam).

This was when i decided to take another look at the game, and i noticed how they added a Levelling system, kind of like Killing Floor's (This was heavily requested by the game's community) some new Maps, and fixed tons of the bugs that had been plaguing the game since release.
While still being a quite flawed game (as you can notice while playing the game for a bit, ESPECIALLY those third-person player character movement animations, they look beyond terrible, sorry it had to be said!) i can finally say that i had fun with this game, and at the current 93% Sale price, it is WORTH IT.

I sat down and said "you're actually gonna finish it tonight" and I reinstalled the game. I shouldn't have to sit down and force myself to play a game, but Mafia 3 accomplished the task of making me feel this way. The story and the format it's told in is great, the gunplay is great, but that's the extent of it. At 30 hours, the campaign feels like an unending slog. A long campaign might seem like a blessing but somehow 2k and hangar 13 turned that blessing into a curse.
The campaign boils down to "do same objective set a, then same objective set b, and kill important person. repeat for 30 hours." This made the feeling of progression basically nonexistent and by the time I offed the big bad I went "Thank god". NO GAME SHOULD MAKE ME DO THAT.
The game's start was incredibly strong. But that's it. I can only recommend Mafia 3 if it was cut down to at most 30 dollars. The graphics are kinda shoddy, the combat is good, the story has a VERY strong start, and the campaign is overlong and not varied enough to engage literally anyone.
5/10

Life is Strange is a story rich game. For those that enjoy a lot of dialogue mixed with some action and truly meaningful choices, this is your game.
The game is kind of slow, however,  it keeps it's pace very consistently. The game's optimization for PC is well enough, although weaker systems can barely push 25fps on even the lowest settings.
[Spoilers Ahead!]
The characters are generally enjoyable and believable, and the acting is great, though there are some flaws. Chloe seems to die... A LOT, and it ruins the player's original first impression of her that she was a rebellious "you can't beat me" kind of person.
Max is a very likable character, though she does use some... very outdated terms in her dialogue.
[OKAY, BIG SPOILERS, TURN BACK IF YOU HAVEN'T BEAT THE GAME, YOU CUCKOLD!]
The Jefferson plot twist at the end of Ep. 4 is so mind blowingly unexpected that when I originally saw it I had to sit there for about FIFTEEN MINUTES before starting Ep. 5. Speaking of which, Ep. 5 is a very strange part of the game.
Now, we're on to technical issues.
There are very few issues with the programming of the game, but there is one thing that, for some, can ruin the whole experience. The lip syncing is absolutely abismal. Their mouths don't even move when they speak!
Despite the bad things I've listed, the pros heavily outweigh them, and the game is very good with some ups, downs, and emotional moments.
I recommend it.
FINAL VERDICT -
8.5 / 10

After the huge success that was season 1 I found myself wondering and worrying that season 2 would just never be able to match up.
And I've never been happier to be proven wrong as season 2 manages to easily deliver an equally intense and emotional ride as season 1, also....
so that's a massive win as well.
The story is once again well put together and certainly manages to catch you off guard with some really gutwrenching and tear-jerking moments.   That said, if you've played season 1 then that no doubt doesn't really come as a surprise and if you haven't.... then why the hell not?
There are some minor negatives off course, mainly that some of the characters in this season are a bit more bland then the ones in season 1.
Also everybody follow and obeying a little kid during the entire story is perhaps logically speaking not really all that realisitc, no matter how baddass that kid might be at times.
Lastly, if you're not a fan of quicktime events stay far far away.... but then if you do, why are you even looking at a telltale games game in the first place?
+ Great story
+ Plenty of emotional moments
+ Clementine
+ A good amount of different endings depending on your choices
+ Cellshaded graphics
- A few really bland characters
- A bit too short for my liking

This game is incredible, in some ways it's better, some ways worse, than Season 1.
Gladly (and most importantly) the story doesn't disappoint in any way, which is great to say considering how strong the story of Season 1 was. Clementine learns to stand on her own two feet in Season 2, and the way that happens is through the decisions you make, considering how young she is, you really feel like the decisions you make with her are really forging her character into how she will behave when she grows up. You really get immersed into this.
While the story quality is high unfortunately the gameplay is more limited here, there are less 'hub' areas than the first, and less actual gameplay segments, shame because it is nice to actually shoot some zombies without it feeling so scripted every once in a while.
Overall, this game is definitely a worthy sequel to Season 1, if you haven't played Season 1 get that one first and it's '400 days' DLC, as the decisions you make in those have any effect in Season 2 (much like in Mass Effect) and doing that will help you craft a more personal story, immersing you further into this world. If you have played Season 1, picking this up is a no-brainer (zombie pun not intended) and get ready for another seriously emotional rollercoaster.

Just about 30 minutes in and already having a great time.
The game is obviously inspired by
and plays like a manic version of that game. Similarities: controls make your character move left, right, jump, and drop, and firing can only be done forwards or backwards, stationary or during movement. There are three planes along which you can travel, and enemies may come either along those lanes (from either side) or may fly independent of them.
Notable additions include a number of unlockable characters that feel like (and, in one case, literally is) Nuclear Throne characters, different strengths/weaknesses, different guns, and a different active/passive unique ability. There is a cumulative score based unlock system, which means even if you aren't good, you'll start getting new characters quickly. Finally, coins collected in game allow you to unlock items which essentially function as perks, giving new or improved abilities, or one time bonuses (like refilling life).
I don't know how much content the game has - I haven't yet reached the first REAL boss (there are a number of short miniboss waves), but the game so far is cute, fun, more than a little twitchy, and definitely scratches my "one more time" itch. I suspect I'll be playing it for a good long while to come.

At maximum stealth level, you can basically walk through most maps entirely unseen, taking the most direct route from checkpoint to checkpoint, entirely invisible to all the enemies.  It's like the game designers realized you'd get bored with the game, so they gave you an option to just skip most of it.  They also gave you a pistol, which at high levels can one-shot kill almost any enemy in the game, if you wanted to skip the bulk of combat as well.
There are at least two easy ways to play the game 'right,' and I found one unfortuante way to play the game 'wrong.'  While the pistol can kill anything, the shotgun can barely kill the starting enemies.  Leveling it up doesn't make it materially better.  If you chose a shotgun build, you've chosen wrong, and the game will punish you for it.
The one interesting aspect of the game is also one of its most frustrating.  Conversations have real consequences and are hard to reset and replay.  It encourages you to research your conversation targets well, like you're supposed to, and to accept convesation mistakes if you make them.  But it's too easy to make mistakes.  The game doesn't tell you what you're character is going to say, it just says something like, "suave."  Now "suave" might be cool and seductive when talking to one character, but creepy and stalker-ish when talking to another.  You don't know until you click the button what ridiculous crap is going to come out of your mouth.  So I never really felt like my conversation choices were "my choices."  It was just a question of whether I pushed the 'right' button, or the 'wrong' one, based on what the online wiki said.  That's not fun.

Don't listen to all the people whining about the micro-transactions in the game. They're literally the most non-offensive micro-transactions i've ever seen. On the same tier as cosmetic microtransactions.
The online portions of the game are also incredibly fun. If your fortress is attacked while you are offline NO DAMAGE IS DONE TO YOUR FORTRESS OR FOLLOWERS. YOU DO NOT LOSE PROGRESS. When you're making defenses for your fortress you're basically making a challenge for other players, more or less a "You think you're tough? Come at me bro". It's really fun too, the fortress fights are incredibly well done IMO. Just, when making your defenses, make everything fireproof so that your captains don't just get ♥♥♥♥♥tomped by someone riding a drake >.>
Captains DO die in invasions but that's honestly fine, if you plan it right they'll survive anyway and it adds a sense of consequence. If they die they weren't strong enough to deserve a spot in your army anyway (Same with the pit fights!).
Caragors and Graugs got nerfed to hell but Drakes are the new Graugs and they're more fun than graugs ever were so don't worry about mounted combat if that's you're thing. I recommend that as soon as you unlock the questline that lets you get the drake summon story ability, you just do it all right away. You'll know which one it is on sight. It's the one with the forest and the big nature woman, because of course it is. Flying across the map atop a mini flying death machine feels amazing.
The actual game is incredibleand I've barely been able to stop playing despite actually wanting to due to other obligations (it's okay sleep is for the weak anyway). Heavily recommended even at current price. I don't know about the DLC yet, just wait for it to come out anyway. No point in essentially pre-ordering extra content you might not want, though if Shadow of Mordor's DLC quality is anthing to judge by I have pretty high hopes.
Game's also huge. Lots of stuff to do. It actually felt overwhelming seeing how many zones there were after you take control of your first region, and as far as i'm aware that's all still just act II, I know there are at least 3.
A little bit too much collectible hunting for my tastes (I stopped giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥about gondor artifacts after my ~30th one). The gondor artifacts actually remind me of assassin's creed, but it's admittedly still much better in that there's a pretty decent amount of lore behind every artifact, though I skip it to get to the real goods, Talion and Celebrimbor's quippy dialogue after you pick it up.
Story's also pretty good, better than Shadow of Mordor's at least. Characters are pretty decent too. Game's definitely not as lighthearted awesomeness as the trailers made it seem but lots of awesome to be found.
It's a really good game that's gotten a lot of undeserved flak, including a bunch of asshats buying the game JUST TO GIVE IT A BAD REVIEW. Even despite that, on steam it currently has a "Very Positive rating" If you're looking at reviews, even if you don't like mine, I recommend completely ignoring anything that even mentions microtransactions, and make sure the reviewer has at least a couple of hours in the game. You do that and you'll realize pretty quick that everyone who came into this game with an open mind and actually tried it has LOVED it. Give it a chance before you regret it!

Pros
- Gorgeous hand-drawn landscapes and cut scene animations. All of the game looks great if you appreciate this style, but some parts are simply beautiful. I enjoyed the Old Woods and the waterfall sequence especially.
- Norse Scandinavian mythos is back in spades. The Banner Saga 2 embraces the traditions of the first game, and shows off more aspects of the Viking culture in a historically inspired tale.
- Battles are very similar to the original. But improved tactical system with new skills and character abilities keep battles interesting, even for a veteran player.
- The epic saga continues! Two amazing story arcs follow the journey of a Human/Varl caravan seeking shelter from the menacing Dredge hordes and a series of apocalyptic phenomena. Plus a giant serpent that crushes mountains.
- Plot twists, hard choices, and betrayals abound, with the lives of your friends and clansmen hanging in the balance. This can be irritating if a seemingly casual choice allows thieves to steal your supplies, or heartbreaking if your battle strategy ends up killing one of your favorite characters. Forward looking and decisive actions will reward your group with supplies, new allies, and morale boosts for both your caravan, and for yourself at making life just that much better in a uncertain world. Regardless of your choices, this gritty, teeth on edge story will take an emotional toll on you.
- The abundance of varying paths and caravan decisions encourages multiple playthroughs, giving the game a nice replay value.
- The option of importing a save from the first game with all of your hard-fought character levels, items, and clansmen is a much welcome treat to fans of the original Banner Saga.
- The music is just frigkin awesome.  Unique, atmospheric, dynamic. It goes the distance and then some.
Cons
- Too many playable characters, which leads to lack of character dialogue/development outside of the primary group. I wanted to hang out with Yrsa and Griss more.
- Some events seem as if they give you a choice in what will happen, but the end result will always be the same. These are annoying false dichotomies in a game that usually plays in a ‘Choices Matter’ fashion.
- The Horseborn, the new playable race prominently featured in preview trailers, seem somewhat lacking. Their playable characters come off as average, and their backstory is very peripheral to the main plot.
- The ending…..I’m coming to like it better when I consider certain other aspects; a sequel like this can’t end the same as the first, a trilogy of games relies heavily on the second part to set the stage for the finale, the developers want to keep us in suspense, etc….but I won’t lie. My initial reaction upon seeing the ending was to yell a particularly nasty string of curses at how poorly the plot was resolved. Way too many unresolved issues. This more than anything else seems to be the most damning critcism in an otherwise spectacular game.
Overall
Great sequel to an amazing series. The artwork, music, and story will capture your heart. The decision oriented chapters will keep you thinking about how best to run your caravan, develop heroes, and use resources. While the combat is pretty much the same as the original, the formula remains an engaging strategy challenge with quite a few new features to liven things up. Aside from nit-picking at an overall great story, and an ending that does leave quite a few loose ends, The Banner Saga2 is a worthy sequel. If you liked the first game or enjoy strategy RPGs, definitely get your hands on this Scandinavian gem.

Was expecting some kind of sandbox GTA-like game; got an LSD-fueled action-packed arcade game instead.
In this game basically you complete one level after another, just like your typical arcade game. Between levels/missions there are intermissions where the plot progresses and you are given a short brief about your next mission. The format isn't unusual, but the gameplay is quite challenging. Imagine stealth game where people die in one hit (old Tom Clancy's?) + brutish shooting and melee combat (Sleeping Dogs in 2D?). Albeit having stealth elements, this game rewards brutality and exposure - so the key here is simply not getting die. There is no health, only checkpoint per stage.
The graphics is nothing special, but the atmosphere and the use of color makes it as if you're playing while on drugs. The music supports the LSD-induced atmosphere. The story can be a bit difficult to follow; it might seem surreal or even odd with only little things explained - especially since most of the secret is hidden in bonus missions and unlockables. But I guess it's not the strongest part of the game anyway.
I finished this game in 8 hours or so. While I usually don't enjoy arcade that much, I can see the replay value in this one.

As soon as Tim Shafer revealed this on Kickstarter I backed immediately. The old Lucasarts games such as Monkey Island 1&2, Day Of The Tentacle and Grim Fandango are among my favourite games ever created and so I jumped at the chance to play a new adventure game from the same mind involved in those classics. I was not dissapointed. The writing takes on a different mood from his previous efforts in this genre and is less about side splitting humour and more about telling the story about the tragic lives of 2 seemingly unrelated teenagers with drastically different lives. That's not to say there are not funny moments, some of the humour is genuinly brilliant. The visual style is the thing that struck me most about this game though with it's amazing storybook visuals which look amazing when the characters are animated on screen.
At the time of this review only act 1 is available and comes in at around 4 hours long. I can already say my money was well spent and cannot wait for act 2. Tim Shafer and Double Fine have knocked it out of the park with this game.

This game plays like a moving painting. The graphics are well made and the animation is sleek. You have to like the (kind of) childish look and feel, tho. The music is marvelous and sets the mood perfectly! The story (up until Act 1) is rather short and linear, but entertaining. It's not like those old Lucas Arts games where you have dozens of items simultaneously and need to gather lots of information to solve the puzzles. Broken Age is way more linear and adresses the casual adventure gamers, rather than the die hard oldschool fans. If you want good, old point and click adventures, you have to play the "Daedalic" games.
Still, Broken Age is a good and solid game.

It took a while for the game to build up. At first I was skeptical to the "world" that Double fine had created, the puzzles were to easy and the world felt empty. As the game progressed you stumble upon characters which are more realized and the plot thickens. Puzzles were also getting more complex, but not even I had to use a walkthrough for this.
The cliffhanger at the end of the game was awesome, can't wait for the next documentary from Doublefine and the next act!

Adventure Game 'Hardcore' Fans out there, you probably have backed this game via kickstarter already. Some late comers might also have backed this game during the humble Double Fine bundle.
But if you haven't and you love adventure games, you pretty much have to play this one.
The art style and visuals are stunning, believe me. It's as if you are in an interactive children's story book / animation movie.
Voice-acting is also good and if you are one of the backers, you probably know the famous people who lend their voices to this game.
Gameplay-wise not much has changed from the traditional point-and-click adventure games from the past or recent time.
When you are stuck, you are stuck and feeling so dumb going back and forth between places trying to find what you've might missed. Well, unless you want to get a bit spoiled and look it up in the internet nowadays compared to the old times when your only options is to find that hint book or walkthrough from your gaming mag.
Sadly, with all that funding, this game's Act 1 felt pretty short. Might've been nice if they put multiple / alternative solutions to given puzzles / obstacles in the game.
Story-wise it's top-notch, kudos to Mr. Schaffer and team.
If you enjoy adventure games this is a must play!

Turn based futuristic stealth game with randomly generated levels.  You play as a spy agency on the run, looking to get back on it's feet on a deadline.  You take missions around the world that offer different benefits such as money, breaking out an MIA operative, getting additional augments for your operatives, and so on.  The operatives themselves offer different specializations and you can level them up by spending credits, as well as equipping them as you see fit.  It seems to be pretty replayable due to the randomly generated missions, and once you move past playing the game on the easier difficulty (about 7 hours for me) the later ones have a permadeath mechanic by default which is pretty cool.  I think the settings for that are customizable though.  Anything past the first difficulty is pretty tough for my tastes honestly, but those who are accustomed to say XCom should find this game plenty enjoyable.
A stealthy mixture of FTL's take on an extended rogue lite experience and XCOM's masterful turn based strategy.

A great turn-based tactics that looks like a mix of XCOM and Splinter Cell. You control several agents as they infiltrate and pillage different facilities.
The main campaign is really short (5-6 hours tops), but there's an endless mode. Even better, all locations are randomly generated with different rooms, guards, cameras, security bots. etc. This adds a lot of replayability, especially since there are 4 preset difficulties and you can tailor a custom difficulty by changing various game settings.
You also unlock new agents and AI abilities (programs & hacks) by getting XP for completed missions. So each time you start a new game, not only you can choose other difficulty settings, but different agents and abilities as well.

Definitely too short and too simple game.  I've passed throught main campaign in 5 hours. Certainly, it's still possible to repeat game with higher difficulty level, but what for? All missions are very similar. Invisible doesn't offer many different strategies and tactics, so gameplay is funny only at the beginning. It's OK to play it for few hours, but that's all what it offers.

As a game I should really downvote this. But there are enough reviews here to show that this isn't really a game, so since we already established that, I am going to review this for what it is, an intriguing piece of art. I am an art lover, and as such I find this interesting.
The concept of a lonely mountain that goes through changes, comments on its existance, has reactions and so on is just a really good concept. It lives up to the creators of Her.
You kind of wonder if this mountain at some point is going to become so evolved that it will go away to a "higher place" with the other Mountains. And you know that this isn't going to happen, that obviously this isn't as complex as the ficticious AI OS starring in Her. But your mind goes places, and then your attention is brought back to the Mountain, even as I type this, as the sound of dawn chimes.
You are there going about your business, doing your own thing, and so is Mountain. So why blame Mountain for living its own life? Yet unsuspecting that you can turn it off at any time, only to resume from where it left off the next time you turn it on.
But you could ask, are we also all unaware of some higher power that is watching us from a computer screen while we go about our lives?
You'll probably say, "You are crazy, of course we are not."
Yet all I have been trying to do here is to embrace and show what kind of concept Mountain really is. At least my artistic interpretation. Look elsewhere if you want a game, but if you want a piece of art, a silent "companion" then you might want to spend the little money it costs. If not, nobody forces you to buy this, you keep going about your business and play the games you enjoy, just as Mountain goes about its own.
P.S.: If you really don't like your Mountain, you can always "as,zb"

It's always the same.
A few questions are asked; sure, they're fairly different every time, but what's relevant is that they're always questions.
The first time? You don't know what to do until it says draw something.
Connections are made. You realize it's making you draw an abstract concept.
Does it do anything? Who knows. Maybe it's a metaphor.
Then it draws you a mountain.
.
You do what anybody else would do. You click on it. It stops. You drag it left. It spins faster to the left. You drag it right. It spins to the right. You scroll for fun. The camera zooms in and out accordingly.
Suddnely, a sound. A wonky chord, played upon a piano.
The mountain says something. Was it you? Did you do anything? The answer is no. You didn't do anything. The mountain has thoughts. It thinks.
Later, a few presses of your keyboard reveal that certain keys produce musical notes, and that there's even one to make the mountain speak, to think. This isn't the natural way of things. The mountain thinks, speaks on it's own terms. It feels forced otherwise.
After playing around with the notes for a bit, you feel adventerous. What happens if you play these notes? What happens if that song plays? What happens, if for no reason at all, you decide to play that five note tune from
?
Maybe it's best you don't right this instant. A time for everything, and such.
Then a loud noise, and a shake of the camera. What happened? What is it?
You search the mountain for any clues. Then you see it.
A giant rubber duck.
It's right there, buried face-first in the side of your mountain. You can't see it from the front to confirm it's a rubber duck, but there's nothing else that's quite got that shape.
So you click on it. Maybe there's a rubber duck noise. Maybe not. Nothing much happens. So you click it and hold it.
It shakes. It pops out of the mountain. In shock, you let go of the mouse. It flies back into the mountain. It makes you chuckle.
The mountain keeps thinking, keeps spinning, just doing it's thing.
Then you remember the
song-tune-thing. You plunk out the keys badly enough to figure it out, then prepare to play the thing for real.
The final note rings out. A giant red eye appears out from nowhere and comes ever closer to your mountain. The tense music begins, growing ever louder as the eye gets ever closer.
And then it reaches the mountain. The eye destroys your mountain. The thing that ou didn't work at all for.
And you feel a loss.
And then you start again.

Banner Saga 2 might seem like more of the same at first, but improves on it's design in a number of subtle, but important, ways. The story continues to be a masterful display of world building and character moments, while continuing to propel the characters forward, never giving you a chance to be bored.
I highly recommend you play Banner Saga 1 first though, as your entire party, their upgrade path and your items are carried over, some of which can even impact your story in interesting little ways.

If you liked BS 1, you'll more than like BS 2. If you didn't like it, well, I don't think this'll do much to sway you.
You play it for the story, which I think is interesting at best and a little dry at worst. I was keeping track of more characters than last time, I was more invested in the story this time as my actions carried over from BS 1 (being who plays the main character) and they do a better job explaining how the morale system works and what the different variety of people in your clan can do (clansmen now gather suplies every so often from the road, so that's a nice touch.)
Combat is the same (though you'll get a new selection of classes and heroes to try out like Poets and Horseborn) and the artstyle is basically the same. I will add there are some fully animated cutscenes that are a nice touch, but there are only a handful of them for the REALLY important plot twists. I beat it in 10 hours or so, I'm sure others can do it faster, but I'm satisfied. Already waiting for The Banner Saga 3.

Let me preface this by saying I LOVED the first entry in The Banner Saga. I have over 80 hours logged on it, gotten every achievement and beaten it at least 5 times. I actually just did a fresh playthrough of TBS1 and I still loved it!
The Banner Saga 2 is a DIRECT continuation of the first one. The first thing I noticed when I gained control is I had the exact same resources, clansman, fighters and varl as my imported save. My characters retained the same level and equipment, however it seems like they boosted all your underleveled characters up to level 3.
I actually didn't expect this and it took me by surprise. Then again, I wasn't sure what to expect.
Everything you liked or disliked about the first Banner Saga is back except everything is a -little- nicer and freshened up a bit!
My only real complaint is about the progression system. Now, all your units can level up to level 10 but the problem is, there's no real reason to. The stat caps on your units hasn't increased at all but instead you have two options per maxed stat that can be put into a related perk. The problem is, they are all minute RNG based stats. Chance to avoid damage, critical hit chance, dodge chance, chance to avoid death are a few of the options you are given.
Not only this but all of the new equipment seems to follow this design, as well, such as giving you higher tier of these random chances or more other tertiary stats that I couldn't be bothered with.
It's no secret that The Banner Saga's combat is just a math battle so giving you more and bigger flat stats on levels and gear might be tough to balance and heavily dependant on how you did in The Banner Saga 1. However, by the end of this instalment, I was swimming in renown and couldn't be bothered to feed it to my units to min-max more. I think the highest level I got a character was maybe 7 and I still did fine.
Overall, I'm sad to say that I doubt I'll be finding the same replay value that I did with the first Banner Saga. The ending to this instalment came more sudden and cliffhanger-ey than the last, to the point where it sapped any real urge I had to start another playthrough, anytime soon.
Still, I am eager to see the end of this amazing series!
Here's to hoping we don't have to wait another two years for the last part of the trilogy!

Breathtakingly gorgeous, and with a hilarious flair that Tim Schafer is known all too well for, Broken Age is a love letter to the classic point-and-click genre that is so rarely ever acted upon in this age of gaming. Growing up playing games like this such as ToonStruck and Grim Fandango, I find a heartwarming and euphoric sense of wonder washing over me with every click of the mouse. The dialogue and story is reminiscent of the days where well-written plots and stellar (not to mention gut-bustingly hilarious) character interaction was a keystone in gaming, which seems to find less and less of a foothole in many modern blockbuster games. Double Fine has always excelled at creating games that have a personality, and Broken Age is no exception. With a terrific ensemble cast of voice actors, a beautifully executed art style, and a charm that only the folks at Double Fine and the creative genius of Tim Schafer could produce, you're looking at one of the best games of the year. Don't pass this one up folks.

Thoughts: I finally realized what was lacking in The Wolf Among Us that made it feel less like a game compared to Walking Dead Season One, and it's also lacking in Season Two: in Season One, there were a few sections where you had to explore and interact with a large open area in order to solve a puzzle or problem. This large exploration area not only gave some meat to the game, it also helped to flesh out the characters more as you could talk to them and catch up with them. This is pretty much lacking in Season Two: instead the game feels more like a series of cutscenes with dialogue options interspersed with QTE action sequences. There are some areas you can explore, but the areas are small, there's not much to interact with and the puzzle-solving element is minimal. The lack of this makes Season Two inferior to Season One, IMHO. All that said, it's still an enjoyable ride. Clementine is a fantastic character and I loved that there were several "little girl" options for her dialogue, like hugging a person or giving them *sad eyes* to gain their sympathy. There were quite a few harrowing decisions to be made (although I have to say none as harrowing as in Season One), one QTE sequence in the first episode that is not for the faint of heart, some interesting and likeable (and a few utterly hateable!) characters, many horrible deaths, a few heartbreaking betrayals, and one dream sequence in the final episode that was an utter gut punch... Ultimately a fun roller coaster ride, but I wish Telltale would put the exploration and puzzle solving elements back in their games.

In this game basically you complete one level after another, just like your typical arcade game. Imagine stealth game where people die in one hit (old Tom Clancy's?) + brutish shooting and melee combat (Sleeping Dogs in 2D?). Albeit having stealth elements, this game rewards brutality and exposure - so the key here is simply not getting die. There is no health, only checkpoint per stage.
The graphics is nothing special, but the atmosphere and the use of color makes it as if you're playing while on drugs. The music supports the LSD-induced atmosphere. The story can be a bit difficult to follow; it might seem surreal or even odd with only little things explained - especially since most of the secret is hidden in bonus missions and unlockables. Nuclear Throne is one of the best games I've played in a long time.
It offers tight gameplay based entirely on your skill and a teensy bit of RNG. The RNG is acceptable enough, you usually get at least something you'll like by the time it actually matters.
You never feel cheated by the game. Any time you fail, it's almost certainly your fault. I can think of exactly one instance where the game becomes unfair, and that's with IDPD Vans. But those only appear much later into the game, and... hopefully they're being fixed soon.
Overall, NT is an excellent game which follows a tenant I hold dear: "It's okay to do only one thing, as long as you do that one thing spectacularly." NT is the same thing over and over again at its very core, but that one thing is so satisfying and JUST varied enough in its own ways that it has a lot of replay value. It tests your skill without being unfairly difficult, it offers responsive and very fast-paced gameplay, and it's everything you probably want from a shooter like this.
I would strongly suggest it.

The graphics (while simple) have a unique, sleek design to them that suits the future noir-esque setting, while the character abilities further refine and immerse you in the world that's developed. The sound design and music all add to the game's effectiveness as well. Nuclear Throne is an awesome game. It's fun, has a lot of content to unlock and is very challenging. Almost everything about this game is solid, from the fast paced combat to the many enemies and guns. So there’s no reason for me to waste your time going into depth about everything awesome about this game. Throw your money at Vlambeer and play this game! So I’ll go over the bad parts of the game, it’s lack of character and mutation variety.
The game has twelve different character to play with, each with their own abilities and perks. But your playstyle doesn’t usually change from character to character. You'll find yourself taking the same mutations and the same guns, so your playthrough's might not differ to much from one another. Two characters are an exception to this, Melting and Rouge. It takes a lot for a game to consume me in the same way that Middle-earth: Shadow of War has. I went to bed seeing parry and dodge prompts, I heard the voices of enemy Orcs and Olog-Hais in my head whilst stood in the queue at the shops, and I’m sure I saw the Bright Lord in an episode of the Great British Bake Off. Point is, this game has bled into my reality due to the amount of time I’ve spent with it, fighting Sauron and the Nazgûl, destroying armies of Orcs and forging my own, riding Drakes and Caragors, dominating Uruks, and simply existing in Monolith’s glorious vision of Middle-earth.
Shadow of War is hands down the best game I’ve played all year, for a multitude of reasons. The combat and movement is excellent, the upgraded Nemesis System is so intricate and superbly devised, the visuals and the score are sublime, and the story can easily rival the masterpiece that is The Lord of the Rings trilogy. I became addicted to fighting Orcs, hunting them down, confronting those that betrayed me or killed my Captains. I fell in love with the different regions and their landscapes, and I formed a bond with Talion through his morals and belief in a better world – a better Mordor.
The story takes place straight after the events of Shadow of Mordor, where Celebrimbor and Talion have forged a new ring of power to fight Sauron, and free Middle-earth of his darkness. It is such a vast tale filled with familiarity, but also wonder. You’re going to see people you’re familiar with, but also plenty of new characters too, and you’re also going to notice places that will be known if you’re a fan of Tolkien’s work. It’s devised in such a way that it’s not as simple as one sole story, but a combination of many constructed into one epic narrative. The different quests see you fulfilling many story points that ultimately bring about massive repercussions for Middle-earth, but you can find out those for yourself.
You’ll do missions set around Gondor, learning about how Minas Ithil has been attacked by Sauron’s army and the Nazgûl (the holders of the nine rings of power). You meet up with a woman called Elitariel who you’ll work with quite a lot before the story is over, as well as fighting the tormented Nazgûl including the Witch-King. There are missions you’ll complete for Shelob, the Olog-Hai called Bruz, Carnan, and loads more. They all play a role in the story of Talion and the fate of Middle-earth in one way or another, and there’s never a mission that feels like filler. Each one is crafted excellently, serving a major purpose for the story, and to give you a fantastic experience.
Playing Shadow of War is immense, and the upgraded combat and movement system is varied and fun. It’s also incredibly versatile, allowing you to personalize your own style to the letter by unlocking a wealth of new abilities across the massive skill trees. You can focus on a multitude of branches such as Wraith and Combat which really open up gameplay the further you get. For example, the Bird of Prey ability allows you to freeze in the air when using Focus and aim your Elf-shot at any surrounding Orcs.
I became hooked trying to get better gear and weaponry in Shadow of War, and the way it does this certainly isn’t revolutionary, but it becomes addictive. Certain Orcs will drop gear, and beating Epic and Legendary enemies will drop special items that form sets, and by completing challenges will let you upgrade them even further. Gems can also be tagged onto gear giving you small buffs to increase the damage a certain weapon does, or giving you more health.
There is an online market where you can buy loot boxes (WHICH YOU DON'T TO ♥♥♥♥ING BUY YOU ♥♥♥♥TARDS WHO SAY "OH MY GOD LOOT BOXES I AM GOING TO LOOOOSE" ACTUALLY ♥♥♥♥ OFF YOU ARE THE TYPE OF PEOPLE WHO PROBABLY CAN'T GET PAST THE ♥♥♥♥ING TUTORIAL OF DARK SOULS), You can also purchase Orcs for your army on the market, but again, this isn’t a necessity because you’ll encounter so many opportunities to dominate them on your journey.
One of the greatest features of the original was the Nemesis System mechanic, meaning Orcs would remember who you were, get promoted through their ranks and increase their level, all in real time as your story progressed. It returns here, but on a much grander scale. There are lots of different classes of Orcs, such as the Archers, Savages, and Olog-Hais. Assassins, Berserkers, and Marksmen are more advanced and are associated with the Captains and above. Each class has a weak point, but also a strength so knowing them becomes commonplace.
It’s essential to learn how each one works, and find ways to exploit them. Berserkers, for example, are brutal and relentless when attacking, but blocking and freezing allows you to attack without any quarrel. Olog-Hais are big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, but you can stun them and climb on their backs, stabbing them to wear them down. There are loads of ways to bring down the Captains and Warchiefs, not just through the types of class they are. Grog barrels are littered around which can be poisoned and blown up, as are the huge sacks of meat for attracting Caragors, so if they have a fear of these beasts, or are instantly dazed or heavily damaged by poison, this is the way to go. You can interrogate Orcs for intel like before, and doing so will make these battles much easier than going in blind.
The real genius of the Nemesis System is how you can exploit it. You can dominate a whole host of Orcs to recruit to your army, send them to kill rival army Captains, infiltrate rival Warchiefs and gain their trust a-la Donnie Brasco, and assign them to be bodyguards to your own Warchiefs or even yourself. This led to many amazing moments where my Captains would stab a Warchief right in the back, destabilizing him and helping to turn the tides of battle in a heartbeat. It also had its downfalls, as members of my army might turn on me when I needed them most, or ambush me when I was already overrun. It’s magnificent because encounters, betrayals, and ambushes can happen at any time, but this feels more realistic and makes everything you do seem important.
There are plenty of Nemesis Missions and Vendetta Missions you can do to kill those that defeated or humiliated you, and they’re only available for a limited amount of time due to death and revenge being a part of every Orc’s life, not just yours. They’ll want revenge as well, and boy, they come in droves. One of the Warchiefs I destroyed hunted me down hours later and faced me on the plains of Gongoroth, where we fought to the death in a long and arduous battle. These kinds of fights happen all the time, and you’ll even encounter certain enemies tens of hours later, in ways you never thought you would. It’s a system that bleeds in the Fortress Sieges as well, because a massive part of Shadow of War is the war side of it.

This is a combined review of Invisible, Inc. and the Contingency Plan DLC.
As my games library has grown larger and larger, I've come to appreciate games which do one thing really well more than big, sprawling titles which try to do lots of things well and only partially succeed. This game is a perfect example of the former.
The core game mechanic - sneaking around, hacking and stealing - is brilliantly executed. New agents, abilities, items and programs become available as the game progresses, each combination with its own optimal strategy. Like any good turn-based game, Invisible, Inc. will get you thinking all the time. No two levels are the same, even if you play through the game multiple times, so it's always a good idea to explore, observe and analyse the situation. And no matter how well you plan, most levels have at least one hairy moment which forces you to improvise, sometimes diverting agents well away from their intended locations to help each other out. The alarm tracker increments every turn, building the suspense and forcing you to move quickly, but my experience is that rushing through levels is hazardous to agents' health.
The game has a great failure spectrum. It would be pretty annoying if getting spotted meant an instant game over, but that's far from the case. If you make too much noise, a guard will come to investigate, but you can try to hide or ambush them. If you get spotted, you have one turn to take cover or knock the guard out. If a guard still has eyes on you after that turn, your agent will be shot, but you can revive them with another agent or just drag them to the exit. Even if you don't manage that, as long as one agent escapes the level, your agency will live to fight another day - and you can recruit more agents as the game goes on. There's also a rewind button, with a limited number of uses by default, which takes you back to the start of the previous turn if things really get out of hand.
The experience system is also well designed. Every time you play the game, you'll make progress towards unlocking new things for your future playthroughs, even if your agency is eliminated. If you try a particular difficulty setting and realise it's too easy or difficult, you can retire that save file, bank the XP and start afresh with new toys to play with, which is not something I've seen in any other game.
The story is fairly simple but interesting enough and the voice acting is excellent. And I know it's a matter of taste, but I think the game looks and sounds fantastic, the character designs in particular. With Contingency Plan installed, the length of the campaign is good for about 15 hours of gameplay, but you can make the campaign shorter, longer or even endless in the settings. I've finished the game three times - once on each of the three standard difficulty levels - and I'm now deep into an endless game, so don't be put off by reviews saying it doesn't have replay value.
The only things I'd change about the game are very minor issues: there could be a tutorial on how to throw items, there could be more storage space for items not currently equipped on any agent, and some of the agents could do with a bit of buffing to bring them up to the level of the others, but that's about it. It's no exaggeration to say I love this game. Highly recommended.

Stoic has done it again! The saga continues. The Banner Saga 2 allows players to import the save file from the original game. All the great items you earned, experience you received from killing dredges, and good/bad decisions you made from the first game WILL impact the outcome of this amazing sequel. If some characters are killed off in the original game, they won't return for the sequel.
The new leveling system has evolved from the original game. Each character's level cap is increased to 10. Incremental renown requirement for each levelup is lowered from 5 to 2 points in this new game. Feel free to try out different fighters from the rooster because multiple members can be maxed out by chapter 15. Many players have ignored leveling up some characters from the original game for various reasons. These characters will start off as level 3 fighters from the beginning of the sequel, so they are still helpful during combat.
The introduction of many new classes have opened up many more possibilities during combat. The poet class can replenish the entire party's will power, the agile horsebreed race can use the hit-and-run tactics, and the berserker class can attack twice during each turn...
The introduction of secondary skills and traits allocation have made the combat more engaging, tactical and fun. Versatile fighters can be created by spending extra skill points to specific traits. All characters are relatively balanced. High armor characters might shine in the normal mode, but others' nifty skills might turn the tide of the battle in hard difficulty. Some impressive skills include beast summoning, invisibility, axe throwing, and overwatch. New ranged and buffing enemies have made the game more challenging.
Storywise, The Banner Saga 2 suggests there are two sides of the same story. For the first time, players can experience the saga from 2 distinct perspectives: the benevolent rook/alette or the impulsive Bolverk. Betrayal is certainly the reoccuring theme of this fantastic sequel. Sefa the starving archer, the risk-averting king, and the oppressed Canary are not necessarily 100% evil per se. Players can resonate with their perfectly reasonable motivations.  New revelations suggest that dredges are not all evil. Juno can be viewed as a heroic valka or a manipulative instigator. The sequel ends with a major cliffhanger, and player's last decision is not only difficult but also heartbreaking.
If you love great storytelling, character development and tactical combat, the Banner Saga 2 will not disappoint!

Found it hard to decide but end up leaning towards positive.
The story is still quite good.
There have been some great improvements, like the training feature being added to, being able to further improve stats with a choice of directions and a choice of abilities, and more. Also some interesting new characters.
A lot of the stuff about the first one that I liked are still there - such as a really surprisingly enjoyable combat system.
HOWEVER:
The story felt very hollow compared to the first one. In the first game I found myself very deeply invested in a lot of the characters and their motivations, but in this one it felt like the devs hadn't really bothered to tell the stories of the characters further, it just felt very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in that respect. Also, a lot of the heroes just felt so pointless. There's too many of them, some of them never say anything and you end up never using most of them for fights because you don't level them up. Although the story did split in two directions, I felt like it could have done with having more storylines to allow a longer game with more diversity, and paying more attention to more heroes.
Also, a lot of the time, especially towards the end, I was very confused, and the final battle and actual end was so unsatisfying, confusing, and left too much up in the air. If the devs delay release of the next one as long as they did this one, I'll have the same problem as I did this time of being totally unable to remember 80% of what happened, and being even more confused!
And also, having fighters in the caravan felt pointless as there were no big battles like in the first one.
OVERALL
Despite all my complaining, it is still a great game, and the issues, particularly with the story, only come because I'm comparing them to an amazing first game and its really captivating story. So, although slightly disappointing after the original, I still had a lot of fun playing this game and will definitely stick with the series.

TL;DR version: This is a Tim Schafer adventure game. If you wanna play that, you should get this.
Now I've been hearing a lot of nonsense about how people don't like the single-click interface. In classic LucasArts titles, you could right-click and look at something and get some dialogue. From what I've read, a lot of people seem to assume you can't do that in this game— and they would be wrong. Oh, there's no right-clicking, but there are plenty of things to look at, and what's more, if you drag any item out of your inventory and try to use it, you'll get a funny line unique to that situation. There is a ton of dialogue in this game, and plenty to interact with.
I'm about 3 hours in and I feel I'm about 80% done with Vella's story and 40% through Shay's. The people breezing through this in 3-4 hours and then complaining about how short it is are missing a TON of content. If you like to take your time and poke everything, this game rewards you like crazy.
Is this Day of the Tentacle? Is it Grim Fandango? No, and it could never possibly be. But it is a meticulously crafted, thoughtful, funny game with a good story, fantastic writing and gorgeous art. Take your time and you will be rewarded.

Adventure games ARE NOT DEAD!!!! And Broken Age is here to slap you in the face and make you love them again!
Thoughtful, interesting, beautiful, engaging, charming, different, story-driven -- this game is a marvel. Run, don't walk and play it.

After a bit of turmoil over their release structure (with the 'solution' being the two-part release), we now have the first half of Broken Age, and I must say, it was worth the wait. If you're a fan of the point-and-click adventure games of old (LucasArts games coming to mind immediately, as well as The Longest Journey), Broken Age is worth playing. The game doesn't have the length that some of the old ones had (assuming Act 2 is roughly the same length as Act 1), though that may be largely due to the puzzles being a little more logical than those in the older games were, so you spend less time aimlessly clicking on the environment and trying to use random items with each other in hopes of finding a solution, and more time enjoying the stylized art, amusing dialog, and interesting world.
Is it a good game? Yes, perhaps even if the adventure genre isn't normally your cup of tea. Is it worth $25? That really depends on whether playing half of the game now and half of it "later this year" bothers you... chances are you'll have the opportunity to get it on sale before Act 2 is released, so that might be something to consider.

[SPOILER FREE, FOR THE MOST PART.]
This game is... impossibly good. It's just so masterfully crafted that it's hard to believe that it's even really possible for game developers to execute a story like this, execute gameplay like this, so well. It's almost as if they time-travelled from the future where interactive storytelling has advanced a fair amount from what it was a year or two ago.
I got this game over the Summer Sale. The free first episode, I mean. After I played that ONE EPISODE, even the one just introducting the characters and the setting, I knew it presented me with more impactful choice than any choice-heavy game I played before. A day later I found myself buying the rest of the episodes, and one day after that (today) I finished the game. I didn't beat the game... I finished it.
During my playthrough I compared this game to Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and the InFamous series. Both of those games (Let's just focus on InFamous 2 for now) were very choice-driven, and it all affected the ending in some way. But Life is Strange blows those games out of the water in that department. Yes, it has different gameplay mechanics than its two comparisons and yes it is a little unfair to single those two games out because of that. But a big pull factor and possibly a defining feature to those games was the karma system, or the player choice system to be more exact. As I said before, this game blows those others out of the water.
Every choice, and this is something most players in other games will say but this is a FACT. EVERY choice matters in this game, it is ALL taken into consideration, and it's easy to miss things here. It's easy to forget things, even when the main character is a time-travelling arts academy student. 'Tis why I say I have
the game, not
it.
There's more than two ways a situation can unfold in this game and given how you handled your past decisions, more than 2 ways they are affected prior. And I don't mean every choice ever made suddenly being assessed at the endgame. I mean every choice ever made relative to whatever character you're speaking to, whatever scenario you're in, affecting the game's world possibly permanently. These aren't just small incidents like a character remembering that you threw their plate of beans on the floor one time, or someone forgetting that another person brought weed into their house one day. These are major events, like a person deciding to commit suicide which will haunt you for the rest of the game, or choosing whether or not to report a crime to an official, which may have consequences driving the game on their own.
With all of this pressure on the player for choice, how is one supposed to deal with it without feeling powerless, or frustrated that they will never get to experience the other 66% or 77% of what the game has to offer?
Enter the Time Travel mechanic. It may sound OP, but the game works it in such a way that not only does it make sense, but it actually encourages you to experiment with this power. You can reverse your decisions to see different outcomes, gather information from the present and use it in the past, even appear in rooms that you otherwise could not get into. You can replay conversations around you, you can re-do conversations with said new info. You can prevent accidents from happening, the time travel mechanic is of course wonderful.
Now, the obvious question would be, can you go to the future? Well, somewhat although I won't spoil that here. But in everyday game, no. No you cannot, because the future is decided by the present. Imagine how chaotic it would be to go into the unlived future, because nobody can predict the future, unless they went BACK in time. All you can do is go back and try to fix whatever you broke.
Most of the game, you're taking pictures (arts school) or manipulating time to fit your needs. It sounds awesome yet boring at the same time. But this above all else is a story driven game, and the story is the main attraction. Speaking of which...
I'll try to keep this as spoiler-free as possible but basically, the summary of the plot and story is this: Maxine (Max) Caulfield is an arts student at Blackwell Academy. She's a photography geek who deals with the usual bullies and has an odd assortment of friends too. Her dorm room has photos spread all across the walls and she has various memorabilia from her home in Seattle. One day while leaving her photography class, an incident erupts in the girls' bathroom at school, and Max, panicked, finds that she can reverse time. By using her power, she averts an otherwise tragic event and tries to come to terms with her newfound abilities. Along the coming days she meets old friends and forms new enemies... but that might depend on your actions.
See, from that basic summary of the beginning, the game's story is what you decide it to be. The events you set in motion truly affect the plot, and while not so much that there's still a basic, linear plot structure leading to the ending (No, you can't just shoot anybody and everything and rewind, nor can you rob banks, nor can you decide to go all the way back to colonial-era American West Coast), it is still substantially influenced by what seems like small actions.
It can be erasing an insult on a whiteboard, taking a picture of somebody bullying another, or even telling a person to watch out for flying objects... maybe even 3 whole seconds before they're thrown. It all affects the future. Which is what this game is all about. It's all about events affecting the future, whatever they are.
The setting is like a young adult mystery novel, except with actual relatable young adults. They don't talk like kids or like they're afraid of being seen as rude. They talk like real high schoolers today. They cuss, smoke, drink, have sex, like any other high schoolers. It's actually a believable setting. For a game about time travel, realism of environments is one thing they do so well in this story. You actually believe that your actions are being met not by NPCs, but by actual people.
When you play all of the episodes and finish the game your way... you actually feel for every character you remember. That's something that defines a good story. A good story leaves you thinking, and that's something every episode here does.
I will not spoil anything. Play it yourself.
At first, Life is Strange appears to be your average indie, hipster girl story, and when you hear the first song with sund lyrics (Syd Matters - To All Of You), you're probably going to prepare yourself for cringe. And I'll be honest I didn't really care for half of the songs that they actually got preformers on, since most of the tracks I only found fitting for the in-game situation, but probably couldn't listen to outside of the game.
There's no heavily dramatic music, no large orchestras, no real wall of sound. It's mostly all acoustic music with some techno and punk here and there. If any or all of those are not your thing, or if you're a rabid metalhead elitist and hate anything that isn't Slayer or Iron Maiden, then you may have a lowered experience because of the music.
But you know, me personally, I found the music all-around amazing even if some songs were meh. Everything fits situationally, and the in-game soundtrack itself (without named preformers) is SUPERB. The pause menu's theme is great, the ending credits theme is deep and emotional after you experience a whole episode. And sometimes where you assume there will be music, there isn't... and in some cases it truly helps to sink in the feeling of a scene.
I'm not really an indie guy anymore, but honestly you don't have to be to enjoy the soundtrack. It's pretty much essential to the game if you want to fully experience it.
I'd write so much more but I've run out of characters. tldr; PLAY THIS GAME. BUY THE FULL PACKAGE. You no regretty.

There is an inherently charming and magical quality Windosill; an enchanting playfulness that can't properly be put into words and is better enjoyed first hand. A point and click puzzle game encompassing ten inordinately imaginative rooms, it's neither challenging nor lengthy, but in the same way a short picture book can be hugely delightful, Windosill succeeds because of its simple design and childish sensibilities.
There is not a whole lot more I could say about Vectorpark's bite-sized treat of a game, and hopefully I don't need to to convince you it's worth your time. It's a brief expedition (about 30 minutes, depending on how good you are at puzzle solving) to another world, full of strange sounds and bizarre creatures, that is entirely unassuming in its execution. A gorgeous artistic endeavor, it shows that sometimes all a game needs to be worthwhile is a clear vision and a lot of passion to back it up.
It's the sort of game that is effortlessly relaxing; best enjoyed curled up with a blanket next to the fire, sipping a cup of cocoa and just enjoying life.

I remember specifically reading when I backed this that it was going to be a game that harkened back to classic point and click adventure games. It had Tim Schafer's company behind. A man that co-designed the first two Monkey Island games and Maniac Mansion: Day of the Tentacle. When I think "Classic Point and Click Adventure" I think of the games listed above as well as the old Sierra games. But I suppose I set myself up for some amount of disappointment by making assumptions based on the information above.
I knew I was in trouble when nothing in the game seemed to stump me. I never really had any moments where I truly had no idea what to do next. This is a huge mistake when it comes to adventure games. When I needed an item to do something, I always knew which item I needed and usually had it or knew where it was. And if a character had it they would, almost always, just give it to me without reservation. Without any puzzles hard enough to slow me down I had it beat in under 4 hours. And I was taking it easy, reading all the dialog choices and trying to click on everything I possibly could for extra story and dialog. Some people had it beat in an hour and some change. Classic point and click adventure games were short but only if you already knew what you were doing. The old games were hard enough to slow people down and give them a challenge so no one ever beat them that fast the first time through.
Now I'm not saying it's terrible. I really like the art style and the story is interesting. It be nice if the game itself could catch up. I'd say if you want to try this, wait for a sale later down the road.

The Banner Saga 2 continues the engaging story of its predecessor with improvements to almost all aspects of the game. Once again the gorgeous art style evokes a feeling of purity and beauty, yet in this second installment there is a clear feeling of loss and danger that comes with it. As you pass through the world, it gives one pangs of sorrow, because it's clear that the darkness is coming to destroy all that is lovely.
To begin, THE SOUNDTRACK ALONE IS WORTH THE MONEY! Austin Wintory (composer of Journey, flOw, Horn, The Banner Saga, and many more) does an exceptional job once again building the perfect rugged and fierce atmosphere for this mystical Nordic landscape. The music fits the brutality of war; blaring horns bombard the listener in fight sequences, and in the time between fights, the soundtrack helps keep tension high. Soulful performances by the vocal soloists tie everything together perfectly.
This product is more of a story than a videogame, and you truly feel like your decisions have weight. The storyline is great-- major props to the writers for creating such a well crafted experience. There is no right decision at any fork in the road, and many times along the journey you will regret your choices. It is virtually impossible to finish this game without questioning some moves you had to make, but that is part of the beauty.
The combat system is not too challenging, but at times thinking on your feet and making sacrifices is going to be required. You are challenged to take on the personality of your character and do not only what you want to do, but also what your character is able do while keeping a good reputation. There are consequences for being too ruthless, but also for being overly-soft or lenient. You have to strike a balance.
In my opinion, the most important thing to keep in mind while playing this game is that it is just ONE part of a MULTIPLE part series, and should be treated as such! Do not go in expecting closure at the end, or even a perfect story-arch. What you get is part of an incredible journey, one that isnt too common in games. I STRONGLY recommend this game, the previous game, and any future games in this series.
On their own, each game may not be a feature-length experience and game, but when put together, you get a 30+ hour adventure that is unforgettable. I can't wait for The Banner Saga 3!

Nuclear Throne is an awesome game. It's fun, has a lot of content to unlock and is very challenging. Almost everything about this game is solid, from the fast paced combat to the many enemies and guns. So there’s no reason for me to waste your time going into depth about everything awesome about this game. Throw your money at Vlambeer and play this game! So I’ll go over the bad parts of the game, it’s lack of character and mutation variety.
The game has twelve different character to play with, each with their own abilities and perks. But your playstyle doesn’t usually change from character to character. You'll find yourself taking the same mutations and the same guns, so your playthrough's might not differ to much from one another. Two characters are an exception to this, Melting and Rouge. Playing as them changes which perks you take and how the game operates, making playing with these two characters a unique experience from the rest of the game. While the other characters are unique and well designed, you’ll fight enemies in more or less the same way, take the same guns and take the same mutations. The mutations (or perks) in this game are cool, but have a clear order in how you take them. Some mutations are always better than others.
This lack of variety is the game’s main downfall in my eyes, but it’ll still keep you playing for a long time and is one of my favorite rouge-likes out there. Despite all I’ve said, I give this a 9/10. :D

This game is absolutely beautiful. Just look at those hand painted graphics. The orchestral score will melt your ears with how good it is. The puzzles are excellent and streamlined in such a way that you don't need to rub every single item together to find the solution. If you get into the right mindset, you'll be able to follow the game's own twisted logic easily.
But as with all adventure games, story is king. It may start off slow but trust me, the story is incredible and will twist and turn in ways you could never expect. The humour is spot-on (as with all Double Fine games) and often had me grinning like a lunatic.
There's only one minor caveat and that is that the game only offers 4-5 hours of gameplay. Of course it's only the first act of 2 so I imagine you'll get another 5 hours when Act 2 releases later in the year. It's up to you if you think playing 2 halves of a game months apart is feasible. Personally, I think I'm going to have to invade the Double Fine offices and hide amongst Tim Schafer's Rubiks Cubes because I HAVE TO KNOW WHAT HAPPENS NEXT AND I CAN'T WAIT THAT LONG.
4.5/5 - Highly recommended to long time adventure fans and newcomers alike.

It's really hard to recommend an unfinished game, but that is essentially what Broken Age is at this point in time. Only half the game is currently playable, with the second half to be released later in the year. Just as it is with buying episodic games, so too do you need to consider that you're paying for something that's not done; something that only the developer can assure us is any good. Unfortunately, Broken Age's issues run deeper than just being half a game. I'm not even sure it's a game at all.
Visually and audibly, the game is a treat. The art style is fantastic and the score and voice acting are top notch, except when the dialogue randomly delays and gets clipped by the next line. It's unfair to judge a story on just its first half, but I found Vella's side to be particularly slow-moving and uninteresting. Shay's story was more intriguing, but as expected, the first act ends before it really gets any good. There is hope that Act 2 will deliver, but hope is not guaranteed to deliver.
But is Broken Age even a game? There's no "decision making" a la Telltale's newer stuff, and the puzzles barely qualify as such. Mousing over something usable changes your cursor, so it's not even a matter of finding the right item to click on. You can't even really say navigating dialogue trees is part of the game, as they are almost always pointless filler. Indeed, most of the game feels like simply going through the motions more akin to an interactive novel. This is something unlikely to change with Act 2, and that's my real issue recommending Broken Age.
A year from now the game will probably be available at half its price. If you can resist the garish hype surrounding the game at present, then I'd recommend waiting until then.

This game is a strategy game in the layout of here's your main guy, if he dies then you lose. Builld more guys to kill the other guys main guy and then you will win. Rather then the game saying "This guy destroys guys, this guy destroys guys in tanks, and this guy destroys guys in planes" the game says "Make some guys you want to make". The vast research tree will allow you to create guys to deal with any large problem the game throws at you, and this is quite fun as you can strap an ultra death chasis to a giant rocket launcher, mass produce forty of them, and throw them at your level one advesary that is still working with level one lollypop chasis and whose only form of defense is flicking boogers at your vast army. Really nice game from a developper that worked alone.
The game is actually a bit hard to handle in the first place but proves really intuitive once the basic concepts of managing energy and creating units are understood.
Positive aspects :
+ Possibility to control directly ANY units you built (from simple assault droid to massive Fortitude Tank)
+ Customization of units. From example, you start with a plain tank (regular armor and basic gatling canon) but later you can modify it with better armor or change its main gun (plasma, rocket,...) and create templates for your factory to produce, provided you've done the necessary researches.
+ Tech tree is cool (it doesn't seem so at first glance but tech tree expands : unlock the "dead-end branch" that is Armored Factory to expand the branch with new vehicles and upgrades, for example)
+ Defensive buildings (Turrets, Chainlink fences, bunkers) since too few games feature those
+ Fortitude Tank ! (Sorry but driving one personnaly, towering regular tanks and firing with its double main gun is just great)
+ Energy management (cut power supply to turrets if you're not attacked to increase iron extraction speed, and so on). Reminded me a bit of Supreme Commander energy system
Negative aspects :
- (it's personnal but...) pointer is hard to handle : it is quite hard to see which units you have selected (no panel with the names and types of units selected, just how many) or to click on a small ennemy to make your army engage it (I had to zoom in to make the small bots big enough to be selected)
- [Can be a positive point for some gamers] AI is quite forward going even in easy (I've been attacked by tanks / aircrafts in my base after just a few minutes from the start, while I was still trying to understand how to build bots)
I highly recommend the game since it's a really nice new concept to RTS and for its strategy side (customizing units one by one is possible, to fit any situation ; researches ; energy management)
Plus its from a single developper, the kind that should be encouraged !

All in all it's a wonderful game i'd say, with great replayability I just beat it with my first continuation playthrough with Rook and have gotten half way through with my second as Alette.
