The first playthrough I wanted to get a feel for it so I went with the Mission Impossible route, some jokes, some professionalism, making friends with poeple you come accross for info. Then I played full bond, just a pistol, no armor, stealth, suave and of course if you are a Roger Moore fan, the corny and suggestive jokes. Then I played as Jack Bauer, agressive, confrontational, but knows when to kill and not to kill. Then I played full on Taken and opened up a can of Liam Neeson on my enemies which turned it into less of a spy movie and more into a Rambo like movie where anyone who got in my way or was a potential threat....they were dealt with. So if you are a big fan of either one here is the playstyle to follow.
Ethan Hunt: Mixuture of everything including armor and weapons, little to no suave but plenty of jokes and yet maintain seriousness and mostly stealth
007: You can be as aggressive as Brosnan and Craig or as snarky and funny as Moore, to the cockyness of Connery and if you feel the need to throw in some Dalton gun play go for it. However everyone besides Dalton does not wear any kind of armor so be warned.
Jack Bauer: Again little to no armor but damn aggressive and up front, you basically carves through anyone he wishes yet spares those he has has to. This would be the hard gameplay.
Liam Neeson: This would be the INSANE game style, no armor, just a pistol, wits and of course you eliminate EVERYONE and I mean EVERYONE. Which makes everyone mad but hey its Neeson we are talking about here.
Then you have others:
The strong quiet types like Steven Seagal to Rambo and the Commando Arnold (which is a specialization option)
So which ever spy you want to emulate go for it. I prefer Bond and word to the wise, download a track or two from the movies, really sets the RPG mood.

Remedy, the same company that gave us
, have produced a superb game in
. And just like with their groundbreaking previous games, Alan Wake brings something new to the party, too.
The game is a few years old now so the character models and environments aren't quite as good as they could be, but the game shines bright on its own for its epic story and gameplay - the plot and characters could have been lifted from a great Stephen King novel, kudos to the writers on this. The levels are woven together in an episodic format, like a TV series, and there are several nods to
scattered throughout the game.
Then there's the gameplay, and Remedy pull off the superb 'Fight with Light' mechanic - you must essentially wield two weapons in tandem, with two different ammo counters, which makes pitched battles much more tense. You'll soon learn to fear the dark in this game, not so much for the dark itself, but for what the darkness brings forwards!
The levels are highly detailed and, whilst somewhat linear, give you lots to interact with - machines you must manipulate (not always just pushing buttons to progress) and a wide assortment of vehicles you can drive in certain levels. You get a good selection of weapons and ammo is always on the brink of scarcity, although you also get some epic showdown scenes with lots to shoot at and blow up. The rural Pacific Northwest comes alive, especially during the night, as the plot unfolds and Wake digs deeper into the mystery surrounding his wife's disappearance.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed
especially for its dark and twisting story, which
proves itself a worthy successor to - watch for some great nods to
further into the game! Also, anyone who enjoys survival horror games, or horror/thriller novels, will greatly enjoy this game. The soundtrack is also excellent, with Poets of the Fall once again helping out with a few songs (and check out
!) and worth getting with the game.
is an interesting game on its own, not directly connected to the original - it uses the same gameplay mechanics with more polished graphics, but with a much shorter story. You still play as Wake, but the story is deliberately ambiguous in its connections back to the events of
. Definitely enjoyable, but a little odd.

I’m not a hardcore gamer so I almost never buy games just when they’re released. The Banner Saga however was an exception for me. I remember years ago when I still carried my Gameboy Advance SP around with me and one of my favourite games was Final Fantasy Tactics. I loved the fantasy genre and I loved RPGs so it was no surprise that I loved the game. Over the years, I’d been searching for a game that could live up to the standard of Final Fantasy Tactics. And one fine day when I decided to google, I came across the Banner Saga. I was hooked and played hours on end until I completed the game. Despite the flaws that many reviewers pointed out (and which I agree with), I completely overlooked them and thoroughly enjoyed the game. While the game’s strength was in its story, the combat (and levelling) was still good enough for me. The story ended on a rather tragic note but it was well-written nonetheless; someone must sacrifice themselves to save many others.
I’d been waiting so long for the sequel that the moment it was released for pre-order, I snapped it up. Not because of the price though
. And I finished it within
. While there were many new features, I couldn’t help but feel that the developers were really just taking the first game and slotting in bits and pieces here and there. It felt like taking Banner Saga and aside from the continuation of the story, you were just getting some extra DLC. I didn’t get the first game at full price so I didn’t feel the pinch but now I’m hesitant to get Banner Saga 3 at full price when it comes out. Below is a breakdown of my experience:
You spent probably 50% of your time watching your caravan travel from one point to the other. I guess the devs felt they should make use of this time to engage the player. Besides occasionally feeding your caravan (btw I spent close to nothing buying supplies), you could train your clansmen to become fighters. I didn’t really see the point of doing that and only did it once or twice throughout the whole game. I only remember a couple of moments where the number of fighters came into play and never once did I think: “Damn I should have trained more of them earlier!” More fighters simply means higher consumption of supplies and fewer people to forage (which is a neat feature). In other words, the devs kinda failed at making caravan management a crucial part of the game.
This was a nice addition to the game. Instead of figuring stuff out through countless battles, you could learn new strategies based on objectives given in this. I thought there was more potential for this part though. I found myself just completing the objectives for the sake of renown. And I got stuck during the training on Bolverk’s side… what makes it worse is that there are no freaking hints so I just gave up.
Perhaps the most important part of the game since this is where you actually do stuff.

Overall, it takes on the first game and builds on some aspects, but overall I wouldn't call this "Banner Saga 2" so much as "Banner Saga 1.5". It left me wanting more especially in terms of story, but has a lot of potential to buildup to an epic ending in Banner Saga 3, if tied togother properly.

This game has a lot of bad press about it, and it doesn't deserve it as much as it did in the past. Things have gotten a lot better since ORION: Dino Beatdown, and even from the original release of ORION: Dino Horde (which people got for free if they already had O:DB, so check if you already have it from the previous name), and the amount of fun you have with the game is linked to your disposition to it.
If you go in thinking it's going to be a terrible game, you're not going to have fun with it. If you think it could be good, then you'll probably give it more of a chance. There's been a lot of updates and additions that probably fixed something you didn't like about it before. (I'm looking at you, TotalBiscuit, and everyone that follows him blindly about his first impressions.)
With that said, this can be a lot of fun with friends, playing by yourself is okay, but it really shines with more people. If you get on Skype/TeamSpeak with some pals (because who uses in-game voice chats anymore, really?), you can coordinate and assist each other in your fight against waves of dinosaurs who apparently find the noise/smell of your energy generators really annoying/tasty. I've found it to be an enjoyable alternative to Killing Floor or especially any of the modes in the CoD games (save for MW1 or BO2).
Sure, it's had a past behind it, and there's some concepts borrowed from other games, but if you wait for a sale (namely right now, it's free to play for the week of Feb 20-27, and you can have it forever if you pay a single dollar), then maybe you can justify the purchase. Personally, I don't think that it's worth it at full price, but once it goes under 50% discount, that should ease the hesitation. Now go ahead and try it on a sale (maybe get a 4-pack to share), bring some friends along, don't be a filthy public match joiner.

This is a brilliantly made 'interactive movie' with some strong gunplay and sandbox fun mixed in.  However, at this time, it has a number of visual bugs and a few crashes.
The devs just released a massive update fixing the 30 fps cap and a number of other PC issues.  Since the patch, I haven't experienced any bugs or crashes, and performance is exceptional.
For people coming from Mafia I and II, this game resembles 2 only in the gunplay.  Storywise, it's much more akin to Mafia I.  The open-world gameplay, which is new for the series, will feel very familiar to players of Saints Row III, Assassin's Creed Brotherhood, or Far Cry 3/4.
Story, voice acting, cutsenes are phenomenal.
Licensed music is perfect, as well as the original score.  If you like late 60's music (who doesn't), you will find you know and love most of the songs.  The talk radio is very well done.
Open world gameplay, which starts after about 3 hours of gameplay.  The racket system is a refreshing take on the aging open-world grind we're so familiar with.
Gunplay is very satisfying, good sounds and the cover system is fluid enough.
The whole 'Eagle Vision' sense mode thing, which I thought I would hate, is done well here and actually feels like a legitimate representation of Lincoln's combat instincts.
Car handling on simulation is pretty fair, don't bother with normal.
Graphics are gorgeous;
.  The city is iconic, especially at night.
Performance is good, with a GTX 970 and i5 4690K I'm getting constant 60 at max settings 1440p.
Some issues with the exterior shadows and lighting in the daytime.  Not sure if the constant shifting from light to dark is a feature meant to represent cloud cover or a bug.
Rain looks odd.
Car sounds are a little off, the samples are very limited and sound like they're coming out of a tin can.
Car customization is less in-depth than in Mafia 2.
Some screen tearing and one crash, and after 4 hours, no other issues.

What looks to be an incredibly polished turn based action game is actually hampered by poor UI design and incredibly boring gameplay. Most of the gameplay consisted of just walking from room to room and passing your turn (to get more AP so you can walk to another room).
I am a big fan of Klei's other games, and the animation and style is clearly polished, but the gameplay and UI are lacking. I had to refund this one.
PROS:
-Great art
-Good voice acting
-Lots of modes (level generation)
-Multiple agents with different abilities
NEUTRAL:
-The "increasing alarm" system is misguided. I assume the purpose is to make exploration a risk/reward system, but this system (combined with the excessive walk/pass, see below) got on my nerves rather quickly.
CONS:
-Terrible UI design (NOT intuitive at all)
-REALLY boring gameplay. The distances that must be covered are too long, so you will constantly be moving all of your agents, then ending the turn to get more AP, then moving them again, then ending the turn again....SO exciting.
-Although different agents existed, their differences were not very clear by reading the stat screens (crappy UI), nor is anything really explained (even starting with the easiest mode).
In my first 4 missions there were a number of instances where I had to stand on a particular tile to reveal the presence of a camera across the room, but there is no way to know that "this" is the tile to stand on ( as opposed to all the ones next to it).

Whether I would recommend this game or not depends on at what price you intend to get it. Ten euros is in my opinion very different from 1.8 which is the price for which I bought Age of Gladiators, during sales.
First and foremost, understand that for once the game uses the label "strategy" in the appropriate way. When you see "strategy game" in reality the developers or publishers refer to battle tactics or something very similar. Strategy on the other hand, pertains to foreseeing unexpected results, calculating the odds, judging whether a risky move is worth its price in case you fail or not - in short strategy means management. Some tactical elements are indeed featured in the game, such as picking certain attributes and armours could be categorised as tactics.
The game is entertaining for several hours, which is subjective indeed, but I would vouch for the first 5 hours to say the least. I still have to play it intesively but I feel a review can be released at this point (6 hours played) because I've seen all the features, mechanics and mastered the game's logic - which is in a sense sad. Sad because, after a couple of attempts you will find out it's very easy to win 99% of the times all fights by using a certain build - which I won't describe here for the sake of the future player.
Art-wise, the game features decent music, but not spectacular, mediocre sound effects, mediocre and few 'cosmetic customisation' options. The most disappointing aspect was the last one and I'll elaborate at once: The gladiators do have their own personal artwork which can be changed at any time, but there are really few of them and the vast majority are drawn without respecting historical sources - e.g. the retiarius, the nest-bearing gladiator type, wearing a helmet; or questionable armour and weapons. It's nice that the artworks comprehend fighters from all the provinces and thus feature different ethnicities, but that isn't enough.
Gameplay-wise the most frustrating aspect is containing the costs, and personally I think the game suffers from great unbalancing and that some costs are just unrealistic and make the controlling of gold tedious. Such as the fact that gladiators must be purchased as if they were slaves (which they are) but then take a regular salary plus a cut of the prize for their  victories.. huh what the ♥♥♥♥? Didn't I pay for their purchase? Gladiators weren't contracted professionals, they were slaves, they didn't get any share of any victory and let alone did they get a regular salary... In short, I found myself pennyless many times even though
, that is because maintenance costs are generally too high per day, and when the game randomly gives you 1 or 2 weeks with no planned games, your money runs short or even below zero.
Another defect is that bigger resolutions than 1566xsomething are not supported, so if you set your game in full-screen you will notice a huge black background covers most of the monitor... a bit disappointing.
To sum it up, when >50% off, preferrably 70-90%, the game is absolutely worth its value. I usually consider a game good when it yields at least a hour worth of
per $/€/£ spent. Since I reckon I will enjoy it for at least 10 hours altogether and I paid it € 1.86, that's a pretty big ratio for me. A you can guess, using this same rule with the full price would result in a 'barely acceptable' grade.
EDIT: My entertainment in the game ended at about the 13th hour, when I put up a squad of 4 unbeatable fighters plus others training to be even better. I am now finishing the game as I write this just for completeness, but I'm not exactly enjoying the experience, which has become pretty repetitive and frustrating - a myriad of useless clicks.

Well this is rather pleasant.
Broken Age isn’t a brash, jaw dropping, impossibly clever, superlative inducing spectacular. Instead it brings an old school charm.
It seems not too much has changed in the 20 years since Tim Schafer last shipped a point and click adventure. The main difference is with the complexity of the puzzles. Broken Age is more story focused than puzzle focused with a simple single click interface replacing the verb system found in the old SCUMM games. But at the heart of this is Tim Schafer’s story, with colourful characters, imaginative settings and witty dialog.
The story focuses across the two protagonists stuck in an absurdity that they are trying to escape from; one on a spaceship that controls their every action, the other in a fantasy land where they joyfully given as a sacrifice to a mysterious beast.
Both of the settings are relatively small, but beautifully realised. Each story is largely independent with nothing like the item passing mechanic of Day of the Tentacle, meaning you can complete each at your own pace, swapping between the two characters at will.
Everything comes together very nicely, from the writing, the excellent soundtrack and the beautiful story book art. There’s some excellent animation work as well and while a couple of lines fall flat, most of the voice work is very good.
There are a few minor issues, mainly with the interface. You can’t chose dialog options with the keyboard, the cursor is unnecessarily large and the inventory system is a bit awkward (I recombined rebinding right click to opening your inventory).
There’s a larger issue if you were hoping for brain teasing puzzles, but if you were looking for a captivating adventure game your only real complain will probably be that Act 1 comes to an end a bit too soon.

The Banner Saga 2 is a terrific pickup... if you enjoyed the first one.
The Good:
The story continues in an expectedly hopeless manner, but it throws a few curve balls and left me excited for the third installment. The artwork remains beautiful and even though you spend the majority of your time watching your caravan trek endlessly left across your screen, man does it look good.  The characters are also much more compelling this go around, but that might just be that it is fresher in my mind. Seriously, Bolverk and Iver and Hakon, hell all the Varl are just amazing. If you really get in the head of the protagonists, instead of choosing what you believe are optimal paths, the decision making weighs heavily on you.  At its heart, this game is a visual novel and to play it like Fire Emblem is just silly.
The Bad:
The Combat.  So many people like the Armor vs Strength combat thing, and its cool but it is so flawed. Turn order needs a serious rework for Banner Saga 3. I learned this in the first one, and  slogged through it in the sequel, but the optimal tactics are not the realistic ones. Often it is advantageous to leave enemy combatants with 2 or 3 strength rather than killing them, because it is better to have a weak enemy in the turn order.  I got it handed to me several times in Banner Saga 1 before I figured this out because I would one-shot all the weaker enemies and then the 2 or 3 remaining big dudes would alternate turns wrecking me.  My biggest complaint with the game.  But like I said, it is a visual novel at its core and there are only I think half a dozen fights in the game that have major story developments attached to them.
Neutral:
Illusion of Choice. This could be good, depending on your outlook I suppose. But sometimes it feels like you are at the mercy of a bad DM. No matter what you do, bad things happen to you and no decision is correct. It really plays into that hopelessness but some of the "Surprise!" bad things that happen to you are super ham-fisted.  For a decision based, heavy narrative RPG sometimes you feel at the whim of the writers. Maybe it plays into the despair more than I am letting on and it does feel like things are out of your control, but to me that wasn't always a good thing.
The Verdict: Play it.  If you haven't played the first one, its like five bucks on sale all the time.  It isn't better or worse necessarily. It's definitely an improvement, but it doesn't quite have the wonder the first one gave you. It's like Pokemon sequels. They're better, but they aren't the same.

So first and foremost, what everyone is talking about, the loot crates.
The loot crate thing, in my opinion, has been totally blown out of proportion. They are entirely optional and I have gotten through more than 20 hours of the game without spending any money on microtransactions. Even if you really want the lootcrates, you can get them for free by doing vendetta missions.
And if you REALLY don't like the loot crates? There's an option to completely disable the market and all online functions (including vendetta missions) when you first load the game.
Would it be better if they weren't in the game at all? Yes, but these loot boxes are nowhere near as bad as people would have you believe. In all honesty people who purchase the lootcrates are just robbing themselves of the game experience. Everything you get from the crates can be attained in game, and doesn't require any major grinding. It's just a way to get Orc Captains faster, and if you don't enjoy hunting down captains to recruit/kill them, why are you even playing this game? This game is all about kill orcs and orc "politics", if that doesn't interest you then you probably shouldn't spend your money on this game anyway.
Anyone who feels the game is actually hindered in any meaningful way by the loot crates, I would ask you to give me a solid, concrete example of this. The final battle (spoilers) does NOT require you to purchase anything. Any reviews saying that were written by people who have zero idea what they're talking about and wanted to hop on a bandwagon for some easy popularity.
In my opinion, anyone who buys these crates is actually robbing themselves; of experiencing a fun and awesome game.
The game itself is not affected AT ALL if you don't buy the crates. Not buying them does nothing to diminish your experience (enhances it really) and there are zero aspects of the crate system that make this "P2W"
Now that the stupid controversy is out of the way, onto the game.
If you liked the first one you will love this one. Pretty much everything has been expanded/fleshed out more. Combat is much more challenging (actually the game as a whole is more challenging now) and there are 3 difficulty settings. Orc captains can really ruin your day if you haven't unlocked the right skills to counter their abilities yet, and even with them all unlocked some captains are just beasts who are immune to almost everything.
The world is now divided into many regions, I want to say there's 5+ but I might be remembering wrong. Each one feels about as large, if not larger, than each of the two areas from the first game. The terrain is varied betweem deserts, snow, forest/swamps, and your typical "mordor" landscapes.
The Nemesis system is amazing now. There is so much more variety in their looks, traits and personality. Orcs that you've branded being able to betray you is so cool in a frustrating way. I had one big War-Troll captain I made my bodyguard. I called him in to help me when I was outnumbered by 3 captains, and he betrayed me instead of helping me.
Orcs will also have more relationships with other orcs, both friendly and hostile. I had one orc who was a "blood brother" to another captain I killed. He now ambushes me constantly, saying that he will avenge his dead friend. I have killed this captain at least 3 times now, but he keeps coming back for more.
The orc voice acting is one again on point as well. They all sound great, well acted and with unique lines. As with the hundreds of hours I spent in the first game, I'm yet to notice any kind of repitition among the orc captains. They all feel/look/sound unique.
Overall, if you didn't like the first game, I doubt the changes have been substantiual enough to make you switch, UNLESS your big complaint about the first was the difficulty (or lack thereof). Even on the "normal" difficulty it is significantly more challenging, once I beat it I will probably do a NG+ game on the harder difficulty.

My actual, full review was too big so I had to cut out a few things, like a couple of the complaints (I didn't like Shelob and the Mad Max-esque tower things) Oh well!
Shadow of Mordor was a great game corrupted by it’s incredible lack of replayability. I have about forty hours on which comprises a full playthrough and maybe some extra on two others. All collectibles on both sections of the map and everything. The problem is, once you figured out orc detection ranges, you could clear an entire camp without them the wiser. The captains also become a bit clear-cut once you figure out how to best kill them which usually amounted to two ways; Stealth stabbing or headshotting. If they happened to be immune to both then, and only then, were you in for an actual fight. However I cleared most of the game stealthing through it and after the initial early game difficulty by not having any skills or stats, it became a breeze and I became unkillable.
We return to him in what is presumably just a few days or weeks after the end of the last game, and he immediately has his ring blackmailed away from him from the spider Shelob, often taking a human form here. For some reason. The majority of the first act is trying to manuever between visions she gives Talion, and saving a Gondorian stronghold from a new assault from the orcs. From there, my first dozen or so hours are largely dedicated to leveling up through the new system and getting geared so that I can handle some of the higher level captains that are running around.
I’m happy to report that the sequel, Shadow of War, has added a lot of nuance to the whole Nemesis mechanic as well as making sure Talion can’t take a goddamn hit in the early game. Very quickly I already acquired a proper nemesis named Grisha, who originally looked like a fairly normal gentleman but after cleaving him in half, he was put back together and was one of the highest level orcs I’ve faced as of this writing, eventually earning himself up to twenty before cleaving him in half yet again.
That’s a pretty tall order for early game, as he had a ton more health than any other orc I’ve faced.
I mentioned nuance earlier, and there’s a lot more to the Strength/Weakness system than last time around. In SoM, it mostly amounted to a random shuffle of a dozen things. Here, they have eight different categories between them from hates, fears, vulnerabilities, traits, bonuses and more. You have to properly plan around each captain encounter and the game emphasizes the summoning of spiders, Ghuls, and beasts to come to your advantage a lot more than they did before.
In addition to that, captains are a constantly flowing force. In SoM you could clear an entire war map for the zone and it only refills if you die or purposefully pass the time through fast travel towers. In SoW, every encounter and power struggle has a “turn” mechanic, each starting with three. Once you do three of them, new struggles pop up as do new captains. I find this to be a mixed blessing, as sometimes I like to clear the map just so that I have less captains to deal with in random world roaming, but instead I hunt down one captain only to find an ambusher popping up on a ledge above or the blood-brother of a previously killed orc assaulting me, bringing a bit of complexity to my usually clear-cut goals.
In yet another addition, enemy captains will consistently evolve to your tactics if it’s take a while to bring them down. Grisha above evolved against two things between four different fights with him; I vaulted over him a lot in the beginning and he earned the Vault-breaker trait. When they stopped working, during the final (or latest) fight against him he evolved against my wraith-stun attack so eventually I just had to slowly earn my fury in order to do a proper execution.
It’s a lot more exciting than before, and it’s a much welcome level of complexity from SoM’s late-game ease.
I don’t recall too much of the domination mechanic from the first game. I remember it being a late-game perk in the final act, which by then I was maxed out on every weapon and skill stat I had my hands on, so I rolled through the story missions very easily by doing the bare minimum. As a result, I cannot recall how complex it really was, I do remember you can attach your controlled minions to warchiefs and the like and have them betray your quarry. Well, that’s still there and much more. You recruit an Olog war troll to this end, whom I assume is fully scripted because it wouldn’t let me use intel to “discover” him earlier, and he has a ton of voiced lines that tutorialize how to recruit captains, use them as bodyguards, and order them around to do different things.
I was hunting a boss and attached not one, but two of my own minions against him. One of my mates axed him and took him down to what was essentially 1% health, “Breaking” him and making him able to be controlled. It was then I found out I cannot recruit orcs that are a higher level than me (I was 20, he was 22) but I did have the option to “shame” him which tanks their levels. If there’s a guy you want to grab because of his epic or legendary status, that is the way to do it as he flees and shows up in another confrontation event, where you can control him as per your level and then level him up through the whole army mechanic in the future.
It’s all rather well done and not at all difficult to do. The ends to these means are the siege battles, which are actual raids against major strongholds. They can be easy or hard depending on what you do, like I discovered that the fortress had some kind of fire pitch they’d use to pour on my siegebreakers but that didn’t happen when I disabled both of the underbosses protecting the stronghold’s Overlord.
I had some fun upgrading my mates, as some of the missions you’re not allowed to intervene (or they’d reveal themselves to be a traitor, rendering your goal pointless) but instead you’re treated to a studio-cam and watch your buddy battle it out with others in a pokemon-esque arena. One of my guys severely overleveled the other but kept getting stunlocked, but it worked out in the end.
As a point of contention that has haunted and bombed the steam review rollout is the microtransactions. Honestly they’re barely worth mentioning. There’s some you can buy with the ingame Mirian (sp?) which the game drowns you with. After you get a relatively decent set of epic and legendary gear, you’ll still be drowning in loot from killed captains which you can break down for their money. Instead of Mirian you can buy “gold” which offers a lot more in terms of loot and guaranteed legendary orcs and gear, which lead to sets that had decent bonuses that cater to a variety of playstyles and to exploit captain weaknesses. (There are sets based around poison and fire damage, for example). It is of course optional, though some personalities across the web still claim that there mere practice is scummy and shady. I don’t necessarily disagree but I’ve yet to be tempted to buy orcs as the few I recruited did the job nicely during my first siege. Surely strongholds will get more difficult and the temptation to outright buy legendary allies may rear its ugly head but until then, the game hardly bashes me over the head with it. Most of my gameplay consists of hunting captains down.
In conclusion, I highly enjoy it. It’s as you’ve probably read from other sources. It’s Shadow of Mordor but more, every mechanic it had is expanded on in some capacity which is exactly what a sequel should be doing.

Hotline Miami melds many commonplace game trappings in an environment both nostalgic and alien, simple and intuitive top-down shooting in a pixelated rendition of 1980s Miami makes you feel powerful and fragile all at once. Your blood boils and your stomach churns.
As stated above, the game stakes most of its playtime in fast-paced, simple, visceral combat; both with melee weapons and firearms, all offering different and equally viable strategies. (besides the OP knife)
Most levels will place you in a cramped, tight-cornered building where you're tasked with the same objective each time: kill
The game keeps things fresh with the smart and deadly level design, where one slip up or overlooked hazard means the difference between victory and defeat.
Apart from one or two minor glitches taking me out of the moment and a disappointing final boss, the game is exhilarating and challenging in all the right ways.
Presentation-wise, the visuals are an acquired taste - if you find yourself turned-off by any form of visual filters or camera sway, (ie: almost everyone who hated Max Payne 3) retro-aesthetic designs (both mechanics and graphic-wise) or are looking for a benchmarker, this game isn't for you.
Looking past all that or embracing it reveals an incredibly unique-looking game. Characters are pieces on a gameboard from above but grotesquely over-detailed and caricatured up close.
Similarly grotesque is the famed ultraviolence, though not as "realistic" as a AAA release, the detail in each wanton murder can give you pause, make you cringe and squirm in your seat. Your enemies don't take death like a vainglorious super-soldier, rather twitching on the floor, crawling about for help and having their various extremities and organs blast out their bodies and stain the floor, bones punctuating the air with a horrific pop, snap and crunch. These are
more than mindless robots and serves to accentuate the strange and disturbing tone the game is bringing about.
The game serves its aesthetic with great aplomb, suffering at random times from a mysterious slowdown knocks a point off.
The game shines above the other categories with its varied but fitting soundtrack from a plethora of indie electronic artists, putting an emphasis on synth bass, and unnerving crescendoes.
Each song feels suited to its setting and though they loop, never gets annoying as each note serves to punctuate each successful kill.
The soundtrack is a must-have if you're into alternative music, electronica or EDM or just 80s atmosphere in general.
Hotline Miami spins a tale that's as abstract as it can get away with given the tone and gameplay style; you play a man in a jacket and animal masks who gets mysterious phone calls to his apartment. These calls are from various business owners and people who give him locations and barely-veiled directions to kill everybody there. These are the only glimpses of regular life in Miami apart from visiting your friend who seems to work everywhere from the local grocer to the nightclub and pizza place, not including the late-game appearance of a mysterious
Revealing anymore of the story would be a crime worse than any the "hero" commits, but it's truly a surreal rollercoaster ride from start to a tentative finish.
Hotline Miami delivers and excels in every category, offering an exciting, thought-provoking and strategic game that is sure to please fans of crime thriller cinema, retro shooters and gamers looking for a tough, challenging beatdown of a game.

I don't really know what I can tell you about FSX, mostly because I know quite a bit about it. Although my current in game hours may seem a bit low to give the game the raving review that I'm giving it,I assure you there is a reason.
I have owned a copy of FSX since it was realeased all the way back on Windows XP, and as it was my favorite game, and I was in gradeschool, I played the game. A lot. How much a lot? Total flight time was over 5,000 hours flying alone. My total landings were over 10k, and my total distance was enough to circle the globe 120 times.
I was very proud of my logbook (all printed about 25 pages), so when I went with my dad to work one day (he's the supervisor of ground operations at Cleveland Hopkins, he basically says if the airport is open or not **not if flights are cancelled or not**) and 12 year old me showed my printed log book to my dad's former boss.
He looked at my dad and asked "Did he really do this?" My dad, although enamored with the game himself, responded "Sadly, yes." (I would rather fly than play baseball or whatever) My dad's boss then took me to a 737 which was about an hour from departure. My dad's boss, my dad, and myself all walked into the cockpit, where the boss said to the pilot "Show me your logbook." (Every pilot has their own, and if they get filled up, they carry over like a checkbook) After looking at the logbook for a considerable amount of time, he said to the pilot "Impressive stuff captain, how long have you been flying?" He responded "Since I was 17 sir, and I'm 27 now, so 10 years."
"Good for you captain, however would you like to see something impressive? Check this out." He handed the pilot my logbook. After the pilot was done leafing through it, he looked in disbelief and said "Hell, you're more qualified to fly this plane than I am." I then looked at his logbook, which had totaled just under 4k hours, and less than a quarter of my landings.
Later that day, we went to the disastrous landings simulator, which tested pilot's abilities to land in the weird extremes of Cleveland weather, and the boss had the people running the simulator set it up for a 5min takeoff session, 5min  at cruise, and landing from 20k ft. I flew the simulator, and when I got out, the boss said to me "If you were 16, I'd hand you your license right now, and take you down to the Continental offices downstairs."
So yeah, thats the reason why I love this game, and it has been such a big part of both me and my childhood.
**My dad's boss is the SuperIntendant of the airport, basically he rules all
**What did 5000 hours do to me? Make me good at flying in simulators
**Yes, I have flown a plane in real life. Cessna 172 and Piper Cherokee
**No, I do not have my pilot's license
**I broke 4 different joysticks out of wear and tear during that time
TLDR: On the original version of this game, I put more than 5k hours into flight time, decide for yourself if I think its good or not.

I know that the game is marketed as a game for those who want to concentrate on the management rather than micromanaging (or playing out) the actual arena combat, but this is too far a step in the wrong direction in my opinion. A simplified combat system (as Sands of the Coliseum manages) would have been all that is required, or a small animation at the very least.
I didn't want to play out the entire combats in 'First-Person Shooter' fashion, but I did expect a little more than a stark textual announcement of the result for all the time and management getting my gladiator into the ring.
As it stands, the game has potential, but it really needs to be wedded to a simple combat game to make it fully rounded.

Perhaps one of the most unforgiving and nervewracking games I have played, Nuclear Throne comes to the point of nearly breaking a person as they play, run after run. To be put plainly, Nuclear Throne is a Rouge-Like Stick Shooter where every moment counts, wether it be dodging projectiles or choosing the perfect mutations. The game is very simple; your goal is to reach the "Nuclear Throne" and to save your friends. To do so, you must progress through different level and areas, slowly gaining more and more weapons, ammo, and radiation as you go along, leveling up and mutating from said rads allows you to take special perks and abilities such a increased ammo and health drops, or dealing contact damage to enemies. All of ssaid weapons and mutations are completly random, and make the game different with every playthrough, for better or worse.
There are also many different ways to play in Nuclear Throne, which revolve around which character you pick, and mostly, pure luck. Personalyy I like to choose high mobility, or incredibly safe characters to ensure an easier time, but if it suits you, you can play as a character that can dual wield laser miniguns. But, most of the time. your play style is determined more by what you get than what you like. Finding some weapons in this game are certianly not going to change how you play, but there are that most definitely will. Take for instance, the Laser Rifle; a high rate of fire energy weapon that if given the correct mutations, can be used throughout a run. Or perhaps you find a minigun, a weapon that rapidly chews through ammo, but with the correct mutations, can become a well sustained bullet hose that may never run out of ammo. While Nuclear Throne may give many choices, to play the game well is to learn how to play with the hand you were dealt.
There are many enemies in Nuclear Throne, some of which you will come to love, and others that you will hate. Wether it be a seemingly harmless maggot, or a crazed abandoned operative of an interdemensional police force, all enemies are unique and dangerous in their own ways. Some enemies can feign death, others will explode, some will run at you with reckless abanon in hoves of killing you, but they all share the common ground that they can be killed. Upon death enemies will drop radiation upon death and the stronger the enemy, the more the rads. As for a rule of thumb with all foes, if it bleeds, you can kill it.
All in all, Nuclear Throne has caught my attention, and taken hold, becoming one of my favorite games and passtimes, and I hope it does for you as well.

Since I really loved The Banner Saga 1, I made sure to pre-order the second as soon as it became available, and started playing it on the same evening it was released. Well, it took me around 12 hours over three long evenings to beat the game, and I'm pretty sure I'm going to begin again very soon. At the time of writing this review, Steam says I've been playing for 8 hours, but it didn't take into account around 4 hours of game time in which I was offline.
For those of you not familiar with the games all, The Banner Saga is a series of Tactical Role Playing Games. While the game's environment is a fictional fantasy world, it is somewhat connected to the norse mythology. I don't know much about the norse mythology, but I did notice some connections, such as Hogun and Mogun, and I suppose there are others as well.
Anyway, just like in the first game, in The Banner Saga 2 you alternate between leading 2 different groups of adventurers (for a lack of a better term) on their continued quest. The game is a direct continuation of the first, so while you can watch a recap of what happened during the first game and start playing the second one immediately, I really suggest playing and beating the first one first, so you can carry your savegame over to the second, and continue with the exact same party you ended the first game with.
The battle-system is interesting, refreshing but simple enough to learn. I know some people have been complaining it's too simplistic, but I don't share that view. The graphics are great and so is the soundtrack, but what makes this game so much fun for me, is the story. It's refreshingly dark and interesting. Also, the choices you make have a major impact on the game, which also means you'd probably want to play through it more than once, to explore different options and see what happens when you choose different directions.
Also, it seems like the developers managed to take some of the problematic aspects of the first game and improve them. For one, The Banner Saga 2 is much more flexible than the first, when it comes to promoting your characters. You get much more freedom in choosing which ones to level-up, which in turn, gives you more tactical options in battles.  Not only that, you also get a much larger veriaty of characters to choose from. In addition, this time there are training scenarios, in which you get to learn to use your characters' most important special abilities.
I really like this game, and would recommend it to anyone who likes tactical and story-driven RPGs.

Invisible, Inc. manages the rare achievement of combining two wildly disparate genres - stealth and turn-based tactics - and somehow managing to feel totally mundane. There's not really anything wrong with it, but as an experiment it seems like a failed one, and even when it works it almost feels like the sequel to a more interesting game.
I realize that reviewing the plot of a roguelike is
a questionable activity, but it's worth bringing up here. The game opens by quickly establishing a fascinating world of cyberpunk duplicity, then immediately blows it up to pit you against a monolithic alliance of evil. Then, after you beat the game, the victory cutscene reveals that whoops it turns out you got totally owned. You're then whisked back to the main menu and asked if you'd like to play - and therefore get totally owned - again. The premise isn't
, but it's certainly wonky.
The gameplay is of course the meat of things, but it similarly smells of missed opportunity. You play as the operator of an experienced espionage organization, yet every mission involves stumbling blindly into unknown office buildings in search of unknown objectives, where even flawless victory might net you nothing of value. The world is full of advanced technology for your operatives to hack, but you do so by establishing line of sight. This makes less than zero sense, which isn't a dealbreaker on its own. But crucially, this funnels the dimension of technology into plain old meatspace. You're not exploring a level to gain access to Network A to gain access to Physical Area B to gain access to Network C and so on, you're just… walking around. It's so fundamentally bad at cyberpunk that I have to wonder why the game uses the trappings in the first place. And the actual sneaking follows suit, relying on age-old tropes of hiding behind boxes to avoid patrolling guards' vision cones, with unique agents who present a façade of individuality but nothing more.
As a whole it's… fine. But the alluring premise is almost completely at odds with the gameplay, to the point that it'd work better with an old-timey detective theme than the futuristic cyberpunk one it sports. And the turn-based nature gives the stealth gameplay extra precision, but it doesn't do anything truly new to set it apart from stealth games of the past unless you're really into procedurally generated cubicle farms. Bottom line, you're better off playing
(from the same devs) or
to get your stealth kick.

Just got through act one as yesterday. I am a backer for the game and absolutely loved all the old lucas arts point and click adventure games. With that being said, I have not had enough time on my hands to watch many of the episodes they have posted on the documentry. However, I watched enough to have an idea of what the game was going to be like.
As I played through my first thoughts were really how unique this game was as compared to some of the older games (i.e the monkey islands, day of the tentacle, etc...) in terms of the art work, the interactions between characters and items and everything seemed very thought out. But there is deffinetly a relatable feel to this game cooresponding with the older ones. I can tell by playing act one that alot of heart went in to this game and that for me was enough for five stars.
However, there is much more than heart visible in this game so far. The moderetly challenging(with harder ones to come in following acts according to doublefine) puzzles give the game the classical point and click feel. However I found when trying to use items with multiple people, there would be unique and different dialoge for pretty much every person! This for me was a huge shift in the right direction! It adds that subtlety to the gameplay that I feel will be vital for the survival of future point and click adventure games. And if that was not enough for you, the plot(so far) is absolutely genious, in my opinion one of Tim Schafer's best! The twists and turns really bring you along for the ride, and you never feel bored or left out.
So with the bar being set with the release of act one, I hope that the rest of the game can live up to the expectations. I hope to see more challenging puzzles, and can't wait to see how the story will develop. I hope and expect to see the rest of the game will leave me jaw dropped just as act one did!
And to the all staff of doublefine on board with this project - Great job guys! This one really blew me away!!! I can't wait to see what adventures await our two protagonist in the story! This one, so far, is truly a stroke of genius! Keep up the fantastic work!!!!

I enjoy tactical strategy but not stealth games; decided to try this given the positive reviews. I wanted to like it but found myself thinking this game could have been much more than it was. The core mechanic can be fun, but I still have to go thumbs down. Three primary complaints:
1. The story and characters are underwritten. This makes the game mostly a sandbox that gets repetitive quickly.
2. The environments are one note. Every level looks and feels the same. The adversary has no personality or variety.
3. The game's economy/balancing doubles down on the repetitive loop that the above creates. On the first playthrough, I cruised to the end only to find myself missing critical equipment to complete the final mission that, in retrospect I was had not been offered for purchase from any of the game's semi-inaccessible vendor options in the first place. The between mission vendor is literally useless, frequently having nothing to offer for sale, thereby raising the question why he's included at all. The game's response is to suggest I replay the entire campaign again as part of a metagame. This would be fine given that the game moves at a decent clip except that the repetitiveness of the core game makes replaying it extremely boring. I only have so much time, replaying a game I'm lukewarm on hoping procedural generation will give me opportunities to acquire needed items to finish it doesn't sound like fun, it sounds like a chore.
I think there is a core for a great game here, either by changing the setting (say to the Cold War or by licensing a spy property like Archer or Austin Powers or No One Lives Forever) or a sequel that focuses more on making the game both challenging AND fun by opening up the inventory more, giving the world more character, and creating a villain worth beating.

I love turn based strategy games and I also love stealth games. But only in my wildest dreamsI ever thought it could be possible to put together both of these styles of games in a single one. Invisible, Inc. turns that dream into reality and does it masterfully. The game mechanics are flawless; the playable characters feature distinct skills, enough to ensure different gameplay experiences depending on how you build and upgrade your team; And, as if it were not enough, also offers us an entertaining story to follow.
The gradual increase system of difficulty levels, depending on how long it take to finish a stage, prevents the player to make reckless decisions. Every action here, no matter how small, carries an urgency weight that makes it much more exciting and fun the whole experience (and sometimes frustrating, I can't deny).
The game's campaign is short, which is quite good as it prevents the experience to become repetitive for players less junkies in stealth or turn-based strategy. However, for the diehard fans of the both genres, Invisible is extremely replayable for two main reasons: every play the maps are randomly generated and the different characters to release every match ensures that the game remains fresh for a long time.
--------------------------------------------------------
Eu adoro jogos de estratégia em turnos e jogos de açõa furtiva. Mas nem nos meus sonhos mais malucos imaginei que veria esses dois estilos de jogo reunidos num só. Invisível, Inc. transformou esse sonho em realidade e o fez com maestria. A mecânica é impecável; os personagens possuem habilidades distintas o suficiente para garantir diferentes experiências de jogo dependendo de como se construi e atualiza a equipe; e, como se não bastasse, ele também oferece uma divertida história para acompanhar.
O sistema de aumento gradual dos níveis de dificuldade, dependendo de quanto tempo se leve para concluir um estágio, impede que o jogador tome decisões imprudentes. This game is a hidden gem, it needs more attention than it gets. Let me be the first to say that though it doesn't present the best graphics and at first seems hard to grasp, this game has alot going for it. Hats off to the developer(s) of this game for doing what most others fail to do. I have been searching for a game like this, an RTS with the option to control the unit. Such a simple addon to most other RTS games, but it makes it a much more enjoyable experience. You care more for your units, because you want to USE them. Let me outline some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Innovative game features (the first person capabilites and the aim of the game takes a step up from other RTS titles)
-Alot of depth in the research system (I was very surprised by the amount of branches and trees there were in this, and just how much you can do)
-Theres alot of promise, potentially alot can be done with this game to make it EVEN better.
-You can customise your units armour and weapons?! f*ck yeah!
Cons:
- I ran across a bug with the jeeps where they fell through the ground on some maps.
-The camera doesnt allow you to zoom out as far as you'd expect, and I often found myself having to scroll up and up and up and up to get to the action in some cases.
- The executive has no sort of crosshair and I dont really see any tracers so if a robot does get in, you have to pray you're aiming in the right place or its game over.
- I feel like you're unable to expand very far at all, and whilst it keeps your base in a tight confinement and stops the game getting ridiculous, it feels a little /too/ claustrophobic.
Whilst there are some cons as listed above, don't let it deter you from giving this game a try. I would reccomend getting it on a sale, I paid the full £10 for this, and whilst i'm more than happy to pay this much, the more picky among you may not be. Watch some videos on it, give it a go. You might like it, you might not - in which case you can easily refund. Again, hats off to the developer(s) of this game, a few bugs here and there but that's to be expected. Keep it up.

One of my favorite games I have ever played, which I was pretty blown away by given the very reasonable pricetag. It's addictive, fast, challenging, and has both an active community and an excellent dev team that interacts with the fans.

It has a ton of varied weapons (everything from a shovel to a super plasma cannon) and they're almost all fun to use, and you really look forward to finding some of the crazier heavy duty weapons late in the game. Shootem up players and others with good dodging skills will see their skills come in handy in this game: there's tons of projectiles! Tried really hard to like this game.  I'm a big fan of Rogue-likes, difficult ones, even; got the Real Platinum God achievement on Binding of Isaac Rebirth, but this game takes it a tad too far.  The difficulty, for ME, is just plain too cheap to be enjoyable.  It's the type of difficulty where you're playing a platformer and there's spikes on almost every floor tile.  The game is a classic example of cheap-shot or aritifical difficulty - there's traps all over the place that will insta-kill you with very little or no time to react whatsoever.  There's even monsters that can fly from offscreen moving 20-30 tiles per second and can kill you instantly.  You can chalk that up to planning and strategy, which may work for you, but for me, it just leaves a bad taste in the mouth.
Some of this difficulty comes from bad decisions on the developers' part; being planted in near impossible situations, unfair boss spawns, for example.  Genuine difficulty and unfair difficulty are two different things.  One can argue that unfair difficulty adds to the experience and sense of accomplishment, requires more planning, strategy and luck, but I tend to disagree, it's just a cop-out.
There is a boss called "Li'l Hunter" (sue me if the spelling's wrong) who will just jump down from the sky with no warning and probably instantly kill you with his ultra powerful shockwave.  Cool, i've played the game a few times, maybe now that I know his entry I can prepare for it.  Nope.  On his stage, you're likely to be dropped into a large open room surrounded by 10-20 dangerous enemies with no route of escape.  Once the boss appears, he flies around the screen like a maniac, spamming all kinds of overpowered weapons, WHILE YOU STILL HAVE TO DEAL WITH THE ENEMIES THAT ARE PART OF THE LEVEL.  Some of these situations would require a complex computer running complex scripts solving their own complex formulas to successfully navigate said situation.  This type of difficulty is not fair even for a Rogue-like.
You may have fun with this game being that it's action packed and (loosely) follows the Rogue formula, and the game feels pretty fun to play overall, but the artificial difficulty ruins it for sure.  I wouldn't recommend.

So this game has been out for well over a year and there's no one new buying this game anyway so there is no point to me writing this review. But I'm going to do it anyway because ♥♥♥♥ you that's why.
As you can see by my stupid number of hours played in this game I actually enjoy it. Seriously I don't know how the hell I played this game for 41 hours without blowing my brains out even once still astonishes me. I suppose it's because I am a big fan of management simulation games and what's cooler than a gladiator simulation game?
To explain why I can't recommend this game let us start at the beginning:
When you first start out in the game it feels like that gladiator simulation game you've been looking for; you can recruit your staff including scouts, doctors, blacksmiths, and trainers, you assemble your own squad of gladiators to send out into the meatgrinder that is the early game arena because you don't know the difference between "massive" and "mild" shows, and everything seems great. It feels like there are actually interesting aspects such as money lenders and a ranking system. Different bosses and a progression from city to city leading up to the colosseum at Rome.
But it's all a ♥♥♥♥ing scam.
Well I guess that's a bit of exaggeration, I don't want to give anyone the impression that this game is lieing to you about what it is....even though it kinda does.The issues of the game might not even become apparent on your first paythrough, but I assure you by your second one it sure will.
The game is painfully shallow in its mechanics and wastes so much potential. The game is just flat out broken, which I knew when I first bought it about a year ago but I had hoped patches would come out to fix it but nope. Dexterity is the only skill that matters so just max that while throwing a couple of points towards strength and your gladiator suddenly becomes ♥♥♥♥ing Russel Crow from...well, I assume you can figure that out. Anyway, the point is that you never need to level anything other than dexterity and strength as long as your fighter has decent health and even then if you've got 150 dexterity/strength it won't matter anyway.
This issue is not as terribly game-breaking in a typical playthrough, even though no one can touch your 56-0 gladiator once you get to Rome so what's the ♥♥♥♥ing point anyway, but it becomes super apparent when you try to play the game on the extended campaign mode. If you've played XCOM then you might expect as I did that the game length would be extended but in a consistent and enjoyable way, but why the ♥♥♥♥ would you think that you inbred retard? All it changes is the amount of red-shirt practice dummies for your team of soon-to-be squad of Russel Crowe gladiators to cut through so they can hit max level before leaving the first town. I'm not even joking with that, in what other RPG can you hit max rank within the first 25% of the game? The whole thing is busted and I have no idea how it was ever put into the game. In my numerous attempts I have never been able to get through an extended campaign. Not because I don't have the time but instead because my family keeps catching me playing this game and having me readmitted.
Moving on to a few smaller things. The ranking system is just dumb. "So maybe you should send your top fighter into the arena. He is bruised up and fatigued – but he also is ranked 3rd overall by the so-called experts and pundits of Leptis Magnus" - The sketchy description for the game. This doesn't mean that he is the third best fighter as determined by a group of intense gladiator channel sports analysts. He just has the third most wins in the town. I have had 2-0 gladiators who I can't be bothered to find on the ranking charts skull ♥♥♥♥ "ranked 3rd overall" gladiators who are 22-2. Also, not like you care or are still reading this, but the market is the simplest thing I've ever seen. It feels like they put no effort into making something creative and just have a list of weapons that deteriorate over time.
Also the settings suck, but none of you care about settings anyway.
So to conclude this review that no one has read, someone finally realized that making a gladiator management sim is cool, but they kinda ♥♥♥♥ed it up.
But hey it's 10 bucks so I'd still buy it again.

It is one of the best stealth games so far, I got the Contingency plan DLC as well so both are so worth the price. It feels like an xcom 2 base game but obviously not the same because of the gameplay, you play as the agents from invisible inc. completing your objectives and rebuild your lost HQ that somehow they got compromise.
The cut scenes of the choice of art style I really like, I just wish they add more cut scenes instead of only two and more like Mark of the Ninja that has several shorter cut scenes. I want to have a small connection to my agents and the head leader, maybe the villains I want to hear their objective in these whole missions we were task on. Yes there is some brief history each of the agents including the leader, but what I meant was having an interaction between my agents as they are doing their brief missions. (After they finish talking to the main objective)
Each mission is important depending on the resource you need and depending on the objective the level will be increasingly harder as you progress into complex buildings. You have an alarm meter that fills the alarm bar each turn and each level of alarm will get the level harder which adds more tension to the game and leaves you an adrenaline feeling when you're trying to complete your objective and will say to yourself of "oh shoot I got to get out of here, level 3 has been activate too many guards."
It leaves you the same excited feeling when xcom did this and invisible inc. nail it right out of the park for the creation of stress (in a good way) of either gambling to stay and get more loot or leave as soon as possible, not to mention the soundtrack they have is suburb when guards spotted you or when you just got to get the hell out, each action counts. You can't kill guards unless you have lethal weapons but if you do kill them the alarm level will be increase by two so watch out if you do. Is all about stealth and is better to not stun them then stun because that means you have to watch over the body so that he won't wake up and start searching for you.
There's your companion AI Incognita which she is a huge life savior at times through hacking, distractions, all kinds of cool gadgets but each skills require power which you need to hack into terminals in order to get more power for use of Incognita. Each agents has its special abilities and I feel frustrated that you can only carry 2 agents at the start but later when you do rescue hostage you can get additional agents, although the only negative thing about the hostage rescue mission is that you can't get their "unique" gear that he/she is special of using it, so you are stuck with a basic "normal" agent until you buy their gears back from shops that you can hack in buildings from your objective.
The game is short roughly around 6 hrs to complete but the modes is what kept the 20 hrs as of this review going because it adds more challenge into the game and having good replay values. The ending is a brain scratch for me and is obviously building up a sequel or hopefully an expansion pack which in my opinion I don't "mind" much because I sort a want to expand the game more to have all new challenges to play.
CONCLUSSION
Don't let my mix expression toward the ending stops you from buying this game, this game is mostly for gameplay value and it is excellent, the story yes could use some more in depth storytelling to really earn an upcoming sequel pack, but the extra modes to fill in the extra hrs is still worth the price to buy. 8/10

This is another winner from Klei - a great, challenging, and surprisingly deep turn-based strategy game. I did find that the initial learning curve was a little steep, and so recommend that beginners actually do not select the Beginner difficulty. Instead, dig through the custom settings and dial up the multiplier for the # of credits you get for hacking / stealing, and increase the KO amount for the guards. This helped tremendously, as even with the Beginner difficulty, I was always getting killed after just the 2nd or 3rd mission.
Once you get past the first few hours, and start to learn all the ways your agents can die (and oh yes, they will die, repeatedly!), then you begin to see just how much depth there is to the game. This game really reminds me of some of the best Euro-board games, such as Tikal, Catan, etc. The thing that makes these games great is the vast amount of choices you have on any given turn, and the very small amount of actions you actually have time to perform. Of course in Invisible, Inc., as you progress, you will gain the ability to gain more actions, but the central strategic element of balancing all of those choices to maximize your outcome still remains.
I foresee a great # of hours put into this game before the year is out.

Once again the developers have released a brilliant game and have made me a devoted fan for life!

Pros:
- The Nemesis system has improved in almost every single way.
- The game looks beautiful and runs very smooth on my 1080Ti.
- The fortress assaults are really fun in my opinion and the open world feels more alive than Shadow of Mordor.
- The gameplay and combat like in Shadow of Mordor is still extremely fun and taking down a group of Orc captains feels rewarding on the Nemesis difficulty.
Cons:
- The size of the game is quite big, with the High Res Texture Pack and 4K Cinematic Pack it reaches almost 100GB and without it it's still a whopping 75GB, that means if you have a slow connection or your HDD is almost full you're well.. screwed.
- Microtransactions -- There's been a lot of controversy on this subject but it hasn't really affected my game so far, however, to unlock the true ending of the game you're forced to do Act 4 which requires you to defend your fortresses which will require strong orcs and that is where the microtransactions come in.
- Terms of Service -- If you accept the TOS but do not allow them to collect data the TOS pops up every time you start the game.
- There were times were I was getting sick of side missions because they were getting repetitive.
Overall I think this game is a solid 7.5/10, I've only played 15 hours, just started Act 2 and am far from finishing this game however I can honestly say that this is a fun game but there are things like the Microtransactions and the intrusive ToS that stop me from recommending this game at its current price.
I got the game for free with my 1080Ti and do not think it's worth the 60€ price tag, I would however recommend picking it up on sale.

Overview:
Star Merchant is a casual business game in a sci-fi setting where you pick a ship, fly around to different planets, buy and sell goods purely on speculation, and fend of attacks from pirates as you strive to meet your pre-determined goal of how much money you want to earn as apart of the victory condition.
Graphics and sound:
Sadly I'm unable to provide screenshots due to my screenshot key not working with Star Merchant, but I rate the graphics as being purely average.  There's nothing stunning about the graphics, but there's nothing I'd consider game-breaking or corner-cutting.  The sound, however, is very pleasing.  While Star Merchant isn't the sort of game that depends on sound, I have to admit, the times I've played it, the game music and sounds were good enough to where I forgot to mute the game and play my own sort of music in the background.  The battle music would have to be my most favorite feature of Star Merchant.
Positives:
Star Merchant has the sort of casual feel you'd expect from FTL, but unlike FTL, you can actually have a realistic chance of winning in Star Merchant.  As much as I'd rather play a management sim involving an intergalactic freight company, Star Merchant is still good fun with simply managing a single ship which you can purchase an auxiliary weapon for, upgrade various features of the ship one at a time.  Escort ships of three varities can also be purchased, but there's nothing interesting about them.
The ability to make money in a large variety of ways is is also enjoyable.  The bulk of your income will come through the act of buying goods at low prices, then traveling around and selling your wares for more than what you paid for them, but you can also collect tolls from planets, put money into the bank (which features a savings account and two different types of funds which can either pay impressive interest rates, or lose money), buy stocks, gamble at space casinos that randomly appear, find artifacts through dumb luck and then sell them, take money from pirates who were stupid enough to attack you, or simply have the governor of a planet give you money in an audience.  There's even the ability to transport passengers, but the pay is insignificant.
Negatives:
Probably the biggest complaint about Star Merchant, is the system for passengers.  You can move passengers even when you don't have the space for all of them, and they travel aimlessly like they were any other piece of freight.  When purchasing upgrades for your ship, passenger upgrades are only one passenger at a time, and on top of which, hauling passengers doesn't pay out good enough money to make it worth the while in the first place.
Conclusion:
I was pleasantly surprised by the overall experience of Star Merchant compared to the last casual business game I played, which was only useful as a substitute for anesthesia.  Star Merchant doesn't cost much, but given the price I paid for it while it was on sale, Star Merchant represents value for money, and an enjoyable experience for people who love money making games.  Even if you prefer a hardcore management sim game, Star Merchant is a great game to enjoy on the side while you're stressing over another game's scenario.

You know that one game or movie you saw/played when you were growing up and it forever burned it's essence into your soul? This game does that.
The story is incredible. The music is even MORE incredible. The gameplay is pretty simple, it's a more advanced telltale style game in that there isn't any quick time events and you actually control a character, but there is a TON of dialogue and choice making. Choices do actually matter in this game unlike the telltale series, they have a lasting effect on the story through out the game.
Episode 1: Starts off slow, it's pretty much a get to know everyone type of episode of the game. I spent 3-ish hours in this episode because I read EVERYTHING and tried to talk to everyone. They show you how to use the rewind time mechanic and it's pretty neat.
Episode 2: Still kinda slow going, but it picks up the pace and by the end of the episode you should have a solid understanding of who is who and your story in the world. Some really cool choices you can make and you get to see how your past decisions start effecting the rest of the game.
Episode 3: Slow moving episodes are now over with. The story picks up full force and locks you in for the ride by the end of this episode. Awesome choices to be made, great easter eggs to see and find, and you really see how your decisions shaped things around you.
Episode 4: By starting this episode you now know why this game has so many good reviews. This was my favorite episode of the entire game and it's so good I don't want to spoil anything but typically I played 1 episode per day, but after the ending of the 3rd episode I HAD to binge the rest of them. 4 and 5 feel like they go by so fast in comparison to the rest of the game.
Episode 5: A wild ride to the end. Super engaging and I couldn't stop until I finished. As a grown♥♥♥♥♥man, I cried at the end. I also teared up at another part of the game, but I won't spoil that.

Memorable, impactful, and inspiring. An experience in which story, characters, and choices stay with you.
Taking place at a senior high school, this game should be nostalgic and enjoyable to nearly any millennial. The main character, Max Caulfield, is inspiring, hopeful, and a bit naive. Traits that we all may have had, or have, at the age of 18. Early on in the story she discovers that she has the ability to manipulate time leading her to become more brave and adventurous. Using her new power she becomes determined to unravel the mystery of what is happening in the Oregon city of Blackwell after her old friend, Chloe Price’s best friend, Rachel Amber, goes missing.
Although a story game in the vein of what a developer like Telltale would create, this game breaths new life into the genre by allowing Max’s power to be involved in the gameplay, itself. You will have the option of using time manipulation to solve puzzles, open up new dialogue options, or simply change a plot choice you immediately regretted.
Life is Strange offers a legitimate mystery and great conclusions based off choices made prior to the end of each episode, however, characters and character relationships will prove to be what you care most about at the end of your experience.
For those even mildly interested, I suggest playing the first episode to know if this game is for you. It was for me (and apparently many others)!
9/10

This is a very fun game about espionage, secret service agencies and world conspiracies. The plot itself is kind of naive, somewhat cliched but the storytelling itself is very fun. The character development is great, there's a lot of attention to detail, lots of choices to be made during the game that will have their consequences in future. The dialogue system is great - you get a mood of reply which you need to choose really fast. Depending on the reply you can gain reputation with the person you're talking to and that can open up different resolutions of conflicts in the game.
The gameplay itself is not terribly exciting. The AI is somewhat dumb which spoils the shooting part, the minigames (hacking, lock- and codepicking) are simplistic and get dull after a while. Stealth is really powerful tool. I've heard a lot about bugs in the game but I haven't encountered many during my walkthrough. I got stuck in a texture once and saw AI do some really stupid stuff.
Despite all it's flaws Alpha Protocol is a great and fun game. It's like reading a good super-spy book and watching a good James Bond movie. I've played this game practically non-stop for 3 days, it is that much fun to get through the plot and see what comes next, how this all will end and how it all will be resolved. This conspiracy/espionage setting is really a breath of fresh air in RPG world and I really can't have enough of it.

This game is boring, monotonous, repetitive, uninspired and feels like a failed attempt to create something like a horror game. There is no horror!
It only provides the player with funless fights versus tons of the same ugly and unscary evil shadow lumberjacks.
You walk 90% of the game through woods at night. The models are recycled again and again, i can't count how often i pressed the same looking button, walked in the same hut, climbed the same watchtower, passed by the same tractor.
The best parts in the game are, when you explore the locations and learn about the story, and even that is not really well made.
The character-models, especially the females, are looking hideous. The textures are blurry and ugly.
The gameplay is a disaster. Always the same fights, running from checkpoint to checkpoint in pseudo-open levels, which reveal themselves sooner or later as straight paths without providing real exploration (not that this must be necessary...)
Using your flashlight to weaken the enemies, so you can kill them, sounds like a good idea and it seems to be fun the first 15 minutes, but after you did that 100 times it's just annoying. The car driving is horrific and futile. The controls overall are just really bad. Why do you have to use the same button for running and dodging?
The game completely feels stretched to a length that wasn't planned before. If there is a cut-scene with Alan in a car or a helicopter or whatever, it will to 100% crash anywhere in the woods. If you have to go somewhere, the straight way will always be blocked suddenly. If the game would consist of 3 Episodes it would be "OK", but playing through this is just really boring. And it is not scary at all, well perhaps for the first 30 minutes.
*Story: Good idea, interesting telling through TVs and manuscript pages
*Gameplay: Boring and repetitive 3rd person shooter, no puzzles, controls feel poorly conceived
*Graphics&Sound: Ugly textures, hideous character models, recycled models for huts, cars, houses etc. everywhere, sound was neither special nor bad.
