Alpha Protocol is a Third-Person Action RPG which feels like it was maybe a half year's polish from being the best game of the previous generation. In it, you play as a recent recruit to Alpha Protocol, a secret intelligence agency of the United States. You carry through a series of missions, some of which can be played in any order, in order to drive the story of what happened to cause an airline to be shot-down to its conclusion.
The primary thrust of Alpha Protocol's novelty is its choice mechanism. In many conversations, there will be multiple options available to the player (typically suave, aggressive, and professional). Different characters will react differently to you depending on what you use, and the player builds a reputation over time. This leads into gameplay perks, new initial reactions from characters which previously haven't been met, and many other branching storyline options. Furthermore, what order you choose to do missions can provide additional intel which can unlock FURTHER branchings in missions, optional objectives, and may other items.
The game is not without fault - depending upon what sort of focus you choose to give your character's skills, some boss fights can prove to be very difficult, and this is where the polish could have been most beneficial. That being said, it's hardly enough of a flaw to remove a recommendation for this game - it's absolutely worth the asking price. Rarely have I finished a story-driven game and immediately felt the desire to go back and play through it again while making different choices.
Highly, highly recommended.

Shadow of War should really be a shining example of what developers SHOULD be doing for sequels: Take what works and what's fun and make it just that much better. That's really what it boils down to; do you enjoy Shadow of Morder? You'll love Shadow of War. It's the same idea, except this time you're actually building an army and upgrading Talion in many ways with various items. The story is neat, though you don't feel like you're actually making that much of an impact on the overall Lord of the Rings story, and there's plenty of cool characters and backstory. Of course the army building and sieges are way too much fun. My main complaint is, honestly, that all the cutscenes are pretended. My cool Rohirrim armour? Yeah, Talion wears his typical ranger armour in every cutscene with his same broken dagger-sword. There's no way he had enough time to change during the siege of Minas Ithil, let's be honest here. Otherwise, the game is absolutely stunning.
Now for the part you're probably scrolling by to see: Microtransactions. Yeah, they exist. Yeah, it's absolutely scummy. A singleplayer (mostly) game with microtransactions? When I heard about this I almost didn't buy it, honestly. Everything you can get in the chests you can get in the game anyway so there is that, but it still doesn't remove the fact that it's kind of a dirty thing to do. This is a full-priced single player experience and here we are being asked to fork out more money for day-one DLC and microtransactions. Developers do deserve to be paid, absolutely, but there's better ways to do it than this. It's like trying to choke more eggs out of a chicken.
This game is worth it though. The experience is so much fun and there's honestly so much to be done that I can't stop playing it. If you're wary on the microtransaction part then buy it when it goes on sale; that's completely understandable. If you do buy it at full price do not, please DO NOT buy ANY of the chests or ANY of the microtransactions. This is NOT behaviour that we should be encouraging from ANY developer. EVER. We need to beat it out of them like my parents should have done when I was a kid.
Oh wait, they did.
I still highly, highly recommend it though.

Middle-Earth: Shadow of War is a great game, the gameplay is fast and fluid and the controls are more responsive then in Shadow of Mordor. While the graphical update may be minimal, it still has a beauty to it unlike most games now of days. The location variety is astounding and I never felt like one area overstayed it's welcome. The weakest part of the game is easily it's story but I happened to still enjoy it very much. And while you do not get much from the main story in terms of character conflict, when you explore the sidequests and hear the banter more and more, you learn more about the characters and their struggles.
While there may be those who criticize it for the microtransactions, it is very eay to play the game without them, especially if you just let an orc kill you, allowing him to raise a few power levels above you, and then killing him to get the better rewards. The nemesis system makes these microtransactions redundant if you can learn how to manipulate it which becomes extremely helpful in the late game grind for the true ending.
I would give the game a solid 9/10, while it breaks some of Tolkien's lore, it fits it into the Lord of the Rings trilogy nicely and the story is a welcome one especially with a universe so proud on boasting about the heroes who came before.

Hotline Miami is something familiar yet feel so different.
It feels so similar to past top-down view perspective games such as the first 2 Grand Theft Auto Games but this game is a linear, and that's a good thing.
The linear approach of this game offers broad and distinct storyline compared to most modern games.You start out as a normal civilian until a masked assassin attempts to murder you in your own apartment.You spend the whole game pursuing the people behind said attempt.
You do missions provided by an unknown caller on your answering machine and other people that will help you along the way. Missions regardless of whether it may be a killing someone, retrieving items,etc. requires stratetigical thinking before you act. Unlike most modern games which requires minimal skill, this game demands you to carefully plan before you engage and execute actions flawlessly in order to have a good "score grade" in the scoring system.
Combo and mobility is a must to acquire a good score grade.

+Replayability
+Leader Boards

Here's my take on the civilian flightsim hobby as it currently stands: More than ever, it is a period of transition and I believe the future looks good. I have and use both FSX and X-Plane and therefore have a foot in both camps. It's a case of fully realized capabilities versus future potential. From another perspective I see one nearing the end of its 32-bit lifecycle and the other very much in its 64-bit adolescence.
Background: I've been flight simming since SubLogic's C64 release, and have been firmly entrenched in the Microsoft FS camp on PC since FS5.1, although like everyone else in the day I had and used Flight Unlimited, FLY! and ProPilot. We loved the variety and happily used them all for what they had to offer. For me FS2004/FS9 was the watershed, and I was entrenched for a decade in the sim using all the familiar add-ons and a full suite of GoFlight hardware. Unfortunately my computer was firmly stuck in 2004 as well, so I avoided migrating to FSX. I was aware of and had messed around with XP during my biannual pilgrimage to Oshkosh, even chatting at length with Austin Meyer, but I was already too deeply invested in the MSFS camp. I'm certain that many can relate.
I've been a licensed private pilot since 1991, with a multi-engine endorsement and lucky enough to have had exposure and stick time on some pretty cool equipment. Now as most real world guys will tell you, flying a computer is NOT the same - I don't care if the flight models are based on lookup tables or basic real-time elemental calculations, it's just not worth arguing over. Get over it.  Where there is tremendous value in simming however, is the 'process' of flight - planning, procedures, checklist habits, instrument scans, IFR approaches. For true immersion in the system look up PilotEdge and add that to your mix no matter what platform you fly.
I was fortunate enough to finally build a cutting edge computer recently. As a treat, I picked up FSX-SE to see how she'd run on a modern box. Looked good and I was enthused enough to purchase Aerosoft's A320/321 (an absolutely excellent add-on BTW). Then the dreaded terrain.dll crashes started on flights lasting longer than about 60 minutes. While I understand these errors may have been largely addressed in the new FSX-SE beta patch, I am very grateful for them. They gave me pause and saved me the hundreds of $$ I was prepared to pour into the scenery and add-ons in order to bring it up to the available standards: Orbx, UTX, ASN, PMDG, et al. It's a slippery slope most know only too well, and when you finally stop and look back at all the resources you have dedicated, the thought of migrating to something totally new seems not only daunting, but is likely financially unwarranted as well.
While waiting for a decade old piece of software to get patched by a third party so that I could run it on modern equipment and proceed to spend a great deal of money and tweaking time to get it to run correctly, the light bulb went on for me. Here I was at a crossroad and I was prepared to reinvest in the same old song and dance. Yes, it's the one tune everybody knows, but there was an opportunity to learn a new one. Even though I tried and failed to get the X-Plane demo working, I purchased the full version (10.35 currently) in order to give it an honest shakedown, flying it exclusively for a week. What that week gave me was an appreciation for just how immersive, smooth and realistic XP can be.
I spent a good deal of time reading the related forums, familiarizing myself with the tips, tricks and FAQs. I found the stock 172 and Baron okay (certainly the equal of their stock FSX equivalents), but added the beautiful Carenado C340 for some GA flying. (Aside - the C340 is a nice looking package and I'm glad I have it but there are some unforgivable faults that required modifications to actually work - in particular the CDI when tuned to an ILS. Basic stuff. For shame.) Then the FlyJsim 737-200 for some good old fashioned radio navigation at jet speeds. Wonderful aircraft, beautifully modelled cockpit and convincingly realistic performance numbers. Definitely a pilot's plane. The coming IXEG 737-300 looks incredible. And I needn't mention that PMDG is developing for XP with a DC6 to be followed by one or more of their 7xx series...
Sparse scenery? To me it looks far and away better than stock FSX. It's nicely scalable to the hardware you're running, and XP definitely makes proper use of modern hardware. The stock mesh is great, autogen works well, the road traffic is cool, and the night lighting is the stuff of pilot training heaven. But here's the kicker - there's so much freely available from the community. I've managed to populate my XP world with all the airport scenery I will be reasonably using with a few visits to the XP ORG. And if you have a look at what's possible using world2xplane... the future looks not only bright, but incredible. Need I mention no terrain.dll CTDs or OOM errors?
Stock XP weather is in my opinion better than stock FSX. Dressed up with ASN and REX however, and FSX has a strong lead. But based on how close XP is getting with aircraft and scenery, the weather engine won't be far behind.
Stock ATC is crap. But so is FSX's. Sorry, it's just not real. I alluded to it above, but try PilotEdge to see what real ATC is. Full stop.
This has become a rather long piece, sorry about that. I suppose I felt I had a lot to say about where we've been, where we are, and where we're going. MSFS has been how it was, and largely how it is now (I include P3D here). Is it time for change? One platform is nearing a developmental dead end, albeit with some wonderful add-ons, and one is just beginning to realize its potential with continuous and meaningful support.
I'll continue to use both platforms for now, I mean why not, I own both and enjoy each for what they offer. Let me be clear though - I will not be adding anything further to my FSX ecosystem, but will simply enjoy what I already have. FSX will be limited to getting my bus fix with that awesome Aerosoft A320, at least until the sim crashes with the latest .dll or OOM error. For the price of a decent FSX add-on, I would urge you to give XP a fair evaluation.
In the end I see FSX as an old woman all gussied up in makeup and a new designer dress. She looks great and is pleasant to spend quality time with, but be careful if you go out dancing - she may fall and break a hip. Now have you seen the new girl in town? Dances funny, but she's smart, modern, and has some really cool moves. You may want to meet her.
My future in the hobby is with XP. I know I am not alone. Developers take note.

Get your action-movie-spy on! Invisible's headquarters have been attacked, its agents scattered, and you have 72 hours of raiding the evil corporations (for money, supplies, upgrades, and rescuing your agents) before you have to make your own counterattack.
As a "roguelike", everything from the levels, to the extra agents you can pick up, to the items in the "shops" is randomized, and you have to build your strategy around what you get. You can't manually save the game, either - though you do get a limited number of "rewinds" to undo your last turn. It's enough to let you control the difficulty, but you can't afford to become a perfectionist.
You can probably finish Story mode in about 25 hours (including the DLC), but there's a fair bit of replayability, and an "Endless" mode that just continues cranking up the difficulty.
The minor irritations:
- What locations will be in cover, and what locations will be revealed as guards walk their patrol routes, can be unintuitive at times. (My agent can hide behind what?!?) It could be handled better in the tutorial; possibly with the guard walk animation slowed down, so you can watch the tile "noticed / watched / hidden" highlights change.
- It feels like there's a steep ramp in difficulty from finishing a "Beginner" game to starting a new "Experienced" one. Thankfully, there are rewinds (unless you choose to disable them!)
- It takes several playthroughs to unlock all the agents. I haven't, yet, and I suspect if I tried it'd feel less like fun and more like a grind.
Finally, you can't solve every problem with a gun. It's not that sort of movie :)

Having (somehow) clocked up 199 hours on record in less than three months, this seems like a good moment to give this game my whole-hearted recommendation for:-
- the fidelity of its stealth experience. With the exception of the final level, combat/gun battles bring in the law of diminishing returns, so your primary resources really are desks, corners, chair backs, potted plants, etc. Confrontation is ultimately unavoidable, but even then because of the escalating alert levels, ambush and misdirection work far better than firepower.
- its exquisite interface. Take the classic board game template with its sense of control and overview. Randomize the 'board' each time and have it unveil itself bit by bit as you move across it (especially clever here is the way electronic devices such as consoles, cameras, safes, act as little 'beacons' within unexplored areas, helping you feel out the edges of the map). Switch between AI and agent-operator modes at the touch of a button, spin the map, and even toggle the amount of wall cut-away to keep abreast of all your options.
- its emphasis on tactical gameplay. Some may disagree with me here, but I feel that there's only a limited amount of strategy involved, as procedurally-generated levels and randomized items mean you are mostly confronting unkowns. It's all about how you adapt your options to each new circumstance rather than sitting back to watch a master-plan execute itself, and this means each turn is as riveting as the last.
- its high tension-low frustration ratio. Despite its crazy odds, perma-death, and fearsome difficulty at the later levels, I've never once felt the kind of exasperation that most games present when ratcheting up the challenge levels. Great pacing and balance keep this game totally absorbing even while you're failing (which is what you'll spend an awful lot of your time doing).
- its charming visual design, characterisation and voice acting, which loads of other reviews have already commented on.
Most of my other games are shooters, but even I can see that Invisible Inc. is what gaming can be at its best...

Though it suffers from the troubled development that so often befalls Obsidian, Alpha Protocol is nevertheless an amazing RPG; It could be described as a superior copy of Mass Effect, adding actual choices and consequences in a more modern setting. The stealth and action are mediocre but the real core of the gameplay is in manipulating people through your actions. You are given about 5 seconds to make all your choices, be they flirting with a journalist on an airplane or deciding whether someone lives or dies and the game responds wonderfully to each one.
Do you extort the arms dealer or arrest him? Do you smash a bottle over your contact's head when he wastes your time or play it cool to get on his good side? Do you bluff your way past the guards or sneak in through the roof? Extorting the arms dealer will get you some cash and a reluctant mole in the area while arresting him will provide you a nice bonus and reduce arms smuggling in the area, the enemy will have worse equipment but you might have a harder time getting gear for yourself. Assaulting your contact might result in him phoning up a friend at the place you're trying to sneak into, resulting in better security. Bluffing past the guards may be frowned upon by a more professional handler you chose while a more aggressive or sly one would have approved.
You can play Alpha Protocol half a dozen times (ignore my playtime) and still find plenty of new things in every playthrough, I   found an entirely new mission in one playthrough that exposed a new side to two characters I had written off before, at another point I antagonized a character so much that they attacked me and left. I can think of few games that even come close to AP's reactivity, characters will call you out for anything from wearing full combat gear in public to leaving a trail of bodies in your wake.
If you enjoy RPGs then Alpha Protocol definitely deserves a try.

Let me just start by saying the Alpha Protocol is one of the few RPGs I know that have delivered on it's 'choice changes the game' mechanic. I've played this game for 80 hours now, and I can say that there's cutscenes I have seen in LPs that I haven't even played before.
Honestly, this isn't the best combat I've ever seen. You can play with stealth, or just shoot everything in the face. You start off with 4 classes to choose from which have perk points already in some predetermined places, but you can mix them up. A 5th option, Recruit, has you starting with no perk points at all, making the game a lot harder. Completing the Recruit option will unlock Veteran for future playthroughs, who has perks from previous experience.
You can carry two weapons with you at a time, ranging from an assault rifle, a shotgun, an smg and a pistol. They can be upgraded and you can even buy more of them in the safehouse.
The safehouse serves as a hub for you inbetween missions, allowing you to read your emails (which sometimes contain funding or other useful information), watch TV about 'recent affairs', or check the black market. On the black market you can buy things ranging from a map of the complex to intelligence on a person.
You can build up intel on people or groups, and knowing it can sometimes give you an extra option in conversations. They also give you a certain damage bonus against some of the bosses.
SPOILERS:
The story is extremely well written and has a very high replayability, only being dragged down by the combat. For that, I'll give it an 7/10

You know that one game or movie you saw/played when you were growing up and it forever burned it's essence into your soul? This game does that.
The story is incredible. The music is even MORE incredible. The gameplay is pretty simple, it's a more advanced telltale style game in that there isn't any quick time events and you actually control a character, but there is a TON of dialogue and choice making. Choices do actually matter in this game unlike the telltale series, they have a lasting effect on the story through out the game.
Episode 1: Starts off slow, it's pretty much a get to know everyone type of episode of the game. I spent 3-ish hours in this episode because I read EVERYTHING and tried to talk to everyone. They show you how to use the rewind time mechanic and it's pretty neat.
Episode 2: Still kinda slow going, but it picks up the pace and by the end of the episode you should have a solid understanding of who is who and your story in the world. Some really cool choices you can make and you get to see how your past decisions start effecting the rest of the game.
Episode 3: Slow moving episodes are now over with. The story picks up full force and locks you in for the ride by the end of this episode. Awesome choices to be made, great easter eggs to see and find, and you really see how your decisions shaped things around you.
Episode 4: By starting this episode you now know why this game has so many good reviews. This was my favorite episode of the entire game and it's so good I don't want to spoil anything but typically I played 1 episode per day, but after the ending of the 3rd episode I HAD to binge the rest of them. 4 and 5 feel like they go by so fast in comparison to the rest of the game.
Episode 5: A wild ride to the end. Super engaging and I couldn't stop until I finished. As a grown♥♥♥♥♥man, I cried at the end. I also teared up at another part of the game, but I won't spoil that.

Memorable, impactful, and inspiring. An experience in which story, characters, and choices stay with you.
Taking place at a senior high school, this game should be nostalgic and enjoyable to nearly any millennial. The main character, Max Caulfield, is inspiring, hopeful, and a bit naive. Traits that we all may have had, or have, at the age of 18. Early on in the story she discovers that she has the ability to manipulate time leading her to become more brave and adventurous. Using her new power she becomes determined to unravel the mystery of what is happening in the Oregon city of Blackwell after her old friend, Chloe Price’s best friend, Rachel Amber, goes missing.
Although a story game in the vein of what a developer like Telltale would create, this game breaths new life into the genre by allowing Max’s power to be involved in the gameplay, itself. You will have the option of using time manipulation to solve puzzles, open up new dialogue options, or simply change a plot choice you immediately regretted.
Life is Strange offers a legitimate mystery and great conclusions based off choices made prior to the end of each episode, however, characters and character relationships will prove to be what you care most about at the end of your experience.

Review of Act 1:
So finally we have the first part of this game! The first things you'll probably think when you boot up this game is that it's frickin' beautiful. That doesn't wear off either, this game keeps up its beautiful artwork all through the adventure, and it made everything go down so much easier. It's also incredibly well voice acted (Wil Wheaton, Elijah Wood, Jack Black, Jennifer Hale and a few more famous voices), and the soundtrack is great too. The puzzles are never too oddball and almost always feel like an entirely logical action - I only looked for help once in my playthrough, and I felt like an idiot when I did!
Obviously the most important part of an adventure game however, is its story. And let me tell you, this one is a corker so far. Of the two, I definitely preferred the boy's story on the spaceship, as it's a lot more charming and funny than the girl's, but really both are great and the fact you can switch between both whenever you like will keep things fresh if you ever get sick of anything. The piéce de resistance is finding out how the two stories may involve each other, and the conclusion really will make you want to play the next act of the game (it can't come soon enough). Also, it took me roughly 3 hours to play this act of the game, I don't know whether I believe that's a bit short, but tbh I really enjoyed what I got and I feel like it was a good place to finish the act,
Considering the development troubles, the non-conventional funding and it being split into two parts, the fact it's turned out this good so far is incredible. Very polished throughout, great story, lots of humour, if you've ever enjoyed an adventure game, I really think you'll enjoy this. Highly recommended.

New features: There are now higher ranked orcs called overlords which rule regions, you can start an intense seige the keeps and overthrow the overlord. This seige feature fits into online too, you can raid other players keeps to earn big rewards and rank up. Rideable drakes are in the game, orcs now seem to come back for revenge more often sometimes coming back stronger and dominated orcs can turn into your enemies. Each orc captain is more unique with its own class and tribe which determines their fighting style and traits. Some captains can be epic or legendary and sometimes come back to life stronger, for example I killed a trickster class captain by burning him, he came back as a legendary fiery machine trickster, he gained a epic trait and legendary trait. You can now find and equip different gear with unique abilities which can hold different gems.Talion/Celebrimbor is more agile now which is pretty useful. Good to also see some more comedy in this sequel, there are also old 'friends' which have returned.
Game isnt quite worth £45 though and the loot chests system is a bit forced on a singleplayer game but you don't need to buy them to play well, not going to give this fun game a down vote just because of it being 'pay to win'.
I got legendary followers very quickly within playing and fairly decent gear so didn't need to buy loot chests.
Clear improvement, story is more interesting with new characters, new features work well, devs just got greedy.
I'd give it a 8.6/10 would ask for a cheeky vision again *wink*

Shadow of War makes Shadow of Mordor look like a prequel episode to the franchise.
The Map is huge which is covered unders different 'Acts' as Talion progresses in the story.The story is directly adapted from the Lord of the Rings which makes it very interesting.Many NPCs like Shelob(Act 1) and The Witch King along with the Nazguls(Act 2) make a terrific apperance quite early in the game,to name a few.
The Skill list is also greatly improved and defeating enemies is not as easy as it was in Shadow of Mordor despite exploiting their vulnerabilities.Anyone who starts the game with the 'Nemesis' difficulty will realize it soon.The overall gamelay has also been improved and made way more challenging in Shadow of War.
About the in-game purchases(Use Gold,Mirian or directly Cash)
1.You can buy Treasure Chests of three types-Gold,Silver and Common.I preordered the Gold Edition and hence,I have the Bonus Pack and a Gold Chest.However,one can buy as much as they want.
2.There is also 'Spoils of War' and 'XP' Booster Packs available for purchase which boosts the quality of Enemy Collectibles and Talion's XP gain respectively for two hours which makes the player to easily(and unfairly) advance in the game.I got two of these each with my preorder.
Important to remember
1.Players can kill as many enemies as they want in the Nemesis to get armors and weapons,but only of the Common,Rare or Epic types.To get Legendary type using this method is very difficult since the enemies dropping Legendary items are very few and are also very difficult to kill(I can't remember how many times I died just to kill one enemy for a Legendary Sword).This is where I think the game is unfair and WB forces us to buy in-game items.
2.If one wants to boost XP without spending money,they can complete as many Online Vendetta missions as possible,but this makes the game unnecesssarily long.
Hence,to conclude,Shadow of War is an excellent game with a very well adapted story from Tolkien's mythology but its shine is shadowed by the mere unnecessary presence of in-game purchases.
Review
1.10/10-Monolith for making a beautiful and unique game.
2.0/10-WB games for meaningless in-game purchases.

Okay, this is a good game, and I've finished it on beginner in about 24hrs according to steam, I'm playing with dlc and I haven't played it with out before. All seems good.
So you beat the game and then sink another 6 hrs in to experienced mode.  Two problems, one, the disconnect from coming from super powered agents way back to basic agents on a harder difficulty setting is jarring, you make too many mistakes.
Second is just how hard this is with out level resets, and the difficulty seems to have been adjusted too much, what is a 2nd or 3rd mission is very hard with out the correct hack tool, which you know from beginner you get later... It's not vastly different from beginner, but the combination of disabling level restarts - so you have to start the entire campaign again - and the addition of trying new characters out is too much. Then also the difficult shield level is way out, you don't have the hack tools needed. This can be fixed by enabling level restarts - but then you're not playing experienced you're playing custom, no awards for that.
On first play through most people I assume would be doing stealth and avoiding kills, the default characters are this way. You happen to get a couple of characters later which are geared around killing which would be best for a second play through - I just don't see myself playing through beginner again though to get use to it.
Also on experienced, even when you ARE experienced, the shield difficulty indicators, the things which tell you how hard something is going to be, were way out. 2nd or 3rd mission in a 2 or 3 level became impossible because I didn't have the right hacking tool (area effect hack), but having played beginner I know that that tool wouldn't be got so early.
(I think I got up to turn 37-45 in one map, dragging a body along a map which was basically one long corridor while 8 guards swamped around, a lot of micro. Obviously it wasn't meant to get like that and should rewind before, but it was fun enough to do.)
This may be a problem of expectation. Because some in beginner which are marked as "do not advice infiltrating" level 5-6 aren't that hard, yet on experienced a level 2-3, what should have been easy, wasn't. I'm wondering if it would have been better to have started the game on experienced, just so the expectation was set, but even so. Or to have my suped up agents from beginner carry over, just so I could tell if it's the agents or the game.

The more I played this game, the more it felt like Wonderboy. But that's not exactly a compliment. What I mean is, the controls are a bit clunky for a platformer, but once you get used to them the game is not half bad, considering I got it for $0.16 in those Steam auctions. I decided to finish it and review it anyway.
Unfortunately the game is backwards! The first world is not really engaging, the sound track chiptune eats away at your brain and the first boss is unnecessarily frustrating. Admittedly the game does get better as you play in to it, as I will explain in detail in a second, but I have to ask why... why not engage the players early? Oh well. Probably why it was $0.16. I'll get all the bad things out of the way first.. but where do I start? Ok, let's start with probably my biggest peeve, the "secret" areas. I put secret in quotation marks because well they aren't really that secret. They're ♥♥♥♥ing everywhere! There are probably 5 or so secrets per level, 8 levels per world, 5 worlds. That's a ♥♥♥♥ tonne of secret areas, you kinda get tired of them after a little while. Mainly because the rewards in them are often petty or you are forced to risk your life or fight a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of enemies to get to a chance of a good reward. Yeah ♥♥♥♥ that. I learnt quickly to skip the secrets. But sometimes you can't skip them! There were times where you see a ledge, and you jump, and then, ohhh ♥♥♥♥ invisible wall - you're dead. Mother ♥♥♥♥er..
What next? The bugs? After collecting a token and entering a secret world where sprint is disabled, when you get back to the main game, sprinting and shooting is still disabled. You have to quit the game and re-open your save file to be able to do it again. How did they miss that? Actually it kinda made the game more fun and challenging the first time it happened. I thought it was intentional, and played the level without shooting. It made me realize that the power-ups are ♥♥♥♥ing stupid and overpowered. There's also a few collision detection bugs, which you do NOT want in a platformer. There were times where things did not even touch me, but they still killed me. Other times where I quite literally dodged a bullet, because the bullet hitboxes are so tiny, they can sometimes pass right through you and not hurt you. In parts where you aren't meant to control your character, you can still press the down and left key, making your character moonwalk or butt-slide. Not game breaking, more humorous actually.
Artwork! Now this is gonna be a bit of a mixed answer. I loved and hated it. I loved the art style on the enemies and some parts of the map, they were really detailed. However, other parts of the map objects and the main character sprite were really lacking. They looked a bit rushed. If you take a look at this video I made of the world 5 boss fight you can see what I mean. The boss is really detailed but some other things like the player, the flag, the user interface are really poorly done. They just don't sit well next to each other and just give the overall look of it being put together a bit quickly. Some improvement here and with the clunky gameplay would have really improved this game substantially.
Alright, better talk about some things that were enjoyable. A lot of the mechanics were ♥♥♥♥ing god awful like the inverse Mario style blocks that broke when you jump on them or cactus enemies that hide behind other cacti so you can't see them. They're also introduced so ♥♥♥♥ing poorly, you don't even know it's coming - it just hits you. You are meant to let players learn new♥♥♥♥♥♥before just throwing it at them! ♥♥♥♥! Ok, meant to be saying nice things. Some mechanics were cool.. I was really impressed with the sinking sand in world 2. I actually really liked where they took that. I was actually thinking "hey they should have a level where you race the sinking sand" and lo and behold, 2 levels later they did it! The snow world was a bit cooler too. Lots of new stuff implemented here, the guys throwing the snow balls were pretty cool, although if you had max power ups you could wreck them pretty easily. The boss fights got more fun as the game progressed too, which was nice because I nearly quit the ♥♥♥♥ing game after World 2's boss fight cause it was so infuriating.. The map design in the final world was really fun in a not-too-easy but still challenging way.Where the rest of the game was either easy, or ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Last world was right in the middle. This may have been because I was slowly getting used to the awkward controls, but hey, that's old school game progression for you, right?
Overall verdict - it was worth what I paid? I guess?

Invisible, Inc. is similar to xcom but without combat RNG or damage scaling. The graphics is quite easy to the eyes and instructive, the music and voice acting are fairly well done, and the character design has decent depth.
The storyline campaign is very short, with an average of about 6 to 10 missions. Even with the DLC (which is well worth it) missions it will only take at most a few hours to finish, which is a great shame as it would make a very dank cartoon show should there be some more effort.
The real content lies in the custom campaign generation, for you can remove the 3 (ingame) day time limit to receive more missions up to endless. This allows you to explore more strategies with your agents and items of choice, and with about 20 different agents there are abundant possibilities to experiment.
What really made it better than xcom for me is its randomly generated maps, even for unique storyline missions. For those who are familiar with xcom EU/EW you should know that all missions use a limited pool of fixed maps, so after a playthrough or two, the only uncertainties are the locations of the aliens (even that you can guestimate) and the mood of RNGesus. Invisible, Inc. on the other hand has no combat RNG, all aggressions either result in a KO (knockout) or kill. However the variety of the maps made gameplay weighs a lot more towards stealth, scouting and planning, qualities I appreciate from a turnbased strategy game; and across the 4 or 5 endless campaigns I barely ever feel the fatigue I felt while replaying xcom.
tl;dr Great game, value purchase, short storyline campaign, surprisingly high replayablility and depth in strategy. 9/10, -1 to the unrealized lore potential.

I'd never have thought that this simple a name for a game could sum up my experience with it so well.
The main gameplay mechanic and the starting point of the story is that during their art class, the main character discovers that they can reverse time at their will. They use this ability to try and save their best friend and get a "good ending" for everyone they know - despite the fact that, as it turns out, it's not always possible. In the second half of the game it turns into a detective game and gets quite dark.
One of the main themes of the game is that your actions will have consequences, and you cannot always predict them. What you do, believing that it's the right thing, might backfire and cause the exact opposite of what you wanted to do.
The characters are all well-written and often deeper than they seem at first glance. Your opinion on some of them might radically change throughout the game, as you discover more about them and their motives.
I really liked the story, except for one thing - the game hypes up throughout the first 4 episodes the event of a catastrophic tornade, however the devs seemed not to have the time (in episodes) to touch that subject until the very last part of the game. This caused the story thread to feel kind of rushed and not well thought-out, in the end.
Nonetheless, the main part of the story (solving the dark mystery of the town that Max, the main character, goes to school in) is very well-written, as are all the characters. Your actions have consequences, and all the effects that they cause are shown in an interesting way, and happen at times you might have forgotten about them.
There's only one more problem with the game: as many people point out, the voice acting isn't very good. Whether that is a deal-breaker in a story-focused game is up to you.

Pre cross-play it was hard to find a match because the game's playerbase has been very small. But I highly doubt anyone should have issues finding people now that we have the ability to matchmake into PS4 players.
The Pros:
-Fast paced and highly addictive gameplay
-Easy to pick up mechanics
-Support for local multiplayer
-Just all around an extremely fun game
The game does have a couple cons to it though:
-Only 1 map to play on as of this writing
-The tutorials can be a bit ambiguous and somewhat hard to execute, needs some re-work.
-Not a vast amount of cosmetics. There are a lot, but definitely needs moar!
-Music can get quite repetitive after a short time, of course you can always just turn it off and play your own music.
Overall though, I've played my heart out on this game and even with some of it's imperfections, namely the 1 map part, even with that I've put over 300 hours into this game and have still not found it to get stale.

Since release, this game has added dedicated servers (enabling 2v2 matchmaking) and cross-platform play. I went from being unable to play with some of my friends through peer-to-peer to being able to find matches consistently within minutes.
Mechanically, the game is incredibly fun and challenging. The push and pull of momentum in a match completely trumps any tennis or sports game I have ever played, thanks in part to the Juiced mechanic, which boosts your throw speed after three successive perfect throws. But don't miss a beat or you'll lose it! Maintaining your Juiced state while trying to make your opponent drop his is just half the fun.
Landing perfect throws is precise and feels great, blocking and charging your Super is satisfying and returning opponents Supers, though tricky, feels amazing. Not to mention you can throw lobs, perform Wall Skips and even return an opponents Super with your own if you're fast enough. Super throws can also stack with your Juiced state. There's plenty of options in how to get an advantage but you always have the tools to counter them.
Whilst there's only a few characters and currently one arena, the game feels like a cohesive whole as it is. High Horse clearly focused on having fun and engaging gameplay first and foremost. They also have more content planned but the fact that they focused on implementing dedicated servers and cross-platform play as soon as possible shows thier priorities are in order. I would even say it's above and beyond what should be expected for such a small studio. Kudos, HH.

Alan Wake is proof positive of the point that a story, properly told transcends all media and genres. A game that could be EASILY adapted for film or TV, Alan Wake is a game that is, in actuality, an interactive novel, and one that is just BEGGING for Star Trek's holodeck. Even in the intro sequence I found myself enjoying the game on a level that I have not enjoyed any other game before. Does that mean it's my favourite game? No. But even still it is a wonderful experience nonetheless. Even the fairly standard horror pacing and formula can't detract from this game, and so intricately tied to and interwoven with its plot the game really manages to tell a story while you battle shadow monsters with a Christmas light wearing sidekick (I am NOT making this up). While I am not a fan of the horror genre, and have never really read any Stephen King (to whom the tilts it's hat many times), the game was nevertheless thoroughly enjoyable. The only down-side to this interactive novel is that like a novel it is not immediately replayable. When you get to the last chapter, you don't feel any pressing need to start over again from the beginning, because what you have really enjoyed is not the thrill of the chase, being hunted by an insidious Lovecraftian shadow-demon, but the content of that story. But I think that is one negative we can all bear if games of this ilk were to become more common in the future. And really that actually makes the gameplay longer lasting easier to savour. Please Remedy, and ALL developers, give us more interactive novels, and less psychotically emotionless space marines killing freaking zombie demons from outer space.

Well, it's here at last after almost two years of development, we get to see what Double Fine did with those 3.3 million dollars they got from backers. So is the game actually good? After playing the entire first act in one sitting, the short answer is yes. Is it 3.3 million dollars good? I'd say no.
The game really shines when it comes to the world that Tim Schafer envisioned. I never felt bored exploring the world of Broken Age. There was always something interesting to see and marvel at. The story is really well done too and I really like how the first act ends and sets the events for the second act. I didn't see the story twist coming even though there were a lot of cleverly hidden clues which is a sign of good story writing. The dialogue is also very well written and as expected from a Tim Schafer game, very funny. I can see the same game being made at a much lower budget though. Voice acting probably cost them more than it should because there are some big names in there like Jack Black and Elijah Wood, but they could have done without them easily as their voice acting doesn't really add much to the game in my opinion.
Gameplay in Broken Age is your standard point and click adventure game fair. There is nothing revolutionary here that will change the genre forever or anything and I don't think Double Fine had plans to do that anyway. Most of the puzzles are on the easy side and there are enough clues to help you solve them quickly without feeling stuck for too long.
Overall, I recommend Broken Age at a sale price. Maybe when it's $10 or less. It's not the best adventure game I've played, but it's worth playing nonetheless. Now the wait begins for the second act and the conclusion of the story.

Nuclear Throne is the best game I've played in many years. I love almost everything about it. However, as with most games to which a community is given Early Access, the matter of full release left a sour taste in some mouths. I will try to explain my reasons for including this in the review, but by and large the takeaway from my thoughts should be: THIS GAME IS BRILLIANT, BUY THIS GAME. It’s a more addictive, faster Binding of Isaac, and I say that as someone who returned to video games after 15 years purely because of BOI. During Early Access, the team diligently provided weekly updates which corrected, evolved and modified the gameplay and game features based on the feedback of the community. The community itself was galvanized by an independently run high-score ranking site ‘Throne Butt’ (The creator of which has now, in 2016, been brought onboard the project to run the official leader boards) which brought fierce competition for the overall top 30 high scorers as well as a place at #1 in the dailies. It would be remiss to not mention the fact that the dailies themselves have, as of the writing of this review, been broken for over a month now. We have been assured that this will be fixed. By and large, the developers are very willing to make the necessary efforts to fix bugs and correct imbalances— though perhaps understandably this willingness has diminished since the unfortunately rushed release date forced by SONY and the PS4 release of the game. This has caused a fair bit of annoyance for long term PC players of the game, who quite rightly regard the PS4 incarnation as a passing fad as opposed to the PC version which, with its strong community and Twitch.tv streamers like SleepCycles and DevilAzite, has much greater chances of being a long-lasting enterprise. All in all, the game is great, as I’ve said, and if the few instances of polishing required (the dailies and weeklies don’t work at all; the game crashes at random for a many players despite a plethora of fixes attempted by the community; textures are improperly layered, especially blood explosions; weapon sprites have rough extra pixels; bolt weapons can be fired through terrain; the mutation Gamma Guts only works some of the time etc.) are implemented promptly, it will definitely go on to be a rogue-lite equivalent in quality, value and depth to other classics of the genre, such as BOI, Spelunky, COTND and Rogue Legacy.

Hotline Miami is fun.
Fun.
Fun, and frustrating.
One thing is for sure though, that with all that frustration comes the reward of feeling as if a weight has been lifted from your shoulders. The weight isn't one you necessarily hate though. It's the weight that you know is making you stronger, and you enjoy the daily burn of marching around with it, but once you get past that weight, you feel accomplished yet left empty inside.
Those are my exact thoughts for a game like Hotline Miami. With each passing level I found myself more interested in what was going on. I'm not referring to the brutal murders I was comitting; I'm talking about everything. The circa 1980's setting is fantastic and colorful, the soundtrack is a masterpiece, and the gameplay is fast/addictive. You're not sure why you're killing everyone at first, or why you're getting strange calls. I felt I was sure that I liked where it was going, and I wasn't wrong.
This a game worth anyone's time, especially if they're a fan of older games from the NES era to the SNES era. You won't want to miss out on the fast, brutal action of Hotline MIami.

Banner Saga 2 is finally here and it carries on where it left off. This review will analyze the amazing amount of fun I had in my first playthrough (many more to come) of TBS2 and the moments that were less than pleasant. I aim at comparing the second game's structure to TBS1, and measuring the good, bad changes. Alright lets break it down.
Very much drawn up like a Tolkien-esque world, Banner Saga 2 plays out like the Two Towers of Tolkien, great fantasy writing accompanies the 2nd novel in a great trilogy that builds up to an upcoming climax in the third. Although it stumbles in a few places, the story proves to drive this epic adventure well into its second episode. The story starts off at a meager pace and suffers from bogged down streaks of fighting(explained in gameplay section).  However, these negative aspects are QUICKLY and STRONGLY forgotten when thrown into the heat of the carvan's struggle of getting to one story sequence after another. Tolkien's Two towers is the worst of the best and the same can be said for this game. The first Banner Saga had a more complete narrative that was well supported by its characters and driven by tension from one scene to the next. Banner Saga 2 struggles to build tension or as intense interest in the beginning than the first game did, but with the option to start where your clan left off, this breathes continuity in the epic and gives it a semblance of being one game. Because of this, the first saga helps drive the second extensively. It does not fail to set up a Banner Saga 3 to outperform this entry in the series.
+Great story is continued
+sets up for a climactic finale
-story does drag in the beginning
--- 8.5/10 ---
The old group is back headed by the two protagonists Rook and Iver. These characters that are brought about from the first installment led with remarkable chemistry prompted by great writing. Unfortunately,   many supporting characters don't get the screen dialogue time to continue developing themselves and create the sense of a united clan that was present in the first game. This is because the cast of characters grows too huge during this game and many characters were left behind either too late in the game or appeared not enough. Many new characters are ho-hum and plagued with some poor character designs that mimic the original cast slightly.  Its only a select few of new characters that shine through and represent the new regions visited. These select new characters bond and become a part of a character driven exchange that works well with the story.
+Original characters are great
+A dynamic interplay between characters
-Too many new dull characters
-lack of further development in some older characters
--- 8/10 ---
The gameplay consists of leading a clan across the tundra and forest making decisions that effect the outcome of the story and the survival of the clan. When battle ensues, characters can be chosen to fight in a tactics style form of combat. Gameplay differs from the original in a few good ways and many uncessary ways. Firstly, the caravan system is now unbalanced. With the ability to find food far more easily and obtain renown especially too easy, management of food is almost never a problem. More renown is gained every battle, almost exponentially as the game goes on and this plays to TBS2's detriment. This leads to mass upgrading of characters and not as great care to tactical upgrading. The renown needed for upgrading is also designed incorrectly. The satisfaction of leveling up a character and feeling as if a distinction exists between levels is muddled. I found myself with the majority of my characters being able to level up 3-4 times in a row because of the previous kills that carry over to the next level. This also led to most of my characters being OP throughout much of the game and very little difficulty in combat. Combat soon became tedious at parts because battles would consist of enemies that presented no challenge at all for stretches of the game. The great aspects of the combat are still there however, and thats what makes this game's battle system amazing despite the related shortcomings.
EDIT: I played this game on normal and that should represent the adequate balance of difficulty and story telling. But in the end, the combat was too easy.
+original combat has not changed
-leveling and character progression is shoddy
-difficulty has been nerfed from the last Banner Saga
-last fights proved to be far too easy
--- 7/10 ---
The main aspect of this game that makes it great and separates it from every other game is and always has been -- its presentation. The atmosphere created by its authentic Celtic/Nordic music and a throwback art style that is captivating and adds so much to the game. The art is beautiful and haunting when it needs to be. The characters are represented well save for a few new characters that look awkward.
+Music is perfect
+animation is classic and unique to games of this day.
+Creates an atmosphere that is an ensemble of perfection
-New characters have questionable designs
--- 9.5/10 ---
The second Banner saga was amazing and amped up the story to an amazing height that can only get higher in Banner Saga 3. It was easy to tell when the first Banner Saga came out that it would turn into something awe inspiring and it has. A game I immediately want to play after beating it is a rarity for me, but now it just seems ritualistic to me with Banner Saga. Don't hold out on this one, it is one of my favorites and the game is truly a gem.
--- 8.25 --- TOTAL SCORE
EDIT: TBS2 is by no means a perfect game, and the story is very well constructed, its gameplay is poorly integrated at times and the 2nd game is a step down from the previous. This game deserves more criticism than it is getting and the amazing story should not blind the analysis of the game as a whole. This game should be paid more attention to, its originality has sparked the creation of other games following its lead.

Better than XCOM! Invisible Inc is my favorite game in my 100+ title Steam library!
This game took me over 100 hours to beat expert-plus mode but it was worth it! The game takes 4-5 hours for a play through and the levels are procedurely generated. There are a wealth of unique agents, programs, and rewards so every play through really is different.
There is a steep learning curve- you will die a lot. This is the point and this is how you learn, don't despair! It's important to balance patience with aggressive exploration. It's ok to usually play it safe, especially in higher difficulties! Here are some hints (or rather basic mechanics that you shouldn't overlook):
1. Always peak or open a door before running into a new room.
2. If you peak into a room with the door already open, the whole room is visible (good for corner cameras).
3. Only hack what you need to for your current situation, conserve power when possible.
4. Don't kill or KO gaurds if you can help it. Let them walk in the same predictable patterns as long as possible.
5. Run when enemies won't be able to hear you (within 5 paces?).
6. Upgrade agents to Anarchy level 1 then steal credits and passcards without KO'ing guards.
7. If you screwed up and are going to use a rewind on this or the next turn, have other agents sprint to scout the map.
8. Use Alt to see a guard's vision lines. You can run in the diagonal red shaded squares to distract them.
Hope this helps. Make Invisible Inc 2, Klei!!!!

One of the best atmospheric thriller games I've played in recent memories. If you're looking for gore and demons and half-naked nurses, move along. If you're looking for something like a Stephen King-esque horror/thriller with supernatural elements and tense combat, pull up a chair. Let me tell you about Alan Wake.
Alan Wake was originally to be a launch Xbox 360 title. But it got delayed. Then it got delayed more, and more, and people started to wonder if it would ever come. Then it came, and it was polarizing. People seemed to either love it or hate it, depending on expectations. But one thing was clear, it was creepy, it had some unique twists and game mechanics, and it looks beautiful now that it's been brought to PC.
Alan Wake is a struggling writer; he just killed off his main character and is looking to start a new series. Alice, his wife, suggests a vacation to get his mind off the pressures of work, and they go to a small town, where they've rented a cabin. The townsfolk seem a bit... strange... and as night falls over the cabin and the lake surrounding it, things take a turn for the worse. Alice's scream pierces the night, and Alan grips his flashlight tightly.
Achievement-hunters may gripe at Alan Wake's collectibles. Some are fun and relatively easy to find with some work; manuscript pages from the novel Alan never remembers writing, televisions that show short "Twilight Zone"-esque episodes of a series Alan wrote for and radio broadcasts that indicate events going on elsewhere in the town. But then there are the can pyramids to shoot over, or the coffee thermoses to gather. Those weren't easy to find, nor did they have a purpose outside of achievements.
Lip-synching is also a bit of an issue at times. When you're dealing with rendered models, it's great, but when they mix up live video with foreign actors trying to flap their lips along to English voice work, it can be iffy. Thankfully, these situations are fairly uncommon, only being used on in-game TVs rather than fullscreen cinematic sequences.
Overall, Alan Wake has a well-written story with some interesting twists and supernatural elements. Some of the writing comes off a bit cheesy, but it's intentional; Alan Wake's character writes and speaks that way in the manuscript pages and cinematic sequences or memories he narrates. The scare-factor is more about creepy atmospheres and shadows that turn into enemies and sometimes just sprinting madly to a source of light and safety. The combat can be formulaic if you don't experiment; try different weapons, use your flares and flash grenades in combat instead of misering them away until you absolutely need them for a crazy difficult fight. Don't get me wrong, there are definitely difficult encounters, but the game usually gives you ammo and weapons in the area.
- Dark, inky shadows that melt into enemies and more create a great atmosphere
- Sometimes cheesy, but always dramatic narration and writing that set the mood for this thriller novel come to life
- The light mechanic is an interesting and fun concept to work with in combat, and the enemy AI can be sneaky. They'll flank you and sneak up behind you and sometimes travel in packs.
- The DLC and extra content are superb to go through after the game, and I normally don't touch that stuff
- Some great plot twists. What can I say without spoiling? Pay attention and hopefully it'll all make sense at the end. If not... well, to the internet!
- Some horror fans may not like it. There's not much in the way of brutal murders or torture or guts. It's about setting a mood and soaking yourself in it. If you're determined not to be scared, you won't be.
- Fights can get formulaic. Flashlight, shoot, repeat. Some areas can even be sprinted through, bypassing common enemies on the way to the next plot point. Don't do that if you want to enjoy the game.
- Driving. Good lord, it's awful. They tried... but it didn't work so well.
- Non-English-speaking actors dubbed with English voices can break the fourth wall when it's so important to have it intact in this type of game.
- Very few puzzles, and they're rarely very challenging. It's usually just a question of finding where the button is to push. This may be a pro depending on your expectations, though.
You'll laugh, you may cry, you'll probably scratch your head in confusion more than once, and you will absolutely want to play this in a dark environment. A second playthrough in Nightmare mode gives you access to some new manuscript pages that often explain an in-game situation in a new light that would have spoiled a first playthrough and gives more explanation if you need it after finishing it once. It also makes the enemies tougher and more cunning, obviously.
And don't forget to count the shadows!

Steam says I "only" have 29 hours in the game, but that's only because I took so long to move my license for the game onto Steam. I've easily put in 150 to 200 hours on this in total.
This game is a blast but does have a bit of a learning curve. That being said, sometimes having horrific failures that end in large explosions is half the fun. If you're interested in realistic space travel, this game offers the perfect balance between real life physics and fun (sometimes comical) gameplay. Launching straight up might get you into space momentarily but you'll just come crashing straight back down to Kerbin.
The real beauty of this game comes down to the fact that you can set your own goals. For some, simply getting into orbit may be a milestone achievement, but for others, you might not be satisfied until you've successfully aerobraked in the atmosphere of Jool and landed on one of it's moons, or perhaps you really wanted to start a base on Duna.
Take a manned mission to the Mun with a simple direct descent setup or build a more complicated Apollo-style CSM/LEM setup. It's all up to you!

I normally do not play simulation games, as I am a big fan of RPG Maker games.
However, out of the blue I decided to try a different genre and pick this game because it was on sale for a low price of about $1 . I had a great time, and once started I spend about 40 hours hooked on the game.
There is a lot of thinks to do in this game.
You can hire scouts, trainers, healers and smiths and decide on what you want them to specialize in when they level up.
You can also hire gladiators, provide them with training and weapons and take them to arena fights or exhibitions (fight with animals).
You started off in a small town with the aim of defeating all the other gladiators bosses (3 of them) with their large number of gladiators. When you eventually get all the gladiator boss in the small town to close down their operations, you get to move to bigger and bigger towns and eventually to the great city of Rome, the center of the Roman Empire.
One of the ultimate goals of this game is to be the wealthiest person in the Empire, even richer than the Emperor.
It's a long and tideous process, and the various steam achievements only add more fun to this interesting game.
After about 40+ hours of gameplay, I was finally able to get all the achievements and retire from the game in satisfaction.
OMG..... considering that I pay only $1.49 for this game and got 40+ hours out of it, I would highly recommend this game.

Obsidian's underrated espionage RPG, Alpha Protocol has amazing malleability and replayability as far as how you shape the story with your mission choices and the way you treat others. The open nature of choosing your missions can cause you to meet allies who will help you in later missions... or remember what you did to them the next time you meet, so be cautious; you may even miss a couple of characters entirely depending on where your travels take you!
The game also has an incredible dialog system, where people will come to know you by your actions and expect you to act a certain way - you can prove them right, or throw them off - something that can come to your advantage played carefully. Enemy or ally, both can work to your favor. Also interesting is the ability to choose a background that further affects conversations and gives your extra points in different categories. (choose Rookie first!)
While the gameplay is your standard TPS/RPG hybrid, this game is a must have for anyone that enjoys games with top tier dialog and freedom of character development such as Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines or Fallout: New Vegas.

Nuclear Throne is the best game I've played in many years. I love almost everything about it. However, as with most games to which a community is given Early Access, the matter of full release left a sour taste in some mouths. I will try to explain my reasons for including this in the review, but by and large the takeaway from my thoughts should be: THIS GAME IS BRILLIANT, BUY THIS GAME. It’s a more addictive, faster Binding of Isaac, and I say that as someone who returned to video games after 15 years purely because of BOI. During Early Access, the team diligently provided weekly updates which corrected, evolved and modified the gameplay and game features based on the feedback of the community. The community itself was galvanized by an independently run high-score ranking site ‘Throne Butt’ (The creator of which has now, in 2016, been brought onboard the project to run the official leader boards) which brought fierce competition for the overall top 30 high scorers as well as a place at #1 in the dailies. It would be remiss to not mention the fact that the dailies themselves have, as of the writing of this review, been broken for over a month now. We have been assured that this will be fixed. By and large, the developers are very willing to make the necessary efforts to fix bugs and correct imbalances— though perhaps understandably this willingness has diminished since the unfortunately rushed release date forced by SONY and the PS4 release of the game. This has caused a fair bit of annoyance for long term PC players of the game, who quite rightly regard the PS4 incarnation as a passing fad as opposed to the PC version which, with its strong community and Twitch.tv streamers like SleepCycles and DevilAzite, has much greater chances of being a long-lasting enterprise. All in all, the game is great, as I’ve said, and if the few instances of polishing required (the dailies and weeklies don’t work at all; the game crashes at random for a many players despite a plethora of fixes attempted by the community; textures are improperly layered, especially blood explosions; weapon sprites have rough extra pixels; bolt weapons can be fired through terrain; the mutation Gamma Guts only works some of the time etc.) are implemented promptly, it will definitely go on to be a rogue-lite equivalent in quality, value and depth to other classics of the genre, such as BOI, Spelunky, COTND and Rogue Legacy.

Shadow of War makes Shadow of Mordor look like a prequel episode to the franchise.
The Map is huge which is covered unders different 'Acts' as Talion progresses in the story.The story is directly adapted from the Lord of the Rings which makes it very interesting.Many NPCs like Shelob(Act 1) and The Witch King along with the Nazguls(Act 2) make a terrific apperance quite early in the game,to name a few.
The Skill list is also greatly improved and defeating enemies is not as easy as it was in Shadow of Mordor despite exploiting their vulnerabilities.Anyone who starts the game with the 'Nemesis' difficulty will realize it soon.The overall gamelay has also been improved and made way more challenging in Shadow of War.
About the in-game purchases(Use Gold,Mirian or directly Cash)
1.You can buy Treasure Chests of three types-Gold,Silver and Common.I preordered the Gold Edition and hence,I have the Bonus Pack and a Gold Chest.However,one can buy as much as they want.
2.There is also 'Spoils of War' and 'XP' Booster Packs available for purchase which boosts the quality of Enemy Collectibles and Talion's XP gain respectively for two hours which makes the player to easily(and unfairly) advance in the game.I got two of these each with my preorder.
Important to remember
1.Players can kill as many enemies as they want in the Nemesis to get armors and weapons,but only of the Common,Rare or Epic types.To get Legendary type using this method is very difficult since the enemies dropping Legendary items are very few and are also very difficult to kill(I can't remember how many times I died just to kill one enemy for a Legendary Sword).This is where I think the game is unfair and WB forces us to buy in-game items.
2.If one wants to boost XP without spending money,they can complete as many Online Vendetta missions as possible,but this makes the game unnecesssarily long.
Hence,to conclude,Shadow of War is an excellent game with a very well adapted story from Tolkien's mythology but its shine is shadowed by the mere unnecessary presence of in-game purchases.

Fair warning: I helped Kickstart this thing. If you think that biases me, there we are.
On the down-side:
First up: This puppy is -short-. I logged about three hours on Act 1, including some backtracking and headscratching, and if there are only two acts... then it's still going to be short.
Second: The puzzles are pretty simple. The interface is point and click, and for the most part you solve puzzles by dragging objects to combine them with the environment. I'm a person with low tolerance for frustration, so I consult walkthroughs pretty regularly, and I only had to do that twice here. Both times, I'd just failed to notice cues, or experiment a little.
On the brighter side? It is pretty as heck. It has an unusual paper art aesthetic that lends a feeling of wandering around inside a storybook... though the story plays fast and loose with expectations. Split into two realms, one is a land where badasses become bakers and damsels -want- to be devoured by marauding monsters, and everyone is horrified that the female protagonist wants to -kill- it; the other is the story of a young man alone on a nursery-decorated starship, smothered by an overprotective ship's computer and slowly drawn into something that -looks- like traditional space adventure at first glance. The writing is fun, and funny... though there is a brief flurry of poop jokes at one point.
The game's big gimmick is being able to switch between the characters' points of view at any time... which isn't actually necessary. It's worth doing from time to time, though: I played through barely the first scene of one adventure, then focused entirely on the other, and I missed a lot of the correlations between the two until after I finished and had some time to think about it. It's definitely something that I'll try to do when I get to play the next part.

At a glance, one might be tempted to conclude that 8-Bit Boy was nothing more than a cheap Super Mario Bros. knock-off. While the game unashamedly barrows from said title (not to mention a number of other classic platformers), 8-Bit Boy nonetheless manages to please. Ironically, it is because it harkens with such transparency back to many-an-old-school side-scroller that this title is such a surprising joy to play.
The controls are very good--much better, in fact, than many of the games from which it models itself. Level-design does not disappoint either; while simple, they are all just about the right length and offer some pretty rewarding treasures for those adventurous enough to explore all the nooks and crannies. In fact, once you have beaten the game, you are able to select any stage in order to collect anything you may have missed on your first path.
The difficulty gets kind of steep in places (I had to resist a rage-quit or two), but it is not so brutal that the challenges cannot be overcome with a little persistence. Keeping at this one and making progress turns out to be very rewarding, and the bosses are fun to tackle and put away.
The soundtrack, while not mind-blowing, is a notch above serviceable, making it plenty good for this sort of outing. The composer certainly succeeds in capturing the old-school tunes of yesteryear, which actually get to be rather catchy after awhile rather than annoying.
Graphically, the game appears a "bit" archaic, but since every ingredient in 8-Bit Boy is designed to evoke late-80's gaming, they are perfectly suitable.
I have returned to old games like Super Mario Bros., Mega Man, and Donkey Kong Country again and again. 8-Bit Boy is like any of these titles in the sense that it can be enjoyed more than once on account of it being well-designed, fun, and relatively short--especially once you get dialed back into the "twitch-thumb" playing you used to do while sitting in front of the old cathode ray tube, Nintendo controller in hands.
So if you have a hankering to revisit those crusty-old NES cartridges, you might want to grab this inexpensive game as an appetizer. You likely won't be disappointed.

Violence is going to be the main focus of this review, because Hotline Miami is violent. Like, really ♥♥♥♥ing violent. If Quentin Tarantino made a movie with an unlimited budget, it wouldn’t hold a candle to the violence of Hotline Miami. That’s how violent this game is, and it embraces that identity while poking it with a stick.
The story takes place in 1989 Miami, which just helps to make the graphics, soundtrack, and especially violence stand out. Mysterious phone calls come in sending the player to addresses full of a gang who will slowly be wiped out, and you slowly delve deeper and deeper into this world of violence, and maybe your own sanity.
I want to talk about this story. I really do. Could go on for hours rambling about hidden meanings justified by the smallest of strings I’m pulling at. But, without spoilers, I’m just going to say that it always asks questions regarding the violence it, and the player, so happily partake in.
Walk up to a guy. Stab him in the face, beat him with a club, I don’t care, just kill him. Take a look at his corpse. It’s drowning in a massive pile of neon red blood. The graphics really push what would probably be acceptable as being not ♥♥♥♥ed up, and if it were made in any other style than pixel art, people probably would think this game is ♥♥♥♥ed up. But it has fun with that idea. All of the deaths are so unbelievably over the top that you can’t help but laugh at them.
One of the most commonly agreed things about Hotline Miami is that the soundtrack is good. Like, really ♥♥♥♥ing good. Hotline Miami’s soundtrack is an adrenaline fueled synthwave barrage. All of the tracks are able to get you to think “Oh yeah, time to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of random people in the 80’s.” And they’re also really good on their own, with...memorable riffs...and stuff. Music critique isn’t my strong point. It’s real ♥♥♥♥ing good though.
And the best part of Hotline Miami? The gameplay. One hit deaths for everyone, very little exceptions. That’s it. It is so simple and so basic, that every game company ever must be beating themselves up for not thinking about it first.
It works. It ♥♥♥♥ing works. The simplicity manages to make this more than just an already violently fun and difficult action game. It’s a strategy and a puzzle game - one of trial and error, one of finding the best way to kill every person in the room in as quickly of a fashion as possible. A stealth game, one of killing everyone undetected. And it's a real ♥♥♥♥ing blast to play over and over again.
It’s probably not the greatest game of all time in many aspects. Technical issues and some frustrating design decisions somewhat hinder this game. But it is my favorite game of all time, that’s for sure. Was it in the right place in the right time? Maybe. Will it revolutionize gaming forever? Probably not. Is it still a very, very good game? Yes.
I cannot recommend Hotline Miami enough. Nearly everything about this game is masterfully executed, with the violent identity just being a bonus. It’s a game that when you finish it, you immediately go and play it again. And again. And again.
One of the best games I've ever played, from the sound design, to the score, to the art. Add on top of that incredibly tight stealth tactical play that often feels nail-bitingly tense. Perfect.

The real beauty of this game comes down to the fact that you can set your own goals. For some, simply getting into orbit may be a milestone achievement, but for others, you might not be satisfied until you've successfully aerobraked in the atmosphere of Jool and landed on one of it's moons, or perhaps you really wanted to start a base on Duna.

Mechanics are a little overcomplicated if you're coming from Windjammers but it's not hard to learn.
Windjammers: one button to dash, knockup the disc, and throw. With a second to lob.
Disc Jam: Throw button is block, have to charge the block to knock disc up for super. Lob button is also dash (which I think should be the other way around at least).
There's an awkward delay after dashing to grab the disc so you can't get rid of it right away like you could in Windjammers.
Curving is pretty easy in this. You can do slight left and right curves with one button press, or you can hit throw and rotate the controller or pad in quarter or half circle to curve it more. You don't rotate controller then hit throw. You gotta hit throw then rotate.
There's only 4 goofy looking characters with minor stat differences and all 4 can have the same super moves.
The bad cam angle makes it difficult to judge the disc path. I think it would be nice if they gave us the option of playing with a top down angle.
If the game wasn't dead I would be playing it like a fanatic even with the few shortcomings, but with no community the game is pointless. Might as well stick with Crazy Power Disc or Windjammers for local multiplayer.
Another thing I preffered with Windjammers and Power Disc is that you could volley almost indefinitely no matter how fast the disc gets. In this the playing field is quite large and it's easy to circumvent  your opponent.

~ 'It's rare to see a game this simple this well done' ~
Age of Gladiators is a simple stats, attributes and management game set in imaginary gladitorial arenas.
This is a text-with-pictures game - nothing fancy or modern like animations - there aren't even any flashing images, and your reflexes will never be tested.
However...
I have some experience desiging, creating and playtesting this kind of game and it's very difficult to get it dead right. Which is exactly what this game does. The scope is narrow, the range of actions available small; but the challenge is great. It has a short, but very steep, leaning curve that is very rewarding to master, and the gameplay is well balanced. You will go bankrupt. Plenty of times.
It's rare to see a game this simple this well done. It's bug free. It has a tiny footprint, it's easy on the eye and it's entertaining.
