The game has a lot of strong points, including seamlessly jumping between RTS and FPS, a strong unit roster, and a huge upgrade tree.  It's very fun to play with others, but the AI gets predictable, as it always does in an RTS.
I can think of a few changes that need to be made for this game to work.
1) the RTS controls are set up so it's incredibly difficult to select individual units, and there is no way to set up troops in a formation.
2) the maps are way too big with not nearly enough in them to keep them interesting.  No secondary bases, no fortify-able hills, not even a lot of small interesting locations.  The Dev needs to either make smaller maps, or spend more time playing with the ones he has and add stuff.
3) The resource system is messed up by the easily aquireable ability to call in resource meteor strikes at any time, virtually eliminating the need for taking over resource points outside of your base.
4) The game has no hotkeys and a UI that needs work.  Want to select all bots on screen?  set a patrol? tell your transports to ferry units?  too bad.  You can select and move your units, and maybe tell them to attack a specific target, but most of it requires micro, which is incredibly difficult with this game.
5) No bullet drop!  if you have two lines of tanks, they will fire into each other's backs rather than over, killing half your troops in a single salvo!  For a normal RTS, this is fine, but when you have an FPS element added to the game, it's a big deal.
For all it's problems, the game is slowly improving.  I give the dev slack, because it's only one guy, and the game is pretty low cost for what you get, but it still has a long way to go if it's ever going to be great.  If it's on sale, get your friends to buy a few copies too, so you have people to play with.  Support the dev!

Middle Earth Shadow Of War as said is a game where you forge an army and try to beat back Sauron after doing it the first time in Middle Earth Shadow Of Mordor. (Which is also a nice game!) You now have the 'New Ring' which can do some more fun things than normal. This is about random generation even for mission based orcs in the main storyline so you don't keep the same experience in some battles.
The story picks up some time after Middle Earth: Shadow Of Mordor once Talion and Celebrimbor decide to forge a ring to stop Sauron.
They progress and Minas Morgul replaces Minas Ithil after it falls despite Talion attempting to save it. I would say more but you can find out.
The gameplay consists of you raiding fortresses and infiltrating them by adding captains and warchiefs to your ranks and killing some captains and warchiefs of Sauron's army. These infiltrations do eventually add up to how your siege may go.
No warchiefs to stop you? Free captures and easy entrances into the fort. You have ologs and they have fire? They'll burn the olog-hai. There is many choices but you must choose carefully as your captains of course don't come back from the dead commonly. If they do, they might be against you for you not helping them when you were able to.
Let's say that you win a fort battle. Great. Now you must defend it. You can add upgrades and choose warchiefs and an overlord. You may upgrade this fortress if you have enough for it in levels or currency. (No not premium.) There is many upgrades similar to assaults though more tier-based rather than situational.
Your orcs are the important part of the game for basically anything battle-based. You lose them, you will have to get better orcs. They of course are randomized and are able to betray you. As happened to me actually. (I think I may of died or ran off too many times. Probably ran.) I still don't have that orc back or dead yet.
So what do I think of this game? Strap your seat-belts everyone!
This game is nicely done. I haven't finished it to admit but so far it seems fairly great.
OKAY -  Random generation can be a bit funny for some orcs with tons of blood brothers or ambushers once you do something specific. (I tried to poison some grog once and got ambushed by an assassin saying I had to put some more dosage in it. Least he told me the recipe!) It does get overpowered but that's random numbers for you.
GOOD - There is much more indepth orc personalities and activity than the previous game and are the core part of the game now. It's harder to see through the system if you think about it than the first, Shadow Of Mordor. You can shame an orc and have some crazy results once you meet him again for example. (A guy I had to deal with went crazy after I shamed him probably 2 times or 3. He said he liked the first shame, he's still out there just saying Bright Lord Dark Lord.)
GOOD - More online capabilities if you don't want to stick with just your campaign. You can raid someones base online, at risk of losing your own orcs. Some don't like it, some do. It's an interesting feature though if you look at it a certain way. You still have vendettas of course. On defense during player raids, you will not lose your orcs most likely.
GOOD - Much more stuff to experience in terms of side-quests(?) You are able to go to Celebrimbor's Barrows and look at Shelob's memories ontop of the other stuff you were already able to find in the first game.
NEUTRAL - Microtransactions are a BIG turn-off for most people. Yea big surprise, right? Besides my sarcasm this system doesn't seem to be intrusive despite the ad that pops up on the menu in the little box that tells you stuff like challenges and you have a store where you may purchase chests with real cash to get yourself some orcs or other stuff. I myself won't look at them but hey. I did have to use chests I got from gold edition to assist in securing a warchief spot with the orcs I got from them.
EHH.. - The controls for stealth and sprint were swapped. I was annoyed about this in my first video and second(?) and had changed the controls to fit my familiarity with the previous game. Spacebar for stealth and shift for sprint. It's annoying but easily fixable.
BAD - There isn't much indication for why you may be betrayed. I was confused as to why but he had said that my army "Could use better leaders!" so I suppose he heard of me running away from battles or maybe he noticed I wasn't helping once in a small skirmish. Could use clarification.
BAD - Glitches seem to be occuring where I stealth-dominate but as it turns out I blow up the heads of anyone I quietly dominate. This is a problem as that is the only quick way for me to quietly turn a group of orcs to deal with something. There is also moments where I just can't move in certain spots and have to get unstuck. Thankfully I was able to get out of all stuck-rocks. This isn't that bad though, but is still bad.
BAD - When a Drake appears, it is annoying as it gets when you are fighting to take down a captain but then you get your health cut off by fire balls and fire breath attacks. This is really horrible for when you don't have drake riding capabilities. It is as nearly as annoying as perfectly generated enemies that can't be defeated in most ways.
How do you know you may want this game?
Do you like randomly generated enemies? Yes? Continue.
Do you like forging an army made out of your past enemies? Yes? Continue.
Do you like sieging fortresses that may be upgraded with you also having upgraded assault bonuses? Yes? Continue.
Do you like trying to challenge powerful odds? Yes? Well if you said yes to everything else, you may want this game.

I have no idea why so many would compare 8BitBoy to Mario. If anything, this game resembles Superfrog - a billion levels with very little to set them apart from each other, and every single one is filled to the brim with secrets of varying usefulness and satisfaction upon collection. The way the stages are mostly built from a sprinkle of narrow little platforms also spells Superfrog, or a lackluster Mario hack rather than the real deal.
The features that
make me think of Mario, such as hitting blocks repeatedly for multiple coins, seem to have been borrowed without much thought. It's questionable whether these blocks were all that fun to begin with, but certainly no new ground is broken by placing them willy-nilly in empty corridors, especially in a game where separate 10-coin pickups exist.
Aside from being a mess of tiny blocks, the level design is repetitive with a noticeable lack of interesting enemy placement and unique stage features. Low-ceiling instakill pits abound. Enemies, on the other hand, usually present no challenge due to the player character's super overpowered projectile attacks that bounce everywhere and kill most baddies before they've properly entered the screen. The projectiles are lost upon death and require multiple pickups to regain, though, contributing to a shifty game balance.
The basic movement mechanics are solid enough, so if you really like bouncing around and finding a coin stash from every block of land big enough for one in an environment where nothing leaves a lasting impression, you will probably love this game. If you've actually played the nonspecific platforming greats this game tries to emulate, I'll be surprised if 8BitBoy leaves you satisfied. Unless, of course, the untouchable classic
were thinking of is Superfrog.

Dear Hangar 13,
Clearly you and I need to sit down and have a serious discussion about what constitutes £53 of video game.
See, I'm one of those "play for the story and gameplay" types, I don't really care that much about fancy graphics and I can't see the difference between 30FPS and 60FPS. That's a category I'd comfortably fit in, given any other situation. However, if I stated I was the kind've person who ate ice cream all the time, you'd sensibly infer to be alive I must also eat other things. In this situation, my former claim must also be taken with an equal pinch of salt and the optical migraine that is this £53 pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥is driving me mad. My intention was to file for a refund although since it's taken me 2 hours to play through the introduction of the game, apparently I am no longer eligible to do so. I suppose that would be my own fault for spending so much of it trying to figure out how to make the game playable in the menus.
I paid £53 in good faith based on the excellence that was Mafia 2. What you have delivered is a visual downgrade from Mafia 2. Hell, what you delivered is a visual downgrade from GTA: San Andreas! It looks like it belongs on a goddamned PS2. This is not acceptable. To add insult to this injury, every few minutes there's a cutscene reminding me how beautiful the game was in the trailers, the end of which I'm forced to readjust my eyes, feel intense disappointment and continue through the objectives.
I simply cannot enjoy this. It's using none of my computer's capability, it's running at maximum settings yet it has about 20ft of draw distance. Anything less than 5ft away is a textural smear which would constitute a reasonable criticism of a £10 indie title.
Now, let's get started on this thing you've coded the camera to do while driving. So, car goes vroom vroom, wheels probably spin and stuff, can't really tell from the graphics, but I digress. You give me, the player, the capacity to make the metal box of vrooms move around. Why is it I'm not given the same capacity to control the camera in order to look where I'm bloody going? Why is it I am given the capacity to move the vehicle, yet I'm considered too irresponsible by your incompetant development team to aim my camera where I mean to look? Was it assumed that I would abuse the system and look around, having an unfair amount of spacial awareness in a singleplayer game or something?
To put this camera situation into perspective, some poor neckbeard in your studio has had to code a coroutine that runs every few seconds to initiate this cancer, then a lerp to move the camera smoothly back where it is of no goddamned use, plus any other bits and pieces in order to ensure it is as far from being a smooth, sensible or helpful thing as possible. What level of incompetancy do you have to be operating at to pay your employees to make your product worse?
Finally, the gunplay. I blitzed through Mafia 2 before this was released psyching myself up for what I assumed would be a better version. I'm intensely disappointed to encounter a combat system where solo enemies yell loudly to themselves about whether or not they can see me. While engaged in an active firefight, I duck behind a building to reload and by the time I move around the other side of it the enemies are either having discussion with themselves or eachother about how I'm probably not even there anymore. It's like gunfighting the developmentally disabled. I just wanna give these poor mentally challenged Haitans a hug. Perhaps not, I don't like being drooled on.
Next up, this inaccuracy thing needs to go to bed and not wake up. I'm supposedly playing as the most badass man in New Orleans here. If I, in real life, can consistently hit a man sized target 5 metres away with a handgun, why can't he? I would intensely like to gripe about a general lack of damage on certain things that should actually do damage, such as the M14, but I understand that lowering damage is a gameplay choice that perhaps makes gunfighting a little bit more accessible for the casuals. So, I'm not happy about that, I'd like a representative damage model for the guns ideally, but there's no way you can justify the need to empty magazine after magazine to kill a guy 5 metres away. Walking forward out of cover, up to the enemy to shoot him should not be the dominant combat strategy on the hardest difficulty level, which at the moment it very, very much is. (Otherwise you have no ammo and the enemy's still alive.)
So in a little over 2h of play I've been about as disappointed as this one time when I was a small child I left my cuddly cat toy on a plane when I came home from a holiday. That's a hell of a lot of first-world disappointment right there.
£53 for this unfinished mess is pretty terrible, but for the disappointment I should be legally entitled to forward you the bill for a professional therapist.

Alright, so you either gotta leave someone behind or drag the guard with you. Except you needed to knock out 3 guards and you had three people. Okay, dragging it is then. Tick tock.

This sim comes with a unique history - it should have been dead years ago but a stubborn community kept it alive, more specifically they kept developers alive who pushed the engine harder and farther than it was intended to be pushed, with some stunningly complex and complete simulations of the flying experience being released as addons.  This new release has met with some criticism, such as dovetail didn't listen to the community and releases addons that are weak, old and overpriced.  There might be some merit in that, but in some ways the complaints are inevitable.  On the good side, the sim is 64 bit, more stable and, like it or not, the future of the software.  The actual flight mechanics are "solid", I would say(X Plane has more sophistication there), but the addons are phenomonal and more and more are becoming compatible with the Steam version as devs see which way the wind blows.
You'll definitely want to get some addons at some point.  I'd go for orbx scenery over the ones being sold here(expensive but just pick the areas you want to fly), ezdok camera(there's a beta for the steam edition that works fine), Accufeel, DX10 fixer, FSFlyingSchool and some of the higher rated planes that interest you(again, the ones on steam are 'meh' at best).  You'll probably want to make a decision on what sort of experience you want - some are really into all the navigation and procedures(real world pilots use them as a decent alternative to a real flight sim), some just want to fly around and look at scenery.  They are two very different worlds.

Alright, so here's the deal.
This game is EXTREMELY fun for me to play, and when playing the beta, i had loads of fun playing with others and playing with my brother in custom matches. I played quite a bit, and even though i didn't get as much time as i would have liked during the beta, this game easily fell into my top 10 favorite games of all time at that time. When i heard the game was releasing soon, i was excited because i thought the playerbase would get bigger, because it was fairly hard to find many people in a game (eg. finding the same person 3 times within 5 games) and i thought the release would come with lots of publicity and more people to play with.
Unfortunately, my predictions were completely wrong, because with the release came a dead game that is now abandoned by many players. Once i bought the game, I went straight into it, expecting at least a few people to easily find and then jump into the game I had loved. But low and behold, i sat for over 10 minutes trying to find a game, with literally nobody joining. I was very confused and sad, because I had loved this game, played a lot of it, gained different skins, discs, and taunts, met many people who were fun to play with and were friendly, and i got pretty good at it. I kept persisting, but never found any games with anyone to play with.
Even with new additions of characters, skins, taunts, poses, discs, names, emblems, integration of deticated servers, crossplay with pc and ps4 (also its apparently free on ps4), ranked stats, and "many more features to come", the game is an absolutely dissapointment when it comes to the community. Because there is none.
I VERY MUCH want to give this game a recommendation, and if anyone reading this wants to re-ignite the community spark that was once in this game, be my guest and buy this game, if you have any friends to play it with, or if you would like to try to contribute to keeping the community alive. It is very, very fun and is easy to get into and hard to master. But for the time being, i cannot give this game a recommendation rating, because i spent 15$ on this game and found that it was a waste of my time and money, because nobody seems to care about or has forgotten about this game. A piece of advice for the devs; try lower price, more publicity, and more content (i know you guys are working hard, but i dont know if it's enough) and MAYBE your game will grow substantially. I do think that those who seem to think the game seems fun and those that wish to buy this game should. But be warned that you are most likely buying a dead game with no player base.
I truly hope this game can once again regain it's charm, and bring back the playerbase so that everyone can enjoy this.
TL;DR: Very fun, but no playerbase, basically a dead game. Buy if you want, expect nobody to find in matchmaking.

Alpha Protocol is a modern-esque style third person stealth game with
an enriching story element.  The first thing to notice is that the sensitivity
in the aim mechanic is just insane, if not annoying to the point of unplayable.
The game would benefit from a field of view slider, or the ability to scroll
out as well.
The story centers around a top secret governmental program created
to  do the governments dirty work, so at the same time giving them plausible
deniability if anything should go wrong.  It is a modern James Bond game,
without the corny puns.  The choices you make effect how the environment
shapes around you.  The result of your choices change the context of the game,making you feel like what you do matters.
The character build comes with many different options for what you can
choose as a specialization, as well as active and passive abilities.  This
adds to the games replay-ability.  In addition, the weapons come with a large
variety of customization options.  The guns feel good, and convey the right
weight and power that you want to have in a shooter game.  You can play the game in the style you want, whether it be melee, ranged, or stealth; the game doesn't punish you for playing how you want but rewards you for it.
The game also offers the option for technical minigames; you are for
the most part not forced to lock pick or hack to get to certain areas; you could, for example, use a grenade to force your way past.  The difficulty of the minigames increases as you level up, but they offer variations so that it's not repetitive and boring.  The only issue I had was with the computer hacking  minigame, in which again the extreme mouse sensitivity leads to not completing the hack within the time limit, which then activates alarms, and can then lead to pulling you out of the stealth mode you had successfully completed until that moment.
The combat is done very effectively.  You can charge in to attack your
enemies, but be aware that the enemy will respond to your tactics, and employ methods to try and counter your approach.  The stealth element was very satisfying, as you can actually ghost through a level if you choose. The enemies level in difficulty, adding to the suspense and requiring that you choose how to level your character carefully, or follow the preselected level design paths for you. As well as making you think more about how you are going to approach any situation.
The level design is done very well.  Despite the fact that it is linear,
each zone looks different, and every mission adds variety in enemies and aesthetic, making the linear aspect a non-issue.
The game interacts with you; your choices make a difference.  You can
create the character you want to create, and play the way you want to play.  This game has been enjoyable to play; I never felt that my time was wasted.  This is an easy game to recommend.
This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to
watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.

--- DISCLAIMER: This review is written by someone who, obviously, was a backer to the project. As well, it must be noted that only the first half of the game is playable.---
After a long wait, the game that truly kickstarted the Kickstarter games craze is out - well, half of it, for now. I liked it.
While it certainly has a more streamlined approach to point-and-click gaming, Broken Age does have the charm that reminded me of that golden age of graphical adventure games, back in the 90s. The character design is delicously original, the storyline starts slow but develops deeper themes of alienation and absence of control over one's own life, the storybook-style visuals are evocative and beautiful, the orchestral music is simply stellar, and most of the cast does a magnificent job of breathing life into their characters - with a special mention going to Jennifer Hale as 'Mother'.
Inventory management is stripped to the bare essentials, and there is no use of verbs or actions - think Telltale Games, not early 90s Sierra or LucasArts. But this stripped-down design does not turn the game into a simple QTE-fest. At its heart, it is still an adventure game, with all the backtracking, item-hunting, and puzzle-solving that is involved. Besides, most adventure games of old may have had multiple verbs and actions available, but most items and interactable objects in the games were usually a one-way thing: if you didn't select the exact right verb or the exact right item, you simply couldn't do anything with said item. Thus, freed from useless time-wasting devices, the game can concentrate on its storyline. And while the first part, so far, may seem short, let's remember that you could finish classic adventure games like Monkey Island 2 in less than two hours.
Some will nevertheless be disappointed, but after nearly two years of development, there wasn't much that Tim and his gang could have done to satisfy the tallest expectations from the hordes hungry for a Double Fine Adventure. But make no mistake, Broken Age, so far, is a gem.

Age of gladiators is a kind of spreadsheet game with some images.
This is very well for me, because sometimes I just want to manage things and not bother with tactical positioning on a map, even turn-based.
So, here you manage your "stable" of gladiators:
- Hire Scouts, Trainers, Medics and Smiths and level them up to level 25. Each has 2 skills and only one of them can be improved per level.
- When you have scouts, hire gladiators, and have them fight in the arena. Each day, there is only one fight. If it is an Exhibtion Day, one of your gladiators may fight against a beast (from wolf to lion). This gives poor money and there are no bets but is an easy way to get experience. Otherwise, there is a fight which will have an attendance ranging from Low to Massive. And you will choose which gladiators fights, against which of the 3 opposing teams in the city (there are 4 cities, the last being Rome). You can then bet on him/her or aginst him/her.
- you can improve your stables to get better morale or more room for gladiators.
- you also must buy weapons and armor, and can get loans at the Market
- at the office you get mail, can view the opposing teams, sell your gladiators, view rankings and Hall of Fame, etc...
So, this is a game where your imagination works from numbers: the images are few and pointless (often many of your gladiators have the same display).
The management part of the game is great.
However some parts could be improved:
First of all, the player should be able to take notes. As your gladiators feel all the same, it is hard to remember what development you had in mind for the 15th or even the 6th. And as you can order them by level, match record or characteristic, they often change places. Which leads to confusion and I tend to have a similar development plan for all of them.
Second, you will soon equip all of them with plate armor: I feel the mitigation it brings is higlhy important. But their proficiency does not depend on Strength or Agility: it is a perk. I feel it imperative to get that perk. Which means there's only 1 kind of gladiator in the arena.
Third, which is bound to 2nd, there's no real difference between weapons: all can be good or bad, according to RNG. And there's no shield or net. Again, it is a perk that gives your gladiators some proficiency in weapons, 1 at start and later you can choose another one. Again this means there will be no real difference between them.
As there's no shield or net, there's no point in planning a retiarius "light" agile guy with trident and net, a "medium" gladiator with gladius and round shield, etc... It just does not exist.
BTW, I did not yet get to Rome, having started out 1st time as a Merchant (like the only guide says), and trying now as an Ex-scout. And then I'll try the Medic way.
While this game can look and be boring to some, I am victim of the "one more turn" syndrome, which is why I recommend it :)

Violence is going to be the main focus of this review, because Hotline Miami is violent. Like, really ♥♥♥♥ing violent. If Quentin Tarantino made a movie with an unlimited budget, it wouldn’t hold a candle to the violence of Hotline Miami. That’s how violent this game is, and it embraces that identity while poking it with a stick.
The story takes place in 1989 Miami, which just helps to make the graphics, soundtrack, and especially violence stand out. Mysterious phone calls come in sending the player to addresses full of a gang who will slowly be wiped out, and you slowly delve deeper and deeper into this world of violence, and maybe your own sanity.
I want to talk about this story. I really do. Could go on for hours rambling about hidden meanings justified by the smallest of strings I’m pulling at. But, without spoilers, I’m just going to say that it always asks questions regarding the violence it, and the player, so happily partake in.
Walk up to a guy. Stab him in the face, beat him with a club, I don’t care, just kill him. Take a look at his corpse. It’s drowning in a massive pile of neon red blood. The graphics really push what would probably be acceptable as being not ♥♥♥♥ed up, and if it were made in any other style than pixel art, people probably would think this game is ♥♥♥♥ed up. But it has fun with that idea. All of the deaths are so unbelievably over the top that you can’t help but laugh at them.
One of the most commonly agreed things about Hotline Miami is that the soundtrack is good. Like, really ♥♥♥♥ing good. Hotline Miami’s soundtrack is an adrenaline fueled synthwave barrage. All of the tracks are able to get you to think “Oh yeah, time to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of random people in the 80’s.” And they’re also really good on their own, with...memorable riffs...and stuff. Music critique isn’t my strong point. It’s real ♥♥♥♥ing good though.
And the best part of Hotline Miami? The gameplay. One hit deaths for everyone, very little exceptions. That’s it. It is so simple and so basic, that every game company ever must be beating themselves up for not thinking about it first.
It works. It ♥♥♥♥ing works. The simplicity manages to make this more than just an already violently fun and difficult action game. It’s a strategy and a puzzle game - one of trial and error, one of finding the best way to kill every person in the room in as quickly of a fashion as possible. A stealth game, one of killing everyone undetected. And it's a real ♥♥♥♥ing blast to play over and over again.
It’s probably not the greatest game of all time in many aspects. Technical issues and some frustrating design decisions somewhat hinder this game. But it is my favorite game of all time, that’s for sure. Was it in the right place in the right time? Maybe. Will it revolutionize gaming forever? Probably not. Is it still a very, very good game? Yes.
I cannot recommend Hotline Miami enough. Nearly everything about this game is masterfully executed, with the violent identity just being a bonus. It’s a game that when you finish it, you immediately go and play it again. And again. And again.

For the money, this is a pretty good time vampire for the imaginitive. It's not going to go over well for people who need lots of flashy graphics, but if you're the sort of person with a strong inner dramatist, and you like games driven by numerical values and an element of randomness, but are more interested in gladiators than baseball or football, this can scratch an itch.
It is not without some pretty gnarly problems though. It's a game that's entirely UI, and in many many ways, the UI sucks. Not as bad as Dwarf Fortress, but it's also nowhere near that level of complexity.
1. Many menus can't be backed out of. If you hit "New Game" instead of "Load Game", guess what: you're making a new game. You can then immediately load the game you meant to and consign the game you just made to partial oblivion, but still, I expect to be able to hit the escape button to, well... 'escape' that mis-click.
2. Mediocre tooltips are only mildly informative, and incomplete. Most things you can work out by trial and error, and as long as you don't play Ironman, you can save-scum to figure out what different buttons do without negative results. Very useful when picking 'perks' and not know in what increment a perk point will provide.
3. It's a management sim with a shortage of management tools. It's very bare bones when it needs to have more fluidity. For example, the only way to move people around the roster is by permanently removing people from the roster. I have some great fighters two or three pages in (too few fighters displayed per page too) and the only way to get them to front page is remove enough fighters in front of them so that the get there.
Another lacking feature is the ability to sort your fighters. You can sort of sort your weapons/armor caches, but not your fighter roster. It's always a FIFO ordering in the order you procured them.
The biggest miss though, is the lack of a way to mark, star, or otherwise tag fighters to track them. Without the ability to put them in an ordered list, you really need some way to help keep track of your best, worst, and most trainable fighters--preferably with different tags. But there is no way to do that. The lack of this feature is especially annoying once your stable grows and/or you end up with multiple fighters with the same name. There are so many useful ways to group and order your fighters that it's a real thorn to have no way to do that--in a management sim!
The only way to keep any sort of records or groupings like that is to pull out a pen and paper, or maybe pull up a text editor to run alongside, but that seems a bit off as those are management tools I just expect to find.
4. Random can be pretty random. Any game that uses randomness runs afoul of this, but in some areas, it's a problem. I'm honestly a bit on the fence as to whether or not it's a problem or just the principle challenge.
5. Levels don't mean that much. This is another one I'm on the fence about. On one hand, I like the idea that a good fighter is a good fighter, and anyone can have a bad/good day. Anyone can die, and a level 1 fighter can trounce a level 10 fighter. Mostly, this is an advantage because it means that you can continue to bring up new fighters even when the common level in the arena gets large. A lot of the importance of leveling comes down to how well you manage the bonuses of leveling up.
The AI seems to be awful at leveling.
6. One stat to rule them all definitely applies. There is one stat that above all others influences the outcome of every battle: Dexterity. It determines your hit rate. The fighter thate scores most frequently, wins most often. The other stats are nice, and all provide value, but Dex is grand high emperor.
7. Managing save games from within the game itself is awful. No custom names, just the date and name of the manager you're playing. But the real kicker is: you can only delete saves you manually made. I've not found a way to delete past autosaves from within the game, and I hope they have a limited number of slots.
8. I have no idea why this game is as big as it is. It's enormous for what it is.
Still, I'm having more fun with it than I've had with games I've payed much much more for. It's worth the sale price for sure. If the interface issues were fixed (escape key, more fighters per page, more management/tracking features) it would be worth the non-sale price.

This is going to be the only the second review I have given a game on steam yet, but I feel this game deserves it.  I will start by saying that rating this game I would give it a 10/10 and words won't do it justice, the game is just that damn good.  That said this game isn't for everybody and without going into detail or spoiling the plot I will try and explain why and to whom this game wouldn't be enjoyed.  The game has a story driven plot that is second to none in any other game I have ever played, basically it ends up being an emotional rollercoaster.  If you are the type of gamer that simply doesn't care about story and is only interested in gameplay then you will in most cases probably not get the most enjoyment out of this game as the amount of things that you can do in the game is extremely limited.  In other words it is not an arcade shooter or a pew, pew, pew lolz you're dead kind of game.  It is more about the story and more akin to watching a good mini-series on cable.  The amount of things the player can do is very limited with most of the moving around being solely so you can inspect objects in your surroundings to help explain aspects of the story and as a mechanism to allow the player to make good informed choices at key story points in the game.  That said it is in my opinion and without spoiling the story very helpful to pay attention and inspect most everything in your surroundings that you are able to.  The game at points does have some problem solving that needs to be accomplished to advance further into the game but most of it is pretty straightforward and the player will not find themselves stumped for hours trying to figure something out.  A playthrough takes about 25-30 hours in total (3-6 hours per episode) if you inspect all items you can carefully and take the time to appreciate the story.  If you are the type of person that doesn't or cannot cope well with an emotional rollercoaster then you will probably also not like this game.  It will have your emotions soaring one moment and 10 minutes later leave the player with a sense of helplessness regarding the characters in the game.  The game does get you involved in the characters and it is in that fact that the game shines, the character and story development is unlike any other game I have ever played.  The soundtrack does an excellent job of accentuating the environments and setting the stage for the moods in the game and is also one of the best soundtracks I have ever seen used in a video game to date.  The story reminded me a lot of the movie The Butterfly Effect and The Time Machine as it deals with the ability to rewind/move through time to change the characters timeline and for those familiar with the movie you will also know about The Chaos Theory and the ramifications inherent with messing around with time.
In closing I love this game and very much look forward to the prequel and the sequel and I hope that my review can convince some to give this game a shot as in my opinion it was right up there as being the best 20 bucks I have ever spent.

Playing this game is like playing a cyberpunk, spy movie.
You and your team of agents teleport in, sneak past security, steal from guards, hack into their surveillance cameras, drones, servers and map database via electronic warfare without getting caught.
You finally arrived at  a terminal. As you grabbed the hard drive, the main objective of the mission, you did not realised that a guard strolled into the room and started aiming at you: “Stop right there! Intruder alert!” Other guards became alerted of your presence. No time to lose, you shot the guard who saw you with your dart gun. You and your team have to bail out.
The next minute is followed by a cat-and-mouse run between the enraged guards and your agents. You and your agents used a variety of cliche gadgets, such as tasers, holograms, door traps and silenced guns.
Just as you’ve reached your limits in running towards the exit, an agent gave you a shot of fast acting steroids. It gave you enough energy to reach the teleporter exit just in time before the guards are able to stop you.
But that’s prolly just a scene from a movie. Or your imagination. Will you be able to reenact the same scene in this game?
Not exactly. Because, every game is different. No 2 maps are alike.The game gives you a different location(map layouts) and different calefares(Guards and drones) every time.
You’re given the liberty to choose between your actors and actresses(agents), your props (gadgets) and your matrix-style command interface (incognita with hacking programs) to run the show.

How do you run the show? Well, it’s up to you how you direct them.
Your agents might sneak in swiftly like the wind, steal and complete the objective and walk out before the alarm detects your presence at all.
Or your agents might sneak through by incapacitating everybody in their way, and end up becoming a cat-and-mouse scene at the end?
Or maybe your agents will use lethal weapons to kill
those guards, take control of drones and turrets and counter attack the guards in the most desperate, Rambo fashion before escaping?
Of course, the first is the slickest, coolest while the last is probably when you make a grave mistake and you’re desperately salvaging your way through. Relying on dodgy stealth consumes little budget compared to gunnery action which is expensive to include in the show.
Ultimately, all of your decision counts, as a tactician. Have fun.

Two Sentence Version:
Do you like management games, the gladiator theme and need a casual time waster?  Buy it when on sale, otherwise hold off.
Short Version:
Age of Gladiators is a fun, casual time waster if you enjoy management games, are intrigued by the gladiator theme and can get it on sale.  At full price, you might feel a little bit let down if like animated presentation.  Read the features section on the store page, as it does cover the aspects of the game well, and decide from there if it seems appealing.
Long Version:
This is a fun, casual game to pass the time if you enjoy management games.  The game doesn't have too much of a learning curve as messages appear when a cursor is positioned over most elements in user interface.  The gladiator theme is welcomed as it provides an interesting backdrop for the game.
The gameplay itself is straight forward with the initial balance of income and expenditure sometimes being a touch frustrating, but once there is a little time investment and experimentation, it comes to together well.  The office portion handles investment decisions, whether it be hiring staff members such as scouts (search for new gladiators), trainers (increase XP for each combatant), doctors (speed the recovery of sick or injured), or blacksmiths (weapon and armor bonus).
The management of the gladiators is also enjoyable enough with points being earned from fighting and training which are then spent on upgrading various skills such as health, dexterity, strength, stamina, etc.  There are various portraits which can be swapped around to change the appearance of each gladiator and their names are all customizable.  Weapons and armor, which deteriorate with use, must be purchased and provided to each gladiator with their effectiveness being based on various skills and specializations, all which can be upgraded.
There is also numerous perks which when earned can be spent to modify certain business aspects and the gladiators themselves.  Office related perks, for example, increase the amount of income from each fight, effect the morale of the gladiators on betting, change the recruitment baseline for future prospects and impact various other aspects of gameplay.  The gladiators can be modified to decrease the likelihood of execution after a loss, be more proficient in multiple weapons and armor, and other various traits.
Perhaps the most disappointing aspect of the game is the combat screen.  Once two gladiators are pitted against each other, there is a back and forth of flashing text under each gladiators portrait with details whether a hit landed, missed, was blocked or dodged, the amount of damage caused, etc.  Once combat is completed, you can view the log from the fight which details the aforementioned information.  It would have been terrific to see descriptive language, such as where the hit landed and its effect, but instead it’s simply missed, hit, this amount of health was lost, etc.  Since there is no visualization of the actual combat, more expressive and rich blow by blow battle accounts would have been welcomed.
Overall, I’d say Age of Gladiators is a solid buy if you are looking for a casual time waster or in between games.  I purchased it on sale for $1.99 and for the price, I’m very happy with my decision.  Despite the fact I enjoy the game, I would not have been as pleased if I paid $9.99, as there just isn’t enough to justify the price for me.  Sure, I’ve put about nine hours into it so far, and by the time I’m done, I’ll have spent less than a dollar for each hour of fun, but as a gamer, I’m finicky and would not have been satisfied at full price.

Banner Saga 1 was one of the most refreshing and intense experiences of the past few years. A good example of an small budget indie game that manages to transcend the limitations and expectations with good balance between simple ideas, good execution and minimalism that leave enough for the imagination to fulfil. There are few realistic big budget 3D games that manage to create as strong feelings as the 2D graphics that Banner Saga utilizes.
Banner Saga 2 is a straight continuation from the moment where Banner Saga 1 ends and if you have played the first game and still have the same game available, you can import the save game and it's situation to the second episode and continue playing. Enginewise not much has changed - the game still consists of mainly three different elements:
- tactical chesslike turn based battles
- camping where you can decide how to divide renknown between your heroes (or save it for shopping as reknown is used both as experience and gold in this game, which makes for interesting choices and isn't as bad concept as it sounds).
- storyline dialogues where you can choose between various options and see how it affects your situation, sometimes more or less drastically
However, there are some major changes in relation to the first episode: the battles are less repetitive and tedious as most of the fights have some extra elements that make them more interesting. Sometimes something happens during the fight that changes the situation and makes it more interesting. There are possible extra elements in the battlefield that can be destroyed or utilized. There are also extra classes that give more choices to your party structure. Bard being one of the most interesting ones. His skill gives boost to one character and he replenishes nearby characters willpower if he's close enough to the place where an enemy is killed by singing a heroic song.
All in all Banner Saga 2 offers an updated and more enjoyable version of the already enjoyable first game with deep and emotional storyline that can contain rough and sad moments - like in real life, no matter how hard you try, sometimes bad things happen and you just have to cope instead of reload.
If you enjoy tactical battles, interesting characters and emotion inducing storylines in a viking fantasy world with sort of minimalistic and streamlined dialogue options, you can't go wrong with Banner Saga. But start with the first game.

"No better burden can a man carry on the road than a store of common sense."- Hávamál, st. 10
In The Banner Saga 2 you again assume the role of a leader of men, as you take up the mantle to guide your clan, and your banner, to safety. The world is breaking (Ragnarok) and this is part of the mystery as the story unfolds.
In many aspects this sequel continues the trend of The Banner Saga 1. But on a grander scale. The enemies are more varied, the battles have more diverse environments and other winning objectives than simply "defeat all enemies".
The battles feel integral in moving the story along and it is paced very, very well in my view. The game's underlying mechanic is essentially getting from A to B via C via X. Confusing? Not really as the story branches out and introduces new main characters such as the war torn Varl (a race in this universe) Bolverk. A stark contrast (depending how you play and your choices of course) to the other main character.
The story, and choices, are multi-layered as you make decisions as to how (not) to protect your Caravan of people at the base level. The stakes are upped when you parley with more powerful individuals, whether in regards to magic, title or simply supernatural beings, and need to make decisions that can affect whole communities or possibly the world.
If you have played The Banner Saga 1, you will want more answers regarding the game's overarching plot of the world breaking apart. These are somewhat passed along to the player just like treats to a pet. They satisfy you for a bit but you stay to get more as The Banner Saga 2 augments the series' universe. The lines are blurred and your morality, as well as your view of people, will get challenged. Compared to other "choices matters" games it does matter here. Main characters can die, or be lost, 10 minutes after using all your ressources leveling them up.
Common sense will get you far in this game, but what exactly is common sense when you are presented with possible world altering consequences?

In my limited gameplay I haven't experienced the weird AI that many people complain about. My problems with this game are the core gameplay and the changes that were made to it.
Using traders to build roads seems like a nice concept, but I liked having workers set up my own personal routes to help me traverse my kingdom. Also, whoever thought of turning workers into 3 use builders made an egresious error in my opinion. I would gladly take workers taking a few turns to build an improvement rather than having 3 use workers.
When it comes to districts I think they are a cool idea, and they definently add something to civilization, but they really take away from the experience in my eyes. It limits your playstyle since the ammount of districts you can make it proportianite to your land and population. In the past I like to do a few mega cities, stacked with wonders and buildings, but this iteration makes it so you basically have to branch out and have many cities.
I have no real gripes with combat. Every civ is a little bit different when it comes to combat, and I haven't really found any major issues with how it is carried out in this one.
Religion seems more annoying. In civ V I could more or less brush it off and manage to keep my cities with my own, but in this game it feels like if I am not 100% on top of my religious game I will get taken over by other civilization's religion.
I actually like how city-states are done. The envoy system really freshens them up and offers players to win over the bonuses without just giving them an endless supply of gold.
Overall, there are some interesting things in Civ VI, but when it comes down to core gameplay I just don't enjoy it as much as I have in previous versions.

It's simply not a good Civilization game(yet at least prior to extra expansions).
All victory conditions are about domination. Want to be science team? Capture enemy towns with academies. Culture? Go ravage those enemy towns because you do want to be cultured after all! What about empire size you ask? Well you could make small solid empire like in civ 5 with wonders, right!? Wrong! Wonders for most part don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥ They are very high risk with low reward. Building a wonder feels kinda like building granary in one of older games, except not anywhere near as strong and it will take waaaay longer and it will take slot from ground and they will have special terrain and resource requirements! See in Civ 6 wonders and districts are built on top of your tiles. Districts? Well these are like town sections that each boost different things(like academy for science, commercial hub for trade/gold and so forth) which are limited by your size and location(which gives different bonuses and decides how you will want to play the game for you!). The idea behind districts actually was pretty good IMO, sadly the execution was worse than horrible. The terrain combined with your start team completely dictates how you will play the game but then again since game is all about conquest I guess it doesn't matter which direction precisely you go for through conquest! Now I will say harbor district was well made, it gives you freedom to settle just near shore as opposed on the shore. Encampment(military district) was also another better district as it gives freedom rather than limits and shoehorns you too much. Wonders though which were biggest enabler for small empires really not a thing. They give low rewards, take tile yelds/resources they are built on top of and frankly you'll get much better stuff from districts to make wonders feel even more worthless. You could and should build/capture a huge empire like civ 4 as it will always be the best choice due to how strong districts, resources and basic buildings are. The biggest downfall of this strategy however is falling asleep from boredom.
Did I mention this game has no puppet cities(civ 5) or automation(civ 4) so you get to manually do absolutely everything even with the most useless towns! No pesky building ques either so you can enjoy putting each and every teeny tiny little item to build manually(well mods have this but for some reason it still isn't in base game). Ohh yeah and you no longer need automated builders either, now you get to(read: you are forced to) manually build every teeny tiny little improvement and with limited build number you get to build more builders manually because we love to micro everything!
Ohh and the lovely diplomacy. You get those lovely trade offers and demands and denounciations every so often. What's even better is you still get to see them in diplomacy screen directly so you get to tap exit for the first minute of every few turns as those dozen AIs keep making worse and worse offers for resource you did not want to trade prior and still do not want to trade. Or you could just trade it because saving yourself from that headache the bunch of diplomacy suggestions will give you. No more tech trading, map trading vasallages or anything like that either because less is more! And not to worry, the AI will still be crazy warmongers always declaring war on you with no chance of winning. You capturing a town or two will make you the warmonger so you get to be denounced by the whole world or some idiot AI will praise you for 60 turns till they declare war on you. Naturally the whole world will eventually declare war on you but you need not worry too much.
The AIs strategic thinking is that of a toddler randomly moving different units generally into the worst possible locations. Naturally builders and archers are the best frontline you will ever need. They can then be backed up by the melee units followed by cavalry so everything that actually wants to fight at close range will be blocked. The AI is literally dumb as a box of rocks. It has no clue when it should send and what. Even on highest difficulties you can easily defend army 5 times your size for they are just lambs to slaughter when AI is in charge. The AI has no sense of terrain, chokes or target priority. The AI also fears hights, for that reason it keeps the air units tightly grounded in their hangars(it builds them, just doesn't use them)! I should mention that unit promotion options in this game are also very very limited compared to civ 4 and 5 so don't expect units to feel different from one another. One good thing I will say about civ 6 combat is the barbarians. They are hell of a lot bigger threat than all nations combined in early game. If you cannot stop a barbarian scout in time from reporting to camp you can expect serious threat possibly from multiple directions. Naturally this is the reason you have to build army in every game so you don't need to feel like matches would be any different from one another as you will always get to build and research the very same stuff each and every game!
Speaking of research you might have heard of Eurekas? These very innovative "quests" give you so much fun if you love doing long excell sheets! You get to check culture tree, then science tree and then again culture tree every few turns to maximize free gains in science and culture techs through the quests. Not to worry, many city states have the same quests so you get to check those too. On the bright side once you learn the worthwhile stuff you will do the same techs practically every game, just change the order slight every now and then if you find some natural wonder or continent. I will say the idea behind them sounded fun, but the min-max nature it brings to micro everything is the exact opposite. It also didn't help that the quests are always the same which leads you to build and research always the same which doesn't really help when you also always have to play conquest so every single game feels exactly the same. I'll just jump to conclusion as I simply get tired, angry and frustrated just thinking about the game.
Frankly this game makes me angry when I think about playing it and bored once I start playing it. It has sooooooo much micro it's not even funny and it doesn't feel like it adds anything to the game. You could micro in old games and it felt more rewarding but it still didn't feel necessary either. I always do a lot of min-maxing, but this game just feels like a chore with no reward anywhere.
Positives:
+Caravans create roads, cool and natural addition
+Barbarians with scouts to bring in the reinforcements, another cool addition.
+Unique great people
Negatives:
-AI is dumb as a brick
-Poor diplomacy
-Wonders are anything but wonderful
-Very unpolished idea of districts and Eurekas, both do have potential.
-Poor balancing, playstyles and techs don't really change. Domination, war, large empires > everything else
-Tons of small and big features/things/QoL missing or not finished.
-Poor replayability, the leaders/nations feel like they both dictate the game too much and still at same time won't allow you the kind of freedom in playstyle as in previous games.
-Tedious as hell micromanaging.
-Unclear map, once you lose vision you can't even tell the terrain properly(this looked cool in beta demo, was anything but once I actually started to play the game).
Conclusion: Just buy Civ5 GOTY if you are looking to get into the series or you're old fan. It has much more features, freedom of playstyle and is way more user friendly. I don't even know who civ6 is aimed for, it feels dumbed down in many ways to deter veterans and super mega hyper micro intensive to deter new players(heck it has deterred everybody I know).

Windowsill is an adventure game in the purest sense: a series of beautiful, whimsical, and highly interactive collages that you need to "solve" in order to make progress. You'll be spending half your time poking at the scenery to find out what delightful bit of interactivity is hiding under your cursor. It's not long, but it doesn't have to be: I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of my playthrough.
As a programmer, what really amazes me about this game is that it doesn't use 3D acceleration. Instead of being composed of triangles in 3D space, every single object in this game (to my knowledge) is defined by basic shapes and vectors in 2D space. You might think that this would be a detriment, but instead it allows the game to produce fluid, smooth, and very organic looking effects that would be almost impossible to with traditional 3D graphics. If you're as interested in this as I am, get the iPad version instead: once you've beaten the game, you can play through in wireframe mode and check out the way it's put together.

The Binding of Isaac is a wonderfully difficult game which takes time to grow into. Combat is similar to that of The Legend of Zelda, but featuring projectiles fired instead of relying upon a sword which only hits directly in front of you. You work your way through multiple levels of dungeon fighting enemies and bosses, collecting power ups, and ultimately becoming a God of Death before facing the final enemies.
It is VERY important to note up front that you will be dealing with some questionable content in this game: religion, abortion, various physical deformities and problems, and many other subject matters are treated without particular care, so those who are could be offended by these topics should avoid.
Additionally, I will note that while the DLC is well worth it, if possible, try not to install it from the outset if you're starting fresh. Wrath of the Lamb makes the game even more difficult, and new players should start with Vanilla before moving on to something more difficult.
Regardless, highly highly recommended.

I had to check to make sure this game was no longer in Early Access, because even finished it still feels like it isn't quite done.  Part of that is the rough art style (chosen), and part is just that your deaths are frequently very random and often unavoidable.
Nuclear Throne has a lot of 1-2 hit kills, and sometimes just flat out screws you with a level starting position.  Spawn in the middle of a boatload of high damage enemies with no cover to  be had, and all your progress can melt in an instant without you really haven't any meaningful choices to make to avoid it.
Similarly, if you happen to kill the final enemy on a level, the spawned portal may appear and detonate a nearby car or other inopportune object and send you to a pointless and undeserved grave.
Other than a number of fairly cheesy deaths, the basic gameplay is pretty enjoyable.  The game encourages you to use the terrain as cover, and has some mild bullet hell where you weave and dodge to avoid a hail of projectiles.  There is a nice collection of different weapons to choose from, though having played Chicken extensively in beta, I'm always missing better options for melee weapons (which are great, allowing you to bounce bullets when timed correctly and trading range for unlimited ammunition).
Your character gets to pick one from a few different potential mutations every time you level up.  These are not particularly well balanced, and it is entirely possible to get to choose really good mutations, or to get stuck with some completely pointless ones.   It tends to be less a matter of choosing between play styles, and more a matter of hoping you have at least one good mutation on the selection list.  Go a couple levels with all bad mutations, and your run is effectively done for, without you having done anything to deserve it.
Kind of seeing a trend there.
Still, there's enough enjoyable moments that it is worth picking up and playing.  I think it could have been architected to be a more satisfying experience, but it remains worth trying out.   Levels are very short, and the style of terrain and enemies changes every couple levels, so play throughs are quick and contain a mix of experiences.
Go ahead and give it a run.

Memorable characters, with what seem like interesting arcs as well as a classic revenge tale all set within 1960's Mob era New Orleans. If that doesn't get you excited you've got a problem with your pickle. I'm not sure that this game feels like a traditional point and click adventure to me. There is no really difficult puzzles, no pixel scanning with the cursor and no revisiting areas and dialog trees over and over again, causing that all familiar frustration that comes with most point and click adventures. I know from being a backer and watching the documentary that Tim Schafer wanted to avoid this type of frustration and he certainly has achieved it. At the expense of more difficult puzzles? Yes. But that's not a bad thing. I kind of do wish they were just slightly harder, but truly I am not that bothered at all.
Instead, this game is smooth and fun to "play". It's like walking into a piece of art, not only visually but the music and voice acting are also brillant. I have seen a couple of comments where people have mentioned the Spoon character, which is just awesome. He reminds me of "Talky the Toaster" from Red Dwarf.
The best bit about playing this game is that it takes you into another world from a collective (double fine) imagination, where you really want to see what happens next and how it all pans out. The story is really quite compelling. And just wow, that ending :)
Vella's side of the story is the most artistic and fun to play, but to get the best from it play Shay's side first right to the end. Although, you can of course switch between the girl/boy side at any point and continue from where you left off. Just don't complete Vella's side before Shay's. At least for me, I'm certainly glad I did it in this order.
It should take you around 4 hours to complete Act 1, not the two hours that many mention. I wonder if they have even played both sides yet? Or just followed the first guide that was released? At the very least they didn't take the time to explore the content and dialog. ALthough I did get stuck on the helmet puzzle for a bit (no spoilers!).
To all those wondering about the cost of this game (£17.09 with 10% off pre-purchase) all I can say is.. How much does it cost you for a ticket to go watch a movie nowadays? £8-10 for 1.5 hours of entertainment? If Act 2 is another 4 hours long, you do the math.
Overall, I really enjoyed it and couldn't put stop playing just for the story.
Can't wait for Act 2!

Forget about the microtransactions. The orcs you get from the crates are generally as good or worse than what you find in the world with a little work. The final act is only grueling if you didn't bother to level up your orks. The fact of the matter is that Monolith could have left the loot crates out completely and it wouldn't have made a difference, its very clear that it was something that was forced on them by WB because the words "tacked on" are what describes the "loot crates" best. Now that that is out of the way lets focus on the game.
Gameplay:
Its Shadow of Mordor but massivley expanded and refined and with the improvements to the nemesis system the game really comes to life. Turning a Warchiefs bodyguards to your side then watching them murder him like a scene from Gladiator is more than satisfying. With new ablities to expand your arsenal, taking the fight to Sauron has never felt better.
Story:
The story picks up right after Shadow of Mordor with Talion and The Bright Lord forging a new ring to challenge Sauron and The One Ring. The Story is pretty predictable but that doesn't mean its bad, its actually quite good and is frankly better than anything Tolken came up with. But in the end its Lord Of The Rings, it pretty much defined the fantasy setting for the last 50 years. Everything it does has been seen before but Shadow of Mordor/War does it so well you don't notice.
Overall the game is probably the best game of the year so far but has taken a beating due to some bad PR and sales tactics by WB. In the end Loot Crates and Microtransactions are not going anywhere anytime soon, with the rising costs of development and inflation, the massive success of CS:GO and Overwatch crates, and mobile gaming its going to become the industry standard just like season passes and DLC, its a fine line that the industry is still learning to walk and there will be mistakes and legit preditory tactics, Shadow of War is not preditory its stupid and redundant and its system is 100% ignorable and NOT Pay2Win.
TL;DR:
9/10 Very much worth your time and money

Alpha Protocol is frequently overlooked but it's an RPG game made by Obsidian, which is enough in itself to justify a purchase, however unpolished you might think it is.
One interesting take on the genre is the conversation system, which gives general demeanours (suave, professional, etc.) for responses.  This can occasionally hide the intent of a choice in a way that reminded me of Mass Effect's conversation system.  However, you have limited time to respond in Alpha Protocol, which means you have to think on your feet during what's normally a passive situation.
Alpha Protocol presents a dynamic story in a way I don't remember seeing elsewhere.  Some games claim to provide branching storylines but this one genuinely varies impressively, which can lead to truly satisfying end results as you see the outcome of your choices.  You can become allies with one faction or turn them into enemies, trust someone or be completely suspicious of them, etc., depending on your mood.
The combat's a bit unbalanced and some skill trees break the game.  Still, I don't remember too many situations that were completely frustrating (but it's been a while since I played it).  I played in a somewhat stealthy way and the most annoying part was one particular boss, who seemed very unbalanced for my given player build (you'll know which one when you run into him!).  I was able to take him down eventually with some Brave Sir Robin-esque kiting.
Some reviews mention how buggy the game was.  I didn't hit any of these bugs, for what that's worth.  Your experience may be different if you're unlucky, I suppose.
If you're into RPGs with a bit of action then this is worth a go as it has interesting ideas and you can really affect the story in big ways.  Plus, it's an Obsidian game.  Did I mention that already?

Invisible Inc. is an incredibly enjoyable turn-based stealth game. This game combines certain aspects of my favorite games. Of the most important aspects is a feeling of anxiety when you see your alarm level rise, and you know you're in a bad situation, and the feeling of: "I need to figure out how to get out of this mess". The feeling I get when I play this game is matched by no other and is truly exemplary of what stealth games should be.
Notes(I feel pros and cons lists are inadequate):
-The top-down viewpoint of this game makes it very easy to plan your movements and greatly increases this game's ability to be an effect stealth game.
-The characters are very diverse, I found of my favorite things to do in this game is come up with, and create very interesting synergies between your choosable agents, abilities and findable items.
-The story is a bit disappointing, and I don't think this game is story-driven in any way. This game is much more based on gameplay
-This game is only replayable if you enjoy what I said earlier: "I found of my favorite things to do in this game is come up with, and create very interesting synergies between your choosable agents, abilities and findable items."
-This game is difficult. I feel guilty writing this review because I have only beaten this game once...on beginner. Perhaps it is because I suck, but this game is very difficult and takes patience.
Tips:
-Hide. Make sure that you are always hidden behind some structure. You never know when a bad guy will barge through a door and spot you.
-Only KO enemies if absolutely necessary. I have found in my everpresent experience that it is best to avoid confrontation, and killing especially. Lethal/loud weapons should only be used if absolutely necessary.
-Know your strategy going in to the level. Know what you plan to have accomplished by a certain alarm level and be prepared to leave early if necessary.
To conclude, I will say that this is a great game created by a great developer, and is certainly worthy of it's price tag. I would recomment this game to all age groups as it has something in it for everyone.

It would be tough to not recommend this game. Everything is nearly perfect; it feels like a superior Telltale game with more exploration and choices with the setting of Alan Wake. Choices definitely feel like they matter more here than in any other game of this style.
What on the surface seems like a corny teen drama quickly evolves into something much better; the whole thing gets much more interesting and mature, and the characters are great. The visual style complements everything here well. No problems with the controls, either. The game recommends you use a controller though, which I did, so I cant speak for M+K controls.
I do have some minor gripes, though. First, I did run into a really annoying bug where the main character's mouth didn't move for about a solid 10 minutes straight right towards the end of the game. It was during an important series of events and it kinda rips you out of the moment. But other than that, I never encountered any bugs or crashes of any kind. Second, the length and pacing of the episodes is a bit inconsistent. Episodes 4 and 5 are brutally long, while 1-3 felt much more reasonable. Third, this is a game about time travel, and 95% of the time any sort of media involving time travel has to have an incredibly convoluted and confusing ending about "messing with the timeline and alternate realities." It's overdone and boring. Life is Strange does an okay job of roping you back in right before everything comes together for the big finale, but it definitely was a bit of a black mark on the whole experience.
As a whole though, Life is Strange is definitely a game I would recommend and legitimately enjoyed. I definitely will not be replaying it soon if ever due to its exhausting length (it's a slog towards the end) and due to the fact that I was relatively happy with how my choices turned out.

I tried to like this game i really tried but i just don't like it. The game tries to copy the feel of old games but doesn't quite manage to do so. I will use Super Mario Bros. (SMB) the NES game for comparions.
In SMB you can run full speed through early levels.
In 8BitBoy this isn't the case, you have to go very slowly, not only because of the rather floaty controls but also because in some of the very first levels there are a ton of things that will instakill you.
In SMB the enemies are very different from one another.
In 8BitBoy there are like a million types of different owls, all of them have different behaviour. So you have to go slow trial and error to figure out why the green owl is different from the yellow owl. Once again, this is not fun.
In SMB every enemy is easily identified as enemy, it is very obvious what will kill you and what doesn't.
In 8BitBoy in the 2nd world one of the first enemies is a cactus that ambushes you, he blends in with the background and once again forces the player to go slowly to not get killed by something that is hard to see.
The game also tries too hard with secrets and branching paths, not every level needs a million secrets. I don't like the music, i don't like the visuals and the controls are not very good.
I don't recommend this game, it just isn't enjoyable.

Unlike the title might suggest, we're not talking about a RTS. This is basically a tycoon game and the title's premise quickly caught my attention, so I decided to give it a run to see what this was all about. For starters, there's not much of a plot. I mean, you have a certain goal to meet but there's not really a story to offer some immersion. You can hire certain staff members to assist on your quest and just like the gladiators that you recruit, they also evolve through time. You have to pay them all salaries and the value keeps on rising the more you play. You can also build facilities to improve the morale of your fighters. Besides, you also have the opportunity of purchasing some better gear at the market and the stock is always renewed after some time. Ok, overall we're talking about a fun game and everything, but there're a few things that could be improved:
1-) No tutorial: Well, the game isn't exactly that complex, as long as you know what you're doing. If you try to play it without reading any guide first, you might have a hard time (such as I, until eventually I decided to look for more information about it).
2-) Soundtrack: I'm not saying that it's bad, but it's so repetitive that it gets old quite easily. It didn't take much for me to mute the game and listen to something else
3-) Micromanagement fest: As mentioned earlier, the more experience your crew has, the more they evolve. That shouldn't really be much of a problem, except that depending on the size of your party, you've gotta distribute all the points and that process gets quite annoying after some time, especially because if they're tired / injured / sick, their stats are affected so unless you have an elephant memory, it's better wait until the debuff is gone. Another thing: Your fighters' equipment decay after some time and you've gotta keep that information on track. Although you can have a blacksmith, they won't actually repair your stuff, they'll just improve their efficiency. That said, although you can manage several gladiators, such process is so tedious that it's better to stay with a just small elite force and focus on them.
4-) Grinding, holy grinding: The nature of that game can't be hidden, after all. In order to reach to the top you've gotta fight to get there. No worries, as there are plenty of battles to be fought. The closer that you're to the end of the game, the harder it is to kill the other gladiators in battle, so I seriously advise you to choose your skills with care because that will make a lot of difference on how much you're gonna click.
Well, that's basically it. The game isn't really perfect but it's surely fun and I really hope that some similar titles may be released in the future.
