At this point in the development of the Civ6 game, I would recommend for those interested in this type of game to purchase Civ5 instead.  The basic mechanics of this version need some serious work, in essence it plays you - you do not play it.
Don't get me wrong, there are several things that Civ6 improves upon over Civ5 but many of the great features of Civ5 have been lost or thrown out for whatever reason.  These can truely make the game extremely tedious (at best) and utterly frustrating  if you are already familar with the mechanics of Civ5 already.
Pros of Civ6 over Civ5:
+Better political game play - definitly a large improvement in working with AI players, better information available on how to play/trade with the AI leaders.  Not perfect by any means but an improvement none the less.
+Slightly better graphics - I really did not need better graphics or additional animations from Civ5, but I can appreciate that Civ6 did make some improvements in these areas.
Cons of Civ6 over Civ5:
-Over reliance on automation of play with a complete lack of tunable options.  There are lots of examples of this but a very simple one is 'auto-select' of next unit.  When you issue an order for a unit to complete it's turn the program forces you to the next unit in the list (it's list, not yours) and whips the screen immediately to that unit - nevermind that you are attempting to coordinate and concentrate on the actions of a group of units and not just that one.  1/2 way around the world we go...  I swear, all of that whipping around on the screen is going to give me epilepsy.
In Civ5, there is a simple checkbox in the options menu to disable the auto-selection of units.  (huh, imagine that - an option to play how I want.)  You will not find any of the Civ5 selectible menu options in Civ6.
-Failures of Available Information.  Two simple examples: 1-the trade route menu & 2-the help menu.  In Civ5, if you wanted to find out what was the best trade route to use next, then you would click on the trade menu and a nice graphic matrix would pop-up and allow you to sort it by all of the different information columns, typically in 3 or 4 clicks I could sort it out in a minute and be on my way.  Alternately in Civ6, you have a single long list - no sorting, lots of repeats - it really is an information cluster-f***.  To be fair, it looks like there are buttons that should be available for some simple sorting but they don't work (at least in my game) and even if they did, this still would not fufill even 1/2 of the possible options of play.  Sometimes when I click on the trade-route menu, nothing shows up at all - so maybe its a bug of some sort, IDK.
The help menu: in Civ5, if there is something in the game you can find it in the help menu - may take a bit, but for the most part it is there.  In Civ6 there is a lot of information missing - if you don't have access to the internet, forget about it - you may have to save the game and just try it.  But you should be prepared to go back 10 to 15 turns to undo that attempt at learning.
Which leads me to my last major Con:  Time to complete.  It takes forever to accomplish simple things - This is partially just how the game is but it really seems to me that it is easier to speed things up in Civ5 with the right resources and build options then it is in Civ6.
Some other thoughts on Civ6 deficiencies -
One of the new items in Civ6 is the "stackable" units - they sell this as the ability to create armies, you know, a whole army: infantry, machine gunners, tanks & artillary.  Nope.  It's not that - It is just a slightly more powerful unit of the same type.  Of course, you can't easily determine if this is actually an improvement or not - what is the cost benefit?  Can't tell, there is no information available to determine the cost of a 'corps' vs. a 'unit'.  But now you have only shot from that corps instead of two shots from two units.
The Districts.  The new concept of building districts around your city instead of buildings in your city is interesting but currently flawed.  The failure to provide additional workable tiles around the city (still stuck at 3 tile radius) really makes this difficult in many situations.  Especially if you are working with a captured city from an AI player.  The AI cities do not play under the same rules, which is fine - until you capture one and have to work with what they left you.  At least in Civ5 you could build a settler and then raze the AI city at a later time.  That is not an option now.  You can choose to raze a city only if you capture it by force, and only at that exact moment.
Also, you cannot move districts.  Pick the wrong spot and did not figure it out until later in the game?  Tough cookies - your stuck with it now.  Want to trade a district from one city to another that the AI built to close?  Nope, can't do that silly - why would you want to do that?
City-State Envoys - great concept.  Why do they have to all die when an AI player takes over the city-state?  Taking with them thousands of years of effort also?  Not sure - not happy about it either.
Some other thoughts on the Civ game, in general:
Why can I not buy and sell land?  This seems like a perfectly reasonable way to negoiate with neighbors and make sure that we can actually get along?  The land tiles are the most important aspect of the game -  why is the concept of trading land rights so foreign & unincluded in these games?
Also, why do I need a city to hold on to captured land?  I need a city to work the land obviously, but if I capture a city and raze it to the ground, why do I have to give up the land rights?  I only need an army to hold on to land, not a city.
Anyway - buy Civ5 at a sale event.  Wait a few years for Civ6 to fix itself.
Myself, I am going to learn how to Mod Civ5 with the good parts of Civ6 and then play Civ5.

Sure, on a tile-based strategy you cannot expect realistic scaling, but the one-tile cities of Civ V made you actually feel like building a vast Empire with strategically placed cities and lots of productive countryside and infrastructure between them. Now, half of your tiles are cities and there is simply no feeling of distinction. The second great sin is the utterly horrible, outrageous, disgusting, ugly, mind-blowingly idiotic art style. I said districts remove the immersion from cities, but even worse is that they now have about four buildings and look more appropriate for a mobile game where it's all about gamey min-maxing and nobody cares about building a nice empire.
In Civilization V, I would always enjoy having a long single-player game, building my empire not to achieve victory, but to have a nice empire, even to RP a bit; I would be immersed in the experience and forget about time. If someone forced me to play Civ VI again, I'd probably just click whatever my advisors say and watch a good TV show or a football game on the second monitor.

An honest review. 2.4hrs Of play. Gameplay video this review covers is below
The game so far, has bad reviews, mostly because of the 30 frame limit, and not "expected high def graphics"
However.
Usually I will jump on the graphics bandwagon, and say oh I expect more from a game brought out on todays market, graphically. But Mafia 3 does something rather strange that makes me change my usual approach.
Animation - This really helps with the graphics I feel, from what i've played (Up to the  betrayal video time "1h 46m") the animation in all scenes is really done well, and it looks like care has actually been taken to make the story cinematic. For me anyway, it has helped me look away from the fact the graphics arent what you'd possibly expect. There are ofcourse a few things that need worked on, but this is Mafia 3 day 1, it's expected in todays gaming market for patches required after release, its become norm.
Graphics - In they're own way, they are pretty good, they arent great, but they are good, certain things have been given great detail, such as you're clothing, cars, buildings and the random objects in the game such as Lamps, fridges etc.
The sky however, is a bit different, not at all sure if i like it, or if it will grow on me slowly, the clouds do a pretty invasive change of light across the roads etc, and at first I thought it was some weird distance/load bug, personally I reckon they need to give that a  bit more attention but who knows, It's not game breaking, there is an odd somewhat non smooth sky reflection on you're vehicle, which is kind of annoying, but again, not game breaking. Shadows are ok, nothing amazing but so far they havent had any major issues that I have noticed.
Sound - So far, the games sound has been incredible, the music for one is very well added and comes in so far at good times, guns sound and feel amazing ( I use a xbox one elite controller ), explosions, car doors, and overall world just sound good.
Driving - I have to be honest here, when i watched the trailers originally way back months ago, the driving looks like some odd crazy taxi arcade style crap, however, I think they have died it down a little, I've chosen the realistic driving setting in the gameplay menu and prefer it over the normal driving mode, and so far, it's good, the hand break is a little action hero but It's incredibly easy to use which is nice, i've not used much other than the starting car and a few car's somewhat similar, but so far it's nice, and the boats drive pretty well with the water.
Story - So far i'm not too far in the story, i've only really revealed what the trailers showed us few weeks back "the betrayal" etc. But, for once, not often recently, I had to actually stop myself continuing after looking at the time and realising i've got work in a few hours, like previous Mafia's the story so far, is well done.
It's different going a black guy, and some would say they took 2 major risks. 1 You are against the mafia, and 2 You're playing a black character lead, for me  I couldnt care about colour, I do however love the Mafia side of play, and I was worried and somewhat dissapointed upon first information release that you will not be following the roles of the previous games "being the gangster" so to speak. But so far, it's working, while playing I never even said to myself oh wait...but I aint the mafia, I aint the Italians etc.
Give the game a chance, the negative reviews are  beyond stupid, to review the game negative on the basis of its 30 "atm" fps cap, is stupid, the game still works, it still has the good story, and everything i've mentioned above.
Sometimes I wish steam reviews had some kind of idiot free mechanic, but hey. Play the damn game.

This is what the AAA PC marked has come to...
70€ "next-gen" AAA release on PC, locked to run at headache-inducing 30 frames per second.
Just when I thought we were making progress on that, with JRPGs and other long-term console exclusive series being ported to PC with unlocked framerates or at least 60 FPS options being more and more common, Hangar 13 decides to be the puppy that♥♥♥♥♥♥on the rug and releases this game, showing complete disregard for the PC platform and reality itself.
Under 2K's supervision no less, a publisher that has had a stellar record with PC games, releasing series like Bioshock, Borderlands and X-Com, none of which had locked framerates.
Furthermore the game refuses to render at the desired resolution. At 1080p it looks clearly upscaled probably from 900p or lower, there is no option in the settings to force it to render at 1080p. Probably a remnant of the console version, and not relinquishing the control over this "feature" is just not acceptable. As a result the game looks blurry and washed out, the UI is pixelated and has many glitches.
Patches are good and fine, but releasing a game in this state is a terrible testament to the developers inability and complete detachment from the target market.
The story is probably great, but since I cannot play the game, I won't be finding that out.

'Mass Effect' and 'Splinter Cell' had a child named 'Alpha Protocol'. It turned out to be a flawed genius.
There are a lot of faults with this game. Broken gameplay mechanics, PS2-era graphics, inconsistent frame-rates and an uninspired beginning. But if one can look past its many shortcomings, this game turns out to be an absolute gem. A global espionage-RPG in the true sense.
To start things off, you first pick your character's class: Soldier (firearms), Field Agent (stealth), Tech Specialists (hacking) or Freelancer (a combination of skills of the player's choice). Each class determines how well you perform a specific task in the field.
With regards to gameplay, I'm sure the devs were targeting a realistic approach to combat. For instance, you have to aim at a target for few seconds to let the reticule converge. Thus, ensuring that every gunfight turned out to be a challenge. The melee system comprised of martial arts which allowed you to knockout enemies either stealthily or engage them head-on. All character abilities were upgradeable with sufficient experience points (XP).
Hacking was one of the highlights of the game. There was a unique system in place each for hacking computers, opening locks or bypassing keypads and alarms. Many people found the hacking system frustrating but I think it was fairly straight-forward. Challenging, yes, but very rewarding in the end.
The graphics were rubbish, plain and simple. Character animations were clunky, anti-aliasing horrible, lighting awful, movements jerky and texture loading very slow. These were some of the biggest down-sides of an otherwise fantastic game. Level designs were very good though with plenty of alternative routes to complete objectives.
The plot is where this game really shines. The story is gripping and opens up once you're done with the Saudi missions. And it hurtles you head-first into a global conspiracy mess. Allies (and enemies) are made along the way and your treatment of them has future implications in the form of gaining intel, weapons, money (if allies) or facing problems and hurdles (if enemies). Reading their dossier in advance helps you choose favourable options during dialogue sequences. Characters are interesting and unlike many other RPG games, dialogue never feels bland.
Alpha Protocol needs a sequel to set its problems right. It requires perseverance and patience to overlook its many problems and bear with its frustrating nature but underneath all that, this game is a true gem. One not to be missed.

Enemies by comparison are quick and accurate and have a tendency to snipe you outside of your field of view. The developers compensated by making the AI exceptionally dumb. It's easier to win by abusing geometry than toeing the AI in a firefight, and it feels like cheating. This is not a satisfying experience.

BUT, the plot also adapts really well to the decisions you make along the way, and your play style. It feels like your actions carry weight, and the plot develops accordingly. I've power played this game for 24 hours already on Nemesis and not because of any reason other than I couldn't stop playing.
Shadow of War is a better, slicker game than Shadow of Mordor was. Similar to Shadow of Mordor there is a first act where your domination abilities are limited however this time around I did not mind as the Minas Ithil storyline was good and kept me interested.
The skill system is better, the loot system is better, the Nemesis system is expanded with much more enemy variety and best of all there appears to be a lot more playable content than the first game.  Also Drakes are a hoot.
As for folks saying it is just the first game again I disagree as someone that played through and beat the first game (for the second time) just 6 months ago - Shadow of War is the refinement of that game and superior. But if you didn't really like the first game... don't expect a revolution. I can understand folks that think it's more of the same the same way each Assassin's Creed game is more of the same. On some level, it's the same basic game system but you should know that before you buy it.
I'm running on a 970 at 3440x1440 and it stays mostly above 30fps with a few tweaks down from High - par for the course with this card and UW display. Unlike some titles I didn't have to hack anything to get the UW to work right.
As for cons?  Yes I've been ambushed tons of times - my favourite was when I picked up a Godorian Artifact and one started to taunt me over it - and I've died my fair share or had my prey escape but honestly it hasn't really annoyed me like it did in the first game. It can be frustrating when you send a favourite Captain into the pits and he loses or when you miss a dodge prompt and get destroyed by a nasty Captain build but that's the nature of the game... death doesn't touch you, it just sets you back.
As for a real con - the gold and mithral loot crates can be ignored with no real impact aside from the online fortress challenge stuff that is purely extra. That said I am the guy who will buy a few here and there just to get a cool captain upgrade but not at the prices they are set at... 5x too expensive.
Bottom Line: Shadow of War is my new favourite Revenge Simulator and one of the best Mordor experiences out there.
I'll leave with a pro-tip; dominated Captains will turn on you no matter how much you buff them if you kill their Blood Brother right in front of them... who knew?

I had basically sworn-off Day One game purchases - prefer to see some credible reviews before buying - but on this I figured "I enjoyed the first one a lot - how badly could they screw up a sequel on the same game engine?"
Turns out - a lot. Combat is both stupid and stupidly annoying now. Feels like the game is playing me instead of me playing the game.
I would have happily paid for and enjoyed a new game consisting of nothing more than a new map using exactly the same game mechanics as SoM - instead they dumbed-down an already geared-toward-consolers combat system to make it blisteringly idiotic.
I understand that you unlock new moves and combos as you progress - and that adds complexity - I guess my mine gripe is the auto-targeting of enemies whether you're facing them or not.
Part of the challenge of these types of melee-oriented games (Assassin's Creed series, Mad Max, the first Batman) is maintaining situational awareness so you can time your attacks, blocks and dodges and build up your hit streaks or land combos.
In this game, you can literally do nothing but close your eyes and hit the left mouse button for as long as it takes to kill 30 (regular) orcs.  I actually went into the options to see if there was a way to turn the auto-targeting off, because not having to maintain situational awareness removes a lot of the challenge from the combat.
I'm a moron for buying this on Day One. Pick it up on the first massively-discounted sale if you have to, but don't be a moron like me and pay full price for this.

Invisible, Inc. is fantastic. I've never gotten all that excited about games with randomly generated levels before, but I guess I just had never found one that did it so well. The biggest differentiator for me is the mechanic of limited turn rewinds per level, which is the compromise I've always wanted (but never knew I wanted) between the drudgery of quicksaving and the masochism of perma-death. Now that I've seen it, it seems so obvious. Maybe people have been doing this for years and I just haven't been playing the right games.
The other aspects of the game are excellent too, even if they don't merit their own paragraphs. The campaign is long enough that you can build a good team, but short enough that you have to make some tough tradeoffs along the way, so you end up playing different strategies on different playthroughs whether you want to or not. There's a satisfying array of items, augments, and Incognita programs to vary how your characters behave. The suggested difficulty progression is very well tuned and eases you into the game without it ever feeling overwhelming. The stealth mechanics work well, with a clear distinction between hidden, noticed, and watched squares and the ability to observe guards to predict their future movement. The artwork and animation look great and make the game feel polished.

I have about 80 hours in the original game, which is finishable in 10-15. You might say I like it a little. So I'm probably a little biased in writing this review, but I honestly wasn't guaranteed to like this game upon release, since I was mildly skeptical of some of the changes the devs had hinted at implementing. I think a lot of times when devs try to change up a formula in response to criticism, they end up creating new problems that are sometimes worse than what they'd started with (looking at you Bioware and the way you stole my dialogue wheels in Mass Effect).
But Stoic Studio, in my opinion, successfully navigated the balance between resolving criticisms and weaknesses of the first game without undermining or changing what made the original great. Every little tweak made the game better, not worse. A few important changes: the morale system  is so much clearer-- in the original game it took me multiple playthroughs to pick up on the interaction between some choices and morale shifts; the cutscenes are more dynamic and the voice-overs more frequent so that it has even more of a 'cinematic' feel (but runs in 60 fps!) in the sense of watching a classic animated film; the music is even more beautiful (was that even possible?? Austin Wintory is fabulous) and most of all, the combat is much better.
I was among those who actually liked the original combat, so I was worried they'd throw the baby out with the bathwater in their promises to make it more complex (especially in response to criticisms that it wasn't enough like other turn-based strategy games). But I think I can safely say that really do think they hit on just the right notes for it. The fights and mechanics feel familiar and still absolutely approachable. It’s the same bones and sinews of combat. But the tweaks they’ve added blend with the old instead of conflicting with them — like instead of just slapping a new face on top of the the body, they gave it more muscle. They took everything that was good from the old combat and embellished on it instead of throwing it away, while trimming away the weaknesses, where I think a lot of devs might’ve said ‘people don’t like the combat? Better start from scratch.’
TL;DR is: If you liked the original, you'll absolutely like its continuation because it builds on its strengths; if you *didn't* like the original, you should definitely consider giving its sequel a shot because it's fixed what made it weak before.

Executive Assault is, in short, a magnificent game that has an extremely slow development time. It takes place on an unknown planet(s) where you must destroy your opponent for control of it's resources and or to gain control of the entire planet. To do this you use a real-time strategy playing style to create robots, with a dash of FPS in the mix.

The goal of Executive Assault is to either kill the Enemy Executive, or force their power core to self destruct through the use of robots. All while protecting yourself.
Executive Assault does real-time strategy quite well. You must gather in-game resources to construct different factories that creat robots. These robots vary from small cannon fodder to giant mechs of doom. Using these resources you can also create defensive walls, turrets, gates, and bunkers. Even a giant force field to defend against the occasional missile barrage. You cannot get to these without the use of a research system however. This system is not complex in the slightest, you simply find the option you want and begin research. After completing research you unlock new research options. New weapons and armor for robots and a personal shield for your executive are a few of these options.
Like every real-time strategy game, you control your robots by selecting whichever oens you wish to move, then select where you want them to move. The game also has a handy teleporter as a research option, great for moving your cannon fodder.
Executive Assault, like advertised, has an FPS system. Which is not complicated at all, and sadly it is very limited to what you can do. You simply select any unit you want and go into FPS mode. From this mode you use the standard WASD keys to move and left mouse button to shoot the currently equipped weapon. This mode is essential for self destructing the enemy power core, and possibly killing the enemy executive
The AI itself is decent, it moves units, builds buildings, and eventually destroys you early game. That's the sad truth, you will almost never win against the AI. They get overpowered units WAY too fast, and like all real-time strategy AI, begin to spam them until you lose. It is sad to see such a great game have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI.
I give gameplay a 7/10. It would be a solid 9, but the AI is so bad that you cannot play this game solo. It also needs to be developed a bit more.
The graphics are not the best, but to me they meet RTS indie quality standards. The enviroment is bland, and the textures are not that detailed. But seeing how this is created from a small indie studio that does not bother me much, as the gameplay far outweighs the graphics.
I give graphics a 4.5/10. With some improvement to the landscape and better textures they can reach a solid 6-7.
Executive Assault is a terribly overlooked game that just needs a larger playerbase. If you plan on purchasing this game please do so, but only if you want to support the developer, have a friend to play with, and the development has gone further down the line.
Overall score: 7.5/10

Engrossing mystery thriller with unfortunate gameplay weaknesses.
Alan Wake is an immersive experience filled with mystery. Its greatest strength is definitely its plot. It captures its audience by presenting an interesting premise and questions that need answers, which ends up being the main driving force of the game. It did a fantastic job of keeping me interested throughout the game. The story is complemented by (mostly) well written dialogue and some (not all) well constructed characters. The issue I have with the plot is its ending, which contains no real closure or catharsis, which I imagine is due to a possible sequel. Another strength is the atmosphere. The dark tone of the game is achieved by a meticulous attention to lighting and a carefully picked soundtrack. It all blends together to form a dark engrossing mystery.
Unfortunately the gameplay is its greatest weakness. It is thrilling and exciting at first, but quickly turns into a tedious routine that just stops you from exploring the storyline. The formula never changes: shoot the "taken" with light, then shoot them with weapons, rinse and repeat. The game does try to add some variety by adding elements of platforming, puzzles and even the illusion of exploration. Gameplay is in and of itself not bad. The problem with it is that the gameplay sections are too long. They're so long that whatever fun you had killing the taken dissapates very quickly. This is unfortunate, because I believe if those sections were made shorter, the game would feel a lot more immersive and connected.

I went into Civ6 not entirely sure what to expect. I've played Civ5 and enjoyed it immensely, and most of the reviews about Civ6 I had read said that it didn't hold up to its predecessor in any way, so when I bought it I did not have especially high hopes. I will also note that when I bought the game, it was half off, and I most likely would not have bought it otherwise (or at least until the price was reduced).
Despite my low expectations, after playing multiple games and difficulties, I can definitively say that Civ6 is an incredible game and a worth successor in the line of Civ games. It's beautifully crafted and the gameplay is actually improved somewhat over Civ5, especially in terms of fighting and the overall victory and game mechanics. It's still a challenging game that makes you think ten steps ahead of your opponents, but the difficulty settings make it so that even novice players can have a fun, engaging experience.
With regards to the characters one can play, all of the new additions are fun and challenging, and as a history nut I love the wealth of lore and backstory we receive about each leader. The gameplay is just as exciting as Civ5, and in Civ6 I find it a lot easier to figure out what you need to do and where in your victory progress you are with relation to the other characters.
The only thing I will say that I genuinely dislike is the new interaction menu for city states and leaders; it's easier to navigate in Civ5 than in Civ6 and for players who are new to the game, it can be a little bit frustrating to try and make heads or tails of.
I don't use a gaming laptop, but Civ6 runs well on my normal Lenovo. I've had a few issues with exiting from the main menu where the game will freeze up and I have to get creative to close it, and there are a few bugs here and there with the ingame map, but nothing too serious and nothing that's made the game difficult to play.
Overall, Civ6 is a fun, immersive, and challenging addition to the family of Civ games, and I would recommend it both to veterans of the franchise and newcomers who want to try out a turn-based strategy game. However, because it is a pretty expensive purchase and there are a few bugs, I generally would advise people to wait for a sale or discount on the game.

If you loved point-and-click adventure games when they were big (think Monkey Island, King's Quest, Day of the Tentacle etc) and enjoyed the irreverent, cheesy, innuendo-laden humour of the Al Lowe Leisure Suit Larry games, MEBtST will be totally up your alley.
I grew up on the aforementioned click-and-point adventure games, and I loved them, and I really enjoyed this. It's silly, over-the-top fun, with some great one-liners, some amusing pop culture references, break the fourth-wall moments, and a space opera to boot.
The art, on the whole, suited it, with loud colours and quirky designs, though in places the background art seemed inconsistent with the rest of the game. The music was great and suited the upbeat space opera mood, and the sound effects were unobtrusive and fit the mood well.
My only complaints were that at times it felt like it was running slowly; it seemed to take ages for Tycho to walk from one end of the screen to the other, and there were a couple of typoes in the dialogue I noticed. A little more character development would have been nice, too, but for a fun, silly, and slightly surreal game, it was most enjoyable.
(I'm seeing a lot of "I'm offended" comments on here, or mentions of it being "unrealistic": a fair call, but I never felt like the game was meant to be realistic or taken too seriously: it felt like a gay-themed Leisure Suit Larry, which was equally silly and unrealistic in its portrayal of both female characters and heterosexual relationships. While it's nice to have serious games and accurate representation, it's also sometimes nice to have a bit of fun and some smutty humour which isn't really hurting anyone.)

Great game, lots of fun.
You play as an agent.  You can select what categories to spend your action points in.  From assault rifles, pistols, stealth, sub machine guns, etc.  There are also dialog sequences where you choose how to respond.  Including things as major as whether or not to shoot key people.  These choices influence the course of the game.  You have some leway in how you play.  Whether you go for the Splinter Cell approach or go in guns blazing.
I played the game as a stealthy silenced pistol wielding agent.  It was cool having some control over the outcome, with the dialog choices.  Gameplay was a lot of fun.  Some people seem to get frustrated by the hacking mini-games, but I didn't mind them.
A few minor complaints: in certain parts of the game you're forced to play a certain style.  I was being a stealthy pistol using agent, but at a few parts I had to pull out the assault rifle to deal with the enemy.  This generally happened during the boss fights.  It wasn't terrible, just threw off the Sam Fisher style I was playing.  During some of the dialog choices it was a bit difficult to tell from the single word description how you were going to respond.  Sometimes the physics were a little wonky when you died, but that's just cosmetic.
Overall it's a great game, lots of fun.  I'm tempted to replay it to see what different choices might lead to.

I really want to give this a thumbs up and down, but since that isnt an option, I'm giving it a up, as trying lots of the options can be rewarding/challenging and can eat a fair amount of time making the $ to playtime equation pretty good.
But a warning: this game can be brutal!
First whats good: Unique setting/graphics/abilities.  Fun tactics and sneaking around. every level is randomly generated, meaning it never plays the same.
Whats so/so: The story is weak, and very short, and annoying by the time you have played through a few times. Some of the "agents" dont even get to start with one extra ability point(balancing?)
Whats bad: Due to the complete randomness of everything, levels, stores, guards etc: you may not have the tools you need to survive later levels.  For instance I didn't get a single item or ability that would allow me to affect guards with armor, and on the last level every guard had armor.
Personnal Opinion - good/meh/bad - You decide: Due to the randomness of everything you cant rely on one play style/tool setup to get through. This can give you a unique challenge on each play through.  But hurt you if you perfer one play style.  The game seriously penalizes you for taking your time, so its a constant struggle of pushing too far vs keeping your agents safe.  Some levels (randomly) spider out in several directions, meaning if you take the wrong path you waste a ton of time exploring a dead end, and then have no time left/there have been too many guards spawned that you can't make it down the correct path, decide: cut your losses and run, or chance ending our play through/loosing agents to get to the goal.  On the other hand I have had level randomly have all the goals on the room right off the start. Risk Reward decisions are huge since both Power and Cash are almost always in short supply for you.
In all I have played for 30 hours, beaten the first 2 difficulties, and been stuck without the tools the final level needed on expert a few times.  I havent scratched all the different agents yet, as I have been trying a few related play styles, perhaps its time to try something else ;)

tl;dr If you can say "Okay, WB did some stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥ but let's see what kind of game Monolith made", and you liked Shadow of Mordor, you'll have a fine time.
To start off, obviously, WB's practices have not been spectacular leading up to the release of the game. Loot boxes in a single player game are sketchy, season passes are generally not popular, and the charity debacle has been discussed time and again. But while these are certainly bad choices, they're not AS bad as people make them out to be.
The loot boxes get a bit of reference in the game, but aside from a bit of glow in the menu, generally to indicate you have a chest you can open from something, it really doesn't affect gameplay. Honestly, most of the loot from the crates is on level with (or worse than) what you can find in the world, and the content feels balanced enough to not need them. The fourth act has a significant difficulty spike, but a lot of it is a challenge from your average captain not being a candy♥♥♥♥♥any more. With some thought and strategy, it's not that hard to get through.
Season passes are more of a preference thing. Some people like them, some don't, I personally don't care much one way or the other.
There is also the issue of the charity DLC, but I don't have anything I can contribute that hasn't been said already.
With the WB shoveling done, there's the actual game. It feels like a solid continuation of Shadow of War, once the first bit of the game is done.
(Small spoilers ahead, primarily abilities and enemies featured in the game)
Some of the abilities that you started out with in the first game require you to put points in to them here, but after that, there's a lot of new looking stuff. Each ability has upgrades, which you can only use one of at a time, allowing things like elemental damage, special effects, and quality of life improvements. Early on, you gain access to a double jump, and it feels great, for both mobility and the occasional "Oh I didn't mean to jump off of that". Later upgrades allow you to do things like summon a dragon on command (with a cooldown) and kill grunts when you counter with proper timing.
The maps each individually feel a bit smaller than the two in Shadow of Mordor (including Nurnen, which is in both games). However, there are four primary zones in the game, with smaller zones such as a city that are used intermittently, and definitely more area to play in overall. The load times also seem to be a good bit shorter in Shadow of War.
One of the new mechanics of the game is Sieging. While the first siege requires you to go through the motions of disassembling the setup as a tutorial of sorts, future sieges allow you to choose how much setup you want to go in with. Your own captains, who can be given a choice of three upgrades similarly to your abilities, will be assisting you in capturing a series of points in the siege before you go in to the keep to fight the Overlord solo. Any hostile Warchiefs left at the time of the siege will contribute upgrades to the fortress, such as fire and poison traps, and specific groups of enemies. You can kill them to remove these upgrades, or take it a step further by putting your own captains in place as Warchiefs in the fort. They have a chance to be caught (and killed) at the start of the siege, but will help you by having points in the fortress ready for capture at the start, and blowing open extra openings to the fortress. When you finally enter the keep, you bicker with the Overlord for a short bit before taking them (and some goons) on.
For better or for worse, the game follows a lot of the formula set up by Shadow of Mordor, but with pleasant additions. Ologs give a bit more variety to the grunts and captains you'll run in to, and while the side bosses don't give much more variety in mechanics than they did before, they are more interesting storywise, pitting you against Nazgul and a Balrog. The AI varies between comical and frustrating, and generally flips between smart and stupid like Shadow of Mordor, but the true trolling comes from ambushes. Certain types of captains, as well as some of those whom you've killed but aren't really dead, will come in to your most carefully laid plans to either mildly frustrate you or destroy everything you love, depending on their abilities and level. There doesn't seem to be a limitation on what mission they will attack you in, or even where, sometimes following you to areas that orcs seem to normally be incapable of reaching. This can also happen consecutively, with little to no time in between dropping one Captain and another one coming in for a chat, and can really screw with you and make your game a lot harder.
It also feels necessary to take a second to talk about the look and theme of enemies, because some of the Captains are wonderful. Someone returning after being killed with poison or having limbs removed is a good detail, but a well dressed Captain singing (mostly in rhyme) while he attempts to kill you with his guitar-axe is a magical experience.
All in all, if you can put aside the WB fiascos, Shadow of War is a fun game. If you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor, the game is definitely worth a try, and if you find yourself writing a review for the game, rate it on the gameplay, not on what the publisher did before it came out. It deserves to be mentioned, but it shouldn't be the singular thing you base your opinion of the game on.

If you can get it with a massive discount for less than €5 I would recommend it, but I would not recommend playing this clunky mess of a game without quite a bit of tolerance.
I actually completed it twice, but apparently it was before Steam started counting or maybe that was broken too..
Obsidian used to make remarkably well written fully fleshed out dialogue options with a lot of branching options and you had all the time in the world to consider and enjoy them. In AP you only get one word, an "attitude" or a "stance" that represents an entire tree of dialogue that just plays out by itself and you only get like three seconds to decide AND find the right spot to click. You can highlight a response, thinking it's all good, but you need to click on the text inside to enable it.. Clunky. How can you assume that there is any roleplay in conversation if you have no idea, what you are saying? It's just a gamble then and gamling is not roleplaying. The most annoying part in this regards is that game autosaves AFTER each conversation.
The game has a bit of replay value, because of the non-sensical dialogue system of course and in different ways of playing it with focus on different guns (i.e. different combat strategies) and skills, but unfortunately the more you play it the more it falls apart and reveals the inconsistencies. Advance too fast and sneak around and enemies will literally spawn in your face and fail to see you right in front of them. You can master the game and break it.
The game itself doesn't play on the same conditions as the player. There are lots of scripts and triggers to ruin your gameplay like enemies that alert everybody to your presense in a split second before they pass out. I can't prime a grenade and when I throw it there is always a delay before it explodes that pretty much makes them useless to me in combat, but when an enemy lop a grenade my way it explodes almost instantly. It's also quite rare that I actually manage to complete a throw, because it will bounce off or against walls that I didn't notice.
For a game with the title Espionage RPG there is a remarkable lack of espionage and barely any RPG. You can't spy on anyone, you can't select your own targets, nothing happens unless the game serves it all on a platter for you. You can only request information if it's for sale, not because you want to check up on somebody. There should have been an option to request data on anyone you want to check out, but there isn't. There is no spying. Calling this game RPG at all, that's really far fetched. It's much more of Action Adventure with skill-progression than anything else.
I had a lot of mouse issues with this game. There is some hyper-sensitive DPI scaling which turns all minigames into a total wreck. Combat was fine, but Sniper mode was hyper-sensitive and the cursor in minigames moved in completely erratic patterns, which made it impossible for me to use the Sniper at all and made me fail pretty much every minigame.. I had to fiddle around a lot with ini files to lessen the pain, but I couldn't remove it completely.
The main character is in a bit of the same vein as Shepard in Mass Effect i.e. boring and forgettable, but there are a few colourful characters that adds all the fun and sexiness of the game.. Take those (two) away and the game would have a been a total disaster.
It happened on numerous occassions that enemies respawned in my face and just stared blankly at me.. Always weird and immersion breaking.
It was mostly clunky and frustrating to fight with controls, sometimes a bit entertaining, rarely awesome and funny, but it happened. It's very much a - Been there, done that - kind of game.

If you liked the first game, you will like this one as well. They've basically taken everything good from the first game, and worked to make it better. Gameplay is extremely smooth, and I've yet to see any large frame drops (and yes, variable framerate is OFF).
As for the loot box situation... well, people are making it way more than it is. Throughout the game you are rewarded credits which can be obtained via missions & item disposal. After roughly 2 hours of gameplay, I had earned 2.3k in credits (which I used to buy 3 lootboxes at 750 a piece). The boxes contained gear which had some neat passive abilities. Like other items in the game, you also have the ability to dispose or "recycle" this gear for a reasonable return as well.
I understand that certain things were said pre-launch regarding the state of store-items, and I understand some things may have changed.... but they do not hinder the overall experience of the game. For those of us who enjoy playing games on the hardest difficulty, with as little external assistance as possible, who cares? The loot boxes give gamers with money to spend a way to keep making games of this caliber.
We're living in the era of - "PRE-PRE-ALPHA: PLAY AT YOUR OWN RISK - PRICE: $9.99"  - that we seem to forget how much money is involved in AAA games. The devs have bosses too, and unfortunately, they want to make their money back (and have a reason to fund another game).
Please don't let what you read deter you from playing this game. You WILL enjoy it if you enjoyed the first .
PS-- Change the resolution scale instead of using TAA or FXAA (for 1440p and below). It looks much better, and they have a tessellation toggle (which smooths a ton of jaggies).

I've power played this game for 24 hours already on Nemesis and not because of any reason other than I couldn't stop playing.

As for folks saying it is just the first game again I disagree as someone that played through and beat the first game (for the second time) just 6 months ago - Shadow of War is the refinement of that game and superior. But if you didn't really like the first game... don't expect a revolution. I can understand folks that think it's more of the same the same way each Assassin's Creed game is more of the same. On some level, it's the same basic game system but you should know that before you buy it.
I'm running on a 970 at 3440x1440 and it stays mostly above 30fps with a few tweaks down from High - par for the course with this card and UW display. Unlike some titles I didn't have to hack anything to get the UW to work right.
As for cons?  Yes I've been ambushed tons of times - my favourite was when I picked up a Godorian Artifact and one started to taunt me over it - and I've died my fair share or had my prey escape but honestly it hasn't really annoyed me like it did in the first game. TL;DR = This is a tentative no. It's easily the best game of it's type on Steam (yes, there is more than one gladiator management sim), but replay value comes down to what you like in games.
Review proper:
Alright, pretty straightforward on this one. It's a management sim, where you are the lanista of a ludus (there's some Latin for ya!). You control several aspects of your gladiators, their stable, and their matches, with the ultimate goal of crushing everyone who gets in front of you.
You start in a small arena in Carthage, working your way through the ranks until you reach Rome.
The Good:
Essentially, the gameplay is pretty solid. There's some neat mechanics, a few simple side quests, and the early game is very much a "oh crap, I need to do X or we're out of business" type thing. It's also easy (for me anyway) to get fairly immersed in it, and grow attached to a gladiator, imagine a backstory, etc. etc. In essence, it's not a bad story creator if you're imaginative, and a person could write a good AAR or two due to this.
Finally offing the dude who's been the terror of every (abstracted) tournament and is the most feared and famous fighter in the Empire feels great.
It's artistically very pretty, too.
It's also possibly the easiest game to 100% in terms of Steam achievements. You can get all of them in one playthrough.
The Bad:
So here's why I don't recommend this - if you know what you're doing, the game is much, much too simple, you can ignore the majority of the mechanics, and it devolves into "click this, click this again, click it again, more click".
My first playthrough was exciting, because I didn't know what I was doing, and everything felt very tense and on the edge. By my second playthrough, I understood how to min-max everything, and went 1100 odd matches undefeated. Which honestly kinda sucked after I hit 200 wins, because it turned into me just clicking through everything in order to just kill off the last 100 or so other gladiators.
No lie. There is no save scum involved there either.
It doesn't matter if you have the most famous gladiator, money becomes irrelevant, and there's just no way to fix any of these issues. Certain game settings do make things harder, but the only one that makes the late game remotely challenging (Let The Gods Decide) can also make it just about impossible to progress in the early game. The only real way to keep things edgy is to make up your own restrictions, which might work well for some, but not me personally.
In the end, it suffers from the same problem a lot of 4x games have - at some point, once you're doing well, it just becomes uninteresting.
Conclusion:
In the end, I can't really offer much in the way of a solution for the above problem, or think of any way to make it a better game. I can't say it's a bad game, because it isn't, but I can't say I'm going to go for a third complete playthrough either. I got my 30 hours out of it for the price of a pack of smokes, so I'm not dissatisfied, but that's it.

This is going to be the only the second review I have given a game on steam yet, but I feel this game deserves it.  I will start by saying that rating this game I would give it a 10/10 and words won't do it justice, the game is just that damn good.  That said this game isn't for everybody and without going into detail or spoiling the plot I will try and explain why and to whom this game wouldn't be enjoyed.  The game has a story driven plot that is second to none in any other game I have ever played, basically it ends up being an emotional rollercoaster.  If you are the type of gamer that simply doesn't care about story and is only interested in gameplay then you will in most cases probably not get the most enjoyment out of this game as the amount of things that you can do in the game is extremely limited.  In other words it is not an arcade shooter or a pew, pew, pew lolz you're dead kind of game.  It is more about the story and more akin to watching a good mini-series on cable.  The amount of things the player can do is very limited with most of the moving around being solely so you can inspect objects in your surroundings to help explain aspects of the story and as a mechanism to allow the player to make good informed choices at key story points in the game.  That said it is in my opinion and without spoiling the story very helpful to pay attention and inspect most everything in your surroundings that you are able to.  The game at points does have some problem solving that needs to be accomplished to advance further into the game but most of it is pretty straightforward and the player will not find themselves stumped for hours trying to figure something out.  A playthrough takes about 25-30 hours in total (3-6 hours per episode) if you inspect all items you can carefully and take the time to appreciate the story.  If you are the type of person that doesn't or cannot cope well with an emotional rollercoaster then you will probably also not like this game.  It will have your emotions soaring one moment and 10 minutes later leave the player with a sense of helplessness regarding the characters in the game.  The game does get you involved in the characters and it is in that fact that the game shines, the character and story development is unlike any other game I have ever played.  The soundtrack does an excellent job of accentuating the environments and setting the stage for the moods in the game and is also one of the best soundtracks I have ever seen used in a video game to date.  The story reminded me a lot of the movie The Butterfly Effect and The Time Machine as it deals with the ability to rewind/move through time to change the characters timeline and for those familiar with the movie you will also know about The Chaos Theory and the ramifications inherent with messing around with time.
In closing I love this game and very much look forward to the prequel and the sequel and I hope that my review can convince some to give this game a shot as in my opinion it was right up there as being the best 20 bucks I have ever spent.

A trip back to the classic adventure games of old.
Broken Age tells the stories of two teenagers, Vella and Shay, as they experience their own coming of age stories. Shay is a teenaged boy stuck on a spaceship run by a motherly AI who still treats him like a baby even though he has long since grown weary of her childish games and patronising tone. He seeks a new adventure, and the shifty wolf Marek living in the underbelly of the ship may be just the solution.
Vella lives in a bakers community called Sugar Bunting, where every 10-20 years an event called the Maiden's Feast is held. During this feast, the great monster Mog Chothra is offered several sacrificial maidens as an appeasement to keep him from destroying the city. Vella is one of the lucky maidens, but she refuses to just lie down and be sacrificed. There must be a better way. Couldn't we just kill Mog Chothra?
Broken Age is the long awaited game made by Double Fine which was successfully kickstarted in March of 2012. Today, Act 1 is being released with Act 2 coming around April. This game is a callback to the classic point and click adventure games of old. It has all the charm and humour of those games, with a modern animation, voice acting, and art style. Voice actors like Elijah Wood (Shay), Jack Black (Harm'ny Lightbeard), Jennifer Hale (Shay's mom AI), Whil Wheaton (Lumberjack), and others are really funny and really bring the characters to life.The game ended on a jawdropping cliffhanger that left me begging for more and I cannot wait for Act 2 to come and pick up the pieces. My only real complaint is that the puzzle systems have been simplified when compared to older adventure games, and I really never struggled for too long on any of the puzzles. The story, art, and voice acting are top notch though and the game was an absolute blast to play.
Bottom line is this, never before did I ever think a stool could provide so much comedic value, and never before did I think that a SPOON of all things could be one of the most genious characters in a modern game. If you have any interest in this type of game then this is a must have.

If you’re a fan of point-and-click adventure games of yesteryear, look no further: this is the game for you, especially if you’re also a fan of gay-friendly and gay-oriented entertainment. I’m always happy to support gay-friendly endeavors, and I have a special affection for Joe Phillips, who is a genuinely nice guy and a superb artist.
But it’s a case of point-and-click adventure games not really being my thing, coupled with a terrible, depressing story made even sadder by the fact that it thinks it’s funny. There are a few jokes that work, but most of these are misses, not hits, and only accentuate how dismal the story and its universe are. I left this game feeling unhappy and regretting I had ever played it. It has grisly, macabre moments that are incredibly disturbing and upsetting, but the writer apparently thought they were hilarious. Hint: they don’t get any funnier as the game goes on, it just gets more and more depressing and awful.
If you can look past the wretched tone though, you might have a little fun with this game. It is good to support the community, and it is nice to see a gay-friendly universe populated with a lot of gay characters. You’re not really saddled with the best choice for a protagonist though, as Tycho is an insensitive, selfish goody-two-shoes whose stupidity more often than not leads to significant inconvenience for the player. By the end of the game, I hated him. What a scumbag!
There’s no real payoff, nothing actually sexy about the game. The closest thing we get is the fact that his clothes keep vanishing through the transmat beam…except when they don’t. It’s more of a pain than an amusement after the first couple of times. It’s like watching a late-night movie just to find that it’s not only depressing, it doesn’t actually deliver any of the goods it promised and, when it gets close, it's with the character you find the least appealing.
If you want a legitimately fun game that will make you happy to play it, look to Kitty Powers’ Matchmaker instead. My Ex-Boyfriend the Space Tyrant is something that I could only really recommend to point-and-click adventure fans or people that just want to support everything gay that comes out, which is admirable enough.

Growing up in the early PC gaming era, I came to love point and click adventures such as Space Quest and The Secret of Monkey Island, etcetera.  If you have fond memories of games like those, then you'll love "My Ex-Boyfriend the Space Tyrant".  It has the same silly comedic style that I'd come to love from those sort of games, only with a gay theme that's suggestive, but didn't go too far... though I'd have been okay if it had!  I really enjoyed this game; it was light-hearted and fun and took me back to when I was a kid.  In fairness, if this had been a non-gay themed point & click adventure, I may not have enjoyed it as much, but since it appeals to me as a gaymer, I was much more willing to overlook some of the minor flaws of the game, the pros and cons of which I've listed below.
There are only a few down-sides to this game, one of which being that it was quite short. I finished it playing casually in under 5 hours of total play time.  I wasn't disappointed from a monetary value perspective, but from a gameplay perspective, because I wanted to keep playing.  I only now learned that there's a sequel planned and I really can't wait for the release!
=====
HIGHS
=====
- LGBT themed game that makes the story interesting for gaymers
- Silly humour that I LOVE, similar to that of the Space Quest / Monkey Island franchises
- Suggestive themes that didn't go too far
- Amusing story that captured my interest
=====
LOWS
=====
- Encountered a game crashing bug one occasion
- Short game - finished in under 5 hours of total gameplay
- Would liked to have seen a wider variety of items & interactions
- Would liked to have seen a wider variety of dialogue choices
- Voicing over the game would've added an extra level of fun
Overall, if you're a gaymer, you'll more than likely enjoy this fun game and get a few good laughs out of it!

A truly engaging title that allows you to either create and manage your own space agency, or simply mess around in sandbox mode and explore your creativity. Although, far from just letting you fly ships into space, this game also challenges you to take into consideration your allocation of resources, atmospheric heating, drag, Delta V, gravity and a whole multitude of other Newtonian laws which incidentally can/will teach you an awful lot about orbital physics & mathematics if you have the inclination to to so. This surprised me even when playing it in mid-2013 during its early access.
Now, this game is for the most part a simulator of sorts (one that is initially very difficult to play) and as such will have a slight learning curve & requires a little patience to get used to, especially considering the exploration into aerodynamics and rocketry, but as someone who has more than 1,450 hours logged I can promise the rewards are more than worth it.

This update does some things well, but mostly it is too complicated to be enjoyable. There is too much to keep track of, too many changes from the previous versions, and absolutely no help to walk you through the multitude of changes. This all results in a game that is not fun because it is too complicated. And then there are quirks that make it annoying For example, it used to be that when you pressed C the screen would center on a selected unit, not anymore. It used to be you could use the number pad to move a unit, not anymore or at least not by default. It used to be you could move the screen by moving the mouse to the edge, that is off by default. It used to be that when a turn started the screen would center on a unit, not anymore. (I accidently moved the wrong unit by mistake several times thinking what was in the middle of my screen was what was selected.) You get no in game help as to what makes a city grow in size. And other annoyances. This is not to say everything is bad. The ideas of limiting all wonders to places with appropriate tiles is a good thing. The idea of doing certain actions to advance similar research is a good thing. How the game approached civics is a good thing. How the world leaders react to you based on what you do is a good thing. But all the good things are drowned out in the morass of complication and confusion. If Civ6 just took the few good things I listed and merged it with the way Civ5 is, then it would be an awesome game. As it is now, I am uninstalling it and going back to Civ5. I am just glad I did not pay full price.

If you can get it with a massive discount for less than €5 I would recommend it, but I would not recommend playing this clunky mess of a game without quite a bit of tolerance.
I actually completed it twice, but apparently it was before Steam started counting or maybe that was broken too..
Obsidian used to make remarkably well written fully fleshed out dialogue options with a lot of branching options and you had all the time in the world to consider and enjoy them. In AP you only get one word, an "attitude" or a "stance" that represents an entire tree of dialogue that just plays out by itself and you only get like three seconds to decide AND find the right spot to click. You can highlight a response, thinking it's all good, but you need to click on the text inside to enable it.. Clunky. How can you assume that there is any roleplay in conversation if you have no idea, what you are saying? It's just a gamble then and gamling is not roleplaying. The most annoying part in this regards is that game autosaves AFTER each conversation.
The game has a bit of replay value, because of the non-sensical dialogue system of course and in different ways of playing it with focus on different guns (i.e. different combat strategies) and skills, but unfortunately the more you play it the more it falls apart and reveals the inconsistencies. Advance too fast and sneak around and enemies will literally spawn in your face and fail to see you right in front of them. You can master the game and break it.
The game itself doesn't play on the same conditions as the player. There are lots of scripts and triggers to ruin your gameplay like enemies that alert everybody to your presense in a split second before they pass out. I can't prime a grenade and when I throw it there is always a delay before it explodes that pretty much makes them useless to me in combat, but when an enemy lop a grenade my way it explodes almost instantly. It's also quite rare that I actually manage to complete a throw, because it will bounce off or against walls that I didn't notice.
For a game with the title Espionage RPG there is a remarkable lack of espionage and barely any RPG. You can't spy on anyone, you can't select your own targets, nothing happens unless the game serves it all on a platter for you. You can only request information if it's for sale, not because you want to check up on somebody. There should have been an option to request data on anyone you want to check out, but there isn't. There is no spying. Calling this game RPG at all, that's really far fetched. It's much more of Action Adventure with skill-progression than anything else.
I had a lot of mouse issues with this game. There is some hyper-sensitive DPI scaling which turns all minigames into a total wreck. Combat was fine, but Sniper mode was hyper-sensitive and the cursor in minigames moved in completely erratic patterns, which made it impossible for me to use the Sniper at all and made me fail pretty much every minigame.. I had to fiddle around a lot with ini files to lessen the pain, but I couldn't remove it completely.
The main character is in a bit of the same vein as Shepard in Mass Effect i.e. boring and forgettable, but there are a few colourful characters that adds all the fun and sexiness of the game.. Take those (two) away and the game would have a been a total disaster.
It happened on numerous occassions that enemies respawned in my face and just stared blankly at me.. Always weird and immersion breaking.
It was mostly clunky and frustrating to fight with controls, sometimes a bit entertaining, rarely awesome and funny, but it happened. It's very much a - Been there, done that - kind of game.
Everyone should have it. 10 out of 10

Being able to make choices in a game is a big deal these days. It's just a shame few do it well. And out of those few that manage it, Alpha Protocol stands tall as the prime example. It’s third person shooter/RPG that is most similar to Deus Ex: Human Revolution and Mass Effect. The plot is very reminiscent of James Bond and other rouge spy movies.
The story is actually pretty intriguing and decently written, involving different factions of spies, mercenaries, terrorists and secret police; taking you to places such as Moscow, Rome and Taipei.  Its interaction mechanics with NPCs during cut-scenes is the highlight of this game.  It allows you to chose different dialog choices that influences the story and character relationships. The cast of characters is colorful and they are all very interesting. Each NPC has a unique and different personality and a huge part/theme of the game is manipulating people to get what you want, that means acting aggressive, professional or suave depending on the person. Your relationships and interactions can also influence the way a mission plays out, whether or not you’ll receive back up, determining who are going to be fighting, and what items on the black market you can purchase. The game also emphasizes dossiers and gathering intel, which gives passive combat bonuses to specific factions and helps you learn about a character’s background so that you can learn how you’re supposed to talk to them if you want them to like you. Missions offer multiple paths, approaches and options. You can also bang MOST of the chicks in one play through, if you play your cards right (this is, hands down, the best part).
Combat and controls can feel clunky, it seems like they wanted to make weapon specialization and stats like accuracy, stability and recoil matter in a third person shooter, so it forces you to ‘focus’ your cross hair on your target before you can shoot or else your shots will be all over the place.  This can make early game very annoying because your shots won’t focus fast enough, and any kind of long ranged combat becomes a pain.  The game forces boss fights, there is no stealth solution, you have to straight up fight them so it's highly reccomended that you pump up the stats in at least one weapon (fun fact pistol is over power). Regardless of the boss fights, playing stealth is generally over power, it rewards you with more stuff than a straight up commando/aggressive play, and it trivializes a lot of missions. There are 2 hacking mini-games, a word search and clicking tangled wires in a specific order. They get repetitive fast and are not really fun. The game can also be glitchy at times; there have been times when I’ve been spotted and never should have been (through a wall), times where I’ve gotten stuck in walls and had to die or reload my save, and the game had crashed on me 4 times throughout my play through.
I’d recommend it if you like the talking parts of the Dues Ex and Mass Effect or just enjoy a good story driven game. You’d have to deal with the par combat, missions and maybe a rough early game.

tl;dr If you can say "Okay, WB did some stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥ but let's see what kind of game Monolith made", and you liked Shadow of Mordor, you'll have a fine time.
To start off, obviously, WB's practices have not been spectacular leading up to the release of the game. Loot boxes in a single player game are sketchy, season passes are generally not popular, and the charity debacle has been discussed time and again. But while these are certainly bad choices, they're not AS bad as people make them out to be.
The loot boxes get a bit of reference in the game, but aside from a bit of glow in the menu, generally to indicate you have a chest you can open from something, it really doesn't affect gameplay. Honestly, most of the loot from the crates is on level with (or worse than) what you can find in the world, and the content feels balanced enough to not need them. The fourth act has a significant difficulty spike, but a lot of it is a challenge from your average captain not being a candy♥♥♥♥♥any more. With some thought and strategy, it's not that hard to get through.
Season passes are more of a preference thing. Some people like them, some don't, I personally don't care much one way or the other.
There is also the issue of the charity DLC, but I don't have anything I can contribute that hasn't been said already.
With the WB shoveling done, there's the actual game. It feels like a solid continuation of Shadow of War, once the first bit of the game is done.
(Small spoilers ahead, primarily abilities and enemies featured in the game)
Some of the abilities that you started out with in the first game require you to put points in to them here, but after that, there's a lot of new looking stuff. Each ability has upgrades, which you can only use one of at a time, allowing things like elemental damage, special effects, and quality of life improvements. Early on, you gain access to a double jump, and it feels great, for both mobility and the occasional "Oh I didn't mean to jump off of that". Later upgrades allow you to do things like summon a dragon on command (with a cooldown) and kill grunts when you counter with proper timing.
The maps each individually feel a bit smaller than the two in Shadow of Mordor (including Nurnen, which is in both games). However, there are four primary zones in the game, with smaller zones such as a city that are used intermittently, and definitely more area to play in overall. The load times also seem to be a good bit shorter in Shadow of War.
One of the new mechanics of the game is Sieging. While the first siege requires you to go through the motions of disassembling the setup as a tutorial of sorts, future sieges allow you to choose how much setup you want to go in with. Your own captains, who can be given a choice of three upgrades similarly to your abilities, will be assisting you in capturing a series of points in the siege before you go in to the keep to fight the Overlord solo. Any hostile Warchiefs left at the time of the siege will contribute upgrades to the fortress, such as fire and poison traps, and specific groups of enemies. You can kill them to remove these upgrades, or take it a step further by putting your own captains in place as Warchiefs in the fort. They have a chance to be caught (and killed) at the start of the siege, but will help you by having points in the fortress ready for capture at the start, and blowing open extra openings to the fortress. When you finally enter the keep, you bicker with the Overlord for a short bit before taking them (and some goons) on.
For better or for worse, the game follows a lot of the formula set up by Shadow of Mordor, but with pleasant additions. Ologs give a bit more variety to the grunts and captains you'll run in to, and while the side bosses don't give much more variety in mechanics than they did before, they are more interesting storywise, pitting you against Nazgul and a Balrog. The AI varies between comical and frustrating, and generally flips between smart and stupid like Shadow of Mordor, but the true trolling comes from ambushes. Certain types of captains, as well as some of those whom you've killed but aren't really dead, will come in to your most carefully laid plans to either mildly frustrate you or destroy everything you love, depending on their abilities and level. There doesn't seem to be a limitation on what mission they will attack you in, or even where, sometimes following you to areas that orcs seem to normally be incapable of reaching. This can also happen consecutively, with little to no time in between dropping one Captain and another one coming in for a chat, and can really screw with you and make your game a lot harder.
It also feels necessary to take a second to talk about the look and theme of enemies, because some of the Captains are wonderful. Someone returning after being killed with poison or having limbs removed is a good detail, but a well dressed Captain singing (mostly in rhyme) while he attempts to kill you with his guitar-axe is a magical experience.
All in all, if you can put aside the WB fiascos, Shadow of War is a fun game. If you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor, the game is definitely worth a try, and if you find yourself writing a review for the game, rate it on the gameplay, not on what the publisher did before it came out. It deserves to be mentioned, but it shouldn't be the singular thing you base your opinion of the game on.

It would be tough to not recommend this game. Everything is nearly perfect; it feels like a superior Telltale game with more exploration and choices with the setting of Alan Wake. Choices definitely feel like they matter more here than in any other game of this style.
What on the surface seems like a corny teen drama quickly evolves into something much better; the whole thing gets much more interesting and mature, and the characters are great. The visual style complements everything here well. No problems with the controls, either. The game recommends you use a controller though, which I did, so I cant speak for M+K controls.
I do have some minor gripes, though. First, I did run into a really annoying bug where the main character's mouth didn't move for about a solid 10 minutes straight right towards the end of the game. It was during an important series of events and it kinda rips you out of the moment. But other than that, I never encountered any bugs or crashes of any kind. Second, the length and pacing of the episodes is a bit inconsistent. Episodes 4 and 5 are brutally long, while 1-3 felt much more reasonable. Third, this is a game about time travel, and 95% of the time any sort of media involving time travel has to have an incredibly convoluted and confusing ending about "messing with the timeline and alternate realities." It's overdone and boring. Life is Strange does an okay job of roping you back in right before everything comes together for the big finale, but it definitely was a bit of a black mark on the whole experience.
As a whole though, Life is Strange is definitely a game I would recommend and legitimately enjoyed. I definitely will not be replaying it soon if ever due to its exhausting length (it's a slog towards the end) and due to the fact that I was relatively happy with how my choices turned out.

TL;DR: Takes place about a year after the events of Season 1 and 400 Days, a lot (if not all) of your choices in both will affect the situations and how you talk in this season (400 days not so much, mainly season 1). This one focuses on Clementine. Choices are HARD.
+ Graphics look nicer - a bit more colourful i think.
+ The continuity of things is very well done imho and its nice to know that your prior decisions still play a big role in things.
+ Great quality storytelling as is to be expected from Telltale. Manly tears were shed quite often (especially at the end *sniffle*)
+ Thought the quick time events were better this time around, also had more scenes where you can wander around a bit freely.
+ The ending is a lot less linear than the first season, from what i can see there are some drastic differences with each. Awesome, but... how will then reconcile all of them in Season 3?
+/- I think the Season 1 story of Lee and Clementine was a stronger one, this season lacked a bit of the magic of the first, but that said it is an exceptionally high bar to reach again.
- Did not really like the new UI, i don't think it should have been changed.
- Not quite as much character development as the first one imho
Overall i liked it immensely, especially the second half (chapters 3-5) and, while not quite as good as season 1, it is still one of the best choice driven narrative games i have played. An absolutely essential purchase and experience!

Can they make Season 2 still interesting after Season 1? Hell yeah they can!
This review won't be so much about the basics of the game, since it's a sequel, so I will talk more about the differences/improvements of this game. If you like to hear more about Season 1, you can read about it in my review for that game, which I REALLY recommend playing it before this game (of course). I will avoid spoilers as much as possible from now on.
In this sequel, you play as Clementine. She has aged a bit, so she's tougher and more careful about her environment. The game continues on the choices you made in Season 1. You can still make a lot of different choices, but none of them seemed out of place for her in my opinion; she's still the sweet caring girl as you knew her.
This game is way more cinematic, and by that I mean the cutscenes look more different. They're taken from more different angles, the (face) animations are way smoother and the music can be intense. It also has way less glitchy animations, for example: if someone was staggering in Season 1, their model would shake/trip a bit. And in Season 2, I've only seen it once or twice in the whole playthrough, so that's a lot better.
Another difference between the games, is that in Season 1, you could investigate a lot of things, walk around and talk with other people between the cutscenes. In Season 2, they have limited this a lot. It didn't really bother me that much, since the story and the decisions you make within the cutscenes are still good, but it could've been a bit more I guess. Also, the story was more diverse in Season 1 and had more emotional moments, but that doesn't mean Season 2 doesn't have them as well.
Although this game is shorter than Season 1, it's still really good. It has a lot of improvements, the story is awesome and it feels like a true sequel. I liked both of them, since I see it as one big story. If you played Season 1, I definitely recommend getting Season 2.
