Invisible Inc.'s gameplay is a good implementation of a great cabal of ideas. It is turn based and all the interactions are fairly clear and deterministic, so it's easy to play in that sense. It is a stealth game, so it has the classic mechanics of running away, hiding, and using gadgets to set traps. Also, it is randomly generated and loseable, which removes the chore of replaying stages over and over again like in a traditional stealth game.
It also adapts those mechanics in a novel way, since the game focuses more on stealing money and gear in preparation for a final mission than clearing specific objectives in individual missions. This adds a nice risk management element, and valuation is required to know what to steal. It also has loads of characters and customization options, all of which are very welcome.
So I really recommend this game. That said, it's not without its flaws. Unlike most modern strategy games, most of invisible's flaws are related to gameplay and are very difficult to even notice. It took me 70 hours of gameplay to really notice anything wrong with it, which is an incredible testament to its design. I strongly recommend this game, and if you are thinking of buying it maybe it's best not to read about its flaws, and just stop reading now. But otherwise, here:
-Character balance is bad. Some characters are miles and light years easier to win with, some are much harder to win with. Same thing with the programs you can start with, once you realize which ones are good, you realize they are good by a huuuuge margin. I guess you can still play with the bad characters/programs, if you want.
-The game has LONG arcs. One playthrough is something absurd like 150 minutes (even longer with the DLC), which is very long considering you should be replaying it a lot. As a result you get feedback as to if your strategies are working very slowly, and a loss will cost you many minutes of thought.
-The game's risk management... Well, it took me 78 hours to realize this, because of the second problem, but it turns out that the final mission is very doabe with little more than the equipment that you start the game with, if you pick the right starting agents and programs (even on the hardest difficulties). So the idea of trading risk for resources... If you are playing optimally just do the least risky thing if you've picked a good enough starting team.
Anyways, in spite of its flaws, the game delivered almost a hundred hours of high-quality enjoyment to me, so I strongly recommend it.

Age of Gladiators could be one of the menu screens on a higher rent title. The game is largely carried by the theme and lacks character depth, plot, and visuals. That doesn't mean I'm not enjoying it though. AoG is pure management: Your gladiators to fight for you. you hire staff to find and maintain your gladiators. If one of your good gladiators dies, making money becomes difficult. When making money becomes difficult, things start to go wrong. Gladiators have a morale system and may leave if you don't pay them, let their comrades die, and a variety of other circumstances. All of that sets up for a pretty cool game (the higher rent title for which this is the menu system).
Remember those gladiators and support staff? Stat monkeys. Staff are litterally just functions of two stats depending on if they are (talent) scouts, trainers, doctors, or smiths. But, this is a management sim, so you probibly care less about Dr NPC's relationship with his wife and more about how his ability to dislodge a spear from your gladiator's spleen compares to another doctor, and a numeric score acomplishes that. (note gladiator injuries can be that specific but only add a mod on recovery time).
Gladiators are also mostly stats and one of about a dozen generic portraits. Battles play out basically as turn-by turn dice rolls, which makes sense from removing you from control of the gladiator's actions to the coach betting money on him/her on the sidelines. (the hypothetical higher rent game would really add something if battles were visualized, especially if it were tied into the betting system so you could place prop bets as the battle played out).
So why am I recomending a game that my major comment about is that I wish there were more to it? Well, that's it really: my problem isn't that it's a bad game, it's a good game that could be a great game. Could be a 30-40$ gladiator game that I could rave about rather than a 10$ game that is merely pretty decent. It is very possible to fail at this game, and if you do it is probobly your own fault. That is the sign of a good game, when poor descisions have consequences and good decisions have rewards. It's pretty rewarding when you start being able to take down opponent's top fighter's, or looking at their roster and trying to decide if you could take them at the next fight where they are likely to drop their top fighter or if you have to cringe and let the opportunity to make bank (or lose everything) pass you by. There isn't all that much to this game (compared to what I would like it to be), but what is there works pretty well.

Age of Gladiators is a first game from a 1 man development team. Basically it's a spreadsheet management simulator hidden behind an easy to use and clear graphic user interface, and while it can seem simple on the surface, there is a lot of hidden depth when it comes to min/maxing your gladiator's stats to get the best results. Scouting potential new fighters and rival boss stables is essential. Learning what stats have what effects is also important. The first few playthroughs can be brutally difficult until you learn how to manage your budget. In addition to managing your fighters and their development, you also manage their living conditions, hire staff, buy weapons and armor, send gladiators on side quests, manage your expenses between fights, try to increase your reputation to become rich and famous, and that's all before you get to the fights and the gambling!
The developer is constantly releasing updates, many suggested by the player base, and what excites me the most is the potential this game has. History and facts could be added via an encylopedia, the fights could move from text based to 3D, your stables could move from sliders to a mini city builder, many more side quests could be added, multi-gladiator fights could be added, creation of gladiator events sponsored by you ... so much potential in either this or the sequel.
The game is not perfect, if you are expecting an action game involving gladitorial combat, this isn't it. It's more like Football Manager for ancient Rome. The learning curve is steep, but once mastered, becomes much easier. However, the game and it's setting is original, it's not expensive even at full price, and can suck you in so that the hours disappear while you have that "just one more turn."

As a backer of the Kickstarter for this game, I was given early access to Act I. So I won't spoil any of the story, but I will say that this is a very good adventure game experience, on par with the classics of the Golden Era (80s & 90s). I've been waiting for these games to come back and what better way to re-usher them in than with a brand new game from Tim Schafer himself, an adventure star who designed the likes of Full Throttle, Grim Fandango, and Day of the Tentacle. He also had a hand in designing the first two Monkey Island games by Ron Gilbert. These are adventure gaming classics. I've only played half the game so far, but the other half is coming in a few months as of this writing. That said here are my thoughts:
The Good:
-Story. Very intriguing. I was very invested in both the girl and boy's characters and was quite interested to see where their stories would take them and how they'd eventually intertwine. The experience was not unrewarding and definitely wasn't a disappointment!
-Writing. Tim's humour is expectedly very present in the game. His trademark sarcasm and wit are strewn throughout the dialogue and even into some of the look of the locations. It's a very bizarre and funny world Tim has created, but not too bizarre. Just recognizable enough to not seem too far out and unrelatable.
-Art style. The 2D painted artwork style is fantastic. I was initially skeptical in the beginning of Bagel's art style, once I'd seen some of his work in one of the hidden backer forum threads on the Double Fine forums. But I have to say that my skepticism was misplaced. This game has a lovely quality and very pleasing aesthetic. The artwork truly does resemble a beautiful painting come to life. And despite this it is absolutely brimming with detail in every scene. It's beautiful to just sit and watch, but it also works very well for the gaming experience and story. Some of the girl's locations actually reminded me of Curse of Monkey Island, even though the styles are wildly different. While the boy's space ship is unlike anything I've ever seen for a space ship. It's all very unique and with just a dash of familiarity in it as well.
-Animation. Truly charming and natural. Everything seemed so alive. Not like puppets on strings, but real characters that were moving on their own. Special care was given to these animations. Every one showed amazing attention to detail and added a great deal of character to everything that moved. Every character in the game had their own unique persona that spoke volumes about their motivations and intentions. One of my favourite aspects of the design of the game!
-Voice acting. Top notch. Every voice puts a life and an identity into their characters in a way that binds them to their personas where I could not justify turning voices off and just reading subtitles. The voices are truly special and unique and are really part of the experience in a huge way. So don't mute them.
-Soundtrack. Peter McConnell did a fantastic job with the soundtrack. The themes are very fitting and atmospheric, yet the themes for the boy and girl and their locales are separate and distinct from eachother, as should be expected. Peter doesn't disappoint. As a backer, I also received the soundtrack to the game which I immediately put straight on my player for my long drives to work. And it's played by a live orchestra. Can't beat that. Truly effective work. Bravo, Peter.
The "Wish-It-Was-Better":
-Puzzles. The heart of the adventure game experience (combined with story). There
some great puzzles in this game, but as a veteran adventure gamer I was expecting a bit more of a challenge. Especially in the beginning, the puzzles were fairly simple. I assume to ease in new or rusty players. Luckily these simple "tutorial" puzzles didn't last long at all end began to become more complex soon enough, to my relief. As long as I was thorough, however, I never missed anything. Years of adventure gaming has taught me to leave no stone unturned and to keep a mental map image in my head of where certain characters, objects, and puzzles were located. This made it easier to deduce when and where I'd be needing certain objects or what objects I might need in certain areas. I ended up acquiring all of the objects I needed ahead of time before I needed to use them, which sped up the gameplay a bit. But that's due to my obsessive style of exploration. Other gamers might not share this and thus wouldn't run into the same problem, which would probably extend the experience for them. There was no so-called "moon logic" in this game, which many classic adventure games were infamous for. Personally, I never had a problem with extremely hard puzzles and enjoyed them, but many others (especially nowadays) don't share this feeling. Luckily, they won't be disappointed with this game as a result.
-Length. Keeping in mind that I have only played Act I, I still have to say it was somewhat shorter than I expected. If Act I is truly an exact halfway point in the game, then I can only hope that the puzzles in Act II are much more difficult. I wish it was longer. I'll have to put it away for a year or two after completing Act II and come back to it to see just how long the game actually is with a fresh perspective from beginning to end.
Overall, the world of Broken Age is an immensely pleasing and fun one to live in and explore. The story is gripping and mysterious. By the end of Act I you are left wondering just
in the world is going on! It left me wanting more, but in a good way. Luckily we
be getting more! I encountered no bugs whatsoever. The game played extremely smoothly and there were no unexpected quirks. I was finding myself missing the skip dialogue function from the older LucasArts SCUMM engine games by pressing '.'. Instead it only lets you skip entire "cutscenes" of dialogue. Not a huge issue, as there never really was anything that I needed to skip specifically to get at something new from a repeated conversation. I would like a "retro" filter shortcut for the game to make it seem all pixelated and 90s looking if only for the novelty. ;)
I highly recommend this game to those who enjoy a good story in gaming and those who appreciate a work of art. Newcomers to the adventure genre who are mildly curious but fearful of ominously difficult puzzles needn't worry as everything is intuitive and logical, but still challenging enough I feel to give you a great experience without seeming too easy or too short. Adventure veterans may find the challenge a little lackluster, but what little it may lack in puzzle challenge it makes up for in pretty much everything else. It won't be the next puzzle masterpiece adventure game, but it is surely a very good start to the great Adventure Resurgence! It appeals to old and new fans alike and, I feel, is the perfect bridge to link the two together. Take us onward, Double-Fine! Here's hoping for more adventures after Broken Age!

There are some downsides though.  It is short.  Expect it to take you three hours in its current state.  When the second half comes out, assuming it is about the same length, the total play time to complete the game will probably be around six hours.  Adventure games have always tended to be on the short side, so I expected this going in, but I still wish it was a bit longer.
I also ran into a few crash bugs.  One room consistently crashed for me, and I had to delete and reinstall the game to fix it.  The game also quit to desktop at another random point, though that did not require anything more than a reboot.
Over all I love it.  I can't wait to play the second half!   8.5/10

Many people claim that it's the most difficult and the most frustrating game they have ever played. SO..if you aren't into rogue-lite and bullet hell, you can stop reading right now. If proceduraly generated content is not your thing, or you are not particularly skilled FPS player (even thought that entire genre), it may be hard for you to really enjoy chaotic nature of Nuclear Throne.
However…if things mentioned above check all your boxes, and you feel strong enough to overcome first several hours full of frustration, then feel free to continue reading.
Organized chaos (the good)
There are many thing that I like about Nuclear Throne. The thing that stands out the most to me is not the sheer amount of content and possibilities, but the way they've tied it all together. The game has many ways how to keep you moving and thinking, and punishes you for every misstep you make. This is the level of depth and that special "something", that will have you coming back over and over again.
Despite the random nature of the game, I found Nuclear Throne to be more skill based, than, let's say BoI or Risk of Rain. Sure, those games are a lot of fun…when you get the right drops. At least, that's my take on it. Nuclear Throne takes part of that problem away. You won't ever be completely OP, because the game is so unfair, that mutations don't make all that much of a difference…and they certainly won't get you to the throne by themself. And if you're good enough, even with bad build, you can have a great run. You're getting better yourself, your skills get better. Doesn't matter if RNG has a bad day.
Also, let's not forget to mention sound design, that is perfect. Everything, and I mean everything in this game, has it's own sound. Once you'll get into, it will help you a great deal to understand what the hell is going on on the screen. I can't stress enough how important this is in the game, where you can get killed by something you can't see at the moment. Also, soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing great, and I still listen to it from time to time even when not playing.
The last big possitive, that is kind of hard to describe, is the overall gameplay and the feel of the game. That's something that Vlambeer excells at, and you will know what I mean if you've played Luftrausers or Super Crate Box. Controls are tight, everything feels right even though you are not sure why. There's something very visceral about the wa it plays. And the most important thing - the gameplay is fun, even though you are not very good at the game yet.
"It's not fair, it's not right." (the bad)
It's little bit hard for me to talk about what's bad here, because I see the game differently after the time I've spend playing it. But I'll try my best.
The biggest downside to this game may be the time you have to put in, to actually get skilled enough and be able to see more, than just first couple of levels. That's pretty funny, because this is actually game that you can play, when you have just a couple of minutes to kill. Playthoughs last 10-15 minutes, of course they can strech to hour or more, as you get better and better. To fully explain what I'm trying to say here - I've beaten throne for the first time after playing the game for 60 hours. SIXTY. That just may be too much for some. That said, I'm someone who can get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥very much, very quickly…so if it wasn't fun for me to try and beat the game, I would ditch it half a year ago.
Also, the whole game is locked on 30 FPS, which may seem like a terrible idea for a game as frantic as this one. Not only that, but there are times, where the framerate dips even lower, because there's just too much stuff going on at the same time. Now, I know this may sound stupid to you, but I don't mind any of that. Freezeframes are an actual feature of the game (no, really). They are actually helpful, as they give you those fractions of the second to realize what's going on and act accordingly.
BUT, I know some may have problems with that, so that's why I'm telling you about it. Also, I don't know what's up with that 4:3 format.
At the time of writing this, we are at update 97. As of now, there are still some bugs; also daily/weekly modes are pretty much unplayable, since leaderboards don't work. That said, I believe that Vlambeer will fix this as soon as they can. Nuclear Throne is imo one of the best examples of Early Access done right…
Last, but not least - the game is ridiculously unfair at times. You will encounter situations that seem absolutely hopeless, because they really are. And even though the game lets you try different play styles, some just won't work very well…and that's a bit frustrating, to say the least.
Conclusion
Nuclear Throne is the best game in it's genre imho, and my personal GOTY. If you're looking for a hardcore shooter, that will provide you with endless hours of fun and tears, for the price, this is the best deal. Despite being procedurally generated, it doesn't feel completely random and your success actually depends on your skills, and not just RNG. However, it will take you a great amount of time to reach the throne, and that might just be too much to swallow for some.
Nuclear Throne covers the surprising amount of depth behind it's cute, yet weird pixel-art aestetic. But once you get into it, every beaten boss will be one of the most rewarding videogame experiences. You'll try again and again…and with the amount of content and replayability, you definitely can! But as I've mentioned before, this game is not easy, and it sure as hell isn't fair. You have to be the special kind of masochist to truly understand the beauty of Nuclear Throne.
Rating: 9/10
+ amount of content and replayability
+ fun, arcade-like gameplay
+ guns and mutations
+ sound design
- daily/weekly not working (at the moment)
- occasional bugs
- sometimes ridiculously unfair

I wont lie to you as this game is far from what Civ 5 is like, and at first is a bit challenging with how they introduced a way to combat hoarding wonders with needing specific locations to build them, and brought districts to the table that are essential to building a grand empire for any win condintion. Each of this new additions, including a variety of others, really changes the pace of Civ 6 from any other Civ game, and at first I was skeptical as it took me awhile to get the hang of it, but once I learned how to build my districts according to the way I wanted to win, it was surprisingly alot of fun.
The graphics in Civ 6 is very well done, but sided more on the cartoony side though I'm not s against it as the A.I have so much more life to them in both units, and the leaders themselves. Though I would like to address how the A.I have some new tricks called hidden agendas that can be very annoying, like Cleopatras is likeing people with large armies, and if you don't have one she bombards you with snarky soments. This just adds character to the game in my opinion as I grow enough hatred towards Egypt to build an army large enough to conquer her entire empire.
With city placement its no longer just about finding spots with good growth, luxury resources, etc..., you also have to be wary on where districts are going to go, and can you build the right wonder in this city? This is the make it, or break it with every leader as location is even more important then anything else for if you dont have the necessary land to build your empire can not grow.
Some other fun new implements to the game is how caravans now automatically build roads when sent out on trading missions though the down side is this is only one of two ways to build roads now as the other is with engineers. What about the workers you ask, well thats the next fun item on our list as the workers now have charges to them, and once all the charges are up they disappear, but that dosent mean you need to spend multiple charges on one improvement infact once you decide on an inprovment for that tile it will automatically be built with no wait time, so you must decide which resource tile is most important.
Lastly, as I could go on forever, I want to mention the win conditions with faith, yes faith, being the first. Faith in Civ 6 is vastly different from 5 as you can actually win with it, but it is extremely difficult. From the beginning of any game faith supplies us with paragons that have nice bonus to our early game, and once a religion is made even more bonus's are granted, but thats usally where faith tends to drop off as we progress through the game. With the introduction of religious districts faith now has more building options, and can really speed up the process of converting other civ's, though that is alot easier said then done.
Science victory still requires space ship parts to be built, but takes alot longer then you would think as all the parts cost a ton of production with needing a ton of science just to unlock the parts, and need the new space project district to build them, and I would say is the second hardest victory condition.

War, war never changes, but I guess we have incampent districts now that are required to give units promotions instanly, and give and extra layer of defence. I would say War is the easisest victory condition depending on who you start with.
Culture also requires thearter districts to hold multiple pieces of art to prduce enough tourism if you remember that from Civ 5, and can be realitvly hard to combat if left alone. Culture I would say is the second easiest way to win.
TLDR: thumbs up, recommend buying when on sale as you never know if this game might be for you as it was for me.

My problem with Civ 6 is that it is too repetitive. It seems like nowadays whenever they add a new civ they are guarunteed a pretty trashy unique tile improvement or building that is extremely limited in use and doesn't really add anything special to the civ, and it seems like all of the unique abilities now are just 'extra (insert yield) for adjacency bonuses next to (insert land feature here)'. There is no variety in the game, and I am tired of looking at the same old boring Cleopatra and Frederick Barbarosa every game.
CIvilization 5 was better in my opinion because each civ had an extremely different unique ability, from Morocco's extra gold for trade and Babylon's free Great Scientist. The games felt much more fun, as it took more strategy to beat and counter the several different civs in the game, because they were all extremely varied in playstyle and strengths. Another thing that I liked about Civ 5 compared to Civ 6 is that the games felt a lot more involved and interesting, and getting the victory in the end felt like much more of a challenge, as the AI or another player would always be right at your tail threatening to win another victory type, leading to some extremely fun and close games. Winning in Civ 6 however feels too much like a chore, as the victories themselves are extremely boring and tedious, and the AI is either never competitive or way ahead of you in everything, and the games feel like they are decided long before it actually ends. Getting a science victory or religious victory in this game is extremely boring and tedious, as the theological combat mechanic is bland and uninteresting and the micromanaging of buying the missionaries and spreading the religion is too boring. Civ 6 has some interesing ideas, but they are executed extremely poorly and they fail to capture any sort of interest from the players, i.e. the extreme inactivity in the Workshop compared to Civ 5.
It's a great game no doubt about it and a classic game too!

A truly engaging title that allows you to either create and manage your own space agency, or simply mess around in sandbox mode and explore your creativity. Although, far from just letting you fly ships into space, this game also challenges you to take into consideration your allocation of resources, atmospheric heating, drag, Delta V, gravity and a whole multitude of other Newtonian laws which incidentally can/will teach you an awful lot about orbital physics & mathematics if you have the inclination to to so. This surprised me even when playing it in mid-2013 during its early access.
Now, this game is for the most part a simulator of sorts (one that is initially very difficult to play) and as such will have a slight learning curve & requires a little patience to get used to, especially considering the exploration into aerodynamics and rocketry, but as someone who has more than 1,450 hours logged I can promise the rewards are more than worth it.

Quick-review for previous Civ V-  players: it's now worth it to buy this game. I'm an old fan from the series, this game has a LOT of potencial but needs some improvments to get a gold medal. And probably many changes will come with the Rise and Fall expansion.
Here are some things that i think need to change. I wish the devs read it:
- Difficulty: AI has improved but, still, i'd like them to be a little bit smarter, specially at the Immortal dificulty. Civilization V was very challenging at the Immortal level. Basically you go Sumeria or Schythia and do what the Mongols did on previous games: conquer everything with your horses, then it's just city building at mid game, and a little bit effort to beat the top opponent. Then, the game is won. The AI isn't as treacherous as it was in Civ V. In fact, the AI is stupid. I was 3 eras above the Nubia and they declared war to one of my city states. Basically they gave me permission to wipe them out of the planet without receiving warmongering penalties! It was Jet bombers and modern armours vs pikemen, crossbowmen and catapults. Even with my civ aside, they were getting a good beat of the city state that was taking almost no damage from their 20 unit army. Australia was the second top civ after mine and they declared war without planning. Like, they had no real invasion force and i just conquered them all.
- Early envoys: i've played a game where i met first 2 military and 3 commercial city states, so, basically i had +4 production for military units and +12 gold to support a huge army early on. There should be a limit. You could only send envoys to the first N city states(maybe letting you chose which ones, if you discover them first). It shifts the game balance a lot, it should be balanced.
- Tech three: right now you could build facories and launch rockets and build robots without knowing how to print a book! That's ridiculous! I like how the techs follow a linear branch. but, at certain point, some branches should need previous ones like the printing tech. It happens with steel but should be shortened early on. This also lets one advance quickly over eras, so, adjusting it would balance more the game. It's still 720 AD on a Immortal level and i'm already at the industrial era, almost reaching the modern.
- Consequences: i kinda like you being able to conquer cities in the begining of the game without heavy penalities. I don't like ZERO penalities as it is right now. You take Schytia or Sumeria and rush with their horses early on and you can conquer every neighbor without consequences at all! I think there should be at least a light wermonger penalty here.

Framed as a disturbing yet cutesy retelling of the Bible story in which Abraham is asked by God to kill his own son, 'The Binding Of Isaac' includes almost all of the elements you loved about losing yourself in those old randomised dungeons. The striking resemblance to Zelda's NES years (inclusive of hearts, arrows, coins, etc.) is twisted into the art style of Edmund McMillen and accompanied by a hauntingly retro soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky (both having previously worked on Super Meat Boy). The dungeons are peppered randomly with the variety of 40+ enemies, 30+ bosses, 130+ items, and plenty more to make each game unique. As environments and items change with each game there is no feeling of grinding, or impulse towards memorised repetiton to reach 'fresh' ground.
Grotesque, hysterical, addictive - 'The Binding Of Isaac' revisits Shigeru Miyamoto's original dungeons with a headfull of bad acid... in the best way possible.

The story is gripping and the way that it branches really gives the player the power of choices that matter. You really feel like the decisions you make have an impact on the game world and that there are consequences, both positive and negative, for the things you do and say. Some people may not like the dialog system, but I think its absolutely genius! Limiting the time you have to choose dialog responses makes you have to think on your feet and pay close attention to detail. Not to mention, it allows for great replayability of the game. The characters are also really well constructed, each with their own personality, likes and dislikes, that you have to find out to successfully navigate conversations. Voice acting is pretty good too.
Another large aspect of the game is the RPG element: choosing your skills, specializations, weapon loadout and customizations. Although the interface could use some work, it isn't the most cumbersome of console-ported interfaces. That said, I think the mechanics are well done. The skill tree is reminiscent of Mass Effect 2 except you have more individual skills to choose from which is nice. I've read that the skills can be unbalanced and lead to "power-leveling", but I've chosen to ignore reading what particular skills those are because I like finding out for myself. I'm going to defend the game here and say that unbalanced skills in an RPG is perfectly acceptable; Of course not every decision you make is going to be the right one and that is the beauty of having choices--having consequences to those choices.
The weapons customization is also slick and adds a good bit of depth to gameplay since you can customize your weapon mods to suit your play style. For example adding a silencer may decrease damage but gives you the advantage of stealth.
I also like the experience/achievements system which rewards you differently based on your approaches to situations in the game. I never felt like I was missing out by not making a particular choice, because the game would reward me either way, but the rewards would differ.
Now for the bad parts: Enemy AI is lacking. For example, anytime you sprint, guards have the uncanny ability to hone in on your location. Also, this isn't Splinter Cell: Enemy bodies disappear almost instantly and guards don't really get suspicious when you kill their friends as long as they don't directly see you doing it (or hear you). Also, the alarm system is kind of broken. The game works on a checkpoint system so even if you trigger the alarm in one checkpoint, there are no negative consequences for the following checkpoint area. This means the game is very forgiving when it comes to stealth. Trigger the alarm? No problem, just bust out your assault rifle and kill everybody in the area then continue to the next checkpoint.
The other large annoyance is the save system. The game uses checkpoints for saves and overrides each checkpoint save when you reach a new one. This can be frustrating when you want to go back in time, only to find your last manual save was 2 days ago because your checkpoints were overwritten. Now when I first found out there was no ability to quick save, I thought it was a stupid design decision. But now, I see that it falls inline with the rest of the game's design philosophy: You're choices matter and there are consequences to your actions. Allowing you to quick save whenever you want takes away from the gravity of your actions since you can redo them infinitely without consequence. Overall if I could change it, I would keep the checkpoint system, but have it save each checkpoint separately.
That said, I think the save system and the poor AI are excusable, given the very engrossing story and the very well executed branching and dialog system. That's not to say that the action and actual gameplay are not fun in their own right, just that the former elements steal the show. I'm sad to hear Alpha Protocol received such poor reception from the press and initial users, but I hope others will give this diamond in the rough a chance. And just hopefully, Obsidian will be given the chance to do a sequel.

I'll start off by saying this game was an unexpected gem. Alpha Protocol is one of the best RPGs I have every played. The premise of the game is original, the dialogue is superb, and the story kept me interested. I felt that the characters were quite easy to get attached to after a few dialogues. There is one major flaw this game has, and that is the combat and stealth systems.
Combat and stealth, or just interacting with enemies in general, is extremely clunky in this game. At times it is frustratingly bad (for example, shooting enemies from <20 ft away and missing with half the magazine), but in my opinion the excellent dialogue, story telling, and decision making all make up for it. As other reviewers have said, another notable aspect of this game is that the decisions you make in this game actually change the way the story unfolds, unlike most games where they only change the ending. I think this gives the game more than a little additional replay value.
Other notes: the graphics are excellent compared to other games released around the same time. The sounds are of high quality. The voice acting is great, in my opinion. The level design is rather simple, but it works. The AI are pretty stupid, but that can be a pro or con depending on how you look at it.
If you are looking for a game that is rich in story and is addictive, this is the game for you. If you are looking for a combat oriented game with developed combat mechanics, you may want to try something else. I have to take 1 off for the crappy gameplay, but this game still gets a 9/10 from me.

I've power played this game for 24 hours already on Nemesis and not because of any reason other than I couldn't stop playing.
Shadow of War is a better, slicker game than Shadow of Mordor was. Similar to Shadow of Mordor there is a first act where your domination abilities are limited however this time around I did not mind as the Minas Ithil storyline was good and kept me interested.
The skill system is better, the loot system is better, the Nemesis system is expanded with much more enemy variety and best of all there appears to be a lot more playable content than the first game.  Also Drakes are a hoot.
As for folks saying it is just the first game again I disagree as someone that played through and beat the first game (for the second time) just 6 months ago - Shadow of War is the refinement of that game and superior. But if you didn't really like the first game... don't expect a revolution. I can understand folks that think it's more of the same the same way each Assassin's Creed game is more of the same. On some level, it's the same basic game system but you should know that before you buy it.
I'm running on a 970 at 3440x1440 and it stays mostly above 30fps with a few tweaks down from High - par for the course with this card and UW display. Unlike some titles I didn't have to hack anything to get the UW to work right.
As for cons?  Yes I've been ambushed tons of times - my favourite was when I picked up a Godorian Artifact and one started to taunt me over it - and I've died my fair share or had my prey escape but honestly it hasn't really annoyed me like it did in the first game. It can be frustrating when you send a favourite Captain into the pits and he loses or when you miss a dodge prompt and get destroyed by a nasty Captain build but that's the nature of the game... death doesn't touch you, it just sets you back.
As for a real con - the gold and mithral loot crates can be ignored with no real impact aside from the online fortress challenge stuff that is purely extra. That said I am the guy who will buy a few here and there just to get a cool captain upgrade but not at the prices they are set at... 5x too expensive.
Bottom Line: Shadow of War is my new favourite Revenge Simulator and one of the best Mordor experiences out there.
I'll leave with a pro-tip; dominated Captains will turn on you no matter how much you buff them if you kill their Blood Brother right in front of them... who knew?

Story is a man becomes unemployed starts feeling inadequate and magically gets sucked into 8 bit gaming/console. The game is a tribute to Giana Sisters, Wonderboy in Monsterland, Psycho Fox, Rick Dangerous, Megaman, Super Mario Bros and Sonic the Hedgehog as it has an element of all those games in one way or another, still it has a significant feel to it, to be an independent title.
The sound can be grating and the graphics slightly cheesy/corny, but that is the way it is designed, again giving homage to that era of gaming. The game's strength is it's game-play. There are five worlds, 56 levels, 300 hidden locations, and 50 secret coins to find in order to get the TRUE ending.
The game literally is what saved the designer Ramus from unemployment and gave him the ability to support his family somewhat, so this game is close to his heart. You can tell this as the designer is by no means finished with it and is still continuing to update it. He has redesigned levels and is planning to add achievements and a 'secret finder' tally.
It's the most fun I have had with a game for a long while. It's challenging and enjoyable finding all those secret places. If you love games like Mario and your one of those people who has to get every coin. GET IT!

I had basically sworn-off Day One game purchases - prefer to see some credible reviews before buying - but on this I figured "I enjoyed the first one a lot - how badly could they screw up a sequel on the same game engine?"
Turns out - a lot. Combat is both stupid and stupidly annoying now. Feels like the game is playing me instead of me playing the game.
I would have happily paid for and enjoyed a new game consisting of nothing more than a new map using exactly the same game mechanics as SoM - instead they dumbed-down an already geared-toward-consolers combat system to make it blisteringly idiotic.
I understand that you unlock new moves and combos as you progress - and that adds complexity - I guess my mine gripe is the auto-targeting of enemies whether you're facing them or not.
Part of the challenge of these types of melee-oriented games (Assassin's Creed series, Mad Max, the first Batman) is maintaining situational awareness so you can time your attacks, blocks and dodges and build up your hit streaks or land combos.
In this game, you can literally do nothing but close your eyes and hit the left mouse button for as long as it takes to kill 30 (regular) orcs.  I actually went into the options to see if there was a way to turn the auto-targeting off, because not having to maintain situational awareness removes a lot of the challenge from the combat.
I'm a moron for buying this on Day One. Pick it up on the first massively-discounted sale if you have to, but don't be a moron like me and pay full price for this.

Invisible Inc.'s gameplay is a good implementation of a great cabal of ideas. It is turn based and all the interactions are fairly clear and deterministic, so it's easy to play in that sense. It is a stealth game, so it has the classic mechanics of running away, hiding, and using gadgets to set traps. Also, it is randomly generated and loseable, which removes the chore of replaying stages over and over again like in a traditional stealth game.
It also adapts those mechanics in a novel way, since the game focuses more on stealing money and gear in preparation for a final mission than clearing specific objectives in individual missions. This adds a nice risk management element, and valuation is required to know what to steal. It also has loads of characters and customization options, all of which are very welcome.
So I really recommend this game. That said, it's not without its flaws. Unlike most modern strategy games, most of invisible's flaws are related to gameplay and are very difficult to even notice. It took me 70 hours of gameplay to really notice anything wrong with it, which is an incredible testament to its design. I strongly recommend this game, and if you are thinking of buying it maybe it's best not to read about its flaws, and just stop reading now. But otherwise, here:
-Character balance is bad. Some characters are miles and light years easier to win with, some are much harder to win with. Same thing with the programs you can start with, once you realize which ones are good, you realize they are good by a huuuuge margin. I guess you can still play with the bad characters/programs, if you want.
-The game has LONG arcs. One playthrough is something absurd like 150 minutes (even longer with the DLC), which is very long considering you should be replaying it a lot. As a result you get feedback as to if your strategies are working very slowly, and a loss will cost you many minutes of thought.
-The game's risk management... Well, it took me 78 hours to realize this, because of the second problem, but it turns out that the final mission is very doabe with little more than the equipment that you start the game with, if you pick the right starting agents and programs (even on the hardest difficulties). So the idea of trading risk for resources... If you are playing optimally just do the least risky thing if you've picked a good enough starting team.
Anyways, in spite of its flaws, the game delivered almost a hundred hours of high-quality enjoyment to me, so I strongly recommend it.

Alan Wake is an interesting 3rd person action game featuring intense-yet-flawed gameplay, thankfully held up by the gripping, 'Twin Peaks' style plot.
In an unusual choice of protagonist, you play as an author suffering from writer's block. You're taken on a holiday by your ever-supportive wife, but things start to go a bit wonky. Before you know it, the whole place is falling apart, your wife has been eaten by a lake, and you keep finding pages from a novel you don't remember writing. Between the episodic nature, and the overall presentation, this is a game that feels like it wishes it was a TV show.
In terms of gameplay, Alan Wake is a solid 3rd-person action game, but it's let down by a lack of variety across the board. There are scarcely half a dozen different types of enemies, and five weapons (two of which are shotguns), of which only two can be held simultaneously (although the pistol can never be replaced, leaving the player with very limited choice).
The gameplay revolves around the concept of having to burn away the 'darkness' around an enemy with a flashlight, much like armour, before you can harm them with physical weaponry. This is an excellent concept in itself, but by the end of the game it feels extremely worn. With every enemy you encounter, you'll have to follow the same routine: get far enough away to burn them with the light, then put them down with a handful of bullets. I cannot think of a single exception to this from start to finish, even including prominent antagonists.
Aside from being extremely repetitive, the game suffers from the play-style enforced by this mechanic. In a game which wants you to feel panicked while you run for your life, you're constantly forced to stop and stand still while you tediously point your flashlight at yet another enemy. And yes - by and large, this is the only possible tactic.
You might think that running away would be a good choice, especially given the thriller/horror tone of the game, but you have an extremely limited running ability, and the enemies run faster than you. Making a desperate break away from a group of enemies turns into an exercise in frustration as Wake puffs and pants like an asthmatic, before being set upon, exhausted, by the same group of enemies you were trying to run away from in the first place.
Alan Wake's saving grace is the plot and the atmosphere it generates. I expected nothing less from the studio which created Max Payne (and there are a handful of knowing winks to Payne within this game), and Remedy really knocked it out of the park here. I was genuinely gripped by the story, which is split into six 'episodes' in the style of a TV show. The daytime segments, where you are given more free reign to explore the environment, are particularly excellent.
If you enjoy being sucked into a game's world, Alan Wake will not disappoint, provided you can slog through the gameplay to reach the next bit of story. The only real let-down here is the lip-syncing on the character models, which is laughably poor for a game of this time.
Part-way into the game, you're given perhaps the greatest spectacle that Alan Wake has to offer - the signal flare. It's hardly surprising, given that this is a game focused so intently on light/dark contrast, but the flares look absolutely stunning. Having obtained them, the most effective tactic when encountering a group of enemies becomes to hunker down.
Pick away the shields of the strongest enemies first, waiting for the group as a whole to get close enough. Once they're within arms reach, pop a flare and watch as the screen erupts into ruby red pyrotechnics. Even with the repetitive nature of the overall game, I never got tired of the almost messianic sound and visuals of the flare - Alan Wake's true saviour (aside from the plot).
The game also has a number of driving sections, which provide a generally enjoyable change of pace. At worst, they were short enough to not cause any problems. At best, they reminded me of racing over the sand in Half-Life 2. The number of replacement cars scattered throughout the levels does, however, make me wonder if there's a chronic problem with people abandoning perfectly good cars by the roadside in America's north-west...
So, as a game, Alan Wake is mediocre at best. If you're looking for a horror game full of scares, or solid 3rd person action, this is not the game for you. But would I otherwise recommend it? Absolutely. For me, it all comes down to the plot, and how easily I can become absorbed in a game's environment and characters. Remedy did a great job on that.
The real problem with Alan Wake is that it really feels like Remedy wanted to make a TV show, and accidentally made a game. Given that their upcoming game, Quantum Break, is reported to have an accompanying TV show, I can only hope they get the balance right the next time around.
I recommend this game for anyone who likes to play games that aren't garbage.

So I'm giving this review another go, seeing as to how I've been trying a whole lot more platformers since my last review, which sounded very unforgiving.
Unfortunately, my statement still stands that I can't recommend this game to anyone I know.
Last time I reviewed this, I couldn't exactly put my finger as to why I couldn't get into this. I wondered if my bar of expectation was too high, especially since this game had a nice percentage of positive reviews from the community, and that I just expect too much from indie platformers.
But after playing games like  "You Have to Win the Game", as well as the more well-known "Super Meat Boy", I can safely say this game is too dragged out, punishing you for mistakes harsher than it should.
I understand that half the fun and adventure comes from learning your own mistakes, but as you progress, the zones get longer and harder. And personally, the zones get too long for me to even quickly remember what I've done wrong on my second try on that zone. Sometimes, the game just punishes you for not even being psychic.
Honestly, how was I supposed to know I need to jump onto a safety block after going through 3 conveyor belts and onto a deteriorating platform?
How was I supposed to know I'm not supposed to hyper dash on conveyor belts, and my jump was going to be no higher than if I tried to blast off my seat with my fart??
And how was I supposed to know that my invincibility frames after getting hit was as small as my mom's height!? What the ♥♥♥♥!
I
tried to like this game. But with the lack of checkpoints, there's no point in having a live count. You're better off reloading your save with all your power ups intact before you get mauled by another set of fat quails.
And because there's lack of music variety, it just makes the game all that more frustrating. Yes, I have the option to turn off the music, but why am I going to change a feature that obviously was meant to be there by default?
The game is supposed to be played with said settings intact.
So I play it.
And I hate it.
The
first world is fun, I'll give this game that much of credit.
But after going through 8 zones and a boss zone, you already feel worn out.
And then you go through another 4 worlds with 9 more zones each?
And the game says you're not done yet when you reach the end, and you have to go through all 5 worlds again to collect coins just to get that ending??
I can't do that, especially when I know that I can die at any point. And if I don't learn fast enough, then I have to start that zone all over again. And if I exhaust all of my lives, then I get that unsatisfying boss/gameover music with a bull skull above my ahead, as if it's mocking me.
Unless the game is supposed to be Dark Souls, I don't like being treated an idiot.
That said, I can't give a thumbs up to this Mario clone.
If you want to try some platformers worth your time, try the ones I've mentioned above.
A game should feel rewarding when you reach the end, not frustrated that you
go back to collect 50 not-so-obviously-placed achievement coins.
But...don't take my word for it.
There's a good portion of people in this community that love this game to bits, and while I have the hardest time understanding why, I'm not one to give a death sentence to a game just because I hate it.
If you love this game, then kudos. Perhaps the $4 retail value is good enough for you. I would personally wait for a sale before buying.
And if you didn't like my review by the end of this (which by the way, thank you fo reading this long essay of mine) then that's fine too. I just don't know anyone personally that has the patience to play this game from start to finish.
And to the game developer: If my words hold any value to you, then all I can say is please make the zones shorter, or at least cut the amount of zones in each world by half, and please add checkpoints to the game. It would make the game more fun for people like me if you did that, and would actually add value to the lives count system.
Thank you for your time in reading this, and I hope this helps give you some more insight to this game before buying.

In 2014 I had the pleasure of playing through Banner Saga 1, and I had this to say in my review:
"There's something about this game that I can't put my finger on. It might be the entracing music, the Disney quality hand-drawn art, or perhaps it's the fact that everytime I play this game it's always 30 minutes later than I expected it to be.
The combat is simple, for the uninitiated. As you begin to dive into the character types, their respective special attacks, and equipable items, you'll soon realize that there is a depth to the combat that will keep you coming back. When the odds are seemingly against you, and you do in fact manage to reduce your foe to a single unit vs. one or more of your own, you will feel like a champion. A real champion.
What has surprised me the most about The Banner Saga is the number of choices and chances the game allows. Every combat decision, every discussion, every step on the map brings consequences.
I can't tell you whether or not you should buy The Banner Saga, but I can tell you that you would almost be a fool not to."
Even though I've (so far) only played Banner Saga 2 for an hour, I am happy to tell you that 2 years later everything I adored in TBS1 is alive and well in TBS2. The art, the music, all of the hard and rewarding decisions are back.
Anyone that loved The Oregon Trial, enjoys turn based combat, or just wants to experience a really well made game should pick up The Banner Saga 2 now.
Oh, and your save from TBS1 can be imported. If you didn't play the first (and I highly recommend doing so!) you can press a Recap button on the main menu to get up to speed.
I look forward to playing this game over the next 15-20 hours and salivating over The Banner Saga 3 for the next year+ :)

There are usually two type of responses you receive when mentioning Alan Wake.  The first response would be the following "Oh My God!  What a great game!  What do you think happened at the end?!  Ugh, my mind is melting just thinking about it".  The second response " ... um ... never heard of it".
Alan Wake is probably what most us would call a cult classic.  It has a following and those who follow it, love it.  It's one of those games that flew under the radar but once dug up truly grips you.  I compare the game itself to a music album which after the first listen doesn't blow you away but over time becomes one of your favorites without even realizing it.
Alan Wake has many unique characteristics to it but yet stays familiar with the controls and 3rd person shooter concept.  The story grips you from the beginning and constantly unfolds before you but leaves you still thinking "Um, what just happened?".  The gameplay surrounding the darkness and Alan Wake's companion the light gives you a bleak and desperate feeling through out even when you have the comfort of friends (and very capable ones) to help you through.
Wake is stuck in his own nightmare and quickly finds out he has already written it.  He follows the trail that leads him to the darkness.  The question which you must answer is if Alan will defeat the darkness, his fears, his nightmare or will he fall victim just as others have in the past.
A must play!

You don't just play a game - you really ARE Alan Wake. You doubt reality as he does, feel remorse as he does and gets cheered up by the comic relief, Alan's manager Barry. The darkness force Alan to write a story for her if Alan wants to see his wife again, but then the story he wrote has become real before he could wrote the ending, now Alan is trapped in his own story and has to do what he must to survive.
The gameplay of Alan Wake is quite good. You play alone by yourself but in the near end you will have some companion to help you. You don't just get to shoot the enemy, as they are ghost like enemies protected by darkness aura around them, you have to neutralize them with your handheld flashlight or any kind of light source first before you can completely kill them with your weapons. Ammo is not unlimited, in fact they are very limited so you have to conserve your ammo very smart.
Alan Wake has great graphics. The acting and the voice looks great. All the effects and the environment settings are so convincing, makes the game scary to play alone in the night.
If you like adventure and horror story, this game is recommended for you.
Rating 9/10

The game is fun in a way but very unpolished and grindy.
Seriously, if you don't like grinding this game is not for you. The gameplay never changes and mainly consists of beating 3 bosses in each of the 4 areas of the game, which is done by killing all of their gladiators in combat (which usually takes several attempts per gladiator as the crowd will often vote in their favour).
Apart from that, it's quite a simple game but there is definitely an appeal to managing your own school of gladiators and seeing your fighters rise and/or die in the arena.
Unfortunately the game is lacking in many areas.
-Lack of variety in fighters: There are not enough portraits and names to go around to begin with. You'll just keep seeing the same names pop up everywhere and you'll probably have around 3-4 fighters with the same portrait in your stable. Apart from that there's also nothing that gives them any kind of personality. There's the "history" tab to be fair, with a short bio, but said bio often made the fighters seem more ridiculous than believable to me, so I generally ignored it. Something like a tab with "traits" relating to the fighter's personality would be nice but sadly there's nothing of the sort.
-No classes: Each fighter has a prefered weapon, and there are probably around 6 weapon "types" (meaning they have different names). Good start, unfortunately nothing was done with it. All weapons do exactly the same and the only thing to consider really is damage value and your fighters' prefered weapons, as they'll have a damage bonus when using them. There's nothing specific to consider when leveling up your fighters either, as their specialization only affects raw damage and is independent of attributes. I went with dexterity as the number one attribute for pretty much all of my fighters and ended up having a record of around 1300 wins and 30 losses.
-Unbalanced player perks: Some of the player perks are just completely broken and seem more like cheats than valid choices. You can completely disable morale loss for not sharing any of the price money with your fighters, stop your fighters from wanting to retire and completely remove weapon and armor durability loss to name the worst/best ones. You can disable player perks when you start the game and of course you don't HAVE to take the really broken ones but well, I'd still prefer it if there were player perks that were useful but not cheat-tier.
Those were probably my main grievances. I didn't particularly like the music either. To be fair though, I only had it on for about a minute before switching to various Total War soundtracks, which worked fairly well.
So yeah, the concept is pretty cool and the game is basically well thought out, it just seems a bit low effort. It's an ok game as it is, altough very repetitive, the sad thing about it is that it feels like it could be a brilliant game if they just added a couple of features and more variety.

Welcome to Disc Jam! The competitive sport you never knew was your absolute favorite. A Frisbee disc/Action game hybrid.... but this isn’t just ultimate Frisbee, so put your putters away. This is Pong on steroids all ramped up with special moves, dives, and lobs shots! THIS is the vision Windjammers strived to be years ago, but revamped with the technology of the Unreal4 Engine.
The goal of Disc Jam is simple. You take 2 players (or 2v2) on a court similar to a tennis court, and take turns throwing a frisbee at each other in an attempt to get it past your opponent to score some points. First to 50 wins a set, and a match is best of 3 sets. The gameplay is fast and frantic with diving, lob-shots, special moves, curve shots, guard plays and an arsonal of tactics and mechanics to keep each player guessing and keeping each new game fresh. And it’s always crazy when you throw out a special move, and your opponent catches it and shoots a special right back your way. I especially recommend this game for adrenaline junkies. There is always something exciting going down, and as soon as the match is over you just want that rush again. With frantically fast gameplay, easy co-op to comp, loads of unlockables, and  simple-to-learn-but-arduous-to-master style, you and your friends are going to have limitless amount of good times.  I give Disc Jam a well deserved 8/10, with room to grow

The rightful successor of Windjammers, Disc Jam uses its mechanics and adds more. You have a shield to deflect the disc and you can charge it to use a Super throw if the disc is slow enough. If you throw right away the disc you get a boost and it can happen 3 times, 4th time you can use a Super. Of course multiply this with all the different curves you can create, the lob to throw the disc on the ground,  quick curves, dashes etc  and you can really outsmart your opponent. Mindgames ensues.
Very rewarding arcade game, suitable to play 5mn or 2h, you can play single or 2v2 games, 2v2 local online, 2v2 online with a friend etc.
If you just want to play localy, you have to go to offline and everything will be unlocked by default, which is nice to have fun right away and for each player to have a personnal color and such.
The game is a little barebone as I write this, you have 4 characters, each slightly different, 1 map, 2 musics, ~10 colors (haven't counted), ~8 taunts and victory poses (haven't counted again), something like 50 Titles and 50 Icons. So you can really customize your character and player profile.
You get all of this by playing which will make you earn money(even in loss), which you can use to the prize machine to randomly get an item. There are colors and rarity. If you get an item that you already have you sell it for 500 coins ( each usage of the prize machine costs 1000 coins).
Ranked matches, leaderboards and statistics are coming soon, crossplay will follow with the PS4 online.
Talking about online it's very good, seems to be P2P, you can see your ping at any moment and can narrow your search to lower pings.  I find games in 10/20 seconds, it can take more time depending of the number of players.
On PC you have a chat box to write what you want, even though you have very little time in game to talk between rounds, that's why the devs have added a quick message feature like in rocket league using the Dpad.
Overrall the experience is very enjoyable, the mechanics are simple to understand yet hard to master with a great skill curve (not talking about the mechanic which is also called skill curve haha) like Windjammers has. (the arcade game it is based on).
The devs are following the game very very closely and are updating/adding things weekly. It has a great future ahead and I think it deserves to be bought even right now.

There are usually two type of responses you receive when mentioning Alan Wake.  The first response would be the following "Oh My God!  What a great game!  What do you think happened at the end?!  Ugh, my mind is melting just thinking about it".  The second response " ... um ... never heard of it".
Alan Wake is probably what most us would call a cult classic.  It has a following and those who follow it, love it.  It's one of those games that flew under the radar but once dug up truly grips you.  I compare the game itself to a music album which after the first listen doesn't blow you away but over time becomes one of your favorites without even realizing it.
Alan Wake has many unique characteristics to it but yet stays familiar with the controls and 3rd person shooter concept.  The story grips you from the beginning and constantly unfolds before you but leaves you still thinking "Um, what just happened?".  The gameplay surrounding the darkness and Alan Wake's companion the light gives you a bleak and desperate feeling through out even when you have the comfort of friends (and very capable ones) to help you through.
Wake is stuck in his own nightmare and quickly finds out he has already written it.  He follows the trail that leads him to the darkness.  The question which you must answer is if Alan will defeat the darkness, his fears, his nightmare or will he fall victim just as others have in the past.
A must play!

just don't.
the microtransactions have definitely left their mark on the fun and balance of the game, and the story and its pacing are worse than the original.
i'm mostly just disappointed more than angry, because the nemesis system was absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing fabulous in its first showing, and the game is still extremely solid, but the overall enjoyment factor has been crippled by the loot boxes and their effect on gameplay.
edit 10/17/17: the entire game feels like a chore. it takes a great deal of effort to kill any captains that don't have mortal weaknesses and a significant number of bonuses (which happens plenty around level 30+), it takes even more effort to recruit, then level them, there's an unskippable up to three minutes of watching your captains duel when you put them in the pits to level, it takes longer than that to send them on nemesis missions, and god forbid you try to get legendary, or even epic captains through RNG.
there's too much side content (and some of it gates powerful upgrades) as per the average open world game, and while you can argue "but too much content is a good thing," it's really not, many of the side missions take more time to get to than they do to do.
the change to the rune system, and the fact that there's now "equipment" with stats, instead of just growing more powerful over time, means that you have added farming for gear on top of farming EXP to unlock upgrades you need, farming captains you need for siege/defense, going through esoteric and arcane processes (getting yourself killed repeatedly without getting all of your weapons broken by the enemy that kills you/getting rescued by one of your allied captains) attempting to create epic and legendary captains, and upgrading each and every single piece of gear through specific challenges, some of which are more of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥than anything (kill a captain with an execution while under 25% health, for instance). then there's also farming gems for yet more upgrades.
10/10 hardcore farmville simulator i guess, i still can't really recommend it though, it practically demands the time investment of an MMO, especially with the fact that some captains or warlords could potentially gear wall some players by doing ridiculous amounts of damage and taking an excessive amount of damage to kill that basically screams "grind out some more levels and upgrade your equipment in our store!"

At first glance, Alan Wake is a third-person shooter with puzzles and horror themes. And yeah, that's true at the second and third glance too. But what makes Alan Wake so much more, what makes the game grow on me, is the intruiging and chilling story, the breathtaking level design and aesthetic and, to be frank, the collectibles and lore in the town of Bright Falls. The levels and stages within the levels are divided up in chapters and jumps through time and space, making the game more immersive and the characters even more relatable. You don't just play a game - you really ARE Alan Wake. You doubt reality as he does, feel remorse as he does and gets cheered up by the comic relief, Alan's manager Barry. The game is story driven and very linear, but the game benefits from it.
Oh, yeah, and the biggest selling point - I'm a huge fan of Stephen King. If you are too, this game is definetly for you, 'cause it's basically a gamification of a King novel.
9/10, a really good game!

Alan Wake is adventure third-person shooter game. You play as Alan Wake, he's a writer. Alan is going on a vacation with his wife when something has gone wrong. His wife gone missing because of something called the darkness. The darkness force Alan to write a story for her if Alan wants to see his wife again, but then the story he wrote has become real before he could wrote the ending, now Alan is trapped in his own story and has to do what he must to survive.
The gameplay of Alan Wake is quite good. You play alone by yourself but in the near end you will have some companion to help you. You don't just get to shoot the enemy, as they are ghost like enemies protected by darkness aura around them, you have to neutralize them with your handheld flashlight or any kind of light source first before you can completely kill them with your weapons. Ammo is not unlimited, in fact they are very limited so you have to conserve your ammo very smart.
Alan Wake has great graphics. The acting and the voice looks great. All the effects and the environment settings are so convincing, makes the game scary to play alone in the night.
If you like adventure and horror story, this game is recommended for you.

Age of Gladiators is a turn-based, classic strategy/management game.
By "classic" I mean it combines the best elements of turn-based strategy with RPG, and when you situate it in a compelling environment (i.e. the brutal, ancient world of gladitorial combat), you have the makings of a great game.
This is the first management game I've come across where you play a Lanista (i.e. boss) of a Ludus (stable of gladiators) set in ancient Rome. The game doesn't have fancy graphics, flashy cut scenes, etc. but it does have solid gameplay -- from the time I started, I kept going, and the next thing you know, it was 5am...
Things it does well:
1. Unique setting: i.e. managing all aspects of a ludus -- this includes hiring/firing staff, fighters, upgrading your facility, etc.
2. RPG elements: You get to upgrade your fighters (and yourself) when they level up, as well as send them on potentially profitable (and risky) missions. It's always fun when there are RPG elements inserted into strategy games, as the player develops a "bond" with the gladiators in this case. The perks are useful, and the game is well-balanced.
3. Strategic layer -- you have to decide what kind of gladiators you want (e.g. tanks with lots of strength and health, or nimble fighters with high speed/agility/lethality), who to send to what types of matches (of increasing difficulty), who you want to develop and level up, and so on. What kind of staff do you want? How do you level them up? When do you fire them? When do you hire them? These are all decisions you have to make.
You also have to plan around the fight calendar (because fights earn you money, and you have daily expenses), manage the health of your fighters, and most importantly, manage your finances (although you can borrow money in a pinch). You have to purchase armor and weapons too, which add bonuses to your fighters' performance -- this is a secondary benefit, but every bit helps when you're trying to squeeze out an advantage against your enemy in a tough match.
Oh and you can also place side bets on the fights, that can earn you a LOT of extra cash. Lastly, you have to decide what kind of lanista you're going to be -- ruthless (i.e. kill your own fighters and steal their winnings), benevolent (always give them a higher share of the purse and best living conditions), or somewhere in between.
Things it can do better:
1. I find it a little strange that you can't see who your fighter is facing until you've committed your own. I mean, in ancient Rome, weren't these matches planned in advance? Knowing who you're facing adds yet another (positive) element in the strategic layer. It really shouldn't be left to chance. That said, there isn't a whole lot wrong with this game.
Final comments:
I like the fact that you can choose the "type" of lanista your character can be too -- a merchant, doctor, negotiator, and so on. Each background gives you certain benefits. The fights themselves are dice rolls, but you can pick a combat strategy based on your fighter's strengths and weaknesses as well as your opponent's. e.g. if your fighter is not as strong, but is really agile and accurate, a defensive posture may yet triumph over a stronger (but slower) opponent.
Best of all, what I really like about AOG is that it does all this without fancy graphics, high frame rates, videos, actors or voice overs. It's just a great example of a classic strategy game that gets virtually everything right.
Age of Gladiators is a fun, well thought out and executed game, and I highly recommend it. The devs did a great job!
