I was really looking forwards to this game, it looked like it might have some interesting gameplay and a great story. I was disappointed.
The gameplay started off good, but then didn't change at all for the whole 12 hours I played of it. AT ALL. The whole having to shine a light at things for a while before you could shoot them got incredibly annoying (while it started as quite good).
Sadly, the story is an utter mess. Normally I'm fine with having to think over a story a while after it, and maybe chat with some people about it. That didn't do anything for this. It was still an incoherent mess. About halfway through, it looked as if the story could be going somewhere really great but it just didn't. Sad. It didn't help that Alan Wake was just not a very interesting character, but the supporting characters were actually pretty good.
The UI is quite annoying - I really wanted to turn the map and objectives off (don't lead me by the hand, let me explore and do what I want - it's not like it's hard to navigate this mostly linear path), but still keep ammo and weapon information on there (or at least have some indication of how much ammo I had left - like spoken cues, as in that King Kong movie tie-in game) to heighten the whole atmosphere thing, but the game only offers HUD on or off. A minor annoyance, but an annoyance nonetheless.
The game looks really good, but there are only really two settings (town, wood), though those places do look fantastic. The game isn't at all scary in the slightest. The atmosphere starts off decent, but doesn't ever ramp up or introduce anything at all terrifying. Or even hint at it. There aren't even any cheap jump scares (which I am totally fine with, cheap jump scares need to go die in a fire).
As with the gameplay, the sound during levels was really repetitive and kinda dull - though the songs at the end of each chapter were pretty well done (if not particularly great as songs sadly). The whole chapter thing was actually a really good idea as well, but I remember one of the chapters being ridiculously overlong and that didn't really make any sense and just broke the flow of the game.
This game was a big disappoint - I expected a lot, but it just didn't deliver. On anything. I suppose you could buy it, but don't spend too much money on it. It's really not very good.

No way in hell am I paying full price to be treated as a second class citizen.
The game is locked to 30 fps. I don't care if they're gonna patch it later. These companies need to learn that if you don't care enough about PC gamers to make it run as PC gamers expect on release, you don't get a cent. Locking a PC game to 30 fps is UNACCEPTABLE.
Other than that, the game seems unfinished, and it seems they've had no PC play testers whatsoever. Otherwise DELETE and PAGE DOWN wouldn't be part of default controls. If you think having to lift my fingers off of W,A,S,D or my mouse to press a key on the other side of the keyboard is a good control scheme, you haven't put a single thought into the default control scheme.
Sprinting is extremely cumbersome. I constantly find myself pressing the sprint key over and over because the game simply doesn't react to it. The sprint key only works if your character is in a situation where he is able to sprint. What I mean by that, is that if you jump through a window, and you hold shift on the last frame of the jump-through-window animation, it'll ignore it. You have to wait until the very moment he's all the way through the window, and has started jogging. Then you can press sprint. Same goes for everything. To run out of cover, you press shift, then to continue into a sprint, you must first wait till he's jogging. If you do it a frame too early, you'll have to let go, then press again.
In the game, you can sneak (crouch) by pressing X. You can go into cover, and when you go back out, he'll still be sneaking; so far, so good. However, you can't toggle sneaking WHILE in cover, which means that if you entered cover out of sneaking mode, to leave the cover in sneak mode, you must first get out of cover, which makes him stand up, then quickly activate sneak mode before you get spotted.
Now, the next thing is what makes the game really seem alpha to me. Some actions makes your character interact with other characters, like sneaking up to someone, then performing a stealth takedown. You know how in games like Splinter Cell, you sneak up behind someone, and then your character and the target character smoothly transitions into a takedown maneuver? Well, in Mafia 3, they don't. Instead, they instantly snap into action, then cover it up by either randomizing the camera rotation, or making it a cutscene, so you can't see the lack of transition.
If you sprint up to a guy, and hit melee, your character will charge into his back, knock him down and stump his head. But again, there's no transition, you just see your character teleport to behind the target character.
Same goes for picking up bodies. They've only made animations for picking up enemies from the front. That is, your character standing at their feet, with them on their back, and then he picks them up. So if you're standing at their head and start to pick them up, their body will instantly be turned around the other way so the animation fits. This is again covered up by an instant snap of the camera.
In general, the gameplay is very non-smooth. Like, after knocking someone down, you have to wait for your character to stand back up, and get into an idle animation, before you can continue moving. Furthermore, there's like a 2-3 second delay from you have finished a takedown, until you can pick up bodies, so you're basically sitting on top of bodies just waiting for the prompt to appear so you can pick them up. All of this makes your character just seem like a lot of cutscenes stitched together very badly.
Driving physics are pretty good ones you set the game's driving to "Simulation". The camera is really bad though, and makes it hard to drive. On top of that, the camera resets to looking straight ahead, about a second after you stop moving the mouse. So if you move the mouse to look at something, it'll snap back to forward, so you constantly have to shake the mouse around to look at things  that aren't straight ahead.
Shooting is hard due to input lag, probably caused by the 30 fps lock (which in its own doesn't make shooting easier).
I have two monitors. The game does not lock the cursor to the game, so every other minute my mouse will move to the other monitor, so that when I attempt to shoot, the game minimizes.
The 30 fps lock also makes it difficult to navigate the menus due to input lag.
The game crashed 3 times in an hour.
I think those are my biggest gripes with the game.

Despite the promise shown, this is released as a finished product. As it currently is, I cannot recommend this game.
The FPS side is pretty alright. Being able to take control over any unit gives you a breadth-over-depth, so any lack of sophistication in any single unit's controls is more than made up for by swapping over. The issues I have are mostly with the RTS side, since this is primarily an RTS game.
Unit and gameplay balance is currently significantly skewed - one research path is always, always better than others, leading to lack of variety in play. The FPS mode is fiddly, and is difficult to keep in - staying in FPS mode too long will cause you to fall behind on research.
The AI is very lackluster. "Pylon spam" is an AI exploit, by which you build a free building repeatedly. This will consume AI forces, as they attack the building you built for free, allowing you to destroy their units. They will continue attacking the pylon, even while under attack! The differences between AI tiers are done alright, but they all work off the same basic script - and it's a script. Early scout, two bots left iron, three bots right iron, vehicle, lasers, upgraded lasers, assault with tanks, holding pattern, cluster rocket infantry to take out CEO. You can do the same thing, of course - this is the most effective strategy, in fact! So it's down to how fast you can execute this.
Graphics and sound should be evident from the above videos and screenshots - with one addition, being that units are in-scale to the surrounding buildings. Usually, FPS units are significantly out of scale - this is so that they are visible and selectable. You'll be constantly changing your zoom level.
Options are fairly bare-bones, without in-game rebindable controls. The control scheme evokes a much-earlier populus-style or Citizen Kabuto-style controls, rather than a more recent title. It's surprising to see that this title was released in 2015.
While the RTS/FPS concept is very cool, and done fairly well, as it currently stands I do not recommend this game.

Personally this game did not feel like a true adventure game.  I wasn't given the task of finding random items to use for various tasks.  I never seemed to have more than 2 or 3 items, and generally it was obvious what to use them for (not really a puzzle, just situational uses). You could see the rough, chalk-like edges that really didn't look as sharp as the screen shots on Steam.
One of the more annoying things about the game was the needless repetition at times.  Especially with the boy, there were times I was going through the same cutscene (thankfully can be skipped) without really any sense of purpose or diection.
I also saw several graphic bugs (i.e. the girl's neck moved to be in front of her face, 2 on-screen blocks of text overlapped, etc.).  These were minor and could be overlooked, however.
I'm afraid this does not feel like the traditional point-and-click adventure games of the 80s and 90s.  King's Quest VII had better artistic quality than this.

As other reviewers have noted, there's a lot of boring and pointless walking backwards and forwards and back again in this game. Similarly, some dialogue could use work: some opening conversations were relevant earlier in the game, but are bizarre when they're repeated. Surely it wouldn't have been too difficult to throw in a generic greeting?
Those are fairly minor squibbles - or should be. The walking, though: slow, frequently illogical, and at times frustrating enough to make me question whether it was even worth continuing. As the lead character thinks later in the game: "This is going to be a long game." He forgot to add "needlessly".
There was some jarring change in artwork at one point late in the game, for what amounted to an extremely lame joke (or at least, that's the only reason I can think of); and I'm still not sure what happened in the grand final scene, other than by imputation: it's almost as if there's a part of the scene missing.
On the plus side, the eyecandy is great - Joe Phillips is always reliable! - the humour generally good, and the storyline interesting enough to keep me playing - with enough "I didn't see that coming"s to keep me on my toes. Some of the puzzle solving, while usually logical, can take a bit of nutting out (although some others are  telegraphed a bit too much).
On balance, thumbs-up wins - but it was a close-run thing. And the sad part is, the things that brought this game down were easy fixes. If the game testers had done their job properly, or the developer followed up on their advice, this could have been a MUCH better game.
All that said, though, I look forward to the already-overdue next project from this developer: it's nice to have a gay-themed game that is not embarrasingly over-the-top (Joe Phillip's artwork aside, but I happily forgive him that). Sure, some of the dialogue is corny - I'm looking at you, lift - but overall the game is not nearly as corny or stereotyping as some reviewers would have you believe.
Having unlocked the alternative play version, will I play the game through again?
Yes - but not for a while.

The advantage of taking control of units yourself is things like micro and sniping beyond the AI's detection and firing range giving you an edge. The ability to customise your vehicles with a huge selection of weapons as well as a slider based econ/research system means there are multiple ways to play and win.
tl;dr If you ever wanted to play Supreme Commander type game where you can pilot the experimental, this is for you.

This is more like comparison for new Flight Sim enthusiasts
FSX:SE
Pros:
- Cheapest Flight Sim with flexible payment methods on steam.
- Steam multiplayer and also some other steam features (like download, easy community access, home streaming...)
- Increased performance and better VAS usage over FSX:MS (boxed)
- Many add-ons already working, others also getting update for being compitable.
- Limited Support
Cons:
- Its not 64bit so still OOMs
- Not %100 FSX:MS add-ons compitable
- Limited Support
- SDK is not included
FSX:MS (Boxed)
Pros:
- Main game for Add-ons
- DVD installation (no download required)
- SDK included (Gold and Deluxe edition)
Cons:
- No support
- Unused copies can be expensive, hard to find in retail stores
- Only on DVD no download option or official online store
- Performance issues
- No official multiplayer servers. (Other multiplayer options still available)
Prepar3d
Pros:
- Most advanced FSX engine
- DX11 support
- Better system resources usage
- Updated landclass for some regions
- Many FSX add-ons already updated for it
Cons:
- Its not for "ENTERTAINMENT"
- Still not looks like new Flight Sim more like FSX with DX11
- Not developing by game studio
- After almost 10 years still no big changes on FSX engine
- Price is high, only sale on their own website (60$ is high for DX11 update, you should also re-buy some FSX add-ons)
- Some add-ons are expensive then FSX,
- Bad UI
- FSX add-ons not %100 compitable (FSX:SE more compitable)
- EULA restrictions (also for add-ons)
X-plane 10:
Pros:
- Only 64 bit and OpenGL flight sim on market (so its supports Mac PC)
- Steam support, flexible payment methods.
- Its actually very different Flight Sim then FSX engine based games so you should read its own reviews. Because there are too many new features
Cons:
- Limited 3rd party support, limited add-ons
- Huge Download Size
- Worst UI

Fearing that his Chinese neighbor will one day launch a rode from space on the Russian capital of St.Petersburg, Peter the great of Russia authorized his generals to wage a full on nuclear war against China. The first launch was a tactical nuke that targeted a recently captured German settlement where the Chinese had their mechanized infantry, artillary and tanks amassed near the Russian border. The next several launches however utilized Thermonuclear bombs that unleased destruction on Chinese cities and armies. The Russian army managed to penetrate 800 miles into Chinese territory before being stopped by irradiated fields that seperated it from the dying Chinese army. The launches continued over the next 5 years and primarly targeted three cities with space ports and their surrounding areas. After the space port cities where destroyed the launches where focused towords industrial towns towords Siberia and agricultural farms in the east.  Peter the great wanted to make sure that these cities and their space ports could never rise again, that CHINA would never rise again.
By the time of a ceasfire was signed, China has lost more than 90% of it's population and production. Radiation has reduced the acres of farmlands to rubble and the ones promising and thriving space centers have been reduced to molten piles of steel. Only the Chinese colonies in the Americas never experienced conflict. But as part of the ceasefire, the Chinese had to relinquish their American colonies aswell as a few towns close to the Russian border one of which luckly has a space port.
The Russians quickly got underway to to decontaminate and rebuild the infrastrucure of their newly aquired prize. The Chinese however where not so lucky. With the loss of arable land and a complete destruction of its infrastructure, the Chinese economy tanked to the bottom. The government soon found itself unable to pay the wages of it's soldiers once memmbers of the largest amy in the world. The soldiers in turn sold their weapons on the black market or joined warlords who now roam free.
The warlords pillaged Chinese villages as they pleased with no resistance from the Chinese government. Infact the warlords felt so confident that they started crossing  into former Chinese territory and kidnapping Russian workers tasked with rebuilding the Russian side of the new territory. The Russian military had to be called to secure the border and to prevent intrusion from Chinese warlords. Peter certainly did not expect this as a side effect of his victory,
20 years after the war not much had changed. Radiation has largely disappeard (no one knows why). The Chinese economy never recovered and warlords still roam the Chinese landscape with occasional attempts to enter the border. Chinese cities on the russian border have been rebuilt but have not recovered to pre-war levels. While the Chinese space ports rust on into history, the newely rebuilt Chinese-Russian space port on the other hand shows signs of promising. A few of the surviving and captured Chinese scientists and enginneers have been working with their Russian counterparts on launching the first Russian sattelite into space (more than 80 years since the Chinese went to Space).
As he looks eastward from an army observation post near the border, Peter of Russia still wonders. Was it necessiary to drop the bombs on the great cities where innocent people ones thrived? Was it right to condmen the people of China into the hell and misery they live in? Peter after all got want he wanted but at what cost? Should the Russian government try to rebuild China either through refinancing the Chinese government or "integration"? Or should China be left upto God and the mercy of those who rule her?

This game was a very grateful surprise. It is a management game that doesn't bother the player with micromanagement, and its mechanics is so simple that very quickly you understand how it works and operates, in such a way that it becomes very fast-paced for quick fun.
The different stats your gladiators have guarantee different strategies in battles, but also makes clear which are the strong points and weaknesses of each, so that even if you are facing a higher (or lower) level character there is a real possibility that not only chance, but also the interactions of their different stats may favor the underdog sometimes.
That is not to say the game couldn't be improved. The galadiators are very bland, and even though they try to make each unique by having their own "background"history, it comes down to a generic text that doesn't create any empathy between the player and the characters.
It is also a pity that the game doesn't try to deepen a little bit its complexity by adding different characteristics, pros and cons of each weapon. The coice of weapons was one of the most importante and strategically meaninful choices in a gladiatior match, and the game simply ignores it.
All in all, it is a good game, specially if you find it in a bargain, such as during steam sales. It also shines some clever lights not only for its developers, but other independent developers who wish to undesrtand how simple mechanics and programming can go a long way providing fun if you are clever and creative.

Really hard, great concept, fun but deeply frustrating
This is a fun game with a good concept - turn based strategy meets stealth.  The graphics look good, the scenarios are randomly generated, complex, and require significant thought.  The story is good enough for what it is, however, I will say despite what you are supposed to be doing, it feels like you're just doing random missions, getting more buff and waiting for the game to just move on - like the missions are meaningless obstacles.  They don't really play into the actual story.
What I really want to talk about is how frustrating this game can be.  Things that make this game so frustrating include not being able to see enemy vision cones - it's not very helpful when you can see what an enemy's path is, but not whether they can actually see you - you want to plan ahead but you can't.  Hacking 'power' points - saving them up is complicated, you can easily find yourself in a situation where you just don't have enough to complete a mission, and there is no way to get them.  So you automatically lose.  If you want to open all the safes and disable all the cameras, at least make it semi-feasible to do so.  As it stands at least in my game, I need to save every point, or I will easily find myself in an unwinnable scenario.  This problem sort of bleeds into the next, which is how much it costs in power to hack terminals that let you buy upgrades/weapons/etc.  You don't know what's for sale, but the out of mission shop barely carries anything, so you are encouraged to hack them and buy - but they may have nothing of value, or you may just not have enough money - wasting a ton of power points that you likely can't get back.  Lastly, getting spotted - it is very easy to die in this game.  Which is fine, we're all doing this Dark Souls-hard game thing now.  However, it is such a slog to get back to where you were, it's really depressing to lose.
So, in summary - this is a good turn based RPG and gets credit for incorporating stealth in a very meaningful way, but it has balance issues when it comes to supplying you with power points, and there are some tweaks it could make to its userface that would decrease moments of death/failure that feel "cheap".  Also, if you want to play this game, you have to enjoy the experience of smashing your face against the wall because of frustration, because you will be doing that often.

This is a terrific game. The real kickers of it are the story and the atmosphere. The story involves a writer named Alan Wake who goes on a search for his missing wife, Alice. But is he really searching for her or is there something bigger, more devastating going on here? The atmosphere envelopes the player in moody darkness as Alan traverses the great outdoors and fights his way past the possessed dark known as the Taken.
The gameplay can get quite repetitive, but different segments diversify it up (such as surviving an assault with loads of ammo and batteries for your precious flashlight). Light is the key in this game, as the player must make his way to each lampost emitting light which is always another checkpoint. Some may find this repetitive as well, but I was always relieved to get to the next one as many of my resources (my batteries and ammo) were quite exhausted. I played the game on normal and while there were some moments that inflicted great frustrations, all in all it was a great experience.
It is a survival horror game, and while it is not as scary as Silent Hill or Amnesia, it definitely gives you moments of panic and/or fright. For me, these moments typically came because Alan can not run fast for too long as he gets tired and slows down. This can prove to be frustrating if you are being chased by too many Taken (as I was on many an occasion), but I believe it was purposely done this way, else the game would be too easy if Alan could just run faster than the Taken to each checkpoint and never have to stop, turn around, flash and kill as many Taken as possible, and go back to running.
Overall, I had an enjoyable experience with this game. I would recommend that everyone who plays it, also play the 2 Special DLC chapters upon completion of the base story. This will provide closure upon finishing the two specials, or at least more closure than the ending of Alan Wake by itself.

I can't say that I'm in any way thrilled or impressed by this. I understood that it could never live up to the hype generated following the financial debacles that had plagued mid-development, however this just is a bit sad.
I went in expecting something to the likes of Grim Fandango, Stacking, Day of the Tentacles, or any of Double Fine's (or Tim Schaeffer's at Lucas)  previous adventure games. I wasn't expecting much for four hundred-thousand, perhaps something more on par with the Hamlet game, a few good puzzles, and a simplistic story. Playing Broken Age I feel like despite its sizeable (taking into account original plans) three million dollar budget (which isn't even enough) it still falls short even for my initial expectations.
The gameplay is standard point and click if you can find it between the cutscenes that take up every other action and the puzzles are simplistic (I wont fault them for that though because stacking was too and i still could look past it for the artstyle and world design), the characters just dont really click with me (not a fan of overdone angsty teenager trope no matter what the backdrop), and the dialogue left much to be desired and really doesnt stand up to previous titles such as Grim Fandango or even spme of the liekable dialogue of Brutal Legend.
However the greatest dissapointment for me was the artstyle. It just looks rather generic and there really isnt anything memorable here for me. The music is forgettable, the voices sound a bit stiff, and on the whole the audio is nothing to write home about.
All and all I wouldn't have necessarily minded this all as much if it was the original game proposed with a few modifications such as voice acting, but given that this was touted as a three-million plus game, a game that double fine could really be set free on, I am extremely underwhelmed. Not to mention the fact that for a four hour 2D game that was years in development with a budget in the millions, its stoll incredibly buggy.
Overall, most of my arguments could be counteracted with the argument that this is a kids game. This is true (granted we are talking closer to ec than E here), but that may be why I am a bit upset, this really wasn't pitched as a early childhood game. It was pitched as an adventure game. My reccomendation would be to skip this and pick up kentucky route zero. For around the same price you get another episodic point and click, they have more episodes in the works that will likely give you some longer playtime overall, and despite being pretty pretentious it will give you a bit more to think about than this and I like the soundtrack a bit better, but that last part is just me.
Full disclaimer I couldn't really get immersed in Mass Effect either, and I find myself perhaps thinking this as an issue of immersion, there is some lore here that some may find interesting but once again I find it just falls short.

Alpha Protocol is the most reactive game ever created. Every other RPG you've played where "choices matter!" and "you shape the story!"? Complete bunk compared to this. There are SO MANY things you can manipulate that it is entirely possible to end the game with the entire main cast dead or every single one of them alive. If you enjoy good writing (the game was developed by Obsidian who have created some of the greatest RPGs in the business), semi-cheesy spy fiction and interesting characters you will fall in love with this game.
Now for the bad parts:
The start of the game is pretty slow and fairly linear. After completing the tutorial and the first "hub" the game opens up hugely in both options of where to go and the impact of your choices. Many reviewers never got past this first area and therefore never got to experience the 'real game', leading to a lot of fairly negative reviews.
A lot of people dislike the gunplay and combat. Personally I found it solid and enjoyable, if not particularly special. However, the build balance is slightly out of whack - the pistol's Chain Shot (similar to Mark and Execute systems found in other games) is way better than any other weapon's special ability. However if you just embrace the cheese you can run a Martial Arts/Stealth build that leads to you, about halfway through the game, being able to turn invisible and punch every single person in the room in the throat, which is wonderful fun. Be aware that some bosses are really really hard to melee though, so pure martial arts builds might suffer.
Despite these and some other minor niggles, however, I wholeheartedly recommend this game. There's nothing on the market that compares to Alpha Protocol for reactivity.

Become the ultimate spy in this highly stylized, turn-based, cyberpunk masterpiece.
Cloak past guards, hack into enemy turrets, and steal valuable technology right from your enemy's pocket. Escape without being detected. Or, if you're feeling blood-thirsty, equip your agent with a hand cannon, and augment them to become a stone-cold killer.
Each of Invisible's agents offers unique traits and advantages, and they're a lot of fun to experiment with. For example, Sharp is a heavily augmented machine-man who can knock down even the toughest guards with brutal efficiency. Draco scans the bodies of the dead to gain his upgrades, which introduces an entirely new resource to the game.
Personally, I had a great time playing through the game with Internationale and Dr. Xu:
Internationale allows the player to explore each map quickly by wirelessly scanning through walls, which is a very cool effect. You don't have to risk being in sight of enemy guards to gather information, which is incredibly helpful.
On the other hand, Dr. Xu's melee-range EMP ability is one of the most useful abilities in the game. Dr. Xu is a master safe-cracker,  and will make short work of corporate firewalls. He will disable enemy drones, heart-monitors on guards, and even short-circuit your opponent's advanced cybernetic armor.  Plus, Dr. Xu has a modded Shock Trap that can be placed on any door, which ignores enemy armor! This provides a perfect "get out of jail free" card when you're up against increasingly lethal enemy guards.

The biggest problem I had with this game is the short time frame the main story mode campaign is based on. You have 72 hours to gather your forces and prepare yourself for the final showdown, and the very first mission you do takes 10-12 hours off that clock.
While that doesn't exactly lend itself to in depth gameplay, allowing you time to figure out the game, that doesn't matter. Every time you fail, and your spy agency is destroyed, you gain experience. Enough experience, and it unlocks new Agents and Programs.
What I found worked very well for learning the game though, is the Custom campaign mode. You can use it to configure just about every aspect of the missions, from the number of safes and consoles available to hack, to the number of guards on duty, and even what the alarm does. You can even set it to Endless mode, which takes away the three day time limit.
I don't recommend sticking to Custom though. Changing all these options is great for learning how to play, but it does take away the actual storyline.
As for the style of gameplay, it's like a cross between Evil Genius, and XCOM. Evil Genius in that you have the world map, and select your missions on there, and XCOM in that the missions themselves are turn-based and have the same top down view that XCOM has. Unlike XCOM though, you are not there to shoot stuff. In fact, if you have to shoot stuff, chances are you're losing.
Killing, or even tasering, is an option of last resort. You really want to stealth it, sneak around behind the guards, picking their pockets as you go, but try not to kill them, and if you stun them, they wake up after a few rounds and go hunting for you. Not the most ideal situation to be in.
All in all, a very fun game that offers something a little different.

Alpha Protocol.
Underrated but still quite an awesome game. I was pleasantly surprised as i entered its world of espionage and from the beginning, it shows you that your decisions have weight. They actually matter, unlike in other games that promise that your decisions have outcomes, this one delivers. You can be a really suave spy, a really aggressive 'roided up spy or a professional killer spy or even a combination of the three. You can make people hate you or like you. Both of those have corresponding consequences/rewards. Makes for interesting conversation choices throughout the story.
The graphics of this game are okay in my opinion. It hasn't aged that badly actually.
The combat mechanics aren't as bad as i was expecting but there are exploits that players would discover.
For instance, melee attacks are OP as well as pistols. In my playthrough, i never needed to use my rifle or any other gun for that matter.
Why? Chain Shooting. The Chain Shooting skill for the pistol makes for quick and deadly executions. (think today's Splinter Cell: Conviction/Hitman: Absolution's Execution/Instict kills.)
I found stealthing the whole map to be an enjoyable experience as the enemies barely have time to react to you punching their lights out.
The story is well told and your decisions have an impact on how the game tells it to you. I can't say much about it without spoiling so you'll have to play it.
This game is well worth the full retail price, but if you're on the fence or just don't wanna spend a lot, you can wait for a sale so that you can pick it up and enjoy some espionage.

text:
My first introduction to Adventure games was way back (perhaps not as far back as some), to the days of "Day of the Tentacle". This led to a lifelong enjoyment of Point-and-Click Adventure Games, including King's Quest, Full Throttle, Grim Fandango, Deponia, Whispered World, etc. This game piqued my interest early, and I was VERY happy to back the project.
As a Kickstarter backer, this game has met and exceeded my expectations. It's a well-developed throwback to the Adventure games of yesteryear and has a good amount of heart. The humor is on-target in almost all cases, and never groan-inducing. The animation is WONDERFUL, and the world is detailed and has a very Double Fine feel while still feeling fresh and new. There are a few spots where it feels as though the animation is not as fluid as others, but it doesn't interfere with the enjoyment.
As for the gameplay, the puzzles aren't terribly hard, and make a good amount of sense if you take a moment to think. This is the game's strongest ally; many adventure games rely on randomly assembling/using objects to progress the plot. This does an excellent job of helping you through puzzles through clever dialogue writing and timeliness. No more carrying around 10 useless items for the duration of the game HOPING that one will be useful.
This is easily one of my most favorite games of the year so far, and no Adventure fan's library will be complete without it. Bravo, Double Fine!

That said, this game made me remember what a good adventure game is actually like after playing a bunch of lesser efforts recently. The story is absolutely captivating, the puzzles are good if on the easy side, and the art style is this gorgeous "construction paper art project" sort of thing. You split your time evenly between two very different characters in very different settings, and each grabs you immediately and won't let go. Hilarious writing, characters, and voice acting too. The ending will make you slam your head on the desk because you will need to know RIGHT NOW what happens next, but instead the long wait begins.
Buy it so we can discuss and commiserate.

This game was really funny. I bought this game as a laugh to play with my girlfriend, but instead, it turned out to be an engaging story for the short time it lasted. I've noticed that every review for most of the games on this site often contains a lot of personal bias, so I figure I should be fair to this game and to everyone else and show my viewpoint from two different perspectives.
As a straight guy examining the game's gender tropes, this game was fun. Characters break the third wall and talk directly to the gamer, a tool that showcases a lot of the games true humor. The most often trope in video games is "hero saves damsel in distress", but here, the main goal is a reunion between the main character and a past love interest, who is by no means a damsel. Several other homosexual characters and comments made by them shine a light on how few other video games defy stereotypes and show that relationships can come in any shape or form. I REALLY enjoy a game defiant enough to turn common tropes around. Creativity is really the only thing that keeps game development a fluid marketplace.
As a gamer, this game was a short, funny adventure. The nature of the point and click game genre often requires a lot of going back and forth between different areas of exploration, and there are some moments where a detail that you didn't catch may end up making you explore an area you have already been to several more times. The game has a high contrast mode for vision impaired players, a nice touch if you're having too much trouble searching for the right things to grab. However, despite this, the game itself is fairly short; you should be able to finish the whole thing in under a few hours. The art style is not exceptionally thrilling, but the dialogue is hilarious and finding all of the hidden jokes and sexual innuendo was exactly what I expected.
All in all, I would recommend this to others, but only if the price for the game falls below $8 or if you have some money burning a hole in your pocket. The ending scene makes the whole game absolutely worth it.

An updated review for an updated game...
Since their last patch, the simulator platform has become quite stable and changes the experience quite a bit.  I actually have some flight experience and while certainly this is not a true measure of flight, it is a very good introduction to it as well as a means to maintain your skills.
PRO'S:
There's a robust support group out there, seasoned and developed and happy to help.
The missions supplied are very well arranged and developed, the presentation is enjoyable as opposed to a ♥♥♥♥♥ing betty.
The radio traffic is excellent, allows newer pilots a chance to get in some communication practice out of the real world.
This game still has collisions, which is great for those wishing to ensure they are "not hitting" obstacles.  The new simulators require that collisions are turned off, so if you're testing your skills to make sure you're clearing that 50ft tree at the end of that short runway, this simulator will definately let you know if you cleared or not.
CON'S:
Very few with this latest patch.  The graphics are getting a bit dated, but they're not bad.
Some of the missions do have dead spots or don't really give good instructions on what to do next to advance in the mission.  Most do very well.
Overall, I've enjoyed this Steam Edition very much and am regularly using it to keep up and develop my pilot skills.

At first glance, I wasn't especially impressed with 8BitBoy, but a few of the reviews were positive and the game was heavily reduced in price so I thought I'd give it a go. To its credit, it does evoke a sense of nostalgia; the visuals and music are very reminiscent of a Genesis/SNES game (thus making 16BitBoy a more appropriate title, but that's splitting hairs). The graphics are simple and cartoony, everything is brightly-coloured and you can clearly see what is an enemy, what is a powerup, a platform, etc. The game's presentation is fine.
However, in an attempt to emulate some of the classic platformers of the 8-bit and 16-bit eras, I feel that 8BitBoy has not quite hit the mark in terms of quality gameplay; your character seems to slide around very easily, almost as if every level were an ice level. I've also noticed that the main character's hitbox when it comes to platforming is smaller than its sprite; classic platformers like Mario and Sonic allowed you to land your foot on the edge of a platform and be fine, yet in 8BitBoy you had better make sure you land square on a platform, otherwise you're likely to fall and die.
Death is another problem with this game. Lives are in short supply, and the levels have no checkpoints. Granted, they're not really long enough to warrent them, and there is little downtime between dying and respawning. However, because of the aforementioned hitbox detection, death is very likely. And the power-ups you'll have collected (which amount to a series of slightly different projectile attacks), will be lost. There is a plus-side to this; the game autosaves at every level, keeping track of your lives total and power-ups when you enter a level. Hence, when you get a game over, you can restart the level with everything. However, this completely invalidates the point of having extra lives. If I die in a level and lose all my power-ups, why would I want to play the level without them, when I can just suicide until I get a Game Over and restart the level with my arsenal intact?

The biggest problem I had with this game is the short time frame the main story mode campaign is based on. You have 72 hours to gather your forces and prepare yourself for the final showdown, and the very first mission you do takes 10-12 hours off that clock.
While that doesn't exactly lend itself to in depth gameplay, allowing you time to figure out the game, that doesn't matter. Every time you fail, and your spy agency is destroyed, you gain experience. Enough experience, and it unlocks new Agents and Programs.
What I found worked very well for learning the game though, is the Custom campaign mode. You can use it to configure just about every aspect of the missions, from the number of safes and consoles available to hack, to the number of guards on duty, and even what the alarm does. You can even set it to Endless mode, which takes away the three day time limit.
I don't recommend sticking to Custom though. Changing all these options is great for learning how to play, but it does take away the actual storyline.
As for the style of gameplay, it's like a cross between Evil Genius, and XCOM. Evil Genius in that you have the world map, and select your missions on there, and XCOM in that the missions themselves are turn-based and have the same top down view that XCOM has. Unlike XCOM though, you are not there to shoot stuff. In fact, if you have to shoot stuff, chances are you're losing.
Killing, or even tasering, is an option of last resort. You really want to stealth it, sneak around behind the guards, picking their pockets as you go, but try not to kill them, and if you stun them, they wake up after a few rounds and go hunting for you. Not the most ideal situation to be in.
All in all, a very fun game that offers something a little different.

Alpha Protocol.
Underrated but still quite an awesome game. I was pleasantly surprised as i entered its world of espionage and from the beginning, it shows you that your decisions have weight. They actually matter, unlike in other games that promise that your decisions have outcomes, this one delivers. You can be a really suave spy, a really aggressive 'roided up spy or a professional killer spy or even a combination of the three. You can make people hate you or like you. Both of those have corresponding consequences/rewards. Makes for interesting conversation choices throughout the story.
The graphics of this game are okay in my opinion. It hasn't aged that badly actually.
The combat mechanics aren't as bad as i was expecting but there are exploits that players would discover.
For instance, melee attacks are OP as well as pistols. In my playthrough, i never needed to use my rifle or any other gun for that matter.
Why? Chain Shooting. The Chain Shooting skill for the pistol makes for quick and deadly executions. (think today's Splinter Cell: Conviction/Hitman: Absolution's Execution/Instict kills.)
I found stealthing the whole map to be an enjoyable experience as the enemies barely have time to react to you punching their lights out.
The story is well told and your decisions have an impact on how the game tells it to you. I can't say much about it without spoiling so you'll have to play it.
This game is well worth the full retail price, but if you're on the fence or just don't wanna spend a lot, you can wait for a sale so that you can pick it up and enjoy some espionage.
I want a sequel to this game so bad.
But sadly, Beta Protocol is still in Alpha.

Don't bother with this. I'd heard it was pretty poor, but since it was cheap I decided to give it a go due to it's interesting spy espionage theme.
Basically everything is just badly executed. Stealth is too easy due to the braindead AI who will sit and stare at you for about 10 seconds before walking off. Combat is just boring because of it's generic structure and fairly odd aiming system. You can basically get around most of the areas with the standard grunt enemy through bugs and glitches - I know I did. Then you go up against a boss. These are pretty unfair and the only way you'll win is by hiding behind cover, slowly picking off each of the boss's goons and then shooting the boss in the face for about 20 minutes until their stupidly large health bar is empty.
The only thing this game really has going for it is it's storytelling, with all that choices and branching stuff, ya know what I mean? It was alright I guess, but since all the characters are cardboard cutouts of generic spy movie stereotypes I found it hard to be invested in the story at all.
So yeah, don't bother with this game, unless you're willing to devote some time into it. Personally, I couldn't be bothered to play more than 4 hours because it just had too many floors for my taste. However, I can appreciate why people do defend this game.

I finished this game like 4 times before buying it from Steam (Or, perhaps, I got it with a Humble Bundle. I don't remember correctly) and I enjoyed every single bit of it.
You play as Michael Thorton, a brilliant and promising trainee to join the ranks of Alpha Protocol, a secret agency. Prove everyone and yourself that you're the best agents around. As the world around you seems to collapse, you always find a way out.
Introducing a similar, but much more interactive, dialogue system like Mass Effect, you decide the attitude you want Michael to have towards people, depending the personalities of the others and what you have read in their dossiers.
Be a spy lurking in the shadows or a tough soldier ramping your way inside compounds and bases. This amazing third person shooter game also have RPG elements allowing you to make the agent you want to be.
The story is not so long, I think. Depending on the difficulty, 20 hours should be enough for you to finish it.
Perhaps you've heard about some bugs and glitches this game have. I will not deny it, it's not a perfect game. As everything, it has some flaws. But, trust me, it's an experience hard to forget.
Would I recommend it? Hell, yes!
So, feel free to buy it, my friend. I'm sure that, if you like RPG's, you will totally love it.

As soon as you get into your HQ and start doing missions, the game becomes extremely boring because its very repetitive.
Here a summary of the first two hours:
Arrive in HQ, look around and explore the rooms in your HQ, buy stuff for your inventory/gear, go into a mission in mid east, kill bad guys, return to HQ, buy stuff for your inventory, go into mission in mid east, kill bad guys, return to HQ, ...
and so on.
After two hours I was fed up with the game, and uninstalled it.
The teammates seemed rather dull and boring, I didnt feel any obligation or interest to listen to the stuff they wanted to tell me, so I just tl;dr´d 75% of the conversations as soon as I noticed that it was going to be a boring dialogue.
The many ways to kill or not kill and move or sneak around the maps are there, but not necessary nor effective. There hasnt been a single scenario where sneaking around the whole map and silently killing enemies would have been as efficient as just going full Rambo-mode on them.
The weapons feel weird. Extremely inaccurate even when you crouch and aim down the sights. So I mostly took them out with stationed MGs.
Overall... meh. Its kind of okay, but it gets boring very quickly.

Disc Jam is a solid competitive game, and can be a lot of fun to play! It's easy to pick up, and hard to master. There are a number of characters, skins, emblems, name tags, and discs to choose from. However, as of right now, the amount of content is pretty limited.
Here's why:
After going through the basic and advanced tutorials, if you're playing alone, there is nothing to do except for free play, and customising your character. The playerbase is small meaning it can take a very long time to find a match online. There is no option to enable bots for offline play, and, in doubles, teams are required to be balanced regardless.
Do I recommend Disc Jam? Definitely yes if you have others to play with. If you're playing alone, then it can get a little boring after a while. That's mostly because this game is underrated and needs a bigger playerbase.
It's still a new game so hopefully the devs can add some new features in future updates.

I just wanted to say the MT's aren't as bad as people are making them out to be. The game really opens up in Act II when you can finally start to recruit your own Orcs. I've killed an Orc only to have him come back, kill me, upgrade to legendary and be promoted to a Warchief. It's rare but it does happen. And I was in turn able to dominate him and have him join my side. Not to mention you find a ton of legendaries/epics just through playing the game and sometimes they aren't even as good as normal Orcs you may find due to their weaknesses.
The MT's are there to reduce the grind for the final chapter. It's not necessary to complete the game or get the best end result. It just allows you to buy better Orcs instead of having to look for them yourself or send the ones you already have out on missions to get them stronger. From what I have seen they can gain up to 7 levels (maybe more) for one easy mission and you can even assist them to assure success. And it's a lot easier to get a worm to give intel and pick Orcs that way rather than to rely on boxes.
The online function is also there if you really want loot boxes for free, as well as daily quests which do give cash currency at times. A good bit into Act II you open up the ability to siege other people's fortresses that they set up with their Orcs. This in turn gives you gear depending on how well you did and points to redeem for spoils of war chests. I've only gotten one Spoils of War chest  since I have mostly been playing the storyline but it seemed slightly better than the gold chests that you can buy off the market. It may have been luck, but the point is there are ways outside of MT's to earn what everyone is complaining about. Like most games, MT's are just a means for speeding up progression that you can easily do yourself if you just play the game rather than spending more money than you already have.
Can the game get repetitive? Yes, absolutely. I feel like I might only be half way through. After 30-40 hours most games are going to get repetitive for most anyone. Don't get me wrong though, there's a lot of variety in the story missions and what you can do in the open-world but a lot of it does revolve around killing and subduing Orcs. If you don't enjoy the battle system the game probably will not last long for you.

This is the sequel to Shadow of Mordor which expands upon every dynamic aspect from the original game.  Deeper story (the end of act 1 was amazing), improved combat, enriched Nemesis system, larger skill tree, gear upgrades, more challenging and sufficiently punishing game play.... with about 25 hours of play time put in thus far I can say that this is probably my favorite game released within the last couple of years.  While I enjoyed the original Shadow of Mordor, I found myself bored of that game after short periods of play time, not at all the case with Shadow of War.
I was initially concerned about the developer's decision to implement micro-transactions but to be completely honest, I barely even notice that they are in the game and they very much seem to be an after thought.  I have been steadily gaining character levels after just 1-2 missions and sometimes find myself with an excess number of skill points to drop into the skill tree (which is ~3x larger than the last game).  Gear upgrades also come regularly and I find myself swapping gear up every hour or so of play.
If you played Shadow of Mordor and have access to the Nemesis Forge, I highly recommend playing that first.  There was a period in the game where my Nemesis from the forge showed up which ended up turning into a 15-20 min battle.  It was intense and at a level of difficulty that you could only find in games like Dark Souls.  My particular nemesis was especially challenging due to the fact that his only weakness (heavily damaged by beasts) was offset by one of his many strengths (Beast Slayer).  I was sad to finally plunge my sword deep into his chest as he bled out into the arena.... it was apparent to me that he had earned his "Champion of Sauron" title.  I sincerely hope that he returns later on in my game.
I would not be surprised to see this game pick up several "game of the year" titles.  Definitely recommended.

Let me tell you the story of Kuga the Unashamed.
Kuga the Gentle was originally a fairly plain looking Orc Captain in Nurnen until one day his Blood Brother, Flogg Eagle Eye, was forced into the service of the Gravewalker. Kuga was never aware of this, but one day he encountered the Gravewalker. Knowing that defeating the scourge of Mordor would increase his fame, Kuga decided to fight him in hand to hand with his mace. After a hard battle, Kuga was beaten into the ground and the Gravewalker tried to turn him as well, only to find his will too strong. The Wraith within, enraged, attacked Kuga's mind in an attempt to shame him.
But Kuga was too strong for this and, rather than being weakened by it, he came back stronger and prouder, determined to get vengance for his humilitating defeat. Hearing of this, the Gravewalker hunted him down and decided to test the Uruk's newfound courage. The Ranger found that Kuga's attacks had become much stronger, his fury reckless, and his resolve almost unshakable. After a long, tiring battle, the Ranger finally defeated Kuga the Unashamed, bending him to his will. As a Captain in the Bright Lord's army, Kuga gained a reputation for savagry, single-handedly wiping out entire hunting parties. Eventually, the Gravewalker decided one of the War Chiefs, Hura Pathfinder, needed to be killed to weaken the Stronghold and sent Kuga to infiltrate his bodyguards.
Kuga happily accepted his mission, easily becoming a bodyguard after defeating his opponent with two swings of his dreaded mace. After the fight, the Gravewalker informed Kuga that they would be putting the War Chief down and that all his bodyguards would assist. When Kuga arrived to meet up with his prey, he found Flogg Eagle Eye waiting. It was then that Kuga learned the truth, that his Blood Brother was a spy for the Grave Walker since shortly after his arival in Nurnen.
When the Gravewalker dropped off the cliff in front of Hura, the brothers nodded before Flogg shot the hulking Uruk in the back, knocking him over before Kuga brutally beat the War Chief's skull in. It didn't matter who they followed or who they killed. The two brothers would always have each others' backs, and the Gravewalker made sure they wouldn't have to kill each other.
...And after all this, I realize I created a Kruk Blood-Axe with the savagery and invincibility of Prak Jaws. Mordor will never be the same again.

Quick Summary: The Walking Dead Season 2 is obviously the sequel to the first Walking Dead game by Telltale. If you haven’t played that one yet, you really shouldn’t start with Season 2. Your choices from the first game carry over from your save files, but don’t be too worried about how old choices impact Season 2’s plot because mostly they’re just mentioned in throwaway conversation lines. “I remember when we first met and you said blah blah blah…” Season 2 is shorter than the first game by a couple of hours, and has a little less puzzle solving, so you spend less time wondering what you’re supposed to do next.  It’s still not an action game though, so if you’re looking for a shooter you may get bored.
The story picks up a little while after the ending of the first Walking Dead game, with the main character being Clementine this time around. Clem is a little older but still for the most part can’t go hand to hand against the “walkers.” Most of the walkers you meet will be a threat to be evaded or struggled with, unlike the television show where every dude with a knife can headshot 20 walkers per minute. As you might expect, the biggest threats in the game will be other humans, all struggling to survive in this post-apocalyptic world.  Group politics and conflicting loyalties will be your main decision points, with 5 possible game endings. However, the ending is basically “chosen” in the last 10 minutes of the game, so your earlier decisions won’t limit your decision.
Just like in the first Walking Dead game, Season 2 is kind of an interactive movie where the plot unfolds through unskippable cutscenes and dialogue, and every once in a while you get to choose how you want Clem to respond to a question. Usually you get 4 dialogue choices (saying nothing is a choice) and about 5 seconds to choose which one you want. Just like in the first Walking Dead, don’t worry about saying the wrong thing. You’re not going to♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone off so much that it affects the main story unless it’s one of the few critical choices (such as saving one person and letting another die). The critical choices will be showed in a list after the end of each episode comparing your choices with other game players. So just choose whatever option you think will provide the most amusing response, the game’s plot is mostly fixed.
Pros:
+If you accept that your decisions are mostly for entertainment purposes, the game is easy and relaxing. It’s not a “choose your own adventure” book where a wrong choice leads to your death. Generally speaking you will know when your life is in danger, and even if you die in a failed quick-time event, you only need to replay about 5 seconds to get back to where you died.
+Well written story, although there’s a mysterious gap in time near the beginning. Perhaps a DLC is planned?
Cons:
-Just like the first game, the auto-saves can be a little far apart so set aside an hour or two to play. Don’t try playing for 15 minutes at a time. Also, the ending credits of each episode are unskippable. You need to sit there and watch them scroll through before moving on to the next episode.
-Not much replay value for the game. Play through it once and you’re basically done with it.
Overall, I recommend Season 2 if you’ve played the first game and liked it. It’s basically the same game with a new storyline. I’m glad I got the game despite mostly being an action game fan, but if you’re not a fan of interactive movies / point and click games, both Walking Dead games may drag for you.

The Rating System: Good refers to the obvious positive qualities, the Bad is reserved for nitpicks and gripes that don't necessarily ruin the experience, the Ugly is for the worst parts of the game, meant for serious consideration before purchase.
The Good:
Who hasn't wanted to talk about this game once they've played it? What can be said that hasn't already been said? This part of the review will be difficult to write, but I'll do my best. Hotline Miami's gameplay isn't very original by itself. It's a perspective brawler, how many other games can wear that hat? But Hotline Miami is much more brutal than others of the genre, and it relishes in that fact. Every sound effect and visceral spray of blood is deliciously satisfying. This is a game of superlatives that banks on its coolness to carry it. Even its creators poke fun at how its gameplay is all style and satisfaction over any real substance. "Was any of it worth it?" "Didn't you at least have fun?" The gameplay is extremely unforgiving of any mistakes, and if you love challenges as much as me, that will only entice you. If you take the game's own advice and stop being scared of dying, getting into the mindset of a remorseless killer rather than a careful planner, you'll find success coming a lot quicker and easier - yes, easier. The game will become a lot more fun if you stop trying to treat it like other games and indulge in as much suicidal behavior as you can. You have to deprogram the mentality that you are valuable or you'll find many repeat deaths. If you cease to care if you die, you'll have fewer deaths and generally less frustration with them. Once you hit your stride, you may become as addicted as Jacket himself to the act of senseless killing. It's a heavy drug, so try not to overdose. Its stylish presentation and pulse pounding gameplay is worth the already relatively cheap price in my opinion.
The story is thin, but has just enough interesting moments and plot elements that it never becomes boring, it simply leaves a lot up to interpretation. If you like speculative fiction, Hotline Miami may satisfy that part of your tastes too. It takes place in a reality where Russia won the Cold War, about a man who recieves mysterious messages on his answering machine that tell him to murder the Russian mafia living among us. I won't give any more spoilers about the game, as to say more would be pretty much summarizing the game's entire, scant amount of story outside of simply exploring the mind of the player character, Jacket. The top down perspective and retro aesthetic are wonderfully over the top, but there are problems and limitations with it that I'll get into later. If you like the 80's and all its bravado, from cheesy Arnold Shwarzenegger power fantasy movies to gore filled horror ala Friday the 13th, this is a must own as the atmosphere is so thick with synthesizers and blood that you'll almost choke on it.
It would almost be a crime to talk about Hotline Miami and neglect mentioning its soundtrack. The music is perfectly implemented, and I'm probably reading too much into it, but I feel that every track has its purpose. Bright and exciting when in combat, seeming to imply that the only time the player character feels alive is when he's murdering, but the second it's over the music turns ominous and unsettling, symbolic of how the horror of what he has done has sunk in for our "protagonist" and all he wants to do now is run away. The post-mission results screen's music is hauntingly soothing, growing more upbeat the further away he gets from the crime scene, showing how relaxed he's becoming again. The track at the start of each job is otherworldly and jarringly different from the rest of the game. I believe that it's symbolic of him "giving in" to his dark urges as he gets another reason from his phone to kill again, grim yet satisfying like a drug addict getting their next fix. He always had this addiction, and the gentle pushing from anonymous messages on his answering machine is all the excuse he needs to indulge that addiction.
The Bad:
The top down perspective and 8-bit art design can make it difficult to interpret the environment correctly, leading to a lot of deaths on that alone. You'll often find it hard to tell what's solid, what's cover and what's low enough to the ground to be shot over (for example, bath tubs provide cover, but pool tables do not). I'd often get killed trying to take cover behind something that isn't actually cover, and all of this is due to the limitations of a top down perspective. There's many secrets in the game, some of which are literally pixels worth of size that get lost in the intentionally undetailed 8-bit environments, but thankfully these aren't required to be found in order to beat the game. The AI, if you are playing carefully, is very unpredictable. Sometimes they'll wander out of rooms they were previously walking in circles within, sometimes they'll just snap-aim at you, while other times taking a full 2 seconds to realize you're near. If you're trying to take this game slow, it will become a teeth grinding chore to beat. Combine that unpredictability with the fact that any damage you take will instantly kill you and you will initially find yourself tip-toeing through the game's stages, which the game will actually punish you for. In order to acquire new abilities and gear, you have to earn a high score, and the game will detract from your score for playing it safely. You must play this game the way IT wants to be played, rather than the other way around. Taking your time gives few unlocks, and the game will even give you sarcastic ratings like, "Playstyle: Coward". Hotline Miami is like a party-loving bro friend: A magnetic personality and amazing fun to be around, but you're going to have to put up with a lot of its obnoxious habits and demands to prove your worth through suicidal challenges ("UPSIDE-DOWN BEER CHUGGING! WOO!").
Oh, and this is without a doubt the pettiest thing I can gripe about, but half the achievements have blatant grammar and spelling mistakes. Please proofread your stuff, fellas. Hotline Miami has achieved cult classic status and is a gaming phenomenon, treat it like one.
The Ugly:
Dear Christmas will this game crash on you. It will crash and crash and crash, and after so many deaths and time spent on even one stage, you may feel the urge to take a baseball bat to your computer in frustration. If you're running on Widows 8.1 like me, try going into the game's installation folder and right clicking on HotlineMiami.exe, then setting its compatibility settings to Windows XP Service Pack 3. It'll crash a lot less, but using the Steam overlay (shift-tab) will sometimes make the game crash too.
Final Verdict: 6/10
Despite me harshly criticizing it and despite that cold score above, I actually am somewhat addicted to Hotline Miami. I come back to it again and again, I want to indulge in every bit of lore and fan art I can find on it, and can't wait to try its sequel to find some answers to the questions the first game left for me. However, the issues I find with it are so glaring and hard to deal with that I admit that my love of it is probably a symptom of gaming Stockholm Syndrome. It's absolutely not for everyone. The skull-breaking difficulty combined with frequent crashes and half-random AI is enough in my mind to justify warning readers that it might not be for them. If you aren't into the game's atmosphere and retro NES level difficulty isn't something that appeals to you, maybe pass on Hotline Miami. That being said, I still believe that said flair and atmosphere are worth the price on their own, and for that reason I can still recommend it.

In "The Walking Dead: Season 2" you play as Clementine, the 9 year old, now about 11, girl from Season 1. This takes place around 1 to 3 years after the events of Season 1, and with this you see how Clementine has to move away from how she was in the first season. Without Lee, you experience everything Clementine is without her having some trusted figure protecting her most of the time.
This installment in the series focuses more on how Clementine survives and deals with the situations she is forced in. Bringing into light that Clementine can not be sheltered as she once was to survive, you can not keep everyone alive or trust just anyone even if they have the means to take care of you. From the beginning the game shows this, and it is strongly placed within the first chapter. It can trick you into thinking the situation is as innocent as it seems, while deep down it isn't. As Clementine learns everyone and everything is out to survive first, you do too. It was a good choice choosing Clementine as it might not be the same if Lee was still there or in control of a totally different character. Everything seems more harsh, more dire, that Clementine uniquely brings to the series. It brings more perspective when you see another kid being sheltered and how they handle it in comparison to Clementine; you can't help but think how Clementine would of survived if the events in Season 1 didn't take place or wasn't taught how to survive.
Telltale kept the main aspects and built more upon them. Moving is improved (and unlike the first, you actually stop when you hit an invisible wall) and the combat system feels better especially when you have to think fast. It's smoother, and when you fail it feels like you were too slow, not that it was the game. There also seems to be more detail within the artwork to convey the gore and facial expressions especially in key moments and the voice acting only adds to the experience. I often found myself cringing at certain moments as it was painful to control Clementine through harsh situations, wishing the scene can finish to stop the feeling of heartbreak or pain. This edition includes multiple endings, and I wonder how Telltale will address each of them in Season 3.
There are some things they could of done better story-wise, but it didn't totally affect the experience. Walking Dead Season 2 imports decisions made in Season 1 and 400 Days dlc, but it isn't required to play those beforehand as it does randomly fill in decisions for you if you haven't. It easily conveys how Clementine is attached to characters in Season 1 that do show up so you won't entirely be left out. It will certainly be interesting how Telltale handles the differentIf you're a fan on The Walking Dead, or generally Telltale games, this is definitely a must buy.

After the acclaimed success of 2012's The Walking Dead (Season One), it's no surprise that TellTale Games released a follow up less than a year later; what is a surprise is that we don't have a Season Three yet. During that short time, the company managed to add some additional mechanics that made the experience still feel as fresh as ever, despite its familiar graphics and linear styled gameplay. If your feelings and conscience were strained with the series' first installment, you haven't experienced anything yet.
Continuing nearly a year after where the first game left off, The Walking Dead: Season 2 puts you in the shoes of 10 year old Clementine. Since Lee sacrificed himself to save her, Clementine eventually regrouped with Omid and a very pregnant Christa. It doesn't take long for things to heat up, and within a matter of minutes the first character is killed off, proving to the player that this title is going to be filled with even more dramatic, hard-hitting events than its predecessor. After this event, sixteen more months pass and eventually Clementine is alone in the world, left to defend herself and scavenge for food and water without the aid of anyone. It's truly a horrific plot if one thinks about it, and how dangerous a world like that would be for such a young kid, especially a little girl.
Sticking with TellTale's signature design, the game is split into five episodes. As well, the player is given the choice of four dialogue options in any given conversation; jerk, nice, apathetic, and no response generally speaking. If you have a save file of Season One, the game will take the choices made from there and implement them into the storyline. While the quick time events are still present, there's also the addition of a slightly more sophisticated combat system that requires aiming with the mouse or controller. As well, the player can move Clementine around the world more in this title than Lee in the sophomore release. Basically speaking, there's more freedom of movement in this title. Other than that, the core mechanics stay the same; including the "remember" system where characters will remember your conversations and actions toward them.
The graphic style has pretty much stagnated from the first release, although Season 2 does feature more luminosity with a few brighter colors scattered sporadically throughout; such as the sunset sky, or a campfire. It still features cell shaded comic graphics, as it should given the history of the series. It also seems to be a little more detailed, and a lot more gory than its predecessor. All are a welcomed upgrade. As usual, the voice acting is in an unrivaled top tier, and the emotions of the characters really bleed through wonderfully.
If you enjoyed TellTale's first Walking Dead game, then The Walking Dead: Season 2 will not disappoint you at all. Some, like myself, may not enjoy playing as Clementine as much over Lee or another "grown up" character, but there's a deep appreciation for how adventuresome the storyline is. Playing a ten year old girl in a harsh environment such as the zombie apocalypse is genuinely unfathomable, and psychologically horrifying if one sits down and thinks about it deeply enough. Even though to some people it doesn't stack up as well to the first game, it's still a worthy successor and amazing story without question. Again, given its age I do recommend this title on sale.

Positives:
+Dynamic story that reacts to the choices you make, and not in a cheap, inconsequential way like the Mass Effect games have.
+Deep dialogue system that allows for great roleplay possibilities and character development.
+Memorable characters and locales, all very well realized.
+High replay value, no two playthroughs will be the same, and no two Agent Thorton's will be the same.
+Excellent writing.
Negatives:
-Poorly balanced. Not all skills are created equal, stealth and pistols are game breakingly OP and many other skills are just entirely non-viable for "builds".
-Somewhat buggy. While not frequent in my experience, many users report small bugs breaking a sequence and forcing a reload to fix.
-Arbitrary checkpoints are the only real means of saving your progress.
-Controls are rough around the edges, and unfortunately this extends to the shooting as well.
Conclusion:
Alpha Protocol is a game I'm hesitant to recommend for anyone who values mechanics over storytelling, as Alpha Protocol fails in the former while blasting expectations of the water with the latter. If you can forgive the games many failings, you will find a captivating RPG there within the rough.

Alan Wake is an exercise in "what could have been cool." Did George Lucas have a hand in creating this? It's disappointing enough to have his stench about it and it smells of cheap coffee.
The game starts you out in a nightmare sequence as a tutorial, which is appropriately concises but also effective. I actually liked the shooting mechanic of using the flashlight to aim. Then you're dropped into a little town out in the wilderness and it feels genuinely alive. Being someone who currently lives in the middle of no where, I really get the feeling the developers took a trip out into the Heartland and visited little towns in the USA and Canada. However, that's where all the positives really end.
What you get is a shallow, boring, and sluggish thirdperson shooter with very little elements in survival and absolutely nothing creepy about it. When will video games figure out that seeing silhouetted outlines of humans isn't scary, at all. Hearing voices that have been distorted isn't scary. Being forced into arena shooting galleries isn't scary. You never feel vulnerable in the game, at all. That's a huge problem for any kind of game trying to be survival horror. If you're not threatened, you're not scared. Also, seeing the familiar outlines of humans in this situation isn't scary.
Alan Wake is like the Charlie Brown Halloween Special: You see all the cliches like witches and vampires, but you're never once even unsettled since the imagery your seeing is as overplayed as possible. Mix that in with iffy controls because, once again, a developer is too lazy to make a decent PC port and you have Alan Wake. Skip.

A very shallow game masquerading behind difficulty to give the illusion of depth.
It's extremely enjoyable as finger crack but that's about it.  All of the games interesting mechanics revolve around the fact that you are constantly forced to obtain money in order to sustain your Gladiator empire and the game is at its best during the establishing period where you have to wrangle your way to survival by killing off old Gladiators to steal their savings or betting against a sacrificial lamb you've sent to the slaughter.  But from there on out it's all down hill.  The more stuff you get the more meaningless everything becomes.  After a while I couldn't be bothered to even upgrade all of my Gladiators because it had become so tedious to do so.
How best to sum up the superficial nature of the game?
All Gladiators have an age.  And the game tells you if their age puts them as developing, in their prime or declining.
Great.  I'll buy some old guys to keep me afloat and some young guys to develop for the future.
Don't bother.  It doesn't mean anything.  A complete play through of the game is not likely to cover more than 2 in game years.  And as far as I could tell the age had zero impact on the development of fighters.
I signed a 17 year old to begin with and aged 18 with 39 fights under his belt he wanted to retire.  Meanwhile the 34 year old I signed was still there at 36 and had leveled up exactly the same without losing stats.  And there's not enough customisation of stats, fighting style and stratergy to really feel like you "own" any of the gladiators or that they have any degree of personality.
The grind is a problem too.  You fight all the time.  You have to in order to keep the money coming in.  Each turn is a day in game time so you're literally moving through the game at a snails pace, clicking into a fight every couple of days and hoping the random numbers come up in your favour.
If you like management finger crack, which I do, you'll enjoy this, which I did.  But I won't ever turn it on again.  So read into that what you will.

Tim Schafer and friends made another cool game. The Writing is Double-fine quality: Great writing with bits of humor thrown around.
The Gameplay is what you come to expect from a point and click adventure game. click to walk around, Item Inventory to use for puzzles, etc. Nothing truly groundbreaking but compared to old 90s point and clicks like Day of the tentacle and Sam & max the interface is way better. It serves it's purpose well. Would say it feels better than the recent telltale games.
The Puzzles have a sense of logic to them, they arn't Phoenix-Wright/Ghost Trick style Logic-Leaping but it isn't  "Fit round object into round slot" easy.
The Voice acting is really well done. it is easily the highest quality part of the game. Nothing felt out of place and nothing got annoying to me.
The Characters are great too, From the crazy cloud people to the Blind Guardians of the Dead Eye God. Even the Hipster lumberjack (now named Curtis) which was made fun of early in development is funny.
The Soundtrack is great for what it does, but it's not something i would loop on my Music player when im not playing.
The art style is beautiful. I Pressed the screenshot button alot to get some desktop wallpaper out of it.
It's quite obvious that the ending part was slapped together quickly because it randomly became a two part series in development, But i can't wait for part 2. Don't want to spoil anything.
I would recommend buying it. If you have a longing for a classic point and click adventure or want something like the Telltale Sam and Max Games i would get it. Though if your expecting something like the Walking dead or Wolf Among Us with ~~choices~~ and stuff like that don't get it.
