Age Of Gladiators is a nice little bussiness sim, with lots of RPG and strategy elements.
This game can appeal more to the casual players, giving you the option to complete a playthrough quickly. Yet, all the components needed for a deep, complex and involved experience are there.
It's a game where decisions matter. How you build your gladiator school, how you shape your gladiators, and how you develop your own character, they all add up to affect the outcome of your game.
For a full experience, i recommend playing in the ironman mode. It will push you into studying your opponents, evaluating risk and reward before every fight. You can keep track of your opponent's gladiators, when they might be injured, fatigued, how they improve. It will let you decide when you send a weaker fighter into the battle, to grow him, or to weaken your opponents to give your superstar more chances to win in his next battle (you can also bet against your own fighter, if you decided to sacrifice him...but if he somehow survives, he won't be very happy about it!).
Also, try different gladiator builds, there can be a use for most of them. Don't be affraid to experiment.
I would really like to see a good tutorial added in, otherwise you need a few playthroughs until you figure out all the mechanics and little things.
And now, the essential question:
All in all, you decide how difficult and how in-depth the game can be. I fully recommend it. Especially since it looks like the developer is caring about it and investing more resources into making it better.

This game...
The art style and music are awesome, creative and feel fresh and new. Every step you will take in the world of Broken Age looks absolutely gorgeous. And while you are looking around everywhere and soaking in this colorful world, the sweet soundtrack fits perfectly in every scene. There are some hiccups, when the track starts again after you run around in one screen for ages, but this is not even once annoying or anything near it. Great music, great art style!
The gameplay is as it self advertises: Pointing and Clicking. And that is not a lie. I feels and plays like a good point'n'click adventure. (Somehow I miss the different options like: grab, push, use...and stuff like that) but still it works is very minimalistic and suits the gameplay very well. Overall the riddles are easy and that is a point that bothered me a bit. I never felt like really thinking and searching for solving a puzzle. Don't expect a full inventory and the good old "I try every item combination" method. Most of the time the solution is direct in front of you or only some screens away. And when you can pick up an item, you'll use it at another point.
Nonetheless the story makes up for the most of the time easy puzzles. It will start very slow (you decide when which character is telling his story) but it develops a good pace and keeps it till you reach a great finale when the act ends (no spoilers here :) The question now should rather be: Is that a story for children or adults? I would like to say it is for both, but cause of some puzzles and dialogues it seems to be more aimed at younger players. Still you will have a good time with the story and more than one time a smile will sneaky make it's way onto your face. I found myself mor than one time smiling stupidly at my screen and being happy. (My tip: play the game when you have some free time and do it in one single sitting)
Now that I played through the game: I am hyped, I am pumped and ready for Act 2 and I look forward to play the second part of this great adventure.
You want fun and happiness? This game is a musthave. (Don't get me wrong, the story is not only happy and rainbow-ish, sometimes it becomes darker than you would expect)

Disc Jam is a very fun, fast-paced and competitive multiplayer sports game.
Graphics:
It won't make you go "Wooow" but it is certainly well-made and doesn't look bad at all.
Performance:
It runs well for me and even if it doesn't for you, you can turn down the graphics quite a bit to fix this.
Music:
There are only three different tracks in the game so they do get stale after a while but they fit the game very well.
Sound:
The sound design is good, nothing special to say about this though.
Gameplay:
The matches can be very fun, especially when you're playing with your friends in 2v2. Disc Jam is easy to pick up but hard to master.
The controls are good but playing on keyboard is substantually harder than with a controller.
By playing random matches and voting on game streams, you can also earn an ingame currency. It can be used to get some nice random prizes which are cosmetics like skins, taunts and tags. This also provides another small reason for playing some more.
The characters are all very interesting and for the most part well-balanced with their personal strengths and weaknesses.
The developers are planning to implement even more content so the game should improve even more in the future.
The playerbase may not be the biggest but if you have or make a few friends to play with/against regularly, it's fine.
All in all I recommend this game because it is alot of fun.

If you are looking at this as a veteran of other FPS/RTS games, you're probably wondering why this $13 indie game should be worth your time and money compared to the bigger budget ones. You probably think it's quite a bit like them at a first glance. That's where you're wrong.
First and foremost, this game is an RTS. A proper RTS. This doesn't rely on multiplayer matches with other people to be your groundfolk or play the opposing team or anything like that, everything works as it should in a proper RTS. You can go completely offline in single player against up to 3 AIs in configurable teams and difficulties, or online with other players and AI if so wished. You build your base, you build your units from a huge (emphasis: HUGE) list of weapons and upgrades, and you control them all as you would in any other RTS. It's done well, it's fun, and it has all the things a GOOD RTS needs - massive titanic sized walkers driven by captain martini-in-hand, huge destructive lasers, and a big list of buildings to choose from.
This game adds strategy to a location that most RTS games dont - building your base. Usually, a base's construction is simply a matter of what you've unlocked so far or what you want next, and the way to win is to have a bunch of a single building all producing something. That or they're just tech tiers. The strategy here lies in the small grid given to construct your base - all structures are confined to it and connected via corridors at one of many preset points for each building. The result of the small space and huge number of buildings means you have to be efficient when designing your base and can't simply lay things wherever you please. You can't fit everything into a single base, and some sacrifice will have to be made to specialize in something for the game. For example, if you wanted to completely surround your base with walls, that's going to take a toll on how much space you have remaining for other buildings. If you want an artillery station, that's going to take up a huge amount of room you could use for other things. The whole base becomes an intricately designed puzzle that, for the record, you can fully walk about in when in FPS mode and will -HAVE- to deal with to win the game.
The units are built in a sort of design-yourself ideal, where you pick the type of unit you want, special ability, and weapon before saving it to a slot, of which you have 6 for each type of unit - infantry, vehicle, and aircraft. You can overwrite previous designs if you get better ones. Each unit in the game except the transport aircraft can be controlled by the player should they so desire, and depending on how good at FPS games you are, it can be an advantage over simply letting it control itself.
With that, there's also the Executron mode. Up to 4 Executrons can join each company in multiplayer, up to 16 total. They act as purely FPS players who run about and can commandeer vehicles and aircraft as well as have infantry battallions follow them into battle when necessary so the CEO can focus on other things.
The FPS mode (more so specifically Executron mode) itself, however, does leave some to be desired. I had initially said there was no way to access the menu, this is wrong - you can press F10 in FPS mode to access the menu, not escape. So point 1 is invalid. For two, the Executrons have no way of upgrading themselves without dying/respawning and can only train whatever unit is set as the basic one at factories. For three, the Executrons are quite literally just another unit - they're restricted to what a normal unit can use. This is understandable in most cases, but they're also confined to a single weapon. To help make executron players a bit more involved, multiple weapons and preferably some sort of extra health would probably be desired seeing how they have no RTS control and need other ways to stay motivated.
Overall, this is a game that's gotten me 5 hours of enjoyment in the last DAY and is likely to get many, MANY more with my friends joining me. There are still many aspects of the game I haven't been able to try - that's how big the tech tree is. And what's more, this whole game was made by 1 guy. 1 GUY. Every single thing. The art, the assets, the FANTASTIC music, all of it - 1 guy. (Ok, the music was actually his brother, but still.) It's absolutely outstanding. The game even has a huge amount of polish and is surprisingly stable and bug-free, even more so than many AAA games that come out today. I cannot bring myself to believe a single guy was able to create this good of a game. You expect this quality from higher budget studios with many people working at them, not from a single guy. On that alone I urge you to buy this game. And for $13? I'm surprised you haven't hit buy already.

8BitBoy is a homage to oldschool platformers. It looks a lot like Mario, and a little like Psycho Fox and Wonder Boy, but it has a propose: the main character is a man trapped in a world made of games of his childhood (NES and Master System era).
In your journey through five worlds you'll face different enemies, find a lot of secrets and traps. You'll need to perform perfect jumps in some areas to pass tougher stages. This can daunt some young players, but don't worry, this is not a problem of level design; games used to be like this in late 80's.
The pixel art feels truly retro. Even the menus are oldschool.
The soundtrack...well, could be better. Music is repetitive and kinda sad sometimes.
8BitBoy is made by only one guy (Rasmus Kønig Sørensen) - also, looks like this is the first game he developed. It has some flaws, but for the cheap price we can forgive.
All in all, I rate this game a 7/10

Got this during a Steam sale because someone was pointing out how underrated this game was.
For the money I paid, it was worth it.  It doesn't try to do anything unique or pretentious.  It does one thing and one thing only - be a solid 2D platformer.
You will have to realize the controls may borrow concepts from classic Mario games, but they follow their own "rules".  This was something I had to shake from my ingrained muscle memory of playing tons of Mario games - for example, running does not make you jump higher - longer yes, but higher no.
This makes some level designs mildly annoying, since it's obvious some levels were made exclusively to limit you because of these jumps.  There will be jumps where you just won't be able to make it because of a one block difference, and you're forced to either go around a long way just to reach that jump or use some other means to get there.  Super Mario games had a lot of these, but the level designs for those games didn't feel as... obvious as the levels in this one.
The enemy designs are kinda funny, strangely satisfying to stomp on enemies that look like Angry Birds.  It's like the author knew that people who like these older retro style games have a bit of a dislike for what the "Angry Birds" genre of casual mobile games have caused for the video game industry.
Regardless, if you want a few hours of fun, there's way worse things you can spend your money on.  There's lots of Youtube videos you can look up if you want first impressions of the game, and it's highly recommended you use a controller for an optimal playing experience, seeing how this game harkens back to the console platforms of old.

OK, so anyone over the age of 30 will know this really is basically the arcade game Wind Jammers brought to your home. Yes, i recommend it, but with some caveats.
Disc Jam has the potential to be a truly top game. The premise is there, the foundations are there. Now it just needs some extra floors and bells, and some very-much-needed tweaking.
See, as fun as the game is, it is also equally frustrating. There is so much emphasis on getting the "power shot" right, every time. The margin for error in pulling this off is effectively zero. Let me give you a great analogy. Go get yourself a stopwatch, start it, and stop it at precisely 1.00 seconds. Then do this again and stop it at exactly 2.00 seconds. No hundreths allowed. If you cannot do this 10 times in a row without failure, then you're going to be taking the path marked "Frustration".
Now combine the above ardour with a matchmaking system which currently pits you against the closest player geographically, regardless of skill. What has happened to me just about every time i've played is that i'm put up against someone who was in the beta, and has twitch-learnt the above ABSOLUTELY REQUIRED skill sometime during their hundred-hour playtime.
I don't want to take away from the amazing job the two (yes, 2) developers have done here. But the game definitely needs filled out with better matchmaking, alobby, more stadia, more forgiving power shots and a single player mode. Given how active the devs are, i've no doubt that all those features will come in due course.

A wacky little title that is surprisingly serious about it's core mechanics.
On it's surface, Kerbal Space Program may somewhat resemble a 'crash simulator', especially as new players try to send up their first few rockets only to have them spiral out of control right off the launch pad, Wil E Coyote style. But at it's heart, the game really wants the player to make it into space, in a smooth and graceful arc to end in a peaceful orbit around the planet, then to transfer to another majestic body to touch down on the surface... and then have you realize you done goofed with the design and your pilot is now stuck there. :P You're given all the tools you need, assuming you have the patience to learn them. And even after you've learned the base game, modding support is substantial, with hundreds of active mods to explore, from the tiny UI tweaks to a complete real world overhaul.
Do you have the Kerbal Stuff?

A turn-based tactic roguelike stealth game sounds like a lot of genres smashed together, but Invisible, Inc. is an amazing take on all of them. You control several units tactically moving around a grid-based map, attempting to complete objectives without being caught. The gameplay is asymmetric, with your opponents acting differently than yours and following estimatable AI routines. The game has many levels of strategic depth, where every decisions can produce good or bad results for you, and the game often has interesting risk vs. reward setups in the map, with you pressing your luck to get more money for upgrades, or playing it safe and completing objectives quickly and then getting out. Fans of strategy games should absolutely check this out, and fans of roguelikes and stealth games should also take a look.

Alan Wake is a story-driven game set in a beautiful location. From an early stage you're taught to be afraid of the dark. It's intriguing and obscure as you journey through a nightmare, running from light to light, armed with a flashlight and occasional flare as you're persued by dark creatures. Between the scary night stages are relaxing daytime stages that come as a genuine relief and also serve to progress the story.
I'm pleased to say thart the game unnerved me. It nails the queasy feeling of a nightmare perfectly as small things gradually grow into impossibly large obstacles without you realising until it's too late. There's a strange black goo that begins consuming the world and things start to shake before being hurled at you from across the level. It repeatedly lures you into a false sense of security by giving you other people to hang around with, before cruelly forcing you apart from them again and again. Towards the end of the game I had had enough but it was worth playing up to that stage.
There's a recurring theme with my games collection- it's the games that I wouldn't consider to be my taste that end up being the most memorable and enjoyable. Alan Wake falls under that category. It's a one-off experience, but one that is most definitely worth the effort.

I love platformers.  They take me back to the days when I was a kid, sitting up late at night, trying to get through various incarnations of the genre in the early days of NES.  I've never claimed to be good at them, mind you, but I enjoy them a lot.
8BitBoy didn't seem like much at first glance.  It came in a bundle, which means I was after something else in said bundle most likely, and 8BitBoy just came along for a ride.  One day I was digging through my library to find a cure for a sleepy Sunday afternoon, and I happened to catch the platformer tag when I scrolled across it.  I figured it couldn't hurt to give it a spin.
The first time through?  8BitBoy feels a bit off.  You go in expecting Mario, but the controls just aren't the same.  They're a bit more floaty, not quite as precise.  This will throw you off a bit, but press on.  As you dig a little deeper, you start get the hang of the controls and the game starts to feel more familar.  You're progressing through the maps, you're stomping on birds and making jumps.  Then there's that special moment when you're standing on a ledge and accidentally push the control into the wall, and you slip through and discover a secret room...and now 8BitBoy has its hooks in you!
8BitBoy is a love song to those platformers of old.  You will notice elements of them all throughout.  While looking back so fondly, the game still manages to be its own beast.  It's hard.  Hell, it's very hard!  It's also packed full of secrets, warps to other zones, many many maps and more.  All it makes for a very fun, low budget platformer that you may not have noticed otherwise!

TL;DR: This is the worst Civilization game yet. So many bad decisions, glitches, and idiotic features. Civilization V is far better in literally every way. It looks bad, feels bad to control, and most importantly, it's not fun. "And if the game isn't fun, what's the point?" - Reggie
First, I'll make a Pros and Cons list.
Pros: It starts up much faster than Civ V, you can play as a more diverse and unique cast of civilazations.
Cons: Literally every other part of the game besides the two pros are bad and/or not fun.
Next, i'll talk about the AI. Every Civilazation leader except for one or two per game is a bipolar, warmongering traitor. They either spend the entire game insulting and denouncing you for no reason, or they act like your friend, then declare a surprise war on you over and over, again, for no reason.
Now, The bad decisions. There are so many that I don't even know where to start. You cannot denounce other players, you cannot allow complete kills, you cannot embark land units at most places on the coast because of cliffs, you cannot found a religion unless you have a holy site, also most of your great merchants wont work until you have a holy site which you need 10 population to get which i would have if i could build farms but i dont want to build a worker every other production. Having one or even few cities is straight up not viable in any difficulty abovce very easy. speaking of the difficulty i played on difficulty 3 (4 is the default) so i could have an easy relaxing time learning the game's mechanics and differences. what i got was three samurai in the classical era taking my capital within 4 turns. I had a settler that i could've started again with, except complete kills are not allowed, so even if you have a settler, it's game over if they take your capital. They've dumbed down things that shouldn't have been dumbed down, and compllicated things that shouldn't have been complicated. You cannot view the city screen anymore, instead, everything that you could've done in one place in the city screen is now moved to individual little actions in the bottom right that are hard to see when you click on the city. Except when you click on your city it does something else. So many times I've thought my computer was crashed or my mouse was broken because everything takes two clicks or a click in a place where you don't expect it to be. The game looks terrible, the over-saturated cartoony art style looks like trash and is very hard on the eyes. information is not as clearly visible as it should be. Plus, they seem to try and mix multiple different artsyles, not in a good way, some things seem so out of place. Roads do nothing now, they dont improve on movement for units, they dont connect two of your cities, they are purely cosmetic, which is bad because they look like a child painted them onto the map. The advisor is mentally challenged, and has a very annoying voice. i set it to "New to Civ VI", because i wanted to learn about the features that are different from past civ games, what i got was the most obvious trash advice that applies to every civ game, nothing about any new or changed features, AND, every piece of uselees garbage that she said to me before, she repeats everytime i load my save file so i would spend five minutes dismissing this trash every single time i wanted to play. The government system is dumb, overcomplicated, doesn't make any sense, and takes away from the fun of the game. How would you have a democracy if you're the only leader ever? why do i havfe to choose between fifty cards to do tiny bonuses for my empire? it's just not a good, fun, or easy to use system. They spread out the tech tree so now instead of taking 20 turns to research something that gives you four new things, it takes five turns to research something that gives you one thing that you have to find through an absolute mess of a list, or the 50km long tech tree. There's probably more that i forgot about but pretty much they made everything worse, so now you either play a 30 city military focused empire or you get bullied for no reason by those 30 city military empires.
Glitches: Units move when you don't tell them to, wasting turns because you were trying to go somewhere. Like i said before, everything, including the Next Turn button, doesn't click on the first try, and i dont believe this is a performance issue, as i had a consistent fps >50.The load times between turns are twice as long as Civ v's (which might be a performance issue). your cursor never seems to be in the place where the screen shows you it is. and the ai that i mentioned before, i hope is a glitch, if it's not a glitch, then its just bad programming or decision making.
Don't buy this, even if you are craving a different Civ experience like I was. 1/10

Civilization 6 is quite different than Civilization V, which makes it hard to get the hang of - but it's fun to play. I am quite fond of Civ 5, so I got Civ 6 thinking that it's going to be a good play. I was right.
The Good:
- There are now two trees instead of just one - one for science and one for culture, which unlocks different forms of governments. Social policies from Civ 5 are gone, and in its place are, well, policies. They come in one of four colors - red, which are militaristic, yellow, which are economic, green, which are diplomatic, and purple, which are based around Great People. Each can only be slotted in their own respective slot in your current government (with the exception of the purple ones, which have to be slotted in the Wildcard slots which can accept any type of policy).
- Districts now exist, which force you to build specialized districts in your city before building specialized buildings in those districts. For example, the Campus district must be built before you can build a Library in there, which as a result, can no longer be built in your Capital. Non-specialized buildings, like the Monument, are still built in there.
- Wonders are now built in a separate tile.
- Even though there are different districts, only one building may be built at a time - so you cannot build a Campus and a Holy Site at the same time. In addition, you can only build a district once you hit 3 population, and then every 3 after that (so you can build an Encampment at 3, but you would have to wait until you hit 6 to be able to build a Campus).
- Escort Formations are now possible. This means that you can link a Warrior and a Builder (which is the replacement for the Worker, and gets things done instantly, but only does so 3 times), and moving one will also move the other.
The Bad:
- The AI got worse, in my opinion. It's harder to judge what they think of you, and as a result, how you should play. Each AI has two agendas, one which is visible and never changes, and one which is not visible from the beginning and is randomized. For example, Japan's Hojo Tokimune likes leaders with a strong military, but only if they also have a lot of culture and faith.
- Diplomacy got different, and I'm not sure if it was in a good way. Surprise declarations of war are more common in the Ancient and Classical eras, and it's not uncommon to be the target of one. I myself have been the target of a joint Declaration of War, which means that two AI nations declared war on me at the same time.
- Barbarians got harder to fight against. They are more intelligent and send out scouts to scout out civilizations, then send 2-3 units to fight. If you don't maximize defensive unit production at the very beginning, they're hard to deal with. A good defensive army could consist of 3 ranged and melee units, each.
- The UI was redesigned, and looks more clunky. Several buttons take up a lot more space than they did in Civ 5.
- "Dark" areas (which are areas that have been revealed in the past, but are areas you don't have vision over" appear brown and papery, which is a bit hard to get used to.
Overall, I would say Civ 6 is a good game, but not one that I would get on full price.

One of my favorite kind of games is the kind that knows exactly what it wants to be. From there, every component of the game, from graphics to music and gameplay can then be crafted to create a greater, more unified whole. I think that this is one of the ways that you can make a truly great game.
"Hotline Miami" succeeds in this way in an astounding fashion. It is a frenetic fever dream, combining twitch gameplay with tight level design, fitting aesthetics, and a killer soundtrack. "Hotline" does particularly well with atmosphere, creating an immersive and bloody acid trip. It's easy to lose oneself in the hypnotic beats and waves of psychedelia that surround this game.
To be fair, "Hotline" isn't a game for everyone. It is difficult and can be frustrating. The player can sometimes die from bullets fired from off-screen or by running into the same bad scenario again and again until they solve it. But it's for these reasons that "Hotline" also succeeds, much for the same reasons that "Super Meat Boy" did. Despite its difficulty, the punishment for failure is rather small. The player respawns almost instantly, giving them a second, third, or hundredth chance at murder.
My first playthrough of "Hotline Miami" shortly after its original release was one of my most refreshing experiences in gaming. I can't recommend that everyone should play this game enough, even if it's only to see what happens when you don't try to do too much and instead focus on what makes your game excellent.

All in all, it's a very good game if you like stealth and/or tactics games.

I've gotten this game on early access and having spent some time on it, I must say, I recommend it to anyone who would be even remotely interested in what the game has to offer: turn based stealth mechanics (as odd at it may sound - trust me, it works), squad management, with a dash of roguelike gameplay.
Klei, the studio responsible for Invisible Inc. has a pretty good track record of delivering games that are well thought out,  charming, genuinely fun and challenging. They may not be obvious blockbusters or cult classics, but the game's a gem nonethless.
The game is challenging, but it also offers a load of options which allow tailoring it to your playstyle. You can make it as easy or hard as you want it, it's also possible to entirely switch off some of the features.
The game gives you control over a clandestine organization tasked with infiltrating corporate facilities. First you select a team of two agents (each with unique skills and equipment) and a set of hacking programs to help you bypass security (cameras, locks, robots). After that, it's your job to intelligently select your assignments to gather enough resources to keep your operation afloat. The game is essentially a stealth game, so it pays to avoid direct confrontation, sneaking past security guards and resorting to non-lethal takedowns when it's unavoidable. That's not to say it's not possible to go in guns blazing; however, you will find this option to be quite hard... on your finances. The cleanup costs get pretty nasty.
The game has two modes - story and endless, the first one gives you a certain narrative framework and 24 hours of in-game time to prepare for the big mission. On endless, you just keep playing until you feel that you're done.
It's worth mentioning that the game is essentially a roguelike - each level and each playthrough is randomly generated.
While this can produce extreme arrangements that are either very difficult or near impossible to beat, learning through failure is part of the game's enjoyment, and it's worth noting that the easier difficulty levels give you the limited ability to rewind your turns (or even regenerate the entire level) to ease the learning process.
Still, even if you fail, the game rewards you with experience which is used to unlock new agents and programs. Perhaps the new ones will better suit your style?
All in all, I'd recommend Invisible Inc. to any fan of the turn based genre with a touch of squad management seeking to scratch that itch.

Since patch 1.0.1 introduced 60 fps to the game, i gave the game another chance.
I've played the game for enough hours where i feel like i can give a decent opinion on it.
This game is a very mixed bag..
On one Side there is the great story, wonderfully crafted world. great sound and music design.
But on the other there is the instability, the horrible performance and the bugs bringing the whole thing crashing down.
As of right now i cant really recommend buying it, even though i loved playing it.
Maybe later on when they released some patches, or in a sale if you have a powerful machine and dont mind some bugs here and there.
Here some good and bad points, starting with the bad:
-Settings menu in the launcher doesnt seem to affect the game settings, sloppy,
why add a configuration menu in the launcher if it doesnt work, or for that matter, why include the launcher in the first place..
-Subpar performance, even with the new patch the game performance is terrible.
On my i5 2500k with r9 290x i can barely hold 50 fps with everything on the lowest settings.
(just as a comparison, i can run gta5 with everything maxed out, and keep the game at 60 fps.)
-Keyboard and mouse controls are still subpar, even though they added extra keybinding options, they did not add an option to remove the forced centering of the camera (usually used for controllers, since thumbsticks always recenter when you take your finger of it), which makes driving with a mouse and keyboard a very awkward experience.
-Blur filters make the game look terrible, and you will need a third party filter such a reshade to remove these. Why hangar 13 chose to implement these blurs is beyond me,
They may have used them to hide the low quality textures that can be found in many places in the world, but instead of hiding this it only makes it more apparent.
-The missions are all very similar, you either destroy stuff, or people, and capture a district in that way. (Personally this didnt annoy me too much, but i can see how people would get burned out before they get to the end siumply because of the repetition.
-World feels empty and static at times. Without any side activities and the relatively simple AI of pedestrian/drivers.
-Bugs and instability, the game sometimes randomly shuts down without warning, with a random risk of your savegame getting corrupted. I didnt lose any major progress but did have to play a few missions twice. There is also some strange behaviour with physics.
Now some good points of the game for me
+interesting characters, the character design was clearly a big focus in this game,
from the facial animation to the voiceacting, all of it shows an amazing level of detail.
+great world design
+superb Soundtrack fitting the time period.
+Fun combat, very detailed (People writhe in pain when hit with a non lethal shot,limb if shot in the foot, and stand dazed for a bit before returning to fight you).
+lots of collectibles  (a plus for me since i like collecting that sort of stuff)
+good amount of content, you wont have everything done in a few hours.
+Modable, The game has no intrusive copyright protections and can be fully modded.

Alpha Protocol suffered from numerous delays and was still released very buggy, which at the time made playing the game rather frustrating. The current build is stable, resource-lean and largely bug-free, however.
The game has three major focuses: Stealth, combat, and dialogue. The first two are serviceable, though games like Thief or Deus Ex leave AP far in the dust. Players familiar with more comprehensive stealth games will likely be weirded out by some of the design choices, such as the linear area designs, or the guards in a given sub-area disappearing once you've moved onto the next, even if you can go back to the first -- though often you can't, as doors mysteriously lock up behind you. Combat likewise feels rather clunky, though I myself usually prefer the stealthy approach, anyhow -- almost all combat aside from boss fights can be avoided, as can be killing enemies even when you DO decide to engage them. The game offers various lethal and nonlethal methods of dealing with enemies.
It's in story and dialogue where the game, which is first and foremost an RPG, really shines. Many missions consist of nothing but dialogue, and virtually every choice you make therein has some consequence in gameplay, as do the actions you take. The effect might be slight, such as increasing or decreasing a character's opinion of you (something that may well come into play later on), or it might open up or close off entire story paths. How the end game plays out very much depends on the choices you made and how you interacted with the various characters you meet along the way.
The dialogue is witty and flows along effortlessly, and the characters are interesting, varied and written in depth. Beside the dialogue, there's also tons of documents for the player to uncover and delve into, and acquiring this extra data often offers all kinds of story benefits as well. In short, it is a real treat for anyone fond of story-driven RPGs.

After playing with an unlocked framerate for about 6 hours I can now say that I really enjoy it.
Graphically, it's not as good looking as I hoped for. Definitely not as impressive as GTA V but still not that bad. There is some noticeable blurring of textures and it feels like they have an overall washed-out filter on top of everything however this can be fixed with a SweetFX config that removes the blurring and increases the vibrancy of colours. (You can find it on the Mafia 3 subreddit)
In terms of the story, it really catches your attention and draws you in. Combine that with the really well done cut scenes and voice acting it makes for an amazing experience, on par with Red Dead Redemption imo.
In terms of gameplay it is pretty enjoyable. The sounds of the guns are amazing, much better then GTA V. And being able to call in help from you associates in the form of backup to help you beat up a rival gang or a concierge to collect the earnings from your businesses, along with a few other people to help you out is really cool.
Also, the way you can manage your businesses and assign them to different underbosses who then grant you different rewards but at the cost of loosing loyalty from  the other ones is really cool and acts like an unlock tree in some ways.
There are a few problems however. The car destruction physics are ♥♥♥♥ing dreadful, you can have a head on collision with another driver and all you get is a broken headlight or you clip a small curb and have the car flip over and burst in to flames.
When playing missions, if you choose to go stealthy it can be pretty boring in the beginning of the game where you basically hide in cover, whistle to get their attention, kill them, repeat 20 times. Once you unlock the silenced weapons however, it is a lot more fun and you can do some pretty cool stuff as you run between cover and pop heads of the unsuspecting enemies.
After the patch, the performance has been pretty good for me. It crashed twice pre-patch in the 11 hours I played it but has yet to crash post-patch with about 6 hours of playing.
I get around 70-80fps average with my 980ti, i7-4790K using max settings and with AA on “high”.

So far it seems like a great game but playing it for any more than 20 minutes gives me eye cancer. I will probably refund this if the framerate isn't unlocked in a patch within the next few days.

Apparently 2k have a fix working and they are sending it out this weekend. Why it wasn't just included at launch I will never know.

This game puts you in charge of running a school of gladiators.  You train them, book them in matches, and determine their stats as they level up.
Since the game came out, the developer has shown suppot for it through regular updates which have improved, expanded, and enhanced gameplay.  At the time of writing this, I have completed three playthroughs of the game and logged a total of 43 hours of gameplay, according to Steam.  Not bad for ten bucks.
My only complaint is that the end game gets a little tedious when it feels as though your fighters can't lose a match and you still have to take out two entire rival schools to win the game.  Also, be prepared to fail on your first few attempts to get your school going successfully.  It's hard to stay financially solvent for the first month or two.
All in all, it plays like a good, if not super detailed, sports management game - and I recommend picking this up if that sounds appealing to you.  It's worth the full price, but if it happens to go on sale, it's a steal!

Extremely fun game, probably one of my favorite indie games out there. It's difficult and challenging and if you're not used to rogue-like, bullet hell styled games you might struggle in the beginning, but the game is fun even if you're not doing too well and is simple enough that you will improve relatively quickly. You can play the game as a balls-to-the-wall shooter where you charge in and kill everything the best you can or as a cover-based shooter using longer ranged weapons to pick off enemies. You will find yourself just enjoying the game for its colourful and smooth gameplay that can get very intense and heated in fierce firefights.
Pros:
- Very intense yet simple at the same time gameplay.
- Is challenging and difficult yet also beginner friendly with a tolerable learning curve.
- Colourful, challenging, and interesting bosses (Bonus: The boss cutscenes are a good touch)
- Gameplay is very smooth and polished; haven't run into any bugs or glitches yet.
- Lots of enemy types with varying strengths, weaknesses, and threat levels.
- Lots of fun weapons and weapon types.
- Lots of unique and fun characters that are well balanced and varied.
- Lots of replayability; will likely return to the game from time to time
- Co-Op mode for playing with friends.
- Isn't graphic intensive and will play on almost any machine.
Cons:
- Music can get repetitive at times; not too much of a factor.
I'd rank it 9.5/10, worth its price ($12.99 CAD at the time of this review being written)

I cannot recommend this game in good faith.
Those who are aware of my history with this game may find this unusual and I apologize to any who are offended by my opinion.  However I cannot, under the weight of my conscious, suggest that others play this game.  The issue is not a lack of quality; quite the opposite.  This is a game where people lose hours, days, weeks while just pushing as far as they can.  Spawn, kill, get hit by a Rhino on 6_1, spawn, kill, meet Lil Hunter, spawn, kill, loop all over again.  My time played is staggering, but I am not even close to the most time spent by a single person and it also does not account for all the additional time spent.  The hours I used making posts, talking about things with friends, watching others to see what they did, finding secrets, and getting unlocks.  Over the past years this filled gaps between less interesting games and shows.  Just a seamless gauntlet of spawning, killing, porting between worlds, collecting gats, slaying bosses, and then getting taken out only to do it all over again.  And again.  Deep in it's subtitles, simple in it's concept, hypnotic in it's nature.  A beautiful back hole of time.  If given the chance to do it again I'm certain I'd spend even more time with it...  But-but for others, for those who are not aware; who have not stood at the brink of the abyss.  Have not watched time slip though their fingers run after run; loop after loop.  I say there is nothing for you here.  If you were to delve into this it could make so many other titles appear shallow and lacking by comparison.  It's brilliance would make a library of games appear dull under the same light.
Again I say; under the weight of my conscious and in good faith I cannot recommend this game.  Now if you'll excuse me I have an abyss to peer into once more.

This game is so addictive. I've never played a game like this where I didn't mind to start all over again. Shooting with all the different weapons is extremely pleasant, and mowing down through waves of enemies with the mini-gun is literally the best thng ever. The enemies are all original and threatening in their own ways, and the playable characters all have different play-styles, which are all fun to try out. Although the game can be very unforgiving at times, dying is very much your fault most of the time. The art style and story are both really nice.
The randomness of the dungeons is a downside in some cases, for example when spawning right in the open and dying immediately, or, in the Scrapyard or Frozen City, spawning in a tight corridor with a car in your way, which can accidentally lead to a very explosive death. Although it has some minor cons, this game is a very fresh and welcome addition in my library, and I recommend it to all.

But at it's heart, the game really wants the player to make it into space, in a smooth and graceful arc to end in a peaceful orbit around the planet, then to transfer to another majestic body to touch down on the surface... and then have you realize you done goofed with the design and your pilot is now stuck there. :P You're given all the tools you need, assuming you have the patience to learn them. And even after you've learned the base game, modding support is substantial, with hundreds of active mods to explore, from the tiny UI tweaks to a complete real world overhaul.

I'm really enjoying this one and wholeheartedly recommend Invisible, Inc.  Since it has great replayability, I don't know that I'll ever be done with the game.  I want to spend more time on challenges that other modes offer.
The player picks two agents among team members that have different abilities. As you play the game, two more agents become rescued and are added to your infiltration missions during the current playthrough. (You will also unlock agents to use at the start of your next game when you finish your current playthrough.) The game is turn-based, with your actions being spent from the agent's AP pool. You infiltrate a procedurally generated corporation level and accomplish main and side objectives and try to escape any way you can. There is also an AI computer on your side that sees the map as you reveal it, and it can hack the enemy consoles and units, helping your agents accomplish their mission. You will upgrade your agents by spending money on their skills or by giving them items to use. The AI can be upgraded by buying programs to use against consoles and enemies.
The best thing about Invisible, Inc. is the ease at which it builds tension in a given mission and makes you consider every decision carefully. When you knock out a patrol, they will eventually wake up unless you dedicate an agent to pin him, which means you can no longer use that agent for hacking or taking out others. There is an alarm tracker counter that advances each turn, and can step up when certain things happen in the game. The alarm tracker is an abstraction that signifies that the corporation you're infiltrating senses something amiss when you teleport in. Even when you are perfectly stealthy, the alarm tracker counter will go up regardless and cause some pressure and a little chaos to your game. It's best to accomplish your objectives before the counter gets too high, or you may not make it out alive. The game is at its most exciting when the alarm level is 6 and there are several guards waking up and pursuing you after you retrieved some crucial data from their servers, and you just acquired some new items to deal with them more effectively. You quickly learn that every step in the game counts, and you should always close the doors behind you when you move through the level. The game is always a nail-biter, and I love it.
I love the aesthetic of the game -- the stylish graphics and the cyberpunk music. The story is surprisingly good, and it makes me want to play more and unlock more story bits as I go. I'm not a big roguelike guy, but this game is outstanding.

At 12 hours into the game I have almost completed my first playthrough. The whole game takes about 15 hours to complete, and, while short, they really couldn't have made it any longer, and here is why:
Game Mechanics:
Hacking - Super frustraring when you are first introduced to it, but it gets more fun and easier the more you do it. Its a fantastic way to pick up some Xp, and to gather Money, Intel, and Dossier information. Fantastic mechanic well done.
Sneaking - Yes, yes, yes, ohmygod yes. Possibly the most simplistic sneak mechanic I have ever seen, and in its simplicity is where it shines. Hiding behind a wall works the way you think it would work. Being crouched under a window works the way you think it would work. Staying in the shadows WORKS THE WAY YOU THINK IT WOULD WORK! Everything is line of sight, and the AI is fantastic at dealing with that.
Sound - Breaking glass makes people suspicious or can downright alert them immediately. Sprinting will reveal your position to enemies due to how loud it actualy is. Throwing grenades, even mild ones will alert people in a very good area. And the enemies will talk to each other, so you better make sure you can shut someone up before they alert the whole goddamned compound!
Weapons - Not aiming is not suggested. Firing blind or in rapid succesion is more likely to alert the enemies around you than it is to actually kill the person you're trying to hit. All the weapons have thier advantages and disadvantages, Pistols have silencers, and can make for excellent stealth play, but they lack the rang to accurately hit a guard in a guard tower. SMGs are great for clearing rooms, but are terrible at actual combat. Shotguns, while great for single target and room clear do not work well against enemies spread across large areas, and large areas there are. ARs are all around good weapons, but the accuracy is terrible when firing in quick succesion.
Balance - Probably the best I've seen in a stealth game, or really any game. Even if you decide to go loud, and just gun down all the poor sods that in your way, you are not in a Call of Duty game. The weakest grunt will kill you in you get too close and he has a shotgun. Now, if you do go loud, but are not bent on attaining as much bloodshed as possible, it is more than likely you can make it out of a Taiwanese Embassy without ever disabling an alarm.
Over-all recomendation:
Buy it, play it, repeat. Its fantastic, and the graphics while not amazing, have stood up well against the test of time. This is not an FPS, it is a Stealth RPG. Eevrything you do effects the game, your choices will matter. Think of it as Mass Effect, if it was a stealth game.
Over-all rating:
9/10
10/10 Sneaking
8/10 Sabotage mechanics (Purely becasue it can get frustrating and slightly repetitive)
9/10 Gunplay
10/10 Story writing
10/10 Gut wrenching descions
Buy it, play it, expierience the life of a spy.

I like it.  It is definitely a niche kind of game, but I really enjoy it.  It is easy to learn, but so many ways to play.  My first playthrough I didn't use any tips and ended up getting about halfway, but then just running out of money and fighters who could compete.  The second playthrough I won it all and ended up with 30+ million in the bank by using a few starting tips.  I will definietly go back and play again, and probably again after that - just trying different ways of getting places and adding to the realism each time.
It is a bit overwhelming at first because there isn't much of a tutorial, but jump in and know you're learning through the first time and then come back and play it for keeps.
Pros:
- easy to learn
- with the fighting you don't see anything but the play-by-play, but it can be pretty stressful and exciting!
- Many, many ways to play, win, fail, learn
- Can save often so you don't have to lose it all on one fight
- Is addicting
- Found myself actually attached to the fighters in my stable after a while, and losing them was a huge risk
What's fine:
- graphics, but it is more a dice roll type of experience
- Interface is pretty standard, and gets the job done
- price is good if you get into it
Cons:
- no real tutorial, and the in-game (?) only explains the surface of things
- the odds can sometimes make no sense when you look at the stats
- does get a bit grindy towards the end in some cases
- fighters in your stable can be moved around or hidden by a new page, meaning sometimes you have to hunt around
All in all I say go for it if you can get it on sale and find the concept interesting.  It isn't very historical, but you do get a lot of fun out of it and there are mail updates about actual historical events.  There are very good help discussions to push you in the right direction, but you can play it your way and I have heard people talk about winning in many different ways.

The story is in a nutshell okay, if you like lazy writing. I thoroughly recommend this game.
Despite all its flaws, glitches and errors (of which there are a few) this game is tremendous fun. The RPG side is not well fleshed out but it still has a nice sense of fulfilment to it. The discussion tree is vast with so many choices to go through, I suspect this game can be different every time through up to 4 maybe 5 playthrough’s (if you can stick it out that long).
The characters and story are great and very well fleshed out. I loved finding out things about everyone I met and the world in general around the action seemed deep and rich as well. As for the combat it was alright, for an RPG it was fantastic, for an action game it was average at best. The Ai is either amazing or so stupid it ignores being shot. I found little use for the gadgets but I loved using some of the skills.
As for progression when you gain enough XP you level up and in doing so can add to a number of espionage/weapon skills. You will probably want to specialise in one weapon, doing more than that means you can fill out the full skill tree. Side note: pistol is OP.
If this game is on sale you should pick it up, not recommended at full price unless you love the concept, too many glitches to really justify though.
Have fun ^_^

YET i cant keep myself from coming back to the game, the AI is solid (i cant beat it past the second difficulty on my own), the dynamics are great, you can have up to 20 players in a single game (4 as CEO's and 16 as "Execurobots" which are basically like generals or administrators of your base)
You can outfit your troops to better serve your purpose (maybe you want a heavy attack tank to take down that pesky turrets? or maybe you want it to have a gatling gun to mow down that infantry/air units or perhaps a laser to take on those walkers? maybe a robot meant as anti-armor or anti-infantry? perhaps a close air support with a gatling gun? or a strike bomber? you choose!
You cant just spam your turrets all over the map, you have to manage your resources at least at the start, you have to take care of the space you have to build and guard your iron extractors since they're the main source of income, analyze if you should attack now or if that will leave you undefended.
The tech tree, well its an actual Tree! its HUGE, at start it looks small but more you research more you have and the more you can build, which means more micro and macro management, should you go for that extra bit of iron income or maybe you are in dire need of that extra bit of power? Maybe its best to get that offensive upgrades as soon as posible or will that leave your CEO defenseless since you didn't choose the auto turrets and the blast doors for your base?
This game is a one-man made game, no AAA game here, it means every single asset, sound, bug or glitch has been made/overlooked by a single man, and THAT is great! It recieves regular updates, but you cant ask much since its a 1 man job, but the game is pretty fun, i dont know why not many more peole play this!
It has a lot of flaws, yes of course! but its pro's outbeat them once you play it!

I really wanted to like Civilization VI after enjoying Civilization V (after it got its prerequisite expansions to improve upon what was a pretty mediocre vanilla game), but I just couldn't get into this new version. The art style is a big turn off, and it looks a bit too much like a cheap mobile game in that respect. It has made reading the terrain extremely hard in many cases. I find it almost impossible to pick out the goodie huts on the map, for example.
I found the game at launch to have some significant balancing issues, which may have been bad luck on my part, but it is what it is. I had several games where the barbarians completely overran my position and made it impossible to survive. I had a game breaking bug that corrupted a save file in another game (which sounded like it was a common problem with Kongo?). The diplomacy is uninteresting, and unless things have changed the AI was more or less incapable of taking a city with walls.
There are simply too many design problems that existed in the vanilla Civ VI for me to recommend it based on my playing experience. I've been watching the last year for more positive reviews and feedback to emerge saying that Firaxis had fixed everything in patches or after the first expansion, but the reception has still been largely lukewarm. I'd recommend that anyone interested in this game hold off for at least another expansion to see if Firaxis manages to right the ship or if it ends up sinking to the bottom of the sea -- and hopefully takes the dreadful Sean Bean tech quotes with it.

Overall: 8/10
Ok, I've loved the Microsoft Flight Simulator franchise since the early 90's. I've played tons of flight simulators and none of them come close to FSX. The real time weather is fantasticly accurate and when played on the highest realism settings the aircraft behaves as one would in said weather. The pockets of turbulence above a rise, the shift in heading from a headwind. It's very, very accurate. I find flying on here is probably one of the most relaxing things my PC has to offer me. GET A JOYSTICK.
Pros: 8/10
1. The landscape is decent. It looks dated. But that's because it is. The size relationships between the aircraft and the buildings is a bit off but it works.
2. Very realistic both in aircraft interior/exterior apperance and in flight dynamics.
3. Missions are fun (I tend to re-run them for better metrics like time when I'm bored).
4. The handbook and lessons are helpful.
5. When used properly the ATC radio communications are very realistic.
Cons: 7/10 (points subtracted for cons)
1.  Not a lot of choices for aircraft. Would like to see more jets/jumbojets/helicopters etc.
2. Multiplayer VOIP is broken. Period. It doesn't work right. Maybe ONCE in a blue moon you'll come across a server with a working VOIP system, but that it superbly rare.
3. The airports are... disappointing. Microsoft claims they're accurate representations of the airports. But they're not. They're really not. They're close enough that you can ignore it, but don't make a claim about being "accurate representations" of something if it's really not. And no it's not because it's been a lot of time since the game was released. RDU International Airport never looked that way.
Replay Value: 10/10

If you're buying this game, you're not paying for the gameplay. You're getting this game because you want to find out the adventure of Alan Wake. Vomit-inducing cliche introduction aside, this game's gameplay is so shallow it's only there to be consistent with the plot, and to prevent this story into becoming a spooky film. While the things you can do in the tutorial may be fun, it becomes increasingly annoying and difficult and monotonous as the game drags on. However, this is all worth it for the storyline.
While classified as a horror genre, it's not very scary. It's actually spooky at best even to those who cannot stand the horror genre. The storytelling is just spooky enough to make people like it, and play on to find out what has happened. As for what makes the storyline great, you are a lone harmless thriller/horror books author who is trapped in a town surrounded by perpetual darkness that is trying to kill you, and you're trying to save your wife. The writing and the storytelling and the immersion is great in comparison to many other accomplished games, and you won't regret buying this game provided you don't mind the tedious gameplay in exchange for a good plot with charming storytelling. Like any good game worthy of one's time, it should even deserve a sequel.

Alan Wake would have been a truly brilliant game, if it hadn't had got scared and soiled itself. At some point you start to notice the smell, and it's very distracting. Horror games are hard to execute, and I think we all understand why. A game needs to make you feel vulnerable but also capability; put you through an ordeal but give you hope; panic you but not frustrate you. Alan Wake gets this right, at least in the beginning. The problem is in the combat. It has a terrible habit of equipping you with some new tool, and then rendering it useless. The implementation of light as a weapon is inspired because it slows down combat and makes your guns feel a lot less powerful. Unfortunately the number and strength of enemies thrown at you steadily increases until you’re often overwhelmed. After the third of fourth reload after being mobbed by monsters, it stops being scary and starts becoming a chore.
Oh but what about the story? Its pastiche, but that helps it fit into the groove already chiselled out in your mind by Steve King et al. The great arc of the story, if there really is one, isn’t as compelling as the little moments. The presentation is a bit of a mix, but it most resembles a TV series to me. If I'm not mistaken, there are also several nods to Max Payne.
Visually, it’s wonderful. A lot of care went into level design, and for a game that is mostly about running through the woods at night, it’s quite colourful. There is one little niggle though: as you orbit the camera around Alan, there is a noticeable and distracting motion blur affect applied to his head which doesn’t make sense because he is not moving, the background is. Also what is up with Alan’s teeth and lips? Man looks like a horse sometimes.
Worth a play, but be prepared to abandon it when it stops being fun. Don’t worry, you won’t care.

Season Two is set a few years after Season the first game.
Here Clementine is a preteenager trying to survive without Lee.
You can notice from the first interaction between Clementine and Christa that Clementine misses Lee a lot and that nobody will take his place.
We see a girl becoming an adult and missing her adolescence.
What makes things worse it that we are responsible for this evolution.
It's sad to see a girl like Clementine being forced to take important and difficult decisions.
Her evolution is based on our decisions, what gives us the weight in any choice we make.
The choice that seems the ideal at that moment quickly becomes something caothic, out of control, where we don't know how to react and decide in the next moment.
Sometimes we get a lump in our throats, but also we breathe angry, because we need to survive, and we want to smash the button to kill that character!
Just like in the comics or the TV series, our main goal here is our own survival than the group, whatever it is.
There is always a place or a name to get attached to... "We need to get there", "It's not far from here", "We need to keep moving". These are our incentives throughout the game.
The game is an interactive history, it's the history that drives us, not the gameplay.
The exploration is not the objective, just like the puzzles are not difficult.
It's possible to import the savegame from Season 1 along with the decisions you took. If you didn't play any of the episodes, the game will make random choices.
You can play Season 2 without having played the first game, since most of the characters from the first game aren't present in Season 2, but you'll miss the background history from Clementine.
Just like in the first game, you feel like at any time something will happen that will get us in trouble and as the game progress we are sure that this is a true survival game, because everything is important and every choice we make will lead us to a complicated situation.
9/10

Alan Wake is one of those great titles that tends to go unnoticed until it goes on sale and everyone goes "What in the world is that game?"
Which is a shame, because Alan Wake is an great, atmospheric game quite unlike most others. The best way to describe it is that you play through a Stephen King novel. It's hauntingly beautiful at parts, and a lot of the tension comes from the atmosphere and knowledge that something definitely waits for you around the corner, but it won't show up until you get there.
You even play through "chapters" in the game, which is really the best way to go about it. Each one is just the right length that you won't get burned out on the kind of samey gunplay here. Play one chapter a day, and you'll find it to be just right. The gunplay does get somewhat boring, but a large part of that is because the deelopers don't really make it known that the PC port's "Normal" difficulty was the console's "Hard," turning the enemies into bullet sponges. Just play on Easy.
Overall, a great little gem to add to your library, especially at the sale prices it usually goes for.

This game is beautiful. I was lucky enough to be a backer of this game, allowing me to follow its creation to the point and as it continues in the future. I have been an avid fan of point-and-click/adventure games for a long time now and am a huge fan of Tim Schafer's games and writing.
First of all, it is interesting to point out that you play as two characters in separate, parallel stories, a boy named Shay on a spaceship and a girl named Vella in a village. It is very unique and provides an interesting twist to the genre that I personally haven't seen before. At any time you can switch between the characters using the inventory menu at the bottom of the screen and pick up right where you left off with that character. I'm interested to see if there is a link between the two and when it will appear. It is a very interesting mechanic and I can't wait to see what DoubleFine continues to do with it.
I have to say that everything in this game just... works. The art is done in a very interesting and eye-catching style, and it is a major draw of the game. In any point-and-click, the art is extremely important since you will do a lot of exploring. It is also important to make sure that it is clear what is in the foreground vs. what is in the background as well as make the distinction of what is just part of the backdrop and what you can interact with. The game does a terrific job of all of this. I have enjoyed exploring Shay's ship and Vella's home immensely. I think my favorite moment, in terms of the art, were the different birds you see flying during one of Vella's segments. The art style and direction is incredible.
Complementing the art and story is the music. The music rises at parts and is more subdued at others, matching the mood. Some points will feel slightly darker while others will feel slightly more silly or intense. For every situation, there is a perfectly appropriate piece. They've also successfully avoided one of the pitfalls that can occur with a point-and-click: the music loop. If you spend too long on many games of this genre, the music loops can can become very annoying very quickly. However, if the music looped, I didn't notice it, which is a great thing to see in a game such as this. I have to say that little piece when you first start the game and see Shay and Vella back-to-back in different worlds has to be my favorite piece thus far. I am extremely glad I got the soundtrack with my backing.
The voice acting thus far has been pretty spot on and terrific. I am thoroughly enjoying listening to these actors speak and find them to be believable, which can be tough to pull off. I often find myself listening to them in situations and thinking, yeah, I would be apprehensive also or that I would be just as confused as them given the situation they are in. The voice actors do a great job.
The puzzles are as you would expect. Challenging enough that you don't breeze through them, but intuitive enough that you can figure them out if you put in a little effort and time exploring and putting the pieces together in your mind. They don't reach the point of frustration, at least not for me, which is just where it needs to be. Again, the art helps a lot in this department as well by showing you what you can pick up or interact with and making it clear what various different objects are.
Finally, the crux of the genre, the writing of the story and dialogue. When Tim Schafer writes a story, you know it's going to be good. It's going to be one of the few games that can make you laugh out loud with how funny it is. This game is no exception. Throughout most of my time playing, I was smiling and, on more than a few occasions, I belted out laughing. Mr. Schafer has not lost it. He is still up with the best of them in terms of writing and I enjoyed going through every possible dialogue choice just to see what silly, or even insightful, things would be said next.
Overall, I am quite pleased with what I have seen and am quite glad that I chose to back this game when I did. I have a good amount of trust in DoubleFine and believe they know what they are doing. I can't wait to see where this game goes in the future. Good luck to them in producing the rest!

I've been preaching a RTS/FPS hybrid for as long as I can remember. Just recently pulled the trigger and bought the game full price (which is extremely unusual for me)! The game in it's current state is playable and has quite a bit to offer. Gamers will be hungry (in both good and bad regards) for a lot more once they finish a couple of games. Most games will take around an hour but given on how determine you are, can take more or less time.
I remember when the very first StarCraft came out. RTS Games started striking it big and FPS began making a strong debut. I loved both genres but couldn't have both at the same place or time. I've always wanted to control a single marine or a Goliath and have never been able to until this game released. When the game states you can take control over any unit, you literally can take control over any unit. This is an absolutely beautiful feature that was nailed. In addition to this scenario, players may play against or with their friends. One friend can be in charge while other friends can take control of units (to do this "execubots" need to be approved). This can be handy as players are more independent than AI units. Independent players as well as any player playing in FPS mode can command nearby units by pressing "F" (for follow) and "G" (for guard). Big points for inclusiveness here. The AI within the game is decent at the moment. Depending on what level you set them at will determine the intensity of the game.
The
regarding Executive Assault is the player takes control of an executive business man who is essentially the only human on the battle field trying to take over the world. Instead of directly being involved in the fight, the executive sits high atop of their office with only a pistol in his hand and a computer on a desk. The computer allows the player to enter and exit RTS mode (by pressing "E"). There isn't much reason to control the executive either than if you're being raided. The executive cannot have any other weapon either than a pistol and a upgraded pistol (that needs to be researched) that takes out robots in one shot. Additionally, a desk shield can be researched and a big red button has to be pressed manually by the player to activate it. Robots will have to fight their way through corridors to the executive elevator that will take them all the up to the office. Defenses can be upgraded and added to protect the executive. Auto-turrets can get really annoying if you don't come in with a strong enough presence.
From the executive view, we jump into the RTS view. Before the player can start building anything at all, a power station is needed. Power management is extremely simple in this game but takes a bit of skill to manage properly. Research, drilling power and defenses can all managed through this. Go over the magic number (that keeps everything in homeostasis) and watch the stores deplete faster than instant noodles being microwaved. Power towers can be placed throughout the map in order to expand drilling expeditions. Upon building that, the player can build basic buildings such as unit facility and drone facility. Drones will build towers and drill sites while units are the ones that can raid the executives office. Research is another tab besides the power management tab in which the player will have to closely watch and use in order to advance their technology. There are other buildings that can be built such as airports and vehicle factories but this all needs to be unlocked through research. Some other buildings with neat features include a long range facility which has four slots that can be assigned to artillery or a trion cannon (that bombards every so often) or a missile. All long range weapons need to be assigned a target by the player. Moreover, hallways can be added and defense mechanisms such as turrets, fences/force fields or mechanized doors can be added for a buffered defense.
Research plays a crucial role in what one can do in-game. Weapon options begin to open up once the proper research is done. A unique and enjoyed feature in this game is that there are no set units. When a new building is researched, a default unit is given but there are five empty slots. These slots need to be filled up by the player. Players are able to design their own units to their preference. For instance, basic foot units can be given basic to upgraded armor and equipped with lasers, quantum weapons or missiles. Additionally, defensive sort of measures can be added such as personal shields, timed explosives or electrostatic shock. Vehicles and air units also have option defensive measures although at the moment quite limited. Research unlocks these weapon variants, units, buildings and abilities. Players should be careful as research can take up quite a bit of energy. This uniqueness allows players to add another depth to their attacks. Some players may favor certain weapon types while others find benefits in mixing ballistics with energy.
The HUD for each individual unit is awesome. On one of the bigger aircraft units the player has the view of the action from the bridge. In mech-walkers, it feels like you're walking on mechanical legs and obviously the view is a little different. It would be nice if some sort of sprint option was available for air and vehicle units. Even though most of the

Locking the framerate is bad enough, locking it as low as 30 FPS is even worse, but the move that ensures I'll never again pre-order a 2k game again was the fact that they refused to hand out advance copies to reviewers.
This shows a clear awareness that this was a serious problem that would affect pre-orders and sales in general, but rather than informing us about it before release, they did their best to conceal it and keep racking up pre-orders.
Acknowledging the problem and promising a fix is a good start, but the lack of an admission that they intentionally hid this, not to mention the lack of an apology, makes things crystal clear. This is an attempt to minimise refunds and salvage future sales, not an admission that they behaved poorly, or that they will learn a lesson and do better in the future.
This kind of unrepentant deceptive behaviour is unacceptable, and I for one will think long and hard before ever buying another 2k game, and definitely won't pre-order one again.

Initially, I was miffed that this game was 30fps and in what might be the ugliest, most cluttered fake-isometric perspective I've ever seen. I hated it, but I was also playing it on a TV with a gamepad. This was a bad idea.
Nuclear Throne is a keyboard and mouse game, make no mistake. The controller-required co-op mode is a token add-on that has more downsides than benefits. Play this game on a fast monitor and contrast turned up, and you'll have fewer problems.
The light at the end of the tunnel is that Nuclear Throne is basically a procedural, single-life version of Hotline Miami. Everything is very fast, there are guns everywhere, and there's a ton of content. Nuclear Throne is about variety, difficulty, and how fast it is to get into a new game. That's where Vlambeer got it right and others (like Isaac) didn't. Death is permanent, but restarting is so fast and easy that you hardly feel it. Vlambeer had mastered the art of permadeath long before roguelikes took off, and I do feel like this is a glorious return to the Super Crate Box days, despite running at half the framerate.
