Ok, early first impressions.
So, I LOVED the first game. It was kind of an out of nowhere smash hit for me. I'm a massive fan of the LOTR universe (and yes, I read the books so I'm allowed to say that now leave me alone) so as you can imagine I was pleasantly surprised to find that it did an excellent job of coexisting side by side with the existing Tolkien universe while simultaneously respecting the original material. It felt like someone filling in the gaps of the story. Gameplaywise the original took the standard hack and slash template but added a whole new layer of depth with the nemesis which made it unique and very, very fun.
I had hoped Shadow of War would take those things that were core to the original's success and then just increase the amount of depth and content. It does... I guess... and maybe I'm just being overcritical because of my extremely high expectations (and I'll update the review accordingly) but right now I'm not exactly happy about it.
I'm two hours in and am nowhere NEAR the level of cool♥♥♥♥♥♥you see in the trailers. Conquering regions, taking over forts, building in depth relationships, riding dragons etc are still clearly a ways away. And that would be fine if the intro weren't incredibly boring. It's lots of narration, recap and frame locked cinematics that really aren't that interesting. It may be true that Shadow of Mordor also took some time to ramp up, but at least you were playing during that time, and it had a super dark scene where you watch your family slowly executed in a blood right that fules your motivation for the rest of the game. And then the mechanics kick in. Now instead of draining Uruk's to refill your arrows, you drain for health. Arrows are found by picking them up around the map. No more building up hitstreaks for executions, instead dealing damage permanently fills a meter that never decays (unless you receive damage) and then can be consumed for an exeute. The upgrade tree is now much more like a standard RPG, you get a point to spend every time you level up. There are a few more changes as well, but overall I've just kind of wondered... why? It's not like these mechanical changes are making things worse, they just don't feel necessary.
Storywise I feel about the same as I do the game, lots of unnecessary changes that don't really make things any better, just different. For example, Shelob is a hot goth chick now. Which is stupid. And apparently Palantir are super important, but after seeing how they work in game it's obvious the developers don't really know what they do. So far the game feels much less like a side by side companion to the LOTR universe and more like a fantasy story written by a guy who watched the movies while half asleep and then was told to retell them but in a way that would be broadly appealing to as many people as possible. It's not necessarily a bad thing, just disappointing.
One thing, as others have noticed you CAN disable the micro-transactions at the beginning by not agreeing to the online features. Just do it. For what little I have played the games I could already feel the drop off between this one and the previous.
The first big tip was when a leader called me evil and denounced me on turn thirty five because I had a resource he wanted. This was after him and another leader said really bad things to me randomly for no reason while still remaining friendly. Just, what, how is the player supposed to know what resources each other civilization wants and why should the player be punished for progressing by having other civilizations get triggered by it before they all have even learned what a wheel is.
Then an uncatchable scout walked by and turned off my very first trade route, scouts seem to be far more common now at least during the early stages of the game. Which is quite obnoxious when they are just as capable of pillaging your trade routes as any other unit yet they are far more mobile. So at any point they can zoom by and ruin your progress, just because.
So within an hour of playing, my first trade route got ruined less then three turns after I made it; and I got denounced for taking a resource directly adjacent to my capital.
Although the art style is neat is really does not compliment the game as a concept. The art style is very light and half cartoon like, yet this is supposed to be a game about trying to win at life. Usually by killing entire cultures in the process. It seems like, instead of just giving the game better more quality graphics, they went with cartoon graphics which are easier to make and give the game a more "unique" appearance. Which would work, if the art style was not inappropriate for a real world civilization management game.
Playing for under an hour it just did not feel like any significant changes were actually made to the game, and if significant changes were made they would be noticeable even to some degree because from hour one to thirty you are still working with the same system. Most mentionable changes, builders do things instantly but have charges and there are districts.
Government systems are basically customizable perk systems which you unlock more perks for as you research and unlock more perk holders with different governments you pick. Which they use to pad out the research rewards, since they give out all kinds of selectable perks with the research rewards. Each perk doing a tiny little thing of its own, which is extremely tedious because of how much reading and consideration has to be made for each of these new perks you are constantly unlocking. You have to sift through all kinds of options even in the first hour, and it is just like why is the player expected to make so many choices about their passive bonuses within the first hour. The player should not have to be this concerned with micro managing their passive benefits to begin with, because it is not actually gameplay it is just preperation for gameplay.
In the previous game, you pick a tree that suits the playstyle you want, and start unlocking stuff from it based on which you want first. In this game, you are perpetually unlocking individual small perks overtime. But you are forced to read each one because you need to know what you will be unlocking with your research so you know which research to prioritize. And then, you need to read all of them again when it is time to customize your government since you will likely have forgot what they each were by then. It is just tedious and overcomplicated.
Also religious victory. Every other victory in the game is either a race, or a direct conflict. Religious victory is neither, it is you splashing religion around the map trying to dye as much of it in your colour as possible and whoever gets the majority wins. So whether you like it or not you pretty much are forced to play along with it since if you do not resist the enemy religion will take over. You get to choose whether you want to dominate the world or have a science race, it is your choice which victory you want to try for, but with religion you are forced to participate because it is the only way to directly stop others from winning it. It is just extremely intrusive and detracts from the freedom of the player to play how they want.
Eighty dollars for this, seriously. Yes, this game has a lot of things that you can only get for the previous game as purchasable content. But this game costs eighty dollars up front, with little improvement from the previous game and in other ways it has devolved. And they want you to spend thirty plus more for each expansion.
For eighty dollars, the reaction to this game compared to the previous game should be a whole lot more then two steps forwards two steps back. It improved some things, it ruined some things. That is not worth eighty dollars. Just buy the previous game.

It feels like people producing the game where collecting mechanics, but not designing the game flow and player experience. You end up with crazy things like pacifist Gandhi bothering you in middle ages about his Nukes agenda. Just random nonsense that hard to follow.
CIvilization games never had any historical sense, but it was possible to follow at least some story (and even enjoy replay on a minimap at the end). This version is just a mix of smart and not so smart mechanics that glue together with terrible AI and without much care for a meaningless game progression.

The video settings are as follows:
Graphic Quality
Antialiasing
FXAA Quality
Antisotropic Filtering
Shadow Quality
SSAO Quality
Backdrop Quality
Godray Quality
Volumetric Light Quality

Need I say more? The game is gorgeous.
In general, the original engine created by Remedy which is supported by the Havoc engine is pretty neat. The physics is worked out, the lighting is vibrant, the distant fog is pretty volumetric, the textures are smooth and realistic although the face characters and face expressions can get quite silly and not fully be fleshed out.
As for the gameplay, well, I am finally able to easily avoid getting hit in the head with hammers, axes, crowbars and other similar household items. I am able to do so because I can finally evade successfully, something that I was not able to fully master on a controller, which is not the fault of the controller but my own. The taken (your foes) are still able to outrun you and surround you constantly so the game constantly forces you to fight back with vigor. You cannot jump high, which is realistic and you get tired faster than in any other game. Three hits to the head on Hard mode and you are dead. There are no med-kits so you recover health by being illuminated by light, any light.
Anyway, by this time I assume most people have heard what the game is about so I'll spare further reading. You are a writer who shows signs of his waning ability to write successfully. He decides to go to a resort to attempt to mentally recover however he soon discovers that there is some kind of battle going on between the malevolent and the benevolent forces in the area. Later on, he starts to doubt his sanity and goes on a quest to find out what really is going on. By the end of the game I personally still had no idea what happened. The DLC's did not help to solve the story either. Anyway it's a nice attempt at creating a somewhat vague story on behalf of the developers but I still had no idea wtf happened.
The game is filled with Easter eggs, reference to other icons of American pop culture, miscellaneous videos, paradoxes, logical dilemmas, etc.
In the end, let us all thank Microsoft for postponing this game for as long as possible for us humble PC folk, so we could buy their xbox instead. My hat goes off to those who resisted and waited.

Promising concept, ruined by sub-par gameplay.
The multiple dialogue options and branching story paths add some value to the game, but I just couldn't get behind the boring gameplay.
EDIT:
Gave this one another shot recently. I still stand by what I said so far, but now that I'm a little further in, I've had the chance to see some of the game's stronger points.
The story, while pretty standard spy fare (who's the mole etc etc), is interesting enough to keep your attention. I also liked the cast of characters and the different ways you could interact with them. I haven't done multiple playthroughs or anything of the sort, so I can't comment on whether your choices are meaningfull in any way.
I do like the Mass Effect style dialogue system, however. The only negative here is the ambiguity of choices. Instead of actual dialogue lines, you only get to choose between different attitudes (sarcastic, aggressive, etc.). For the most part, I was satisfied with how those choices were interpreted by the writers. Occasionally, you get some line that makes you wish you had chosen differently. What also doesn't help at all, is the very short time you get to make your decisions. Even worse, though, is that you have to have made your choice as soon as the NPC has finished its line. This frequently results in situations where you need to hear the whole sentence to understand things, but then you're already out of time to think of an appropriate answer.
Gameplay is still clunky as hell. During my first playthrough I made the mistake to go for max stealth for obvious spy related reasons. This made actually playing the game alternatingly boring and very frustrating. Now, I'm just running around with a shotgun, gunning down everything. Still not very fun, but it works and lets me get to the story parts faster.
So, if I had to choose now between recommending and not recommending this game, I'd kinda sorta recommend it to anyone who really enjoyed the type of dialogue/decision system that Bioware employs in their RPGs. Overall, the game is quite mediocre, but most of it is due to the lackluster gameplay. The story and decision components are pretty decent on their own.

Some comments about this game in relation to season 1.
Playing as Clementine is significantly more interesting than playing as Lee. She's a kid and you are (I assume) an adult. A lot of the choices you make are dripping with so much dramatic irony that you can't help smiling.
A lot of the clunky puzzle solving elements in the first game are now gone. It's pretty obvious that Telltale has refined their formula between the first and second season. The pacing is a lot smoother as a result.
However, the cast of characters in this game is significantly weaker and less interesting than those in season 1, and story is nowhere near as subtle. A lot of the plot just feels like the writers were just generating conflict for the sake of making everyone miserable.
On the plus side, your choices matter a little more in this game than in season 1.
Overall, a decently strong showing from Telltale despite a weaker story.

Just finished playing the whole game, all i can say is i've never experienced a more life changing experience from any other game. Life Is Strange has one of the most engaging and emotional stories, along with nice graphics and art. This game shows me, like a few other games, that each choice you make in life has a following consequence either good or bad, "every action has a reaction" and that while we can rewind and change our decisions in the game, we have to be extremely careful with what we say or do in reality. The music within the game was especially beautiful as it gave me a sense of  nostalgia, bringing me back to the time in the early 2000's when life seemed simpler and less stressing.
[SPOILER ALERT]
At the end of the final episode, you either sacrifice the many to save the one important person in max's life, or you sacrifice that one to save the many (damned if you do, damned if you don't). i played both endings, sacrificing the many seemed a little too nice and bittersweet to me...but sacrificing the one...I will admit was one of the most saddening endings i could ever witness to the point i actually had a moment where i had to hold myself back from crying.
[In Short]
If you're looking to play a game with a great story, a game where your choices will carry weight and affect the town around you, a game that will make you wonder why you made the decision you made and whether or not it was the right decision to make, then Life Is Strange is the game you'd want to play.

tl;dr : The best stealth game I've ever played. Buy it
.
Invisible, Inc. is a rouge-like turn-based stealth game where you're controlling several agents through procedurally generated maps filled with guards, traps and loots. Its turn-based nature make it sidestep the central problem with stealth genre : The fact that waiting is boring. In this game, you never needs to wait since your agent is the one observing enemies for you. So instead of wasting your precious time, you're using an agent's action point to make a strategic decisions on whether it's worth it to determine the guards' patrol route or peek through doors.
Since the game is turn-based, it only make sense to make the map procedurally generated. So I guess they just went all in and made the game a rogue-like. And it
. The only time I got bad maps that I'd rather not deal with is during early game of Expert Plus difficulty runs which includes more guards. Every playthrough also feels different since there's a lot of variety with agents, programs and items. Extra point for making the unlock painless, 2 successful campaigns and I already unlocked all agents.
Last but not least, I strongly recommend playing the game with contingency expansion. The campaign on base game is short (around 9 missions, compared to around 16 with contingency) and it feels weird since it's basically just several early game missions before jumping to the end mission. Endless mode fixes that by adding exit pass, but I bet people won't be able to guess that there's some unique mechanics in endless mode. Also, Endless mode is improved with contingency too, so there's no reason to not grab it.
In closing, if you have any interest in stealth games, Invisible, inc. is a must buy. It's a solid blend of stealth and rogue-like, bringing forth the strength of both with many customization options if you find some aspect undesirable.
PS: I strongly recommend playing endless mode until 3rd week after you got decent at the expert campaign. Your stealth experience is incomplete until you got Fractal 2.0 in an FTM facility full of Omni guards with 4 routers and 2 Scanners.

Let me start by saying right now it's not a good game.
With a little help, it could be great.
"So why have you recommended it?" I hear you ask. Well honestly because I don't want to discourage people from investing in this game. With a few updates and patches here and there it could be good, my first impression is they've made the game they wanted and not had a chance to really get much outside input from the people who are actually playing it, if they choose to follow that input we could have a great game here (and if they don't I'll be changing this review to not recommended).
At the moment you'll get a few hours of fun from it as you progress through the bosses and cities, recruiting new gladiators and working their way up to becoming champions.
What it's missing is a more open-ended game, my biggest gripe is how every fight your gladiators will take kills one of the opponents gladiators, he doesn't seem to replenish these and the aim is to kill off all of his gladiators and move onto the next boss killing his gladiators - as the game progresses these get tougher and toughter. It's fun but it's not what I want, I want a more realistic gladiator experience where the combatants involved aren't constantly becoming more and more tough, occasionally I want a great to come along and he'll reign at the top for a while until he's finally defeated but I don't want the champions to constantly be more and more and more challenging as we go. It feels like an RPG where I'm trying to "beat the game" more than a simulator.
While you might expect the combat in a gladiator game to be a massively important thing it's actually just a series of "miss" or "damage dealt" flying across the screen.  I don't really mind it as I tend to use my imagination but it would be nice to have some descriptive text here instead so we can visualise what our gladiators are actually doing. While we're talking about combat it does seem to need tweaking but the games very new and I've read that balance issues will be sorted in the next patch.
TL DR
A nice little game but needs some updates and patches to become great.

That will make or break your enjoyment of this game, because it feels like the difficulty is based around mastering those kind of controls (which I personally never liked in the first place). The music is fine but nothing memorable, and the level designs are pretty blatant knockoffs of Super Mario World and the Super Mario Land games for Gameboy.  Collecting coins?  A plant that lets you shoot projectices?  Springs?  I wonder where you got those original ideas!?
They went for a retro feel with the intro cutscene, but they just look like flat line drawings in done in MS Paint.  Also, no one wants to read a wall of text before they play a goddamned platformer.  If you can't tell the story of a platformer through the gameplay, then the game doesn't need one.
The whole thing just feels like a really generic experience.  It's certainly not a *bad* game, but all it made me want to do was play Super Mario World instead.

a friend saw me playing this game and asked me "hey, is that game any good"
i told him "no" but then i added "but it's fun"
and that's pretty much where i'm at with executive assault right now. the graphics are really not very good, to the point of being silly, and this extends from the first-person unit view to the menus. when in first person view, it has that 'unity game' feel to its graphics that makes me inwardly kinda cringe. your futuristic robots hold generic assault rifles until extensively upgraded, and the cockpits on many of the machines serve to be obtrusive and ugly rather than cool. i'm not the kind of person who can tell you for certain what balancing issues there are or aren't, but i'm sure there are mechanical tweaks to be ironed out in terms of research and unit production and all that.
but i like this game, so i can deal with that. if anything, the almost 2003-era graphics lend a certain charm to it, and it's my hope that this game will eventually improve and replace the graphics as time goes on.
this game has a concept that i love and the execution is competent. from the first time i played an RTS to the last time i did some sprawling base-building in DoW, i've always wondered what it would be like to have a walk around the unit-spewing fortress i've created or even see inside. this delivers on that front and it opens up a lot of exciting tactical options on top of that. being able to hop into the head of one of your units and guide them around is a fantastic concept and it's the very reason this game deserves so much attention.
i would love nothing more to see this game get bigger and sleeker and more complex. i want this to be a new subgenre of RTS and i want this game to be at the tip of that spearhead.

I'll begin by saying...this game is rough. It's rough in many, many ways. It's not just a matter of difficulty, but also presentation, style, and a lot of aspects like that. It's a game that shows promise, but as it stands...is a very niche title. The game's premise is novel and far too rarely executed on. It's a game I wanted to like, and while I do enjoy it, it's a game that is lacking in some areas and needs a lot of improvement.
However, I've found the game...is simple. The simulation aspects are there, the game is sutiably difficult, and the fights are bloody and exciting. Every fight can put your gladiator school to ruin. However, the game just doesn't (yet) have the depth that really lets you get into the nuances of the game. Variety feels rather lacking. There are only really 4 venues to fight - two in North Africa (Utica and Leptis Magna), and another two in Italy (Brundisium and, of ocurse, Rome itself). In each city things grow increasingly difficult as you go from city to city, climbing the ranks. The concept is great.
The management of the teams is simple. It's effective as you buy staff to train and heal and maintain your gladiators. The game lets you choose too how you treat your gladiators. Do you want to build a prison, or a high-quality training establishment? Or maybe something in the middle? Based on what upgrades you buy for your school, what ameneties you provide for your fighters, their skills be influenced rather heavily, though at great cost as maintianing such enhancements can become quite expensive. Thus your goal is to run the most effective school possible, but also a profitable one, and sometimes these things can be at odds, espeically given the rather sporadic nature of fight scheduling and their value (more on that near the end!)
The fights are suitably engaging, in a way, especially if you turn the combat text speed to 0.5 to really hype the suspense, or a more brisk but still intelligible 1.0 (by default it's at a blindingly fast 2.0), each fight can become quite tense, especialy if you're invested in your fighter. That said, the game feels very obtuse in terms of what a crowd's desires are. There's no indication until you're actualy committed to the fight what the crowd may be feeling - whcih is understandable, but you'd think that a city would have a certain 'flavor' or the crowd coudl be a little more predictable, at least over time. Instead, it seems that there's a straight up random chance (20% to start) that a gladiator will be spared at the end of a fight, which can only really be increased by investing perk points into them. More talk about those later.
Sadly, there isn't really many ways to invest in them. It's simply a matter of very hands-off training, increasing the facility ammenities, and giving your fighters weapons or armor. While armor feels like it's well-done, in that wearing armor is a trade-off of dexterity, stamina, agility... Weapons are lacking.  I just don't feel like weapons exist in a very engaging or interesting space. There are nominally over a half dozen weapon classes, but they merely exist to make you buy weapons as a gold sink, as there is no differentiation between them. A sica is no different than a gladius which is no different than a fascina (trident), or pugio, or any of the other weapons. And while any gladiator can use any weapon, there is a bonus to using particular weapons - and given that all weapons share the same damage ranges, have no speical characteristics, and generally cost the same...well, it feels like a missed opportunity mechanically speaking
The parks are a novel feature that I rather like; and the perks for the individual fighters feel well balanced. However, many of the Player Perks, designed to simulate, I believe the school's traditions, history, inclinations, over time, feel very unbalanced. There are a few (the Reputation Boost perk in particular) that feel outright broken! It states that it raises your reputation to the maximum simply by investing into it. That sort of bonus, naturally enough, just kind of kills any purpose for the mechanic. The same could be said of a lot of the other perks - such as being able to ignore fatigue, or retirement ages, essentially making your team into an emotionless juggernaught as you can choose to ignore morale penalties with certain perks. Things like that are wonderful boni, but they can seriously unbalance the game. That said, other perks, such as Opportunity Chance increases, starting level bonus, weapon bonuses of various types, gladiator health increases.  Things like that make a lot of sense and play into the whole notion of Ludus Traditions...the others just feel outright game-breaking and need to be reconsidered.
It would have been nice to fight across the whole Empire than merely North Africa and Italy. It could have also allowed for a degree of variety too in the fighting styles, or the sorts of fights you can manage, or increase the scouting possibilities, creating a regional fame system so that if your team fares poorly in one area you can move to somewhere else where your style is more interesting to the crowd - whether through the crowd's preferences of fighter style. It just feels like a bit of a missed opportunity to not be able to play with gladiator types, city preferences. Besides the obvious style choices, cities could have had meanignfully-sized arenas. Smaller venues would of course be less favorable to spear-wielders, for instance... Or massive arenas might be the only ones capable of putting on mass displays where you send your whole stable out to showcase an entire roster against an opposing school. Second, you always start in Utica, then advance, city by city, through Leptis Magna and then to Brundisium, and finally to Rome. It could have been more interesting if each city had a certain bonus or style or some other aspect to it, and then you chose where to start of the three other cities - and your goal was to 'conquer' all 3 of them, then move on to Rome. It's currently a linear path that I do wish had been a little more interesting.
There's also no way to arrange matches. A big part of being a Lanista, as I understand it, isn't JUST building your stable of fighters, training them, and keeping them in prime shape, but finding fighters to go against your men that will make for interesting battles.  It'd be nice if, instead of 'merely' choosing your fighters, and your chosen school, you could also 'suggest' in negotiations who you fight against. And based on relative skills, purse size, crowd attendance, venue, and other factors, the opposing Lanista will agree or disagree to the arrangement. ALso, not being able to fight non-arena fights, is kind of disappointing as well. While the schedule of fights goes primarily towards the main arena(s) in a city, it wasn't uncommon to have schools supplement their income by providing entertainment to dinner parties, funerals, and frankly - to not have this option can lead to massive gaps in the game where you sit there for days or weeks on end hitting 'next turn' until you find a fight that matches your needs.  And this isn't an issue that occurs only in the beginning when outmatched and seeking only less hyped fights. It happens also later on in the game too, when you find that it's simply not worth it to risk your less-skilled men in the less-hyped fights that occur.
I'd also like to note that the developer is quite active and open-minded for suggestions in this game, and while the game is technically a full release, I see ample probability that there will be some major game enhancements, mechancis, patches, etc, that will make the game better over time. In full disclosure, I have talked with the developer relatively recently and have been in contact for modding purposes. Further, in the course of our discussions, he asked that I write a product review here - however, it has not affected in any way the content or my opinions on this game.

Just gonna put this out here first: I am a huge fan of turn based strategy games. I've spent THOUSANDS of hours playing different Fire Emblem games, I love XCOM... Hell, I even play competitive chess outside of gaming. Strategy games are my jam. By all means, this review will be a bit biased because of that.
First, I'm gonna break a cardinal rule of positive reviews, I'm going to start with the game's cons.
First thing to note, this is NOT a turn based strategy game. It is a turn based strategy STEALTH game. This is one thing I really wish I knew more about going in. If you attempt to brashly plow your way through levels, you will lose quickly and painfully. Planning becomes key, and strategically dissecting the levels becomes a necessity at experienced difficulty and beyond. This game is extremely punishing, and will annihilate you for the first 10 hours that you spend in it. The fact that your range of options is as cyrptic as your sentient AI companion doesn't help at all. You WILL die, you WILL get aggrevated, and you WILL feel cheated early on.
But then, 10 hours in, something clicks.
As you play this game, you will begin to crack the code on the gameplay mechanics bit by bit. The better you crack them, the easier and more fun it gets. Within 15-20 hours, you end up pulling off some complex tactical manuvers without even thinking about it. Once you get into the meat of this game, it is a MASTERPIECE. Let's get into why.
Most of the game involves finding an objective, breaking into and stealing something from the objective, and leaving through a teleporter. When you enter a level, you have no idea where anything is. Your main job is to explore the area, find both the objective, and the teleporter, then execute a plan to get to both. While it may not seem that genius at first, the stuff that you may have to come up with to get there is remarkable. The game tests not only your ability to think, but also your ability to work under pressure. There WILL be times when you have to make the best of a bad situation. This is where Invisible Inc. is at it's best. In my time playing the game, I've ran into plenty of these situations, and when I have, it is the most fun I have in modern gaming. It's tense, it's tactical, and the problem solving involved is devious. However, if you can get out of those situations without a scratch, you walk away feeling like a champion. You will fail occasionally, but that's OK. The game wasn't meant to be easy. To me, that is a definate positive. There are also multipe side-quests throughout these levels as well. Stealing credits, and hacking nanofabricators so you can buy prime gear become almost as important as your original goals.
So, overall, what's the verdict? The first few days playing it may seem tedius, but play on beginner difficulty, beat it once, and then try it on experienced and expert. Once you can get past the firewall of a learning curve, the game reveals  a vast network of strategic options and amazing gameplay that is unparalleled in the market today. I fully recommend this game to any fan of turn based strategy, or indie games in general. If it's on sale, you have no excuse not to buy it (bar an empty wallet... dangit Gaben).
As your boss, Olivia Gladstone would say: "Good luck operator!"...You'll need it.
Edit: October 19th, 2016
After sinking 40 more hours into Invisible Inc. since I wrote this review, I love this game now more than ever. It's climbed past all other games in the turn-based-strategy genre and is now my second favorite game of all time (barely behind my first ever completion: The Legend of Zelda, Ocarina of Time). For anyone who is on the fence about this masterpiece, I cannot recommend it enough. It's also now available on the Apple App Store, so if you ever game on mobile, it's there for a much cheaper price. 9.9/10. One of the best games that I've ever played, and an amazing experience from begining to end. BUY THIS THING.

Need I say more? The game is gorgeous.
In general, the original engine created by Remedy which is supported by the Havoc engine is pretty neat. As for the gameplay, well, I am finally able to easily avoid getting hit in the head with hammers, axes, crowbars and other similar household items. I am able to do so because I can finally evade successfully, something that I was not able to fully master on a controller, which is not the fault of the controller but my own. The taken (your foes) are still able to outrun you and surround you constantly so the game constantly forces you to fight back with vigor. You cannot jump high, which is realistic and you get tired faster than in any other game. Three hits to the head on Hard mode and you are dead. There are no med-kits so you recover health by being illuminated by light, any light.
Anyway, by this time I assume most people have heard what the game is about so I'll spare further reading. You are a writer who shows signs of his waning ability to write successfully. He decides to go to a resort to attempt to mentally recover however he soon discovers that there is some kind of battle going on between the malevolent and the benevolent forces in the area. Later on, he starts to doubt his sanity and goes on a quest to find out what really is going on. By the end of the game I personally still had no idea what happened. The game is filled with Easter eggs, reference to other icons of American pop culture, miscellaneous videos, paradoxes, logical dilemmas, etc.
In the end, let us all thank Microsoft for postponing this game for as long as possible for us humble PC folk, so we could buy their xbox instead. My hat goes off to those who resisted and waited.

Several elements they did really well, like disticts and wonders. I quite like planning my city and finding tiles that would be perfect for certain wonders.
Overall, I would say this game is not worth full price, and I'm rather upset that I was one of the poor saps that paid full price on release (especially since they have yet to bundle/have a sale for any of their DLC). Give it another year, then come back and look at this game. My only -real- gripe, in its current state, is that is it overpriced for the amount/quality of content you receive. Other than that, and the three points I made above, I really enjoy this game.

Overall:
Screwed up, creepy, and oh so amazing!
Takes a little bit of time to get good, but once you get into it, well...for such a low price, it's a very deep game.
Visual:
Your standard flash graphics taking a disturbing turn as the decrepid enemies and landscape you encounter feel so morbid, yet so alive. The simplistic nature of the graphics is something Edmund McMillan is known for doing well, and this is definitely the case here.
Gameplay:
This is just touching the surface of what's on offer here, as more of a "how the game works", as much of the fun comes from finding out the game and its combos.
It's been called a rogue-like, a Zelda-like, many things, but what does that mean? Essentially, you are able to shoot in 4 directions using WASD, and can move using the arrow keys.
You explore rooms of procedurally-generated dungeon floors, collecting coins to spend in shops, on slot machines, or to give to beggars, all of which can give you items which change stats, show the map, or change how you attack. You may also collect keys to enter golden door rooms to get other items, and bombs, which you can break rocks with, and possibly find hidden rooms with. Each room has a (high) chance of containing enemies, which must be killed to open the doors to other rooms.
Each floor has a boss room, containg a more difficult boss, which, upon defeat, reveals a hole into the next dungeon level.
Other characters with different stats can be unlocked through play, shaking the game up a lot.
With the Wrath of the Lamb DLC, it's a whole lot more. More items, more dungeons, some dungeons can change, more bosses, more storyline. Well worth the tiny price.
If you've ever played Super Smash TV, it's a similar affair, but maybe a bit toned down on the constant spawns.
Narrative:
Isaac's story is revealed through some cutscenes, the levels themselves, some bosses, although much of the story is left to the player's interpretation, if they so desire.
A slight commentary on heavy-handed religious activist perhaps?
Anti-abortion?
Pro-abortion?
Euthanasia?
While many people may have different thoughts on the story, you can simply play for playing's sake.
Just know that this rabbit hole can go pretty deep if you care to look.
Should you buy it?:
Come on. Even at full price, this game is CHEAP. And it's a long game, rewarding a LOT of run-throughs.
There is only a few possible reasons not to buy this.
a) If you get too creeped out by the gameplay trailers.
b) If you are interested in EPIC GRAPHICS above gameplay. (Debatable)
c) If you're waiting for The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, the remake in development (Although owners of this version will get a discount on Rebirth, so not too big an excuse)

This is seriously one of the best games I ever played. Yes. Seriously.
Not only is the gameplay is really good (you can approach your missions in any style you like - sneaky or brute force, lethal or non-lethal, solo or with help, etc.) the story is very engaging. It's a true spy story. It takes you all over the world (which leads to very different areas in both style and atmosphere) and brings you in contact with all manner of organisations with their specific style of members and a number of very interesting NPCs. The roleplaying aspect - where you choose from different styles of answers in dialogs (like professional, sarcastic, casual, suave, etc.) has a true impact on the gameplay, as do you choices during your missions. It gives you different allies or enemies.
Except for the good old violence, there are also locks to pick, electronic locks or alarms to disable, and computers to hack, all tree done through minigames that decrease in difficulty if you have the right skills.
Progression is level based. Your PC goes up in levels by earning experience, which gives you points you can spend on several skill tracks, things like stealth, pistol, assault rifle, sabotage, etc.
There is also a sort of underground black market where you can buy all sorts of weapons and armor and accessories for those, as well as gadgets like grenades and spy trickery, but also intel, like maps, dossiers on NPCs or organisations, support, extra mission objects, etc.
So, yes, I love this game. It really has it all.

The premise of this game is a physics simulator for exploring space science. It has been enhanced from a simple sandbox with a "career mode" in which you unlock technology through exploring the Kerbol System. You will also need to earn funds to build your rockets by completing missions. The difficulty level is very tweakable, so you can challenge yourself from the start. If you want to create your own goals you can use the sandbox mode in which all the technology is unlocked and there are infinite funds.
There is also a productive modder community, making new parts, developing the user interface, and tweaking all manner of aspects of the game. You can also download other peoples' rocket creations and attempt to fly them yourself. There are even alternate scenarios with different solar system setups, including recreating the earth/moon system and recreating the earth's space program development.
If you have any interest in physics you will find it at least diverting. If you are more curious, you will find it riveting.

Often called a Doom clone, Star Wars: Dark Forces opens the Jedi Knight tetralogy with a solid action-packed galaxytrotting story set during the Original Trilogy.
Released in 1995, Dark Forces introduced the gaming world to Kyle Katarn, a former Imperial who offers his mercenary services to the Rebel Alliance. The plot is relatively straightforward; the first level is effectively a prologue where Katarn infiltrates an Imperial base to steal the Death Star plans. I don’t even know why they made Rogue One when Kyle Katarn achieved the same objectives in only a few minutes. Anyway, after the first level, the main plot begins: the Empire launches a devastating attack on a Rebel base using Dark Troopers, an elite variant of stormtroopers with overwhelming firepower and none of the inaccuracy issues of regular stormtroopers. Katarn and his partner, Jan Ors, are assigned to investigate and ultimately destroy the Dark Trooper project. While not the most complex Star Wars plot, the story serves its purpose to compliment the emphasis on action and gameplay.
Unlike its three successors, Dark Forces strictly adheres to gunplay only. There are no lightsabers or Force powers, only the many blaster weapons of the Star Wars universe. There are ten weapons, some of which will be used more often than others, particularly the standard stormtrooper rifle. Still, other weapons have their uses, especially the heavy weapons you’ll need to fight the Dark Troopers such as the mortar gun, concussion rifle, and assault cannon. While it’s fun to shoot enemies, mindless gunplay isn’t the only gameplay feature. Oftentimes you’ll need to locate keys and codes to unlock doors; other times you’ll need to solve challenging puzzles to advance through levels. Expect lulls in the action when puzzles appear.
Aside from the small stash of weapons, there are two distinct groups of enemies: Imperials and mercenaries. The Imperials are the most common enemies while the mercenaries generally appear most often in the middle levels. Outside of the two groups are wildlife enemies: dianogas and kell dragons. The oft-feared sewer level gives the dianogas their notoriety, and there’s an unpleasant twist when you encounter your first kell dragon. The titular characters, the Dark Troopers, are the toughest enemies of them all, wielding dangerous weapons and appearing with increased frequency as the game progresses. The variation in enemies depends on the level’s setting; classic planets such as Nar Shaddaa and Coruscant appear, as do obscure planets that seem to stand in for well-known locations such as Hoth.
Dark Forces was not originally developed for Windows, and as such some technical issues persist on modern hardware. The game runs reasonably well in DOSBox but a few tweaks are required to improve performance. The game’s graphics have not aged well twenty plus years after release. On a modern computer monitor, the graphics look pixelated but it’s nothing serious enough to disrupt gameplay. You also cannot look up and down with the mouse, a strange feature absent in modern first-person shooters. Instead, you must use the page-up and page-down buttons to look up and down. Curious technical choices were made in this game, but perhaps nothing out of the ordinary for a game from the mid-nineties.
Despite a simple plot, dated graphics, and minor technical issues, Dark Forces delivers an enjoyable overall experience as the first game in the Jedi Knight tetralogy. If you’re looking for a classic Star Wars game for a low price, Dark Forces is an excellent choice.

The Adventures of Shuggy follows a feline vampire who just inherited a new house. Unlike a certain other popular Vampire; Shuggy doesn’t get along with the undead, ghosts, monsters, or even robots. Instead, these foul creatures are haunting his new home and wrecking havoc. In order to boot these pests out of the house, Shuggy has to collect a mess of gems and bop a few bosses, over the course of 116 levels. It is an impressive number no doubt, but the game is reasonably paced as all of the levels should take no more than two minutes a piece to complete. Although, you’ll be replaying those levels over and over again, because two minutes is an awfully long time to spend on one level. If you want to compete on the leaderboards, your best times have to be in seconds.
The puzzle-platformer is about as simple a genre to explain as anything. In order to collect all of the gems in each level, Shuggy will probably have to do more than just jump on top of things. Each level is defined by its gimmick. This could be something direct like Shuggy being able to jump really high, or it could be something obtuse and unique. For example, Shuggy could have to use multiple versions of his self or direct little buggers called Shmus to unlock gem-holding cages. Shuggy’s mansion is divided into five different areas, and some will focus on a particular level-type more than others. Even though the gimmick changes constantly, the basic mechanics are very sound, and it takes mere seconds to figure out what to do. This aspect of the game so well done that I don't think it's fair to even call them gimmicks. Shuggy rotating the entire level to reach gems or switching between clones to reach switches is just as natural as running & jumping.
Shuggy is the fragile type, so he has to worry about nasty creatures that walk, jump, fly, fall, and roll. Also questions must be raised about anyone who decorates their home with spikes. Worse still there are also time-distorting levels where Shuggy must use his past selves to step on switches and open paths to gems. Ever seen Time Cop? What happened to the villain can also happen to Shuggy, if he ever makes contact with one of his selves. Thankfully, in this game it isn’t quite as gruesome but the result is definitely something to be avoided. I’m particularly fond of these levels, since they require Shuggy to take differing paths around the room, and to pay attention to where Shuggy-from-5-seconds-ago is going next.
All things considered, death will become the least of your worries before long. Even after you have figured out the solution to the level and grabbed the key, chances are high you’ll want to go back after seeing your position on the leaderboard. Where this game really shines is in replaying levels, trimming seconds or even half-seconds away. There is also an absolute #1 ranking, so the satisfaction of taking that coveted spot, just might be worth the trouble. Some will say that puzzle games lose their purpose when the puzzles are figured out, but thanks to the great controls and mechanics, there is almost always room for improvement.
There is multiplayer support, but my advice is the following: Look into making an open-minded friend in your town OR convincing whoever your dating that this isn’t like those murder-simulators you usually play OR worst comes to worst, begging your parents to have another child. There are 36 cooperative levels, and some additional competitive modes to play, but you need a couch-buddy to coop. From what I can gather the cooperative mode is more than just two Shuggys grabbing gems instead of one. You actually have to work together and co-exist in a fashion, that does not lead to harm for one another.
Game reviews are to nitpicks as an octopus is to ink, so while this game is a quality affair, I can’t very well say I’m done with my review until I get my nitpicking on. Whenever a level begins I would prefer if there was something like a countdown before control is handed to the player. It takes a second or two for Shuggy and all of the objects to spawn into the level, but while those things are happening, Shuggy can move around. It doesn’t take much to memorize what I want to do in the first couple seconds of the level, so thankfully this isn’t a serious issue. There is also a certain random element to the game which I’m kind-of iffy about. A couple of enemies have unpredictable movement patterns. This introduces an element of randomness, which doesn't gel with speedrunning. This isn’t an easy fix since the nature of these enemies gives them their identity, and their change or removal could possibly worsen the game. I’m not quite 100% sure either way, but I still think it is worth mentioning.
While I have my reservations about particular aspects of the game, and the lacking multiplayer support is quite a shame The Adventures of Shuggy is a charming and fun bit of entertainment that I definitely believe is worth your consideration. Again I’m not an expert on the subject of puzzle-platformers but I am a veteran when it comes to recognizing quality. As far as I can tell this game does most everything right.

Okay, so the many user reviews I've seen on this game have said its Doom + Star Wars.  I will tell you from the get-go, it is NOT a direct clone of Doom.  Yes, it has pixel art.  Yes, it is a FPS.  However, Star Wars - Dark Forces expands on the Doom formula to bring a whole different experience to the player.
Playing through this game, it does not have that run-and-gun feel of Doom.  You are meant to analyze your environment critically for ways to complete the level (not just for secrets).  It does contain the same things like get key cards for certain doors, but you will also need to do do things like pulling different switches from different parts of the level to advance, blow open secret passageways with mines to get further in the level, or pick one of 4 routes to correctly progress through the level.
There were some levels I had to stop and think about and backtrack a lot before I figured out what to do.  You cannot complete this game just by blasting away stormtroopers.  It requires more thought, and I enjoyed every minute of it!  This made each level its own challenge especially with the diverse environment changes between levels.
Regarding the story, I thought it would be a simple "Kill Imperials A, B, C" type of game like the first level implies.  However, it goes into its own segment on the Dark Trooper program of the Imperaials after Episode IV, which I really enjoyed learning about.
Lastly, the sound design is just great.  If you've played Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire, it seems they originally created those sound bytes for this game!  From the shot of a blaster to the whirring of a turbine, it all felt very Star Wars.  The stormtroopers even yell as they see you like the typical "Stop Rebel scum!".
The main complaint I have about this game is that there is not in-level save system.  To save your progress, you need to play through the entire level.  This can be difficult as some of the levels can drag out if you are figuring outhow to progress.
Another unfortunate point is the music.  I respect the person who has digitized John Williams music and have enjoyed it to a some degree, but range of instruments is very small!  I understand the reasoning why they made that decision with storage size, but this is where the game shows its age more than anything.  You'll have to wait for later games like Shadows of the Empire to get the original score into your game.
Main Recommendation: Play past the first level.  This is mainly a warm-up level to get you used to the controls.  The real meat of the game comes in with the later levels.
This game is a hidden gem and I would definitely recommend you pick it up.

Awesome game! That a turn-based game can create so much tension in almost every single randomly generated level I've played is just amazing. There are so many memorable moments emerging from the tight design and brilliant procedural generation!
Like the time my whole squad played ring around the rosies to narrowly evade the one guard with armor we could not neutralize,.. Or the missions played with 4 agents with 3 weapons between them after starting the campaign with 2 rescue missions... Or that mission where I thought I could go deeper to  loot some safes and ended up barely making it out while running out of lethal ammo... Or the one where the financial executive we had stolen the codes from was running around like a panicked, headless chicken and kept spotting my agents...
One thing that makes it work is that you can pick your risk vs reward... if a missions starts out easy, you tend to try to explore/loot more, until things start getting too dangerous, which can happen quite suddenly if you make a mistake or just overextend. Another thing that helps is the full information and zero randomness (once the level is laid out), so that you never lose an agent to an unlucky shot (as is the norm in xcom). This, combined with the relatively short campaign makes iron-man-like modes viable for me.

If you like turn-based-strategy and roguelite, this game is just a gem.
When I tried it during  a free week-end, I was not convinced: tutorial was OK, but I decided to play on expert level on my 1st try... and I got beaten on first level in about... 2 minutes... yes even though it's turn-based !
Even by playing it in beginner difficulty then, I felt like I was missing something as I was dying a lot.
But if you take into consideration that you have to hide and not shoot (which is what I was doing at first: shooting guards - but this is wrong), that you can cross a room full of guards without being noticed, then you go "level-up", and the game becomes much more enjoyable... and easy... well at least through the beginner campaign... then comes the experienced campaign... and it becomes even more deadly challenging... in a good way... but don't expect to finish it on 1st try even if you easily finished beginner campaign... I can't even imagine what expert campaign is about !
Well all in all, this game should be seen as a chess game mixed with roguelite based on turn-based-strategy principles:
- you have  to think a lot and anticipate your next moves like in chess games,
- levels are ramdomly generated, you can choose the characters and AI powers that you want to play in many optimised ways (or leave it to random selection).
- Plus you get to manage and optimise the use of your credits efficiently depending on if you want to spend them for you AI abilities, for your characters powers, or on the items which can give our characters advantages.
All of these give you a lot of possibilties gameplay-wise, and thus provide a very good replay value even if it does not look like, but don't be fooled: this game is a roguelite. So don't be frustrated if you fail a campaign and don't stop after you finish the beginner campaign, this is not the end of the game, and that's the purpose.

While this game is fun to play, it's ridiculously difficult even on the beginner setting. If you like turn based strategy games you'll enjoy it, but getting out alive is an extremely difficult task. It takes a full playthrough of the game (about 3 hours) to even begin to understand what you are doing.
This game is challenging, but sometimes it seems unfair. The procedural generator can be very unforgiving, throwing you into a difficult map including many rooms where the objective and exit are on wildly different parts of the map, forcing you to traverse back through the mess of guards that just woke up. The game world is already set up for you to lose. Because the maps are procedurally generated, you can get maps that literally are not possible to beat without sacrificing a large portion of your team.
Unless you might like a very challenging spatial strategy game, I'd save your money until they deal with the difficulty.This is all on Beginner mode. Each approach you take has HUGE consequences down the line and the game's alert level system just brings the crushing weight of time down on you. The cost and armor level of the guards go up very quickly without providing much to help you in return.
The game feels polished, but they've got a lot to do difficulty wise. I'm still coming back to the game, but my first playthrough I didn't complete any objectives because of the level of difficulty. If the DEV wants the players to play perfectly, they should make it a bit easier on beginner mode.

Balancing patches, as well as optimization patches have been implemented and the game now runs like butter on my computer. You've got player vs dinosaurs, player vs player dinosaurs, player vs player, player vs harder dinosaur waves and Conquest which is coming up soon.
My only gripes right now with it are the animations being a little rough, dinosaurs can be a little derpy and the music is the same in EVERY map. I know that old music from Beatdown will be implemented once Conquest rolls out, but not sure if that's just for the Conquest maps or for all the maps.
But other than that, it's a pretty great game that has my full love.

Ok, early first impressions.
So, I LOVED the first game. It was kind of an out of nowhere smash hit for me. I'm a massive fan of the LOTR universe (and yes, I read the books so I'm allowed to say that now leave me alone) so as you can imagine I was pleasantly surprised to find that it did an excellent job of coexisting side by side with the existing Tolkien universe while simultaneously respecting the original material. It felt like someone filling in the gaps of the story. Gameplaywise the original took the standard hack and slash template but added a whole new layer of depth with the nemesis which made it unique and very, very fun.
I had hoped Shadow of War would take those things that were core to the original's success and then just increase the amount of depth and content. It does... I guess... and maybe I'm just being overcritical because of my extremely high expectations (and I'll update the review accordingly) but right now I'm not exactly happy about it.
I'm two hours in and am nowhere NEAR the level of cool♥♥♥♥♥♥you see in the trailers. Conquering regions, taking over forts, building in depth relationships, riding dragons etc are still clearly a ways away. And that would be fine if the intro weren't incredibly boring. It's lots of narration, recap and frame locked cinematics that really aren't that interesting. It may be true that Shadow of Mordor also took some time to ramp up, but at least you were playing during that time, and it had a super dark scene where you watch your family slowly executed in a blood right that fules your motivation for the rest of the game. And then the mechanics kick in. Now instead of draining Uruk's to refill your arrows, you drain for health. Arrows are found by picking them up around the map. No more building up hitstreaks for executions, instead dealing damage permanently fills a meter that never decays (unless you receive damage) and then can be consumed for an exeute. The upgrade tree is now much more like a standard RPG, you get a point to spend every time you level up. There are a few more changes as well, but overall I've just kind of wondered... why? It's not like these mechanical changes are making things worse, they just don't feel necessary.
Storywise I feel about the same as I do the game, lots of unnecessary changes that don't really make things any better, just different. For example, Shelob is a hot goth chick now. Which is stupid. And apparently Palantir are super important, but after seeing how they work in game it's obvious the developers don't really know what they do. So far the game feels much less like a side by side companion to the LOTR universe and more like a fantasy story written by a guy who watched the movies while half asleep and then was told to retell them but in a way that would be broadly appealing to as many people as possible. It's not necessarily a bad thing, just disappointing.
One thing, as others have noticed you CAN disable the micro-transactions at the beginning by not agreeing to the online features. Just do it. WB, if you're reading this, ♥♥♥♥ you and ♥♥♥♥ off with your micro-transactions in my SP games you moneygrubbing out of touch sacks of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Just... ♥♥♥♥ off. I only bought this because I liked the first game, if this happens again I'm never buying another Shadow of Mordor game. ♥♥♥♥ you.
Lastly, optimization. Surprisingly I'm running the game on high settings on my RX 480 and it run's well over 60 fps almost at all times on 1080p. That's one thing I can definitely say I'm impressed with, for a brand new IP to be this smooth on release is impressive, to say the least.
TL;DR So far I'm not super impressed. I'm going to go ahead and recommend it because it seems ok for now, and maybe as I get more into it it will get better. But right now the story seems to be taking a bit too much creative license with the universe and the gameplay doesn't feel that much improved, if at all. But for what it's worth Im going to push through and hope for the best.

As a long time Civilization game player since Civilization II, I found Civ VI to be a tedious, slow board game filled with repetitive micro actions that emphasized optimizing game mechanics for war over all else, with inferior AI, subpar diplomacy, and inexplicably irritating game design.
The incredibly slow and cluttered one unit per tile unit movement made the all too frequent wars by every AI opponent  a boring chore. The AI opponents do not strategize interestingly nor are there multiple strong strategic warfare options for the player. Manually moving around units without the ability to construct permanent roads is dull and breaks immersion, Most of my game time felt like clicking and waiting. War is also unavoidable first with agressive early barbarians and then with the frequent inevitable surprise wars that every friendly AI declared. For example, the Vikings denounced my completely landlocked civ for lacking a strong navy, then attacked!
The map art design makes it hard to see information at a glance such as where resources are located and oddly the areas already explored but out of view look almost like the fog of war, and many quality of life features from earlier versions of the Civ series are simply missing.
Now that I have played Civ VI, I realize that I prefer earlier Civilization series games' more immersive simulation, strategic open-endedness and role-playing aspects. The earlier Civ series games Civ 4 and Civ 5, as well as Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, and the Civ 4 Fall from Heaven 2 mod, offer a much wider range of interesting decisions. Their one more turn addictive charm came from both superb game mechanics and an immersive world in which to play out decisions.
Civ VI's focus is board game-like mechanics that focus overwhelmingly on competitive war among players as a path to victory. This, combined with the irritatingly limited AI/diplomacy and tediously paced gameplay felt unfun to me despite 40 hours of trying to enjoy the game.

This was an OK experience. I like to think of AP as a cross between Mass Effect & Batman Arkham...Maybe even Deus Ex!
But...you can really pass this up.
If you're REALLY considering reading this whole review, let me tell you why
AS A STEALTH GAME
First of all, gameplay is mostly stealthy. That is: Hiding, waiting for enemies to have their backs turned, then kill them without being detected. That is pretty cool. But the feel of the rest of the gameplay just didn't do it for me. Combat kind of blows. It's just not FLUID at all and the amount of control feels like I'm prodding a pregnant cow. For everything it can offer, I would rather be playing a Batman Arkham game when said and done. If you're looking for a Stealth game, do not buy this game, go buy Arkham Asylum.
"But...COMBAT?!" Yes, you can customize your character to be more run-and-gun...but it just wasn't polished enough to really make it feasable alternative. Shooting with that silenced pistol was really cool though. Expect to take a long♥♥♥♥♥time trying to get unreasonably lucky on some hard bosses.
AS AN ESPIONAGE GAME
There is hacks, gadgets, electronic sautering, lockpicking... yes. They are nice little minigames to make you feel espionagey. But by the end of the game, you want to stick a lockpick up your♥♥♥♥♥if ONE more of these just gives you money (money is used to buy better gear...but you really don't NEED better gear). Nothing that is actually mission-changing at ALL. The integration of these into the actual missions were below expectation, but it was a good effort especially as sometimes it would give you some story.
AS AN RPG
This is where Alpha Protocal helps to outshine it's not-as-good-as-Batman stealth gameplay. This I went IN not expecting to like the story, but it was actually pretty cool. The protagonist is way more likable than expected. Not the most AMAZING story, but still pretty OK!
Like MASS EFFECT, you get to CHOOSE how you want conversations to go. You can indicate the mood throughout the conversation. Very cool. A LOT like Mass Effect, but with it's own little twist! Kind of felt like a cheaper version of it.
You can Romance women you've kept close near the end, but don't expect anything dramatic...could be a horribly animated kiss, then a "Mission Completed". Not close to even Bioware romances.
But, the transitions are kind of cheesy, almost immersion breaking to an already semi-bland story. The things/coroprations that are "mysterious" in the story, are uninteresting, and I really couldn't care less about learning about them.
The story is run on semi-tracks. Kind of like Mass Effect...linear...but you get to choose your linearism to some degree. Emphasis on SOME degree. Little freedom, but what it is is very appreciated. Go to Saudi Arabia base. Then to Taiwan, Rome, Moscow (those 3 in any order). Then final mission. The safehouse feature was very cool, but honestly I couldn't help feeling like implementation of overall RPG elements was an EXTREMELY poor effort.
"What about the SKILLS?!" To put bluntly, choosing your class isn't really important. It's not really a necessary feature even (you choose whatever skills you want anyway)... the skills aren't very diverse and your choice in them don't really change your gameplay in an already linear game. If you choose anything but spy...you're going to have a ♥♥♥♥♥ier time because combat is not feasably enough implemented to go run-and-gunning.
Don't expect Mass Effect skill options/progression...and DEFINITELY don't expect Skyrim status on this. Very basic, not worth getting worked up over.
REPLAYABILITY??
It's OK...but not really unless you have a strong desire to watch this a second time. Like Mass Effect, the story is pretty much the same, but with different outcomes in the middle if you choose a different dialogue option. But it's importance is severely lessened in Alpha Protocal. I have no interest to replay the story again for another 10 years. Like I said above, class/skill variety is way too lacking to expect replaying just for that as well.
CONLCUSION
Look at other games like this closely before buying. There are a lot of similarities Alpha Protocal shares with other games, but is absolutely sub-par compared to them.♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm always optimistic & thumbs up in reviews, but I just CAN'T be with this game. It's just OK. The story was pretty cool, but it is just another game touched by Obsidian. Alpha Protocal = don't worry about it

EDIT: So the fps unlocking patch has been released and behold the game can't run stable 60 fps on a 1080 GTX even, it fluctuates between 40-58 fps using the 60 fps limit and G-Sync seems to be handling it quite well. However there's till frame timing issues every now and then that cause major stuttering even if it's running at around 50 fps.
Game has three major technical issues that makes it very hard to recommend this game to anyone who has issues graphical issues.
1. 30 FPS lock, controls are very sluggish and it basically feels like playing on a console when you try to aim with the mouse, it's actually preferable to play with a controller at all times for me right now at least.
2. The lightning in the game has some very bad issues. First of all light sources have a very low view distance keep popping in. Secondly shadows seem to render on and off just by turning the camera a bit back and forth without moving yourself on certain objects.
3. THE BLUR... everything looks like someone smudged it with some acid or something, like it isn't enough that the textures look a blurry mess from the start they decide to blur it and then blur it some more! NOTE: It's mostly the anti aliasing technique (FXAA) causing this, setting it to low actually improves the graphics as long as your resolution is high enough to compensate the jaggies.
Other bugs would include some very strange physics in the game with ragdolls bouncing around as well as objects not rendering at all (Had a bunch floating stuff that I could walk into in a garage only to suddenly spawn a table underneath when I entered the car). Had a single CTD crash just as loading screen started about 1 hour into the game but then no problems for the rest of my session. Seen the exact same rendering and CTD issue on some streamers so it's a game issue.
The good part so far is that voices, lip syncing and close up models look good and the story has also been quite intriguing and fun. However the missions themselves are starting to feel very repetitive.
Will update the review as I go along but seriously why would you go some much backwards from Mafia 2 or even Mafia 1 from a technical aspect....

In each game of Nuclear Throne, you start as one of a handful of characters, each with their own strengths, and at times, weaknesses.  That's it.  You're thrown straight into the action, with only the barest whisper of an over-arching narrative.  Upon your first death, you're told 'you did not reach the Nuclear Throne', thus fixing the games objective squarely in your sights.
Perhaps I am getting old and slow, but I find Nuclear Throne fiendishly challenging.  As with most rogue-likes, progression is determined by a combination of luck, and of pure skill.  Your character levels up by collecting rads from fallen enemies.  Collect enough, and you can select one of a handful of mutations when you finish the level.  I find that luck of the draw at the earlier levels can be key, and collecting enough rads in the first stages to level up a couple of times can make future runs much easier.
To assist in your quest, the game features a diverse arsenal of weapons, also dropped at random.  These range from melee to ranged, and players will come up with their own preferences.
One thing the game does really well, is synergise the various systems.  On one of my most successful run throughs, I played as the Robot (can eat weapons for health and ammo, and has a chance to collect higher tier weapons).  Early on, I picked up the steady aim and shotgun shoulders mutations.  When combined with a double barrelled shotgun, a single blast would see a tight grouping of projectiles bounce off walls almost endlessly.  On constrained levels with few open areas, it was a very effective, and safe way of clearing levels.
If that is a moment where everything has come together, I can cite many more where bad luck has lead to an unfortunate death.  One point of frustration involves the portals that are created when you clear a level.  These burst open, destroying all items around them, whilst pulling you toward them.  One set of levels feature cars that explode, and it seems to be my like that the portals open right on top of them, dragging my character to a swift explodey death.
But, even with these moments, I'm still having loads of fun.  The controls are sharp with a keyboard and mouse combo (haven't tried with a controller), and death is but a momentary setback.  Games run so quick, that it's possible to recover lost progress in only a few minutes.
Nuclear Throne is the perfect game to play when you only have a sneaky fifteen minutes or so, but also a great choice for longer plays.  Also a great option for mates, as the short game times work well in a 'life by life' arrangement.
Solid.

Age of Gladiators, doesn't hold your hand, it doesn't let you make mistakes. It is unapologetically hardcore, and when it finally clicks, it is insanely addictive.
GAMEPLAY:: Age of Gladiators puts you in control of a Gladiator stable and lets you manage them through their fighting career. First off, you create your character, choosing from a few character slides, you choose you're former profession whether it be former scout, gladiator, doctor, merchent or others. This gives you special bonuses, such as the ability to accurately scout a fighters real scores and abilities, or so your fighters never getting sick. Once you've chosen the economy you want (this games version of difficulty), you're thrown in the deep end.
Don't let this get you down. You will fail, quickly and often. You will put fighters into competition, and learn through trial and error how to win them fights and make money and you will watch your favourite fighter, your best competitor fight and be executed by an unforgiving crowd, you will get frustrated. Actual fights, are text/turn based, you watch as each action is displayed infront of you and your fighters stats falls as he tires or gets hurt. Dispite how simple this looks, these fights are very engaging and suspenseful. Watching your fighter, begin to lose a winning battle, only at the end to hit a critical hit and win is as exciting as it is generally suspenseful, early on.
The forums, so far, have been a helpful tool. The developer has given handly tips on how to stave off bankrupcy, as well as the easiest way to learn the game.
GRAPHICS:: This is a simple menu driven game. Dissapointingly, the game has no real animation, or even a real full screen. Simply put, it's not winning any awards  for art, but it gets the job done. Character pictures are well done, and the UI, while simple is adequate to what you need.
SOUND:: The game's background music, is a long hum of wardrums and sets the mood perfectly for the game. Interface sounds, and even the fights themselves, are good. The sound of two men fighting is conveyed nicely, if not, albeit simply.
OVERALL:: Age of Gladiators, is a game that looks simple, but soon becomes an intense cat and mouse game against you, the other bosses and bankrupcy. You won't like the game at first, and there is no tutorial. If you are into management style games in the vein of Football Manager, or are looking for a genuine challenge, pick this game up. The game is well put together, and the developer (one person) is open to feedback and responsive on the forums. If you have never played anything like this, I would suggest a lets play before picking it up.

The concept is simple, build an army, kill the enemy CEO. The fact that you can go into first person with almost any unit means that you can personally pull the trigger on the assasination rather than just send in a squad and view from above.
This game is about the gameplay. There is a varied tech tree and the route you take up that tree will decide your fate. That and the route your opponent takes. You can choose to build big weapons and huge troop numbers and bust into your opponents base or you can choose the more subtle sneaky assasinaton attempt.
The game is a lot of fun and the ability to go firts person adds a fun extra to the game. There's somethig awesome about building a base then taking a tour of it in the first person to admire your work. And despite the opening sentence to this review... it looks pretty good!
There are elements that I would like to see improved though. The tech tree although expansive allows for a limited number of basic unit types. I'd like more research options for unit types and i'd like to see larger and more maps. Perhaps more options for the assasination than a blaster to the face.
To summerise, the game is immensly fun despite it's basic designs and unit limitations. These are made up for by some other subtle minor details that i didn't expect.
You can tell that it was made with a very small budget and to a small degree it feels like only half a game but that just doesn't matter. £10 well spent.

I reached out to be a beta tester for this game, so I've played a pre-release version that appears to be consistent with official release.
I completely recommend this game as a comprehensive management sim that allows you to control every aspect of a team of gladiators, from skills and attributes to weapons/equipment, lodgings and supplies, and your own finances. It's like a sports sim in which you, the owner, literally owns your team.
Gameplay is highly detailed and requires you to focus on several things at any given time. Nothing is static - fighters can become ill just before a big match that you were counting on them to win to keep you afloat financially, buildings need repairs, opportunities for trades and side quests arise, etc.
Highly addictive, difficult at first but once you get the hang of it, you will be driven to keep pushing your fighters through the map and all challengers. I personally found that, if you're lucky enough to get a star gladiator and train him well, managing loans and finances will be more difficult than winning fights (stars aren't cheap). I appreciated the detail and historical realism. Definitely try this one out!
