Nuked my own city just for fun. Was immediately contacted by two of the AI civs: Aztecs to congratulate the improved alignment of our interests and Nubia to congratulate the effectiveness of my districts.
My biggest complaint with the game is that it feels like the game is playing me, rather than me playing the game. My actions were more driven by controling war declaration than doing what I want. Don't build enough of the right military units quick enough? AI declares war on you. Try to use your envoys on the city states? AI will declare war on you. Build wonders? AI will declare war on you. Upgrade your form of government because you are ahead in the civic tree? AI declares war on you. Have too many luxury resources? AI declares war on you. Not enough? AI declares war on you.
Some people will enjoy the puzzly nature of babysitting the AI's temper tantrums or the frequent small wars with higher numbers of AI civs, but if you found yourself enjoying the more peaceful routes of Civ 5, I'd watch a lot of playthroughs on YouTube before buying. No matter what victory path you aim for in Civ 6, war will be a part of it.
PROs:
+ I like the new district mechanics, though I wish there were more (quantity and variety of effects) buildings for each district
+ I like the new builder mechanics
+ City states are more interesting
+ Split research and civics trees is more good than bad
+ Better than Civ 5 was pre-expansions
CONs:
- Religion is painful
- No diplomatic victory option. It was janky in Civ 5, but it enabled some gameplay options that are missing from this game (like focusing on economy with mostly peaceful intentions).
- The AI is as bad as all the reviews say
- The start location scripting/city placement issues are as bad as the reviews say (I once had another civ spawn in the hex next to mine, I captured his settler with my warrior on turn one)
- I appreciate what the devs attempted to do with the AI agendas to give them some diversity, but it turned the AI civs into loose cannons. With almost non-existant diplomacy, it's a bad combo.
- Large maps and the higher difficulty settings just aren't fun.
- No penalties for building wide, no benefit to building tall
- No Venice
Wait for post-expansion reviews or pick up when on sale.

As a longtime civ player, I just can't get into this latest version. I avoided the game at launch due to the goofy graphics and the 80$ price tag. After getting it on 50% off, i've tried very hard to enjoy it but I just can't. I'll be trying for a refund but after 30 hours played, I don't think i'll have much luck.
It seems to appeal much more to a mobile RTS style of game whereas I prefer the immersion and civ building aspects of the franchise. I also feel like I need to use the strategic view to actually see what's going on on the map. This only emphasizes the mobile aspect of the art style and makes the immersion more difficult, which is ironic because the art style change was suppose to make things more visible and easier to see. I don't feel like i'm guiding a civilization to greatness, everything is a game-mechanic decision to maximize your pursuit of a win condition, routes that are very narrow and linear to chase.
For example, civ policy cards are being constantly swapped out based on whatever your next immediate goal is, contrary to any sense of persistent or organic cultural development and, on standard at least, tech and policy advances happen at a very rapid pace. I always disliked how quickly tech becomes obsolete and replaced in the civ games, I always wanted to feel like each era was actually an era you play through but this rapid development (first game the AI hit modern era in 1200 AD) just makes it feel like a mad dash to the end and Civ 6 is much worse than the previous games for this.
The new distrinct and wonder placement system feels cumbersome to manage and plan for. With each using a tile space, thus losing the tile yields, and requiring specific hex conditions, it makes trying to plan city placement and the development of a civilization annoying even after managing to learn and remember those requirements. The rate of border expansion is also very slow without specifically pursuing culture or buying tiles outright. It feels more complex than deep, which just leads to ungratifying work on my end. At times the research and policy process felt more like starcraft build progression paths than a civilization growing through the ages, too linear and too obvious.
The civs and mechanics are utterly uninspiring. Admittedly much of this was due to not fully understanding all the mechanics and how everything works now but even after reading and watching walkthroughs, I couldn't get excited selecting any particular civ. Many of the civs are hyper specific to a map type or play style and useless otherwise. This kind of sucks. At the least i would have much prefered each civ having multiple leaders that are designed to pursue different win paths so I could play a civ I liked for the historic, aethstetic or narrative aspect. Again, the civ builder in me wanted more immersion and playing a leader or civ that FEELS exciting outside mechanic bonuses would have been nice.
Another option would have been to separate the narrative and mechanics from each other more like Stellaris, which has an awesome, though content limited, system. I understand dev choosing civs and abilities based on historic presendent has always been a part of civ (and I do like that) but when it's all about mechanics, it stops feeling like civ for me. Why not allow default civs and custom ones? As a side note, the custom religion symbols are really boring and all of the same animal theme. A wider variety of art and styles here would have been nice. Also, why can't I use an existing religion and just rename it?
Seafaring also has little impact on anything unless required on specific map types. Most games, even with coasts, I barely made use of water units(or tiles) other than exploration. Seafaring was a huge part of asian and european development, this isn't at all present in the game and feels really wierd that there is no significant benefit to seafaring.
tldr; if you want a mechanic heavy time-sink with an RTS/Mobile feel, civ 6 might be for you. If you want an immersive, historic rich civilization builder, this one probably isn't gonna work for you anymore than it did for me. I think Stellaris or Civ 5 are still my go-to for that type of game.

Hotline Miami is a 2D top-down action video game by Jonatan Söderström and Dennis Wedin, collectively known as Dennaton Games. The game was published by Devolver Digital and released on October 23, 2012 for Microsoft Windows. The game blends top down perspective with stealth, extreme violence and surreal storytelling, along with a soundtrack and visuals influenced by 1980s culture. The game itself was influenced in part by Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 neo-noir crime drama film Drive, as well as Cocaine Cowboys; Refn is specifically thanked in the game's credits, and the game even features a similar "Driver" jacket lying on the floor in several levels.
○Gameplay
Hotline Miami is divided into several chapters, each of which is further broken down into several stages. At the start of most chapters, the unnamed protagonist wakes up in his apartment and listens to cryptic messages on his answering machine. These messages tell him to perform an arbitrary task at a certain location, which in each case is inferred as a metaphor for killing every person at that location, such as giving VIPs at a hotel a 'great stay', or taking care of a 'pest infestation'. Prior to commencing a mission, the player is asked to select an animal mask to wear, each of which provides unique advantages or handicaps.
In each stage, the player navigates a building from a top-down perspective, and the goal is almost always to kill every opponent therein. Occasionally the player must also defeat a boss at the end of the chapter or find key items as they explore, but most levels are very straightforward. Some levels will also include hidden masks for the player to find along the way. The player has access to a wide variety of melee, thrown, and ranged weapons, and will need to handle challenges through either stealthy tactics or overwhelming force. However, the player character is no more resilient than the enemies, so mistakes are usually fatal.
Enemy AI varies slightly, causing them to occasionally move unpredictably, making it difficult to plan a perfect approach. To make up for this, the game allows the player to restart each stage the moment they die, allowing them to quickly fine-tune their approach over several attempts. The game grades the player's performance at the end of each chapter based on a number of factors, also granting them points that unlock more weapons, and may also unlock additional masks depending on their score.
○Storyline (Spoiler-free)
Hotline Miami employs an unreliable narrator and events are sometimes presented out of chronological order. The player takes the role of an unknown man; he is frequently referred to as "Jacket" by fans due to his distinctive letterman jacket, but he is never referred to by this or any other name in the game. He is plagued by visions involving three masked strangers who discuss his identity and actions. The first is a man who wears Jacket's clothes and a rooster mask ('Richard') and asks him cryptic questions, the second is a woman wearing a horse mask ('Don Juan') who expresses concern over his mental state, and the third is a mobster who wears an owl mask ('Rasmus') and expresses disgust at his behavior.
Jacket wakes up in his apartment on April 3, 1989. He receives a voicemail about a supposed delivery of 'cookies' to his home. Jacket finds a package outside which contains a rooster mask and instructions to perform a hit on a group of criminals and steal a briefcase in their possession, threatening that he is being watched and that "failure is not an option." After delivering the briefcase to a pre-arranged drop-off, he is attacked by a homeless man and is forced to kill him, after which he removes his mask and vomits. Jacket continues to get more voicemails, each of which presents itself as a client or employer demanding that he take care of an innocuous "problem" at a specific address, which invariably contains a criminal operation that he must eliminate.
After each level, Jacket stops at either a bar, convenience store, pizza place, or video store. He finds the same bearded man working at each store, who gives him encouragement and free samples of merchandise. Between levels, Jacket collects in his apartment news clippings relating to his deeds, including speculations from the police that his massacres have some relation to Russian organized crime. Following a voicemail directing him to attack the estate of a movie producer, Jacket rescues a drug-addled girl who was being sexually abused and brings her home. Eventually, he begins a relationship with the woman, while continuing to murder mobsters at the request of the voicemails. At one point, while exiting his building to attend to a 'mission', Jacket notices a green-clothed janitor, who leers at him while he heads out the door.
After a few missions, Jacket receives a phone call insisting he come to the phone company's office to deal with a 'prank caller'. When he arrives a plot twist happens which makes the make more clearer. (I can't write more of story as spoilers will come).

Invisible Inc is a fantastic game. Graphics and voice acting are whimsical, yet elegant (the latter is rare in games). The game mechanics are so very well thought out. The missions are surprisingly un-repetitive, and have just the right lenght for a nice little session. There is not much of a story, but a good tension arch with a not too long campaign that gets progressively more difficult.
What it somehow manage to do, is that I'm getting just barely through the missions, yet I manage them. This combination of just barely dodging the bullet and outsmarting the level gives a nice sense of achievement.
That this happens so often, and so many, shows that it is not a coincidence, but rather a result of a couple of well designed game mechanisms. Moreover, this happens on procedurally designed maps, that could be unfair or easy just out of luck. Somehow the game gives you enough tools to compensate it. Rock paper shotgun analysed this, and found that the flexible structure of objectives and a risk level that increases with every turn are responsible. It is up to the player how much they chose to risk, and how much reward they get. Immediate mistakes are forgiven, due to a roll-back function. However, strategical mistakes can get one in a situation where roll-back does not suffice. Here one has to improvise, accept losses and recover, or get busted. Failure is part of the game.

Assuming you are aware that this is not a gameplay oriented game but a story driven, graphic adventure, click game, it's absolutely amazing. You should definitely play the first season before you start this one, obviously.
The story is insanely good. It has a very emotional flashback/dream scene that on its own already captures the brilliance of the game. Furthermore, the entire while the game keeps you excited for what is about to happen, what insane plot twists are going to happen next. And it doesn't disappoint. Few moments in the game are predictable and you'll want to binge play all episodes in one go.
Just buy. You won't regret it. It even has some form of replayability to it as you can go back and make entirely different choices although that never really charmed me.
P.S.    -    Season 1 choices influence season 2 story and this season will likely influence season 3 story.

Invisible Inc. is a meticulously clockwork strategy game. The only uncertainty here, is information you do not yet have, and AI decisions. Yet, even in these areas the game gives you extensive information to play with. You can see at a glance exactly which of the areas you can see, are also observed by guards. You know enemy health and traits. Even the destination and object of a guard's interest may be divined. This is very empowering, and puts most failures squarely on the player.
At first, you'll want to avoid ever being seen. Soon, you'll be satisfied with escape when spotted. Eventually, you'll confidently pull the strings of the enemy to send them hither and yon, as you scamper about your business. It's an awesome feeling when you pull it off.
I love the slick sci-fi setting; the characterizations are nice and refreshingly diverse. Unit upgrades are fun, and the stage dressing is nicely on theme. The worst I can say is that like all roguelikes, you must first learn the game before you can win at it. Also, you're going to rely on a bit of luck to have the options that you want. Overall, the limited "rewind" system is a good way to offer a safety net, although I do miss that tool on the higher difficulty settings.
The best I can say is, I loved the challenge and was glad to be able to complete it. The unlocks on failure were a great way to spin straw into gold. I liked the expansion, but that difficulty really gets up there. This is a good game to play if you enjoyed X-Com, FTL, Dungeons of Dredmor or Mark of the Ninja. The fusion of stealth and turn based strategy is, in the context of a roguelike, exquisite.

What is Nuclear Throne? What is expenses? Could it be possible that ancient civilizations were visited by outer space travelers? Let's find out.
Nuclear Throne is an isometric bullet hell shooter with roguelike elements. Esentially, the goal of the game is to clean seven 'worlds' or instantiations of a nuclear wasteland by killing every moving thing in them. To do so, you are armed with a broad range of weapons, from classic assault rifles and revolvers to more futuristic stuff like laser cannons and lightsabers. Also, your character mutates as you kill more enemies, obtaining certain buffs like extra health, lower enemy bullets, the ability to push through walls, etc.
From the first moment it is clear that the game has a very arcadey setting. Lots of bullets, screen shaking constantly, low health both for the player and the enemies. Some enemy faking death gets up and instakills you. A boss spawns right next to you. A cop reflects your bullets back, killing you in the process. In Nuclear Throne, everything happens very fast, especially your death. This is a hard game. This is the most important thing to bear in mind when purchasing Nuclear Throne. It is a ♥♥♥♥ing hard game. And I'm not talking about Dark Souls-like hard. If you're ok with dying against the easiest enemy, for any bad decision, for any second of doubt, then go ahead and buy the game. Otherwise go buy any PS3-gen game.
As mentioned above, Nuclear Throne has some roguelike elements, namely random level generation and permadeath. The former is well implemented, although in a simple way. Most levels have nothing remarkable about them. Some people complain about spawning in the middle of a room full of enemies. It is true that some spawning scenarios may be overwhelming at first, but in my experience I have found that it is possible to deal with this situations. Regarding permadeath, there's not much to say in a time when every indie roguelike has permadeath because it is trendy.  You can argue that it is a way to artificially extend the game life, you can argue that its a way of mastering the game. That's up to you.
The setting of the game is pretty bizarre. You find yourself in an unexplained nuclear wasteland, where the survivors fight for some reason not really clear, but who really cares about lore in a arcade shooter? Most of the characters and enemies are mutated animals, which is quite original. The art of the game is simple but effective, and matches the tone of the game. The music is amazing, go check it out for yourself (the ♥♥♥♥ing ending song dude, the ♥♥♥♥ing ending song).
Nuclear Throne comes with some very welcome features like many playable characters with different strong and weak points and lots of different weapons, which leads to different gameplay styles. There are crowns, which act as game modifiers, and also some secret levels. Recently, daily and weekly challenges were added. Not that they are a completely different game, but these things add some replayability.
In conclusion, Nuclear Throne is one of the best roguelike games right now. If you like the genre, and don't mind dying a lot while slowly getting better, then this is your game. And, by the way, yes, aliens built the pyramids. You said it. Not me.

After Season 1 left my heart shattered, I got right on to Season 2. While Season 1 was an amazing joyride of action and drama, Season 2 is the same joyride, but on steroids. Each episode gives you hope, tears it back down, and then makes you forget "hope" ever had a meaning.
Review with spoilers:
Episode 1 ended a little sloppier then the other episodes, but the action made up for it...in my game, you fight bandits, walkers, a dog, and you even have to do a little 007 around a house.
Where Episode 1 fell short, Episode 2 was there to clean up. You get to know more about the group that saved you, including their flaws, their strengths, and their worries. And despite their being lots of action, the most exciting part was reuniting with Kenny, who was one of the many characters whose death was unknown. Key things that made this episode special were the forshadow, the VERY important desiscions, and of course, the internal conflict with each of the characters.
In episode 3, you once again find your charcater jailed up, but since you play as Clementine, you get to do all the risky infiltration to take down Carver's house of nutjob. IF you bought the "400 Days" episode, you will be in awe as you realize where the survivors of that episode end up. Episode 3 may not feel like as much of a roller coaster as the other episodes, but I assure you, the desperation of revenge really makes the episode unqiue. And by far one of the funniest moments was me screaming "CUT THAT ♥♥♥♥♥'S ARM OFF," as I attempt to save Kenny's girlfriend, only to have her die immedietly.
Episode 4 is a mostly feel good episode after the rescue. Jokes are made, "good times" are had between survivors, and Alvin Jr is born... All this feel good only to have to make one of the hardest desiscions of the game.
And last, but certainly not least, Episode 5, the episode that always ♥♥♥♥s you up. It starts off with an intense gunfight, but the episode progresses to where the main threat for the survivors is the mental state of Kenny. If you are evn 50% attached to any character after the lake incident, you're gonna get ♥♥♥♥ed, because I guarentee you'll hate everyone by the end of the episode (except maybe Kenny). The only thing I can complain about is there not being an option to shoot Jane once Kenny dies and the baby is found.
Season 1 ♥♥♥♥s you up by Lee dying, and you wondering what will happen to Clementine.
Season 2 ♥♥♥♥ you up by everyone dying except Clementine, and you still wondering what will happen to Clementine.
Although, there wasn't a season summary like in Season 1 so I'm waiting for that Episode 6 TellTale.

Adventures of Shuggy had potential. There's a nice soundtrack, colorful animation, and cute characters. Unfortunately, it seems the developers put too much effort into the visual look and not enough into the actual gameplay. What good there is here is unfortunately ruined by annoying enemies and too much flash over substance.
Shuggy's controls are way too floaty and it never feels like he's going to actually respond to your commands, even though he does. Despite having a fairly standard jump height, The vast majority of jumps will have you diving into a platform, getting two pixels of your foot caught against it and losing all forward momentum, then BARELY managing to float up with the rest of your vertical momentum.
Lots of minor optimization issues exist here. Every time the level starts, there's a burst of particle effects as all of the enemies and elements appear, but you maintain full control of Shuggy during this time, so it's entirely possible to run into an enemy or spike and die before the level has even fully appeared, which is especially noticeable in levels where death and restarting is not only common, but expected.
Enemies same tailor made to♥♥♥♥♥♥the player off. There is no way to kill them; they must be avoided, and the developers took careful action to make sure to put them in the most obnoxious place possible. Most of them move in predetermined patterns, so avoiding them is simply a matter of pattern recognition, but the mosquito enemies called Mozzies are the absolute worst. Their movement claims to be random, if the meaning of the word random has been changed to "in the worst possible spot and right up your♥♥♥♥♥every second they are on screen" and I wasn't informed. Also, they make a buzzing noise right in your speakers every time they get nearby. Lovely touch, developers. Isn't that what everyone loves? The sound of mosquitoes buzzing around your head when you're trying to play a game?
That's not to say Shuggy is completely without its merits. The real key to this game is the wide variety of powers and gameplay features that change up in every level. Each section of the game  has a different theme and seems to focus on one or two mechanics for most of its stages, but the problem is that there is no rhyme or reason for where or when these powers exist. The stages aren't laid out in any particular order or categorized beyond their visual style, so in some levels you will have an infinite jump, then in the immediate next level you will have no control at all, only being able to rotate gravity. The only indicator of this is a rather obtrusive text box that appears on screen and seems to be more interested in wobbling awkwardly than responding to your spamming of the A button going "Yes, I know, go away!"
Unfortunately, while Shuggy has a wide variety of gameplay mechanics, it never feels like any of these are used to their full potential. In a better designed game, every mechanic and power would be given the spotlight and levels would be designed to showcase all aspects of these powers. Instead, each level seems to be randomly placed, with a random arbitrary action assigned to the Right Trigger, and the developers just decided to roll with it.
But the REAL nail in the coffin is this: Whenever you close the game, you get an ad. Yes, an ad for another indie game. I don't know if it's by the same developers, but I don't care. This is absolutely inexcusable! This is what pushed the game firmly into the "Do not buy!" category. I already bought the game, and you're going to use it as a platform to sell me more of your crap? Maybe if you focused on making a great platformer, your studio would have a more positive association and fans will actually want to seek out your other work. Shoving it down our throats is just plain offensive.
Without the more annoying aspects, Adventures of Shuggy would be slightly above average, but when you add in flashy effects that distract from the gameplay, annoying enemies, and obnoxious, poorly optimized menus, it falls into the mediocre-to-bad category. And the ad at the end just clinches it. Avoid Shuggy if you like good games, but REALLY avoid it if you hate pop-up ads.

Nuclear Throne is one of those games which have great core gameplay, but lack content and maybe a bit polish too. Because of that the game didn't provide a satisfying experience to me although the gunplay is really satisfying. What I basicly expect from every rogue-lite game these days is the following:
The only unlocks in Nuclear Throne are new characters, but those I would normally count as a bonus, since they don't affect your next playthrough at all, they just offer a new playstyle, but if you don't like most of the characters then these unlocks are worthless to you. And that was the case a bit for me in Nuclear Throne. Some of the characters are useless if you ask me, but the most fun to play character was definitly Steroids, and I just play as him. He has the highest DPS and is just the most crazy character which makes him by far the most fun to play for me. But at least the character design is really creative and cool. You can also unlock crowns but they are useless and don't have a big impact on the game, and you can unlock golden weapons which replace your starting weapon, which isn't a big deal, because you get new and good weapons really fast anyway.
There are only a handful of upgrades (mutations are they called) in this game and a third of those are completely useless. Because of that your character build will be same more of less for every run. Also there is a mutation which heals you when you make kills, this is BY FAR the best mutation in the game and has a too big impact on the game. This wouldn't be a problem if the HP drops weren't so random. In some runs the game is generous and gives you lots of HP drops, in other runs you will rarely see one. What is the point in this extreme randomness?
What I mean by this is how similar the runs feel because of how the levels are generated. The enemies you encounter for every region will be the same, the types of weapons you will find will be same, just the paths you have to go will be a bit different but the difference won't have any impact on how you will play the levels, they are just different so the game isn't completely the same every time. But this is not enough. In very few instances sometimes a rare enemy appeared in a level. This game needs more of that, don't have a set ensemble of enemy types per region and use them all, but have a big pool of enemies per region and only use a few of that pool, so you will encounter different enemies every run. The weapon drops could also use more variety. Maybe give weapons status effects like burn of freeze damage (that exists in the game but just a bit).
What I mean by this is how Binding of Isaac does things. For your first run there are only like 6 regions, when you beat the final boss you permanently unlock a new region after the final one for your next run which is more difficult. Then you unlock another region maybe, but then after beating the main boss 10 times the whole game gets more difficult, but that also makes sense because by this point you have unlocked tons of items and upgrades. Nuclear Throne has the "looping" mechanic and hard mode, but that's it.
Another thing which is extremely infuriating in this game is how sometimes you can be nothing but unlucky and just die, especially in 5-3 where you sometimes spawn in the middle of million enemies while a boss appears which shoots 100 projectiles, flys all over the places while making explosions when landing, spawning more enemies AND when you beat him he will randomly fly in a direction and explode. You beat the boss but because RNG decided to make him fly in your direction and explode you loose anyway. There are lots of really cheap deaths like that in the game. Even more infuriating is when a portal spawns near a car and make the car explode which can kill you even if you have lots of HP. And the thing is I don't understand why this is, because apart from these cheap things the enemy design is GREAT with a lot of variety and depth.
One last thing. The game's core gameplay is already really good and has depth, but it could have even more depth by allowing the player to carry more than 2 weapons. I think it would be great if you just could carry a weapon of each weapon type at the same time. This is would give the game more depth because then you would have to consider more criteria when making more decisions. Obviously enemy design and balance and other things have to be adjusted as well for this to work. Just think Doom and Serious Sam.
The game still gets a REALLY good score from me, because the core gameplay is just really good, great character design, great enemy design, great weapon design, great sound design and great soundtrack. All the ingredients for a 10/10 game are there, but there is just not enough AT ALL around that. The game "Downwell" has the same problem, but that game costs 3€.
Oh, also: 30 fps lock is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid especially for this type of game.

Invisible Inc. was already solid in Early Access, and after catching up on the full release with the Contigency Plan DLC...I love it even more.  One of the few experiences where procedural levels are fundamentally essential to the core experience.  Instead of stealth in real-time where being caught just means restart and memorize the space, you're forced to explore.  Peaking and hacking your way into these randomized spaces, gathering intel and using what's in your toolkit to deal with slowly mounting threats.  Each decision becomes more important, tension rises, the risk for reward sits in the back of your mind, and the surprises will make you cheer or despair.
Turn-based games live and die based on whether they provide interesting choices, and Invisible Inc. has them in spades.  So many stealth games now feel like I'm an action hero with a silencer, but this makes me feel like a secret agent in more ways than one.

A delight of turn-based strategy game. I have completed one campaign (hours not recorded by Steam, I was always off-line) and am now going for the second.
Many many times I have consumed myself over what shall be my next move, my choice of target, or upgrade or equipment to buy. Resources are scarce, you race against time, and every decision is tough.
The stylized graphics are pretty but run on modest hardware, and the music compliments the mood of the action beautifully. If you are cautious, minimize risks, your agents will have better odds at first... but you won't collect enough resources, and the enemy keeps upgrading, and becoming more dangerous. To stand a chance to win the campaign, you need to be bold; it is fear, excitement and thrill all the time, building up to that nearly desperate last mission. And you can make the campaign as hard as you like. Random generated levels and different outcomes give re-play value. Worth snatching with its DLC right away.

The thing about rougelikes is that they make you feel like a complete moron. You find yourself tutting at yourself, ashamed of your own ineptitude. Nuclear Throne is no different. In fact it's probably harsher than average. And that's a very good thing.
Maybe I'm just a noob. I think I am. I get massacred every time: on numerous ocassions an irradiated rat has knawed me to death. Cars have exploded from stray enemy rounds and sent me spiralling across the level. A crocodile with a shotgun once made me wish my father had never had that dirty glint in his eye looking at my mother. I mean, they're divorced now, and that whole experience was probably less rage inducing than Nuclear Throne.
I may be a sadomasochist for this type of thing, but I keep going back. Each run, each easily avoided slaying, simply drives me on to discover more of the complex progression system. The depth of game's secrets, weapon management and characters are all of incredibly high standard. All lures in their own right.
But I think the main reasons I love this game are its weird sense of humour and beautfiul graphics. Any game that has a mutated Fish rolling around fighting robot assassins, giant maggots and really angry turtles, all rendered in an eye-wateringly lovely arcade art style, has my support.
Buy it. Die. Die again. Stop playing for two days. Be drawn back like a fly to a steaming turd. Die some more. Relish every second.

Nutshell: 10/10 - Great game, just keep in mind this is a REALLY, REALLY old game, and there are many things we take for granted in games, which this game doesn't have because it would be too intensive for computers back then to have these ammenities (HD resolution support, not even SD resolution support, incapable of going beyond 25-ish fps, lack of support for screen recording software like Nvidia Shadowplay in fullscreen mode, etc)
Setup: 10/10 - Really simple, Windows 10 appears to natively support this game with no mods. HOWEVER, do NOT try to force this game into 1080p or really any resolution other than what it gives you, this game, again, is really old, and does not support HD or even SD resolution.
Will it Run? 12/10 - Yeah, it'll run perfectly, for those wondering, this game ALWAYS runs at about 17-25fps, even on my high-end rig, and the same is true on my laptop, why is it such a low framerate? Cause this is an old game, again, don't try to force this thing to run higher than the framerate it gives you, the game was meant to be played at low framerates.
Graphics (relative to games of it's era): 10/10 - This game was INCREDIBLE back in it's day, it can wipe the floor graphically with Wolfenstein 3D and almost beats Ultimate Doom graphically as well.
Graphics (Compared to modern games): 0/10 - Well, honestly I don't even want to bother comparing this game to modern games, again, this game is incredibly old, but, some graphics-hogs want to know, so I put it here.
Gameplay: 10/10 - Love it! Really simple, only complaint is even on hard difficulty the bots are dumb, and, when you have a mouse, that you can't physically look up or down, both of which actually have perfect explanations, first, this was from an era where CPU's ran at 10-30Mhz with only one core, and also, not everyone had a mouse plugged into their computer back then (you can use the arrow keys to look around, and wasd to move).
Overall, this game is awesome, just keep in mind that it's an old game, and some things we take for granted nowadays don't even exist in this game.

+++ A more than 20-year old, now cult-classic FPS game set in the Star Wars universe - the first instance we controlled Kyle Katarn, a gun-for-hire mercenary working for the Alliance whose initial task is to steal plans for the Death Star (Rogue One, eh?) then to make sure the Empire cannot go forward with its super-deadly-storm-trooper-exoskeleton project throughout 14 missions.
+++ Varied environments & familiar characters: we go to mines, a robotics facility and even "visit" Jabba on his ship. Beside Jabba it's nice to see Vader in the story.
+++ Graphics & cutscenes: although it seems Dark Forces uses the Doom 2 engine it was actually LucasArts's own engine in use here. We can look up and down but this is unnecessary due to the appropriate auto-aim function. Crouching and jumping are also possible. The game has around 10 minutes of cutscenes incorporated - these are pixelated videos, of course, but at the time of release this was a big deal.
--- Controls & DosBox: DosBox is used here to make sure the game can run on modern machines. Unfortunately, it has its limitations (no steam overlay) and the game's menu already misses a lot of features (checking keymapping is not possible; controls have to be guessed along the way)
--- Dark XL: graphics are nice considering its time but today it leaves something to be desired. With the XL component downloaded from the internet it is possible to apply greater resolutions and to check the keymapping. I put this under the negative items considering you have to apply it if you want a better experience but, of course, the XL extension being available is actually a good thing.
A recommended classic from the '90s if your rig cannot run the new Battlefront title.

Star Wars: Dark Forces is a classic FPS game made way back in 1995 in the style of DOOM and Wolfenstein set in the Star Wars universe. A great game back in the day, but is it still fun to play even after all this time? This is what I think of Star Wars: Dark Forces.
I have a confession to make. I have only finished this once, and that was the time I played it through just now to write a review on it. I tried it some years back but bounced off it hard and never bothered to play it again. This time was different. I was in the mood for clicking on things until they died and by chance I decided to pick Dark Forces up again. In this series, I've played Jedi Outcast and beyond and thought it only right I at least play the early entries. And I'm glad I did.
Graphically, it looks like a game from 1995. It's charming in its own way, running as it does on Dos Box. It might not look pretty, but it packs a punch in its gameplay. It's still fun to play today, with some tight level design and interesting locations. Variety in the levels is great and as a long time Star Wars fan it's always a joy to see more of the universe. A short trip to Nar Shaddaa was especially awesome, a favourite world of mine. There is also a great selection of weapons to choose from and all are pretty satisfying to use. I thought it was brilliant.
The story follows Expanded Universe legend Kyle Katarn as he is hired by the Rebellion to investigate the Dark Trooper Project, and shut it down. It's a fairly basic FPS story as you follow leads until you find where the Troopers are coming from. With help from partner Jan Ors, and some cameos via cutscenes including Darth Vader, Boba Fett and Mon Mothma, you travel the galaxy gunning down Stormtroopers with an array of weaponry. If that sounds like a good time, it generally is. One ludicrous part of the story though involved being tossed into a pit with a kell dragon. Tense stuff! Until you realize you have to punch the thing to death and I nearly died from laughing. I know Katarn is a badass but come on.
As an older game though, there are some issues. Lack of any kind of tutorial is a heinous crime in level design. Hitting random keys in the hopes they do something isn't a good idea.  A quick mention of pieces of gear like the headlamp and the nightvisison goggles would have helped me early on, as I found them by accident. FYI, keys F1 to F8 are useful indeed, especially F1, which lets you see what you have in your inventory and what the mission objectives are. You'll need that in a few of the levels. You also have to use separate keys to look up and down, which is strange to say the least. It's quite fiddly, but it isn't as game breaking as it sounds. Merely an inconvenience. Some of the levels are also a little tricky to navigate with little hand holding. Some will love it, other won't. It's old school game design, it is what it is.
Overall, I think Dark Forces is a great game to play. Having not liked it as much playing it before, I didn't think I'd enjoy it this time either but I was pleasantly surprised. Despite showing age in graphics and occasionally level design, it's a strong start to Katarn's series of games. This one is a classic, and you should definitely consider giving it a try.

Alan Wake is an amazing game, very well written and with a great ambience and characters, however that doesn't mean it's perfect.
First of gameplay, the basic combat mechanic for fighting is very interesting at first, basically you need to use a flashlight to drain the enemy's "shields" until you are able to take him down with a gun, but over the course of the game it grows a bit stale and repetitive, with little to no change at all. Trying the different weapons and traps whoever is pretty fun, you'll spend a lot of time trying to find creative ways to take down your enemies, although sometimes it is better to run. Ammo is scarce, which is nice for a thriller game and the way the story develops in game is pretty interesting (like finding the pages).
Now for story, this is where the game truly shines. It's incredible, worthy of a book even. Wake's story place nicely as a psychological action thriller that is well paced and keeps you engaged, the game also features some pretty interesting plot twists, making even the chapters in between battles pretty thrilling. The dialogue and characters are very well written, I can even recall several quotes now.
If you are a fan of Stephen King esque novels than this is the game for you, sometimes it may grow repetitive but that can be easily forgiving by the engaging story and amazing atmosphere.
Alan Wake is a game that proves to be more than what it seems, truly defining that "It is not a lake, it's an ocean".

It's worth the time you'll put into it, but get ready for some frustrating, cheap combat, and some long, meaningless sequences whose only point seems to be to extend gameplay time. On the other hand, this game is pretty damn gorgeous, and the production is really impressive. The attention to detail helps immerse you in the world, despite the poor-man's-Dean Koontz story. The combat is occasionally fun, and sometimes there's a new mechanic to spice things up, but mostly there are far too many encounters with the same enemies, requiring the same strategy, in basically the same setting.
I realize I'm not painting a pretty picture, but I do need to emphasize that the story, while not great, is ocasionally engaging, and does sometimes delve into the psyche or certain characters to refreshing extents. There's even the occasional shock scare that got me going.
It's not Silent Hill, even though it clearly wishes it was. It's more like a third person Condemned: Criminal Origins, which isn't necesarily a bad thing. And if you enjoy games along those lines, then Alan Wake should definitely be worth the mediocre portions that you'll need to slog through to get to the more exciting portions.

I can't believe I haven't written a recommendation for this game on Steam yet.  Isaac is brilliant.  I have put more hours into this game than any 'AAA' title this year.  At its core, Isaac is a pretty basic game.  Dungeons are randomly generated with a different tileset every two floors.  You die, you start over.  Each level, there is a treasure room with one of about a hundred powerups.  These are cumulative, and not only alter Isaac's abilities, but change how he looks visually.  Repeated playhthroughs are awarded with over ten different endings, unlocking new floors and, most importantly, allowing new items to be found randomly in the treasure rooms.  Gameplay itself is a bit like the original Zelda - you move around an isometric map, taking out enemies in order to progress to the next room.  Thematically, the game is defiantly twisted and irreverant, carried along by an excellent score.  For just a few bucks, Isaac offers endless challenge, replayability and depth.  Buy it.

Despite the controversy surrounding this game, especially the art style, I really enjoy it. Civ VI vanilla is much more fleshed out than Civ V vanilla and Gods and Kings ever were. Here's my review:
Pros
- More fleshed out than Civ V vanilla was at launch
- Workers actually have to be produced on a regular basis, no longer are there 5000 year old workers roaming the planet
- The road building system is fun and is more historically accurate than having state workers build roads (except Rome)
- Gaining influence over city-states is no longer a matter of being wealthy, its a serious challenge compared to Civ V
- Districts and wonders being present on the map make territory and strategic planning of city development vital to success
- The eureka/inspiration system is fun and makes research more interactive
- Introduction of the civic tree makes culture just as vital as science, making player strategy more well rounded than it was in Civ V with social policies
- The religious victory is a new option for peaceful victory and allows you to finally fight off the religious units of other civs w/o declaring war, which was a pain in the butt in Civ V
Cons
- Not enough wonders from non-European countries especially from Asia and Africa.
- Art style isn't for everyone
- Diplomacy game is lacking because there is no world congress
- Combat AI is still poor, and can easily be defeated, even with inferior numbers
- Qin Shi Huang's character model is seriously weird
- Agenda system attempts to rationalize AI aggression, but feels like more of an afterthought as the AI is aggressive regardless
- Diplomacy AI is still bad, AI refuses to make peace unless you hand over all of your cities, even when they are down to a 3 population tundra city themselves.
- Religious warfare is never-ending and the AI is obsessed with spreading its religion so it never relents on sending wave upon wave of religious units to you. The introduction of a non-interference treaty for religions, or something along the lines of that, would go a long way to preventing endless religious warfare
Overall:
Despite its many, many flaws, Civ VI is still a lot of fun to play, and builds upon the foundations that were laid by Civ V. City development and war mechanics bring the landscape to life and force the player to build and fight more strategically. Civ VI is definitely worth the money, and while it certainly has its issues, it is a worthy successor to the Civilization series.

30 FPS has been patched swiftly.
The game can now be run at a 60FPS cap, or at an unlimited framerate, which has finally rendered the game playable for me.
I played it for a solid amount of time, and I must say it is quite engaging
despite it being a seemingly repetitive open-world sandbox.
The story is excellent. Voice acting is top-notch and so are the facial animations, which are quite realistic and do a great job at expressing the emotions of the diverse and intriguing cast of characters.
The soundtrack also features many classics and is entertaining enough to compensate for the relatively lacklustre driving.
However, assets are reused copiously throughout the game. Most missions are uninspired and are uniform even throughout all districts. The only ones that really stand out are the ones in which you confront district bosses, which, in the later missions, become lieutenants and capos.
I really hope there are more twists in the story and that it ends in a satisfying way, as it kind of gets a bit monotone throughout the midsection of the game. I'll update my review when I finish the game and expand in that regard.
This game has a few redeeming qualities that save it from plummeting into the abyss with the rest of the trash, which is why this review is a positive one.
Overall, I'd give it a solid 8/10 for now.
I hope all the other customers who wrote negative reviews due to the FPS cap alter said reviews, as this game definitely deserves a moderately positive rating.

A delight of turn-based strategy game. I have completed one campaign (hours not recorded by Steam, I was always off-line) and am now going for the second.
Many many times I have consumed myself over what shall be my next move, my choice of target, or upgrade or equipment to buy. Resources are scarce, you race against time, and every decision is tough.
The stylized graphics are pretty but run on modest hardware, and the music compliments the mood of the action beautifully. If you are cautious, minimize risks, your agents will have better odds at first... but you won't collect enough resources, and the enemy keeps upgrading, and becoming more dangerous. To stand a chance to win the campaign, you need to be bold; it is fear, excitement and thrill all the time, building up to that nearly desperate last mission. And you can make the campaign as hard as you like. Random generated levels and different outcomes give re-play value. Worth snatching with its DLC right away.

Alpha Protocol was an amazing surprise. You’d expect a game that got savaged by most reviewers to be bad, or at least only average. But Alpha Protocol is an amazing RPG, and a passable third-person shooter.
The Good:
This is one of the few RPGs that offers actual choices, instead of illusionary choices that have no effect on the rest of the game. Every choice you make could come back to haunt you or benefit you. And most of those choices are shades of grey. The game won’t directly tell you whether your choice was good or bad, you’re left to judge that for yourself.
On that note, the sheer amount of characters that can be killed in the course of the game is staggering. If there’s a major character, odds are that there’s some event that could result in their deaths.  This is a game where you can’t save everyone. You can’t pull a Mass Effect 2 and have everyone walk away from the suicide mission. You have to make hard choices, and those choices will get people killed.
What makes that more interesting is that the characters you have to make decisions on are, with few exceptions, very well-developed characters. Everyone has their own personalities and agendas, and it’s up to you to decide how you interact with them.  You can ally with almost anyone – or stand against them. The main limits are your relationships with the characters, the intel you have on them, and your own creativity. But there is literally nothing stopping you from doing things that other games wouldn’t even think about letting you try.
The Bad:
In typical Obsidian fashion, the game suffers from bugs. Reloading checkpoints, in particular, can cause some strange behavior with enemy spawns. They may behave normally, reposition, or even vanish entirely. Very, very rarely, a reload of a checkpoint can cause a black screen that forces you to quit.
While most of the minigames are well-designed and even enjoyable, the hacking minigame appears to have been designed by a sadist. Hacking the wall panel in the tutorial may be the most difficult part of the game for some people. However, it’s not that difficult once you get used to the initially confusing controls. The game also allows you to ignore hacking entirely with a single-point investment in the Sabotage skill and a supply of EMP bombs.
The shooting, while more than passable for a third-person shooter, could have benefited from a bit more work. Some weapons (such as the pistol and SMG) are much better choices, while others (the shotgun and the assault rifle) are not. That’s not to say you can’t succeed with any weapon – you can – but some are clearly better choices. Additionally, the controls for mounted weapons like the sniper rifle and the heavy machine gun have an absurdly high degree of sensitivity.
However, all of these are minor issues that shouldn't stop you from buying a criminally underrated RPG.

As of late, with all these new games coming out that require a high powered computer to play with high quality graphics and maxed out settings, I've been circling back around to the classic games. I grew up playing this game and absolutely love it just as much as I used to when I was little.
The game is pretty straightforward and in my opinion fits into the Star Wars Universe brilliantly with its well formed story. The first level has a very cool connection to Episode IV: A New Hope and it's also where you're introduced to Kyle Katarn, a "mercenary for hire" who is a total boss at wiping out Imperial bases. Each of the levels are great fun and provide a very good challenge for the player that can be changed depending on the difficulty level that you choose, whether it be Easy, Medium, or Hard. My favorite level happens to be level 10, which features a cool cameo of a certain character that stars in the original trilogy. You start off the level with nothing but your fists to defeat enemies but in due time you get back the things you've taken for granted in all the previous levels to escape!
I do have a paperback guidebook for the game that I love to look at every now and then to read character bios and all the descriptions of the enemies and weapons. I must've utilized it quite a bit when I was little because I'm certain that's the only way I got through certain levels that I still have trouble with even today. The particular levels (The Detention Center and Imperial City) are presented to be quite a challenge but it's still all good fun!
Whether you're new to the universe of Star Wars games or have played many in the past but just found this one, give it a chance! I'll admit it does have very dated graphics but everything else the game offers tips the scales in its favor. The protagonist and deuteragonist, the incredible design of the levels, the new deadly enemies that are menacing in the climactic final battle and all battles leading up to it, the vast array of weapons that allow you to wipe down enemies with each blaster shot/explosion, and the simple fact that it's set in the world of Star Wars make this game not only memorable but absolutely amazing!

While I have been a
fan for over fifteen years, I have only picked this series up recently. As a kid I played
, so now I wanted to play the entire story of Kyle Katarn, since I picked up a
bundle in the Steam sales.
Graphically, the game is what you would expect from 1995: DOOM-style 2D which is stylized to amazingly look like 3D. I actually think this style of early 3D has aged much better than the early days of polygonal sprites, but hey, it's all opinion. There is a certain charm to this style, and the enemy animations are not bad. The MIDI sound files contribute to a nice and coherent, stay-in-with-hot-coco-while-it's-snowing-outside, feel, which is the feeling many
old games give me.
The story is okay, better than fan fiction but definitely worse than most of the expanded universe, but then again this was only the first game in the series. It's a very basic FPS story, especially for its time: Badass guy goes on mission, uncovers big and sinister plot, spends rest of game trying to uncover and sabotage said plot. A great variety of worlds and weapons make sure the game feels fresh in each new level. Some levels are quite short and straightforward, while others are large and elaborate, and feature difficult puzzles that will have most players scrawling to the webz for a strategy guide or video walkthrough. The game could have done a bit more hand-holding at times, while other puzzles are almost insultingly easy. I am not one for puzzles, though, so that may be my personal issue with the game.
The game holds its own in controls even today. One thing players nowadays will really have to get used to is the lack of vertical aiming with the mouse; looking up and down has to be done by buttons. That said, the game plays a lot like doom, so most enemies will be at your level and there is rarely ever any true need to look up or down. The guns all feel very different and have varying efficiency. Sadly, this also means you will mainly use two or three good weapons throughout the game, largely ignoring the rest.
In all, this is still a very enjoyable game. Fans of old school games, fans of FPS games, fans of action-adventure games, and of course
fans will really be able to enjoy this game. For the rest of you: approach with caution, but you might just find it to be a lot of fun!

Civilization 6 is a game in which you control a country and try to lead it to victory against its opponents - whether they be AI-controlled or real players. Because of its nature as a turn-based strategy game, it is appropriate for anyone, even those who don't want to be pressured into bad decisions by the lack of time, which may be the case in some RTS titles. So far it sounds pretty good, doesn't it? Well, there are a few other good things about this piece of software but sadly the negatives outweigh the positives by a, in my opinion, way too big amount.
Let's start with the price: Yeah, I understand, people need to be paid, the developers want to earn enough to make a decent living out of it and so on. Still, for 60€ I expect nothing less than a complete game. Not some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t where I am given a buggy and in some parts not even feeling like it's finished version of a game that I have the opportunity to upgrade into a somewhat enjoyable strategy game through the purchase of various DLCs. At the moment there are 5 Civilization packs and 1 Scenario pack released, which total in 38€. Out of those you get 7 civilizations and a few scenarios. The thing here is that the scenarios are only of minor interest to the players and also not that hard to create as far as I'm concerned. Also, if you have the wish for more factions in your game you can also go to the workshop, which makes those DLCs extremely overpriced. Additionally, there is the announced 'Rise and Fall' expansion pack that is going to cost 30€. It brings, of course, new civilizations, some features with great inspiration from former titles and some new stuff which actually looks interesting. You know, not everything about this game is bad. Except the fact, maybe, that 30€ is the money I pay for a game like PUBG and not for the expansion pack of some 60€ strategy game. So, in total for Civilization 6 + the minor DLCs + the expansion pack you pay a whopping 128€, in which you have to add that this isn't the final price as there are still many great additions coming, I reckon.
If the price was the only bad thing but otherwise you'd get a completely perfect tool for recreation I could perhaps live with that. IF. It's been 1 year and 2 months but still there are bugs and the AI that is an insult to anyone even thinking about playing the singleplayer. Bugs can and should be fixed, especially since there hasn't been a real change in content except for the additional civilizations since the game's release. Interestingly, there are still cases of defense values being shown wrongly, enemy planes remaining in the airport whose city I just conquered and made peace with its former owner, players having to reload the game every single round in multiplayer or outright not being able to connect to the lobby and so on. Now let's get to the AI. Anyone having been involved in the development of an AI or simply possessing a brain and some imagination will know that creating an AI can be incredibly hard. Still, 2K Games gets their money for that and thus making the computer-controlled civilizations more than just a waste of space shouldn't be impossible. At the moment, the only variations between the different difficulties seems to be the amount of cheating the AI is doing. On the hardest difficulty, named Deity, you start with 1 settler enabling you to create a city and 1 warrior to defend it. The AI starts with 3 settlers and 4 or 5 warriors. This does, indeed, make the game more challenging, but not because of the superior strategy of your opponent. Instead you simply are in danger of drowning in a flood of enemy troops that also possess a bonus when fighting you. That's at least the case for the beginning. After you have recruited enough troops to defend yourself the game becomes boring. The AI will show a notionally higher aggressiveness compared to lower difficulties. This aggressiveness basically only consists of your opponents declaring war on you more often and then sending a few, perhaps technologically superior, troops to one of your cities, only to be  destroyed by you. After that the AI begs for peace and is often enough willing to give you incredible amounts of gold, resources and sometimes cities, even though they are, in theory, a lot stronger than you. This repeats itself a few times until you are either strong enough to stop the cheating AI from achieving an early non-domination victory by snowballing them to pieces or the AI manages to do what you succeeded in stopping them from in the first scenario. I used the term 'non-domination victory' because as dumb as your enemies are they sure as hell ain't gonna win against you in open warfare, even if they have all the advantages that you can possibly have over another player.
That leaves the multiplayer which can be fun as long as you manage to fill every slot with a real player, since a computer-controlled one would simply be prey for the first one to find it.
There is other stuff to write about as well, but I don't think at this point it is necessary anymore to elaborate on my reasoning for giving this game a thumbs down.
TL;DR: The game is too buggy and has a frustrating AI, which makes the singleplayer aspect of it almost unenjoyable. The multiplayer can be fun, given that you have enough human players to fill it. The price for the game with all its DLCs and expansions is outrageous but this kind of DLC policy seems to be quite common nowadays. My conclusion: Don't buy it, at least not yet and not if you mind to pay extra for all the downloadable content.

A very interesting game that brings a lot to the table. I got this when it was 90% off (crazy deal), but I honestly would have payed more for what I got.
The combat is a refreshing take on the third person shooter. It requires tactical management and forethought not found in a typical shooter: enemies are invincible until you remove their shield with a light source. The enemies are limited, so it might get somewhat stale toward the end, but still worth the experience.
Graphics are pleasing and creative. They definitely won't distract from the play experience.
The story was very intriguing.  Without giving too much away, it was an interesting mind game that plays with the idea of the player character being led what appears to be himself to reach the goal. The story continues to build upon itself, one new crazy idea after another. A+ grade horror fiction here.
To narrow what you may be looking for, this is a horror third person shooter, but don't expect disturbing images or twitch shooting. This game is meant for the tactical of us that want an interesting new perspective on the genre.
Overall, I'd offer an 8 1/2, with the only detracting point of the game being that the combat becomes repetetive toward the end of the game, as no new challenges are offered. Still, a powerful experience.
As with any steam game, I recommend waiting for a sale, especially because there have been multiple 90% off sales of this game in particular in the past. More money saved is more games purchased!
TL;DR: If you are looking for a combination of the following:
-A tactical third person shooter
-A great horror story
Then I highly suggest you get this game.

Overall, Shadow of War is a good game. It's more Orc slaughter in a nice, fun way. The Fortress system is a good addition to the game, gives you a feeling of real epicness in the fighting.
However, upon reaching Act III, you're put before a wall. To even get the ending and End Credits, you're put on a road to grind Legendary quality Orc for your army. You need quite a number of them and after 30 hours of playing I've got... 2.
The game offers microtransactions in the way of "Loot Boxes" which offer Legendary Quality Orcs behind real-money wall, as opposed to being able to buy them with ingame currency.
And while the game is good, I can't help but NOT recommend it until such thing is patched or modded out, or made easier with other means.
9/10 as a core game until you reach last Act. 1/10 because of the loot boxes and a grind that's been put in the game JUST to make you pay those extra 10-30 Eur.
EDIT: I've been told I've only reached Act 1 by achievements, let me add some explanation.
Indeed, the power of the all-mighty O2 ISP tends to do that. As in, with my net connection I'm surprised I even kept connection for those achievements xD
The issue isn't getting one legendary Orc.
You can get a legendary Orc by finding the same Orc over and over and letting him kill you. He will rise in rank, as they level, they lose and change abilities sometimes.
Sending Death Threats (the worm mechanic, not actual ones) also helps with that.
You can also "craft" the Orc during encounters. If you keep using Fire, he grows resistace to Fire. Same with Arrows, using Stealth Attacks, Finishers.
So, you can pump quite a bit of time into "Crafting" one Orc. But you need more than one of Legendary, alive Orcs to even get end credits.
Also your hand crafted time-pumped Orc can not only die in the online part, but can be just captured or randomly killed by regular enemy Orc.
Both me and my partner have and play the game, except she took a week off to play the game, while I have to work.
It is just way too grindy. The game is good, but the addition of loot boxes kill it for last Act. Could as well go play GW2 and start crafting a Legendary weapon over one menstruation cycle. So until that changes...
Nope, can't recommend it.

When I was 15 years old I played the Thief: TDP demo for the first time on my family computer. It ran like a slideshow and since my PC didn't support fancy 8-bit colors it looked terrible. Despite all of this I sensed there was something deeply amazing there and when I got my first job I saved up enough money to buy a computer so that I could play the Thief games.
Now many years later I still have a deep affection for stealth games. The feeling of being both powerful and vulnerable. Using your wits to navigate a situation that could turn deadly at any moment to accomplish your goals. Unfortunately as I grew up and began to consume more stealth games I discovered that most didn't live up to this experience. Although I have played every Hitman and Splinter Cell game, I never really felt clever or vulnerable, just powerful. The worst of these games were corridors of stealth set pieces that I could just shoot my way through if I wanted to. It was easy and often optimal to solve every problem with bullets.
I was skeptical about Invisible Inc. when it first released and I dismissed it for a few months. I bought it on a whim one day though and I quickly fell in love with it as my 151 hours (as of this writing) will attest. It is the first game since Thief to elicit that same feeling I had as a kid and one of the only well-made stealth games that I can think of. I love its procedural generation and how you have to work hard to gather the information you need to be successful. I also love its weird mix of cyberpunk and 50’s noir art style. I love its characters, design, and setting. Every character is very powerful in their own way, but also very vulnerable. It’s the first time that I felt that I understood what it meant for a game to be “well designed.”
If any of this resonates with you, I sincerely recommend that you buy a copy if Invisible. As someone who typically never cares enough to write reviews for anything, I feel strongly enough to write too many words about this one.
30 fps aside, great game, no crashes so far. Calm the ♥♥♥♥ down everyone.

* Alpha Protocol is a unique 3rd-person-action/RPG hybrid. Truthfully, though, it caters more to the "twitch" side of stealth than the "methodical" side. Keep this in mind if you like your Stealth games slow or medium-paced.
* Alpha Protocol laid the groundwork for some of the games that you are playing right now. It is the reason current-gen iterations of Deus Ex, Borderlands, and Fallout exist in their current form. And, because of this groundwork, AP has similarities to all three of these series, but it is unfortunately a worse game.
* It is widely-reported that the game has a number of game-breaking bugs. This may have been true upon release, but is NOT true now. I did not encounter any game-breaking bugs.
* The method of gameplay caters to the players' choice: it can be played multiple ways: run-n-gun, stealth, etc. However, playing with stealth is quite difficult compared to games like Metal Gear, Splinter Cell, or even Oblivion. This difficulty leads to many more twitchy fire fights than you would typically desire in a stealth game. And it's not a "good" difficulty. It really feels cheap or unfair when the enemy detects me while I am in full camo in the dark, crouched and not moving.
* Most levels are essentially hallways, with only one or two alternative routes that can be used.
* Some animations are a bit stiff. For example, the open scene features your avatar's bicep and forearm occupying the same space at the same time. Enemies will also "slide" into cover at times, and the normal guard's walking pace is way too low for the length of his stride.
* Character animations are incomplete. Most games feature some sort of "turning" animation as your avatar changes direction. Turning is automatic in Alpha Protocol: your character is facing one direction and suddenly faces another direction.
* The computer hacking feature is definitely the dated relic of a game developed for a console. Rather than allowing a click and drag interface using the mouse, the player must move two "passwords" across the screen using the keyboard for one and the mouse with the other. Although I have done a poor job of describing it, believe me that the interface feels dirty and and the controls are alarmingly poorly-designed.
* UI Features, such as the item selection menu, are a little unintuitive. They are confusing but are not hard to get used to.
* Pausing while in the middle of a conversation is really inconsistent. Sometimes the game allows you to pause, other times it doesn't. This is especially frustrating because the game allows you to choose what to say, and if you step away from your computer to give the baby a bottle, you may come back to a conversation headed in the completely wrong direction, essentially ruining your game up to that last checkpoint.
* On one mission I was instructed several times to use dust storms to hide my approach. There were no dust storms. On another mission I was told the sound of trains would disguise the noise of my bullets. The trains: they did nothing.
* Bugs encountered: (1) after dying, I loaded my last checkpoint and the game crashed. (2) On one mission, I found an invsible wall in the middle of a hallway, got my foot stuck in a rock, and found a health dispenser floating in mid-air. (3) It is impossible to do a stealth takedown on an enemy near a door, you will simply knock the door down instead of killing the enemy.
* Alpha Protocol's method of encouraging the player to be stealthy works by making the combat mechanics horrible. One example of this is that in order to shoot accurately, you have to wait 4 or 5 seconds between each shot. Deliberately making your game worse to encourage a particular playstyle is a horrible idea, why did Obsidian think that would help their game?
* Playing the game 100%, or even "somewhat fully," requires lots of extra (boring) dialogue. Even worse, and the reason why I don't think this game will be remembered, is that the game "features" hours of reading extra dossiers to find clues.
* Alpha Protocol is neither solid nor decent, but a game that you may enjoy if you are a fan of Bioware or Bethesda games. The game is an interesting combination of stealth, gunplay, and mind-numbingly boring conversations and reading segments. I only recommend picking up this game if you are interested in game design so that you can see how pacing, genre-hybrids, and player agency became such important concepts in newer games.  Alpha Protocol experimented with these methods and was successful in some ways and a complete failure in others.

This puzzle platformer uses tons of different mechanics to make each of its levels unique and interesting. There is time travel, clones, rotating gravity and much more. The closest game would be Braid, but where Braid takes itself maybe too seriously, this game has a very cheerful, humorous approach. The graphics are cute, and the music is in "feel-good" style, reminding circus attractions and theme parks.
The only thing I really didn't like is the platformer-typical challenge to manual dexterity such games usually present atop their puzzles. Namely, even if you already guessed how a puzzle level needs to be solved, it still can take many frustrating attempts to execute the solution without a mistake to the very end, especially with this game's 1-hp instant death rule. Also the character here has this annoying "sliding animation" which makes him slide for a while after landing on a platform. This may make the simplest task of jumping across a series of small platforms surprisingly difficult to perform for a new player. You either slide over the platform after landing and end up on spikes below, or you try to slow down while in mid-air, press the button to move in the opposite direction, but hold it for just a fraction of a second too long, and end up falling straight down, not reaching the platform you wanted to land on. This inertia is actually not very typical for 2D platformer games and probably shouldn't be in this game at all.

Here we have a fun little-big sandbox of the physics variety.  The concept is simple, but the magnitude of options are incredibly detailed. Strapping adventurous little Kerbals into your haphazardly cobbled, and most certainly dangerous, rockets and aircraft you aim them towards the heavens and thus towards glory.  Why you ask?  For Science!  That delicious, delicious science.
From this title I learned some of the intricacies of orbital mechanics, the methods of calculating delta-v, and the anguish (or pride) of blasting little green people into the depths of interstellar space ... never to return.  When played in CAreer Mode I must say, "Buyer beware!"  This is a game not for the feint of heart nor those who are easily frustrated by extremely repetitious failure.  Laugh, learn and launch towards the howling abyss that is Space!
To quote aptly, "Fly Safe" ...

Before I type this, I *never* write game reviews, but this is a must. This game, how do I put it.... It's absolutely amazing. The concept is very simple. You play as an executive commanding a bunch of units to kill another executive (hence the name). You can control these units either through a typical RTS manner or through FPS and you can customize the loadouts of these units. It plays out like any other RTS (research, resource management and the works), but unlike many others you can manage the distribution of power into a few departments: automatic defenses, iron mining, research and I cant remember the rest off the top of my head. The first person aspect adds a lot to the game and is my preferred way to play. I mean, sure, you can send a few units into the enemy base and have them fight their way to the command center, but I'd much rather assume the position of a robot, get a gang to follow my by pressing F, clear the halls and personally assassinate the other executive. Anyway, the main reason I type this is because it opened my eyes to the fact that many indie developers who have great and innovative ideas are going unnoticed and the more popular game companies who keep re-using the same concepts and mechanics (I'm looking at you, Activision) are getting way more money than the people who actually deserve it. But anyways, this game is a 9.5/10 in my personal opinion and is frankly a lot more fun than the vast majority of non-indie games out there. I highly recommend this game.

You'd be forgiven for looking at this in the Steam Store and dismissing it as a cheap mobile port. Well, yes, it is both of those things, but it also happens to be excellent in every respect. The graphics are clear and atmospheric and, depending on your tastes, the music and fx are relaxing and unintrusive. The game's design is also very friendly. Checkpoints are frequent and you can restart a level easily. There's even a story if that's what floats your boat.
Where the game really shines though is in the puzzles. The mechanic of absorbing lights and transferring them to lamps and switches is simple but used to great effect. There's not one part of the game that feels lazy. Every puzzle on every level has clearly been tested and refined by hours of playtesting. The difficulty curve is perfect. This is not a platformer. There's no tricky timing stuff involved. It's all about finding elegant solutions, especially if you want to get 100% achievements.
It's a couple of quid for 25 - 30 hours of quality playtime. I loved it.
