I bought Flood of Light primarily for the art, sound, and premise from the game's summary. Further, even tags like "Adventure" and "RPG" are still sitting on the page, and those also gave me more of an idea to try it out after looking at the quick trailer and screenshots.
It turns out that the only good things in the game are the
and
. There is not really any adventure to the game, and there is
related to RPG's to be found within Flood of Light.
Literally, the game is a handful of linear rooms with puzzles where you drag light from lamps to fill up certain pedestals that cause the water level in the flooded city to lower down, thus allowing you to progress further. There is no exploration whatsoever. Everything is insanely linear and just boils down to each room's puzzle, with the puzzles very rarely depending upon what you did in the previous room.
In fact, most of the puzzles require "perfection." You will likely hit the "Replay" button often, because certain lamps are out of reach if you arrange the lights in the wrong order.
The game adds in some new mechanics in the latter half, but they're relatively short-lived, and for the most part the puzzles become boring and monotonous. I had no excitement or sense of accomplishment progressing through the game.
Depending on how well you are at figuring out the patterns, you can probably finish (maybe not at 100% completion) within 2 to 3 hours. Which might be fine for the game's price tag... but honestly, I didn't get any enjoyment from the game.
When it comes to the story of the game, there's some sense of dystopian future, experimentation, and some deity-like notions, particularly in the main character's ability to move around light. But it's all done pretty badly. You encounter robots that speak to you, but the majority of them repeat the same generic information. Besides that, some little story messages explain more about who you are, but never really get far enough into a sensible story. Nor does the game have any sense of completion or progress with the plotline other than learning bad details in the past.
(Side Note: The English translation is not well-done and learning from the story messages just sort of kills the moment when certain things don't make much sense to read.)
Even worse, there are two endings to the game and both of them just drop everything immediately. Note that the achievements publicly mention both endings, so I'm not spoiling that they exist. In any case, if you go out of your way to get the "true" ending, all it does is change the final cutscene to something that's just about as bad as the original ending, considering that both of them only last about 10 seconds. They give no more expansion upon the story. Then you are just handed a "Thanks for Playing" screen, rendering the already very small story even more useless.
Honestly, I feel like Flood of Light
have been an exploration game with more focus on the story instead of a small-scale puzzle game that left the story in the backseat. The art style and the music and sound are the only positives I give to the game. They are really nice and definitely give off the sense of loneliness in this drowning city. PWND is an amazing game.
The movement is fun, frantic, and fluid.
The combat is powerful and punchy
The satisfaction from kills and the strategy behind PWNs is nothing short of extremely gratifying.
The characters are all incredibly unique, but still able to synergize in diverse and fun ways.
The balance of the game is very good, with the best matches having you on the edge of your seat as you fight for the PWNstack.
To top it all off, the whole thing has an excellent dev team behind it that knows what it's doing and is in tune with their playerbase.
So, what's not to like? The lack of players.
As you can probably see from the other reviews, the amount of people playing this game so far is pretty low. Usually when a new patch drops you'll be able to get into games just fine for a few days, and the devs have done a good job of hosting events that draw in the crowd, but on an average day, you'll probably be waiting a while and you might not even find a game. The bots are very well done in this game actually, but they still lack the human element everybody wants in an online game. A tip to anyone who buys the game: Join the Discord server so that you can better judge when people are online and playing.
The promotion for the game has been a bit lackluster so far I'd say. The devs have given codes for the game to several YouTubers and Twitch streamers who have sizable audiences, but it hasn't been enough. In the future, perhaps leading up to the game's full release, I'd really like to see the developers get a nice big advertising budget so that they can run a lot more online ads, show up on more YouTube channels, and maybe sit on the front page of Steam for a while too.
Should you buy PWND? Absolutely. It's a fantastic game, and if nothing else, I would buy it just to keep it alive. The community is small, but there's a lot of great people in it already and it is in fact growing, no matter how slowly. As well, even if you play it casually only during the peak times that people are on, I think you can still have a lot of fun this game, but of course the final decision is up to you.
This game gets a 10/10 for me because as a game, I just love every single thing about it. I just hope more people will eventually see its greatness too.

Flood of Light is a charming and experly designed puzzle platformer that challenges you to light a series of lanterns in each level, to proceed to the next. The lanterns power monoliths which lower the water level in an abandonded flooded city, and your ultimate aim is to save the city from the flood.
You are able to absorb light from one lantern and transfer it to another, or if lanterns are close enough together, you can transfer light directly between them. Later levels introduce even more variables such as different coloured light, pressure plates that move lanterns, water that can extinguish light and lanterns you can place yourself, which prevents the game from ever getting stale and also keeps you having to find new ways to complete each level.
The puzzles vary from easy to extremely challenging. There is also the added award of an achievement for completing each level with an "S Rank" which means doing it below a certain number of moves, and also lighting some optional lanterns along the way, which really ups the difficulty, but also gives a great sense of satisfaction when you finally figure it out.
Going for the S-Rank really made me appreciate how intricately the levels were designed, so that every lit lantern, unlit lantern, switch, platform and monolith were laid out in such a pixel perfect way that there was only ever one solution. My hat goes off to the developer as it's rare to see a puzzle game with such tight design.
The story isn't one of the games strongest points, and takes a back seat to the puzzles. It is relayed to you by robots that you repair, and terminals you find throughout the game and is all text/picture based. Howver, story is not generally of great importance to this type of game, and I was personally happy just going from one puzzle to the next.
The game has a beautiful 2D art style, and the sound is also of a high standard. It has nice relaxing music which helps keep you calm during those moments where you just can't find the solution, and although the sound effects are quite minimal, the ambient sound such as rain/thunder really adds to the atmosphere.
If i had one criticism of Flood of Light, it would be that the controls can be a bit finicky at times, and you may occasionally find yourself having to replay a level because you accidentally absorbed a light you didn't want to, made the character walk when you didn't mean to, or placed a lantern in the wrong place.
However, this is a minor niggle and one that certainly didn't spoil the game for me, and to the developer's credit, they have included a mouse control scheme and a keyboard control scheme, and for me the keyboard control scheme did alieviate most of the issues i had controlling the character. There are however a few puzzles where using the mouse gives you more fine control over which lights you absorb so you may want to use both together for the best experience.
Overall, this is the best game i've played for quite some time. I enjoyed it from start to finish and was really pleased when I managed to get 100% of the achievements as it felt like a real accomplishment. It is also a massive bargain at £2.79 (I paid £1.39 in the Steam 2017 Winter sale) as it has provided me with over 20 hours of absorbing and challenging gameplay for that low price.

Wow!
I'm a huge fan of tactical turn-based games and have played almost all of them.  To date the high water mark for me has been Jagged Alliance 2 (+v1.13 mod) with the XCOM reboot and Frozen Synapse filling the other spots on my podium.
XCOM2 has been at the top of my "eagerly-awaiting" list for some time and I figured I'd bridge the wait with Invisible Inc.  Turns out (pun intended) I hugely underestimated this game.  It is brilliant!  Not only is it better than Enemy Unknown/Within but even my prized JA2 may need to step aside.
Why?
ESCALATING TENSION
The stealth gameplay works wonderfully. As combat and time quickly escalate efforts against you, the need to be efficient in your infiltration is always at the forefront. This prevents idling/turtling as every turn matters. You need to know how far to push and when to cut and run. The pacing is excellent.
MINIMAL LUCK
There are no probabilities to hit or variable damage. Even the path that enemies will move on their turn can be known. You might think this predictability would reduce the fun - it doesn't - it enhances it. All the information is there but you have to know how to get it.  This makes you supremely responsible for the outcome of your decisions and it is eminently satisfying.
REPLAYABILITY
This is not a story dependant game. It's about the process, not the ending so repeated playthoughs do not feel repetitive. As the maps are procedurally generated there is no repetition here either. Even character builds are kept fresh between playthoughs as you only pick your initial two team members. Additional members (and their unique abilties), as well as available gear, are random. Rather than min/max a single favourite build, each playthough requires a solution using different tools.
There is more to praise about this game but the above are what I consider the key points that set it apart and elevate it to the top of the genre.
This is Game-Of-The-Year worthy.  If you like this style of game, I cannot recommend it enough!
*EDIT: I stand by my original review as this is still one of my all time favourites. However, for what I consider the best experience, I'd suggest playing with the following mods:
UI TWEAKS
This adds a few really handy features to the UI that handily fixes some of the very few interface shortcomings.
CUSTOM AGENT MOD:
While this mod offers several options you may be interested in, the ability to remove the stat limiting auments introduced in the Contingency Plan DLC is the main reason to get this. Those augments are junk and just water down the odds of finding decent items in game.

Taking the Mafia franchise into a new setting in the South of the United States has allowed the developers to create a great envrionment to play in. The New Orleans stand-in (New Boudaux) gives us a great mix of rural and urban locales to drive around and play in. The new setting also means the story can be written differently to the previous games in the franchise (and genre too) which go for the tropes of all the classic mafia films like The Godfather or Goodfellas, this setting is new for the genre.
Compared to Mafia II, the world is very much alive and the game is truly an open world game, where you can enter many buildings (without loading screens) and walk/drive freely, sure, it is linear for the opening act of the game, introducing players to all the characters and mechanics but after an a few hours the game opens up and allows you to explore the map.
The game runs smoothly, I've only noticed two instances of AI bugging out for a minute, right after a transition from a cutscene to gameplay. There is a bit of stuttering for a few seconds after alt-tabbing back into the game but that clears up quite quickly.
The best thing about the game so far is the soundtrack, they've managed to pair songs to the storyline in a meaningful way, yet also have great classics come on the radio when you're driving around. Nothing beats cruising the streets of New Bourdaux than some Elvis, Rolling Stones and CCR coming out your speakers.
Fans of the first two games will be pleased to know the mob story is still core to the game, despite not being the typical italian mob setting, the characters, twists, and turns have met and exceeded the themes of the predecessors.
But the moment Paint It Black comes out of your speakers early on in the game... you know you're in for a good ride.
Edit: Seems others are complaing about the 30fps lock, I'd wait for the patch before calling this one 'the worst game'. A new studio working on their first game, this is a solid effort. No doubt things will only improve, give them more than 6 hours though.

I'm a sucker for cute games, especially cute platformers (thanks Kirby) and this is one of the better ones I've come across. Adorable little bat...thing Shuggy inherited a mansion from his uncle, but it's all haunted and stuff. To get the place in order he has to collect gems (it is ALWAYS gems) through more than 100 puzzle rooms and beat up some equally adorable bosses along the way. It's standard fare for a puzzle platformer, but what makes Shuggy shine is the variety in the puzzles. The devs took every gimmick they could think of short of an actual portal gun and mixed them up to round out the rooms. There are rooms with low gravity, reversed gravity, rotating gravity, rooms where you can fly, clones you can switch between, time travel, a personal teleporter, and my favorite, the magic rope. The rope trails out from a box in the room and you can use it to tangle up machinery, swing around like a monkey, and other neat tricks.
In addition to the 100+ puzzles in the base game, there's also a fully separate co-op campaign and an additional level set that gives you an extra teleporter on top of the other gimmicks. All this comes in a charming package with sharp, colorful graphics and some sweet jazz accompaniment. It hooked me hard enough to finish all the levels in the base game and try my hand at the achievements, some of which are surprisingly challenging. For the money, it's well worth your time if you love adorable platformers at least half as much as I do.

I don’t get all the hatred that’s been directed at this game. I picked it up for $2 during a sale, and some professional game reviewers were warning to not even buy it at that price. Naturally, I had to see what all the fuss was about and…well…Alpha Protocol is really not a bad game.
Not terribly original (a cross between Splinter Cell & Mass Effect in the CIA) and the story isn’t particularly memorable but the gameplay is solid & enjoyable. It’s not the best thing I’ve ever played but it is most certainly not the worst, either. That is, it’s strange to me when professional media praises total garbage like Dragon Age 2 yet trashes Alpha Protocol.
I’ve seen other reviewers complain about the AI in Alpha Protocol and various other glitches. Never had any problem with either of those things. Graphics were nice, music and voice acting were both acceptable. The story is nothing groundbreaking and a bit predictable given the way espionage stories go these days (America is the REAL enemy! Dun dun dunnn!) but it’s still fun to engage in the different relationships and choices you can make which have a real impact on the plot. And the gameplay is the glue that holds everything together; not revolutionary but good enough.
The only drawback to Alpha Protocol is that it’s rather forgettable and you won’t have any reason to replay it unless you want to witness some of the multiple story paths. You can expect to spend somewhere around 20 hours and will have a good time during that, though. It’s a shame that this first entry got savaged because it really could have turned into a good series. Instead we have Assassin’s Creed Part 8 and Final Fantasy 13 Part 3. Oh well.

Star Wars: Dark Forces
All the way back in 1993, Doom was released, which created a new genre the 'first person shooter' . Early adopters to the FPS style were called Doom clones and two years later a Star Wars DOOM clone cam in the form of Dark Forces
Released in early 1995 this was a highly anticipated game and it was one of the most notable games of that year. This game was released the same year as Full Throttle and Command and Conquer, times have changed, Lucas Arts was gutted by Disney and EA have milked every last bit of money and goodwill possible out of Westwood's fan base. The Jedi Knight series was shelved in 2004 when Raven Software released their second attempt at the franchise. EA DICE are developing a Star Wars Battlefront game but that is considered separate from the Jedi Knight series. Its a depressing thought that most game franchises don't last the test of time or the reboots don't do enough to kick start another run of games.
It's now 2017, twenty-two years later and I picked up the Jedi Knight series on Steam for €7.50. I had a lot of questions and a lot of interest to see if this game can still hack it after all this time.
You play as Kyle Katarn, a mercenary employed by the Rebel Alliance, he gets pulled into preventing a secret Imperial weapon from tipping the balance in the struggle between the Empire and the Rebellion
Being called a DOOM clone can have a lot of negative connotations, DOOM is a finely balanced game even after all these years. DOOM has seen a regrowth in popularity with the release of Brutal DOOM and mod that pushes DOOM over the edge of sanity and into sheer bloodthirsty madness. Dark Forces is not a DOOM clone per se, Dark Forces uses a different engine, the Jedi game engine which allows for multiple floor levels, ducking, jumping, fog, haze, and lots more beyond what id software had created before.
However the level design is quality, it is the same high standard of DOOM. Each level has its own signature feel and while you do go the snow and the sewer levels this is no simple palette swap. Was Dark Forces released before snow level, lose all your weapons level, and sewer levels were a cliche filler of mainstream gaming? The levels try their best to put the player into new and dangerous environments to keep the gameplay fresh. There are lots of Star Wars themed interactions with force fields, lifts, and other mechanics. There are some awkward platforming but there are some very good puzzles. Armed with only basic mission instructions, it was rare I got lost in the non linear levels, again top quality level design even by today's standards.
The graphics unfortunately are very poor, more often than not you'll be firing at a mess of white pixels that you know is a storm trooper down a hallway. Enemies up close do resemble their movie counterparts but it's a little silly trying to blast a mess of pixels down narrow hallways. Dark Forces has some nice cut scenes and its presentation is holds high with mission briefs and an inventory/map menu. The lack of a crosshair and vertical axis mouse aim is not the end of the world, you do get used to it after a while. The music is straight out of the movies which is great for the first few levels but it is the same rolling tune for each level and it starts to wear thin after a few deaths.
The guns feel big and chunky just like DOOM. It was a nice surprise that some weapons were better for different enemies but some of the weapons were just useless. Most of the enemies are very easy and the guns make short work of them but there are the Dark Troopers and they are difficult to beat and should be taken with care. Even there walking sounds kept me on my toes in the latter half of the game.
The game is single player only and is about seven hours long. This feels a little short in retrospect but in reality it doesn't feel repetitive. There is no saving inside missions, a checkpoint system is in place but you don't know where or when they trigger. Without multiplayer there is little replayability.
Dark Forces has not aged well, strip away all the Star Wars layers and this game would not have stood well against its contemporaries. DOOM was released two years previous and its looks miles better, DOOM's levels were not logical manifestations of human buildings, id focused on gameplay before decoration. When id was designing it enemies, they made sure that they were easily recognised. In Dark Forces, your memory and imagination of the films fill in the blanks when you see a mess of pixels that are the textures. When Duke Nukem was released a year later, the quality was high enough for you to see a real world form in the game.
For all its extra mechanics, features, and Star Wars nostalgia, Dark Forces just can't top DOOM.
Storm Trooper Laser Rifle doesn't beat Shotgun but it is still a worthwhile experience.

Sometimes you buy games based on how it looks. Maybe just due to the genre it is associated with. Or perhaps something interesting you heard about grabbed your attention. Sometimes researching a game beforehand or waiting on reviews simply can not wait. Arguably this makes for some impulse decisions in purchasing a game, especially when there is a high chance of it being horrible. Flood of Light is one that I absolutely loved how it looked and decided that was enough to give it a try.
You immediately start off on the roof of a 8 floor skyscraper in Hope City. How did you get there? Who knows. All you know is that there is a path in front of you and a whole lotta water under you. The mystery on what this place is, how it came to be flooded, and who you are is what drives the story aspect. The way the city came to how you see it now is told by Doctor S through his entries available on various terminals around the town. Informing that all humans evacuated before the rainfall fully submerged most of the buildings. As there are only a few terminals on each floor, and each entry gives you more and more information, your curiosity brings you to a better understanding of the city’s situation.
Not only is the story told to you by entries, there are various robots that were left behind when the humans evacuated. Instead of the robots recounting a more personal account, they instead only want to help you save them. Talking about a Revelation Code detailing that a Guide with an appearance of a human will come and save all of the robots. As well as telling you the general history of that floor, and where the pedestal is, and explaining when you get more powers. Same as the entries, this reveal goes slowly as different robots have different limits on how much they can tell you.
Of course you can totally ignore the story. The terminals and the robots are placed in obvious spots, only one or two can be missed if you are only paying attention to the puzzle area, and it is very easy to skip through it.
The girl you play as has the ability to absorb light as long as a lamp containing it is close enough for her to. In addition, if a lamp contains an unattached light, or light orb, she can redirect it to another close lamp. The light is also used to power switches so elevators will activate or doors will open. However, you will not be able to continue unless you lower the waters as the girl will stop way before you have the chance to submerge her head. This is where the puzzle aspect comes in.
This would not be a puzzle game with just being able to control light orbs. Each room you have to complete contains one or multiple light monolith(s). As you progress along, you will get more and more complicated paths that have you think about how that action will affect the room and if it will help towards that goal. Will doing this move let you have enough light orbs for all of the monoliths? You can, of course, restart from your last savepoint as there are some instances that you will not be able to get the light orb back if you make the wrong move. This all leads to the pedestal, which each floor has, to give you the sweet reward of a massive water drainage and getting closer to the ground floor.
If you think just absorbing light for eight floors will get boring after knowing all the ins and outs, it was addressed. Mechanics are added to keep the game fresh and challenging and it helps that it does go in line with the story. Wicks are placed around each floor, earning a sort-of collectable and a challenge on. If you collect all of the wicks you will be able to see the second, and true, ending. You can also try to get an ‘S’ rating to test your skills. The easiest goal is talking to the robots, but the hard part is getting the minimum amount of steps possible. This does include wicks, so even if you talked to all the robots and got the same or below the minimum steps but you missed a wick, you will only get an ‘A’ rating. If you are an achievement hunter, all floors have an achievement where you need to get an ‘S’ rating.
Just talking about the puzzles and the story will undermine how the atmosphere was built around you. It would be unbelievable if the city looked like the sun was out but there were obvious clouds hovering above. Each area looks like the rain drained the colour out of them while you look nice and bright. You will also note the constant rain and water below you. I do like how that reminder of what the purpose of doing this is constantly there.Though what I think is a cool little thing they added was the telescope. When you first look through it, you see the drowned city. However, once you get a few light pedestals activated it will reflect in the telescope image. As the water level will correspond with the floor you are on, it might not seem you are doing much, but this does put it into perspective.
The piano that accompanies the rain is great. It easily gives the feel of being alone in a vast city that used to house humans. Bringing the feeling of sadness throughout the gameplay, but yet seems to hold hope. I even teared up a bit at multiple parts. The piano does stop most notably at the end of most of the floors when you walk towards the pedestal, only having the sound rain pelting down and any other sound effects needed.
Arguably the ending is pretty lackluster, especially if you do not collect all of the wicks. You spend all this time learning about the background of Hope City (if you chose to) and working through all of the puzzle rooms to activate all of the pedestals. If you just missed one wick, the ending will stop early. Without an ending that has no pay off, the players have no reason to go back and collect all the wicks as it will be assumed the true ending is the same way.
+ Visuals
+ Music
+ Story
+ Puzzles
+/- Some lines were not translated (never fear, the entries and the robot dialogue is translated)
- Lackluster ending
Flood of Light is a relaxing puzzle game. As the puzzles are simple, but having just enough challenge for you to think it through, coupled with the music makes this one of those games that can be played to wind down for the day. With a goal set in front of you, and curiosity taking the helm, the four to ten hours is enjoyable with little to no frustration. Just expect the ending to be weakest link to the otherwise great story and atmosphere that was built up.

While I can't recommend it for the story (what is kind of a first for me), I can and certainly will recommend it for the puzzles.
As the description goes, in
you play as a little girl who needs to light her way through a city submerged by rain. You start on the roof of a building and your objective is to activate the pedestals at the end of the level on each of the floors. However, in order to reach said pedestals you must light different lamp posts and activate a few stone posts along your way.
For the most part, the game does a pretty good job introducing you to the different ways in which you can manipulate light, how you can absorb, store, and transfer it, as well as the different types of light that will be available to you (blue can be submerged, yellow cannot). I say "for the most part," as there is some trial and error in order to get the most out of the available light. The game encourages you to be efficient and thorough, suggesting a maximum number of steps (how many lights you move in order to reach the pedestal) and indicating what discoveries you need to make to achieve a perfect 'S' rating. Achieving a perfect rating on all floors unlocks the 'true' ending.
I cannot emphasize enough how addicting this game is, a feeling that is undoubtedly exacerbated by the drive to solve each and every puzzle in the least amount of moves possible, not to mention some achievements require an inordinate amount of patience and perseverance (more on this later). I would sometimes stare at the screen for a few minutes, mentally transferring light from one lamp to the next, activating and deactivating switches, tallying the number of imaginary moves I was making. It felt incredibly rewarding solving the puzzles on each floor and I instantly took up the challenge to achieve a perfect rating on every one of them (which I did).
The game however, is not without its flaws, and one of the most glaring ones becomes apparent right away: there is no manual save. What does this imply? Well, for one, it means that if you quit the game before you have completed a floor, then all your progress on that floor is lost (what contributed to my 45-hour playtime as I sometimes left the game open and went to bed). Sure, there are checkpoints throughout the floor that allow you to replay a particular segment in order to optimize the total number of moves but if you quit the game, you'll have to start that floor over from scratch. Also, these checkpoints are sometimes quite inconveniently placed, making it easy for you to make a mistake and not having enough time to get back to the menu to hit replay before your progress is automatically saved.
This lack of manual saves is particularly maddening when you're trying to unlock the "Being the prophet" achievement, as you cannot use the aforementioned replay function. I mean, you can, but if you do, you won't be able to unlock the achievement. That means if you make one false move, you'd better start the level all over again... and there is a noticeable ramp-up in difficulty on that last floor; I must've replayed it ten times, maybe more. A friendly tip: favour the keyboard on that floor instead of the mouse. Sometimes the mouse doesn't respond correctly when you're trying to place a lamp or absorb light, but you can be sure that won't happen with the keyboard.
This repetition can certainly get on your nerves but, fortunately, the game has a soothing (if simple) soundtrack to ease the tension. Combine that with the lovely artwork and this is definitely a most inviting game to play and replay.
As for the story, while you do collect letters that try to explain what is going on, and you interact with robots that give you a few tidbits here and there, the issue lies in the fact that all of the writing has been translated from Chinese to English... and the translation just isn't very good (to say the least). Sure, you can understand most (if not all) of it, but at no point did I feel engaged by it. I know there's probably a good story there, but the issues with the grammar took me out of it.
Considering its pleasing aesthetic, high replay value, and relatively low price-point,
is a great game if you feel like flexing your brain muscles. While I would've preferred that the soundtrack had been included with the game, I have no qualms recommending this title at full price.

The reason to play Flood of Light is its art. One of its promotional images shows the protagonist kneeling in a cloak in front of a darkened cityscape, bright bursts of pink  (cherry blossom trees, it turns out) on either side of her and rain drizzling in the background. It's that image that caught my eye, and even though I read some brief impressions and looked at a few screens after that, I was probably always going to buy it after I saw that initial artwork, assuming it didn't end up being some kind of call center simulator. But honestly, I'd probably buy even that if it were attached to art this pretty. The same aesthetic carries through the entire game, with muted grays and blues punctuated by splashes of more vibrant colors. It's surprisingly evocative for such a small game; the city itself reverberates with an eerie stillness, while the more whimsical character designs lighten the mood ever so slightly.
The puzzles are better than they probably needed to be, too, particularly for what was originally a mobile game. If the mechanics aren't particularly novel, they are soundly executed, and the gently sloping difficulty curve is ideal for this more casual type of game. You're introduced to simple set of rules early on, and though there are a small handful of new mechanics introduced throughout the game, those same rules will always apply.  Crucially, it never violates it's own logic, and never asks you to come up with solutions it hasn't taught you. A pet peeve of mine is when a puzzle game pulls solutions out of thin air, as if it's so very clever for expecting you to solve a puzzle in a way it never even communicated to you was possible; none of the puzzles here even approach that. There are a few telltale signs that Flood of Light didn't originate on PC; it's very mouse-oriented even when that isn't the most intuitive input option, and character movement is sluggish and occasionally imprecise. Overall, though, it's a very solid port, and I think the fact that I didn't even realize it was a port until I was nearly halfway through says something about the quality of the game.
If it has one major downfall, though, it's very clearly its writing, or more accurately, the translation of that writing. Flood of Light comes from a Chinese developer, and I strongly suspect they translated the game into English themselves, perhaps with some help from Google Translate. The result is incoherent at best, and complete gibberish at worst. A kind steam user volunteered to fix its grammar, which removed some of the most egregious errors but it essentially amounts to a band-aid on a chainsaw wound. What the game really needs is for every line of text to be rewritten from the ground up by a proper translator. Do I begrudge a small studio for not having the resources for a better translation? Not at all. Do I think you should be aware of its translation issues before buying Flood of Light? Absolutely.
I can imagine some players criticizing Flood of Light for being too easy, but I think to do that is to fundamentally misunderstand what type of game this is. It's not trying to force your brain into mental gymnastics like The Talos Principle,  or make you feel like a small, worthless and very stupid pile of organic refuse the way Stephen's Sausage Roll does; it's trying to be the game you play to relax after work. Think of Flood of Light like a lazy brook in the summertime; it's pretty, gentle, and will have a decidedly calming effect on your mental state.

First and foremost, the most obvious attraction of Flood of Light is the art and music. The art is beautiful, and the music is absolutely gorgeous. The gameplay itself is fairly simple (at least it starts simple). You manipulate orbs of light to power lamps and switches to open doors to get to the next level. It's a slow-paced and thoughtful puzzle game, and the music and atmosphere fit it perfectly. It does what all good puzzle games do and slowly ramps up the complexity and adds more elements as you progress. Things like blue light orbs you can use underwater, and the ability to create your own lamps.
Flood of light has a story, which is conveyed to you by message logs you find throughout the levels. They're in pretty poorly translated, broken english. They're difficult to read through and don't make a whole ton of sense. Fortunately the atmosphere created by the mechanics, visuals, and music evoke emotions in such a way that a concrete story isn't really necessary. Overall, I loved my time with this game. Took me about 5 hours to beat, and at $4 that's an absolute steal. Very much worth buying.

I don't normally write reviews, but the bad rep this game is getting for the micro transactions is just ridiculous.
Gameplay
If you've ever played Shadow of Mordor, you most likely have a general idea of what to expect here. Superhuman wraith powers with Assassin's Creed like movement (mostly). However there are some important additions here that really add a lot to the whole "Push one button to run, jump, climb, cook dinner, etc" formula. A particular move in here includes a 'double' jump that adds an extra layer of precision on top of the semi automated parkour. While it may not sound like much, it adds a dynamic that makes you feel like you're doing something engaging, rather than just holding forward and spacebar.
A variety of new moves were added that creates extremely satisfying moments, like aerial bow sharpshooting, which looks awesome and feels awesome to do. While there are a ton of extra additions, there are some caveats that I feel were almost a regression in a way. The execution move is no long tied directly to your combo meter. Instead, you have to build up a second bar called "Wrath", which then allows you to unlock the ability to execute. While I understand the mentality most likely was to prevent spamming executions, the Orcs now can adapt to moves you use repeatedly, so is it not redundant to throttle them? It's not a horrible change, just a questionable one.
Map Layout
The map is separated into sections, cutting off the somewhat openworld aspect that we saw in the previous title, but this is, in my opinion, better. Free roam games have taken the market by storm lately, but lack the substance and variety you'd find in games such as this. While it is free roam, it isn't just one giant map that some bloke made in Blender out of a plane using some topology tools. The different areas that are presented to us include a wide variety of environments, making each one feel refreshing when you travel to them. Also, the new fast travel locations are spread about thoughtfully, yet sparingly around the map. You wont always be able to fast travel directly next to your destination, but hey, that's why you spent your skill points on those movement perks, right? Maybe brand some Captains on the way there? Little bit of travel time isn't an issue in this game.
Graphics
Seeing the reception for this one is a strange one for me. I feel the game looks great (Note: I haven't tried out the HD texture pack as of writing this). I have seen a few complaints about recycled animations and whatnot, but it seems like nitpicking at best, whining at worst. Yes, some animations were present in the first game, but we're also playing as the same character as before. What, is Talion and Celebrimbor going to completely change their attacks just because of a new game? That's like saying Goku shouldn't use the Kamehameha for more than one episode. The animations never looks bad to begin with, so it's definitely not the issue everyone makes it out to be.
Also, watching all the characters interact with eachother, from Graug's duking it out with eachother to Captains having a scuffle, it all looks very organic. The animations are fluid and quite honestly sets the bar for how seamless characters should interact with eachother visually.
Story
The story is absolutely a step above it's predecessor. While I haven't completed it yet, the first character you brand in the game is hilarious and extremely likeable. I got a few good laughs out of him and was slightly sad to move onto the next area without him.
*Side note: I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me against a captain and when I respawned, the dialogue was as follows:
Celebrimbor: Maybe next time we cou-
Talion: Don't. Just- don't.
This is funny, but also helps you bond with the character. I believe it's called a personality? Haven't seen one of those in characters in recent games.*
Micro transactions
If you are seriously so upset about the fact you can pay to speed up game progess in a primarily single player game, you need to get your priorities straight. During my time playing I never found the microtransactions to be overly intrusive, and have not myself taken part in them. Is it a questionable business tactic? Sure. Want to make a statement? Don't complain and moan about it, just don't buy anything off the store. It shouldn't be your reason for downvoting the game.
Technical Issues
Framerate wise, the game has run perfect at 60fps for me on Ultra, however I did have a rather strange issue. When I first booted up the game the cutscenes and audio were all playing as if they were an old VHS tape on fast forward. After some tinkering with my audio settings I found the solution was to drop the quality of your primary audio device down to 48000 Hz. I don't notice a difference in quality, and the game now works properly, so that's something I don't particularly have positive or negative feelings for. Seems odd to have the issue, but it's not impossible to fix. If some techno guru could explain what it is about your audio quality that would do that to the game, I'd like an explanation just out of curiousity.
Final Verdict
Like LOTR? Go ahead and buy it. Like Assassin's Creed still, somehow? Go ahead and buy it. Get butthurt over nonintrusive micro transactions? Probably not the place for you.
The game is great and I feel like it was money well spent at full price.

Taking the Mafia franchise into a new setting in the South of the United States has allowed the developers to create a great envrionment to play in. The New Orleans stand-in (New Boudaux) gives us a great mix of rural and urban locales to drive around and play in. The new setting also means the story can be written differently to the previous games in the franchise (and genre too) which go for the tropes of all the classic mafia films like The Godfather or Goodfellas, this setting is new for the genre.
Compared to Mafia II, the world is very much alive and the game is truly an open world game, where you can enter many buildings (without loading screens) and walk/drive freely, sure, it is linear for the opening act of the game, introducing players to all the characters and mechanics but after an a few hours the game opens up and allows you to explore the map.
The game runs smoothly, I've only noticed two instances of AI bugging out for a minute, right after a transition from a cutscene to gameplay. There is a bit of stuttering for a few seconds after alt-tabbing back into the game but that clears up quite quickly.
The best thing about the game so far is the soundtrack, they've managed to pair songs to the storyline in a meaningful way, yet also have great classics come on the radio when you're driving around. Nothing beats cruising the streets of New Bourdaux than some Elvis, Rolling Stones and CCR coming out your speakers.
Fans of the first two games will be pleased to know the mob story is still core to the game, despite not being the typical italian mob setting, the characters, twists, and turns have met and exceeded the themes of the predecessors.
But the moment Paint It Black comes out of your speakers early on in the game... you know you're in for a good ride.
Edit: Seems others are complaing about the 30fps lock, I'd wait for the patch before calling this one 'the worst game'. A new studio working on their first game, this is a solid effort. No doubt things will only improve, give them more than 6 hours though.

Do you like roguelike games? Do you like stealth games where getting into combat is not advisable?
If you answered yes to these, then this game will be for you.
To sum it up, you have to manage 2 people (to start) who are very good at hiding behind small objects against guards that have the attention span of an egg timer.
Combat is simple as there is no accuracy at all. You either put the the enemy to sleep, or kill them. So your rewind turn won't be wasted on accuracy checks. Also a great function is the "pin", where you can keep an enemy asleep as long as you hold him down.
As you go through each randomly generated area, you have a hacking ability to take over electronics around the building using a limited power source. The enemy has their own viruses called Daemons that will infect you to provide random debuffs as you go.
As you progress into the game, you unlock new agents to play as, and new starting hacking abilities to change out.
The game has a few minor flaws, such as you will be able to easily tell which items and abilities are ridiculously useful and the ones that are so specific, they fall under: "Why is this even in the game?"
Another flaw is that without the DLC, the difficulty on Endless may get too easy once you get good at the game.
With the DLC, I haven't tried Endless yet. But I'm hopeful that it'll turn out good.
If you aren't going for achievements, the game can be played as ruthless, or casual to fit your playstyle. They have all the basic customizable game settings unlocked by default. So if you want to cruise through the game or go ridiculously hard, it's up to you.
Just got the DLC, and very impressed by the new side quests that were added in to accumulate a new arsenal of tactics.
If you still are curious, google "Totalbiscuit Invisible Inc" - Watching his overview sold me to the game.

This was a real buried gem of a game. I grabbed it during a sale for less than $5 on the thin promise of "Mass Effect with Super-Spies," and that turned out to be more or less exactly what was delivered. For all the negative press this game received, I found few flaws worth spiting the game for, and after two playthroughs I'm only disappointed I didn't find Alpha Protocol earlier.
AP is a great find for people who enjoy RPGs with an emphasis on 3rd person action - not the other way around. The combat is fairly simple with a few nice twists, though certain combat styles are a touch overpowered while others feel heavily handicapped. If you're a gamer who looks for deep, challenging 3rd person combat, this isn't really what you're looking for. But it
offer rewards for people who are heavily into role-playing characters and only enjoy the action as a means to that end. Once I got a few of my combat skills ranked up enough, I started to feel like a serious Bond-level super-agent, which is exactly how I wanted to feel while playing.
What Alpha Protocol brings to the table is a solid narrative with a few twists, a rich cast of interesting characters to inetract with, and a series of complicated moral quandries to navigate. The way you shape your character and his reactions makes a real difference in how the game feels - even if the levels you fight through are the same either way. Characters react to you differently depending on how you treat them (and others). I played through twice; once as a suave rookie agent in over his head, the next as a hard♥♥♥♥♥veteran willing to go to any lengths to get results. Each character felt unique, and my interactions with the NPCs felt different each time.
My favorite parts of a great RPG are being able to shape a character, being surrounded by NPCs I care about or are interested in, and taking part in a story that grips me - or at least holds my interest while delivering enough surprises to keep me guessing. Alpha Protocol delivered that experience, along with a combat system that was fun and streamlined and made me feel like I was playing the kind of big screen super-spy I was hoping to create. So long as you go in without high expectations, but willing to overlook previous reviewers' complaints and have a fun time, I think you will. It was well worth it for me.

Alright, I guess a few more words are in order.
Being a pretty late arrival to LiS's mere existence (never heard of it until about two weeks ago), I purchased LiS during the recent Steam Sale for next to nothing, but now that I've played it, I'd pay the full price again without a second thought.
Finally there's a game that foregoes polished graphics in favor of amazing storytelling, deep characters, non-standard gameplay and a cool soundtrack. What good is a game that looks great but gets boring after two hours tops because the gameplay has nothing to offer (looking at you, GR: Wildlands)? I'm so sick of almost all modern games going this direction, so I love LiS for breaking that pattern alone. Sure, it probably won't get your adrenaline pumping, but it managed something no other game  did in many years: it made me cry, and that's among the highest compliments I can give to any work of fiction.
Interactive Movies and similar adventure genres are a divisive topic, no doubt about that. The average action-oriented (multi)player probably won't get much mileage out of Life is Strange, but if you're looking for an incredibly well-done combination of paranormal mystery thriller, detective story, coming-of-age tale and a tribute to the power of friendship and love in a world that's otherwise devoid of it, look no further and play this game. I'm certainly glad I did, and all follow-up titles are already earmarked in my budget.

While this game lacks some essential features, the amount of gameplay available for the price makes this game definitely worth the buy. It has some performance issues that persist even in a high end tier gaming machine, and the graphics aren't the prettiest, but it offers quite a bit of customization options for the units and the FPS perspective is very neat and unique. I definitely recommend you support this game!

This is a step in the right direction for FPS RTS hybrids. There other games that have tried to mix the two before to varied success or unsusccess, but this one seems to understand why anyone would mix the two in the first place. It's the epic grand battles of an rts and the heated action of an fps.
The plot is non existant, but what do you expect? It's an indie title and not the artsy indie title. From what little I can understand of this universe is that there's corporations of bot manufacturers (not CIS from starwars) that are waring over planets. There's not single player campaign and the AI skirmish doesn't count.
It's not the prettiest game and it's certainly not the most well animated with the no wheel turn on jeeps and the CEO's walking like robots. The music is still epic though, especially when you finally build the highest tier mech.
Gameplaywise, there is a combination of good ideas that I remmember from other games. For one thing it will mark units on the map if you zoom out like in Supreme Commander. This allows the game to keep the infantry to scale when compared to vehichles and buildings. The buildings themselves are detailed and mapped out making them fun to explore. There's enough attention to detail that you can even see the process of which the infantry are made. There's even a game mode where you play as just the infantry while someone else does the rts mode. Your goal is primarily to kill the opposing CEO in his building by sending infantry in to theses structures and up his tower to shoot him. Then I found out how to break this game.
You see, once I realized buildings were indestructible, I surounded my CEO tower with hallways and left no openings. This meant no one can shoot me all the AI can do is look at my tower with it's ary of giant ships and robots. At that point I had to wonder if anyone else figured this out and tried pulling it on multiplayer. No wonder I can't find any servers. Even the AI seems to forget how to win once it's tech tree is high enough since even the Chairman level AI focuses on building giant war machines instead of infantry.
This game still needs tweeking but as it stands, it's a fun concept and I hope this gets popular.

is a very atmospheric puzzle game with a stellar soundtrack and beautiful backgrounds. Gameplay is focused on limited-space puzzles where you have to move the light in correct sequence. If anyone is wondering there is no reflex based gameplay like platforming etc. Aside from few issues like unrewarding ending and translation, I very much enjoyed the relaxing experience.
Still not sure what the game is? If you ever played a box moving game with limited space it is a fancy version of that. Instead of boxes, you have to move lights between lamps in correct order. That is the basic idea but it gets more interesting later in the game. Character movement is there only to get in range of lamps and get around the city.
The difficulty was very good in terms of progression. Overtime game adds new elements to the gameplay and puzzles become more complex. I thought the solutions were very creative and I found myself cheering every time I beat a hard level. Surprisingly I never felt annoyed or completely overwhelmed by difficulty. I think great soundtrack just makes the game so soothing that I can't even feel frustrated. It has tutorial throughout the game with images and tips (translation might be a bit off but I had no problems learning mechanics)
Save system was ok for the most part. There is a bit of a problem when it comes to puzzles that require light from previous areas because you may have to backtrack to get them (after loading or restarting)
Presentation and atmosphere of the game were near perfect. Backgrounds are very consistent with tone but I probably would have preferred a bit more variety in color. All levels have a suburban theme with some occasionally unique locations.  Maybe the character could have looked a bit better but overall pretty game. Music was just fantastic and perfect for thinking gameplay ( I will actually buy the soundtrack when it goes on sale). Combinations of good visuals and chill soundtrack made it very immersive.
It took me about 4 hours to beat the game and I will have to do 100% to unlock some secret. Good length for this type of game and it did not overstay its welcome. The mystery behind the story kept my interest but that ending was anticlimactic in regards to how much build up it had. You can get a better conclusion by collecting wicks which takes a lot of extra effort. However, I expect a better regular ending because casual players won't get a satisfactory closure.
( Was thinking 8/10 but the ending really ruined my overall impression )
If you like limited-space puzzle games this one has the right amount of difficulty and the wonderful atmosphere created by art and music. I enjoyed it and I hope developers adds something to the ending to make it more satisfying.

Flood of light is a 2D puzzler that offers a number of challenging puzzles in a beautifully drawn environment.
You can find 25 minutes of gameplay with commentary here:

I choose to purchase this game based solely on how nice the art style was. Through the game this does not falter, and it is a joy to look at. The music is also enjoyable to listen too, and you can purchase it as DLC for an additional cost. While I wouldn't go that far, it adds to the atmosphere of the game and help overcome the games shortcomings.
You begin by entering a city that has been flooded by an endless rain. The goal is to reach the end of each stage an activate a pump, which lowers water the water level and provides access to the next level down. Throughout each stage you will come across a range of puzzles that involve using orbs to illuminate lights. The orbs can only move from light to light, and all of the orbs you carry are used each time, with any excess being attached to the last light in the chain. This mechanic is deceptively simple, but gets more complex as you move through the game. Most new stages also introduce additional mechanics that effect the use of, or the orbs themselves.
Story wise, as you progress through the game there are terminals where you can gain information on what happened in the city. There are also robots who explain new game mechanics or provide a glimpse into the history of the city. It is a fitting way to learn about the game but text has been translated from Chinese to English, so the words used and context is sometimes slightly off. Its not to the point where you can't understand the story - just that some of the text could have been written better.
For controls the game uses mouse and W S A D for movement. There is no real way to die, but if you use the orbs in the wrong way, you will have to reload from the previous save to try again. The game also has 4 measurements at the end of a stage - "wicks" lit, moves taken, robots spoken too and story elements collected. Apparently if you get all four items for all of the stages, there is an additional ending.
This game is a port from iOS and Andriod, where you can find it under the same name. The levels have changed slightly from mobile, but not enough to warrant buying it again if you already have it. The PC implementation works and does not feel like it is missing anything.
All up I would estimate about 4 hours of gameplay, depending on how quickly you progress through the stages. There would be much more if you want to go for the full completion, as many of the puzzles left me clueless how to get the wicks. I have enjoyed my playthrough so far and feel its worth the 3.99 price tag.

So when reviewing an old game like this you basically have to address two questions:
1) Was it good when it came out?
2) Is it still good now?
When it comes to Dark Forces and question one: Absolutely yes. The sound design, the feel of the motion, the complex but not confusing level design, all great.
But when dealing with question two there is the issue of nostalgia. I can play some games that have not aged well simply because it brings back memories of how much fun I had playing them back in the day. But to actually recommend an old game the gameplay needs to still stand up to scrutiny today. Some of the classic Star Wars games fall flat in this regard (I'm looking at you Rebel Assault).
But the fact is, Dark Forces is still fun. There are certainly criticisms to be made about the game, and the inability to look up and down will feel very awkward for a little while, but I honestly got sucked into this game far more than I anticipated. In the end, it's still a quality experience that I suggest any Star Wars fan try out.
TWO NOTES:
- Make sure you adjust some DOSBox settings to get the best experience. Check out the Steam Discussion board for Dark Forces to get some ideas of what you should do.
- DarkXL is a neat modern port of Dark Forces that allows playing in modern resolutions, high res textures and more modern controls (i.e. YOU CAN LOOK UP!). It's a really cool project. However, I find that I enjoy the game more when playing the original via DOSBox. DarkXL somehow loses the "feel" of the movement (even if that's a bit of a nebulous concept). I think if you're a fan of Dark Forces and have already played it through DarkXL is a fun tool to check out. But for your first time through stick to the original.

Walking Dead: Season 2 builds on the success of its predecessor to provide another enthralling story. But, while the original was near flawless in its story telling and character building, the sequel doesn't quite hit those lofty highs.
Once again the choices are not designed to provide radically different experiences but rather provide you the choice on how to sculpt the character of the protagonist, Clementine. Your choices will ellicit different responses from other characters in the game and will influence how they interact with you. But won't massively alter their fate, if a character is supposed to die, it will  eventually die. This is not a bad thing though as the writing is sharp and the overarching plot is pretty great.
The crucial element missing from Season 2  is the relationship dynamic of Lee and Clementine. Playing as Lee I had done everything to protect Clementine and put her survival/happiness above everything else.
As Clementine in Season 2 you'll be hard pressed to find someone you'll develop a similar strong bond with.
But the game still provides a thrilling, if slightly bleak story. The growth of Clementine and the return of a major character from Season 1 show how people growing up in a zombified world develop (or just lose their grip).
As with all Telltale titles the game is simple enough for anyone to pick up and play, so you can get 'non-gamers' to have a go at this.
Overall a great game that falls just short of its predecessor.

Microsoft Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition is, as you probably guessed, a Flight simulator and a game which I have loved since it first came out back in 2006. In FSX: SE you get in to the cockpit of a number of different aircraft ranging from jumbo jets to ultralight aircraft in Free Flight or in a number of missions of increasing difficult made by the original development team all over the World.
FSX: SE has always been a game that I have loved due to it providing me with an opportunity to fly aircraft I'm legally unable to fly (due to a long term health condition) and when I upgraded to a Windows 8.1 PC and found I could no longer play this game I was bitterly disappointed. When I heard about DoveTail taking over the game from Microsoft and updating it to work with Windows 8.1 I was over the moon and for the most part I was pleased with what I got when purchasing it through Steam.
I'd also just like to say that despite only having 9 hours in the game on Steam I have at least 50-60 hours logged on the boxed edition.
+Over 24,000 locations to visit which are all realistic based on the locations in 2006
+24 Aircraft, including fixed-wing and rotary craft, each with a number of different variations
+You can customise how realistic the game is ranging from a relatively easy game to a very realistic flight sim
+DoveTail did a fantastic job at increasing performance and making it work on new operating systems
+It's very easy to get in to thanks to its fantastic tutorials and increasing difficulty
+A wide variety of missions ranging from simple cargo delivery missions to emergency landings after complete engine failure
+Multiplayer works again, I've never played it myself but I know a lot of fans of the series were very happy to see this
+A huge modding community (most mods are considered third party addons and do cost money)
+FSX: SE includes the Acceleration addon pack which was developed before DoveTail took over
+A huge number of hotkeys for the vast number of different controls in this game
+Very good settings menus which make it incredibly easy to customise your FSX: SE experience
-The graphics, scenery, flight models etc. still look just as bad as they did when the game first released 7 years ago, this could have something to do with DoveTail's deal with Microsoft but it's still very disappointing
-The DLC that's being pumped out by DoveTail is both overpriced and according to other reviewers not particularly high quality which is bitterly disappointing as I wanted high quality first party addons
-Despite being called 'Steam Edition' it has zero Steam integration, that means no cards, achievements, workshop or Cloud support
-The SDK and modding tools have been patched out of the game, my guess is DoveTail don't like the fact that no one is buying their addon packs in favour of the vast number of far better quality addons available elsewhere
Worth a mention:
-I play this with a combination of a flight stick (with hotkeys) and keyboard for less important operations and I can't imagine it playing particularly well with M&KB or Controller only
Verdict:
8
Despite some flaws the Steam Edition of this game allows me to play a much loved game that I would not otherwise be able to play. Overall a fantastic flight simulator which gives easy access for people new to this kind of game while also providing a great experience for regular fliers or fans of Flight Sims.

When I first played shadow of mordor, I thought the idea of the nemesis system was something super unique, and although it had its problems, it was a work of art nonetheless. Shadow of War brings that Nemesis system back and builds upon it.
First things first, microtransactions:
Yes they are absolutely stupid, the game does not need them whatsoever. And I do think that there is shame to WB for trying to bring that into a single player game. I also think that if you liked the first game enough, the microtransactions are just something to ignore. Because literally everything else about the game is amazing.
Although we oppose the microtransactions, I think there are people (such as me), that do not really care. We won't be paying extra for these chests. We will, however, be immersing ourselves into the different regions in the game. Commanding our followers, infiltrating our spies, and playing every mission until we get to the finish line (with breaks of course). If you loved Middle-Earth Shadow of Mordor,  don't steer your head away from this game, because there is still so much else to offer.
The game builds upon the nemesis system and makes it even more complicated. I found myself being ambushed randomly, shaming others, as well as "building my army". When too many orcs were on the screen, things would get hectic and trying to kill my nemesis or revive my followers would lead to decisions having to be made, and consequences thereafter. The game does a great job of personalizing every orc I come in contact with. The story is alright, obviously we can't expect it to live upto to the hype of the original LOTR. But it does a decent job nonetheless.
To summarize, I would recommend this game 100%, if you were a fan of the first game, I think the $60 price tag isn't something to worry about. But I also think that if you have your doubts or just aren't as big of a fan as I am, then wait for it to go on sale. It will, and I think you will realize it's still an amazing game even if you have to put tons of hours into the game to get the true ending.

Adventures of Shuggy has a ton of content for its price tag with over a hundred levels, with a healthy variety in design and difficulty level. It has a bunch of interesting mechanics ranging from fairly standard tried and tested ideas like rope swinging or a super jump to more unique mechanics such as the time travel levels in which an echo of your past self follows along your exact path and kills you upon contact, forcing you to consider your steps so that you can come back later without bumping into yourself, normally with multiple past Shuggys running around at once making it fairly hectic. New mechanics are introduced at a healthy pace rather than throwing them all at the player at once, allowing for a fairly intuitive game experience. Boss levels are also mostly well designed with only minimal exceptions. You will die repeatedly and frequently but rather than cheap, frustrating deaths they can normally be learned from and then avoided. The soundtrack and art style especially give it a lot of character too, and you are not required to 100% the game in order to complete the main story which given the difficulty of some of its hardest levels is a blessing. Overall a fun little platformer with plenty of content and personality.

As someone who played Civilization III - Current, including both Sci Fi versions, I've seen quite a few improvements throughout the years. I am disappointed to say that I do not find this game nearly as enjoyable as the rest of them.
Each game felt as though it was adding new content, new avenues to invest in, and down right new content. With Civ 6 though, I do not get this at all. I feel like nothing new was introduced. Don't get me wrong, there is pleanty of "new" content in this that was not in civ 5. The introduction of cultures own tech tree was pretty neat, although it was already sort of in Civ 5. There are a few new civs to play as, but nothing ground breaking or that mods didn't already introduce. Government types are probably the most note worthy change as they allow you to have certain policies that impact the way your civ grows, but becomes a mangled mess of honestly pretty useless perks that become so cluttered with a max of 200 cards all with unique qualities that you have to read, memorize, and use on a whim with no organization. I actually did like the mini quest system which boosted the speed of research for a specific science or culture after completing a simple task.
If anything, this game is just a rebalance of Civ 5. The civs all have new perks and attributes, but nothing game changing. Religion had one or two new aspects added to it but is still more of a chore than a feature to boost your own religion while fighting the others. The map is probably uglier than ever now that the fog of war completely devoids the map of color. The tech and culture tree icons are very cartoonish which at times makes it difficult to even identify what you are looking at at first glance. The action buttons on units were also re-arranged and workers now have a "harvest resource" conveinently in the exact location of the generic improvement button in civ 5, which can become infurriating when you accidentally destroy a luxery resource you meant to set an improvement on. City states are no longer bribed by simply coin which is nice I suppose.
I just don't see what this game offers as an improvement to the last game. I understand that each game has it's own flair and qualities, but sequals usually have SOMETHING that new and worth it's own game and not just a DLC to the last one. I see nothing that merits this game as a sequal, nothing ground breaking or major at all. None of the changes positively enhanced the game or even remotely improved the experience from civ 5. It is as if they simply re-arranged some buttons, changed the civ perks, and changed the graphics and were just preying on the fans to buy it because the of the name, which is exactly what happened unfortunately. I actually waited 3 months after release because I was worried about this and I am sad to see that I was right.

Bitesize Review - STAR WARS™ - Dark Forces
The Good:
- Sounds really remind me of the movies
- Great doom shooter feel
- Quite a few different levels and enemies to encounter
- Puzzles were difficult but really rewarding to solve
- Simplified Digitized Star Wars music is great
- There are cutscenes and mission briefing screens that add a lot in terms of story
The Bad:
- The default game does not allow looking up and down with the mouse
- Much like Doom there are moments where you will get stuck
- You CAN NOT SAVE AT ALL in the middle of a level ("power through and finish it all in one go" or "quit and go back to the start")
- The graphics can cause my eyes to strain while playing this, with the mix of low resolution 2D and 3D models (but this is just a personal thing, can't really fault the game for it, it happens to me with Doom/Duke as well, but I did want to mention it etc.)
The Verdict:
Others have said it and it really does sum it up perfectly - this is essentially a Star Wars doom game.
I will say though in terms of things it does better then Doom include having an actual story with characters and cutscenes, and there are complex puzzles in the game that are really rewarding to solve that really set it apart from Doom and similar games.
However since the game is so much like Doom it does have a lot of the same issues as Doom - namely fixed X Axis aiming, getting stuck and not knowing what to do in the level is also common (often you just missed picking up a key or finding the object you can interact with), and the graphics (atleast for me) caused my eyes to strain a bit after playing it. Also the fact that you can not quick save really should be mentioned, it's not a deal breaker but it does suck when you want to turn off the game but you're 2/3 through a level and can't save your progress.
All in all though if you are a fan of old school shooters like Doom or Duke Nukem and like Star Wars as well - this game is great. Highly Recommended!

Honestly, I was ready to give up just a couple hours into this game: the camera was constantly zooming in and out when I walked by nearby objects (which is the entire time), the controls felt off no matter how I set the sensitivity, and the stealth mechanics seemed inconsistent.
It's a shame that this game makes a terrible first impression, cause the first 2 problems can be fixed off the bat (look in community guides for the 'Camera Jerking Fix') with a little text file editing. The dev team should have done that for us PC users anyway. With those initial nags out of the way, I could focus on the gameplay better and got a grip on the stealth mechanics after a couple missions.
Don't expect a really tight action game (this is an action RPG after all), but DO expect the action to be fun on its own terms. I beat the game twice; taking a stealth route the first time, then a guns-blazing route the second time. Both approaches worked well and were almost equally satisfying. Generally, the levels were easier playing as a stealthy character, but the boss fights were much easier as a walking tank character.
I haven't even touched on the story which is the meat and potatoes of this game: it is AWESOME. You have a limited time to answer to other characters in a 'suave', 'aggressive', or 'professional' manner. As far as I know, this game originated the type of dialogue system also found in The Walking Dead. Your timed responses actively shape the story and you must deal with the (sometimes serious) consequences. Occasionally you don't get enough time to think things through but it's usually timed in such a way to make the conversations flow naturally. I won't ruin anything, but will mention that I immediately started a new game after the first go-around to try and uncover more of the story. Can't think of the last game I was that eager to play though again.
Overall it has rough but enjoyable gameplay, and a great story with high replay value. 8/10

I ended up having to alt tab between the game and a wiki to find out my abilities on the fly.  That coupled with the fact either no one spoke English or spoke at all made it frustrating.
All that being said, the game play is solid and tight.  Shots feel like they are landing and missing when they should, lag is at a minimum and abilities feel well thought out. The diversity between these heros and the ones in other games is enough to give it a place next to them.
I am guessing the ballance system starts you out at 0; after playing overwatch for a few months I feel like I was playing with slow motion bots.  I guess that is better than starting you out as a pro and getting your face smashed in to the ground when you start.  But in my 5th game I was still consistently getting 10-15 kill streaks.
I would guess the game is 85% there.  A few more maps, maybe different game modes and an in game system to let you see what your skills do is all that is really see missing.  Worth the price of free for sure, maybe even the 20 bucks they are asking for "all heroes".
The only real down side I see if that it can’t ever truly be competitive when RNG drops determine your stats.  I am guessing as people collect cards and the playing fields are evened out they will introduce new ones for us to buy.

After seeing all those positive reviews my expectations were high. The main thing that made me refund it was the 30 fps cap, the game didn't feel smooth at all and the camera movement felt very twitchy for lack of a better word. Especially with a Xbone gamepad, it was a little better with the mouse and keyboard. My problem with mouse and keyboard was the re-binding of keys were limited, I could not use my extra mouse buttons and I could only add more bindings to the keyboard, not remove existing ones. So space will always change weapons for instance, you couldn't use space for something else, which I wanted. Well, you could but then space would do 2 things, change weapons and whatever you added, which made it unusable.
The game itself wasn't that bad, but certainly not worth the "Overwhelmingly Positive". I expected more of the mutations, I was hoping they were unique to the characters and changed the appearence. But they were more like meh powerups, such as deal damage when you take damage, slower enemy bullets, "extra-life" and stuff like that. The characters didn't feel that different to each other either, each character basically has a gimmick ability, for example one character can roll and another character can pull enemies and items to him. But the gameplay still felt the same betweeen all the characters. There wasn't enough difference between them. It came down to shoot stuff with guns + 1 gimmick ability.
The game didn't feel very random either which rogue-lites normally do. Generally you want a new and fresh start whenever you die. But the maps, albeit randomly made corridors, always were the same in the same order and you always encountered the same bosses in the same order. Take bindings of Isaac for instance, there is a chance you encounter boss X on floor Y, but in this game you always encounter boss X on floor Y. This, the not so different characters and the meh powerup mutations made the game feel very similar, too similar, between playthroughs. Not something you want in a rogue-lite.
The game feels very overhyped and I can't recommend it at full price. I might give it another chance when there's a big discount but my impressions is that it isn't that good and the 30 fps cap stands out like a sore thumb.

Microsoft Flight Simulator has been THE simulation program for many flightsimmers out there for years.
From the smallest prop planes to the biggest jumbojets, people have enjoyed FSX, and surely will for the coming time.
Many add-ons have been made for FSX, and while FSX:SE is slightly different, a lot of add-ons have been updated to work under this version as well. Also, while Gamespy is no longer, multiplayer has been fixed to work via the Steam platform itself.
Does this mean it's the holy grail for home user simulation? Not really. While at the moment it's a working platform, Dovetail does not have the appropiate license to make big changes to the program like Lockheed Martin is allowed to in their Prepar3D program, based on the same Microsoft software.
In the long run (years) FSX:SE in its current form will be obsolete and outdated. While LH Prepar3D and LR X-Plane are actively being developed, FSX:SE does not have that luxury.
At the moment it's still an awesome platform, and anyone who wants to fly can do so no problem in FSX:SE. Including all those awesome add-ons that have been made for FSX over the years.
Hopefully Dovetail Games will be able to upgrade the program in one way or another in the future.
