Honestly, I was ready to give up just a couple hours into this game: the camera was constantly zooming in and out when I walked by nearby objects (which is the entire time), the controls felt off no matter how I set the sensitivity, and the stealth mechanics seemed inconsistent.
It's a shame that this game makes a terrible first impression, cause the first 2 problems can be fixed off the bat (look in community guides for the 'Camera Jerking Fix') with a little text file editing. The dev team should have done that for us PC users anyway. With those initial nags out of the way, I could focus on the gameplay better and got a grip on the stealth mechanics after a couple missions.
Don't expect a really tight action game (this is an action RPG after all), but DO expect the action to be fun on its own terms. I beat the game twice; taking a stealth route the first time, then a guns-blazing route the second time. Both approaches worked well and were almost equally satisfying. Generally, the levels were easier playing as a stealthy character, but the boss fights were much easier as a walking tank character.
I haven't even touched on the story which is the meat and potatoes of this game: it is AWESOME. You have a limited time to answer to other characters in a 'suave', 'aggressive', or 'professional' manner. As far as I know, this game originated the type of dialogue system also found in The Walking Dead. Your timed responses actively shape the story and you must deal with the (sometimes serious) consequences. Occasionally you don't get enough time to think things through but it's usually timed in such a way to make the conversations flow naturally. I won't ruin anything, but will mention that I immediately started a new game after the first go-around to try and uncover more of the story. Can't think of the last game I was that eager to play though again.
Overall it has rough but enjoyable gameplay, and a great story with high replay value. 8/10

After seeing all those positive reviews my expectations were high. The main thing that made me refund it was the 30 fps cap, the game didn't feel smooth at all and the camera movement felt very twitchy for lack of a better word. Especially with a Xbone gamepad, it was a little better with the mouse and keyboard. My problem with mouse and keyboard was the re-binding of keys were limited, I could not use my extra mouse buttons and I could only add more bindings to the keyboard, not remove existing ones. So space will always change weapons for instance, you couldn't use space for something else, which I wanted. Well, you could but then space would do 2 things, change weapons and whatever you added, which made it unusable.
The game itself wasn't that bad, but certainly not worth the "Overwhelmingly Positive". I expected more of the mutations, I was hoping they were unique to the characters and changed the appearence. But they were more like meh powerups, such as deal damage when you take damage, slower enemy bullets, "extra-life" and stuff like that. The characters didn't feel that different to each other either, each character basically has a gimmick ability, for example one character can roll and another character can pull enemies and items to him. But the gameplay still felt the same betweeen all the characters. There wasn't enough difference between them. It came down to shoot stuff with guns + 1 gimmick ability.
The game didn't feel very random either which rogue-lites normally do. Generally you want a new and fresh start whenever you die. But the maps, albeit randomly made corridors, always were the same in the same order and you always encountered the same bosses in the same order. Take bindings of Isaac for instance, there is a chance you encounter boss X on floor Y, but in this game you always encounter boss X on floor Y. This, the not so different characters and the meh powerup mutations made the game feel very similar, too similar, between playthroughs. Not something you want in a rogue-lite.
The game feels very overhyped and I can't recommend it at full price. I might give it another chance when there's a big discount but my impressions is that it isn't that good and the 30 fps cap stands out like a sore thumb.

It's tower defense. Is it the best tower defense I've ever played? No. Is it good? It's... OK. It's fun. That said, there are some flaws to the game, and pretty glaring ones, too.
Difficulty is... off. The ramp in difficulty outpaces the cash reward per shell destroyed. It also outstrips the end of round bonus. This means that while the first few rounds are fine, and seem almost trivial, your ability to place and upgrade towers lags far behind the damage output required to keep up with the waves.
Multiplayer is pretty broken. The address in the Join Multiplayer box is 127.0.0.1. That's not multiplayer. That's connecting to yourself to play with yourself. To join a multiplayer game, you need either the IP address, or you need the domain... and the host has to have configured their router properly. We had a network engineer to figure things out on his end to allow us to play, because none of this is readily apparent. And once the round is over? You're kicked back to the main menu, and have to enter the domain information again. Every single time. Same difficulty problems exist in multiplayer as in single player. In fact, they are exacerbated, as rewards and end of round bonus is divided among players. Five of us played, and it took one person saving all of their cash until round 17 to be able to afford a plasma turret.
Even the enemies have issues. Have a color deficiency? Good luck. Finally managed to kill that last D4 working its way around the track? Oh, no, that was just the first set of shells... it was a D4 of Get Bent, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥, because now it's back to a D... A Lot. Furthermore, nothing seems to correspond to anything else in terms of how many lives lost. Was that enemy that got through worth five, or HOLY POOP, WE ARE DEAD!
The numbers need to be reworked. Badly. The network issues need addressing. Post haste. And yet... it's fun. Five of us spent a lot of time playing this in spite of the network and difficulty issues. We would spend a lot more time playing it if these problems didn't exist.
I was going to recommend it, but for a game billed as 3D CO-OP Tower Defense, it fails pretty hard on the allowing you to play cooperatively. It has too many flaws to really recommend it. Fix a few of these, and maybe I could give it a thumbs up, but as it exists now, no, I'm not sure I can.

I don't scare easily and while Alan Wake didn't scare me outright, it provided a constant state of creepiness that was continuously chilling. The characters and story along with the storytelling are awesome. The graphics, photography, and camera work are stunning. The one major blemish is the gameplay which isn't all that bad, it just isn't all that good either. However using a flashlight to fight off the darkness is a pretty cool concept and the execution comes off pretty nicely. Although I have to admit the game didn't draw me in to play non-stop from start to finish--ultimately starting the game in September and not actually finishing it until November.
So what is it about Alan Wake that makes it so standoffish? Well for starters, the gameplay starts to get repetitiously dull. Some of the forest paths are really long laying ground for more hordes of Taken than one person can deal with before it just becomes mundane. It is kind of broken up with some areas to explore in between, but it wasn't enough. The other aspect which may sound weird is that I never really felt like I took the role as Alan Wake. Instead it felt more like I was just moving the story forward and watching Alan unfold as opposed to being a part of critical decisions. Fortunately the chapters are broken up very nicely into roughly two hour segments with good musical intermissions allowing players whatever amount of time they need before jumping into the next chapter.
Overall, a fantastic game and a must play in my book.

For many, Alan Wake is "the flashlight game". For Remedy, it is their love letter to Steven King. For me, it was the only exclusive for the Xbox360 that looked good. Whichever of these camps you relate to, you are experiencing some of Alan Wake's best qualities.
The flashlight mechanic is simply inspired. I have never seen anything quite like it before. The surprisingly large environment is a fantastic combination of dark, foggy, and forboding. The PC version of Alan Wake includes the soundtrack, two (excellent) bonus episodes, and the fantastic song (and music video to) "War" by Poets of the Fall. Although Alan Wake is not a straight-up horror game, there are also some "make you jump"  (and memorable) moments regarding the enemies, especially when they come from behind. It is also quite thrilling to be running through the woods, out of ammo, madly scrounging around in a shack for some shotgun shells as an enemy wielding a chainsaw stomps your way.
As good as all this is, there are some downsides to Alan Wake.  Most controls are competent, but the dodge mechanic is completely useless. The plot, although solid, is quite long and very complicated, although playing the game frequently can help you understand it. Animations are rather rubbery, especially during cutscenes. Environment graphics are some of the best I've seen, but even with a computer well over the recommended requirements, I can only play it on "Low" settings without enormous framerate drops. I also had some strange issue with the sound not coming through correctly (I couldn't hear someone speaking until I had the camera facing them--and I was right next to them) until I upgraded my processor from a Dual Core to a Quad Core.
Overall, Alan Wake is what I consider a great "B" game. A bit like some of the movie adaptations of Steven King's books, Alan Wake's shortcomings keep it from greatness, but it is nowhere near broken enough to be ignored. Rumors abound that there may be a sequel in the works. I certainly hope so. I would like to see where this story goes.

I don't normally write reviews, but the bad rep this game is getting for the micro transactions is just ridiculous.
Gameplay
If you've ever played Shadow of Mordor, you most likely have a general idea of what to expect here. Superhuman wraith powers with Assassin's Creed like movement (mostly). However there are some important additions here that really add a lot to the whole "Push one button to run, jump, climb, cook dinner, etc" formula. A particular move in here includes a 'double' jump that adds an extra layer of precision on top of the semi automated parkour. While it may not sound like much, it adds a dynamic that makes you feel like you're doing something engaging, rather than just holding forward and spacebar.
A variety of new moves were added that creates extremely satisfying moments, like aerial bow sharpshooting, which looks awesome and feels awesome to do. While there are a ton of extra additions, there are some caveats that I feel were almost a regression in a way. The execution move is no long tied directly to your combo meter. Instead, you have to build up a second bar called "Wrath", which then allows you to unlock the ability to execute. While I understand the mentality most likely was to prevent spamming executions, the Orcs now can adapt to moves you use repeatedly, so is it not redundant to throttle them? It's not a horrible change, just a questionable one.
Map Layout
The map is separated into sections, cutting off the somewhat openworld aspect that we saw in the previous title, but this is, in my opinion, better. Free roam games have taken the market by storm lately, but lack the substance and variety you'd find in games such as this. While it is free roam, it isn't just one giant map that some bloke made in Blender out of a plane using some topology tools. The different areas that are presented to us include a wide variety of environments, making each one feel refreshing when you travel to them. Also, the new fast travel locations are spread about thoughtfully, yet sparingly around the map. You wont always be able to fast travel directly next to your destination, but hey, that's why you spent your skill points on those movement perks, right? Maybe brand some Captains on the way there? Little bit of travel time isn't an issue in this game.
Graphics
Seeing the reception for this one is a strange one for me. I feel the game looks great (Note: I haven't tried out the HD texture pack as of writing this). I have seen a few complaints about recycled animations and whatnot, but it seems like nitpicking at best, whining at worst. Yes, some animations were present in the first game, but we're also playing as the same character as before. What, is Talion and Celebrimbor going to completely change their attacks just because of a new game? That's like saying Goku shouldn't use the Kamehameha for more than one episode. The animations never looks bad to begin with, so it's definitely not the issue everyone makes it out to be.
Also, watching all the characters interact with eachother, from Graug's duking it out with eachother to Captains having a scuffle, it all looks very organic. The animations are fluid and quite honestly sets the bar for how seamless characters should interact with eachother visually.
Story
The story is absolutely a step above it's predecessor. While I haven't completed it yet, the first character you brand in the game is hilarious and extremely likeable. I got a few good laughs out of him and was slightly sad to move onto the next area without him.
*Side note: I got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me against a captain and when I respawned, the dialogue was as follows:
Celebrimbor: Maybe next time we cou-
Talion: Don't. Just- don't.
This is funny, but also helps you bond with the character. I believe it's called a personality? Haven't seen one of those in characters in recent games.*
Micro transactions
If you are seriously so upset about the fact you can pay to speed up game progess in a primarily single player game, you need to get your priorities straight. During my time playing I never found the microtransactions to be overly intrusive, and have not myself taken part in them. Is it a questionable business tactic? Sure. Want to make a statement? Don't complain and moan about it, just don't buy anything off the store. It shouldn't be your reason for downvoting the game.
Technical Issues
Framerate wise, the game has run perfect at 60fps for me on Ultra, however I did have a rather strange issue. When I first booted up the game the cutscenes and audio were all playing as if they were an old VHS tape on fast forward. After some tinkering with my audio settings I found the solution was to drop the quality of your primary audio device down to 48000 Hz. I don't notice a difference in quality, and the game now works properly, so that's something I don't particularly have positive or negative feelings for. Seems odd to have the issue, but it's not impossible to fix. If some techno guru could explain what it is about your audio quality that would do that to the game, I'd like an explanation just out of curiousity.
Final Verdict
Like LOTR? Go ahead and buy it. Like Assassin's Creed still, somehow? Go ahead and buy it. Get butthurt over nonintrusive micro transactions? Probably not the place for you.
The game is great and I feel like it was money well spent at full price.

Alpha Protocol is a fairly decent game.  It has a lot of promise as an action-espionage game that combines stealth gameplay with social intrigue and roleplaying.  While it falls short, the target it was aiming for was a fairly high one, which puts the game at above average in my book. Negatives:  The game is pretty buggy, the save system is a course checkpoint system, and the action element is really lackluster.

I would recommend this game to people looking to invest their time in the setting and story, but not to those looking for to blow up some bad guys.

Rough Around the Edges, but a Gem Nonetheless
Obsidian's Alpha Protocol is like a cross between Deus Ex, Mass Effect, and Espionage. Deus Ex from its multi-method approach to your missions, Mass Effect for character choice and customizaion, and the three JBs (James Bond, Jack Bauer, and Jason Bourne) form your character Micheal Thorton's personality as the situation calls for it.
The game is a first person RPG akin to Mass Effect, but with more emphasis on the RPG part. You need to invest skill points into your skills if you expect yourself to be compitent. Even after mastering some of those said skills you still will experience a bit of a challenge, at least on Hard. The game isn't molded around 1 play style, either. Wanna sneak in and sneak out on a mission? Do it. Do you want to leave the mission occasionally worrying about tripping on one of your victims? Do it!
Also, unlike Mass Effect which has to factor the choices of a trilogy and trying to please everybody, Alpha Protocol didn't have such an expectation. Your choices will have an active impact on the missions. NPCs may have some kind of impression of you from actions and may or may not want to work for you because of it, or simply eliminating an arms dealer can jeopordize intelligence acquisition. And there's not always the "everybody lives" choice either, so you have to stick to the choices you make and how you influence NPCs.
The presentation could have used some polish. The character animations  really show their seems sometimes, and Michael's dead ragdolling can cause him to rocket off somewhere. The inability to quick save really hampers some of the problem solving aspects, but somebody could argue that it's to prevent save-scumming. To me, it's a pain in the butt. Also, bodies just disappear. Having to hide them could have introduced another aspect to stealth, but alas the bodies just vanish like in Metal Gear Solid 1. Also, like most Obsidian games, expect a bug or two, but nothing gamebreaking.
All and all, Alpha Protocol is a great game well worth it's price. The dialogue is sharp, snappy, and often times funny. The story has plenty of twists and curves to keep you interested, along with some well-designed characters that can keep you guessing. I'd recommend it regardless of the lack of needed polish. If you like your Action getting on your RPGs, this one is a winner.

STAR WARS - Dark Forces is one of my most favorite nostalgic and memorable DOS Video Games of all time, that I use to play when I was a child. Though it's considered apart of the extended universe, there are several accounts in more recent STAR WARS titles that have encorporated the ideas of the Dark Forces series as Kyle Katarn, the protagonist, assists the rebellion in stopping the Imperial General Rom Mohc and his plans to spread Project Dark Soldier. Gameplay is akin to a classic Doom format, control-wise, and visibly. However unlike Doom, Dark Forces allows the player to use the Num pad to look around the environment, using 3D multi-layered maps, opposed to id's raycasting 2.5D top-down level configuration. Dark Forces can be VERY dim and rather claustrophobic at times, and can also be very punishing to straightforward players. However to its credit, Dark Forces paces itself as it gradually builds in enigmatic atmosphere, difficulty and anticipation of the ever looming Dark Troopers. Coinciding with this, it has surprisingly decent voice acting, satisfying weapons, and a rather unique DOS MIDI soundtrack. This is definently a game I think anyone new or more accustomed to the franchise should check out.

I bought this game when it was in its early access period(For 13 dollars multiplied by 4. Yes, my currency sucks) and I recently exprienced most of the content, meaning I can finally review it.
Nuclear Throne is a hard(and I mean HARD. at about 9 hours you'll be just getting used to the third area) roguelite top down shooter with a huge variety of weapons(above 140 I believe), a roster of 12(and a few secret) characters, 7 main areas(split into levels) with secret equivelants of most of them, and full of content.
Every session is quite short, and there is no end unless you choose to end the run.
Every enemy drops EXP upon death(rads), and when you level up you can choose 1 mutation(modifiers) out of a selection of 4 every time for 9 levels, and get a special choice on level 10. Mutations vary from trivial things such as faster move speed to kills reducing reload time.
The devs are extremley helpful and active on the forums(at least during the early acces period and until they finish updating the released product) and the community is the last one to be called a toxic community.
The game's lore was told partly through little references in-game, lore bits and pieces from twitch streams of the dev and more, and is worth a read on the wiki(Also run by a great guy). Nobody knows all of it(except for the developers), but what we do know is pretty damn good.
After defeating the first final boss, if you do a thing the community will eventually notify you about(or wiki), you will loop. Looping is going through the entire game all over again and will never end until you die/get either of the 2 endings.
It includes new exclusive content and so much more. The loops are late game, and since they can last forever, the game has to become even more brutal with each loop, and on loop 1 already, without spoiling, you will notice a difficulty spike.
-Full of areas to explore, enemies to shoot and die to, weapons, synergies and more.
-Will keep you playing for a good amount of time, but still is fit for short sessions if you're just passing time
-Amazing and helpful community
-Fantastic soundtrack(Personal favorites are Frozen City's B-Track(Ode on the official soundtrack) , and The Nuclear Throne)
-Great pixel art that is just beautiful to look at.
-It takes a while for RNGesus to make some good weapons become common in the pool after the first time they drop
-Sometimes the game would do flat out unfair actions, such a certain telefragging enemy
-Inconsistent difficulty curve. Its smooth until the third boss, spikes, stays that way, lowers down a bit in the 7th area's boss and on loops spikes up again and goes through the same curve
-Sometimes you just get screwed(even on spawn). RNGesus may not have mercy.
-Some secrets that without a wiki/datamining no one would have found.
TLDR: NT is a great game to sink hours into, as well as to play in short sessions, is hard, but rewarding and fun, as well as full of content to exprience.

For many, Alan Wake is "the flashlight game". For Remedy, it is their love letter to Steven King. For me, it was the only exclusive for the Xbox360 that looked good. Whichever of these camps you relate to, you are experiencing some of Alan Wake's best qualities.
The flashlight mechanic is simply inspired. I have never seen anything quite like it before. The surprisingly large environment is a fantastic combination of dark, foggy, and forboding. The PC version of Alan Wake includes the soundtrack, two (excellent) bonus episodes, and the fantastic song (and music video to) "War" by Poets of the Fall. Although Alan Wake is not a straight-up horror game, there are also some "make you jump"  (and memorable) moments regarding the enemies, especially when they come from behind. It is also quite thrilling to be running through the woods, out of ammo, madly scrounging around in a shack for some shotgun shells as an enemy wielding a chainsaw stomps your way.
As good as all this is, there are some downsides to Alan Wake.  Most controls are competent, but the dodge mechanic is completely useless. The plot, although solid, is quite long and very complicated, although playing the game frequently can help you understand it. Animations are rather rubbery, especially during cutscenes. Environment graphics are some of the best I've seen, but even with a computer well over the recommended requirements, I can only play it on "Low" settings without enormous framerate drops. I also had some strange issue with the sound not coming through correctly (I couldn't hear someone speaking until I had the camera facing them--and I was right next to them) until I upgraded my processor from a Dual Core to a Quad Core.
Overall, Alan Wake is what I consider a great "B" game. A bit like some of the movie adaptations of Steven King's books, Alan Wake's shortcomings keep it from greatness, but it is nowhere near broken enough to be ignored. Rumors abound that there may be a sequel in the works. I certainly hope so. I would like to see where this story goes.

Asguaard is a potentially-intriguing retro RPG that suffers from a bad case of quantity over quality.
It has an expansive world, with no usable world map and several areas with caves full of monsters that will kill you in one hit if you wander into them while going through the otherwise-on-level area.
It has sprawling dungeons, with no way to keep track of where you are other than pencil and paper, and where the only healing points inside cost half of your gold (literally, that's how they work).
It has hidden areas and bonuses, often completely invisible so no matter how much you explore, you always feel like you're missing out.
It has a wide variety of abilities you can learn, by tracking down NPCs scattered across the world (and make sure you track them down in the right order, or you'll just have to come all the way back).
It has its fair share of boss battles, which mostly consist of slowly whittling down the boss with basic attacks while desperately hoping it doesn't kill too many of your party members in too short of a time. Beyond some initial stat-boosting skills, you're basically stuck with basic skills unless you want to run out of mana - and don't even think about using real skills against anything other than bosses, or you'll barely get a room into the dungeon before you're out of mana. Combat in general is not a great experience.
It has a reasonable amount of dialogue, which you'll likely want to avoid reading as much as possible. It's pretty rough.
It contains about four different art styles, interspersed randomly - enemy art in particular often seems to come entirely out of left field.
I'll give it the benefit of the doubt and assume it does indeed have an 'amazing fantasy soundtrack', but regardless, I can't recommend this - certainly not at this price point.

An ingenious, abstract & minimalist 3D tower defence game. Watch little geometric shapes crawl around labyrinthine objects as you build increasingly ridiculous trees of laser-death to make them explode into a rainbow of carnage.
Gameplay is a mix of classic TD optimisation with plotting & extending your nodes to give the maximum amount of turrets (which each have a hemispherical firing arc) the maximum amount of roadspace to fire upon. "just clump a bunch together around a slowing-turret" definitely does not get you through levels alone here- Expect to fail a few times before you get the a) swing of it & b) unlocks to compete, even on easy mode. Thankfully the unlocks are frequent & generous, and can often change turrets in quite radical ways.
Highly recommended, and an utter no-brainer for such a price. Mindwarping but hypnotic, minimalist but deep.

When I first played shadow of mordor, I thought the idea of the nemesis system was something super unique, and although it had its problems, it was a work of art nonetheless. Shadow of War brings that Nemesis system back and builds upon it.
First things first, microtransactions:
Yes they are absolutely stupid, the game does not need them whatsoever. And I do think that there is shame to WB for trying to bring that into a single player game. I also think that if you liked the first game enough, the microtransactions are just something to ignore. Because literally everything else about the game is amazing.
Although we oppose the microtransactions, I think there are people (such as me), that do not really care. We won't be paying extra for these chests. We will, however, be immersing ourselves into the different regions in the game. Commanding our followers, infiltrating our spies, and playing every mission until we get to the finish line (with breaks of course). If you loved Middle-Earth Shadow of Mordor,  don't steer your head away from this game, because there is still so much else to offer.
The game builds upon the nemesis system and makes it even more complicated. I found myself being ambushed randomly, shaming others, as well as "building my army". When too many orcs were on the screen, things would get hectic and trying to kill my nemesis or revive my followers would lead to decisions having to be made, and consequences thereafter. The game does a great job of personalizing every orc I come in contact with. The story is alright, obviously we can't expect it to live upto to the hype of the original LOTR. But it does a decent job nonetheless.
To summarize, I would recommend this game 100%, if you were a fan of the first game, I think the $60 price tag isn't something to worry about. But I also think that if you have your doubts or just aren't as big of a fan as I am, then wait for it to go on sale. It will, and I think you will realize it's still an amazing game even if you have to put tons of hours into the game to get the true ending.

This is a puzzle-platformer broken up into a ton of different short levels. The levels each use one of several different mechanics: pressing a button to rotate the level, trying to get little circle dudes to run into boxes, making clones of yourself to step on switches. The constant variation in mechanics gives the game a WarioWare-like feel, particularly in the shorter early levels. Much like in WarioWare, my enjoyment of the levels has varied and it feels like a game that does a number of different things decently rather than doing any one thing well.
Perhaps the worst levels are those with roving enemies. Usually in a puzzly game like this, the enemies follow a set pattern. You analyze that pattern and figure out how to avoid the enemies. This game elected for seemingly random movement, which can lead to essentially unavoidable deaths when an enemy unexpectedly moves into your or traps you in a corner. Thankfully most levels don't have enemies and you don't need to complete every level to progress.
It is worth noting that while I would call this a puzzle-platformer, the puzzle aspect of the game is much less prominent than in something like Braid. Perhaps only half of the levels have puzzle elements, and those puzzle elements generally boil down to stepping on switches or rotating the level.
The game has support for an Xbox 360 controller and that is how you should play it. Playing with a keyboard is awful.
The music is kinda bad and the sound-effects don't add anything. Mute the game and put on your own music.
For only $5, I would recommend Adventures of Shuggy to anyone who enjoys short bursts of platforming with relatively light puzzle-solving.

The strategy games of my youth were all turn-based because of the limits of the processors. The older I get and the slower my reaction become, so my desire for turn strategy grows. Unfortunately developers have moved away from the Laser Squad/Sabre Team stylings of yore and demand ever-twitchier players.
Fortunately Klei, famous already for the amazing Mask of the Ninja and Don't Starve, have turned their talents to the action-point loving genre and produced a masterpiece. Everything is beautifully balanced, level generation is partly randomised but always feels cohesive and, like any good roguelike, there is plenty to unlock.
The graphics are excellent and the sound equally so, but the real stroke of genius is how flexible and adaptable it is. You can tune it to anything from a game that makes Peggle seem complex into the most difficult game since a blindfolded Dark Souls run. Hugely recommended with masses of replayability, and now with the expansion even more options to try out.

This is a difficult one for me to review. I was really mixed as I loved most things but hated one
thing with a passion. This is a first person shooter like doom but with jumping and puzzles.
It starts with a character named kyle katran who is hired by the rebels to steal the plans to the death star. The strongest points are as follows. The story while minimal is effective. The shooting is good with plenty weapons and while it doesn't seem like it at first, lots of enemy types. I also like some of the puzzles as they are a nice break away from the action. The sound is really solid despite limitations, and they put the star wars music in the game to good effect. And the graphics really nail the star wars feel. Though it can be hard to tell the diffrence between the switches and walls since everthing looks colorful and high-tech.
But this leads to my biggest problem. The level design is awful at some points. Even with a map I would get lost so much. The first few levels are fine. But levels like mission four was terrible. I followed a narrow path that lead to a switch. A door opened and...dead end. Turns out I was supposed to go to a door hidden in a path you could only see if you branched off and looked down. In the games defense not all the levels are like this. Mission six and seven were good. But it was enough though that it halted progression for a while, breaking the flow of the game and made me frustrated. Over all this IS a good game despite any issues I have. Though I think there are much better star wars games.

Synonymy is a different kind of puzzle game. It has a simple way of scoring you, based on your path through words and if you reach your target word. It could sometimes stand to be a little less vague on how scoring works, but if you're doing poorly or great you'll know soon enough. English or lit majors might like this.
It doesn't go for platforms or mazes or simple shape rearrangement, but rather finding a path through different words to get to a target one. A little confusing at first, but the clues such as sound and a way to go back to previous words is good for one to get a decent score. A way to 'mark' words that you've already tried would be a good system so you won't have to backtrack and keep guessing through a sea of words. Good for the cost if you're tired of the dozens of other tan gram puzzles on Steam.

Very nice alternitive if you do not like / if you can't spend money on Overwatch.
The most important question: "Is Paladins an Overwatch clone?"
Well, short awnser: I do not know. I've never played Overwatch, so i can't really compare. However, as a free to play alternitive to the Overwatch-"genre", it does it's job.
The game features 5v5 First person champion combat in 2 different game modes. Either game mode is ultimatively down to a single thing: Push the enemy back and the cart into their spawn. Being close to the cart makes him move forward, so it's quite objective-based.
The Champions available are divided into 4 different classes: Tank, Heal / Support, Damage, Flanker. The names speak for themselves. Getting the champions is quite easy, specializing their abilities as well. The only thing not so easy is changing a champions appearance because all the nice ones do cost real cash.
Of course the Dev's are up-to-date with their free to play model, so you obviously get the most stuff only by buying cases with random contents. Money-wasting intensifies.
The game does feature a competetive mode, but that one requries you to have lots of champions on a certain level to ensure people do know how to play the game.
Overall i do recommend the game, but only if you stick to your choice: Don't pay for a free to play game. If you like the game, consider buying a founders pack as if you were buying a full game, but do not start spending cash on skins on the like.

Hilariously over-the-top and thrillingly addicting, PWND is a crazy shooter game that combines rocket arena-style combat with “excessive celebration.” This game is as enjoyable as it is obnoxious, and it unapologetically encourages every player to be a bad loser and a shameless winner. In each match, two teams of three face off and try to kill each other as many times as possible; however, that is not all. A kill only counts if you “PWN” your opponent, which basically means taunting and dancing over their dead body. Moreover, it takes a small period of time to complete a “PWN,” and within that time, your opponent’s team member can find you, kill you, and PWN you instead. Each PWN gives your team a few points (in some “PWN zones” you can earn double the points), and the first team to get to 80 points wins the match. Not surprisingly, each match is full of death and destruction, stolen victories, and a whole lot of dancing. It taps into your competitive streak and hunger for vengeance, so definitely do not play this game if you are looking for a peaceful, relaxing activity. But the endless activity and interesting variety of characters is so exciting that you find yourself impatient to start the next round of exhilarating chaos.
Because the game is so fast-paced, speed and mobility are imperative to success. I am personally fairly new to playing PC games, so it was initially very challenging to orient myself and navigate my way around the map while trying to stay alive, let alone kill anyone. It was a steep learning curve to be sure, but once I got the hang of the controls I was able to earn my fair share of PWN’s with ease. Moreover, there are four different characters to choose from and play as, and they differ noticeably in terms of speed, power, and stealth. This allows you to find one that compliments your personal strengths and weaknesses and boosts your chances of victory. For example, my favorite character is Mack “the Law” Lawson, who takes the longest time to PWN an opponent but possesses the most stealth and defensive capabilities. The most stimulating matches take place when every team member fights as a different character, as it vividly showcases the best assets of each hero.
The one and only downside to this game is the wait time in between each match. The only game mode is playing with other live gamers on the server, and sometimes it can take 10 minutes before you get matched up with five other people. 10 minutes may not sound like a long time, but because the actual matches are so quick and short, it really breaks up the momentum of the game and tests your patience. Oftentimes it was the only reason why I stopped playing, so it would be great to even be able to play with computer bots while waiting for live players. Because I only played the Early Access version of PWND, I could not access the Custom Matches or Challenges. Hopefully these new game modes will not require as much waiting around.
To conclude, PWND is all about the adrenaline rush. Do not expect a serious storyline; rather, expect your inner immaturity to unleash itself in full force. But as long as you enter the game with a lighthearted attitude and play with enthusiasm, PWND will reward you with rollicking fun and epic action.  9/10

this game is an all time favourite of Aldorlea- it is a story based around 2 earth children Glen -male 17years - and Rayanne - female 19 years who find themselves transported to another world -Asguaard - home of dwarves and fairies. There they meet Grom - a dwarf who tells them that someone has opened up Pandora's Box and let out plagues to destroy their home and only earthlings with souls can save it. So begins a story that depicts friendship, trust, dependancy. loyalty and sacrifice as each character grows and develops throughout the story. The game itself is a long game taking the player through many areas on a world map. There are 99 hidden areas and 51 hidden magical rooms to find. Some areas are only assessible once  so saving often is a must. Saving can be done on the world map but in dungeons and some parts only faries can be used to save and full heal with these cost gold. A guide  is a must if you wish to find all the hidden areas.
There is a 4 level option- starting at story mode and a choice of step encounters for enemies. Combat system is mostly the same as other early rpg's  and Grom can learn a skill that helps with enemy knowledge.
There is a skill list to customise and improve the party- some of the skills are only available to 1 member and specialized skill for their chosen weapon. Each member can choose 1 0f 2 weapons to use ( these cannot be changed throughout the game but  of course you can re-play the game using the other weapon or level). Skills are available from hidden areas and talking with npc's. each skill has 3 levels - expert, master and guru
The ending is rather sad and does leave the player with many questions to be answered. It would have been wonderful if the dev, could have made a second game to follow on from the ending to tie up loose ends.
The overall graphics are beautiful as is the music and a lot of effort was put into the making of the game.
There is a lot of walking in the game and returning to the same areas until you get the airship which then makes moving around the world map much easier.
It is not a dungeon - slogging game more a discovery and exploration type.
Overall it is a great game to play and I would recommend it to players

I am writing this review due to receiving a free guide. I've played lots of RPGMaker games and several Aldorea games. Aldorea games are enjoyable but they usually stick to their game mechanics with each game which i personally don't like. To explain:  The biggest peeve i have with Aldorea games is that they hide way too much stuff; areas, rooms, gear, items, money. This leads to 2 problems. With such a large amount of hidden things they force you to buy the guide to be able to get a complete game experience with their games forcing more money out of customers. The other thing this leads to is searching every nook and cranny which quickly becomes boring and tedious. Not to mention a huge amount of unnecessary wear on a controller. Another thing they tend to do is have random encounters which becomes frustrating because it ruins your ability to explore. While exploring you are frequently thrown into battles and when its over your left with remembering what you were doing and what you have already done. They do this mostly with their earlier games. The last thing they tend to do is allow missing during combat. What makes the combat enjoyable is being able to implement strategies but it screws off your carefully planned strategy when your big killer blow that would drop them misses and since they are still alive they swiftly proceed to kick you in the nards and now you are taking damage and what not when you had a solid plan - this to me takes out most of the strategy for the player and is frustrating and annoying. Even after all that they are still enjoyable games for the money. I mean, how can you not have fun. I have been playing video games since pong, com64, asteroids, i was there. All that time, my first and last love has always been old school turn-based rpg games and I really love RPGMaker games. These kind of games have it all- Exploring and dungeon crawling, character and party development, cool equipment, skills, and spells to create a party to your style, quests, adventure, and you even get a story and often enjoyable music. I believe that the only reason that you wouldn't have a good time is that for whatever reason you decide you don't want to because even though during play there are some things I don't like I always have a great time. Don't poo-poo on old school RPG games and RPGMaker games, they are always fun and if you don't like them, I think it's more on you than the games. I really hope that Aldorea and all the other RPGMaker game developers continue to keep pumping out games forever. Even though they can improve they still put out very enjoyable games. I appreciate all the hard work that they put into what they do. I have talked to the developers and they put their hearts and souls into these games, earning a living doing what they love. My hats off to all involved. These games are inexpensive and a great value for the gaming hours to price ratio. Love it!!!

Slightly boring till about half way, when it suddenly grips you and you realise you're playing a great game!
Alan Wake is a writer who becomes trapped in a genuine horror story about darkness and an obsession with light. Is this simply a nightmare? Or is there something more to this twisted, dark version of the little mountain village named Bright Falls?
He's attacked by monsters that are only vulnerable in the light, so his greatest weapon is his flashlight. This is greatly embedded in the gameplay, where enemies take no damage until you've exposed them in the light, and you're constantly hoping you have enough batteries and ammo while you run from street light to street light, fending off the darkness. Batteries and ammo are scarce, so count your bullets well, kids!
The combat is very frustrating to get control of but once you've got it, it becomes really fun! Especially dodging takes a while to master, and this in combination with its considerable difficult makes this game frustrating at first.
The game makes it easy on you in regards of horror, though. There's lots of scare-effects but overall the game is more scary in terms of atmosphere than in jumpscares or gore or anything like that.  So it never gets INSANELY scary. I myself, being the big wimp that I am, didn't mind this at all.
The Good: Original concept and gamplay, great and complicated story, teaches you to save ammo the best you can, creepy atmosphere very well done, viking rockgods (you'll see)
The Bad: Combat pretty hard and very frustrating to master, lip sync and faces are messy, the purpose of episodic gameplay slightly nullified by having large episodes.
8/10

KSP is an almost perfect space sim, it's easier to point out the flaws. So let's begin.
Kerbal Space Program nails both the design and piloting aspects of flying a spacecraft. But none of the two is without flaws. Let's start with flying the spacecraft. The missions on career mode are sometimes quite repetitive and turn into chores after a while.

First, Disclaimer. I bought this without knowing about the supposed MV Update, I bought this for VX Ace. Therefore, my review will not talk about this update, but rather the software itself, used by me for VX Ace (As I didn't use other versions of RPGMaker)
This Game Character Hub is exactly what it says it is: in short, it's an upgraded version of the Character Generator from RPGMaker. There's some very useful features in here that you cannot find in the Character Generator from RPGMaker: changing to color of various parts to exactly the color you want, moving some pieces, layering different clothes/body parts for your own amusement. With this tool, and a little imagination, you could make your game having entirely different NPCs, not one will look exactly the same. It's a big plus for me who always disliked how in various RPGs, several NPCs always had some long lost identical twins scattered through the world.
Pros:
Tutorial when you start the program for the first time. USE IT.
Ability to generate 100 characters at most with a simple click. Just choose basic characteristics, and you have your characters.
Change color hue/Saturation/Lightness.
Ability to move/create parts. Want a green alien with 6 eyes? Easy to do.
Possibility to add extra parts in the generator. Always useful.
Cons:
Even if it's a convinient program, there's nothing here that you cannot do in picture modifier programs. Everything I've tested here, I could do on GIMP (even if it takes me more time)
I do not know if I didn't find it, but so far, there is no way to create a face and making a Sprite generates itself along the face. It's one thing RPGMaker Character Creator has over GCH.
I got this software on sale, and I figure it's worth the money I spent. I would recommand it on sale only though. Like I said, everything you can do here, you can do elsewhere. It will only take you more time to do. The price you pay is the price for speed and convinience.

Not an obvious no-brainer, but this game really grows on you. The gameplay is sort of unique, given the rest of the indie scene right now. It steers away from the retro-pixelated feel the Super Meat Boy implemented so well, and focuses on brining a surprisingly satisfying experience with random playthroughs, random items and bosses. Actually, the non-deterministic nature of the game is its main source of appeal and addictiveness.

Pros:
- Devs are nice from my experience and are open to criticism, and carry themselves like regular people.
- A lot of the mechanics of this game seem pretty smooth. This includes movement and whatnot. I find it very relaxing to just jump around the map like a majestic meathead during warmups.
- Each character that is currently available has their own feel, but you're definitely not limited to only one playstyle.
- Games are relatively quick but action-packed. I can get really invested in a match if it's super close. If you're familiar with old arena shooters like Quake, this game will probably feel pretty familiar to you.
- Games will always keep you on your feet. Even if you're getting absolutely stomped, there is always a possibility of catching back up by getting a fat pwn stack. Keep in mind that the opposite can happen, so don't get complacent if you're in the lead ;)
- Includes a single-player parkour challenge mode that I think is pretty tough, but also fun. I've spent a couple of hours on this alone and I still havent 100% it yet.
- The bots that sometimes take place of real players (if someone leaves or if your game isn't filled up) are actually kind of smart. I know in some games if you're up against bots it's usually a stomp, but this doesn't feel much like that at all. This definitely does not replace the feel of playing againt real people, but it certainly beats sitting in queue for a while.
Cons:
- There is a bit of a learning curve. The tutorial (which I highly suggest all new players to check out) is helpful, but I do not feel that it fully prepares you for the game. I believe this would be remedied by a sort of "live combat" tutorial.
- There is no Ranked mode, but that makes sense given the game's current status.
- As with essentially every Early Access game, this one has a few bugs. For the most part I've only experienced bugs regarding the party system , in-game voice chat, and sometimes the main menu interface. Sometimes I'll crash when loading into a game but I've usually been able to get back in.
- Some of the abilities don't necessarily feel responsive sometimes. In other games you'll definitely know where your abilities are going and how impactful they are to fights. This clarity isn't present sometimes during combat -- especially during giant cluster♥♥♥♥s in choke points, but that could just be me.
- At the current price, there is a slight lack of content. When new content is released, I will update my review to better reflect how I feel about new content and the method of receiving it (whether or not the store prices is the real price of the game, or if you have to purchase more characters).
- The playerbase is pretty small and it is definitely noticeable. While this isn't necessarily a problem with the game, it does impact the overall experience. However, the developers have been working hard to bring new players in.
Other notes:
I've had a LOT of fun with this game in the few days that I've owned it. The community is pretty positive overall and I believe many of us want this game to succeed. In my opinion, it is a tad overpriced in its current state. However, I am looking forward to new content being released in the future. If the developers manage to work out some of the more problematic bugs and continue treating the community the same respect that I've been seeing then they will eventually build a dedicated fanbase.
Currently the FPS market has several strategy-based games such as CS:GO or Rainbow 6 Siege. This game goes against the grain with a fun and light-hearted shoot 'em up style. In my opinion, it's easy to pick up (just do the tutorial first!) and there isn't much memorization involved beside remembering what buttons to push.
I touched on this earlier, but I need to elaborate on this a bit more. I believe the amount of content in this game is lacking for the price, but I believe that will change in the future. I'm not a big fan of early access games that offer substantive content that you must purchase separately. That being said, I do not believe that is going to be the sales model of this game. I believe that the game will release free updates in the future, with optional cosmetic microtransactions -- much similar to the Overwatch system. I should note that this is entirely speculation and I will definitely update this review to confirm or deny this prediction whether it is accurate.

Every now and then we come across a game that takes us by surprise and reminds us not to be so quick to judge. Asguaard is one of those games. At first glance, this old-school RPG fantasy game from
looks like a small indie title that you would expect to offer you a few hours of simple gameplay. I assure you that's not the case. I have been pleasantly surprised at how much depth this game offered. Asguaard is a diamond in the rough, a nostalgic throwback RPG made in the same fashion as so many of the Nintendo RPG titles I fondly played in my youth. I thoroughly enjoy playing this 16-bit adventure  and strongly recommend it to any true RPG fan.
The story behind Asguaard is rich and well-developed even though its typical for these types of games. Our hero is a sometimes relunctant and sarcastic teenage boy who has somehow been summoned to the vast world of Asguaard by a village of Dwarves in order to save their world from peril. As with most RPG's, you will encounter friends along the way who will join you in your epic quest.
The characters themselves offer a variety of abilities and talents. Players even get to decide which type of weapon they want the characters to specialize in. Plus, you can teach your characters a number of useful skills along the way. Particularly useful in this expansive endeavor is a skill called "Pathfinding." Trust me, this is one skill you definitely want to make use of. Asguaard is littered with over 500 locations and 150 secret places so using this skill will help guide you through the numerous maze-like dungeons and keep you on the chosen path to progress the story. Without it, one can easily get lost because this world is huge. Other skills can be just as useful, especially later in the game. The characters all have unique personalities and while the tons of dialogue can be monotonous at times, there are some funny "LOL" moments included.
Like the 16-bit graphics and anime-styled artwork, the sounds and music of this game help add to that classic RPG feeling. None of these things will leave a big impression on you, but they are good for a game like this. The controls are simple and the game does offer full controller support if that's your preference. There is also the option to play in either full-screen or window mode. There are several difficulty levels to choose from and you also will also get to choose how often the random encounters occur as you explore the dungeon and world maps. These are definitely worth considering before beginning your adventure because Asguaard is quite long. In fact, this game offers between 50-100+ hours of gameplay from start to finish depending on your gaming style and how much grinding or exploration you choose to do.
Asguaard is not your typical 16-bit game. In fact, Aldorlea Games offers some of the best RPGMaker titles on the market and Asguaard is a perfect example. The game is well-designed, runs smoothly, and offers many hours of exploration and adventure. While the full-price may seem a bit much for a game of this type, its not unreasonable by no means considering all of the content included. True RPG fans will want to add this game to their libraries, especially if they can grab it during a discount promotion.

This is a hard game to review. A lot of games I don't review, but there are some I do feel the need to, as a personal encouragement or warning to others.
Problem is, this game is both. It's a solid retro RPG with very high production values, from art to music to game mechanics.
Which may make the faults more glaring, since everything else is just so darn good.
I do love the game but yet my recommendation of it is cautionary in nature.
For instance, the main hero comes across as whiny and juvenile because other characters get something that he doesn't, so he has to make their lives totally miserable for it. And it does grow very tiresome and damages the storyline.
There's a lot of abilities to learn, and they come in three stages, but if you can't find the first stage then you'll never have that ability the rest of the game. The kicker? At an early point in the game you can't return to the areas that have those first lessons so you're completely locked out even though you don't even have your full party yet.
Kicker #2 - a lot of those abilities are hidden somewhere on the map and if you don't criss-cross every pixel of the overland map and bump into every wall every step you can miss the hidden area entirely, so no skill for you.
Games that have a "too bad, so sad, sucks to be you" penalty on players is a big turn-off. As well as making games deliberately difficult in order to "encourage" the added purchase of game guides.
Kicker #3 - Finding the skill-giver is only half the problem. The skills cost gold to learn, per character. So you'll be offered the skill at say 300 gold per character, while you're fighting mobs that drop 2-8 gold per fight, 13 if you're lucky. This is on Normal difficulty.
So if you don't have the money and have to leave the hidden area to grind a few hours to build up the bank, hope and pray you can find that pixel again within that huge expanse of open nothingness, or twisty tunnels when you want to return to it.
This is why the game may take 100 hours to finish. The male hero's constant whining will make that seem much, much longer.
When they say exploration game, they're not kidding. This is both and OCD'er dream and nightmare wrapped up in one. There's enough grinding and backtracking to make Aveyond seem like the length of a comic book.

I love that the solution to running out of fuel in space is to get out and push.
But seriously, This game is fantastic.
Doesn't matter if you want to have fun screwing around, or have fun being super serious, This game has them both. If you want a game about going to space and landing on the moon, THIS is the game for you. want to build crazy contraptions that look like various body parts and watch them explode and take out several nearby buildings? This is also the game for you. Want to build and fly the SR-71? yep, they've got you. Want to fly a pinecone made of tiny wings and airbreaks and use strange physics glitches? yep, we got that too. Worried about physics glitches getting in the way? if you want to play seriously and you know anything about what you're doing, you wont' really notice them unless you use a really unconventional method like forward-swept wings for example, don't even work well in real life, why would you ever try it in a phyiscs based videogame, that's just asking for trouble, but you should totally do it anyway.
and when you get bored, you can always try it the other way around. instead of playing seriously, just screw off in sandbox mode. Instead of trying to build edgy symbols made out of fire, try actually learning something about rocketry and managing a space agency.
because yeah, that's a thing too, in career mode you actually have a budget, and parts cost money, and missions have payouts, maybe you have two missions that are really close, but you can only afford one rocket, Can you fit both missions in one launch, or do you have to do one at a time?
all in all, if you think building things or experimenting with in-game cration stuff is cool, and you think space is cool, I cannot recommend this highly enough. Do you like flight sims? grab it. driving sims? grab iiiit. Think NASA and ESA and SpaceX are cool? get it. want to go to mars? get it.

I purchased this with a Humble Bundle, but my review won't be humble.
This game is 10 out of 10, top-notch, prime-cut, cream-of-the-crop, awesomesauce. I grew up on Doom 95 and Doom II. Do you like Doom? Are you a cool dude like that?
Then this game will be your everything.
This game is all of the fun of Doom, but with more meaningful missions and gameplay, better mechanics and smoother production, and modern story-telling devices packed into a fast-paced, no-bars instant classic that just so happens to be STAR-WARS! Did I mention that part? Take Doom II, make it 10 times better, and then change everything to STAR-FREAKIN'-WARS. Yeah, this game is THAT awesome.
Here are a couple examples of how this game clobbers Doom with a quality-control club.
You can jump.
You can aim with the mouse.
There's a standard 'use' key.
Your armor / shield overdrives and stays there.
If your armor, health, or ammo are full, you won't pick up any more. (Remember dodging enemies in Doom at 100% armor and accidentally picking up that critical armor boost that you needed to save for later? Yeah, no more of that...)
Punching is better. And punching from behind is a stealth takedown.
The BIG One:
Missions are no longer "Collect 3 keys, make it to the exit." You  have meaningul missions with real objectives. And more than one of them!  You can't just collect your way to the finish line.
Because of this, the game doesn't devolve to "kill every enemy and win" either. If you set off an alarm in a storm trooper base, they will spawn like mad, and you will have to run, not fight. And they won't "spawn", either. They'll come out of rooms and doorways and up elevators or stairs.
Imagine you're in a ruined city, destroyed by a star-destroyer, and you must restore back-up power to the city so you can gain entrance to a crumbling base. You traverse the city, the ruins, the rubble, but everything is dark and doors won't operate. Elevators are still and bridges won't extend. You KNOW there are secret areas to explore in those places, but you just can't get to them. Then you restore the power and BAM! the level just multiplied by two. All of those areas are now open and accessible. The lights are on again, the bridges bridge, the elevators elevate, the doors... do door-ey things. *pneumatic hiss* Now the map is suddenly fresh again - and freshly populated with enemies too!
There are secrets to be found, puzzles to be solved, special gear to be discovered, and, ooh! an extra life? Sweet...
You still get that great element of strategy with planning your pickups and backtracking for that vital medkit or weapon you nearly missed, but all of the annoyances and low-production quality folly of Doom and Doom II are gone, replaced with a dynamic, colorful, exciting, and all-around memorable experience that only the name Star Wars can bring.
This game was released in 1995. It's currently 2017, and I'm playing it for the first time. It's 23 years later, and I've stopped playing Mass Effect 3, Assassin's Creed Syndicate, Dragon Age Inquisition, Skyrim, Elder Scrolls Online, The Division, Far Cry Primal, and hell, even Goat Simulator, because Star Wars - Dark Forces has taken their places. This is my main game now.
Move over, next-gen AAA titles, this old school DOS game just stepped into the ring and KO'd the lot of you in three missions flat.
I recommend this game to anyone. Everyone.

The most important question: "Is Paladins an Overwatch clone?"

Getting the champions is quite easy, specializing their abilities as well. The only thing not so easy is changing a champions appearance because all the nice ones do cost real cash.
Of course the Dev's are up-to-date with their free to play model, so you obviously get the most stuff only by buying cases with random contents. Money-wasting intensifies.
The game does feature a competetive mode, but that one requries you to have lots of champions on a certain level to ensure people do know how to play the game.
Overall i do recommend the game, but only if you stick to your choice: Don't pay for a free to play game. If you like the game, consider buying a founders pack as if you were buying a full game, but do not start spending cash on skins on the like.

I've only played through two of the four operations so far in the game, but so far, I've enjoyed it immensely. Although the game totes itself as allowing the player to use different playstyles in order to progress, it is incredibly difficult to beat the game with a pure stealth build due to the boss fights that the player will inevitably come across. It took myself at least ten checkpoint loads in order to defeat the Russian mafia boss through the abuse of a low-leveled pistol skill that I had among the handful of higher leveled stealth skills that I had at my disposal (which were useless for anything other than for repositioning).
Alpha Protocol is incredibly story driven where your conversations with the other characters in the game will affect future missions; if your handler doesn't like you, you get reduced mission bonuses and they will be less inclined to give you good information. Building and reading dossiers are also an important part for these conversations since it's possible to be intentionally mean to one character in order to boost your standing with another. You are warned in-game that a character that has too high of a good standing with you can potentially cause that person to act irrationally and cause problems for your missions, which is quite interesting.
The combat is functional, but it doesn't really bring a ton of enjoyment. Stealthing the game is viable and you are rewarded if you sneak past enemies without taking them down (though you are also rewarded if you defeat/kill them). In fact, making it through missions undetected can affect future missions.
It's something I'd recommend to those who enjoy espionage/thriller stories, though the game is not flawless.

Synonymy is an interesting thought experiment in game form. However, I found that it gets old quickly and the enjoyment fades in about an hour. 3.0 is a major improvement, though, and it's good to see that progress has been made. I didn't run into any glitches this time around and the game was much more achievable.
Still, Richard Dawkins actually does not narrate the whole game, just the tutorial. I'm convinced that this game is polarizing -- either you really like the concept and can play it forever, or play one or two rounds and are done with it. In my opinion, most people are probably in the second camp.

Create a mountain based (presumably) on your random scribbles, and then watch it slowly rotate around. Or increase the rotation speed and zoom in and out with your mouse.
Occasionally music will play and some supposedly thoughtful texts will appear.
And you can play the keytar with the bottom two rows on your keyboard.
Not so much a game as a relaxing piece of barely interactive art, I don't feel ripped off for €0.99. Recommended if you buy it knowing what you're in for -- don't expect gameplay.

Firstly, this is a mobile port to PC/Mac, so the controls are very basic keyboard & mouse click. I experienced some overlay issues within the game when I was reviewing the tutorial and wanted to interrupt it to go back to the main menu. There's no intuitive "esc" to main menu, or anything similar. This is a straight up port, so you have to "swipe" back to menus through the arrow or AWSD keys.
The gameplay itself is quite simple to pick up: you start with a word, given the definitions, and set off with a completely unrelated word to find your way through synonym choices to get to your target word. Remember those "change one letter at a time to get from "Bear" to "Cake" type word puzzles?" This is exactly the same only with synonyms. If you click on a middle word, you are given the definition, and just randomly clicking on words may increase your vocabulary but it won't necessarily get you to your target word. With weekly challenges, and an ability to give a fellow player a code to try and compete against one another, Synonymy is a nice change of pace to other word games.
Gameplay isn't complicated (outside of the word-linking; puzzle-solving) but your mileage may vary with the controls. It is, after all a straight from mobile port, so you may find you prefer that interface than your PC/Mac.
As of this review, the Steam Overlay doesn't work with the game, so you can't screenshot, etc.
The game does however feature a set of 5/5 trading cards (this isn't yet referenced in the Store Page).
Also of note, is this is listed as a "non-profit" game. Proceeds from this game go to Richard Dawkins charities which are listed on the game's actual website (store page has a link) and worth a look if this sort of information is important to you.
I recommend this game purely based on its educational value and change of pace gameplay. There is some longevity to it, depending on how much you like to play with words :)
Pick it up in a bundle or on sale.

Asguaard is like paradise for everyone who loves to explore!
The story is very nice. Asguaard is a land of dwarves and fairies. A wonderful place, but now in danger because the Pandora Box has been opened and seven plagues are about to destroy the land. Only a human can save the world and the dwarves manage to summon even two of them, Glen and Rayanne. Accompanied by the faithful dwarf Grom and a little unicorn they set off to find what's necessary to prevent the worst from happening.
If I should choose one word to describe Asguaard, it would be HUGE. Huge world maps and huge dungeons with many many secrets to discover. There are countless Hidden Locations (on the world maps) and Magical Rooms (in dungeons or villages ...) to be found and if you explore thoroughly you'll be well rewarded.
Someone asked, what's the point of secret rooms. Well, just the fun of searching and the satisfaction of finding them! If that's something you like, then you'll really get your money's worth in this game! But even if you don't - finding the secret rooms is not mandatory at all, and if you decide to leave them be, you'll still get hours and hours and hours of fun playing this game!
Optically the world of Asguaard is just beautiful. The maps are very detailed. A lot of effort has obviously been put into creating them.
Another feature that makes this game outstanding is an extremely elaborate system of skills your characters can acquire. There are almost 30 different skills, each to be learned in 3 levels (Expert, Master, Guru). They are being taught by dwarves you find all over the world and you decide what to spend your money on. Most of them prove themselves very valuable throughout the game. Just one example out of many: If you learn "Path Finding", little arrows will lead your way through dungeons, and no matter how big they are, with this help you'll never really get lost.
Also an awesome asset is the "Friendship" skill that all characters have. You can choose who is your best friend, and according to your choice the characters will collect friendship points with each battle. For certain amounts of points they will achieve friendship statuses that will help in battles. They might heal each other, boost each other .....
The choice of who's your best friend can be altered anytime, so you can get the best out of every combination.
The game has invisible encounters. Fights are turn-based. Glen is a fighter, the other three characters can fight and use spells. There's not such a big variety of different spells as in other Aldorlea games, but the ones available are by far sufficient. How hard the fights are depends on the difficulty level you choose at the beginning of the game - easy, normal or hard. You can also adjust the encounter rate.
To top the game off there are several additional locations you can visit, that have nothing to do with the main quest and are optional, but you can find nice stuff there. They are to be found on the world maps.
Also there are a few caves with monsters. If you defeat them, you'll get nice rewards, like money or valuable items. Sometimes the monsters are fairly easy, sometimes really hard, so you better keep them until later in the game. With those monsters you can test your fighting skills too if you dare to attack them at lower levels.
There's just one thing in this game that I'd like to change: making traveling easier in the first part (later there is a way to travel that's easy and quick).
More teleport points would be very helpful. There are very few teleport crystals, but in order to get skills and other things you need to travel back and forth quite a lot and all the walking can become a bit annoying sometimes. A teleport station in each and every village would have been great.
Also, a "Go through" option for caves like in other Aldorlea games would have been very nice too.
Other than that I really enjoy this game a lot. There's so much to do and so much to discover. Definitely a very recoommendable game!

Asguaard has arrived on Steam, and it is easy to see why it is Aldorlea's most popular game. This game is a complete masterpiece that offers a marvelous storyline that is long and involved featuring excellent character development, interesting plot lines, tons of exploration, and, of course, great battles with a huge arsenal of monsters to deal with.
As with all rpgs, so much depends on the story being told. And this tale of dwarves that summon humans to fend off the plagues being released by the opening of Pandora's box (where and by whom to be discovered) is captivating from the very beginning. You are drawn in to the story immediately, and the adventure and its goals are made clear at the outset. So you are off to discover what is going on in Asguaard, and the adventure sprawls over a huge land without ever becoming tedious. In fact, there is so much to see, so much to discover and accomplish, and so many variables that the game becomes one of those "just one more scene" type of games. It is very hard to find a point where you feel ok taking a break.
Part of any good story is the presentation of the characters, and these are ones that are fun, well thought out, and unique. Even the NPCs (dwarves, fairies) are integral to the plot, and almost always offer help or guidance in your journey.
Music and sounds of the game are remarkably done, and add to the game beautifully.
The artwork (main screens, backgrounds, monsters) are all appealing.
With 4 modes of difficulty (including story mode), over 150 secret locations, and lots of attack variations, the replay value is high. I am playing the story mode primarily, and have also started another game on "Normal", and the differences mean I'll go through the game twice.
The gameplay is smooth as can be with no glitches whatsoever. The text is laid out in a manner that you can easily follow through on what to do next and when to do it. (And not a single misspelling to be seen).
The high production value, and the care that went into this game are obvious and outstanding. Aldorlea's Asguaard is a high quality classic that deserves to be in any collection. Very highest recommendation.

This game....how do you describe this game?  I've seen so many people negatively rate this game and everybody definitely has their own opinion, and I was ready myself to cast it aside after just a few minutes of playtime.  There is something about this game though, more the environment, music, and theme than anything else, that defines what has been missing in the horror/suspense genre for so long.
While the plot might be slightly convoluted at times, and you might hate the main character initially, the deeper meaning attached to a man trying to find and rescue the only woman he has ever loved is permanently endearing even if it is unoriginal.  In ways, the woman is not even a woman, but a light in his life that chases away the darkness that has become the world.  With all his effort and might, he chases after this light and attempts to protect it from all harm, much as we all do every day.
Instead of going for straight gore and action like so many games/movies/books of this genre seem to be doing these days, the real horror is losing his light in the world and never being able to recover it.  This is truly terrifying as the shadows and inner demons of people and the world around him start to manifest physically.
The gameplay is nothing too original or even exciting, and can even be very frustrating at times, but the core and theme of the game easily overpowers its small shortcomings.  I'm an avid gamer and huge fan of the horror genre in the entertainment world, and it has been awhile since a game of this caliber has popped into my sights.  I think an excellent comparison for Alan Wake is the original Resident Evil, but obviously not in the gore factor.  The comparison rings true in the theatrics of the games.  The developers of both games focused on not only what horrors we could see, but even more so on the ones we couldn't see.  The horror in our minds of what could exist around that corner in the Spencer mansion, or in the dark forest of Bright Falls, is what truly terrifies us.
This game has picked up a small cult following since it's release, and I can now count myself as one of them.

Sure some of the dialogue is cheesy, teenage nonsense. But it is a game about highschoolers. And it does quickly become about something more...dark. I think what sold this whole experience though was the way everything interconnects. The visuals with the handpainted look, the warm, gorgeous lighting, the beautiful soundtrack, the great voice acting from the lead characters and a good pacing to the whole thing that, while it starts a little slow it quickly picks up and I can't imagine not being able to play all 5 episodes back to back.
I absolutely loved my experience with this game and while I'm not sure I'll ever play it again, it has kept me thinking about it for a few days now and only really good stories are capable of that.
