It's quite sad to see the true reviews go away and be replaced with the typical fanboyish comments. Notice how all of these positive reviews claim this game is great but fail to give an accurate description as to why (whereas the negative comments stated their stance properly).
1. Orc lines can't be skipped, makes fight intros way too long.
2. The game is not huge, those claims of "huge sandbox" are false. It's not a sandbox world, there is very little to actually do. And using any beast makes the map even smaller.
3. The missions in this game are incredibly short and easy. This whole game was a breeze even with the ending fight against Sauron. While there was a good concept behind each story path, most were also terribly written.
4. Whiney and annoying characters. Daughter of the Minas Guard Captain, whiney. Talion, whiney. Occasionally, you'll find other characters dip into being a tad annoying every once in awhile.
5. Multiplayer is a joke, I saw the meta the moment I viewed orc stats. "One shot" was going to be the meta. If they even take a sliver of the last bit of  health away they instantly are given the finisher which you can't escape out of. And with no multiplayer fix in sight, it looks like this game will die off quickly.
6. Still a very idiotic AI, I've watched my captains stand around doing nothing for some reason in the middle of a siege outside the walls. And it's not just a bug/specific fix. This goes for all captains in every setting. Just a terrible AI.
7. Re-using skins for cosmetic purposes. You'll find many armor sets match even though they are completely different sets. Very lazy devs.
Summarizing all of this, you have a good story concept but it's extremely short and poorly written with annoying characters that serve little to no purpose besides their own personal story of whining. On top of that, a dumb AI and terrible and boring multiplayer with developers showing no care in the world.
Worst part, those of us that bought the game before the sale paid the full price if not more for a garbage game. Do not recommend in the slightest.

and then arbitrarily limited campaign length and added things that unlock via playthrough to encourage replay.
For what it is, it's not bad. I remember feeling that Shadowrun Returns was surprisingly heavy on the combat and light on the core of the tabletop game, which was always espionage and stealth. Invisible has a saturday morning cartoon feel to it that keeps the tone light as your little trenchcoated minions ambush and taser unsuspecting security guards.

I have spent many hours in this program making original pixel art for a game I'm helping create, so I figured it was about time for a review. Now, I am still fairly new at pixel art and don't have experience with other programs, so please take this into consideration while reading my opinions.
As a beginner pixel artist, this program is fairly easy to pick up. The tool selection is not over-cluttered and easy to navigate, and the layering system is perfect and easy to learn.
Some things about this program I really love:
-The preview box allows you to see your animation as you are making it. You can zoom in, zoom out, and adjust the speed and frames of your animation. It helps me see if my pixels are off on one frame flowing into the next, so I can easily detect the problem and fix it.
-The program allows you to have many different tabs and images open at once, though your preview box will not change in size and frame number for each tab.
-You can drag the tool boxes to any corner that you like, allowing you to customize your screen display.
-Though I don't often use the pre-made assets, the program also allows you to add in your own assets so that you can easily go in and layer your original art for sprites if you want to easily randomize for npcs and such.
-The tileset merging tool helps you easily merge and format assets for easy integration into RPG Maker.
-Original assets you make in this program can be used for game engines that are not RPG Maker.
Some things I wish this progam could improve on:
-The program crashes sometimes when you try to copy and paste from a larger file to a smaller one. This has resulted in a lot of lost work for myself and my team that we had to recreate because we didn't save beforehand. I have found that expanding the tile size of the image I am copying into help the issue, but it is rather tedious to do this every time.
-A slider to adjust the overall contrast of an image
-A better fill tool that doesn't need to have a selected area to be used in, and only fills based on colour.
-I would really, really love a way to save my animations into .gif format.
Overall, this program has been very useful to me even though I am not making an RPG maker game at the moment. It's not entirely perfect but it does the job for me and is not too complicated to get into. I do hope the devs see my review and consider changing some aspects of the program to make it a powerful competitor to other pixel art programs. I rate this program 7.5/10.

When I say that Invisible, Inc. has “virtually” infinite replay value, I mean to say that while it is not mathematically possible to comprehensively experiment with all the variables, such as starting agent duo, I do not believe that this is the kind of game that should be played exhaustively, and that is why I struggle with it as a package. I do believe that it is a good game, but I feel that what keeps it from being a great game is a palatable lack of balance and direction.
The regular campaigns are brief enough so that any single session does not overstay its welcome, and that is intelligent design. However, a consequence of deriving inspiration from a roguelike is that not every playthrough is fun. Even when I win, it’s because I am scraping by with skill, although I would prefer to experiment with cool gadgets. Endless mode is a solution to the abbreviated campaign, increasing the likelihood of maxing out four agents to a certainty as long as the player is talented enough to not lose. At times, I feel that endless mode the best, “unintentionally intended” way to play Invisible, Inc., but then again, as of this writing, I am on day 11 of endless and my agents seem invincible even at alarm level 6 (based shock trap III). I feel challenged, but I don’t fear losing. Then again, I routinely play games involving heavy strategy.
Overall, I would recommend Invisible, Inc. to gamers looking for some strategy in their lives, but are disinterested in a game with a skill ceiling as high as the nosebleed section.

There is a similarity with Firaxis' XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It's nicely polished turn based tactical strategy game but with shorter playthrough in compare to the second mentioned game. Understand, the shorter does not mean worse. You get to the end (win or lose) just faster. Each mission takes around 30-45 minutes and the whole game composes from approx. 10-12 missions (overall 5-7 hours).
The general "research" element is replaced by gathering credits (in-game money) for which you can equip new items (some require a particular level of agent's stats), implant new augmentations to your agents' bodies, increase their statistics, or install new programs for hacking. Credits are gathered by stealing from safes, guards or by selling unwanted items. And like in XCOM, you are facing tough decisions and desperate situations many times. Your mission time is virtually limited by the system of increasing alert level. In each level, it all gets tougher and harder. Thus you need to balance between quick less cautious play and slow progress when you risk high alert level in the later mission time.
If you like turn-base tactical strategy you should try this one too.

Ok, I bought the game thinking one thing and it was another, but I’ll try to be fair.
It’s not an action game, focused on playing; it’s an interactive storytelling, focused on the story.
You go along beautiful scenarios and interesting puzzles to unveil the story. The sound, the music and the images are good. The story itself… Let’s say it starts as a dramatic emotionally-driven tragedy... it continues as a dramatic emotionally-driven tragedy... it extends the dramatic emotionally-driven tragedy… and it ends in a final dramatic emotionally-driven tragedy. As a writer I can’t avoid feeling bad about it. The main point is the story, so the plot could be better – much better.
Gameplay: it works all right, pretty simple commands and it’s possible to explore (with scenario limits). But you walk really slowly, even when “running”, what made me give up of playing it again for achievements, like finding the memories. I don’t have the patience to go all through it in slow pace again.
I wouldn’t say it’s not worth the price because you can see there was good work put on it, art is expensive. But being honest, I wouldn’t pay the full price if I knew what’s about and I don’t recommend it unless you are really into shallow drama, beautiful scenarios and puzzles.

All my life I was plagued by an unsettling awareness that something was missing. I was incomplete, a person born into the wrong body and unable to come to terms with myself as a human being. Who am I? What am I doing with my life? What is all this even for? These questions gnawed at me, eating me away from the inside until I was hollow and thinking I couldn't live with myself anymore.
Then I played Mountain.
I realized what was missing from my life, there was a cavernous hole in my psyche in the shape of a mountain. A chunk of myself spinning in the void, disconnected and fragmented, completely without purpose. I watched as it slowly rotated, each angle subtly different, like a babe beneath a jingling plush mobile I was mesmerized.
What am I doing? I pondered as a placidly watched the seasons pass me by, weathering me down, making me smoother, gentler, capable only of idly commenting on the notion of time and how something so indifferent to my existence can affect me so greatly. Has this face changed since the last time I gazed upon it? Its creases and angles seemed inherently familiar, yet the pattern of life across its surface strangely foreign each time I see it anew. I was always getting older, spinning in place as life moved on around me, embedding me with memories of a life once lived, leaving me with impressions, pieces of the world around me, seemingly random and yet unshakable.
Where am I? Lost in an endless and empty vacuum, suspended in a spherical prison pieced together from the materials of living matter I've sorted and categorized to be able to comprehend as existence. Unable to see beyond it to greater meaning. Unable to feel the difference between moving through space and space moving through me. I cannot fathom a reason for my being, why I ended up one place and not another, if I am alone through action or if I am made alone in my awareness of self.
Who am I? I knew there was more beneath the surface, if only I could dig my nails into that crust, pull at its crumbling edges and explore what skeletal frame held up this facade, knowing... Nay, praying, that there was something more to me than this ponderous slope of earthen matter. Something to express in more than a few staggered notes, something greater than the deafening silence. Keep in mind that this is a very hesitant recommendation. Adventures of Shuggy is a simple but challenging platformer that has a huge amount of levels for you to work through.

There's a good 20 to 30 levels per room, and you need to complete at least two-thirds before you gain access to the boss level and then unlock the next room. Each level has a gimmick associated with it; being able to rotate the entire level or sections of it, clones that spawn and carry out what you did within a specified time limit, rope machines that allow you to swing down and even up through levels, embiggening/shrink potions etc. They keep it fresh and as you advance you're expected to tangle with more complicated variants.
On a personal note I just got sick of the game; I loathe time-clone platforming and I am particularly awful at it ('sup Gateways!). There are better platformers around but this is certainly worth picking up on sale if you've run out of options.

I can't recommend this game. It's true that I'm not exactly english for a start, so playing an english-based word game is tricky, but it doesn't matter, really. That game fails to do what it claims to do in the first place.
The rules are simple : you're given a target word (say "Silence"), and given a starting word (say "Crash"), and a cloud of synonyms you can pick from. The goal is to get closer and closer to the target word by picking the right words from the words cloud. The thing is, there's not only synonyms in the cloud, but also antonyms, sometimes just analog terms (otherwise you wouldn't get very far)... but not always.
So for example starting with "Crash", goind towards "Silence" you could expect to go through "Crack", then "Noise" or "Sound", and then choose the antonym "Silence"... but only IF the game knows that "Silence" is an antonym of "Noise". but when you get, for exempale, to the word "Real" you can choose "Lawful"... and also "Unlawful", but can't pick "Silence" out of "Noise".
And there you have it : this game is not about knowing your english, it's about guessing what words are linked with what other words in the game's database. And without knowing what dictionary it was built onto, there's NO WAY you could play this game properly.
This is more a data mesh exploration game than a word game. Therefore it is pretty bad. I know it's cheap, but that doesn't make it any better

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: oh boy another puzzle platformer brought from XBLA time to not recommend it- Wait what? It's actually not half bad? ...you sure? Huh, so it is. Adventures of Shuggy is a puzzle platformer whose main attraction is many stage gimmicks. One stage may have you rotating the entire stage, another one may have you teleporting all over the place, another may have you be zombified so that you can jump and only jump... there's a lot of gimmicks. There's a lot of stages as well; 112 stages in the main game and 40 extra in the teleporter-focused mode. Out of all these levels, there were only seven or eight that I felt were legitimately kinda terrible. Fortunately, there's a lot more than that for levels that are really quite clever with, y'know, actual puzzles.
The platforming itself isn't bad, and in fact there's really only one complaint I have about the platforming, and that is inertia. Shuggy actually has a lot of inertia, meaning that you can very easily end up falling off of a ledge due to your own inertia. You can kinda deal with it after a while, but it's still kinda obnoxious even once you get used to it. Another thing that could be a problem for some is that Shuggy is actually pretty dang fast. There is a bit of precise platforming here and there that could prove tricky for some due to how fast and how inertia-laden Shuggy is, but it never was the top speed that gave me any problems.
There's also boss battles in the game, although they're more akin to boss battles from a game like Donkey Kong '94. I did quite like all of the bosses, and they all took at least some thought and careful planning to defeat. Again, they're, y'know, actual puzzles. It's hard really to talk too much more about this game's gameplay, as the core mechanics are quite simple, and the complexity of the game comes from these gimmicks. There was one gimmick that I enjoyed only about half of the implementations of (Shuggy temporal cloning) and one gimmick that I didn't like at all (wall-crawling Lemming carting around). Apart from those two gimmicks - and they're largely toward the beginning, so if that's causing you duress, just push through; it gets better - I had a great deal of fun with this game. Some other reviewers mentioned a lot of waiting around, but honestly; it's not all that bad. Unless you have super-ADHD, it's really not going to ruin your day. Unlike a lot of puzzle platformers, I can see myself coming back to this game in the future. For $5, it's a great deal. For the $0.49 I picked it up for during the Winter 2013 sale... that's highway robbery. 8/10.
Story: There's not much, really. It's all told through a faux-comic book style presentation. It's honestly not worth rating, as it for the most part stays on the backburner for the gameplay to shine through.
Graphics: It takes a bit of a hit here for two reasons. Reason one is that this game either windows in 720p or fullscreens in 720p. The portiness of this game is quite obvious here, since the 360's maximum resolution for gameplay was 720p. As for the art style... it's alright, but it really does have that "XBLA-look" to it. I'm not the best at pinning this sort of thing down, but I think it has to do with how the XNA kit handles gradients and sprites in general. It's not bad, but once again, it shows that this was once an XBLA game. Kinda disappointing, honestly. 2/5.
Sound: Sound design isn't the biggest deal for this game; it's mainly some obvious sound effects and that's about it. As for the OST, it's not a thing that I'd get to listen to on my own time, but it's good enough in the context of the game. It's a decidedly jazzy OST which is partly why I'm not too keen on it, but that's because I'm 2dumb2jazz or something. If you're into that kind of thing, maybe you'll want the OST for yourself. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 8/0/2/3; 6.5/10. A game with great gameplay design that is unfortunately hindered by some less-than-amazing AV stuffs. Again though, for $5 (and especially for $0.49), this game is a great deal, and will provide you with a day or two of mostly good times.

Man, good music always delivers the best atmosphere for movies and games. So maybe this  is the secret of Hotline Miami. Since it’s music is one of the best for a video game and played at least once in my office on our Radioplaylist. But of course there’s more to Hotline Miami than just the music.
In Hotline Miami we run around and kill everyone on the floor. And once we finished that we continue to the next floor and so on and so on. Is there a true meaning behind killing all these pixel faces? Not really, it’s not a real spoiler that in Hotline Miami one there is no real story, other than a Hitman getting assignments and executing his orders.
What really makes this game unique at least is the mixture of a whole bunch of difficult game mechanics. The Top-down view, the one shot or one hit kill and the pumping music mixed with the different masks our killer can wear to get certain small advantages make the game to a toxic, annoying and yet very satisfying experience I really enjoyed. There are also a whole bunch of weapons in the game as rifles, shotguns, pistols, bats, samurai swords, ninja stars, hammers, and many many more. Some weapons are not that different from each other, but you still need to plan some steps ahead to know how many enemies you can take out with your shotgun until you have to switch to another weapon for example.
Within my 6 hours of playtime and 19 chapters + 1 one bonus chapter the levels sure differentiate in enemies, tasks and difficulty. Normal guys with baseball bats, sticks or knifes sure need a quick reaction, but enemies with guns and rifles need planing. One of the main points that has been told about Hotline Miami 1 is that there is somewhat of a rhythmn, but I can not say that running into a level without a plan would let me survive long enough to finish a level. Sure, the more I died, the more I was able to predict and use patterns of later levels, yet I still needed a plan for my progression.
The game mixes some special enemies later into the game as we have different miniboss fights with a knife encounter, a guy inside a van that throws molotovs at us and the final boss against 2 panthers, a ninja and the miniguns of that boss.
From time to time we will have small visits by 3 masked guys that can be interpreted as you like, I think it is like the concious of our killer. Sadly this is not explained in any way later in the game. But again, this game is simply about the best gameplay that I had in a long time with a top-down view!
Hotline Miami costs 8,49€ or your local equivalent and I can say it’s worth every coin. Go buy it and enjoy the bloody pixel mess as the challenge and excitement give you the greatest gratification later if you manage to survive it.

Right off the bat, Life is Strange meets the requirements of what I would consider a great game: an engaging story, memorable, nuanced characters, and a
soundtrack. I'm not one who cares much about graphics but other than the oft-mentioned lack of lip movement in some scenes, I saw no need for improvement in the semi-realistic art style and motion-capture animation of Life is Strange. I loved the hand-painted textures and felt inspired to paint digitally again because of it. The cinematic Moments of Calm, the montages at the end of every episode, and even walking through the environments while the aforementioned soundtrack plays in the background do a lot help you relate to Max Caulfield, immerse you in the world of Arcadia Bay, and make you truly feel a part of the story. Kudos as well to the developers for their focus on real issues and their realistic depictions of relationships, especially from the perspectives of females characters.
However, the game still has its limitations. Many of the secondary characters fall under popular tropes so it isn't difficult to predict how things go with them. Its point-and-click gameplay might feel tiring and linear if your expectations are not set to playing a story-driven game where you have to interact with objects and people to fill in the big picture. You may think that the variety of choices will mean a variety of outcomes or endings but that is sadly not the case (however, I would also argue that the binary ending is what makes Life is Strange so compelling). In other words, if you are looking for an open-world game with an über customizable player-character whose in-game personality depends on your choices, Life is Strange is not that game.
I urge you to think of Life is Strange not as a traditional 'game' with the objective to win. When I told my friend about how distraught I was about a certain choice, he replied, "Oh, well. It's just a game." But
, Life is Strange reveals itself to be more than just a game. It lets you to face truths about friendship, about ethics, about life in general in a way we likely won't experience in real life. In the same way we discern works of art like paintings, literature, even certain movies and songs, games can carry profound meaning for its players, too, and DONTNOD has achieved that with Life is Strange.
: While Life is Strange leaves much to be desired, it deserves credit for providing a whole new gaming experience, one where the player is prompted to undergo philosophical and personal reflection to understand its message. Developing the choices-and-consequences element to allow more complex variations in endings would make this already fantastic game more enjoyable, but the game as it stands is already very satisfying. It is simple, moving, and beautifully made. Despite the predictable plot and characters, the voice acting, cinematography, music, and overall ambience of the game make it truly something special.
I cannot stress enough how good the soundtrack is for a game of this type and style; every song captures the emotions of the scenes they are in. But besides that, there are so many references in the game -- from quotes by Robert Frost to obscure graffiti referencing David Foster Wallace -- that give the game nuance. Life is Strange is a game that you will not likely forget, if not because of its story and characters, then at least because it made you reflect on your own life.

I often say that Alan Wake is one of my favorite games. When I first beat it back when it came out, I was very impressed. Being an aspiring young writer, I made a connection with the protagonist, However, time has gone by. I've learned a lot and the gaming scene has changed. I also never got to see the two Feature DLCs. Thus, I have gone through hell and back to write a better review for a game, which I'm glad to say is still one of my favorite games. Even though it went a bit lower on the list. Keep in mind, this is a spoiler-free, objective review of the game, looking at it as a potential artpiece.
I must begin by saying that the concept of the game is simply genious. And it's a concept almost superbly executed - the entire atmosphere is spot on, with colours and locales that go perfectly with the chosen theme. And to top it all off - this game has textbook-perfect polish throughout. From voice acting and the soundtrack up to presentation and implementation of certain captivating ideas, like the flashlight's beam being the crosshair.
Most people will notice that the game is not aging well. While some parts of it still look the part, others are now lacking. Cinematics show a particular type of aging that we've come to see, where the framerate seems low and at times it's obvious the models are models. Depending on the type of person you are, this might bother you.
The important thing here, this being a horror title, is that the game is still terifying. Some of the mechanics at work around combat and level design are awesome ideas and they almost always work. A not-so-small remark I must make here is that the game's "easy" setting is far, far from a true easy setting. This game is hard, and at times - it's hard for all the wrong reasons, like the player simply not wanting to deal with the same damn thing for the 15th time this chapter. But otherwise - gameplay is solid, even though some mechanics never feel truly explored. Personally, I still think that more supernatural enemies should have been present, but I guess that is subjective.
Problems, however, start to errupt a few hours into the game. The first thing you'll notice is a style of monotony, typical of games who want to artificially prolongue themselves. Alan Wake has a solid plot, ergo - no need for that. At least 8 hours of the game can be removed entirely and it won't change nothing at it's core. It often time seems like the game looses it's focus for the sake of being a game. It's like it's afraid to cross a border of some type, but given the year it was originally released in - it's understandable. That's a trait most mid-gen games carry.
Another thing some players might notice is the iffy writing. For a game about a writer, dealing with the stress of writer's block, it's expected for the script to be very well written. And it times it is - spot on and clever. But other time it ranges to borderline garbadge. This includes the fact that some characters do not get any proper character developement. At times, the game expects us to care for these said characters, even though it never gave us reason to, presenting them as rude ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. It's a paradox that often breaks the immersion of the game.
Ultimately, there is also lack of any real ending to the story. Not to mention that the two DLCs offer an ending that could be understood significantly differently from the original ending. What's worse is that we are left with too many unanswered questions. To some extent, I feel this was intended. But that does not change the fact that it's never a good sign in any piece of media, when it leaves your audience wanting more answers to important, core questions, which the story asked in the first place.
The obvious hints at the sequel we never got don't help much either. Hope never dies, they say, but with Remedy releasing that heartbreaking video, in which they feed us some bull about them not having the funds to make a seqel, I really doubt we will ever see one. Except if Remedy remember the era in which we live in and turn to a crowd-funding website. Let's hope they see the light.
All in all, Alan Wake seems much more of a mixed-package the second time around. The plot-holes and game time really made it tough. But even at that, everything else exceeds and still keeps it on point. So what I had previously said is absolutely valid:
"Alan Wake" is one of the most marvelous horror experiences available. Everything from the story and presentation to the combat and exploration is not only a horrifying joy, but it's also a extremely memorable one that will keep haunting you for quite some time. Even though part of that haunt will turn out to be unanswered questions.
This game absolutely deserves your time. I recommend it to everyone, especially to horror fans and people who like a solid plot. The game time might turn you off at times, but the addicting atmosphere will probably keep you coming back for that long period.

A thriller action adventure that plays with light and darkness. You take the role of Alan Wake, a writer, who goes on a vacation with his wife. Too bad their cottage (or the lake around it) is haunted and the darkness takes his wife hostage. Alan hits his head and is confused, alarmed and out-right horrified to find himself attacked by shadowy but unearthly shapes of townsfolk, friends and enemies alike. To survive he has to use light and gunmanship.
Basically Alan meets a number of horrors along the way and beats most of them with elaborate use of light, guns and fast feet. Story advances smoothly along six chapters, each of which brings new kinds of enemies, tools and of course lore and insight into the destiny of Alan.
After enjoying the story once you can play it through on a higher difficulty level, dubbed Nightmare, with stronger enemies and due to that scarcer resources. There are also two bonus chapters that are situated after the main story. The whole game takes anything from 15 to 25 hours to play through, more if you play it through with the higher difficulty level and even more if you go looking for all the extra stuff that gives you achievements. The main attraction however, at least to me, was the story that is enhanced by the immersion provided by believable body language and good voice acting.
Get it for full price and you probably won't regret it anyway, but the game is frequently on a high discount that gets you a nice thrilling story with a price of a large soda.

I've enjoyed the game alot so far. Lots of improvements over the first. I would watch some gameplay and decide for yourself if the lootboxes are obtrusive or not. People love to be miserable.
LOOTBOXES: In my 11.6 hours so far, I feel that they are extremely unnecessary to purchase and even though I see advertisements when I pause, it does not bother me or feel obtrusive. Every piece of gear I have equipped is of Epic or Legendary rarity, and all I've done so far is play story missions and a few vendetta missions. I have not felt underpowered at all, if anything I'm OP.
GRAPHICS: I have encounter a few graphical issues but after I updated my driver to the recommended, I have had no further issues. I'm using a gtx 770 and let the game recommend settings based on the card, and it looks and runs much better than I expected.
GAMEPLAY: Some people will not like combat in this game, but I feel that it is much improved over the previous game. Thanks to changes in the flow of combat it can feel more difficult at times, especially if there are a ton of mobs on screen.
It is still very simple and Assassins Creed like. The combat isn't very important to me personally because it doesn't need to shine for me to enjoy this game.
The Nemesis System is fantastic. I have yet to play a game where I care so much about the enemies I face and the allies I recruit. The orcs are almost like pokemon, and have positives and negatives. They can betray you. You can send your allies in to spy on the enemy and even assassinate their warchiefs. You can work together with your orcs to complete tasks or send them out on their own. For me this scratches an itch that I didn't even know I had. Will my favorite orc stab me in the back? Will he stay with me til the very end? Will he get cut in half, burned alive, or poisoned? This is where the game shines.
I will edit the review closer to 25 hours and probably again around 50.
All in all I would highly recommend this game so far, but I would ask that you watch some *SPOILER FREE* gameplay, as its clearly not going to be for everyone.

There are other complaints, but everything else has been said already and I cannot get myself through the effort of writing them all out.

((This review is shortened due to character limitations. You can read the full review here:
))
Overview
Released in 1995, Dark Forces hit the market right at the height of the early FPS craze that had been created by games like Wolfenstein 3D and Doom. Lucas Arts had already explored the series as flight sim, a platformer, and an on-rails shooter at this point, and they of course were well known for their point and click adventure games as well. Creating an FPS was uncharted territory for them, but did they manage? Let's take a look.
Gameplay - 1.5/5.0
Gameplay is, by far, the weakest part of this game. If you've played just about any FPS, you'll know exactly what to expect- be it Wolfenstein, Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Quake, Unreal, Half-Life, Halo, Call of Duty, take your pick. You have a gun. You point at the enemy. You click. You shoot. You win. It really is that simple for the most part- well, that and strafing when going against sturdier foes.
There are a variety of weapons- your standard blaster pistol actually remains useful throughout the entire gameBeyond that, you'll have a variety of other weapons- rapid firing weapons like the Stormtrooper Rifle, Imperial Repeater, and Fusion Cutter, Thermal Detonators to use as grenades, IM Mines, and even some heavy ordnance in the form of a Grenade Launcher, Concussion Rifle, and in the late game you even get access to a Plasma Rifle which can make quick work of just about anything but the final boss.
Aside from the running and gunning, they do try to keep things a little interesting with various puzzles- most of these are in the form of mazes of some sort, but a few of them seem really... Obtuse. There's also a fair number of platforming segments- and while I do love a good platformer, first person platforming is rarely done well, and this is certainly not one of those times. It also certainly doesn't help that looking up and down has a very limited field of view, and on top of that, there's no perspective correction, so any time you try to look at any angle other than straight ahead, you're going to see some weird issues with the polygons. Boss fights are petty uninteresting, they feel like more of the same of enemies...
On a final note, the levels can drag on quite a bit- now granted, this is also true of the sequel, but in Jedi Knight, you could save anywhere you wanted to, whereas in Dark Forces, you're expected to complete a level in a single sitting... And with many of these levels, they can take a good 20-30 minutes if you're not familiar with the layout.
Visual Presentation - 2.5/3.0
Old games can't look good, right? Wrong. This is far from the only example I'd pull up if making a list, but this game actually looks amazing for a DOS game. Other than the aforementioned lack of perspective correction, the visual style of the game actually holds up really well, environments are expansive, detailed, and atmospheric, enemies are detailed enough that you can pick them off at range with your more accurate weapons, and the cutscenes especially hold up extremely well despite their age. My only complaint here is that many of the environments do look somewhat "samey".
As for the story, it also receives high marks. While not the most complex and intricate story in the world, it does a great job of feeling like Star Wars. It knows how to get the atmosphere of the series right, and it has a few cameos fans are sure to appreciate- no major Expanded Universe cameos, though this is largely because this was the time period when the EU was just starting to take off thanks to the release of the Thrawn Trilogy a handful of years prior. In Dark Forces, you take the role of Kyle Katarn, a mercenary for hire that once served in the Empire, but like so many of the Rebellion's best soldiers, defected once he realized the truth of the New Order. It opens on a single level prologue representing Operation Skyhook- those of you that aren't Star Wars afficianodos may be wondering "What's Operation Skyhook?". Quite simply, it was the stealing of the Death Star plans and relaying them to Princess Leia's ship. Yes, before Disney got their hands on Lucasfilm and completely changed everything, THIS was how it was presented in the old canon. After that, the game's story truly begins with President Mon Mothma (for non-enthusiasts, the lady gives the briefing before the attack on the second Death Star) telling Katarn of his next assignment: A rebel base has been wiped out by a rather small contigent of Imperial forces, and it's up to him to investigate. Along the way, he finds out that the attack was carried out by Dark Troopers- droids produced in small numbers that weild ordnance and armor too heavy for any human to use, and designed by one of his former commanding officers from his time in the Imperial Navy, no less. The bulk of the journey is discovering more about the Dark Troopers, disrupting their production, and inevitably facing off against their inventor, General Mohc. It takes a simple story, and presents it in a way that makes it exciting and grand- not unlike the Star Wars films themselves.
Audio Presentation - 2.0/2.0
I have to give the game top marks here- there's really not too much to say. The voice acting is spot on, the actors playing characters from the movies do an excellent job of immitating their roles (primarily Vader, but also Mon Mothma as well), and the MIDI renditions of the classic John Williams' score are very well done (although admittedly, even Into the Trap gets tiresome after hearing it for the fiftieth time or so).
Conclusion
Dark Forces is a mixed bag for me. On the gameplay end of things, it's the same boring, tired, dumbed down gameplay that I always expect from the FPS genre. On the other hand, I do see that the team put a lot of genuine effort into it, and it did serve to bring us Kyle Katarn and Jan Ors- while they never reached the popularity of Zahn's characters (non-ethusiasts... Just nod your heads and ingore me for a moment), these are two of the most beloved EU characters, and for good reason. They show a lot of personality despite the game's simplicity. All in all, I find it hard to recommend this game, especially if you're not a fan of generic FPS titles in the first place. That being said, if you want a fun Star Wars story with memorable characters, I'd definitely say it's worth playing on Easy just to rush through the game for story purposes. Beyond that though, I'd say that it's a game better left to the past.
Verdict: 6.0/10.0

My first clear gaming memories were of this game (Plus hazy recollections of Doom) and at the time, it blew my young mind.
I've been revisiting it on and off every couple of years and every time it seems to have aged even worse. Back then, two hands on the keyboard was the way to go, fingers on the direction arrows, everything else scrambling for ctrl, x, space, you name it. It was clunky, and for the time period, it worked, but along came mouse-look, WASD movement, and that two handed keyboard control felt slower than hauling a ton of bricks.
However, I finally found a solution in a GoG thread (Which may or may not work with the steam version, I'm curently running it thrrough the GoG version) which provides mouselook (I rebound pageup and pagedown to my mousewheel, as the current preset is too sensitive) and WASD movement, while maintaining the feature complete game that other source ports like DarkXL can't provide.
(The fix, in question)
With that added, it's a much more functional game. Is it on par with a modern shooter? Honestly, no, but with that bit of control update, it matches the charm of old school shooters such as Doom, Duke Nukem, and Quake - a lot of bad guys between you and your objective, with a Star Wars flair.
I really like the avatar-like plants and other nature objects, it's a nice game to lay back and enjoy the world you are present in

First of, this is not a game at all. Now let me describe it in detail so you won't misunderstand.

So... yeah. It's not a video game. It's more like a software "labeled" as a game.
You just watch the mountain moving, changing, and sometimes talk back to you. The developer could add some interaction to keep the "game" from becoming a boring screensaver. But no, that would be too much to ask appearantly.
Do I recommend others to play this? I don't. For a "game" costing only 99 cents, it barely has any content at all. There are some graphical glitches in around the shadow texture and it always makes my dark side of the mountain looks ugly. I don't consider this art because there are more better looking "game" that have the same low price and have better "art".
For you people who got an extra 99 cents and wanted a screensaver labeled as a "game", well, here you go.

Negatives/Gripes:

It's no more educational than any dictionary.
Example of what I mean:
When you pick a synonym, the previous word is usually listed on the first page. Instead of being able to "undo" a word and try a different synonym, the game just keeps adding your choices together. Synonymy is a game where you are given a starting word and you have to travel trough synonyms of synonyms trying to reach the goal word that you are also given at the start.
The game has a difficulty selection, making it enjoyable to people of all ages. The easiest difficulty usually gives you very common words, where the paths are more obvious. But on the hardest difficulty, the words start to be a little more complex, not so common, making it challenging for older people. Since you can see the definition of every single word it's a very educational game - even for adults - you may learn a word or two that you didn't know before, specially on the harder difficulty settings.
You probably won't play this game for hours and hours in a row but rather on short bursts of time several times.
The game also features "seeds" (or pass-codes), a 5 character code that you and your friends can enter on the beginning of the game to ensure you have the same starting word and goal. That way you can compare your scores at the end.
There's also a global leaderboard, where you can see the the score, starting and goal words of the most recently played games around the world, along with its pass-code in case you want to try the same challenge by yourself.
I absolutely recommend it. It is very cheap too. Get it.

Executive Assault is a RTS (Real time stragey). Unlike most RTS games, Executive Assault has a FPS (First Person Shooter) mode where you can take control of your robots without leaving your comfy CEO chair. In FPS mode you track your enemys (even through walls) with a red square being placed around them. It is better then just commanding and leaving your robots to shoot down your rivals because in FPS mode, you can see as far as the eye can see (well the whole map if theres nothing blocking your view.) The robots in normal mode will only shoot things near them that they can see (this also depends on the weapons that they are using). In FPS your weapons do have a range limit but you can actually shoot further. You can command any nearby troops by pressing F (Follow) or G (Guard) in FPS mode.
There are many differnt ways you can play this game. You could play against AI or real people. You could play 1v1 1v2 1v3 1v4 2v2. Multiplayer makes any game much more fun by having differnt people have differnt stratergies and some people will be easier to destroy as they have had less game time. Some people will be tryhards and murder everything in there path.
There are ways that you can shoot giant green lasers shoot your enemys down or make meteors fall and give you reasources. You can create hackerbots to break into enemys bases and open all the doors without having to shoot them down which takes forever. You can make turrets, towers, walls, bunkers and there is probably much more coming to this game.
The tech tree is very neat and split up into differnt tabs on a wheel. Sections like Units allows you to upgrade or create new units. Energy, Ballistic and Trion weapons allows you to create and upgrade your weapons for your units. Structures allows you to reasearch radars (which eventually lead to giant green death laser) and a reaseach facility (where you can pick up iron from meteor strikes and bring them back).  You can also customise your units by pretty much choosing a shell, weapon and ability for the unit. Theres mechs, infantry robots, tanks, more tanks, more mechs, planes, more planes, and of course a jeep.
Graphics
Executive assault supports a reasolution up to 1980x1020 (i think). The graphics arent the best i have seen but this game is made by a single man! The maps look slightly man made and could use a bit of natureisation (not a word but meh) The terrain seems too flat and you cant climb the mountains that some of the maps have. The units could use a bit more detail and the overlay is confusing and ugly. (but the graphics dont make up the whole game right?)

Pros:

Updates flowing through frequently

Lots of buildings
Many ways to win/lose (Stupid rouge robots)

I had to wait until I had a substantial in-game time to actually review this fairly.  I think I've came to a conclusion.
This is not a game, as anyone who sims would tell you.  Sure, there are little missions and things like that that you can play through and complete an objective, however, the core of the simulator is simply that: simulation.
If you're thinking about buying FSX simply to play through and complete the missions, this is not for you.  Get a game like "DCS: World" or "War Thunder".  But, if you're part of the small niche that enjoys simulating real life flights, planning flights, practicing VFR or IFR, or anything along those lines, get it.  Even if you don't know much about aviation in general, but you are willing to learn, FSX is a great place to start.
That being said, FSX isn't flawless.  Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition is not an exception to this.
FSX: Steam Edition is simply a way to get into the wonderful world of flight simulation easily over the quick and painless Steam platform.  There are very minor improvements behind the scenes, but in terms of content and things like that nothing has really changed from what you can get out of the boxed Flight Simulator X.  The only big changes are the fact that "Out of Memory Errors" seem to barley ever happen.  (I've personally only experienced it once, and that was because I didn't tweak much of my game at all.)
But that brings me to the next part of the entire Flight Simulator X experience, whether you're on the boxed version or Steam.  FSX needs addons, tweaks, and bugfixes.  Stock FSX, simply and quite frankly put, is rudimentary.  The flight models of aircrafts aren't nescessarily accurate and scenery isn't beautiful or photorealistic by any means.  On top of that, FSX can be heavily improved by turning on the buggy DX10 and using Steve's DX10 fixer, but that's another story.
FSX also needs some tweaking to it's config files to work better on modern hardware.  But I'm not going to go into that, there are fantastic guides on the steam page, and internet, that will help you with that.
The jist of what I'm trying to say is that FSX is something that you're either going to fall in love with, or become just another game that sits in your Steam library untouched.
You'd want to expect to buy some nice aircraft.  (I personally recommend the "A2A Cessna 172 Trainer", fantastic attention to detail and flight model.)  Those cost money, and while there are freeware aircraft out on the internet, you aren't going to get the level of realism and immersion from big names like A2A or PMDG.  Scenery can be easily supplemented with addons like "Active Sky" or "Orbx" but even then it costs more money and more time from just simulation.  On top of that, you need either a joystick or a yoke and rudder pedals.  You're not going to get away for long just using keyboard and mouse.  It's just not fun.
So in the end, yes I do reccommend this game.  Very much so, actually.  But you have to be willing to put forth the time and money it takes to get this game looking and feeling as real as it can.

This is my favorite game of all time. Intelligent writing, near-flawless gameplay and enough horror elements to keep fans of the genre happy, and keep people who don't like horror on the edge of their seats. Right off the bat, Life is Strange meets the requirements of what I would consider a great game: an engaging story, memorable, nuanced characters, and a
soundtrack. I'm not one who cares much about graphics but other than the oft-mentioned lack of lip movement in some scenes, I saw no need for improvement in the semi-realistic art style and motion-capture animation of Life is Strange. I loved the hand-painted textures and felt inspired to paint digitally again because of it. The cinematic Moments of Calm, the montages at the end of every episode, and even walking through the environments while the aforementioned soundtrack plays in the background do a lot help you relate to Max Caulfield, immerse you in the world of Arcadia Bay, and make you truly feel a part of the story. Kudos as well to the developers for their focus on real issues and their realistic depictions of relationships, especially from the perspectives of females characters.
However, the game still has its limitations. Many of the secondary characters fall under popular tropes so it isn't difficult to predict how things go with them. Its point-and-click gameplay might feel tiring and linear if your expectations are not set to playing a story-driven game where you have to interact with objects and people to fill in the big picture. You may think that the variety of choices will mean a variety of outcomes or endings but that is sadly not the case (however, I would also argue that the binary ending is what makes Life is Strange so compelling). In other words, if you are looking for an open-world game with an über customizable player-character whose in-game personality depends on your choices, Life is Strange is not that game.
I urge you to think of Life is Strange not as a traditional 'game' with the objective to win. When I told my friend about how distraught I was about a certain choice, he replied, "Oh, well. It's just a game." But
, Life is Strange reveals itself to be more than just a game. It lets you to face truths about friendship, about ethics, about life in general in a way we likely won't experience in real life. In the same way we discern works of art like paintings, literature, even certain movies and songs, games can carry profound meaning for its players, too, and DONTNOD has achieved that with Life is Strange.
: While Life is Strange leaves much to be desired, it deserves credit for providing a whole new gaming experience, one where the player is prompted to undergo philosophical and personal reflection to understand its message. Developing the choices-and-consequences element to allow more complex variations in endings would make this already fantastic game more enjoyable, but the game as it stands is already very satisfying. It is simple, moving, and beautifully made. Despite the predictable plot and characters, the voice acting, cinematography, music, and overall ambience of the game make it truly something special.
I cannot stress enough how good the soundtrack is for a game of this type and style; every song captures the emotions of the scenes they are in. But besides that, there are so many references in the game -- from quotes by Robert Frost to obscure graffiti referencing David Foster Wallace -- that give the game nuance. Life is Strange is a game that you will not likely forget, if not because of its story and characters, then at least because it made you reflect on your own life.

.Story.
N.E.R.O is a game that relies heavily on its story and so, to avoid spoilers, I’ll just say that it’s a sad one involving a family of three—mother, father, and son. It keeps you guessing until the very end before wrapping itself up (for the most part) in a nice little bow.
The story is narrated via cutscenes—usually after you’ve solved a puzzle or completed a segment of a chapter—and the narrative voice is good.
.Gameplay.
You use WASD to move around and the mouse to interact with the environment. Movement is very, very slow even when you’re holding shift to run. Once you’ve met the second person, you can use space bar to direct them, but you’ll only really need their help on two occasions.
There are a handful of little puzzles, most of which have to do with timing and sequence, but not many. You’ll have the ability to lob a magical orb in order to activate switches and you’ll use it frequently. For the most part, however, you’ll be roaming and reading the glowing text that tells you the origin of the area you’re wandering. There are two colours of text: the white serves as a narrative that describes the area before you while the blue reflects the dialogue exchanged between the members of a family of three.
There are also collectibles, which appear as floating picture frames. They’re pretty easy to spot as long as you look carefully, and collecting them adds a sense of purpose. Once you’ve collected enough of them, they form a full portrait. There’s one portrait for each of the four chapters the game is divided into.
.Atmosphere.
The game looks fantastic. It’s dark and somber save the brightly-glowing flora and fauna that battle the gloom. Each of the four chapters all look very different and the levels were well designed for stumbling into secrets and seeing little details that make the story hit that much closer to home.
.Pros and Cons.
.Longevity.
This game will take you, at the least, two hours to complete. And that includes reading the text. If you skip the puzzles that aren’t required, brush past the glowing, floating text, and gun for the end… You could probably finish it in less.
.Bottom line.
N.E.R.O makes me wish, yet again, for the ability to leave a neutral review because I can’t recommend it as a game—and especially not considering its price—but I can recommend it as a beautiful, albeit brief experience. If it has a price cut of at least 75%, I could say this is worth picking up for the sound and visuals alone. Otherwise, save your money for something that will give you a little more bang for your buck.

N.E.R.O is a beautiful game, in fact the opening cut scene is dare I say beautiful.  It left me engaged, drawn in and waiting to play the game.  Once the game started I was thrown into a world that looked like something painted by a world class painter.  The colors game the numerous areas a vibrant and alive feel to them.  I found myself taking in the scenery while in awe.  Looking at the multiple colors, thinking to myself this terrain could be something out of an animated film.  Dark caves lit by glowing creatures, water that actually looks like water, animals which seemed almost real enough to touch.
While N.E.R.O is a simple walking simulator it's set apart from other games in the genre by the graphics, I can't stress enough how beautiful the game looked.  If you're a graphics hound you'll love it..   While other walking simulators looked good, they lacked that special something that made the scenes look alive.. N.E.R.O clearly had that it factor going for it.  Aside from the graphics the game also has an amazing soundtrack, which further lent itself towards making the game feel alive.  Hearing a waterfall get louder as you approach, and lower as you move away..
I pretty much covered the graphics already, but the store page doesn't even begin to do justice to this wonderful piece of interactive art.  Well drawn, well population and well animated.  If you're like me you'll be drawn into the game immediately.. The only down fall of the beautiful graphics are the character moves at a snails pace..  Even when sprinting it seems like you're walking in a mud puddle heading up a hill.  While I can understand the need to slow things down and give the gamer more time to enjoy the scenery having the character move that slowly is kind of detracting from the experience..
Similar to other Walking simulators, you walk around at a slow pace, reading signs, and solving simplistic puzzles which give you access to the next area..  Generally speaking if you enjoyed other walking simulators you'll enjoy this game.  It really shines above in the artwork and sounds.  Like other walking simulators the game has collectibles, in this way you collect pictures.  Small fragments are scattered around each chapter of the game, which you interact with, collect and build a completed picture.  The game also features numerous puzzles, most of them are rather simplistic, press the button and then fire your energy ball into it.  Others require you to use another character that joins you mid way through the first chapter.  Yet others require you to aim your energy ball at a distance and complete an arc shot.  Although the aiming mechanic is slightly broken and the only challenge comes from the ball needing to be aimed nearly perfectly in order to count.  This can leave the gamer frustrated as they line up what should be a perfect shot only to have it explode early, or completely miss..
The story is a wonderfully told tale, I won't spoil it here but as you move along in the game it unfolds before your eyes, while it's a bit easily figured out fairly early on, the story is engaging enough that you'll find yourself pressing forward to find out what happens next.  Depending on who you are and what you've gone through in life, the game has a chance to leave you feeling emotional.   The story is told through sentences and statements spread throughout the world.  A few cut scenes are sprinkled here and there as well, although 99% of it is reading..
Beautiful visuals and scenery
amazing music
moving story
Totally in love with the Final Fantasy 9 mage design for the characters
Slow moving character (speed that fella up a bit)
puzzles are a bit underwhelming, easy and repetitive
The aiming puzzles are more difficult than they need to be, and the aiming mechanic is a bit broken, (it's made slightly better if using a K&M, but still not perfect)
The game is kind of on the shorter side..
Price tag is a bit steep for the content offered
You can really tell this was a labor of love from the developer, the scenery is beautiful, the music is perfect, and the story is engaging.  The game isn't perfect, but it's very well worth a purchase for nothing more than seeing the beautiful scenery and hearing the ambient sounds, which are nearly perfectly blended together to create something I'd consider a masterpiece.  Gameplay wise it's a bit on the weaker end of the gene pool, but as a walking simulator that isn't a PewDiePie jump scare fest it ranks up there pretty highly..  Then again most walking simulators are lacking in the gameplay department, only so many ways exist to walk from point A to point B...  With that said I'd recommend picking this game up, but if you really aren't sure wait for a steam sale.. You'll love the atmosphere, and be completely and utterly drawn into this amazing game..

N.E.R.O.: Nothing Ever Remains Obscure is a short, story driven walking simulator adventure with puzzles.
Throughout the game, the lighting is absolutely obnoxious, especially In the first chapter. I was actually squinting because the crazy bright lights were flickering, and hurting my eyes. I tried playing with the settings, and completely turning the lens flare off, but no matter what I adjusted, there was still way too much glow on everything. In addition to the rather unpleasant lighting, the game also suffers from constant texture changes, and texture popping, and it was a major distraction. For a game that is predominately a walking simulator, these severe lighting and texture issues have a very strong negative impact on the game overall.
I’m not sure if the game just got better as it went on, or I just started to enjoy it more because of the story. I really enjoyed the story; it wasn’t anything mind blowing, but it was emotional, and I admit that it got me all choked up, and had me in tears. The story is definitely the highlight of the N.E.R.O., and it’s disappointing that the rest of the game isn’t as polished as it could be.
I played the game about 2 hours, and while I don’t feel the need to replay the game, part of me wishes I had explored a little more thoroughly because I know I missed some things. Then the other part of me just wanted to be done with the visual issues that the game suffers from.
Even though the story was good, and did evoke an emotional response, I still don’t think it was quite good enough to carry the rest of the game; considering how short N.E.R.O. is, and all the graphical and lighting issues it still has. It’s a shame to say, but right now, the game simply does not justify anywhere near the full $20 retail price.

Shuggy is a great indie game with tons of levels to explore! It's an old school Halloween-esque platformer with puzzles and challenges around every bend. The game play is smooth. The graphics and sounds are acceptable. Each room has an array of new traps and foes to overcome by various means -- fly, float, and swing your way to victory! The developer regularly visits the Steam forums and listens to ideas and suggestions. An expansion pack is soon to be released. Which is good, because despite it's charm, once you have completed the game, its replay value is somewhat limited. While the single player campaign is stellar, the multiplayer aspects also need to be addressed. Offline co-op mode for a PC game is impractical. These two minor aspects would make it a solid 8 gaming score, but I always respect a developer who interacts with the public on a regular basis and is constantly improving game play.

N.E.R.O.: Nothing Ever Remains Obscure is a visually stunning game. Taking even the briefest look at the screenshots and trailers will let you see that for yourselves. If you enjoy slowly walking through almost breathtaking vistas, then you should enjoy this game. If you are looking for the next big puzzle game, this might not be the game for you.
You can easily see the time and care that went into making N.E.R.O.: Nothing Ever Remains Obscure’s visuals. Each of the four areas of the game has a different feel. The first is a bioluminescent cave which leads to the second area, a lush vibrant forest. The third area takes you inside a rundown building and the fourth to a desert. Each distinct area looks starkly different from the last so the visuals never really become boring. As you slowly walk/run through the game, you will see story fragments floating around the map, guiding your way to the end of the level. You are welcome to just follow the path to the end, but if you are more adventurous and want to take in all the beautiful visuals, you will be rewarded by finding picture fragment collectables and optional puzzles. With the floating text, the picture fragments and the interjections by the narrator throughout your adventure and after puzzles, the cryptic story will unfold before you.
The stunning visuals in the game are marred by the excessive use of bloom and lens flare. It can almost blind you at times with how overly bright things can be. You can adjust the lens flare and gamma, but it doesn’t really help that much. Even moving the lens flare slider all the way down, doesn’t stop it from occurring. Adjusting the gamma can dull it, but it also dulls out passages to the point where you might walk past the formerly dimly lit passage you were supposed to take. If you can look past the glare, the game is, as mentioned, visually stunning all the way through. Even the character details are incredibly well done. The glowing eyed figures in their light trimmed cloaks made for a fun and different take on the usually standard character design. Even the scenery is well detailed, it feels like a lot of time and effort went into making this one great looking game.
The ambient sounds, the lilt of the narrator’s voice, all went into making the experience better. The overall story was very realistic and believable. It is entirely possible that people playing this game will actually be able to relate to the story and feel great empathy for the characters. The story attempts to be particularly emotionally stirring and I have no doubt that it will indeed have that effect on many of the players who play it, particularly those with children. The story was a bit predictable as it has been done before in movies and other games, but it still had its own unique flavour here.
If you looked past the blindly bright bloom in this game, and ended it here, this could be one of the best story-driven walking simulator games to hit Steam this year. Unfortunately it isn’t really classed as just a walking simulator, it is a puzzler too. Sorry to say, it falls a bit flat here.
The puzzles basically fall into two basic element categories, buttons and target practice. Buttons are the standard trope in puzzlers, so odds are you know how those work. You press a button and it does something. Sometimes it is a constant effect until turned off, other times it is a timed effect or needs to be held down. Your job is to figure out the right combination to do whatever it is the puzzle wants you to do. These puzzles, while incredibly easy for me to solve, were not bad. I have played so many puzzle games that it is very likely I can just visualize the solution instantly and get it right my first try which makes the puzzle seem too simple to me. Someone who is not as practiced, might find them challenging, and I am going to assume that to be the case. The other element is a royal pain in the posterior in my opinion. I have never been good at playing sniper in games that have snipers, so maybe that is why I found this element so annoying. You have an arced shot. The further it goes, the lower it will fall. Eventually it will just explode. The puzzles involving shooting typically have you hitting a tiny unforgiving target somewhere off in the distance. The short range ones I had no issue with, but the ones that required you to line up the shot just right and fire it over a long distance took me more trial and error than I am willing to admit to. Now if getting close worked, I would be fine with it, but getting close doesn’t count for anything. I had many shots that appeared to have narrowly missed the tiny opening and exploded just outside. Despite enveloping the target; it didn’t count as a hit. The thing is you can’t even really tell if you actually did get close or if it just looked close because you can’t really zoom in on the projectile to follow it. Overall, I found this element kind of ruined the fun of the game. Sure I felt relief when I finally managed to nail a shot, or felt joy when I managed to get it in the first try, but in the end, I really disliked this mechanic.
Despite the fact this says I have played it for over 9 hours, the game itself is actually incredibly short. Even without knowing where anything is, or knowing the solutions to the puzzles in advance, it took me under two hours to 100% it. I replayed certain areas of it to piece together the story better, and I also left it running to gather its card and forgot it was alt-tabbed for about 8 hours.
Overall, would I recommend you buy it? I personally think for the length of the game, it is a bit over priced. The visuals are stunning and probably took a lot of time and effort to make, but the weak puzzle elements and short game length makes it hard for me to justify the price tag. If you see it on sale for half price or less, you might be interested in it. You will get a visually stunning walking simulator with a compelling story that is only slightly hampered with inconvenient but mostly optional puzzle elements. If you are looking for the next big puzzler, stay away from N.E.R.O. You will be disappointed by the puzzle elements I can almost promise you that. I am going to give it a positive rating since I can’t do neutral and don’t want to be negative because for a walking simulator, the visuals are incredible. The story is compelling enough, and I had no major technical issue others than the slow walking speed and excessive bloom. I am going to assume the puzzle elements were added just to break up the flow to slow you down and not actually meant as a draw to the game.

Right off the bat, Life is Strange meets the requirements of what I would consider a great game: an engaging story, memorable, nuanced characters, and a
soundtrack. I'm not one who cares much about graphics but other than the oft-mentioned lack of lip movement in some scenes, I saw no need for improvement in the semi-realistic art style and motion-capture animation of Life is Strange. I loved the hand-painted textures and felt inspired to paint digitally again because of it. The cinematic Moments of Calm, the montages at the end of every episode, and even walking through the environments while the aforementioned soundtrack plays in the background do a lot help you relate to Max Caulfield, immerse you in the world of Arcadia Bay, and make you truly feel a part of the story. Kudos as well to the developers for their focus on real issues and their realistic depictions of relationships, especially from the perspectives of females characters.
However, the game still has its limitations. Many of the secondary characters fall under popular tropes so it isn't difficult to predict how things go with them. Its point-and-click gameplay might feel tiring and linear if your expectations are not set to playing a story-driven game where you have to interact with objects and people to fill in the big picture. You may think that the variety of choices will mean a variety of outcomes or endings but that is sadly not the case (however, I would also argue that the binary ending is what makes Life is Strange so compelling). In other words, if you are looking for an open-world game with an über customizable player-character whose in-game personality depends on your choices, Life is Strange is not that game.
I urge you to think of Life is Strange not as a traditional 'game' with the objective to win. When I told my friend about how distraught I was about a certain choice, he replied, "Oh, well. It's just a game." But
, Life is Strange reveals itself to be more than just a game. It lets you to face truths about friendship, about ethics, about life in general in a way we likely won't experience in real life. In the same way we discern works of art like paintings, literature, even certain movies and songs, games can carry profound meaning for its players, too, and DONTNOD has achieved that with Life is Strange.
: While Life is Strange leaves much to be desired, it deserves credit for providing a whole new gaming experience, one where the player is prompted to undergo philosophical and personal reflection to understand its message. Developing the choices-and-consequences element to allow more complex variations in endings would make this already fantastic game more enjoyable, but the game as it stands is already very satisfying. It is simple, moving, and beautifully made. Despite the predictable plot and characters, the voice acting, cinematography, music, and overall ambience of the game make it truly something special.
I cannot stress enough how good the soundtrack is for a game of this type and style; every song captures the emotions of the scenes they are in. But besides that, there are so many references in the game -- from quotes by Robert Frost to obscure graffiti referencing David Foster Wallace -- that give the game nuance. Life is Strange is a game that you will not likely forget, if not because of its story and characters, then at least because it made you reflect on your own life.

About a year ago, I found FSX: Gold Edition sitting on my shelf from a few years ago, collecting dust. I opened it and found 3 discs: one for all the military aircraft, and 2 for public aviation. I was (and still am) more interested in public aviation, so I plopped in Disc 2, but it didn't do anything. I inserted Disc 1, and installation started. About half-way, it asked to insert Disc 2, so that's what I did, and installation completed. I played with it for a little bit, and closed it, just to do something else. When I came back and re-opened the application, it asked to repair or un-install the game, so I selected to repair the game, and of course, half-way there it asked to insert Disc 2. When repairing was done, I clicked "Finished", and nothing happened. Disc 2 was apparently for installation ONLY, so when I re-inserted Disc 1, it asked to repair or uninstall, again. I set the box back on my shelf, and let it collect dust again.
A few days before Christmas, I noticed that FSX:SE was out for a discount of $4.99, so I purchased it immediately. I was very pleased to now have a permanent flight simulator.
I don't understand why Dovetail is releasing useless DLC's for ridiculous amounts of money.  Instead of falling for Dovetail's useless DLC's, you should get third-party payware (i.e. Airbus X Extended, 737 NGX, GSX, etc.), or save up for it. Otherwise, enjoy using the default aircraft. Not much payware is yet compatible with Steam Edition, so if you really want something that's not out yet, simply wait or request the developer to make it compatible. The game can't be played offline, so if your internet cuts out, you'll have to wait until it comes back so you can start up FSX. If you have the original FSX, KEEP IT, unless you want multiplayer. If you are going to get FSX, but only have Steam Edition as an option, good luck trying to keep yourself from writing a negative review. Remember that you should not rely on Dovetail to make this game better, as it seems they're doing nothing to fix any bugs.
Otherwise, I recommend this game for enthusiasts who don't mind spending their savings on third-party payware, or if they just want to fly around.

So after playing this game for about an hour and a half, I really struggle to find anything negative to say. The game is a birds eye run and gun bullet hell type of shooter with roguelike elements including permadeath, leveling, and randomly generated areas. Now the graphics here are simple, and the music may become a bit repetitive after dying a bunch, but wholistically the audiovisual presentation is fantastic. Everything has punch and pizzaz. While the character designs I've seen so far arent really anything unusual, besides maybe the crystal golem character, they all have a lot of charm. The gameplay is fast, energetic, and challenging. There is no wasted time between the action either. The longest downtime youll see is when you mull over switching a weapon or which perk to take when you level up. When you kill the final enemy in an area, you get sucked directly into the next level, no meandering about. Bosses show up a little unexpectedly and depending on the number of supporting enemies around can be quite the death knell. Weapons are spaced fairly evenly and ammo and health arent exceedingly common. These and experience can be picked up with a fair amount of magnetism, but what is really clever about all these (besides the weapons) is that they disappear in only a few seconds, which encourages you to move into areas where you risk taking damage. Vlambeer doesnt want you to be too cool and calculated. The game can be a bit ambiguous with the perk descriptions, and you have no real way of knowing how a weapon compares to what you already have without trying it out. For the energy weapons particularily, I had no idea what to expect. You can only carry two, so you have to choose carefully. Whether these things are positive or negative is up to your perspective, this sort of try it and see what you get attitude is common to roguelikes. Ultimately I found the game to be extremely fun and well worth its farily low price point.

This is where the game shines.
I will edit the review closer to 25 hours and probably again around 50.

There are other complaints, but everything else has been said already and I cannot get myself through the effort of writing them all out.

I have almost 900 Hours on Civilization V and I am going to be honest: This game doesnt have that "One more turn" feeling Civ5 has. I will however recommend it because the base game is pretty good. Sure it can get annoying sometimes, and sure it might be near impossible to build wonders, but it changed how I traditionally played Civ.
In Civ5, I would simply start as a nation, try to get as many ruins and start my religion, then policy my way to victory until the Industrial Era, get an Ideology, then declare war as I saw fit until I could choose my desired victory condition. I did this for all victory types. This game however, doesnt let you use this fool proof plan.
Civ6 is more of a micro manager. You have to make sure some cities have certain districts, and those districts need to be worked on or your people might get unhappy, or there might not be enough housing to promote growth. And now that Worker immortality is gone as well, decisions must be made between if you really need that farm or that luxary resource you could trade off.
War was heavily reworked as well. I cant go into full detail since I have only declared war once or twice since this review, but you basically need a real reason why to declare war without everyone you know hating you for the rest of the game. A denounce usually helps you, but sometimes a good ole fashion holy war might be needed, or a protecter war to keep your city states around.
I recommed this game for those who are new the Civilization series, very beautifully designed and a nice feel for it, and very easy to get sucked into the game as well.
