This game is really cool if you're into tile/turn-based strategy games, and it also throws in the "roguelike" components of randomized dungeons, items, and playthroughs.  My first playthrough lasted 5 hours on Beginner difficulty, which seems short, but it's meant to be played multiple, multiple times (with like 7 difficulties shown from the start).  You gain experience each time you finish the game, win or lose (so you always get credit for your work), unlocking more stuff as you move on to higher difficulties.
Randomized hacks and items have been really interesting so far, with me feeling as if my limited choices and combos of those choices really matter.  You also choose what kind of missions you will undertake as you prepare for the final mission, unable to complete them all (and they're also randomized each game as are level layouts and guards/drones/etc), deciding whether you want to steal agent implants, heist a vault of credits (to upgrade your agents or buy items/hacks), rescue new agents, and more.
I didn't think the game structure would be as interesting as it is until I won once and started on the second difficulty.  It was noticably harder and I failed, but felt just fine about starting up again and trying out a different agent's abilities and hacking loadout.
Not to mention the awesome futuristic "hacker" world and art style, complete with the nice touch of "demoscene" music when you're buying abilities from random hacked terminals in a level.  A damn good game.

I want to start the review off by saying I wish I could choose a neutral recommendation, but Steam doesn't give me that option. The isn't good, nor bad, as long as you know exactly what you're going into, and enjoy that genre.
It really pains me to give N.E.R.O a negative, because I fell in love with the aesthetic. I love glowy stuff, and the world looks very fantastical. Well, I fell in love with the cinematic trailer on the store page. The game itself doesn't look quite as good. The bloom effect is a bit excessive, and the colours and world overall are a bit underwhelming. They feel lifeless compared to the cinematics. Of course I can see that it's harder to make the ingame world look that great, I'm just saying it was a disappointment.
Although there are puzzles to solve, and a few things you can interact with, the game can still be classified as what many people call a "walking-simulator". I don't really like using that term as it feels a bit derogatory, but you know exactly what I'm saying when I use it, so it's useful. This is because the puzzles are almost all incredibly easy to solve, and the interactivity is reduced to simple things like pressing obvious buttons. You don't really feel like the world is real.
Just to make it clear, it has much more to do than games like Dear Esther, because you can actually DO things, just not that many.
With that being said, I still enjoyed walking around the game. There are some cool visuals, giant structures and beautiful plants. It's just a tad bit too slow paced for me, even with the sprinting function. The areas are a bit too big with not much new to look at, or no environment or object to play around with. You're rewarded for exploring by finding some collectibles, whch is nice.
The story didn't really grip me. The narrator does a decent job, but the lines he's given aren't great. It all sounds out of context and doesn't make too much sense. I feel like when you go through a second playthrough, perhaps it'll make more sense, but the game sadly doesn't tempt me into playing it through a second time. It's also quite short.
I like the way the text in the game is actually floating in the world, as opposed to being HUD on your screen. There's even a nice detail where walking through the text will cause it to ripple. Nice way of preventing immersion break.
I really enjoyed the music. It added very well some moments of "woah" when you walk into a beautiful, vast room.
Overall, I definitely don't think it's a bad game. I just think you need to know what you're going into. It's quite linear, doesn't have much actual gameplay, and it doesn't look amazing, but it's still an interesting place to explore. Again, I wish I could give it a neutral, but I'm forced to give it a Negative instead.
Consider buying the game and giving it a try if something about it gripped you initially. Not to undermine the developer's hard work, but perhaps if you're unsure about your purchase, grabbing the game on sale will feel more worth it.

Alpha Protocol is a game that mixes stealth, cover-based shooting, and RPGs. It is very much like Deus Ex, and at times feels like a poor man's Human Revolution: it carries many of the flaws of DX:HR, and plays differently.
Alpha Protocol is much more geared towards RPG development, rather than skill that becomes easier with experience. All of the skill tracks (which cover all the weapons: pistols, assault rifles, shotguns, SMGs, and your fists; as well as stealth, toughness, and a couple other utilities) have a skill with a cooldown associated it-- giving the player some ridiculous power for a period of time. For instance, Shadow Operative, a Stealth skill, grants limited invisibility for a couple seconds, allowing the player to takedown foes without being spotted, even if a guard is staring directly at them and would spot them in any case. Their is a counter to this-- turrets and cameras still spot you-- but this can also be mitigated. The skill system, while well-implemented gameplay wise, makes it feel unrealistic-- the player is regarded as simply human (unlike JC Denton, who is better than human), so why can they turn invisible and slow down time?
However, the skills-- which, in my experience, drive combat-- are fun to play with. Something like Room Sweep, the shotgun skill that makes every shot fired knock foes down for a couple seconds, is incredibly fun to use, even if it's incredibly silly.
The major shortcoming of the game is in poorly implemented bosses, which force players into direct combat-- something that stealth-geared players are ill-prepared for. These bosses usually have auto-blocks after a time for melee combat, as well, making melee oriented players impaired. Overall the greatest weakness of the game is in the bosses, which feel unfair more often than not.
Overall, Alpha Protocol is a Deus Ex lookalike that spins the style of the game towards more fun action and superhuman acts. The game's missions flow well, and it does well in the 10 hour story to convey that your actions and conversations make impact on the story, but grinds to a halt every once in a while as an unfair boss grinds the action to a halt.
I'd buy it... but only on sale.

My CONS section contains a lot of negatives regarding visuals and rightfully so because at its core this game is a visual novel and each time my partner walked through a solid metal gate, or half a building popped in it took me out of the immersion of the story. The only extremely solid visuals in this game are the cinematics which show off a beautiful world that I wish I would have experienced in the game.

Alpha Protocol, more accurately the critical response thereto, is a monument to games journalisms’ need for art-house institutions willing to judge games on non-commercial, non-standard merits. Considering Alpha Protocol as one considers most AAA-titles reveals a failed experiment: a reactive plot with inconsistent characters, gunplay that doesn’t quite land, unbalanced skill-trees that result in a clear hierarchy of character builds, and a floundering finale. These properties are, in some ways, Obsidian’s hallmark: since KOTOR2 and NWN2 the studio (my personal favourite working studio) has been plagued with releasing inconsistent products. In some ways, Alpha Protocol is the worst offender: there are some marring bugs that were never fixed which can lead to very flawed plays. Despite the above mentioned issues—even the slightly bland story and inconsistent characters—I’ve played through Alpha Protocol three times and enjoyed each pass.
Obsidian remind me of a quote from Tony Kushner (American dramatist most famous for Angels in America): Kushner distinguishes between two types of artists, “the ones who ask small questions but give great answers and the ones who ask huge questions and often, as a consequence of the ambitiousness of their questioning, fail to give good answers”. Kushner holds that both are necessary, and I agree with him; Obsidian and their works should be treated as the second category. They ask huge questions about RPG design, and though they fail, the questions themselves are both a merit and a necessity.
Alpha Protocol questions the very foundations of RPGs: it is not science fiction or fantasy, it has a branching plot in which the player is almost fifth business instead of universal saviour, and there is no party. Spies, turncoats, flashbacks take you on a global adventure that feels, ultimately, small: this isn’t fate of the galaxy (KOTOR) or fate of the Great Wheel (NWN2) stuff. We have a relatively localized plot that, while slightly bland and riddled with some forgettable characters, unfolds organically and persuasively. Everything feels like it happens for a reason, and you never question your character’s role in it; the game is quite good at being reactive (or at least appearing so, and illusion is everything) and that’s the whole goal.
And on the merit of its questions, I think Alpha Protocol is an important game. It asks: does an RPG need a party? (no); can it deal with slightly smaller stakes? (yes); can it play like an action game instead of an excel simulator? (yes), etc. I would never absolve Alpha Protocol of its bugs or failures—one particular bug causes all enemies on a map to disappear, which can make some areas of the game unforgivably bland, until you figure out that it’s a bug you can correct by shutting down and reloading, which is still unacceptable—but regardless I recommend the game as a glimpse of what RPGs could be like. And, honestly, the bugs aren’t that bad; if you’ve made your way through STALKER, you’ve played far worse on that front.

The Binding of Isaac is a modern take on the rogue-like genre. Following the theme of Edmund McMillan’s super meat boy, this game has an extremely gory graphical theme. Just like SMB, this game is sadistically hard. It can easily take an average, slow reflexed gamer some half a dozen tries before they beat the game one time. The mechanics and controls are easy; it’s the reflex part of the game that is brutal. If you have slow hands, don’t expect to beat this game anytime soon. BOI delivers a strange derivation of the bible’s “binding of Isaac” tale, I found it to be very good satire. The key part to this game is replay-ability, each replay grants a different ending, resulting in different boss level scenario. You have to beat the game 9 times for total completion. Overall if you’re a huge fan of rogue-likes, buy this game! If you hate playing through the same level over and over again to see a different ending each time, save your money.

She uses this power during the subsequent course of events, where she investigates the dark things happening in her prep school and the surrounding small town. It’s both gripping and beautiful, bringing you into Max’s world as the plot thickens and twists.
1. This game shines in how it brings you into Max’s world. I found myself exploring the detailed environments, examining everything around me with Max’s narration. The graphics are powered by Unreal Engine and are beautiful and sublime. An indie rock soundtrack (I don’t even like indie rock) sets the mood perfectly.
2. Max’s time traveling powers provide fun and interesting ways to solve puzzles. It’s an interesting mechanic, and none of
the quests felt like chores.
3. The plot is what drives this game. While she investigates what’s happening in this small town, Max navigates through the youthful drama of high school, making friends and dealing with enemies. It captures the slice of time that is being a teenager on the cusp of adulthood. Her investigation brings more and more twists as her time traveling ability only makes things increasingly bats—t crazy, warping time and reality itself.
I found myself going through emotional ups and downs, feeling shocked at times, sad at others, and always cheering for Max. The combination of supernatural surrealism and gut-checking reality make for an amazing story and experience. The first episode is currently free, so everyone has the opportunity to try it and see for themselves.

I think I should start by saying that I don't usually play the games that seem to me as a walking simulator but it was the summer sale, and the Episode 1 was free, so I got it out of curiosity.
To my surprise, I actually went through Episode 1 same day I started it and I decided to use the same sale as an excuse to buy the rest episodes, now, what about the game?
The game is a walking simulator in which you make decisions that can and will impact the future events. I was actually surprised that actions that I took in the first episode had their consequences already in it(or at least the game made me feel that way). The whole experience took me somewhere between 15-20 hours(whole 5 episodes), and I like to check every corner of the games I play.
The main character is Max, and she's a student in prestigious Blackwell Academy, at first, I didn't like her, she kinda seemed average, like not the right character for the game but she made up for that in just a few moments. She actually can have a very admirable character....if you choose her to act on it. Only once during the game I was sitting and looking at my screen going "Why would you do that? That's so stupid? Every single person in the world would call for help?" so for me, other than that one moment you can really build a connection with the main character. The game has few rather simple riddles and if you can't solve them Max will show you the way with her words.
Some of the riddles involve playing with time, but I feel like you should try it yourself, not read about it.
Personally, I liked two first episodes the most. I don't really know why. Maybe it was interesting to get acquainted with this type of games and this game in particular. Clearly, designers/writers etc. tried to end up every episode with a good cliffhanger and I think they made it but they impressed me so much at first 2 that I actually expected the rest ones to be at least that good, they were, but it wasn't a suprise anymore. I liked ending also, even if it kinda dragged me trough some unexplained corridors it's still had a good emotional kick during the last choice that you'll ever make in that game.
Great props for the music, I usually hear the music in games only when I like it, if I don't my mind blocks it. I really liked it. If I'm correct the music was actually made specifically for the game, awesome!
As to cons, I must say that Max's lips once stopped working and both in Episode 4 and 5 I had some problems with the screen, it's like it moved a little in upper left and left an open space not finished by the graphics on the bottom and right side of it. Also, there were differences in episodes that kinda bugged me. In the last episode, I felt like they drag me by my hand through the entire ending. The first episodes gave me the feeling of freedom(imaginable of course, but still).
I think that the game should get 7+/10. If you like games where you can made choices that actually matter or you play similar games add one point(8+/10) ;)
+If the first Episode is free when you read this, get it, you won't be disappointed.

This is a space simulation game where you can choose to not do precision math without sacrificing the joy of using 1 finger to launch your own little green men/women into space. As long as you have enough thrust and fuel, you can live the dream of getting into space, orbit, onto the moon, another planet, and back.
The game even has it's own built in engineer report to give design statistics, and an encyclopedia to help grasp everything else from simple orbital mechanics, to intercepting everything from planets to space stations.
There is nothing like turning the TV on (or your computer) to see news from NASA that one can finally understand. Throgh playing Kerbal Space Program, I gained a serious appreciation for the work done to land a probe on a comet.
The only possible con is that it can be demanding on your computer hardware, and there is a late game learning curve. However, the game has a nice array of graphic options, physic options (makes it harder to burn up in the atmosphere), and tutorials (Scott Manley has some great videos) that can help get you over the hump. Past that, the community is very loving. No matter how many times does it, the people who complain about hearing of another Moon landing are far and few between.

Great turn-based tactical stealth game, even if you just want to play 10-20 minutes here and there. What I didn't like is that on every mission the first 5-10 turns must be used to explore the map, and that is a very luck dependent thing. Maps are random, so you will get very hard and very easy ones too. When exploring the map, you don't know where the target is, where the exit is, so in many cases you just flip a coin, and either you are lucky or not. When you start the game, there are several options which you can change to your taste, but unfortunately there is no way to control the exploration (personally I would like to turn it off completely, and just make the whole map visible). Once you know most of the map, the real fun begins. You can then predict everything, even the enemy guards movements, so the random factor will be pretty low after that. You can be deep tactical, and I'm sure you will have missions where you would like to give up, but just at the latest second you can save it with a smart move. Pretty satisfying.

Sid did what he does best and re-civ'd the Civ outta Civs! New game play, mechanics, and well... Civs and stuff (don't wanna spoil it too much). Gotta say I love this one, and dare say it's a huge contender for the title of the best in the series.
The changes are pretty dense, but easy to roll into after a few epic fail plays. When you get down to it, they really add to that feel of grand strategy, think big and plan ahead. No two cities are the same, nor feel the same, even if you follow a pattern for them. No pre-made scheme will work; you'll need to adapt and evolve with the round, every few turns. Everything is alive, like never before.
I've played the hell outta aggressive Civs and laid waste as I haven't in any other Civ, smirking and maniacal laughing all the way. Terrain matters now more than ever, and will be every war's crunch and glory. The hexed grid means that in every battle, you'd better make the most of the spots you can decently use, or pay in blood for it. I do feel like a military mastermind as I lay siege, city by city, and deal with the consequences. THIS is war.
"Passive" Civs shine too, and well played cultured peace makers and science lovers can be utterly unstoppable. "You can't kill an idea" comes to mind every time I play these.
Oh and the multi... Oooh the multiplayer. Sooo muuuch fuuun!
Yep. Sid also decided to jump into the let's-get-every-dime-outta-player-pockets DLC train with Civs V and it isn't coming off of it in VI. It actually threw in the whole egg basket, chickens, Old McDonald with farm and ea-ea-oh's.
If you wanna play this game, the actual complete game, you'll have to chuck out $60 for the shell game (it feels like a fully featured demo), and another $60 for all the DLCs (and that's just so far to date).
Another great one, another love of mine gone down the pay-wall drain... I'm sad now. So sad.

Shuggy is a platformer game with lots of little twists.
Shuggy is in a haunted mansion. The game places you in his shoes as you de-haunt the mansion. The main part of the story in this game is done through cutscenes comprising of comic strips. This does a good job of conveying the story.
There are a wide array of platform levels of different types, with different quirks to each level, be it time travel, teleporters or level rotation. This wide array of quirks makes for a very varied experience, which does a good job at preventing it from becoming monotonous.
I played using a keyboard & mouse setup. I found no issues here, and the controls are re-bindable as you wish.
The video overall seems good, but at some points in the level selection area the screen did flash white occasionally. I'm not sure if this was a glitch or supposed to be lightning, it was a bit jarring. However, this only affected the level selection area and did not impact on gameplay.
The music is very high quality and fits the moods of the different levels well, the sound effects don't go too over the top, which is good.
There are many different ways of playing this game. There are the main story levels, levels with extended use of the teleporter & co-op multiplayer levels.
I found no game-breaking bugs while playing this.
Shuggy is a fun platformer game in the casual horror genre. Give it a go if you like that sort of thing.

I got this game from a free key and am glad.  I would not have been happy paying for this.
The game isn't incompetently terrible or anything, but it lacks focus and originality.  The only really original thing in the game is the rope which has some pretty interesting uses, but I would have been really happy if they had built a game around that mechanic and explored it deeply.
BUT ANYWAY.
Every aspect of this game feels thrown together fairly without thinking about the other parts.  There are a variety of level mechanics that are in the game, but they don't seem to tie to anything beyond what the designers wanted to make that level about.  The visual design is not bad but basically is just a pasted-on theme on the same kind of levels.  Level progression is weird and unclear - finishing levels unlocks other levels, but there's no real clarity on which levels will be unlocked next, nor is there a sense of progression necessarily.  One level might be extremely hard, but it might unlock a very easy level.  Some levels are challenging only because they are incredibly long and, since one hit kills, you have to redo the entire level when you die, which can be tedious.  (there are maybe three or four levels I can think of that stand out as poorly designed this way)
The music and sound effects: again, just functional, but for some reason there is a sound when your character lands (I finally figured out what that noise was!), the gem-collecting sound is exactly the same every time, no modulation at all, and the music is mostly in tune with the game, but one particularly goofy-sounding song (the main theme in fact) just did not seem to fit at all.  I would not be at all surprised if the songs were just public-domain tunes that they used because they were free.  (still nothing WRONG with that, just a more effective use would be nice).
The controls are kind of floaty too.  I mean, I think that's intentional because you have a cape and that's kind of floaty (also this is a mechanic later, surprise surprise) but sometimes momentum seems off, and lets not even start on the different sized characters.
One last note - if you don't do the levels in the order they want you to, you might show up in a level with a mechanic you're not yet familiar with and have to figure it out yourself.  Not too bad really, but poor design nonetheless.
I mean, there's nothing that really makes this game exceptionally bad, but nothing that makes it very good either, and in fact I feel like it turns out to be less than the sum of its parts, simply because it is put together in such a way as to feel disconnected and just bland.
I don't really know why I finished all the levels.  I guess getting it for free makes me feel some kind of obligation or something.  Whatever.  I would say that if you have to pay money for it, pass.

Alpha Protocol is a much maligned gem of a game. I'll not deny that it's rough around the edges; the controls are sub-par, and the level design is occasionally just bad.
But the dialogue, the choices, and above all the consequences of those choices, these are all gold. The leveling system is comprehensive and covers a whole lot of options. The choices you make genuinely have repercussions; treat your handler well and they'll be good to you, but if they get too attached you might miss out on imprtant mission details. How you deal with enemies early on will impact what they do for (or to) you later. The story is extremely well put together and I think it makes up for the flaws.
It's well worth a look.

Should you buy this game? That depends on what you want out of it. The game is a little rough around the edges--but improving all the time. The developer is very active and gets updates out quickly. He just finished a total re-write of the multiplayer code. We don't really notice that as players so much because it's not new content, but the game runs better in MP by a long mile.
Other thoughts: Graphics seem dated--but the art style is cool and original. The gameplay has some glitches--but the concept is well put together and amazing. The sounds are pretty generic--but they are appropriate and add to the sci-fi atmosphere. The music is amazeballs. But it's also only 12-13 US dollars. The RTS mode is generic. And the FPS mode is missing things like lean, crouching and prone. But RTS mode and FPS mode happen at the same time which is so unique you hardly notice the missing "features" of more dedicated FPS titles like Call of Duty.
In the end you have really odd game. It's one that if any one of its components was left alone, it would be mediocre. It's not going to win any graphics fidelity contests, or have pundits talk about the realistic sound-scape. It's certainly not going to supplant StarCraft II as the golden standard of fast-paced RTS nor will it outsell Call of Duty's yearly sequels. But when all of its components are put together it's a one of a kind experience that I recommend to anyone with 13 US Dollars to spend. The thing that makes this game worth getting is its originality, its humor, and its unique blend of gameplay concepts from two genres that are really different--even if neither aspect of the game gets developed to a AAA level. There's nothing else like this game that has been made in over a decade. If you want something different to fill your hours, this is it. If you are looking for the next Call of Duty or StarCraft II, you'll have to move along.

Star Wars Dark Forces follows the Protagonist-Rebel-Mercenary Kyle  Katarn as he uncovers a secret imperial operation known as "Dark Trooper" and attempts to bring the operation to a stop.

Definitely worth the buy- I was fortunate enough to get this game soon after launch when it was significantly discounted, but even now it's worth the money.
In essence, this is a straightforward port to Steam of the 2006 FSX release. It's had some internal tweaks such as improved texture rendering, better Windows 8.1 support and improved multicore optimization (meaning it runs better than the original FSX on the same PC hardware).
Perhaps the biggest change here is the removal of the defunct Gamespy multiplayer mode, replaced with an all-new Steam online multiplayer. It now syncs with Steam social functions and servers, bringing FSX multiplayer back online for the first time in years. A welcome addition.
At the moment of writing this there's a major glitch with the game which prevents it from opening when offline. There's a patch in the works due within a week or so (available as an open beta on Steam now) which fixes this, though.
Overall, 9/10. Good update of FSX.

Yet. The online experience (especially) is and always will be the bane of microtransactions biggest dont's. In my opinion, microtransactions need to be kept to things that don't matter. Like skins and other things that don't effect the balance of the game.
Essentially, if you pour enough money into xp bonuses, captains, gear and orders. You can take down fortresses easier and faster, hence getting better gear and captains faster. The rich get richer and everyone else wanting a fair online experience will ultimately never achieve it.
All in all, it's really not a bad online experience. I still don't understand what you gain from your captains successfully defending a fortress. And it doesn't appear you lose anything either except maybe your ranking.
Attacking a fortress online on the other hand is overall fun. If your captains die in battle they will die permanently. This works the same as in the single player campaign, so honestly i have no gripe here. You decide wheather or not to lead them into battle and take your chances as you would with anything else.

This baby uses it's chapters like episodes to a television series, giving you a recap of what happened, and a preview of what's to come. Ambient noise, suspense, and a non-reliance on jump scares is what make this game great - you are a writer trapped in a story, and it is an experience.

This game is everything a sequel should be. It's everything I wanted and quite a bit of stuff I didn't even know I wanted. Killing orcs is fun, training orcs is fun, and making orcs kill other orcs is fun. Some people have said bad things about the story, but I enjoyed it too. The combat is more advanced with better skills and progression. The gear drops are more varied and can make an impact on playstyle. The Nemesis System has been overhauled with interesting new personalities and styles, plus the orc vs orc combat is way more indepth now. Instead of them playing wack-a-mole with each other they actually duel. If you liked Shadow of Mordor you're going to like this one so much more.
If you're here reading reviews because you heard about the microtransactions and are worried, don't be. The game never pushes them, and it definitely does not force them on you by making the game grindy. I have finished the main story and am in Act IV, all the while on Nemesis difficulty, and this game never feels like a grind. Even the collectibles, which in other open world games feel like a grind, are fun to collect due to the fact that there are normally rewards at the end such as gear or a skill unlock. Not to mention traveling around to gather the collectibles can lead to all sorts of encounters with the Nemesis System.

Great turn-based tactical stealth game, even if you just want to play 10-20 minutes here and there. What I didn't like is that on every mission the first 5-10 turns must be used to explore the map, and that is a very luck dependent thing. Maps are random, so you will get very hard and very easy ones too. When exploring the map, you don't know where the target is, where the exit is, so in many cases you just flip a coin, and either you are lucky or not. When you start the game, there are several options which you can change to your taste, but unfortunately there is no way to control the exploration (personally I would like to turn it off completely, and just make the whole map visible). Once you know most of the map, the real fun begins. You can then predict everything, even the enemy guards movements, so the random factor will be pretty low after that. You can be deep tactical, and I'm sure you will have missions where you would like to give up, but just at the latest second you can save it with a smart move. Pretty satisfying.

Invisible Inc. is a little gem of a game.
"Little" because I completed it in less than 10 hours. It's true that the devs try to create a bit more replayability by having additional agents who can be unlocked, different (harder) levels, etc. but it all still feels like the game falls short on the "depth" bit.
Despite that, I really like this game: It has decent graphics, a good storyline, engaging music and a very capable turn-based combat system. You're basically an "operator" in charge of 2 agents whom you use to conduct covert missions. In these missions, you get to score cash, loot, and upgrades for your agents. It's undeniably fun and addictive.
Here's the best part: The core strategy in Invisible is stealth. IF you jump in, guns blazing, or trigger happy, killing every guard you see, I can almost guarantee you'll lose. And the game does not allow you to save progress while on missions. You only get one save game before and after the mission, though you're permitted limited "rewinds" (reloads one turn before) per campaign.
What could be better: I think the strategic layer of the game could be improved. Basically on the world map you get to choose missions, upgrade your agents (if you have cash, which is always in limited supply) and read some dialog. That's about it. Monst3r should have an expanded role -- you hardly get anything from his black market contacts.
If there were 2, maybe 3 more chapters after the initial 72 hours of in-game time, I think it would be exceptional (especially if you're paying full price for the game, about $22).
Invisible was really fun to play. I recommend this game -- I just wish it was longer.
Update: the devs did release some additional content after. Thanks for listening!

Invisible, Inc. is a tense Cyberpunk stealth game with wonderfully designed gameplay systems that create layers of strategy — ones that are ultimately more satisfying and challenging to grip than its competitors. Klei has taken out the traditional roadmap of tactical turn-based games, and replaced it with an all inclusive roguelike sense, coupled with their success on Mark of the Ninja. All important decisions take place during the missions, not outside of them, which pushes for sensitive 'risk vs. reward' gameplay. The mission is all that matters — every player-driven detail of it. Watch Mark Brown's video analyzing The Swindle, part of the Game Maker's Toolkit series, for a great explanation on this significance:
Invisible, Inc does not pull any punches beyond the first tutorial mission, and it's base difficulty is Expert to further mark that. There are a multitude of decisions to make, other than the default "kill all the enemies", making for an intense espionage roguelike. Buy this game if you like to be bad♥♥♥♥♥

XP content is lousy though. The variety is nice, but you have to manually adjust the size and placement of too many of the items. The software itself is easy to use and if you follow the intro tutorial, you'll quickly get the hang of it.

In the end, it's rather nice software with very poor licensing. If you want to legally make characters for something other than RPG Maker, you could gather enough items from the Workshop so you don't need to use any parts or items at all that comes with Game Character Hub, but even then, you'd have to be watchfull of the creator's licensing.

It's 1670, and all the countries around me are mad at me for war mongering. It is for the glory of Poland! Those city states didn't matter anyways... The Empire of Persia is just south of me, scheming, I just know it! I preemptively declare war on them, hoping to gain a few cities at the very least. Little did I know, China was just a few turns away from winning the culture victory already. I take Persepolis and I am told that I have lost. A grim day for the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
Civilization VI is a game where you build your empire from the ground up with one of many countries. Each country has their own unique playstyle and abilities. For example, Poland gets the glorious Winged Hussars, and if they culture bomb another civ's city, Polands religion instantly becomes the dominant religion in the city. Each civ also has their own ability, some more overpowered than others, but its all pretty unique.
Here's some good things about this game:
- Unique civs
- Unique civ personalities.
- Good visuals.
- Wonders now take up tiles, and have tile requirements (helps prevent wonder spam)
- Wonders look... Wonderful!
- Combat is good 'ol civ.
- New civics tree is a great addition. (It's like the science tree, but instead with culture)
- Policies are handled very nicely. Governments make your policy choices actually matter.
- Districts are wonderful additions.
Some things that I could really go either way with
- I don't like the music in this one. It gets boring really quickly. I do however like that the same tune changes and progresses as you go throughout the ages.
- Workers only having 3 uses. (4 if you get a specific policy) I am on the fence with this one. You decide for yourself!

Things I do not like:
- Why is score victory still even here?
- There are a few really overpowered civs. Russia and China are a few examples of this.
Russia gets culture and science from trade routes with foreign civs if the foreign civ is ahead of them. This allows them to catch up mega quick, and their holy site is ridiculous.
- I do not like the amount of DLC they have already pushed for this game. Its only been about a year and a lot of the DLC have been tiny civ additions, among other things. All of the civs should be available to people who don't want to pay at some point.
- The scenarios suck. (The Poland one is particularly underwhelming.)
- You can't build units from previous techs. This is REALLY bad. If you haven't industrialized your country, and you get replaceable parts by accident, you are not going to have a good time. I accidentally did this and got conquered.
- I think the Religious victory is too easy to get.

Overall, I think Civilization VI is a great game if you are wanting to get into the Civ series. It is definitely the most casual friendly Civ game. Veteran players might find the casualness a bit shocking though. I remember not liking this game very much at first because of how casual it felt. The casual direction is the right direction for the Civ games, and I hope to see it stay this way. If you want a less casual experience, Civ V is a great game, and if you are in for a challenge, Europa Universalis IV is great.

Alpha Protocol is the best spy RPG I've ever played (not that there are a ton of those games out there).
The shooting is pretty good, and melee is a viable option unlike a lot of other shooter games. Stealth is a more challenging option, although the shooting is more fun.
The game really shines with the dialog system, similar to Mass Effect but on a timer. The whole setup really makes you feel like you're actually Michael Thorton, actually talking to real people and making decisions based on how you interact with them. I'd go so far as to say it's the best dialog system I've ever seen in any game, let alone an action game.
The visual character customization is ok. I like to stylize Mike for each type of mission I do. So when I go to Russia I look like a euotrash hipster. When I go to Saudi Arabia I look like a wealthy warlord prince, etc. Not a lot of action games give you that option.
Probably the only negative thing I would say about it is that the mini-games (hacking, picking locks) get repetitive after a while, but still adds to the tension of the game, trying to hack into a computer and if you mess up, an alarm will sound.
The closest game I can compare it to would be XIII. Playing with a gamepad is recommended.

This is probably the most inconsistent game I have ever played. It has its highlight moments where it's fantastic, but then it dumps total garbage moments on your lap and says 'deal with it'.
I haven't finished the game yet (because I struggle - with what? you'll find out later) but so far the story is really tight. Global balance is at stake and it's your job to try and save the world from the imminent confilict. Alpha Protocol features a great Mass Effect-like dialogue wheel with limited time to response. This system forces you to make quick and usually hard decisions on the spot, which in turn makes converstations exciting and believable. There is also a system of reactions - the dialogue choices directly affect relationships with other characters - each individual is unique and responds vastly different to your actions. The relationships are meaningful and very useful where you are in the field - they have a genuine impact on the mission. In between missions you are in your hideout, where you can buy/sell equipments, trade valuable and sensitive intel (for instant embarassing information found during one of the missions concerning high ranking political figure - you can blackmail, sell to the highest bidder or hand over to the press), buy intel and help on your current mission and so forth. All of the above, this is where Alpha Protocol truly shines. Building your conntact networks, manipulating data, trying to find out as much as you can, talking with your partners - it all has its consequences and effects.
Now for the bad part. The controls in this game are probably the poorest I have ever experienced. They are just a pain. Anyone who knows stealth games knows this - the controls have to be tight. In Alpha Protocol they are not. They are simply broken. That's why I strugle in this game. Unfortunately, it came to a point where I pretty much know how this game works and I sometimes have to exploit the game's wonkiness to advance. The AI acts weird. You can approach guard who is pretty much facing you and deliver a swift strike. Other times, the same guard would miraculously spot you and raise an alarm. But you know what the worst part of it is? The animations. To say the guards walk awkwardly is an understatment. They patrol areas and when they turn they occasionally pull off some unbelievable herky-jerky 360 move and spot you sneaking behind them. It's extremely frustrating. The level design is sometimes good, sometimes rather bad. In some areas (probably in general) the game favors certain paths of development (RPG-like skill points and abilities are here) and now I'm in a point where I have to use my martial arts skills, but I have none. Especially at the end of 'chapters' the game pits you against 'bosses' so to speak, and you have to engage them in an all-out gunfight. I was disappointed at this juncture, because it throws the whole 'stealth game' thing into a dumpster and becomes an unrefined shooter. Sadly, all of the negatives break the immersion and erase the joy of playing.
This is a game with a great, albeit wasted potential. I'd really like to recommend it, because of a lot of superb ideas, but I cannot do this - Alpho Protocol will bring you more frustration than amusement and that's a shame. The thin stealth games market could have had a gem under its belt.
TL;DR.
If you are a diehard stealth-espionage fan, buy this, but be warned - Alpha Protocol is badly executed.

I pressed every button, manipulated every control I could think of, and made as many patterns with my mouse as I could imagine, and nothing happened.
I can't honestly recommend it, because I've had more enjoyment from that Windows '95 screensaver about a maze (with the rat in it) than I did from this game. The detention center level in particular features a veryfrustrating situation that forced me to spend a few bucks calling the LucasArts hint line in the mid-90s.
With that caveat in mind, this is a fairly immersive experience in the Star Wars universe (as immersive as things got in 1995). You get to explore a star destroyer, imperial bases, and even Coruscant pre-Phantom Menace. Upon release, this game offered a lot of experiences that were a Star Wars fan's wet dream - all through the eyes of bad♥♥♥♥♥mercenary Kyle Katarn.
I do feel like this game has aged better than its sequel Jedi Knight (1997) in terms of playability. Something about the sprite-based enemies and pseudo 3D experience offers a kind of retro charm that makes this easy to pick up and play.
If you enjoy the Star Wars universe and 90s first-person shooters, I would say this is worth the cost of entry. It is a 22 year old game though, so the sometimes-floaty controls and overall aesthetic will likely be off-putting to the folks who didn't play this back in the day.

Excellent application if you're working with any RPG Maker engine. It's cheaper and more streamlined than Photoshop. (That's what I was using before.) It's very easy to set up the grid so you can rearrange and edit tiles, too. I'm well versed with Photoshop and GIMP. But GCH is a great tool because it's so specialized for 2D spriting. You can see a walk cycle preview, for example. It can convert sprites from XP to Ace so they fit the number of frames. It can even handle the old 2000 and 2k3 sprites. It features random sprite generators that are easy to customize and set up. Some people expected it to have "behavior" bases and corresponding parts, for animations or poses, like dancing or collapsing. It doesn't. (I have no idea where that expectation came from. At least one person already made a "down" base.  Just consult the internet.)
Yes, VX Ace has a built-in character generator, but you can't even adjust colors without an outside editor. GCH allows much more freedom for what parts you're able to use and how you can layer them. The resource sets it comes with are for RPG Maker XP and VX Ace. (If licensing is an issue because you're using some other engine, you can always import your own sprite parts...)
Now, this might not be the best tool for making a sprite entirely from scratch, for a number of reasons. But it's probably one of the best options for editing sprites or piecing them together. If the price is too steep for you, just wait for a sale.

I love this game more than I have time to explain. In fairness, turn-based anything is my favourite game style, but this game  puts that formula to one of the best uses I've ever played.
The game offers so many different way to feel an utter thrill. Getting through a level virtually undetected having raided almost everything there is to grab is a joy. Tripping alarms, creating a seemingly impossible situation and still getting all your agents out without missing an objective is pure refined joy. Never has a stealth game felt so satisfying.
It's also one of the best randomly generated games I've encountered.  Invisible Inc. does a great job of using a library of fairly simple rooms and rules to create endless variety and only rarely creates a set of rooms which seem unfair or unwieldy. The rogue-like template for this game is perfect, tailoring the experience to regular restarts and false beginnings.
There are a few gripes I have: there are some inconsistent rules. Sometimes a character can move diagonally for 1AP and sometimes it costs 2AP. I can't figure out why this is. Also (and I'm using the character with the Holo-camouflage) Prism sometimes gets unmasked when a guard walks past and other times not. One time she got revealed while standing in the stealth spot behind a door when the guard was in the doorway. Additionally, it's annoying that guards react to the presence of a downed agent every time they re-enter a room. Surely if a guard has seen a body already, it's no surprise the second time? It makes it hard to predict guard movement in rooms with a lot of bodies. A few more filters to view layout would be nice too, as sometime there are so many floating icons and bits of information it's hard to actually see the state of a tile or select it.
Also, I was shocked that on the tutorial difficulty the end of the game can be reached and revealed so quickly. The game has a nice plot and it's a pity that the end is blown after a first 5-hour playthrough. Admittedly, the great value of this game is the endless replayability and ongoing challenge (I just skip the plot sections now) but I would have liked the big ending to be saved for the higher difficulties, or if there were different outcomes for different tiers.
But those minor issues are almost nothing in comparison to the fun and endless free choice this game offers. No two playthroughs are the same, with reconfiguration of agents, items and cyberspace hacking tools. For reference my favourite combo is Dr Xu (file) with Prism (archive) with Dynamo and Parasite tools. Those are a great combination which stack abilities well together - I just have to remember not to be too blase with Prism's holodisguise.
One of the best turn-based games ever made and one of the most satisfying stealth adventures, too.

This is no simple remake of Civilization V. There are a lot of pros and cons to it, though. As far as gameplay goes, they've added a lot of interesting new things, such as districts for cities, as well as adding in old mechanics from Civilization IV, like water and, to some extent, housing, which mirrors health. Religion is certainly interesting, but I'm not sure how much I care for it - it adds mechanics from both the Brave New World/Gods and Kings add-ons for Civilization V and mechanics of Civilization IV's religion system to the game. The graphics, however, are hard to follow - nowhere near as appealing as in Civilization V. Diplomacy windows have changed, having to be exited like a normal window rather than by option in the window itself, which is something to get used to. Units are easy to misdirect, if you're not paying close attention, and it gives the player no alert of when a new turn has started, unlike Civilization V. An obnoxious mechanic is that units now heal at the absolute end of the turn, after all other players have gone as well, making it easy for more experienced players to lose units on the pretense of them healing before being attacked. As far as gameplay goes, this game is a few steps forward with possibly a few steps back, in the eyes of some. But where graphics are concerned, I've yet to find any that appeal to me. Overall, I personally feel the cons outweight the pros in this game, and I've returned it (under different premises, but will not be purchasing the game again as intended).

EDIT a year and 400 hours later:
I cannot recommend this game enough, it is a must buy. It's one of those games where it's incredibly challenging and most of your losses are due to poor planning and unthought actions. Stealth is key as much as avoiding violence.
If you avoid violence, this game is a lot easier for you. And that's all you can hope for considering how difficult the game gets later on when guards have armor and mainframes become even harder to hack through.
It's been an emotional experience for me mastering this game, here's a link to my blog post about it that the developers appreciated a lot:
Otherwise, here's my original review below:
40 hours in and I STILL haven't beaten Experienced Mode, but I love this game to death! I've had it for maybe a week or two by now, beaten Beginner, and my own customized version of Experienced Mode with level retries, and I can't get enough of it.
The gameplay mechanics are top notch. It is a turn based, top view, stealth game where you need to be very careful how you spend your Action Points and Hacking PWR. As you progress through the campaign, you can earn a ton of skills and items that help you aide in your missions.
It can range from having armor piercing weapons to take down the stronger guards, to also getting better hacking programs from Incognita so that you can better sneak around corporation headquarters.
The mission types have a great variety: you can find Cybernetic Labs to enhance your team's abilities, recon powerful items, or simply loot heavily guarded vaults for credits that you can use to buy skill points or other items. Even better is the Financial Suite type of missions where you can find corporate executives and steal vault access cards from them for even greater rewards in said mission types.
What I don't like about this game is how short the campaign is. You only get 72 game hours to get to the final mission, and basically when you send your team to a mission, each location has different amount of hours it takes to fly there, so you gotta be careful.
You can always increase the amount of hours the campaign takes, but that changes the official difficulty to custom and, thus might be unable to unlock certain programs and other things. However, there's at least an endless mode where you can basically play forever and constantly beef up your characters to take on even beefier missions.
I highly recommend this game as it is quite addicting! If you enjoyed Mark of the Ninja, Metal Gear Solid, or Tenchu, this, in my humble opinion, is the next level of the stealth genre. Just what's possible really makes this game unique. Tiniest drawback is that all maps reuse the same tiles and look the same at a distance, but at least the maps are randomized and so are always a fresh new experience in how to traverse them in each playthrough.
This game is worth its full price, but if you can get it on sale, don't even think twice! Just get it!

I LOVE THIS GAME, BUT I DON'T RECOMMEND IT.. .. ...YET!
I didn't really get on to the Civilization hype train untill Civ V, but from then on I was hooked. So when Civ VI was anounced I immediately pre-ordered the game (non digital deluxe) and have been playing it since the release date. Yes, the quirky AI still remains, but that never was a gamebreaker for me.
But, why don't I recommend this game?
Good question! Glad you asked! Well, like moste reviewers, I find the business model this game is hinged on to be utterly DISGUSTUNG! If, like me, you would have pre-ordered this game non digital deluxe for € 60 and you wanted to play the complete game with all civs (5 € per civ) including the 'Rise & Fall'-expansion, you would have to dish out another € 67! ....Yes, basically rebuy the game! Seriously though, Firaxis have a perverse way of showing their love to the loyal fans of the Civilization franchise!
So, will I buy all these civs and expansions? ..... ....Well ... *sigh* ... I probably will (or already have done) because I'm already into the game and I'm just that stupid. Though I will say that this business model has somewhat curbed my enthusiasm for any future Civization releases. I definitely won't be getting into any future Civ VII pre-sales!
But, if anything, take my advice; Wait a few christmas sales untill the game is fully fleshed out and it has all the civs and expansions it's ever going to get. Maybe then you can buy the full game (in a bundle or digital deluxe) for a nice price. Because at this rate no game is worth the price they are charging for Civilation VI right now!

The trailer has what the game is missing: playing with your expectations.  When you watch the trailer, it shows a flurry of game mechanics that keeps you guessing what will come next.  In the game, though, an interesting level often unlocks a generic platforming level.  Between the time loop levels, the herding shmu levels, and the multi-shuggy levels, there's a lot of waiting and busywork, particularly when you die and start over.  The enemies don't help either, with many of them moving at arbitary times and directions that stops you from being able to plan your way through the level.  There's not enough skill escalation to be a Super Meat Boy, there's not enough surprise to be a Frog Fractions, there's not enough story to be a Thomas Was Alone,  there's not enough depth to be a Braid.  The game wants to deliver on the discovery that come from such a diverse set of mechanics, but just ends up being arbitrary challenges.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a good game. It looks good, it plays well, and makes me look forward to the third game coming later this year. That said, it isn't quite the continuation I had been hoping for. Season 1 was a fantastic game that had me enthralled from start to finish and in the end I was left in tears. Season 2 just doesn't have quite the same impact on me that the original had. As I progressed through the story I felt like many of my choices didn't matter. It really seemed like only the final choices had any real outcome. I didn't really connect with anyone quite as much as I had with Lee. I did try to care for some of the characters. Luke, Kenny, Jane, and Mike were the characters that at first interested me the most, however by the end I only cared to keep Clem safe and Jane seemed like the best choice for survival. I also wasn't particularly happy about the roles characters from 400 Days played. I wasted time trying to get them all to go to safety, but they ended up being either goons for Carver or traitors, in Bonnie's case. I bought and played this game quite a while after its original release so I knew some of the endings. I teared up a bit at the ending where Kenny brings Clem and AJ to Wellington only to sacrifice his spot for theirs. It was a great ending that really meshed well with the Kenny I knew from season 1, but in my own playthrough I couldn't connect with Kenny. I ultimately ended the game with Jane and the family, which felt like an incomplete ending. Seeing the father's gun and how Clem reacted to it had me interested to see if they would turn on them, but it just faded to black. Also, judging by the first trailer for season 3, I don't think it matters which ending you chose. It may be that season 1 was just too good to follow up, and if that is true I hope season 3 can overcome this. I'm a huge fan of The Walking Dead. I love the show and the comics and I want to continue to see stories in this universe, but next time I also want my choices to matter more. If you're a fan of the series I recommend the game, if only to see how Clem has grown. The story is interesting enough, but the choices and payoff are lackluster. Or at least the ending I got was. - 6/10 -

While not a bad game per se, Alpha Protocol attempts to be too many things at once and manages to be mediocre at all of them. It wants to be an action-RPG like Mass Effect with dialogue branchs and a reputation system, but the depth of conversation seems to be superficial. Choosing to be polite or a jackass illicits different reactions for the first sentence, but proceeds to give you the same information after the reaction. It feels hamfisted and doesn't carry as much weight as it could have.
AP also tries to mimic stealth games like Splinter Cell, but the detection system feels arbitrary. Sometimes getting spotted feels completely random; you may have been perfectly sneaky, in the shadows and out of sight, only to have an enemy spot you from afar anyways. I've seen worse stealth implementations by far, but not from titles that are supposed to be this caliber.
The action also feels a bit dull too. For an agent who is supposed to be highly trained, the protagonist can't aim to save his life. I've spent enough time with guns to know that all the guns in this game will hit point of aim at any of the distances you will find in AP. Shooting basically feels like its a punishment for not sneaking properly, and sneaking is such a gamble that the two combined get aggravating.
Also, most of the characters are boring, and a few of them could have been lumped into one person for all I care.
Anyways, if you're looking for some stealth gameplay, an immersive RPG, or a good third person shooter I'd suggest looking for a game that does only what you're looking for and not Alpha Protocol. This game isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend because it's so mediocre. I could only recommend this if you want to pretend to be James Bond and none of the Bond games out there appeal to you.

I haven't played it for a while, but I do remember playing it when I was in my early teens and having a lot of fun. However, graphics wise, it's literally nauseating to look at. I'm far from a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ (I still play and love the look of the original Starcraft), but early 3D graphics make me want to puke. That's right, talking about you Mario 64 and all of your ilk. Late-era sprite-based graphics beat early 3D for me every time. Finally, there's Rise and Fall: Civilizations at War, which I didn't play too much, either. I remember it being fun, but it was very, very simplistic and watered down compared to most RTS. If it wasn't for the third-person gimick, which wasn't that great either, it wouldn't even be worth a look.
Executive Assault, a one man team job, manages to finally do what I've been waiting for: create an in-depth strategy game that, with a bit of bug fixing, could easily hold its own against other titles. The first-person aspect of it is pretty simple in comparison, but when it comes to RTS/FPS hybrids, I care more for how deep the RTS aspect is compared to the FPS aspect. However, there's enough unit customization and versatility that it actually makes the first person aspects non-repetitive. Every time you research a new unit, you're gonna be excited to hop in it and see how it performs, and damn if it isn't fun holding off an enemy assault right on the front lines with your massive army, or storming the enemy base to kill the opposing CEO.
Oh yeah, that's a big thing that differentiates this from even other RTS: you don't blow up the enemy's base to win. In fact, you can actually see inside your base, place internal defenses, and walk around in first person mode, and you want to keep an eye out for any sneaky infiltrators trying to get inside. Why? Because you technically play as a CEO who controls a robot army, and the only way to win is to cut off the head of the snake: IE, kill the opposing CEO himself.
Anyways, I'll probably write a more in-depth review later once I play the game more, but let me just say for $8, it's well worth the money. That's the price of a couple of Big Macs. To think that this was all made by one guy is astounding. I'd be very interested to see what he'd do with a bigger team (though hopefully the other members of it wouldn't bog down this guy's genius at all :P). Oh, and it goes without mentioning: despite the game already being insanely enjoyable, the developer is passionate as hell about it and is still updating with new content.
Anyway, what the hell are you waiting for? Go get the game!

I loved Season 2 more than the first Walking Dead Telltale game. Why? It felt much more emotional than the first, and there were way more quick-time events to keep me involved in the action as well as the storytelling. The biggest strongpoint of the first game was what happened at the end; in Season 2, that crap's happening a lot more often constantly. The characters weren't so much cookie cutter in this one as they were in the first: There were characters I started off despising, hoping they'd either get offed, or that Clementine would put them in their place, but I grew to understand them and care for them because the zombie apocalypse makes people do crazy things.
The only complaint I had was how the decisions the game made me make shook my inner being because I felt like a jerk regardless of the choices I made.
To summarize how I felt about the game in short: I'm preordering Season 3 when I get the chance. I think I owe it to the devs to actually pay full price for one of these games, instead of being the cheapskate I am and waiting till they're 75% off just so I can get the best bang for my buck. The game's fantastic, and outdoes the first one in my opinion with its action sequences and storytelling.

Alpha Protocol is either the most underrated game ever or the most unknown game ever. Seriously, take a second:
Have you ever heard of this game before?
SEGA and Obisidian Entertainment?
Espionage RPG?
It was mentionated on Rock, Paper, Shotgun?
Yeah. I guessed that.
With this intruduction, let's game to the game itself:
Graphics: Pretty good. Facial expressions and overall quality of the game's scenario is pretty good to look at. It doesn't try to be the most beautiful game ever at the same time that it tries to don't look awful. Since they are a little dated, you don't need a powerful machine.
Gameplay: Overall presentation to gameplay tatics and mechanics are self-explanatory and how YOU will use them is pretty much up for the player. The game let's it quite clear: If you fail, the failure is your own fault, not the game's fault. If i can say one bad thing about the gameplay is the key biding: The Space Bar is, at the same time, the button used to run and to go on cover. No, really, i'm ♥♥♥♥ing serious. Now imagine this situation: You need to go stealth because you're on low health, but then, suddenly, your characters run and now everybody is just going to f*** you up. It's quite frustating to say the least (But at least the death animation is so funny that i can't get frustated when i die).
Stealth system and hacking/lockpicking/etc overall works great and in a good amount of difficult. You WILL need to be careful in this game to not die. Dying is easy even for the hardcore stealth game fans (I'm playing on Hard and believe me: It's gets REALLY hard).
Multiple pathways and overall level desing helps a lot the player and are a good touch in a game that works like this one. Same goes for the RPG system. It's quite balanced and the upgrades are self explanatory and really helpfull at many situations. So, save your AP (Experience Points) and get's what suits you better. Because this game is going to put you at your maximum.
This game also have boss fights and, man oh man, they WILL REALLY PUT YOU TO THE MAXIMUM. You will have to be twice as careful when fighting bosses and they have a relative amount of HP (Depending on your difficult. I'm on Hard, so you guess). If you want a comparation for instance: Imagine Deus Ex: HR. Pretty much THAT.I have to say this: This is a game that isn't made for casual gamers. And i really mean it when i say that they try really hard to make this clear.
Sounds: Voice actting is okay, nothing special. Soundtrack of the game is quite good and always does a good job at putting you in the mood of the mission/warning you when something is going on (Like being detected).
Story: Many people liked it because of the beliavable characters and the construction of relationship through the game (Mostly because of the multiple dialogue choises). It's not really something new, but it does a good job at letting the player wanting for more and more, and keeping going through missions.
Overall, you may not know Alpha Protocol™, but he exists. And is a good game for what it is, and pretty inovative too. I have to say that this is the first action/stealth RPG that i've ever played (I think) and it did a pretty good job at trying to start this new kind of genre. It's a shame that it din't really made a lot of sucess and the sells weren't good enough for a sequel.
But hey, it's still purchasable on Steam. Give it a try, you will find a good challenge with this game.
PS: On Steam i will have just some minutes, but i've played it for 3-5 hours in offline mode because my internet just felt down at the time. Damn good job sycing my play time, uh , Steam? GG WP.

The main reason the game is so difficult for its size is because it is totally random.  Items are randomized, dungeons are randomized--the game is never the same twice.  The only way to win is to play the game over and over until you learn how each enemy behaves and exactly how to defeat it.  This is a game for the people who enjoy a real, but simple challenge and I thoroughly enjoyed it.
My only complaint is the controls.  Why doesn't the game support gamepad controllers natively?  Why do you have to download a separate program that converts gamepad commands to keyboard strokes to play it on a gamepad?  In my opinion it's the ONLY way to play this game, so why shouldn't the game support it?  But once I got a gamepad to work, I flew.

Easy to use, easy to share, easy to implement.
This software is perfect for making sprites for games on RPG Maker. I can make sprites and characters and implement them into my games in a matter of minutes. The developmers made it really easy, and fun! The window for the software is easy to navigate and use, with little destractions. You basicly just add objects from a menu, and the program automaticly puts them into a character. It has a lot of options, but one downside is that only a few have a Hue option. Hairs have hue options, but you cannot make a face with the same hair color, because the Face files don't have hue options.
It's easy to share your content with others! When you make a character, you can select an option to post directly to Steam workshop! I made a Sinon character (Sword Art Online II) and posted it on the workshop in less than fifteen minutes. With this easy Steam Intigrated option, others can start sharing content with others.
It's really easy to add a character into your game! Make sure you save as a Graphic File, and save it in a spot you know where it is. Afterwards, go into RPG Maker VX Ace, and import your character. Its that easy!
I would recommend this program to everyone with RPG Maker VX ace or XP. It's a really well made program, with lots of features. The only thing I would change is to add the Hue option to Everything in the program. This would bring customization to a whole new level.
Conclusion: 9/10 Very easy to use, though could have some more Customization features.

The gameplay's pretty decent - in a lot of ways it feels like what Goldeneye and Perfect Dark should have been, if they hadn't been quite so limited by the technology of the day.  It bills itself as a spy RPG - this is only in as much as how Hollywood defines spies (or rather, how they did in classic movies).  There's a small information gathering feature that gives you some minor bonuses, but it's mostly just a stealthy shooter.  A good stealthy shooter that gets 2 of its 3 technical minigames very, very right.  Alarms rung by enemies can be canceled, but you have to finish a little minigame to do so (while being shot at unless you clear the area first), and lockpicking has its own minigame - both are actually very well done - you can figure out exactly what you need to do given a moment to think, but you're on a timer (every lock is connected to an alarm system, and alarms freeze you out so you have to start over) so you still feel pressured.  Hacking computers, the third technical minigame, is somewhat awkwardly controlled (move around 2 codes - mouse is hypersensitive and WSAD is super slow...and seems to not accept non-default Interact controls (anything but space...why space?) for finishing that side.  Much more challenging than the other two, but it's not game breaking since no matter how much you suck at it, you can level up your sabotage skill once and gain the ability for EMP grenades (wait, I thought this was the modern world) to selectively deactivate just the security systems of the device, allowing you to disarm alarms, kick through doors and hack computers without bothering with the minigame (yeah, definitely not using the standard version of an EMP).  All in all, what could be an excellent game.
That is, until you hit the story.  There's a reason I said this would have been great for Goldeneye or Perfect Dark.  Those games had the sneaky, technical side of gameplay.  They had missions where you planted explosives, evaded detection of cameras, missions where using non-silenced weapons or allowing the enemy to fire their unsilenced weapons brought down what might be literally called an army of enemies down on you.  What they also had, however, and what Alpha Protocol lacks, is an interesting story.  Goldeneye's Dam-Facility-Runway introduction, and Perfect Dark's similarly tense infiltration mission were great hooks.  And while Goldeneye largely relied on you having seen the movie for the finer points, both games had interesting outside-the-box storylines when taken as a whole.  Alpha Protocol might venture outside the box eventually, but, to extend the metaphor of a story hook, you'd be better off using hook shaped pasta on the end of your fishing line than what Alpha Protocol provides.  After a short segment where you wake up confused in a hospital and beat down a number of guards while confusedly trying to escape this facility, you end up in a room talking to your boss as if nothing had happened (slightly jarring, but OK, whatever), you end up with your mission.  You are to kill the public face of an Islamist terrorist organization that used sophisticated ground-to-air missile technology to shoot down a civilian jet liner in the Middle East.
Did I just describe the basic story of about half the modern set shooters out there?  Yes.  Yes I did.  The antagonist is a transparent standin for Osama bin Laden and his organization is equally transparently standing in for Al Quaeda. Except that, since we're an intel organization so black ops that even black ops aren't allowed to know we exist...so black ops that we rely on weapons and information sales to fund our field operations.... we can't have anything big like 9/11 as a motivator, we need something more subtle.  So, instead of hooking you with its premise, the story stabs you with a piece of limp spaghetti.
Oh, and level design is pretty linear.  But then, I've just been playing Dishonored, where there's at least 3 ways to do anything, so perhaps I'm expecting too much.  (On the other hand, Obsidian's core team was Black Isle's core team - the guys who did the Infinity Engine DnD games, so expecting too much of them shouldn't be that easy.)
It might get better with time.  It's a decent game, and, 2 missions in, has the potential to be something great.  It just needs a knife-in-the-back plot twist or two to get things going.  It's already provided me my money's worth of entertainment...but being on sale for $3.75 makes that a pretty easy threshold to cross.

I went into this game with quite high expectations. Obsidian is arguably my favorite video game company, and the guys who worked on Alpha Protocol are also some of my favorite devs and writers. But I got something completely different.
This game tries to be new in many ways, and fails in all of them. And I do say this with a heavy heart, because I love sneaking games. The Metal Gear Solid series are some of my favorite games, and in any RPG I can be a rogue or a thief I chose that on the spot. But Alpha Protocol should have spent more time thinking about the gameplay instead of polishing the story. The controls in this game are beyond horrible, I lost count of how many times I accidently slipped out of cover because I wanted to look around, or ran from soldiers only to hit a random invisible wall and get gunned down. It's a very easy game, but the sheer chaos of the controls alone makes it extremely hard, but not in a good way. In an infuriating way, where you know what you need to do, and you know how to do it, you just need to make the game understand it, and it refuses to do so.
Unfortunately I have to downvote this game and throw a review as a warning: Don't. Go play Metal Gear Solid instead. It's what this tries to be, but fails.

EA is an RTS (real time strategy) in which you can take control of your units once you build them and even make them into squads, this mode is different from CEO mode, as if you die in this mode, you will stay alive, if you die in CEO mode, you have a perma-death. You can play 1v0, 1v1, 1v2, 1v3 or 1v4. There's many difficulties for the AI, AI: The Janitor beign the easiest, you can make each bot have a different difficulty or all of them to have the same difficulty. There's cheats such as: Make resources fall out of the sky (from meteors), have infinite resources or have very quick research times (3 seconds instead of 3mins-10mins). There is no such mod support. There is multiplayer. In order to "take over" some bots' or players' office/company you wll need to use Hackerbots to hack all of the doors down or use Infantry and simply shoot the doors down, shoot the indoor turrets down and finally kill the CEO. The tech tree is very nicely split up into many parts such as Structures, Units, Defence with tons of upgrades in each part. There's tons of units too, you can cutomize your units by combining 'X' chassis (tank, jeep, infantry ect) with 'X' ability (faster moving speed ((infantry only)), shields ect) with 'X' weapon (RPG's, LAZERS! ect) to create the most badass thing you want. The updates are  very common (3 or more per month on average) so there is so much more to be seen, did I mention one guy made this?
The game supports up to 1920x1080 resolutions, the graphics themselves aren't something that are super pretty, but they are still nice, although a bit dull. The HuD could be improved since it is very clunky and is confusing, also, it has many spelling errors. The animations are very smooth, especially the giant robots! The models are absolutely purely made of the most badass material known to man. The effects look very powerful, so do the ammunitions.
Pros:

Constant updates
The most badass models for an Early Access game
Interesting concept

Outside of Star Wars, the other main point of reference is, of course, Doom.  A 1990s FPS was judged based on what it did well or poorly in comparison to the latest id game, to the extent that the genre was known as Doom-clones rather than first person shooters.
Dark Forces was a truly excellent Doom-clone.
Despite not having true 3D levels, the developers were able to hack together a system that gave the levels a verticality that Doom just didn't have.  Rooms could be located on top of one another, and the result was anything from maze-like prison complexes built into cliffsides to simple things like gaps you could jump over and bridges you could walk both over and under.  It was the kind of leap forward that sounds so trivial after it was done, it's hard to imagine games without it.
The improved technology would not have mattered if Dark Forces didn't feel like a Star Wars game though.  iMuse was a system that dynamically mixed the music with the rise and fall of in-game action that had been used successfully in previous LucasArts games.  As with X-Wing and TIE Fighter it sounded fantastic when applied to Star Wars themes.  Voice acting and a handful of cutscenes let the game tell a simple but functional story, itself a somewhat innovative idea for a mid-90s FPS.
Is it worth playing outside of nostalgia or as a history lesson in FPS design?   Many of the mechanics are simple by today's standards.  Enemies shoot at you or walk around slightly aimlessly, and while there is a good range of weapons available to the player, the gunplay is very basic.  Lives are used instead of a save or checkpoint system, which leads to an occasional need to restart the level when you fall to your death too many times or die against the handful of actually difficult enemies.
Ultimately though it's impressive that the game has aged as well as it has, and with the use of a graphics mod like DarkXL, it's still eminently playable.
