I can't remember when I bought Hotline Miami or how much I gave for it, but I honestly regret not playing it sooner.  I also forget how long it took to finish and to get the secret ending, but I clocked in 10 hours to do all that and get a few additional cheevos.
Hotline Miami is basically Ultraviolence: The Game.  Each chapter sees you as the brutally-violent "Jacket" who dons an animal mask at the start of each level, who then proceeds to slay a bunch of guys in nice white suits while pulsing music plays through the brightly-colored rooms.  You're going to leave one hell of a mess, but you have to do it without getting hit.  Using the weapons lying around and in the enemy's hands (or your own bare hands), slaughter everyone.  Die, and you have to restart the current floor no matter how many mooks' brains you left ground into the carpet before.
Hotline Miami plays like a twin-stick shooter with one stick or WASD to move, and the other stick or the mouse to aim.  You don't have many actions but you honestly don't need much.  You move at a set rate, you can move the camera slightly away from you to peek around the map, you can punch enemies down, you can finish off downed enemies, you can lock onto individual targets, you can pick up, use, and throw weapons, and you can interact with a few contextual things during your missions.  You press R or the A button when you inevitably die to restart the floor.  The game doesn't demand perfection but it does ask for accuracy, and being a few degrees off on your swing can be the difference between killing or being killed.
You might look at the screenshots and think the game a rather stylized stealth game.  You can sneak around and off enemies with silent melee weapons, but the game encourages you to be reckless and ballsy with the scoring system.  Playing it safe and going slowly will net you few points.  Killing chains of enemies in a short time gives you bonus combo points, so be quick!  Score high and you unlock new weapons and new masks which give minor bonuses like having lethal fists, moving faster, or making all guns silent.  The game is very actiony and very fast-paced, and I'd honestly say it has some puzzle elements too.  Enemies tend to stick to their rooms and some will patrol in set patterns, so it's a matter of how to dispatch them all quickly but safely.  The game also slowly introduces new elements to keep the gameplay fresh, like doors to slam into enemies, or enemies that certain weapons won't work on, or windows that you (and the enemies) can shoot through.  Trying to plan your next move while keeping all of these things in mind while your adrenaline's up is only part of the fun.
The story is...minimal, but the experience is very trippy and weird.  You're some blonde dude wearing an animal mask and a letterman jacket (hence the nickname).  You don't talk, you don't have a name, you just wake up, answer the answering machine, go to some place, and kill a bunch of people.  You get a score tally, you unlock things, you go visit your friend at one of the stores he works at, and then you go home to repeat the process.  It's a very arcadey experience since the story is so out of focus.  You'll be left with plenty of questions if you stop to think...but who has time for that?  You might be able to piece together the puzzle if you have an eye for detail.
While each chapter doesn't have its own unique song, the music really helps to get you in the killing mood. High-tempo music just goes well with the frantic pace of you moving through the rooms, mowing down scores of mooks.  You might find yourself bobbing your head to the beat or tapping your foot or whatever.  Then you get Chapter Clear and the music...
Party's over, time to go home.
The game is pretty short.  Most of your time with this game will be spent getting that "perfect" run through each stage and chapter, so you'll be repeating content quite a bit until you stop dying.  The game's hard, but I didn't think it crossed over from "challenging but fun" to "frustrating and disheartening."  The individual stages within the chapters are thankfully pretty short, so you rarely lose any big chunk of time to failure.  If you're the type of person who likes to speedrun levels or try to beat your previous score or beat your friends' scores or are just an old-fashioned cheevo-♥♥♥♥♥, there's something here for you.  And there's always some catharsis in cutting a bunch of mooks in half with a katana.
I'd like to think that Hotline Miami is well-deserving of its high praise, but it might not be a game for everyone.  Some people might be turned off by the almost cartoonish pixelated gore they'd be creating, some people might not care for the whatever-genre-it-is music, and some people might want to snap their keyboards and controllers in half after dying for the 30th time in a row.  For everyone else, it'll be a difficult but rewarding ride filled with lots of death.  Maybe you

Combining resource management with tower defense and math, Terrorhedron does well to offer a great challenge as you place several types of turrets in crazy positions to compensate for their 180* firing radius.
Just note that this game can be a bit like Morrowind. You may screw up and fail a few times before you get a hang of it and start kicking orb hiney. Just know where to place your turrets so you can get the full effect of their firepower. It may take a bit of trial and error, but anyone with decent knowledge of geometry should get the hang of it in no time.
Unfortunately, there are only about eight turrets in the game, each with only a max level of 3. There are also only six maps available. And while each of them are challenging, they can get a bit too easy to memorize once you start getting better. Some DLC maps and turrets would be a nice addition.
There is also an experience system for unlocking the maps, turrets, and turret upgrades. The only thing I hate about this game's experience system is that there is no level cap. Once you hit level 30, you unlock everything, which makes gaining any more EXP pointless because unlocking things is the only purpose it serves.
Overall, I'd give Terrorhedron an 8/10. Better bought when it's on sale, since it's $0.49 when on sale

From the makers of Super Meat Boy comes a twisted adaptation of the classic Bible story, commonly known as the "Binding of Isaac".
This difficult platformer tells the story of Isaac and his mother whom, upon hearing the voice of God, tries to take the life of her son. As the frightened little boy, you delve into the basement below and fight horrifying monsters with your tears. Yeah, seriously.
Though throughout the game you pick up some nifty items and weapons to help you in your journey.
As previously mentioned, this game is a bit difficult (though not nearly difficult as Super Meat Boy); there are no continues, you have to complete the game in one shot.
That may sound pretty daunting, but there is no set structure to this game; every room and end boss is randomly generated, so you will never ever play the same game twice.
The interface is simple, story is basic, but the gameplay is stupidly addicting and the Binding of Isaac is a really fun time-kille

Very well written, and I'd dare say that the story is reason enough alone to buy this game.  A very twisty-turny plot that keeps the player wondering.  Not just about trying to figure out what's going on, but also about all the implications and ramifications once it's revealed what's going on.  I'd really love to go deeper into it, too, because there's a lot of awesome meat on the story bone here, but it really needs to be experienced without spoilers.
I like how the story is broken up into segments as well, with an intro and "previously on Alan Wake" segments, like you're watching a TV show instead of playing a game.  It's a nice little touch, and I think an
TV series might do pretty well, in fact!
Overall the game is beautiful (with a single lone caveat mentioned amongst the bad stuff), with great lighting and wonderful textures.
As good as the graphics are for the most part, the lip synching is absolutely abysmal.  Alan might be saying something like "You have to believe me!  These . . . these monster just came out of the forest and attacked me!", but if you turned the volume off and tried to read his lips, all you'd get is "Arrarar!  Rah rah rararar arrhar harar!"  It's all flapping jaw and no real facial expressions, like they're all puppets with inexpert handlers.
The camera - at least on the PC version, I dunno about console - is badly calibrated.  Awful, just awful.  When I played through the game, I was using the mouse and keyboard because I hadn't gotten around to buying a decent gamepad yet, and just the barest touch of the mouse sent the camera swinging around Alan five or six times before coming to a halt, like it was a drunk frat boy doing donuts around the parking lot that was Alan's head.  I had to pull the sensitivity down to almost nothing, and even then it was kind of wild.  I eventually got used to it, but dammit, that's not the sort of thing you should
to get used to.
As an addendum, once I did manage to get a gamepad, I went back into the game to see if that really did help things any, but it certainly seemed like that was not the case.  I didn't play through the whole game again, tho', so that might be just a first impression.  Overall, the combat can be fun, but only if you can get over the initial hurdles the default settings place in the way.
On a more minor note, though I did enjoy running through all the different stages, there were perhaps a few too many of them that simply had "dark and spooky woods" as the theme.  A little more variation might have done a lot of good.
Despite my difficulties with the controls, I still highly recommend this game.  It's a deep and fascinating look into the blurring of fiction and reality as well as a disturbing thriller with great characters and beautiful settings.

First things first: This game is great. It's made by Klei. They rock. Buy it.

The game IS DIFFICULT for newcomers and it took me 2 semi-playthroughs and watching guides to be able to complete the game on beginner, before moving on to advanced. The characters are unque (although there should be more), the story is solid, the graphics look great, and the future theme is spot-on. I will say that the enimies aren't very unique, they usually only differ by appearance, or minor things like extra armor. Also, there should be more types of missions, and more layouts for the locations to make each playthough feel different.
All in all, an enjoyable turn-based stealth that I plan on continuing for a while.

This is the most frustrating game. It's frustrating because it rides the line between great and terrible. There are certainly incredible moments, where you feel completely in control and every touch of the keyboard puts you centimeters away from death. Then there are other times when an enemy appears on top of you, resulting in instant death.
I've played this game since early access. I've seen many welcome improvements and fixed bugs. Now that v1.0 has come I feel it is fair to say that this game will not reach the point where it will ever result in a satisfying playthrough. There are dozens of glitches than have stuck with the game since early access. Many of these glitches cause instant death. It's maddening to lose a game due to something out of your control. The better you become at the game, the more this happens. It has gotten to the point where I die only when the game puts me in a glitched or otherwise impossible situation.
The core loop is addictive and never leaves you satisfied. It's the feeling of pulling the arm of a slot machine. Do not play this game if you value your time and energy.

When I first saw this game, I was pretty impressed by the art style and the idea of a cyberpunk future where you infiltrate places for...stuff (though I'd argue teleporting is more sci-fi based). The more I played, the more I became bored. While its all randomly generated, it all felt very samey to me. The only times it felt different was at the very end, on the last level. The voice acting was more akin to reading straight from a script, the wide array of characters mean nothing when only 3 or 4 of them are useful for anything. It just feels like this game was more of an artistic representation over the gameplay. The times the game becomes interesting is when the game becomes overwhelming with 6 guards buzzing all around you like rabid dogs. Oh, and a lot fo this game is RNG. Guard paths, level rewards, all of it is RNG, which means you can be legit boned by the RNG. While its a 'rogue-like', it...isn't engaging like one. I could never finish the last level due to the overwhelming amount of heresy the game continued to throw at me, forcing either a level restart or game over.
Overall, I'd give this a pass. Artistically, its phenomenal. Gameplay-wise, it plays like potato in your hands: makes a mess and hungry for food.

I don't understand all these overwelmingly positive reviews this game is getting, it's as if they never played season 1.
The game isn't terrible, but is vastly overshadowed by the arguable masterpiece that was Season 1. Just to summarize the problems I found without writing an essay:
1. Severe lack of character development. New characters come into the fray with little to no development, then just die off for drama. Even the "villain" introduced is squandered after having a pretty decent entrance.
2. Severe lack of actual gameplay. Cmon, even Season 1 had you atleast walking around and solving small puzzles for atleast half of the episode. This should have been built upon in this Season, instead you mostly sit there and watch the movie.
3. Very little carry-over in terms of consequences. In Season 1, those "X will remember this" notices on top of the screen meant something more than half the time. You would have characters recall things you said 3 episodes and call you on it. Season 2 has very little of this, which also emphasizes Problem 1.
Like I said, way more issues, but I'll let you see for yourself.
So when all comes together, Season 2 only really stands out because we all want to see/continue the Clementine we developed in Season 1. And now especially with the announcement of Season 3, I suppose this chapter is worth going sitting through to see how Clem turns out. So I would recommend this game, only because it's the continuation of the story we all started in S1.

Pros:
-Fun concept to controll your units in a RTS in first person
-Interesting objective to win games (Kill their Executive)
-Lots of ways to upgrade (Units, Structures, Resource, Weapons)
-Many weapon choices for your units.
-The controlls on most units are fine
Cons:
-The Resources were handled poorly, having no base income your priority is to get resource flow going immidetly by building resource nodes on few selected spots on the map
-The Crystals that exist on the map is just snowballing, get alot of the research boost ones and you will just research everything and snowball. Get the Heskosium crystals that are dropped from meteorites and get access to stronger units. Its just a race to who can get the drone to the crystal first.
-The AI version of your units will not destoy enemy drones. Only way to stop them is to go into 1st person.
-Destroying a drone who picked up a crystal will not make the crystal aviable for you.
-Alot of the weapon upgrades are pretty much useless unless you play in 1st person mode. The only weapons i seen the AI use with some effect are the basic machine guns and laser beams. Simply impossible for them to hit anything with a cannon.
-A match can be won real quick if you buy one robot troop and send it to kill the enemy executive, honestly few people can afford putting out a defense so early on. (Once its inside the base you can rarely catch it before it reaches the CEO who dies so quick)
-The AI version of my units tends to blindly shoot at walls as targetable objects are behind the wall.
-The wall that lets you put units ontop of it is completly useless for AI can't shoot even if the target is right under them. Only useable for first person.
-Once you get artillery, aiming them at the enemy's resource nodes will pretty much ruin their entire income and win you the game by simply having little to no threat left.
-Sound can glitch out if its to many things making sounds at once.
-Tends to bug out when selecting units
Overall: This game had potential but wasn't executed so well. Its more a race of which drone will reach the crystal first than it is a battle. The winner of the crystals is basicly the winner of the game. The only fun i had was messing around with a friend on this, and that was only for 1 hour of fun for us. This game had potential but changes needs to be made, it needs to be redesigned on its rules as this is a snowball RTS more than anything and it needs to have bug fixes for the sound glitches aswell as the bug that makes selecting a unit annoying. Ontop of that they need to improve the AI so more weapons are even useable for the AI units, making all my units use laserbeams since else they will miss everything if not is just not fun simply. The only way i can make use of the more hard hitting weapons like the cannons is to have a private aircraft with the cannon simply there for me to make quick assaults on incomming enemies. I shouldn't have to do that just to make the cannon useable.
This can be fun for some i can imagnen but i simply cannot recommend it unless it gets some patches that fixes some of theese problems.
(Theres not to much wrong with the AI players its just the non firstperson player units that are complete garbage)

Alpha Protocol is a hard game to recommend: it carries many of the hallmarks of a really good game but is ultimately let down by a series of hugely frustrating bugs and gameplay decisions.
Alpha Protocol featuring detailed skills progression, branching dialogue, and choices during the progression of the story that ultimately shape the outcome to your style of play. All great stuff, but the barrier to enjoying all that is running the gauntlet of psychic enemy AI, baffling checkpoint placement, and wonky keyboard and mouse controls (especially during the hacking minigame).
By far the most annoying of these issues is the AI. Various enemies randomly vanish between loads, characters will spot you from across the map and immediately raise the alarm, patrol points will be arranged in a way that makes it almost impossible to ghost your way through most areas, and guard behaviour is often wildly inconsistent: you'll shoot a guard in the head and everyone will suddenly be alerted; reload and do the exact same thing and suddenly nobody notices. Even cover hides you from view one minute and makes you visible to every enemy in the room the next.
It's a real shame: if the AI issues alone were fixed this game would be an instant recommendation. As it stands, it's only worth getting if it's cheap and you love Obsidian.

The strongest part of this RPG is its reputation system. In most RPGs you need to hug, kiss and run errands for NPCs or factions. If you refuse, they don't open their parts of the story. End of the line. In Alpha Protocol reputation gets you bonuses. Bad reputation
gets you bonuses, just different ones. So if you dislike some fellow agent, go ahead, spit them into the face, let them know that.
This gets us to the other part: roleplaying. You know, two letters out of three in 'RPG'. Alpha Protocol is one of the few RPGs that lets you do just that. Not for the sake of some 'alternative ending'. Not for some 'heroeness meter'. Got a character? Got ideas on his psycological profile? Roleplay!
One could complain that the story is 'on rails'. It sure is. This is not an open-world sandbox. This is a tale about the protagonist. And
vision of him. And, in part, about you yourself - if you really do the roleplaying and get emotionally invested.
Absolutely recommended!

Alpha Protocol aspires to be so much. It claims to be a game revolving around choice, a sort of modern-day Mass Effect with M4's and gadgets instead of spaceships and pulse carbines. Unfortunately, when it all tries to come together, it all just breaks down. To put it bluntly, Alpha Protocol is a game with a thousand choices that punishes you for not making the choices it likes.
Alpha Protocol's story is a bit of a train wreck in the Modern Warfare vein. It's a trashy spy epic with overplayed cliches, forgettable characters, and a protagonist who couldn't act his way out of a wet paper bag. That said, the story isn't terrible per se, so long as you take it for what it is: a trashy spy epic. Playing an operation in Alpha Protocol is a lot like watching a season of 24, though without any of Jack Bauer's memorable personality. Think about that for a second. Where the overall plot really falls short are the characters. They are unmemorable, unempathic, poorly voice-acted, and generally unlikable, especially the player character, Michael Thorton, who possesses a particular skill for sucking all of the energy out of a room. The best I can say about the characters is that by the time you meet Steven Heck, you'll finally know from where Rockstar ripped off the character of Trevor in GTA V.
The dialogue system is the game's claim to fame, and honestly, I found it to be a bit underwhelming. There are three "Stances" you can take when talking with Mike, but the way he delivers them always makes you cringe. He can be "Suave", which makes him sound like a pretentious♥♥♥♥♥♥who's trying way too hard to be clever, "Aggressive", which makes him sound like a complete jackass, and "Professional", which just makes him sound boring. Certain NPCs respond differently to these stances, but the way they do so lacks any sort of depth. You just find the one they like (or dislike) and keep pushing that one until you get something. I was unimpressed. To top it all off, the selector for the dialogue stays over whatever stance you used last, so you don't even really have to interact with the dialogue at all. The majority of these portions can be played while AFK.
And then the gameplay happens. And it is terrible. Alpha Protocol just isn't sure whether it wants to be an RPG with shooter mechanics, or a shooter with RPG mechanics, and the combat suffers for it. Gunplay is unsastisfying and enemies are bullet sponges. In addition, because of the way that the aim mechanics work, combat is incredibly slow-paced, causing you to wait anywhere from 3 to 10 seconds to line up a single shot, and it'll probably take two or three more to kill something. That is, of course, unless you choose to specialize in the incredibly overpowered Pistol tree, which allows you to routinely freeze time to instantly kill up to six enemies, or execute perfect critical hit headshots from blindfire. Again, the concept of punishing you for making the wrong choices comes into play here. It certainly doesn't help that the AI is beyond terrible.
Stealth is incredibly janky. The mechanics for it are never particularly well explained or represented in the game, on no small part due to the game's terrible AI. How much does your Sound Dampening stat interact with your Stealth skill? No one really knows. You certainly won't. Sometimes the enemies will walk right by you in broad daylight while you're crouching. Other times they will psychically turn a full 180 and scream out "HE'Z OVA DERE!" while throwing lead downrange while you barely moved an inch. The only thing I can say for sure about Alpha Protocol's stealth is that it really just made me want to play Splinter Cell Blacklist again.
And don't get me started on the minigames. Alpha Protocol has some of the worst lockpicking and engineering minigames I've seen in a while, and it definitely has THE worst hacking minigame I've ever seen or had the displeasure to play. Words cannot accurately describe how miserable and tedious they are. In addition, these minigames are EVERYWHERE. Expect to do one every five minutes on average, and before and after every combat stage. And halfway through the game, these minigames decide to unexplainedly ramp up the difficulty by giving you more crap to do and less time to do it. The only way to counter this is upgrade your sabotage skill, which the game never elucidates the importance of beyond "This is the skill wot does stuff with gadgets". If you don't? Forget it. Many of those minigames, particularly the Bypassing ones, will be downright impossible.
The final nail in the coffin is that Alpha Protocol is not a good port. It's not terrible or unplayable, but it's certainly not good. FOV is locked, framerates stutter when they aren't already running at abysmal lows, textures flicker and tear, and there's a permanent mouse acceleration that cannot be switched off. To top it all off, the game has no Quicksave function. Hell, it doesn't even have a real Hardsave function, instead allowing you to save one of their miserably-placed checkpoints.
Despite its aspirations, the problem with Alpha Protocol just boils down to one simple fact: it's just no fun to play. This might have made a good movie, or a decent dialogue-driven adventure game, but as an ARPG, it just falters and dies. Like the thousand wrong choices you can make in Alpha Protocol, there are a thousand other games I would recommend before this one. You want a proper ARPG with guns and dialogue? Play Mass Effect. Proper stealthy spy game? Plenty of Splinter Cell games out there. Proper modern-day shooter? Too many to count, and some of them are even good. Want to kill someone to Autograph's Turn Up the Radio? Play GTA Vice City.
And unlike Alpha Protocol, I'm not going to punish you for making a choice I don't like.

Game of the Month: NOVEMBER
From the makers of Super Meat Boy comes a twisted adaptation of the classic Bible story, commonly known as the "Binding of Isaac".
This difficult platformer tells the story of Isaac and his mother whom, upon hearing the voice of God, tries to take the life of her son. As the frightened little boy, you delve into the basement below and fight horrifying monsters with your tears. Yeah, seriously.
Though throughout the game you pick up some nifty items and weapons to help you in your journey.
As previously mentioned, this game is a bit difficult (though not nearly difficult as Super Meat Boy); there are no continues, you have to complete the game in one shot.
That may sound pretty daunting, but there is no set structure to this game; every room and end boss is randomly generated, so you will never ever play the same game twice.
The interface is simple, story is basic, but the gameplay is stupidly addicting and the Binding of Isaac is a really fun time-kille

I've played many episodic games but I don't think I can say there was one that made me pause the game several times, process what just happened, and then come back to it after a few hours. To say this game's perfect would be a lie, it's got faults like any other game, but where its strengths lie are in its ability to create a universe the player is incredibly invested in.And to avoid spoiling the story in any way, I've decided just to make a simple pros and cons list.
PROS
- $20 price for the season pass
- Performance was good and there was very few bugs for me
- I really dug the unique art style (simple yet visually appealing)
- The UI is intuitive and very simple
- A solid story from start to finish (there might've been a few plot holes but I didn't notice any really)
- Likeable female protagonist and a well-written relationship between her and the deuteragonist
- Amazing atmosphere
- Great voice talent (I think a few voices didn't feel "right" but everyone else was golden)
- The song selection was fitting and appropriate
- Different endings which were logical and nicely executed, to me, for a story that involves time travel (one ending could've been longer though and I suspect many fans might've preferred something less predictable)
- Real choices that matter early on
- The rewind mechanic wasn't gimmicky for the most part and I rather enjoyed all of the puzzles
- The player doesn't take a backseat to the action like a lot of story games I felt (you feel like you're playing a game)
- A lot of extra content in the episodes (various diary entires, optional photos to take, SMS messages, etc.)
- Explores a number of controversial issues and/or themes (that few games touch on) with tact
CONS
- The pacing could've been slightly better in episodes 3 and 4
- Past choices don't matter as much in episodes 4 and 5 (I won't describe anything more to avoid spoiling the story)
- Some characters are more or less stereotypes but each player will feel differently about this
- The rare corny/cheesy phrase that would stick out (I can't think of an example right now)
This game will obviously not be for everyone but I do think it appeals to a lot of people (as seen by the Steam user reviews). It's quite simply a high school drama with a bit of mystery and the supernatural thrown in. If you had thought it was some feministic sort of game like I had initially - I urge you to give this game another look. I have tried to be as honest as I can about a game which I have thoroughly enjoyed and I hope this review has helped you, the reader, in some way. For $20 I highly recommend grabbing Life Is Strange and if you don't happen to enjoy it in the first hour or so: refund it. I don't think you will though :) It honestly deserves a 8.5/10 in my book.- Jason

Well I'm about 20 hours in *seemingly around half way* btu I already sadly have enough issues with the game to give a  not recommended review.
First I'll start with the fact I pre ordered the silver edition, the extra orc tibe dlc down the line will only be a good thing, the other expantions...well we will see.
Everything was fantastic in the first zone, I had amazing encounters and also found the amazing yet rather terror inducing *lookout* orc.
Anyway all was fine until act 1 where I had My first issue...now I like a ton of people HATE microtransactions in general, let alone in a full priced game but I was willing to ignore it...only you can't.. not only does the market flash in the menu *drawing your eye subtly not an issue for Me, but an issue for anyone with adictive personalites*.
Now to My main issue with it...you're forced to open any preorder bonuses in the market by lookbox, and that'll likely be the case with anything that is weapon/orc based. FORCING you into the market IS an issue as it's their cheeky as ♥♥♥♥ way as to say *hey...why you're here...you know...buy more stuff*
But the biggest insult so far by miles is the fact in a cut scene at the end of your first fortress assault a character as the ♥♥♥♥ing cheek to even say BUY LOOTBOXES. The quote is as follows *If you're ever in need of more boys, look for an orc called the headhunter, he'll help you out.*
Thats the orcs name on the market screen...the headhunter.. Yeah they're not shoving it down your throats at all.
Then the issue with leveling orcs comes in, you NEED the lootboxes for this as they almost never gain traits compared to the first game, so if anything you'd want the tokens to give epic traits otherwise your fav orcs that're not already epic or legendary will never become so, as I have yet to see it happen in 20 hours and if I do see it I'll take this part out.
The only time I've seen an orc become epic or legendary is once when I shamed an enemy orc, once in 20 hours...can only imagine how bad that is going to get.
Honestly breaks the nemesis system really if your own orcs can't become epic or legendary without the lootbox tokens... Clearly this time around the game was built more around the lootboxes than we would have liked.
That is the main issue for Me, not being able to keep my favourite orc around over epics now, might effect end game badly without a legendary orc being overlord and lots of epics being warchiefs...will have to see.
But purely on the fact I can see it's built around the lootbox system I have to not recommend this game, even though messing with the nemesis system is decent at the moment, it would be much more fantastic if it wasn't built around the market.

: Short game, short review. When I first saw this game, I was pretty impressed by the art style and the idea of a cyberpunk future where you infiltrate places for...stuff (though I'd argue teleporting is more sci-fi based). The more I played, the more I became bored. While its all randomly generated, it all felt very samey to me. The only times it felt different was at the very end, on the last level. The voice acting was more akin to reading straight from a script, the wide array of characters mean nothing when only 3 or 4 of them are useful for anything. It just feels like this game was more of an artistic representation over the gameplay. The times the game becomes interesting is when the game becomes overwhelming with 6 guards buzzing all around you like rabid dogs. Oh, and a lot fo this game is RNG. Guard paths, level rewards, all of it is RNG, which means you can be legit boned by the RNG. While its a 'rogue-like', it...isn't engaging like one. I could never finish the last level due to the overwhelming amount of heresy the game continued to throw at me, forcing either a level restart or game over.
Overall, I'd give this a pass. Artistically, its phenomenal. Gameplay-wise, it plays like potato in your hands: makes a mess and hungry for food.

Just would like to start out with one statement, and that is: DO NOT buy this game for full price. Wait until it goes on sale or becomes cheaper. If I had the opportunity to buy this again, there is no way I would pay $60.
PROS:
The storyline (cutscenes) keeps you on your toes with plot twists here and there. There are side quests that tie in to the story that are pretty entertaining and a bit challenging. The game overall is a bit too easy on normal difficulty, though. New skills in the skill tree are very powerful and can be very strategic for certain missions.
CONS:
The Act IV is by far one of the worst things I have played. Talk about repetition and grinding. If you like doing the same thing over and over again, multiple times, then this is your forte. The ACTUAL ending to the game is also very weak. Seems like the developers just called it quits. The game is designed specifically so you will have to buy the XP boosts (don't use real money, do the challenges that reward you with gold) so that you can level up to where you need to be at the end of the game. The DLC is also not free, which is a HUGE negative for the game. If the DLC was free, this would be actually worth the full price. No point in covering the micro-transactions because we all feel the same way about those. Not that they're actually necessary to the game, and you can definitely get away with not using real money.
OVERALL:
Fun game until Act IV, would not recommend buying full price and NOT paying for the Expansion pass aka Season pass for DLC which should be free. I would compare this game to EA's Battlefront in that they went about this game in a bad way.

I played many different tower defence games before but this one is the best.
(+++) The biggest thing in the game giving priority for turrents. It makes everything different and more logical.
--> For example:
Let's say you have two weapon which can hit 80hp and you have two more which can hit 20hp. And your enemies have 100hp.
In other tower defence game because they hit the nearest one;
First hit make enemies hp 20 and the second enemy pass away because as everyone knows power means slowness in that kind of games. If the second powerful one hits one has 20 hp then the second enemy still has 100 hp and your 20hp weapons cannot kill it.
However in this game;
You can give the priority. This one will hit slowest one, this one will hit strongest one etc. This makes your game more logical and if we back the example, powerful ones hits the most strongest one then it compares 20hp with 100hp then it hits 100hp so your weak weapons can kill them.
(++) Second most attractive thing is; there is not lots of nodes to build turrents. In the other games you have a path and you can build weapons on side of path. In this game you can build nodes to build more nodes or turrents. Therefore, you have to find the optimum balance for it. You can manage your money more carefully.
(+) The path is 3D and this is a bit more difficult the other tower defence games.
(+) Price is really funny. Kind of there is no price :)
(-) Control mechanism of 3D view is weird. Sometimes I lost the game :D
(-) Levels are too hard actually.

While this is strictly a tower defence game, the convention will only go so far as having enemies that moved in a pre-determined path and the fact that you construct towers to defeat said enemies. To succeed in this game, you must have to the mental fortitude to plan in three dimensions, as well as an abundance of creativity to maximise and extend the reach of your turrets based on limited nodes to build upon.
In the first hour of play you’ll learn to construct vine like constructs to maximise your firepower, since you can only place turrets on specified nodes or extend upon them via connectors. Balancing between the reach of your foundations and your capacity to damage, you’ll glow new vines across a few strategic points, eventually connecting them all in one gigantic network. All between rounds of steadily increasing waves.
The game can be mercilessly hard at higher difficulties, but it is also a rewarding experience to players that can adapt new tactics in different elevations and angles.
That said, the multiplayer felt tagged on at the last minute and it suffers from sync issues when I tried it. The lack of a map editor is also a major oversight on the developer’s part, as this could have so much potential if it had workshop support; potential that was wasted simply because the devs wished to work on a newer title.
If you wanted a relatively new take on the tower defence genre, you ought to give this a try. The unique visuals and catchy tunes are just icing if you happened to like the retro theme.

Refreshing Game. Turn based strategy.
Simple enough story.
, as they give different benefits. You are racing against the clock here. Every mission you go reduce the countdown period to the final stage.
In the mission,
You have up to 4 to mobilise, starting off in a room with a limited amount of action points each. Each character can walk, peek, stun the guards, kill the guards, steal credits, etc. We are racing against the clock here as well. The longer you take, the harder it becomes.
After a mission, you get to spent credits/points.
Increase stats or buy better augmentations/guns to handle harder guards later.
Finally, you reach the last mission. Are your characters ready for it? Hardly for me on my first round. But here's the interesting part. Even if you fails, all this experience will not be lost, but used to unlock better abilities, new characters. What's more is that the game contents are still getting updated with new abilities etc along the way.

I bought Nuclear Throne in early 2014, while it was still in Early Access. I've been following the game's development since then and have been enjoying the hell out of it along the way.
Nuclear Throne is the modern definition of Rogue-lite. There are many different varying versions of this style of game, and this one surely takes inspiration from others like it, but does so in new and interesting ways.
Do you like to shoot stuff? Do you like pixel graphics? Do you like bullet hell games? Then Nuclear Throne is for you.
Death is permanent, but new characters can be earned by playing the game and reaching certain milestones. Mutations (think perks) are earned as you play and can change the way you play. A whole slew of weapons are available and randomly appear via chests. Ammo is limited. Difficulty ramps up. You WILL die. But you'll still want to come back for more.
About the only shortcoming I can find is that the co-op mode is local only. I'd love to be able to play with friends who don't live locally.
Update: Apparently you can now use a mod to play co-op online with friend. Nice improvement!

The singleplayer is really lack luster, for the general player they aren't going to go to singleplayer that much, they will, on the other hand, go to Multiplayer, this had an array of game modes that you can play, there is Deathrun, where runners go through a gauntlet of traps, that the deaths activate. There is also Trouble in Terrorist Town, this gamemode is about the Terrorist finding the traitors, who betrayed them. There is also a game mode called prop hunt, where there are hiders, people who can turn into props that are in the map, and there are seekers who search for them. There are many more modes to play on, thus giving an endless gameplay. However this game does not have dedicated servers, thus the community runs most of the servers, and thus might cause some problems for example, server host is located in california, U.S and you live in London, your probably not going to have fun then, as you are spending more time lagging then playing. This game, if you can't tell, runs 99.99% off the backs of the community, with just facepunch stepping in here and there to fix some bugs, while making somethings broken even more (aka they make more bugs with every patch, which shouldn't be a problem if you play on multiplayer more than singleplayer.) and adding stuff here and there for singleplayer / sandbox, like I said this is a major downside, if you don't have internet the game becomes really stale, real fast. is a 2D platformer with challenging puzzles. The main character "Shuggy" is a little vampire, who inherited an old Scottish mansion full of various monsters. To clean the castle, he has to go through 5 different areas: The Dungeon, The Boiler Room, The Gallery, The Graveyard and The Clocktower. AoS offering over 150 levels to beat, each level can be done in 3 minutes or even faster. In addition to the single-player campaign there is also co-op and “Shuggy’s Teleporting Troubles” - 40 levels with second teleporter to use.
"Easy to play, hard to master" - that's how I can describe this game. I would recommend it to casual and hardcore players, everyone should be happy. I completed AoS without any troubles, even tried to master one level (3rd place in "Rappel" in The Gallery at the time of writing this). “Shuggy’s Teleporting Troubles” was a little bit harder than single-player campaign, but also didn't take a lot of time to beat it.
4 euro is cheap for this enjoyable game, but I recommend to wait for sale, so you can get it cheaper.
Enjoy!
PS. Because I'm forever alone, I beat co-op alone, yes, it's possible, but it's hard to do it, especially "Get A Move On" level. Good luck.

The interface and feel are polished and stylized.  It's also a pure stealther, which I normally enjoy.
Unfortunately, a number of gameplay issues make it far less fun.
First, your success in each mission is far more subject to the luck of the randomizer than your skill.  Every bad level leaves you less prepared for the final one.  In my case, I only had one chance to add an agent so I was also 1 short for the end mission.
Second, you can't afford to max out all your agents, so you end up specializing each one.  The problem is, due to the random levels, you split them up to cover ground and just hope the right agent encounters the right stuff.
Lastly, it's extremely unclear what is important to improve/buy.  For instance, you might increase an agents loot finding results marginally and then discover that without armor piercing weapons you are unable to handle higher levels.  Then, you "solve" that by exiting levels without clearing them, since the timer makes things dicier the longer you take.
This means you get even less resources for subsequent, harder, levels.   Thus compounding the problem into a gloriously pointless end mission.  My first time on the final mission (which just pops on you) I simply did not have enough power to complete the mission.  I was getting +1/turn but it was clearly impossible to finish the first, let alone second, mission objectives.  The only solution is to restart the whole campaign and "try harder" on the lead up missions.  Since the campaign is so short, that's not so bad, but leaves you feeling pretty crappy about the whole experience.

Alpha Protocol is a single player action RPG game with branching story dialogue based on your choices that will affect the way your game progresses and ends. The game has a modern spy movie setting ala James Bond/Mission Impossible. There are dossiers to read through, webs of secrets to uncover, and enough cloak and daggery to make you question who’s side you really are on and who is playing who, typical spy stuff.
HOW IS THIS AN RPG?:
This type of action RPG game has a single hero, third person camera. You will earn level ups and have dozens of skills to choose from and have different weapons and gear to upgrade. Depending on how you approach some missions you will have access to side quests within your current mission that could potentially benefit you afterwards in areas such as the black market for example.
IS THIS A SANDBOX RPG?:
The game is not a free roamer and is fairly straight forward to keep the story moving along, it is broken up into the main hubs of Saudi-Arabia, Rome, Moscow and Taipei. However the order of what areas you decide to visit are entirely up to you.
EXTENDED REPLAY VALUE!:
Completed the game as the sneaky, non-lethal, silenced weapons, computer hacker, suave, smooth talker type? Why not try playing as the shoot first ask questions later, shotgun toting, explosives expert, confrontational, hard headed type? Or a mixture of both or something completely different. The game has multiple dialogue choices and event outcomes depending on what type of play style you go with. You will definitely get your money’s worth from Alpha Protocol if you decide to do multiple play throughs.
Admittedly most of my time spent on Alpha Protocol was on the PS3 and I basically did a speed run for nostalgia’s sake on the PC/Steam version. If this is your first time going through Alpha Protocol you are realistically looking at around 20+ hours give or take per go through.
It’s too bad SEGA didn’t commission a sequel to Alpha Protocol due to poor initial sales showings, but that shouldn’t deter you from experiencing this gem of a game, very underrated.

As of this review, Executive Assault does have a bit of growing pains, but it's potential as a FPSRTS hybrid is very clear.
Have you ever wanted a game where you, yourself, could walk a unit right into your enemy's base, shoot down a few guards and murder the enemy player at point blank? Because in Executive Assault, you can.
The FPS mechanics are pretty solid, though I'd point issue with the aiming. At the lowest DPI it seems like each registered mouse movement moves a few pixels instead of one at a time, unless you zoom in with right click. It's annoying enough that it made leading and shooting targets fairly difficult.
On the RTS side, I cannot stress enough the importance of getting the crystals scattered around the map. Thorium increases your energy "production" by 25 units, which with 1 or 2 upgrades alone helps immensely. The other one (Celerite, I think?) increases your rate of research, and my God is research important in this game. It's a fairly standard multiple-category research tree but some of the first available upgrades are the most important.
Really, though, as one of the only decent FPSRTS hybrids I've ever played,  I can heartily recommend it. The developer seems to have his head on straight and if nothing else, deserves a bit of compensation for his clearly hard work.

Shadow of War. A very controversial game, for a variety of reasons - some reasonable, some not so much.
To start off - the meat and bones of the game:
The Gameplay.
Following on from it's predecessor, Shadow of Mordor, it hails the revolutionary Nemesis System. It must be said, the Nemesis System is turned all the way up in this game, with many more different ways to interact with both your foes and your allies.
There are 3 modes of gameplay; Easy, Normal and Nemesis. I cannot tell you what Easy or Normal are like since I went straight into Nemesis and didn't look back, as I recommend to anyone who played Shadow of Mordor to the point where every fight was an easy victory. Even then Nemesis mode is a bit of a mixed bag still - there are certainly parts where I am given a massive run for my money, but often enough I come out relatively unscathed.
Being able to not only take control of your enemies, but to issue commands and promote and demote them certainly is very fun. The huge variety of tribes, classes and above all traits certainly makes for an exciting time, with no two orcs being the same (though admittedly, even procedural generation has its limits).
I do have to say, however, that there are definitely features missing with the ability to control your orcs that I would love to have seen - such as the ability to direct exactly what kind of missions the orcs are sent on, instead of merely attempting to pit them against each other and seeing what the game decides to give you.
This element of unfortunate randomness is further compounded by the "saviour" moments, where you are protected from death by an ally when you are about to die, thus killing your opponent. This can be extremely frustrating when it happens, as sometimes the enemy in question is one you did not want killed. This ability cannot be turned off.
Still, the ways in which orcs may seek you out are large indeed. Some will chase you for killing an orc close to their heart, or simply because they disagree with your methods of attack. Some can even chase you through the different areas of Mordor. You're not safe even from your own allies, who may chose to betray you if they feel you have wronged them or simply aren't a capable enough leader - though this sadly often means they are difficult, if not impossible to recruit back into your service.
The large variety of not just enemies, but also equippable gear is also excellent, much improved on the simple runes of Shadow of War. Being able to socket your armour and weapons with varying tiers of gems with different effects provides useful bonuses, and the spectrum of abilities that the gear itself can give you opens up a whole new wave of opportunities. Furthermore you can even upgrade the gear itself, giving it a new name, a new look and often a reminder of the enemy you got it from. Some gear can even be upgraded multiple times.
There are many new abilities and sub-abilities in Shadow of War, though some are locked behind story content. They enable you to change your playing style on a whim simply by switching sub-abilities to complement a new angle of attack. As you play through the game, traversing the world becomes easier and more enjoyable with many new ways of moving around.
And you'll certainly need them - with 5 new regions to play in, more than double the regions in Shadow of War, there's a lot of ground to cover. The terrain is very different, with many visually-striking biomes and all the new fauna and hazards that come with them. Fortunately for those who don't enjoy running around as much, each region has 3 fast-travel points to unlock.
And in every region there houses the most interesting part of the game - the Fortresses. Each fortress is ruled by an Overlord, with up to 6 Warchiefs guarding it. You can put together your own crack team of attackers and besiege the fortress, with each ally you bring adding a new bonus to the assault. Each enemy warchief will also have their own bonuses to be aware of, though they can be hunted down outside of the siege to remove both their presence and the defence.
And once you claim your own fortress and customise it as you see fit, you may be forced to defend it against enemy forces seeking to regain it for themselves. Both of these moments are unfortunately both scripted and finite.
But still, if you should desire to spill more blood and conquer more castles, your fellow players may be happy to oblige, with online fort assault being available. Sadly these are somewhat simpler than one could hope for, being only a one-off fight against a random player's fortress - and the only notice you have of your fort having been taken or having repulsed an invader is a simple, brief message in the UI. Though at least if your fortress is taken, you lose nothing.
But some people are interested in more than just the gameplay, so onto;
The Story.
One of the biggest criticisms of Shadow of Mordor was its weak story. I personally forgave the game for that - I read books or watch films for story, such should be secondary in video games. Still, it cannot be denied that certain elements were less than enjoyable, often somewhat contrived.
Has Shadow of War improved? That's difficult to say. There were certainly areas that I did not enjoy, and simply forced myself to get through without feeling any connection to the characters involved. Other parts I found quite emotionally stirring, though sometimes negatively.
In Shadow of Mordor, much is often made of the final boss fight being a quick time event. While Shadow of War is not exactly the same, I definitely found myself thinking about that in some of the boss fights. The gameplay mechanics involved did not please me at all and left me drained and eager to move on when finished, instead of satisfied and victorious.
All in all, it's really hard to give my opinion on whether or not the story was any good; subjective as it is. There were definitely scripted parts I did not enjoy being forced into, and much repetition on certain subjects became grating quickly. The changing of many events in the timeline of Middle-earth may prove angering to those of a "purist" nature, if you care about that sort of thing, which I don't.
And finally we come to the biggest issue of them all;
Microtransactions (MTX).
Upon the announcement I personally did not see the matter as of much importance - though I certainly did not desire them, MTX seemed a relative non-issue. The statement was made that the balancing of the game was done without their presence being included and nothing that could be gained from spending your money could not be gained otherwise, which I took as honesty.
Was it honesty? Not exactly.
It's true that the orcs you can receive are also obtainable through normal means, but it must be said that you can very easily get a hold of orcs that are significantly better than the *majority* of orcs you find in the regular game. Which isn't to say that the orcs you get from MTX are all definitely better than any non-MTX orc - I have run across some I would wager are just as good, if not better.
There're other things than orcs that you can get though, and sadly those things can't be obtained through regular playing. This is disappointing as they do add a whole extra addition to the customisation of your orc allies - the ability to move your orcs through the world instead of having them in only the region you found them in is gated and a big loss.
Despite this fact it does have to be stated categorically that there's no requirement to spend any real life money on these MTX whatsoever. The advantages are certainly there for doing so, but there are lesser "loot boxes" that can be purchased in the store with in-game currency and even the premium currency can be earned through certain ingame challenges.
In essence, the game is definitely worth buying and playing. Some might be put off by the MTX, which is understandable, but they are avoidable.

If you told me I could only play one game for the rest of my life, I'd choose Kerbal Space Program.
Althought at time of posting my steam time with this game reads as 99 hours, it's much closer to 600+ as I owned the non-steam version since 2013.
The game is adorable yet brick hard. Frustrating and immensly rewarding all in the best possible ways.
The Kerbals although never really characterised somehow have bundles of personality. There is a child-like naivety to them and their fearless quest to get to space on some very questionable equipment.
The game demands precision and has a steep learning curve, yet somehow there is a fly by the seat of your pants approach to everything. The parts have comedy descriptions throughout "A flatter variant of the OKTO, OKTO2 was most certainly not conceived when one of our engineers sat on a standard OKTO."
There is hours of fun in just building rockets and space planes and flying them before you even manage to achieve orbit, nevermind land on the Mun(Moon) and Duna(Mars) and beyond.
The fun doesn't stop there with a vibrant community of modders who have made changes as small as incresing the strength of joints between parts, to adding new parts for even more varied building, to adding in whole other objectives/game mechanics and even changing the solar system itself to reflect real life size of planets.
I highly recommend the game, and would also recommend any new players and intermediates who are finding difficulty progressing to look up a tutorial series on youtube by a man called Scott Manely, who covers everything from your first 3 part rocket to landing on the Mun.

The story is okay, the artstyle is brilliant and the gameplay takes this game home.

Nuclear Throne is a game that I admire for its execution and its unflinching vision for itself--a punishing rogue-like, action RPG with bullet-hell (or, depending on your play style, cover based shooter) elements. I objectively think Nuclear Throne is a great game and deserves to be played--it's just not a game that I particularly enjoyed, so I'm saying it's a Not Recommend if you think that brutal difficulty and repetition aren't exactly your thing.
The best way to show my problem with Nuclear Throne is via numbers: With 21 hours, 32 minutes played, I've unlocked 7/12 characters, unlocked 22% of the game, and gotten as far as the third boss (Lil Hunter), whom I've never beaten. I've died 219 times and never finished a run. This means that I've played the same exact 3 or 4 starting levels almost every single one of those 219 times, killing the same ~3 enemy types per level. Sometimes I get farther, but I always have to play through those levels.
Even with the well-designed, different characters, this repetition starts wearing thin. I'm really sick of these opening levels. This problem is exacerbated by how easily death ends a run. A slight misestimation of a bullet's trajectory, an accidental bump into a hidden enemy, poking your head out at exactly the wrong moment--one misstep and suddenly you're back at 1-1.
The action is fast-paced and frenetic, and, when it hits a rhythm, Nuclear Throng can be fun. But, even as someone who enjoys really difficult games and loves rogue-likes (FTL is one of my favorite and most played games of all time), Nuclear Throne isn't for me--something I realized somewhere between my first aggravating death and my 219th.

This game is
great, but as with many recent indie titles, it has several crippling design flaws that turn it from spectacular, which it is agonizingly close to being, into unplayable garbage.
Simply put, this is not a tactical RPG, this is a puzzle game. Why do I say that? Because the way your "pieces" behave makes no sense within the game's theme, which is "tactical espionage." Your pieces are supposedly spies, and carry tazers. Fine so far, except that none of them have the faintest idea how to throw a judo chop or put a shirt-and-trousers rent-a-cop in a sleeper hold. The absence of guns, and the hugely expensive ammo when you actually do happen to get guns is explained in the in-game lore in a satisfactory way. What isn't explained, however, is the way in which these elite spies you're meant to guide through levels are incapable of satisfactorily incapacitating threats. Taze a guard? Okay. Then leave him on the ground, gun and all. No, they don't have zip ties or knives in the future, and your elite spies don't know how to snap a neck. By the end of missions, you're invariably stuck on tiny maps with convoluted layouts and 10+ guards running around hunting for you as the "level entropy" rapidly increases, some of them the same rent-a-cops you've been forced to taze 2-3 times by that point. And then all your agents get killed by those same rent-a-cops you've tazed multiple times, and that any elite spy with a functioning brain would've either killed or tied up, gagged, and stashed under a desk or in an air vent.
Edit: I'll add another thing: the room layouts. I get that it's procedurally generated, but, unfortunately, not in any way that makes thematic sense. These are meant to be corporate offices, yet judging by the way these rooms are laid out, only schizophrenics are allowed to be architects or interior designers in the future. It's nothing but a mad jumble of squares populated randomly by furniture or game objectives. This would make sense if we were crawling through Undermountain looking for orcs, but corporations today, and probably 60 years from now, when the game takes place, are not going to be hiring Halaster the Mad for their interior designer.
This total disconnect from even the remotest semblance of verisimilitude might be understandable in a new developer, but Klei is hardly new to making stealth games. Mark of The Ninja, in fact, is one of my favourite games. It
that the same people who made that gem are responsible for this near-perfect train wreck, but train wreck none the less. It's torture seeing a game so close to perfection and greatness get turned into unplayable garbage by something so small, and something that could've been caught had the developers taken a more objective look at their own game as it grew instead of adapting to dysfunctional systems and growing unconscious of the blind spots created by their own habits.
Sadly, this is another title that leads me to believe that Klei, in spite of coming up with quite a few excellent ideas, is a one hit wonder when it comes to coherent and harmonious implementation of holistic game systems. Don't Starve has a crippling flaw that renders it unplayable due to its terrible inventory system, and Incognita similarly has a crippling flaw in the way it emphasizes arbitrary puzzle nonsense over even remotely realistically represented stealth, espionage, tactics, and all that good stuff.
Edit2: And a moderator banned me from the Invisible Inc forums and locked my thread discussing these topics. I guess that's how Klei deals with criticism of their perfect award-winning games. Hope you're comfortable in your echo chamber, fellas.

This game combines the gameplay of Deus Ex: Human Revolution with the a modenr spy thriller.
Just don't expect an open world to explore.
The narrative of the game adjust to your playstyle.
Be a rambo and shoot everything in sight? The npcs will notice.
Be stealth expert that leaves no bodycount. They will note that too.
Every NPC has his/her unique personality and will react differently wether you are a rambo or ninja.
The gameplay itself is solid if nothing spectecular. Cover-based stealth and shooting with a few ME2 style abilites.
Really, the moments where the game shines are the character interactions and story moments.
You are pushed into your personal James Bond movie (or Jason Borne, or Jack Bauer) where everyone has ulterior motives and you can never be sure who to trust or who a decision early on might come back to bite you.
And it is all about the decisions. The game keeps track and let the wrong/right person live or die and there will be repercussions. But that is not a bad thing. There are no "right" or "wrong" actions only consequences and it is up to you to manipulate them to your whims.
You can try to play nice with everyone or just keep mashing thier berserk buttons to get the results you want.
Tl;dr version. If you loved DE:HR, you will like this game, if only for the strong narrative full of intrigue and back-stabbing.

That dots above this text shows how speechless I am about this game. The game's screenshots is so unconvincing and looks like nothing more but another dirt cheap indie game (I bought it when it was around ~US$0.17 on my rates), but it REALLY has more than meets the eye.
Gameplay wise, there's nothing new about this game. It's basically place towers to shoot 3D shapes down before they reach their destination. You'll start with a single, unupgradeable tower and some money to build a few of them. You'll have to progress just with that. As you shoot more of these shapes you'll gain XP, unlocking new towers and upgrade levels for the towers, just like Bloons (in fact, the whole game feels like Bloons).
What makes this game unique and nauseating at the same time is that the map is 3D taken to literal levels. Enemies can move through planes just as long as there's road on the cube's sides and so your tower placements (as long as there's deployment zone). You'll need imagination and decent visual interpretation to make your perfect defense, as deployment zone's arcs will affect wheter the turrets can shoot them or not (the turrets can only shoot in half-ball area). You can also build turret platforms to build more towers (of course), greatly enhancing numbers of creation possibilities (feel free to use the screenshots as an example or maybe, spark some ideas).
For the sounds, the SFX's are rather generic (especially the firing sounds) but the music sounds rather kickass, and somehow fits the futuristic feel of the game (even though it isn't, I mean why there's such structure in the space in the first place?).
Visually, there's possibly nothing to say. It's just cubes, pyramids, balls, simplistic to say the least. The amount of health the object have is based on it's color. That's it, nothing else. Even the options only give you options for toggling fullscreen and audio volumes.
Worth one buck? Well if you like old school TDs with 3D twist, then this game is really worth it. Just beware, the learning curve is not for the faint of heart.
Pros:
- Co-op (if you have friends to play with)
- Old school TD experience with massive design possibilities.
- Techno music.
Cons:
- Confusing and nauseating map layouts (takes a while to get used to).

If you liked the original, you'll like this game. They've pretty much taken what was good in Shadow of Mordor and expanded upon it while adding quite a few neat features. The Nemesis difficulty (this games version of Hard) makes every fight an actual challenge which I think was one of the few pitfalls of the last game.
Game looks pretty, haven't run into any game breaking bugs (though the AI can be a bit goofy at times and make questionable choices.) The new equipment system feels fine, getting a new sword or bow isn't quite as exciting as I'd like, but there is enough there that it feels satisfying when I get an upgrade. If I were a min-max sort of player the special effects on each armor and weapon could probably lead to some interesting playstyles but I can't be bothered to put that much effort into it.
The Nemesis system itself is really cool. Its a bit more light-hearted at times with a lot more cheesy uruk personality types, but its not enough that I feel my immersion breaking.
If you are a hardcore lord of the rings fan... well lets just say they play fast and loose with a lot of the lore. That doesn't bother me at all, but I can imagine at least a few LotR nerds are gonna be writing sternly worded tweets towards monolith as they get into this game.
and much as I hate to wade in on microtransactions as it's been talked about to death, I suppose it needs to be included in here. The loot chest are obnoxious, there's not real way around that. I didn't like the idea of getting an orc out of a chest when they first announced it, and it feels just as odd and immersion breaking when I'm playing.
That said, you do not in any way need to get them. I've played through just fine never once touching the loot chest system and not felt at any point that I needed to buy them in order to progress in the game. And if you feel so inclined to buy them, they give you plenty of in-game currency so you don't really need to throw any actual money towards it.
Again, not once have I felt I needed to go buy loot boxes, and even if I had I have plenty of in-game currently and could just use that instead of my actual wallet. They're dumb but entirely ignorable.

Nuclear Throne is a game that I admire for its execution and its unflinching vision for itself--a punishing rogue-like, action RPG with bullet-hell (or, depending on your play style, cover based shooter) elements. I objectively think Nuclear Throne is a great game and deserves to be played--it's just not a game that I particularly enjoyed, so I'm saying it's a Not Recommend if you think that brutal difficulty and repetition aren't exactly your thing.
The best way to show my problem with Nuclear Throne is via numbers: With 21 hours, 32 minutes played, I've unlocked 7/12 characters, unlocked 22% of the game, and gotten as far as the third boss (Lil Hunter), whom I've never beaten. I've died 219 times and never finished a run. This means that I've played the same exact 3 or 4 starting levels almost every single one of those 219 times, killing the same ~3 enemy types per level. Sometimes I get farther, but I always have to play through those levels.
Even with the well-designed, different characters, this repetition starts wearing thin. I'm really sick of these opening levels. This problem is exacerbated by how easily death ends a run. A slight misestimation of a bullet's trajectory, an accidental bump into a hidden enemy, poking your head out at exactly the wrong moment--one misstep and suddenly you're back at 1-1.
The action is fast-paced and frenetic, and, when it hits a rhythm, Nuclear Throng can be fun. But, even as someone who enjoys really difficult games and loves rogue-likes (FTL is one of my favorite and most played games of all time), Nuclear Throne isn't for me--something I realized somewhere between my first aggravating death and my 219th.

This is a very good game indeed. It does a marvellous job in telling a convincing story, and it gives you the felling to be part of a unique setting. This is not done by a large amount of cutscenes or - worse - voice-overs, no: the game manages to give you the feeling to be the protagonist in a good, and scary, movie. Everything in this game is polished to - almost - perfection, but most impressive is the way in which Alan Wake succeeds in drawing you into the story and the setting. After sometime, you feel like being Alan Wake, and like living his story.
Very impressive is the way light is used in a dark setting, both as a weapon against the "dark presence" and as a safeheaven. Sometimes, you are so overwhelmed by enemies, the only valuable option is just to run for the nearest lightpost - which happily double as saving-points.
Ok, there are some shortcomings: the difficulty can be a bit frustrating at times, but the story drives you further because you really want to know how things develop. The frightening part is sometimes a bit predictable, but still makes you jump a lot of times. Even during a second playthrough, I found myself being scared quite often, which is a rare thing in these kind of games. Worst: the camera angle is very weird, one has the feeling of walking not in a straight line forward, but after an hour or so, also this gets used to. Still, this could have been done better and is the only indication of the pc-version being a port from the consoles-version. Graphics happily can be tweaked to everyone's liking, so that this game can also run on a less powerful system. Still, it was one of the first games ever being optimalised for quad-core processors, but I only own a dual core, so I can't tell if this gives a noticable performance difference. On my 6-years' old rig (Core 2 Duo 2,66 Mhz & Radeon HD 5850) it runs very smooth indeed on completely maxed out settings.
Graphics are very fine for a game of some years ago, and the sound is simply perfect. One very important thing: play this one in a dark room at night and set the brightness in the options as low as possible, since the light-dark contrast is an esssential part of the game. It will manage to make you jump quite some time!
And o yeah - the two DLC's are masterfull, sometimes even better than the main game. So be sure to get them, they're worth it.

Overall: 85/100

I grabbed the amazing Humble Bundle deal just to get this and believe me, it was the best $12 I ever spent.
-Sprites are dead easy to create, and the animated preview window is a godsend.
-I can make decent RPG Maker Ace faces with this programme, unlike the hilariously ugly ones in the default Ace generator.
-Tutorials are easy to follow, although it might take a while to get the hang of Move Pixels and Move Frames.
-Instant hair and clothing recolours in just a few clicks!
-Easy zoom in and out feature, which is essential when you're dealing with tiny sprites.
-Pixel editing feature that allow you to make changes to existing sprites.
-I don't use RPG Maker XP as much, but I've tested the tileset feature and it is serviceable.
-Ability to add your own generator parts and choose the frames needed, although sometimes it doesn't work.

Just takes two minutes of dragging and dropping.
: Get it! I can never be an artist but this tool allows me to create a decent sprite in five minutes. Valuable money and time saver.

Wow... I didn't think I was going to beat this mission. Barely recovered another MIA agent.. Was only able to hack the turret providing overwatch to the entry to the interrogation room, to neutralize the lethal threat, before moving in. Had to leave surveillance cameras active in order to have the remaining power to break open holding cells. Brought maximum security alert up pretty quick.
Through a combination of using the turret (until it ran out of ammo), hiding under cover, intentionally catching the attention of the cameras for distraction, and carefully placing an unconscious guard as a lure, we managed to get out of a cornered situation in the interrogation room and evade the elite guards and heavy security closing in on us. After 10+ terrifying turns at maximum alert, we reached the exit. It helped that I left 1 agent out in the other rooms to act as eyes and a decoy while the other 2 broke into the interrogation room.
There were a couple really close calls too with agents tossing what few stun weapons we had between each other when we were almost overrun. Only one of our weapons was able to penetrate light armor, and nothing we had could have dealt with the heavy security. Cleanup cost us a bit with 2 destroyed turrets and 4 dead security guards, but got the whole team out alive. Only missed one safe. Made me feel like a total badass when I had all 4 agents assembled in the escape room.
But never again do I want to put my team in that situation.
I had to think about it beforehand, knowing through early scouting that I'd have to trigger high security to make it into that room. I seriously considered aborting the mission for the first time. Figured rescuing an agent outweighed the risk.
AND there were 2 surprises (stationary guards in highly inconvenient places) that I could have only known about after committing to infiltration. Did I mention I took a huge risk...? 3 surprises, actually, if you count not knowing who I was breaking out of there until we made it to the holding cells.
Turned out the captive was Central's bodyguard/head of security, so it really helped that she knew hand-to-hand combat during one of those close calls. If it had been some kid the corp picked up off the street for ticking them off (which has happened), he would have been enough baggage to be left behind or even lose two of my agents.
Still coming down off the adrenaline 25 minutes later.
Do I recommend this game? Hell to the mother f***ing yes, I do.
