Roguelikes have to be my favorite kind of game, and Nuclear Throne happens to be masterfully made to be a nearly perfect roguelike. I've played my fair share of roguelikes, more than what my Steam profile may tell you, and I have to say this is goddamn near the best one. In the aspect of gameplay and intensity, this is certainly the highest ranking roguelike in my opinion, yet I find myself playing more Binding of Isaac sheerly because there's no way to tell what kind of crazy stuff will happen next. Nuclear Throne is more of a straightforward roguelike, there aren't many "crazy" things that can happen except for a few secrets that you might accidentally encounter, but it still stands to be intense and engaging in its gameplay. Another thing to mention is that most roguelikes have some kind of ending to the game, yet this does not. Sure, it may have a "final" boss, but the game still progresses afterwards and greets you with a few more new bosses on top of stronger incantations of older bosses. The fact that this game never ends, just keeps going and going for as long as you can survive, makes it kind of feel arcade-style, and it makes you want to keep practicing to keep going. So where Nuclear Throne doesn't have as much of a randomness aspect as The Binding of Isaac, it makes up for it by constantly challenging you, no matter how good you are at the game.

My level of entertainment achieved from singleplayer games is so low that I tell people that "I do not play singleplayer games". That said, I don't really know how to go about 'reviewing' this one. I'm just gonna ramble, and you're just gonna read, okay? Good.
It has been many years since I've found a non-multiplayer game that has decent level design and good story, let alone one that doesn't feel like youre fighting repetitive, dull enemies in a completely bland setting. This game is the contrary in its entirety.
The story is so good that it is publishable - I would buy the book, truly! The maps are designed in a way that you actually feel like you're progressing. The enemies aren't anything to write home about, but it definitely didn't let the overall experience down at all.
Voice acting is ace, and so is the soundtrack. I didn't notice any annoying sound effects or anything else I usually complain about in single player games. The cinematics feel like they are professionally directed.
Graphics are suprisingly good and the lighting is second to none. Being what I originally thought was a console-exclusive, the controls are actually ... perfect? I have never felt so comfortable playing a third person perspective with a mouse and keyboard. I'd love to see these controls in a multiplayer shooter.
The camera can be dodgy at times (due to its position over the shoulder, making jumps feel a little awkward if not thought about for a brief moment before attempting), though it greatly makes up for it by keeping the cinematic feel.
As for the story, I will admit that if I stopped playing during the tutorial, or perhaps soon after, I may not have come back to it. But, having gone that little bit further and then started being engaged by the plot, boy am I glad I did keep playing. ...I really want to yap on about the story - it is, afterall, the best part - but I wouldn't want to risk spoiling it.
This game could have a position as one of my top ten favourite games, or at least 'most well-made games'.
Do not overlook this title.

While the software itself and its assets are great, there is a huge problem with the license of its contents.
I purchased this software because it said we could use its results for our 2D games. Unfortunately, and to my knowledge it is still unclear to non-users willing to purchase, the software as of now only authorizes usage of its contents for "RPG Maker".
What does that mean?
It means that you won't be able to use Character Hub production for your 2D Games, not in any way.
At least if you are not a pixel art designer. And if you are a pixel art designer, I wonder what use could be Character Hub to you as you would combine your tiles and sprites on Photoshop for about the same results.

The game descriptiom says that "the elements found in the program should work with other 2D game engines as well." As of now it adds that "RPG Maker assets are for RPG Maker use only". But even some months after, the software only contains assets from RPG Maker! This means that you cannot use it in any game of yours, unless you make a RPG-Maker-RPG. I've googled for other 2D resources for Character Hub to no avail. If you know any legal resource library that we may use for our own games (and not something restrictive like RPG Maker), please tell!

The software should be renamed as "Character Hub for RPG Maker" ; as of now, although a very nicely made software, it ends almost as a scam for programmers willing to use it for their own games. It's very unfortunate as I am sure Character Hub programmer, an indie, has worked on this software, but it needs clarification and efforts to get some license-free resources.

This game is sorely underrated. While the combat can, indeed, feel kind of strange as you play it -- it's far from broken (Well... barring certain late-game abilities, some of which are insanely overpowered). Gameplay wise, there is little that separates this game from any other third person military shooter with stealth elements.
However, what makes this game stand out from the bunch -- and earn my approval, is how reactive the game's story is. Every action has consequences that you will have to deal with later -- for better or for worse. Got spotted trying to bug that outpost? Good work, extra security to deal with on this next mission. Chose not to put a bullet in that person's brain? Hey! They want to be your friend and will repeatedly come to your aid in the future! Tell that person to die in a woodchipper? They may take offense to that and might try to add a second mouth where your neck is!
The story is full of interesting characters, some definitely more memorable than others. Obsidian is very talented at writing up gray moral choice systems -- That's a choice system where every option is painful in some way, not necessarily one where your character is a terrible human being. If you are an aspiring game writer, I recommend you brand that onto your flesh somewhere so you can never forget that, and maybe we will have less games like The Last of Us.
I also get the feeling that those that call the combat broken might have been people who never added enough skill-points into their respective weapons skills. See, that's something you need to note; if you have 2 pistol upgrades in the game, you're not going to be very good at using your pistol! It's almost like you need to make a specialized character or something!
The game is underrated, and I do recommend giving it a try whenever possible. It's not a perfect game, but it's a very interesting game nevertheless -- and it definitely tried to impress in the roleplaying and storylines. The effort is noticeable and I can applaud it for that alone.

Executive Assault is an interesting early access RTS/FPS concept. It is a game about strategy, resource management, and teamwork. It is currently in early access but is frequently updated and has amazing potential. The game is probably 1000000% more fun with a friend, whether you are playing against each other or fighting it out together against a surprisingly tough and competent AI.
You have a large tech tree to experiment and explore inside and you have many routes to choose as far as strategies and army compisition goes. You can "research" different units such as aircrafts, tanks, mechs, or just upgrade you standard infantry. The goal of the game is to kill the enemy "companies'" CEO, who is housed in a tower at the center of the base. Oh, and the attention to detail is also quite surprising. When looking at the structures consisting of your base, you can switch to "internal view" and watch as your army of clanking robots is constructed or as your legion of tanks is assembled.
One of the defining features of this game is the ability to take control of nearly any unit and join the fight instead of sitting back and watching your army sweep the map. This can be very advantageous because you can essentially "snipe" enemy units with a footsoldier or tank from distance.
The game, however entertaining, isnt perfect. Being that it is an early access title, you will run into your fair share of bugs and just things that havent been fully made yet, like meteors containing valuable resources cascading and crashing just out of reach on the peak of a mountain or the fact that every weapon has unlimited ammo (which for all I know, could be intended, but it just seems weird). There are other strange and annoying quirks like the fact that the second your robots destroy a wall on the inside of another companies base, the AI can just immediately construct a new one before you pass through
The map selection, however sparse, is very diverse. You can wage war on the surface of a frozen tundra with a mountain seperating the map into quarters or attack the enemy on a sandy plane in the middle of a desolate desert planet. Like I mentioned earlier, the game has unrivaled potential as far as early access RTS titles goes and is definitely worth the small 13 dollar price tag. If you and your friends are looking for a unique early access game that you can play together and sink lots of hours into, you dont get much better than Executive Assault.

Executive Assault, a well thought out and cleverly designed indie game, is one of the "diamonds in the rough". Executive Assault is one of my favorites on Steam, and my favorite RTS by far. Although the game doesnt have a huge player base due to its early development state and lack of media attention, it has incredible potential for a massive, devoted, creative playerbase.
"What is it?":
Executive Assault is an FPS/RTS conversion with a 2-4 player match mode. The player researches "Techs" which allow him/her to build new buildings, upgrade their units, and create new units. The goal of each match is to kill the opposing team's CEO. The CEO is located at the center of a players base, making it difficult to get to him if the defending player is smart.
Pros:
-The game has a passionate and driven developer
-Executive Assault has a well thought out energy balance system
-Well planned tech tree
-Near endless military compositions/strategies
-Fun with or without friends
-Draws the player in/captivation
Cons:
-Not fully developed yet
-Potential for more variety/even more techs + maps
"Why should I buy it?/Conclusion":
All in all, Executive Assault is a fun rts/fps with a very well balanced game for alpha thus far. Executive Assault has a very well thought out system and surprisingly detailed world. Executive Assault raises the bar for not only Indie games, but the RTS genre as well.
2016 Steam award nomination for best RTS/FPS hybrid (by me)

When creating an RPG, one of the most important things are the characters.  While RPG making tools often come with their own standard characters, it can really set a game apart if the game uses custom designed characters.  But, for those of us like me who lack the ability to create custom character portraits and character sprites, Game Character Hub is a godsend.
Basically, when you start the tool you create a type of character.  Then you pick pieces from the proper character type, select them, and shift their order around, until the character looks right.  The character (or face portrait) is shown in the lower left-hand corner, so you can quickly see what your result looks like.
Once you have a character, you can export it to use in the game or save the particular character, so you can re-load and edit it later.    This is a huge help, in case the character doesn't look exactly right, or if you want to make a similar character later.
And, what if you want a slew of similar characters?  Say you want a lot of minor NPCs that look just a bit different?  Game Character Hub has you covered there.  With one special Export command, you can create dozens or hundreds of characters (or faces) which vary in color (such as hair color, eye color, clothing color), all from a single template.  This is a great way to fill in the roster of minor NPCs, very quickly.
Overall, it's an invaluable tool for character creation and I highly recommend it.

Invisible Inc.
What is there to say about it?
Hm, well, that's the question.
Invisible Inc is often described as roguelike, or in the words of TotalBiscuit "Rogue-Lite". Unless you're playing on a custom difficulty to unwind, expect to die A LOT.
Let's break this down, then.
Story;
Invisible Inc has an incredibly short story, but still a fun one to watch, with 2 very nicely animated cutscenes that to me at least felt reminiscent of The Incredibles. Its cast of characters are fairly fun, for what we get to learn of them. Central in particular has to be the best in the game - not only does she have the best voice, but you also feel for her plight and genuinely feel scolded for letting agents die.
Gameplay:
Being a turn-based stealth strategy game, things will go wrong, a LOT. Often resulting in death. Fortunately there is a "rewind" option which allows you to go back to the beginning of the previous turn. Of course, while this is useful, barring custom mode, your Rewinds are limited and you may have made a mistake much earlier that caused your problems now.
the stealth gameplay is really enjoyable and the combat is simple, and just a little frustrating if you don't have the ability to knock out your enemy before they shoot you, or if you are surrounded.
I would criticise how hard it is to obtain enough money to keep your equipment up to date with the difficulty increase each in-game "day". You'll very quickly find yourself surrounded by armoured guards without armour-piercing weapons while trying to get an extra agent in a detention centre, and that certainly doesn't feel nice.
Similarly, there is a "hacking" feature to change the sides of security features in the levels such as drones and cameras. This is absolutely vital for you to maintain a stealthy approach. However, in an endless mode, even on super-easy difficulty settings, Daemons (programs that activate upon hacking, none of which have positive effects) will begin spawning automatically at the beginning of the level, including one which adds a Daemon into ALL hackable items in the level, severely limiting your ability to do, well, anything.
I do applaud it for punishing killing, however. Though despite this, there have been too many situations where killing EVERYONE is the only way to survive a level.
Also, while the levels are randomly generated, this isn't necessarily a good thing. While it improves replay value, there have been too many situations where the only way to advance is to go through a room with a stationary guard who is watching the only door you can go through, meaning you will have to risk increasing security by killing or KOing him. Bonus negatives if said guard is more armoured than you have the ability to deal with at the time.
Modding:
Currently, there is too little in the modding scene for this game. I would really like to see some modding support for agent creation, items and missions in the future. Right now the only real mods are language packs, which is nice if you speak a different language but that's not really a mod otherwise.
TL;DR:
Great gameplay, nice short story, needs more modding.

After the superb Season 1, which turned out to be one of the most emotional stories I ever experienced, it was going to be hard to raise the bar, understandably.
I felt this season to be a little less impactful, mainly because something like the relationship between Lee and Clementine, which made the bulk of the strength and emotional resonance of Season 1, is not present. Theirs was truly special and made for a magical story. Connection with other characters this time around feels a bit less strong, mainly because there's much more chaos this time, their situation is always dangerous and things change very fast. This actually makes sense in this world, but overall I felt that character development and relationships between characters suffered for it.
That being said, though, there are still all the emotional moments and tough decisions that make you feel your choices very acutely, which is still the main focus of the game. Actually, deciding who to trust, who to follow, what to do is even stronger this time around, as you will be put in the middle of different people and situations and how you choose to interact has different reactions and consequences. Once again, Telltale are masters of the "shades of grey" in regards to every character and dialogue, nothing is linear and obvious, making the experience very engaging. There's also a few different endings this time around, which are interesting to explore and make it so your late game decisions do really have consequences.
The main take away from this season, though, was Clementine: how much she grows in every way as she shifts from being a little girl in understandable need of protection into the beginnings of a capable, prepared and charismatic person, in spite of being only 11.
In conclusion, though I felt that this season was slightly less strong than the stellar first one, there are still lots of emotional moments and tough decisions as you'd expect. And watching Clementine develop and go through everything she goes through, mostly bad and difficult, granted, was a delight.

The excellent title from Obsidian Entertainment (the sadly underrated Alpha Protocol), delivers to gamers a uniquely satisfying experience. Alpha Protocol suffers from perhaps two things only - the admittedly horrible combat system, and the "average" quality of the AI. Most video games boast "average" intelligence; this title is no different, and although that wouldn't make much of a difference in the long run, a game which focuses on stealth mechanics should most definitely have decent AI. Now, what Alpha Protocol DOES deliver is in fact an incredibly mature, well-thought, and gritty story interspersed with above average scripts (some good, some bad); memorable characters, locations, interactions, story pathing, and a decent upgrade system. What makes this game essentially worthwhile though, is the character networking, the scripting. Relationships matter, and the dialogue flows like a good spy thriller. The relationships one makes in the game directly influences the end game conclusion, and it's a most satisfying experience indeed.
I would recommend Alpha Protocol for both newcomers and the avid afficionado of the genre alike.

Alpha Protocol is an espionage RPG that does a few things pretty well.  The conversation mechanic is pretty good for a  port, and the story was interesting enough to keep me interested through my first playthrough.  Its biggest strength is how flexible the game is regarding your choices and style.  There are consequences to certain choices, to be sure, but none that should make you throw up your hands and reload due to missed content.  The combat and stealth are serviceable--nothing great if you're used to smooth stealth games like the original Splinter Cell trilogy.  I definitely recommend playing with a 360 controller over K+M.
The glaring problem with this console-to-PC port is the HORRENDOUS loading bugs.  They are well-established across multiple operating systems.  If you die, you can either choose "Reload Last Save" with a high liklihood of game-killing bugs or manually choose a save with an approximately 70% chance that you will get a black screen that you must Alt-Tab and close.  This alone leads me to recommend that you get in on a compatible console if you own one or only buy it when deeply discounted.

Ya like Star Wars? Do ya also like Doom? Well how 'bout Doom with Star Wars in it? Sounds good? Ok, have fun.
That's basically all there is to the game, and yet it still pulls it off so well. This game follows the adventures of fan-favorite Kyle Katarn, former Imperial Officer turned Rebel mercenary after learning his father was murdered by the Empire and who, in the expanded universe, was the actual person who stole the Death Star plans. That's what the first mission is about, taking place between Episodes III and IV, just before the takeover of the Tantive IV in A New Hope. The subsequent levels deal with a new threat to the Rebel Alliance and the Galaxy: The Dark Trooper Initiative. Kyle is tasked with finding out what it is and putting a stop to it.
Along the way you'll find familar and not-so-familiar Star Wars weapons, like blaster rifles, thermal detonators, and a big♥♥♥♥♥Dark Trooper weapon that is suposedly too heavy for a human to lift, but, oh well, I guess you can lift it after all.
The sound and graphics are really good for a 1995 DOS game, and the graphics shine in the cutscenes and look pretty fluid. In game it might be a little harder to see enemies from a distance as they dissolve into a mess of pixels, but the game still distinctively looks and sounds like a Star Wars game, as you will hear the familiar sounds of blasers being fired and hear the cries of dying Stormtroopers and Imperial Officers.
In terms of difficulty, this game can be played on easy with a challenge. Not in the form of combat, but in knowing where the hell you're supposed to be going. And the enemies aren't pushovers like in the movies. Stormtroopers will regularly hit you before you can hit them, but there's so much freaking health and shield supplies lying around that the threat of death is rare, and you can pick up extra lives in common enough spaces, so getting a Game Over is pretty rare (and disappointing, because you must suck at this game to get a Game Over.)
Overall, Star Wars Dark Forces is a pretty cool game, but I can't see myself playing this very often. It's not a bad game, far from it, but I can't see myself choosing to play this over Doom very often. I'd still recommend picking this game up though, you won't have a bad time, I swear on my life or may God strike me down.

Terrorhedron is an amazing 3D tower defence game.  Its soundtrack is cool and everything else about the game is also cool.  Basically, there is a track made out of cubes and on it there are many circle shaped platforms.  These platforms can have weapons put on them.  The weapons are all turrets.  Some examples of these weapons are Laser Turrets, EMP Turrets and Photon Pulse Turrets.  These turrets can be upgraded to a maximum of level three (they start off at level one).  Also, when you unlock a new turret or upgrade you usually get a Steam achievement.  There are forty seven achievements in total for the game and twenty one of them come from unlocking turrets and their upgrades.  This is excluding the two achievements for unlocking the four and six face turret platforms.  The rest of the achievements are unlocked when you complete different levels at various difficulties.

Paladins is a really fun game that you should definetly try out if you're into class FPS.
I'm pretty sure everyone already knows what this game is about and why you should get it, after all, it is indeed a really good game, despise all the criticism that comes from different communinites calling it a blatant copy of Overwatch, Team Fortress 2 and etc. In my opinion, in games like this, you need some basic character abilities and features that will be present in nearly every game of the same genre, because you just have to if you want a balanced game, and that's why both games are so similar.
I think Paladins is much better in the competitive side of things than Overwatch is, as you can't swap champions in the middle of the match and need to know when to engage and when to use your ultimate, as it takes longer to charge it and respawns are longer.

High-rez did a bunch of things better than Blizzard did, in my opinion. For example:
- Ranked requirement : Their requirements you need to meet to be able to play Ranked are really great. Unlike in other games where you just need to level up to a certain amount and then you're free to play it, in Paladins, you need to reach mastery level 4 in a variety of characters. That's awesome because it means no more one trick ponies and less and less smurfs.
- Ultimate usage : In this game, you don't necessarily need an ultimate to win a team-fight. The game is not as ult heavy as, let's say, League of Legends is, which means you don't need to hold back from using it when you feel like you should that much.
- Healing mechanic : Healing in Paladins is definetly fun to do and I enjoy playing as a support the most. What makes it stand out from the rest is that, in Paladins, there's this regeneration feature that allows you regain a percentage of your health when you stand out of combat for a few seconds. This mean the support only really has to worry about healing the front liner and the people around the objective and care a little less for the flankers, who can just stay away from combat for a few and heal up by themselves. Definetly a great mechanic!
- The game forces you to play against Bots until you reach a certain level : This is honestly great. High-rez knew a lot of players would jump into Paladins because, well, "Free to play Overwatch!" without necessarily knowing how this kind of game works and how to play it. So they simply force you to play against bots until you understand it better.
- You can swap regions whenever you want and there's no punishing : Wow! I can play with Senna, who's a buddy of mine and plays on EU, even though I'm from South America? This is awesome! Seriously, knowing you can change regions at anytime was one of the deciding factors for me. I don't have many friends from over here that play it, so whenever I do play with someone, they're usually NA or EU, and that's why I like this feature so much.
Now. There are a few things I dislike about Paladins that are hopefully going to changed soon. I think the grinding system in the game is a little too much but it's not that bad for a free to play game and getting all the loadout cards you want early on can sure be tiring. I also don't like how Hi-rez treats the competitive scenarion and wish they gave it more attention, wish they would fix a few things here and there about ranked that would make it better, like having an overall rank score or something to show up on your profile rather than only having individual champion ranks.

Pro/Con (4 days of use on RPG Maker VX ACE)
+Easy to figure out and use without a manual or tutorial
- Library includes only default generator parts already found in existing game library
- Only one brush type with no contrast (pencil)
+Multiple Frame are easy to manage, manipulate, scale, etc
+Multi Frames share layers but can be edited individualy without affecting the same layer in another frame.
-Pressing Hotkey for tools more than once goes back to the previous tool. (Lots of accidental erasing, moving, etc)
-Editing tool are limited (if your used to GIMP or PS capabilites. You will still need a graphics editor for many things.
+Making multiple diffrent emotional faces that fit Frames is insanely easier than making the frames in PS or GIMP
+Magic wand tool works as good in any editor
-Can't find a way to freeform select pixels (only squares and eliptical and magic wand options)
-Rotaiting and resizing pixels pixelates the image to unusable standards (smoothing option helps a bit but still takes away)
OVERALL:
I was disapointed in the intial library included but the fast and on the spot editing it provides within your games frame/pixel size was very easy to work with. Cuting images was a bit difficult without a freeform selection tool but the magic wand and its options eventually did the trick. Using it for the first time I created a 8 Frame Charater Face with multiple emotions in about 3 hours (and that was because I used very detailed and specific changes to the faces). I can now create them in about an hour or less with all the details and changes I want to make using default face images.
I would say this application is worth the money you pay. 8/10

You are thrusted in a game that claims every decision you make will change the destiny of it's inner world. Well for anyone who hasn't played it and is thinking about it let me tell you, it's simply untrue. At the very end of the day there are only two decisions that actively change the course of the plot the rest of your choices mean absolutely nothing.
The story itself is meant to be charming, but lacks charm. The main hero is unimpressionable, meaning without impression. The other characters can actively be described as one demensional, with no other traits then whatever their first impression was. (Ex: "Oh look, ♥♥♥♥♥ is being a ♥♥♥♥♥." "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ remains an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥." "Cutie is still a cutie." Etc.) Max herself never seems to grow past her inability to make any active decisions, and is steered along by the wiles of the world in which she lives, or at least by her ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ friend/potential ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ love interest Chloe tells her what to do, say, feel, and think. And she listens, because she simply can't think for herself. And though she was meant to be a blank slate so that I could project unto her, I have never more actively felt so unrelated to a blank slate character, she works against me rather than for me.
In fact, let me delve furth into Chloe, since it can be argued that Chloe is closer to the main character than Max, since it is her life that the story resolves around.
Chloe is such an unlikable and unrelatable character who actively reminded me of my worst co-dependant relationship, at one point Chloe refuses to take responsibilty for her own actions and demands that others do so, instead. Her character is utterly pretenscious while pretending deep and forelorn from an outsider perspective. She actively abuses Maxine's abilities, and therefore also Maxine seemingly because she is aware Maxine can make everything go away. However, because Maxine rewinds the story, her efforts to allow Chloe to unwind is meaningless because obviously Chloe will not remember and continue to be a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. She actively makes Maxine's life worse, and by extension the player's experience of the game.
She was the sacrifice I made without hesitation. And because of this, I felt robbed of the supposed "deepness" of her death, instead I felt glad to be rid of her, and only sad that the storyline did not continue without her. She is the only thing keeping the story moving forward, but also the only thing stopping the story from being greater than what it is.
Life Is Strange is better as a concept of a game, than an actual game, itself. The ability to rewind time should make the player to feel as though possibilities are endless, and you can do anything, but the way it was built around the Chloe as a character only cemented that it would lead nowhere, effectively making the player's time and effort worthless.

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ After five minutes, I thought I'd be up all night finishing this game in one sitting. After about two hours, I've finished episode one.
First of all, this game is chunked into very conveniently-sized episodes. Just like on TV, the beginning of each episode is a recap. Nice touch. So that's awesome. It's got a built-in play timer. I play one episode, then I put it down.
I don't know why, but I'm really into horror games recently, and I'm really enjoying this one. I was expecting a Doom-style hack-em-up, but this is actually a well-built game with a great story. It's like something Stephen King would write if he was more concerned with writing good fiction than with making lots of money.
The controls take a little getting used to (aiming is a crapshoot, but that makes sense in context), but they do what they're supposed to do. The one issue I have is that this is the absolute worst impementation of the over-the-shoulder POV I've ever played. Having said that, it didn't take me all of episode one to get used to it.
Until you play for about twenty minutes, it's really difficult to get Alan to walk where you want him to walk. Most of the time, you have to point the camera where you want to go and Alan runs that way. Unless you're (for example) trying to cross a river by walking across a fallen log. Then you have to pay very close attention to the fact that Alan is actually standing in the extreme corner of your screen, and not dead center.
It's a bit of a hassle, but thinking back I bet it's intentionally off-putting, just to make the game feel a little bit more unsettling. And this game is very unsettling. Dead Space had zombies jumping out at you, but after a while that just got boring. This is walking in the woods at night with a flashlight and a gun.
If you're at all interested in the horror genre, this is one to play. There's just enough mindless violence to keep the XBros interested, but this game really is all about the storytelling and cinematography.
And I haven't even mentioned the graphics. Really a good-looking game, which just makes the ambience that much more ambient. I can't run it at full-tilt, but even on my old Radeon HD 3850 (at mediocre settings), this thing looks great. One must wonder why games like Sacred 2 and Marvel Heroes (both completely unplayable due to graphic slowdown) can't run as well on the same hardware.

tl;dr:
Amazing game.
Pros:
+Religious Victory
+Each AI has 'historical' preferences for allies
+City Structure (each tile has a purpose instead of putting everything in the center)
+Modability (in fact mods can fix almost all of the cons)
Cons:
-Historical Innacuracy of Civolopedia (not a big deal since it is rarely used anyway, and easily remedied by mods)
-Troop Promotion Tree (I like keeping the same scout from the dawn of time and keep leveling him.  The level cap here is low, and many promotions are not that great)
-Lack of random events (earthquakes, good crop yields, plagues, bull markets, etc)
Long Version:
This game is amazing.  The scale is epic (you start with a gew cave men in the stone age and build them up to a full blown civilization in the information era).  It seems as though in this alternate world, no one ever dies of old age (can still be killed by battle/starvation though).  That adds an interesting dynamic (the same ruler in 4000 BC is still present in 2050 AD, and that scout trained in 3000 AD may still be alive 5 millenia later, learning new stuff).  Although on that note, for people who can never die of old age, the level cap is kind of low (there was a mod I had in Civ V that could have that 5k year old scout have 25+ different promotions by the end of the game).
The AI can be a bit silly, but some times that can make it more entertaining than annoying.  Each ruler now has a 'type' of ruler that it will lean towards (Catherine de Medici likes people how are good at spycraft, where as Jadwiga likes rulers who produce a lot of faith).  This is a really nice tough, IMO.
I (personally) like the way religion is handled here, compared with Civ V, although many of the 'historical' footnotes are a bit off and have a decidedly anti-christian feel (see note 1).  There is even a religious victory (although it replaces the diplomatic victory which I also enjoyed in Civ V).
Instead of having one tile represent all of the buildings in the city, the buildings are now spread out between 'districts'.  Each district takes up a tile (including the city center) and building are built in corresponding districts.  This allows much more diversity between cities and allows better specialization than prior games where each city just had every building built in it.
One thing I would like to see is new civilizations spawning throughout the game (it sounds similar to something being added in the expansion though so I am looking forward to that).  This would make the game far more dynamic.
Another thing that would be nice is the addition of 'random events'.  For example, one turn you may have a flood, and that could lead to a good harvest the next turn.  I would think this could be modded in, but have not seen anyone do so yet.
Footnote:
1.) The Catholic Church description ends with "A bit of a shift from the days when it burned heretics and most everyone else9 who differed from Catholic dogma.", refering to a time period which never existed.  While there were instances of hereitcs being burned at the stake (mostly by secular governments without consent of The Church).  The ignore any reference to The Catholic Church being the originators of most universities and the (at the time) bizarre idea that educating non-nobles was a worthwile endeavor, or it's dedication to feeding/housing/clothing the poor, etc.  There are several other examples, but I feel like I've already dedicated too much space to this one note (besides as with most of the cons, this is very easily corrected by a mod and can be an interesting history project to do so).

After I watched Jerma and Star, I was amazed by the concept. A Command and Conquer type of game (boy, the developer must be getting sick of hearing this comparison)  mixed with a FPS element.
Now, I don't really review games much; however, I hate seeing shortassed reviews so get ready for a pretty long but
review. I will also try to keep it entertaining.
I will try format this review very well, so you can read the entire thing or skip to the interesting bits. (Steam formatting sucks.)
Let's begin.
In Executive Assault, you play a rich corporate snob, whom wants to get rid of the competing capitalistic swine on the other side of the map.
Now usually in a our world's economy, one would try to do this by running his golf buddy out of business. In this game however, the businessmen strategy that will be in practice is filling your competitor with a variety of destructive matter.
Which may include: Lasers, Quantum Particles, Rockets, Shells, Bullets.
The game is won when the enemy executive takes damage. The only way to reach the enemy executive is to power your self through the buildings go up the elevator of the HQ and do what I said above.
Usually in games you ( or subjectively I ) will not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the people involved and probably skip the credits. In this game on the other hand it is worth to note the developer(s).
This game was directed by
, the programming was done by
, the graphic design were made by
, and the sound effects were also made by
.
You start the game with your company's headquarters which you can build around.
Like most RTS games you will probably start with setting up a main power grid which you do by building a power plant.
Once you have that ticked off of your check list, you will want to start your economy.
There are three types of resources in the game.
, which you get by building iron extractors on iron fields. You will need this to build basically anything.
, which generate after researching the Trion Generator. You will need this to build unique Trion weapons.
and
, which you can pick up from crashed in meteorites. You will need this to build advanced units.
One thing to note is, that your iron extractors need to be connected to the power plant. You can do this by building a chain of pylons.
If you reached your power generation capacity you can collect Thorium crystals that are spread over the map with drones which increase generation.
To boost research you collect Calcit Crystals.
This game was pretty much just released for early access. So it does not have a huge amount of units, but neither does it have a small amount. All your units can be equipped different kind of weapons which can be researched in the research tab.
There is basic infantry which till now only consists of one type of drones with different armor.
(Also you can build a single invisible hacker drone which can overload the enemy power plant, blowing it up and it can disable enemy defenses)
There are vehicles.
Light Jeeps.
Two different tanks medium and heavy.
And light, medium and gigantic walkers.
(The gigantic walker can make your units ♥♥♥♥ing fly OUT of the map if you get kicked by it in first person. It's hysterical)
There is also aircraft.
One Fighter, one transport pickup, and two bombers.
I will not talk about every building as that would be too time consuming for you and me.
All major buildings must be connected to the HQ, and are made almost instantly. (For now, they also seem to be virtually  indestructible) the  The only exception being the pylon and iron extractor which are made by drones. There is also a limited building area for major buildings that can not be extended.
There are also defense buildings which can be build in the limit area but they do not have to be connected to the main buildings.
There are production buildings for each respective type of unit, there are buildings that allow you to have security (will talk about that later), research, radar, artillery/missiles, and other useful things.
Too keep it short, you can research a lot of things in this game. There are many research tree that upgrade your units, unlock more of 'em, allow you to build more advanced buildings, give you more power. Etc.
You can speed up research by collecting calcite crystals (it's basically ♥♥♥♥ing chalk).
There are plenty types of defenses, most importantly different types of gates, which you can build inside of buildings to prolong the time the enemy takes to get to your executive. Inside you can also build an alarm, which is pretty handy to know if someone is sneaking around in your main base. There are turrets you can build outside and inside. Which can also be pretty handy, and walls outside which I have not build because of the building area being to small for it to be worth it.
This developer has humor, not too much, but still has funny little tweaks to make at least you chuckle. Like the Gigatron's pilot having a cocktail.
I don't want to ruin it for you, but for example when you ride the elevator up to brutally slaughter the enemy executive, some classy elevator music is playing. Also the summer sale trailer is genius.
There are some things the game can improve on, this is entirely subjective though, so don't take my suggestions as absolute ( I have also might have missed a few things). Of course it will be fair criticism as once again, this is made by one guy so I will only talk about game play.

Main enemy buildings can not be destroyed, at least from my experience. This is simply stupid. Now of course I do not mean that the buildings should be destroyable from the outside, neither do I think the HQ should be destroyable, but there should be a spot which you should be able to destroy the building from. Star Wars: Dark Forces is perhaps the most faithful adaptation of a property from one medium to another that I've ever seen. For lack of a better term, it
almost exactly like Star Wars, from the style of the environments to the witty banter between characters to the sound effects to the kid-friendly violence. The stormtroopers, in particular, are pitch-perfect, yelling "Hey! Stop!" and the like at you before getting shot and melodramatically falling over. It perfectly captures the original films' sense of breezy, fun adventure that gets tense at times, but appropriately so, and never enough to kill the fast pace and pure enjoyment.
Aping the style of the original Star Wars films is all well and good, but Dark Forces manages to be a solid game as well. Old-School FPS is a great genre, as wel as perfect for capturing the tone discussed above, and Dark Forces pulls it off particularly well. The gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, the weapon variety is excellent, the difficulty scales well, the enemies are diverse and most fill their niches admirably, and the levels are generally easy to understand and navigate, although occasionally they slip into maziness. There are also puzzles that actually require some thought, but at the same time are intuitive to solve (think of Half-Life's Blast Pit). The story also deserves mention, as it's good by current game standards and fantastic by 90s game ones. Before each mission, you're treated to a briefing that tells you what you're doing and why you're doing it, as well as how it connects to the overarching story, which is always good. In addition, there are some barely-animated but well-acted cutscenes that further the plot. It's an enticing package.
Dark Forces also has some never-before-seen (at the time) technical features that were important to the evolution of FPS as we know them today, including a jump button, a crouch feature, fall damage (for better or for worse), and multiple layers in one level— not the way Marathon has, but instead simply starting a new map whenever the player reaches a certain point, such as the top of an elevator. This simple solution would be the workaround of choice for 2.5D games for years.
However, Star Wars: Dark Forces has a few detrimental design decisions which relegate it from 'all-time classic' to 'flawed masterpiece'. Some of its weapons and enemies are superfluous (Why are there two different rapid-fire weapons that seem to do the exact same damage and fire at the exact same rate, especially if one is more accurate? Why does that more accurate weapon share an ammo pool with a weapon that also seems to do the same damage, but fires far more slowly? Also, I can understand that there might be two basic-level enemies that only practically differ in firing rate and amount of health, but why three?), and the two bosses seem to die far too easily. There're also what appear to be infinitely respawning enemies at some points, and though it's not excessive enough to be a major issue, it's a fundamentally bad decision in a game with finite resources. The levels, as mentioned above, sometimes get a bit too mazelike, and occasionally there's some really unintuitive♥♥♥♥♥♥going on regarding where to go and which buttons to press that requires help from a walkthrough.
However, the greatest problem that Dark Forces has, the one that almost kills the entire game at times, is regarding saves. There aren't any. Instead, each level you are allotted three respawns (plus an bonus one or two each level if you can find them). Once you die, you are sent back to the last invisible checkpoint with one less respawn and 100% health and shields. However, all enemies that you killed and objectives that you completed remain dead/completed. When you run out of respawns, you have to start the level over. Some may not have a problem with this system, but I felt almost dirty using it, mostly because I couldn't come up with a viable explanation for how this was occurring within the context of the game. I actually refrained from respawning at all during the first few levels, opting to redo the entire level instead. I gave this up after it became too much of a chore during the sixth level, but the uneasiness remained. I may just be weird for disliking the system (although I do believe that quicksaves are objectively better), but I dislike it nonetheless.
Even with its serious problems, though, Star Wars: Dark Forces is an excellent adaptation, a good game, and a veritable barrel of fun. I recommend it highly.

True to Remedy's previous work on Max Payne, the tone of Alan Wake is perfectly balanced, with tongue just slightly enough in-cheek to be funny without undercutting the darker and scarier elements of the story. Gameplay mechanics are solid, and, given that this is a horror game, combat is built to ensure that both flight and fight options are useful in most encounters. Although its a strange thing to say, the best praise I can give to Alan Wake's combat is that it manages to make running away from fights tense and entertaining.

Invisible, Inc. is a turn based strategy game set in a technologically advanced future. Players will control covert agents as they infiltrate high powered corporations to raid high security vaults, steal advanced technology, rescue captured operatives, and download important data.  Along the way the agents will face a myriad of threats like armored corporate security officers, drones, laser walls, and security turrets.
Players take turns against the computer moving their agents through the randomly generated levels, doing their best to stay out of site while they hack security nodes through their cyberspace combat program, Incognito.  Depending on the programs you have loaded determines how you’ll bring down cameras, unlock electronic safes, and take control of camera drones. After each level you’ll spend credits on buying and selling equipment and leveling up your agents’ skills.
Invisible, Inc. plays a lot like Xcom, which I personally love. It’s difficult to put down.  You’ll get so engrossed in completing a level you won’t realize time is passing! Difficulty ramps up at a reasonable pace so you never feel like you’re completely in control.  In fact some levels become downright tense!
Each level has an objective and an exit zone.  You can leave any time you discover the exit, but you’ll want to try and complete your mission first.  There are several factors that make this difficult.  First, there’s a security meter that rises one point every turn.  Every five points raises the security level and will add complications like new guards on patrol, turning on more security cameras, and even pinpointing the location of one of your agents on the map and sending a guard to investigate.
If that wasn’t enough, guards you knock out won’t stay that way forever.  And once they wake up, they will start searching the entire level for you.  Eventually you’ll have access to lethal weapons, but using these can raise the alarm level much faster as almost all security guards are equipped with heart monitors.  Games can get very tense as you try and steer the guards away from the exit so you can make your escape with the 3000 credits you just stole from the corporate vault!
I enjoy how accessible the game is to first time players.  It’s not very difficult to learn and the beginner difficulty (which I recommend everyone play, regardless of your skill level with strategy games) explains all of the features in the game while being forgiving enough to not beat you over the head when you make a mistake.  At higher difficulty levels, the safety net drops away and you’ll find that every mistake can have dire consequences for your team.
Overall, I find Invisible, Inc. to be fun and engaging.  The gameplay is challenging without being unfair. I particular enjoyed the art style, which has a retro feel about it.  After 15+ hours, I feel confident recommending this title to anyone looking for a new turn-based strategy experience.

This sequal is what all sequals should be like, it improves on almost everything in the first game, it adds more things to do, it expands on it's design, It legit lets you have your own orc army and orc body guards.
And the new orc system they have put in place i.e common,epic,legendary is amazing it actually gets you giddy when you find an legendary orc out in the wild or an epic.
The equipment system is much better compared to the rune system of the first game, it adds different types of armors with different types of buffs/effects that can vary based on the grade of equipment i.e common,rare,epic,legendary.
To explain how vast you can change up your play style and what not with this equipment system i'm going to explain how i set up my equipment and how it changes the way i play:
First off i noticed that most captains were susceptible to fire and or poison so i got me an Epic sword that had a 41% chance to poison an enemy upon a critical hit then a chest piece that had 22% chance to cause an enemy to catch fire with any critical hit and debuff any fire damage towards me by 60% and a cloak that boosted my poison damage by 18% plus a bow that if i get a head shot with has a 40% chance ot cause the enemy to catch fire and i do 50% more damage when an enemy is on fire. Playing on Nemesis difficulty it is very effective to check what your enemy's weaknesses are so setting up your equipment based on that is quiet fun.
Fortresses are a hit or miss depending on what you like but i find it fun. You can either capture the normal fortresses and set them up or you can do online conquests where you take on another players fortress (which can be tricky especially on nemesis difficulty and how they set their fortress up and no you don't get to keep their fortress you just earn xp and items and they don't lose anything upon you conquering their fortress)

highly recommend if you liked the original, Shadow of mordor and want to sink more hours into middle earth and the nemesis system.

I hesitate to call KSP a game, though it certainly is a very fun one. It can be so much more. New players will invariably start by trying to launch huge rockets and marveling at the spectacular explosions and destruction. This is marvelous, to be sure, but if you keep at it you'll learn how to get a (probably much smaller) rocket into orbit. Your next step will likely be the moon, quite an achievement to be sure. Well, if you can get to the moon surely you can go to another planet... and so it progresses.
KSP can be a transformative and profoundly educational experience. A common joke in the community is "It isn't rocket science... except it is!" and that is absolutely true. You'll learn real orbital mechanics. Concepts which seem almost magical to others will become relatively simple for you. And all you did was play a "game".
Modern chess.

Kerbal space program... Its exactly what it says on the tin. With a friendly appearence and seriously brave little green men. This game gives you nice easy access into seeing what its really like trying to safely put a man (or in this case Kerbal) into space. The physics are ultra realistic and give a great challenge when trying to escape kerbins atmosphere. When you do there is a great sense of achievement. But you always want more. Now you want to get an orbit, and return. Nail that and its gotta be the mun next. Getting a mun orbit is a nice feeling but actually landing on the mun gives you a sense of pride like no other. Getting home safely isnt easy but rewarding if you get it right. After mun... well take on minmus or go all out to duna or eve.
This game has given me hours of fun, with alot of explosions along the way. The game is more than expansive enough on its own but its alot got a modding community that is surreal. The game itself offers all the parts you require to acheive amazing things but adding the modding communities hard work too and you have a game that takes space program simulation to a whole new level. With mods for bigger and better space planes, rockets that dwarf everything on earth, to intricate bits adding life support to your kerbals and allowing for space stations that can almost build a rocket with luna bases serving as a mining facility to produce fuel on the go.
The only negative ive ever had is that when you get into the large part counts, 800+ on my system the game can get very laggy. I dont know if they will ever be able to change this but unless you want to keep everything you have made from the beginning I tend to just loose the older space station parts ect... that new bigger sections can do with 20 parts instead of 100 meaing the part count can stay low and allow me to expand. Ive yet to successfully land and return from another planet although i do keep trying.
If you have an interest in anything spacey or like to build things to overcome problems, this is a game for you. You dont need a degree in rockets but when you return from your first mun landing you will feel like you already have one.

A glorious flop, Alpha Protocol is a highly ambitious project with great ideas but weak gameplay. Sitting in the Deus Ex genre of rpg-stealth-action-espionage, it offers a customizable protagonist and a game world that reacts to your chosen style of play and personality to present a long, branching storyline where your choices really do matter. Friends might betray you, enemies might become allies, and the plot has plenty of ways it can wrap up. Stealth mechanics are passable and easily broken by overpowered skills, combat is fairly generic, but between plot and player choice and overall style, it creates a distinct sense of immersion and does a fine job really making you feel like a spy. Frustrating at times, but satisfying, it's worth a look if you enjoy a game you can play any way you want to.

A fun an challenging 3D tower defense game.
I didn't think I'd enjoy it quite as much as I do right now, but it really is quite fun to build your own constructs to place towers. Usually I prefer games where I can control the enemies path, although sometimes those kind of games get boring after a while when you know the strengths of your towers and it is simply a matter of how fast can you win instead of "can I win this at all".
Since in this game the path is predefined and can't be altered by anything you do, and the path is 3-dimensional this game presents a challenge. First you have to get around in thinking in 3D when placing towers and finding your kill-zone and then you have to plan ahead of how long you can wait placing new towers in order to be able to buy the expensive but effective ones.
Like most TD not all towers and upgrades are available at first, you have to do a bit of grinding to get to the good stuff. After almost 7 hours I haven't unlocked all possible upgrades yet, but it took me a while to get around this 3D thinking required, so maybe it is possible to get all the content faster.
This game definitely needs a mouse to be played, the camera and controls are a bit confusing at first, but you'll get used to it after a while.
PROS:
+ 3D presents a challenge
+ fun an really addictive game-play
+ towers are built within a second (no waiting time for the tower to be completed)
+ upgrading a tower can be done mid-fight without loosing precious attack-seconds
CONS:
- controls/camera take time to get used to
- no in-game description for upgrades you haven't unlocked yet
- you start out with 100 lives and loose lives whenever you let shapes escape, the amount of lives you loose depends on the kind of shape that manages to get through (still haven't figured out how many lives a certain shape is worth)
Compared to other TD games it doesn't offer quite as much content but still manages to be fun for a couple of rounds. Given that it has less content (maps and towers) than other games priced at 5 bucks. I bought it on sale and I'd recommend you get this when it's around 3 bucks or less, that's the price it's definitely worth.

This game frequently gets compared to the famous
Series. To be honest though, all the two have in common are the graphic engine, the 3rd person view and the fact, that you as a player get to choose the direction of your ingame conversations. Still, the comparison can be made in order to help people decide, if this game might be for them, or not.
While
is a lot more RPG (especially the first game) as it lets you wander around, talk to npcs and aquire quests,
is a bit more linear in its storytelling, since only the order in which you complete your missions and the order of your missionhubs can be determined by the player.
The missions itself are pretty action-oriented, even though you might want to take a stealthy approach from time to time in order to take out a few enemies without being noticed or to move into a more favorable position for your assault. It is possible to put lots of talent points into being 'stealthy' and playing almost exclusively like this, but it has to be said that the game is by no means a
and some direct confrontation especially during the last stages of the game is unavoidable.
Mission locations are quite diversified, while the level design itself is very linear. During your missions you'll receive radio support by your 'handler', who updates you with the latest mission relevant information. In addition, you'll frequently encounter locked doors and password protected computers, which you'll be able to open or hack by beating one of the increasingly difficult mini-games.
The graphics are decent, I especially liked the facial textures of the characters and the depth of field effects. The voice-acting is great, the writing is excellent, as it often offers you funny witty responses in dialogues and also features your expected conspiracy theories and the like.
Another note on the subject of dialogue choices in this game: unlike
, where you get to choose the exact response you want to give and have unlimited time in deciding on which one it is going to be, you can only choose the general tone and direction of your answer in
, while at the same time being forced to make this decision within a few seconds. Responses include 'professional', 'threatening', 'suave', 'flirtatious' or a certain subject you want to touch upon. While initially this system felt irritating, once you get used to it, it feels rather dynamic and natural, since there are no pauses during dialogues and you are forced to make decisions on the fly.
Decisions in this game have a real impact on the main plot aswell, as often you'll have to make meaningful choices between making allies or enemies, life and death or something of similar weight. Characters react differently to your approach during conversations, and since the game keeps track of your standing with each character, I often find myself reading up on a character's personal files before talking to them in order to get a better understanding of what said npc might react most positively to.

Less depth than
, less playtime and less production value - but by no means a bad game. The only thing the game really lacks because of this are the big, breathtaking moments. Nonetheless,
has some pretty memorable scenes (including hook-ups, you perv!) and I am quite satisfied with my first playthrough.
Especially if you like the spy-setting, want something tight and less drawn out and prefer a more action-oriented approach to the genre,
is a must-have.

Alpha Protocol is an interesting TPS developed by Obsidian Entertainment. In order to define its genre I'd say it's an action-RPG. You level up throughout the game which allows you to select from various perks. I, personally, went with pistols as weapon specialisation along with stealth which made my gameplay a lot of fun - I have to admit, though, combat is not exactly refined and the boss battle did not leave much room for stealth which was a disappointment.
Alpha Protocol offers you choices during the dialogues. As opposed to Mass Effect there's no indication whether or not your choices are good (no Paragon and Renegade approach) and interestingly conversations are timed so you need to pick an answer rather quickly. Making the bad decisions can have dire consequences at the end of the game which has some surprises in store for you.
While somewhat mediocre, Alpha Protocol has its exciting moments and those in favour of the genre should pick this up. I believe its metascore of 72/100 is not really justified.

TLDR:
8/10 Great tower defense game
Full Review:
Terrorhedron takes the traditional tower defense formula and adds a twist by having the game utilize three dimensions rather than the traditional two. This is an interesting change to the tower defense formula and adds a new layer of strategy. The other main difference Terrorhedron adds is the ability to build connector blocks to tower locations, meaning you can turn a single tower slot into a defensive megastructure.
The music is great and really adds to the minimalist tech feel that the game provides. The enemies are all colored shapes which change depending on how many hits they can take. Towers are unlocked throughout play at a reasonable pace, I never really felt like I was grinding for a new tower or being given too many options too quickly. You can also upgrade your towers which generally provides them with a new ability rather than just a stat boost, which is great.
I can't think of any real problems with this game. I have been having a ton of fun with Terrorhedron and if you are a fan of tower defense games I think you would too.

A success story out of the infamous Early Access program, I wasn't immediately sold on
The premise seemed experimental in a wrong way: turn-based tactics in the vein of games such as XCOM, but with a focus purely on stealth as opposed to combat. I had been so used to stealth gameplay in real time from games such as Deus Ex, Dishonored, Splinter Cell, and even Bethesda RPGs, that I thought to reduce it to a turn-based system would result in a boring game.
I was extraordinarily happy to find out that I was wrong. After seeing TotalBiscuit's "WTF Is..." video soon after the game left Early Access, I bought the game on launch sale and alpined out of curiosity. At the time of writing, I only have 16 hours put into the game, and have unlocked all of the agents, but I still want to keep playing to try out different strategies and combinations.
There's two layers of gameplay: stealth and hacking. Agents have stats that can be upgraded outside of missions with money heisted from levels, and this money can further be used to purchase much-needed augmentations, items, and even hacking programs for your AI partner, Incognita. She functions as your hacking system, and you use her to unlock safes, lower security grids, take control of cameras and drones, and so on. Killing enemies is almost more of a liability than an asset in the game, but you can knock them out and pin them down to prevent them from regaining consciousness. Levels are procedurally generated, but never get too easy or too hard. Even if an exit and your objective spawn in two rooms adjacent to your spawning area, the objective is almost certain to be heavily guarded to make up for it.
The game encourages multiple playthroughs, with permadeath in place that can cost you your progress. However, since the game is on a timer (which you can customize, along with many, many other features), you'll not be losing much. What you lose would be about comparable to permadeath in FTL, if on default settings. The game's customization allows you to tweak the difficulty to your tastes for leisure or for the ultimate challenge. Each playthrough nets you experience points that unlock new agents or starting programs.
All of this is wrapped up in a beautiful artstyle that brings life into an otherwise bleak world. Unfortunately, there isn't a lot of story to get invested in, as it's primarily a story of survival from start to finish, against odds greater than yourself. Sort of like FTL, again, incidentally. There is something of a backstory alluded to through descriptions and conversations, but it doesn't do very much to flesh out the world. But that's fine, because the game simply has as much writing as it needs. Short of a more linear story campaign, there's nothing more that I think really could be done.
The game makes good on its promise of "high-stakes, high-profit" gameplay, to the point that I can find almost no real flaws with the game. If I had to complain about something, I suppose there's not a huge amount of content to discover after multiple playthroughs. It may only take two or three complete playthroughs in order to unlock all of the agents, whereas another game like FTL requires specific accomplishments. DLC is coming, however, and Klei has given the game free content updates. They take fan feedback seriously, and have used it to improve the game, and even expanded their upcoming DLC in response to requests for more substantial content. What's here is great, even if it gives you only as much playtime as I've given the game - and that's
more hours than I get from many $60 games, and not one of those hours feels wasted (even when I lost).
Klei is a great developer, and thanks to Early Access, they were able to make one of their best games to-date. I absolutely recommend it to people looking for an isometric turn-based strategy game, but perhaps want something a little more fresh than XCOM. Hell, I recommend it to stealth and strategy fans alike.

Well, if you can get to the moon surely you can go to another planet... and so it progresses.
KSP can be a transformative and profoundly educational experience. A common joke in the community is "It isn't rocket science... except it is!" and that is absolutely true. You'll learn real orbital mechanics. Concepts which seem almost magical to others will become relatively simple for you. And all you did was play a "game".

You die.
You pick yourself up, then die again.
You keep telling yourself it's not just you.
You learn then you die again.
It may be annoying but will never stop being awesome

Nice puzzle platformer with lots of levels and lots of different ideas for puzzle mechanics, so it never gets old. There are only two problems: Mosquitos and the time warp puzzles.
Dear dev, if you think your game is too easy then adding enemies that move in random directions with random speed to make it harder is NOT the way to go. It makes the game more frustrating, sure, but not more challenging. Solving some of the levels is purely based on luck since you can't predict where those annoying mosquitos move next and sometimes they just hit you like a homing missile in the worst possible situation. Overall the game is relatively easy and thus it's still very possible to solve all the levels, but every level with a mosquito in it is a wasted opportunity for an interesting level since it's just annoying. Unfortunately there are quite a lot of those, especially in the later areas.
The other problem are the time warp levels where you play with Shuggys from different time zones. This is a really nice idea and works very well, but there is no way to plan properly what you're doing - and that is all this game mechanic is about. If you pause the game the main menu comes up and covers the whole screen, making it impossible to have a look at the level to plan your routes. And you don't know what the buttons in each level do either until you push them, so it's trial and error all the time.
Still, overall it is a good game, which could have been great without these flaws.

Fan of Deus Ex, or Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines, and their brethren of immersive sims?  Don't pass up Alpha Protocol.
Be warned, of course.  The game is riddled with severe technical problems; across two PCs and two operating systems, this game has proven more challenging to merely
than any other game I've played in the last five years.
, it is also among the very best.  The setting is lacking any particularly fantastical elements, and the characters are arguably not especially memorable, but the intrigue is well presented, and subtly woven.
The game's dialogue system is superb, reminiscent of Mass Effect, but with the addition of a timer, forcing you to make decisions on the spot and stick by them.  Characters react to your playstyle, and the choice to play stealthily, non-lethally, or  loudly and violently will ultimately impact certain sequences.  Don't expect to notice massive consequences for your choices, but repeated playthroughs show an excptional number of subtle, appreciated differences.
Gameplay is ambitiously diverse.  Certainly, as a whole, it controls somewhat awkwardly, as the game does not master any of its elements entirely, but it offers many options competently enough.  The standard paths are available; stealth, hacking, gunplay, and melee (unarmed, in this case) are all present.  Various abilities, unlocked through RPG-like progression, offer a feeling of meaningful specialization, and nicely allow you to focus on a certain skillset.
If you can tolerate its technical failings, Alpha Protocol offers an experience that's difficult to compare to any other recent releases.  It was clearly a labor of love, and fans of other Obsidian games probably know what to expect, in terms of its stability.
, if you want to take a risk on something different from the norm.

So it was late i was bored and there was a steam sale, nothing seemed good intill i took a look at hotline Miami, so i siad simple Indie game; why not. As soon as i started playing i knew this game was legit everything about seemed to be just right, from the art style to the gameplay Hotline was very soild. then i finished it and i have to say Hotline Miami my be one of my favorite Indie games of all time, and all of this is because of the little things the game didn't turn a blind eye to. First of all there is the head rushing gameplay like a scene out of Super Meat Boy you will have one life and one hit will kill you, but one hit will kill almost everything else. This simple idea grew into hard, fast, and bloody levels in a 80's drug driven high, I spent hours runing through hotel floors smashing and bashing my way through crazy numbers of mobsters. I could run in with a automatic rifle and go nuts while all the mobsters dashed at me or i could sneak in with a knife and take them out room by room. This chocie which seemed so obvious was just as perfect as i thought, but the game also adds a fun perks system in it as well. Now you may be saying damm another perk system to learn and figure out, but actully its as simple as a mask. A slurry of colorful masks give you perks like your fists can be a one hit kill or guns are silent make finding all these masks worth while, and they also tie into the deep story of Hotline. You dont know your name or who you are but you do know one thing and that thing is to kill. You get orders from phone calls left on your anwering machine, but none of the measages mention killing. "i have a rat problem for you to deal with," or "i need you to do some babysitting," ring across the line and you don't know if your crazy or if you just like hurting people. then the end rolled around and from a lifetime playing games with big plot twists like Bioshock i was pretty impressed. All in all Hotlin Miami is a must have on any game system, it is fun and bloody romp through a deep and involving story and it is a must have.

Maybe this game used to be great in the hey days of 2.5D FPSs, but to me it feels more dated than Doom or Duke Nuke'Em 3D. While those other titles seemed to have pixel-perfect, artist made sprites; the sprites Dark Forces appear to get their basis from scanned photos and retain that muddled, pixelated look.
Another fault is there are so many grey walls with low resolution textures that it is easy to get lost in the levels due to the lack of recognizable landmarks.
I am sure that die-hard fans of old-school FPSs or Star Wars will find a lot to like, but for me I'd rather skip this and move on to Jedi Knight 2, which has both the better visual representation of SW and better gameplay.

Neat little game right here. Not aesthetically amazing, the music is kind of meh, but it's quite fun on a gameplay level. Each level is a rectangular room, most of them able to fit on a single screen even. And there's a huge variety in gimmicks to keep the levels diverse. Plus, aside from the main game mode, there's also a teleporter-based mode and a co-op mode (that, amusingly enough, is entirely beatable with only one player, though assuredly more difficult that way than it would be otherwise.) The jump physics can be a bit wonky at times though, and there's an enemy time (mosky) that strikes me as a bit unfair, often ruining otherwise good levels with its presence. Really though with all the creativity on display here it's definitely worth a look, not the most challenging or longest of gaming experiences but enjoyable while it lasts, for sure.

The district mechanic for instance is ridiculous. On a standard sized earth map the entirety of Japan is represented by about 6 or 7 tiles. Because of this game's terrible "district" system, that's not even enough for 1 functional city and yet the real life japan is the size of the entire American eastern coastline. So essentially these districts are supposed to be occupying the same space as the entire island of Kyushu, roughly the size of the state of West Virginia or Republican Ireland. The district system heavily favors continental powers and puts coastal/naval/island empires at a massive disadvantage. Culture or Science victories on an islands map? Only if you like to starve your population and have next to no production at all! Many of these districts also completely do away with any passive resource yields for the tiles they sit on. Want culture or science? Well say "sayonara" to productivity, food, and gold! Absolutely ridiculous.
And don't even get me started on the AI! Yes, real life nation-states have been incredibly capricious throughout the millennia, but they at least give you some warning!!! Hitler swore he would reestablish the German Reich before occupying Poland; the only people he surprised were timid idiots like Chamberlain and Charles de Gaul. Instead Civ 6's AI has what is called a chaos value. Basically, the AI does things which don't make any sense sometimes which could be an interesting feature but firaxis just lazily made it so that your friends can backstab you at the drop of a hat. Civs which you aren't competing with in any way and who are on the opposite side of the map which will take eons to sail to will randomly go to war with you completely out of the blue. No indications at all! No troops amassing at your border, no ships cloaked beneath the fog of war just off your coastline. NOTHING! Absolutely infuriating!
Worse yet, the new "agenda" system is broken. The devs lazily made it so that the AI overweights your opponent civs' agendas. So instead of Cleopatra seeing your powerful navy and generous trade agreements with her, she has this ridiculous laser-focus on your army, land units only. This is not realpolitik in the slightest and its far sloppier than Civ 5's AI. Modders also have no way to modify the AI itself. They're stuck reverse engineering (i.e. guessing) how the AI works and manipulating the information the AI has access to. The AI cheats like nobody's business as well. Ingenious plays like pushing an expansionist opponent into expanding into desert areas fail because AI opponents have access to unlimited resources.
