I have heard much about this game for years but never got around to playing it.  Thankfully, the May 4th sale gave me that opportunity.  Eleven hours later into the game, it is very doom-esque (it uses the same or similar engine as doom) and has very good (90's) shooter mechanics with a Star Wars twist to it.
In this game you play as Kyle Katarn, the smuggler turned jedi, turned back into smuggler, turned back into jedi.  Kyle along with his partner Jan are out to save the day.  That's as far as I'm going to go with the story since it's too good for spoilers.
For a game that was released back in the 90's, the gameplay mechanics are tight, fun and precise.  There are a good variety of weapons which is surprising for a FPS Star Wars game in today's market.  I think the most important part of the weaponry option is that every weapon has a purpose.  You have your traditional blaster pistol & blaster rifle, along with rockets, grenades, and other unique tools used for slaughtering stormies.
The level design for the most part is good, unique and tricky.  There are puzzles implemented into most levels that require some sort of brain function for you to complete them.  Sorry CoD players, there are no hands being held in this game.  There are around 16 missions in this game which have enough content to keep you playing them for a while.  The missions take you to different locations which is cool because who really wants to spend most of their game time trying to pull down a star destroyer in a frustrating QTE scenario? Now back to the game that is Dark Forces,  the pacing of this game is very fast so if you are really up for it, speed runs are available.
Just to conclude on the missions in Dark Forces; THE SEWER LEVEL.
Overall, Dark Forces is a game that I thoroughly enjoyed and it was really surpring how well this game plays for it's age.  I can guarantee that if you are a gamer who does not mind playing a 90's pixelated shooter, then you will most definitely have a lot of fun with this.

I had this game for a good while, but I had major gameplay issues from the start and I kept getting annoyed and leaving it alone for months on end. I had a friend point out a couple of fixes to me, and suddenly, hello - I lost an entire night because I was enjoying the game just that much.
Those fixes, btw - your default interact key [I believe it's Spacebar], should be left as default. In the hacking minigame at least one of the threads insists on Spacebar just to be able to work. You can always assign a different key as the backup key and it'll work fine for everything else, but for hacking to work, Spacebar needs to be left as default.
Also, don't try overriding the graphical settings from within the AMD or nVidia software - it can break the dialogue boxes, leaving them blank and you unable to actually choose your dialogue. Considering how Alpha Protocol works, this isn't a good thing.
Those two bugs were gamebreaking for me originally. Once I knew how to get around them, the game played like a dream. Clunky in a few places [combat/movement wise] and I despise the checkpoint system, but I would still happily play it over and over again. There is major replay value depending on where you'd like to travel to first, your dialogue options, everything else. Definitely worth it on sale, though not necessarily otherwise.

As a fan of the Tower Defense Genre I believe this game to be far too complicated in terms of defense layout creation.
You may begin construction of your defenses upon developer chosen insert points and nowhere else. On these points you may construct either a defense tower or install a triple adaptor and/or extension in order to set up defenses for parts of the level which do not have these insert points. These adaptors can be stacked as much as you like...
I have no quarrel with unlimited creativity but when it stems up, down, left and right with unlimited avenues it begins to lose its charm quite quickly as you have so much option but very little drive to do so. There is no game atmosphere to give you any reason to play...
Infinite ways of stemming out from insert points creates a game based on extreme patience and testing; something I nor most of my friends have.
Also, the theme of this game is very dull with simplistic cube styled levels, mostly unimaginative towers and enemies that are just difference shapes and colours to represent how much damage they can take as they travel through the maze... No, you cannot plan out the maze, only the defenses.
This game just gets boring extremely quickly and doesn't allow you to do a simple restart even if you DO manage to maintain focus upon this game.
If the theme was changed and each tower felt like it provided a more unique and useful design then this concept could become an okay game. The problem really is that this game is just an unimaginative geometrical bore which will most likely find you quitting not because you failed, but because you failed to get to the point of failure.
This is boring and dull but could be made better with the existence of some imaginative graphics and more interesting concepts.
This game I would rate a 35/100 due to its boring gameplay, unimaginative style, Lack of polish and the biggest no no of tower defense games: Leaving out a RESTART LEVEL button.
There are better games out there which will provide more fun and charm, including veteran TD players.

A rogue-like twin stick shooter created by Vlambeer, a company with an excellent track record, no doubt about that.

I have used Photoshop for my custom spriting and animation, but just got this today and found this to be very much helpful in making my animation aligned properly and framed appropriately (I use RPG maker VX ACE, btw). Before, it didn't look bad when I tested my current custom sprites' movements, but this shows me all the directional movements along side each other in the proper frames and it shown me a big difference in the alignments of my previous sprites. Something I would've never noticed, otherwise! And it updates the preview as you work on it.
I highly recommend this as an addition to sprite animation editing, especially if you want to make custom edits, even if they are not the traditional xp/vx size :) It'll let you know if the current grid sizing isn't optimal for what you have (I had imported a custom sheet and though it just barely worked in game, it wasn't the proper size till I fixed it). I may still use my photoshop program for stuff like scenes, very large stuff or minimal to no animated sprites, but this is my new favorite for most character spriting. I also love the ability to layer clothing, hair and items, separating them individually, this is a plus :D And the price is really great, too. Especially compared to another program here on Steam that does something similar. Fortunately it doesn't matter to me if there's limited resources included as I've got tons I've collected and many I plan to make anyways.
Update (and further/clarification tips): Yes, you can adjust the amount of frames to what you need and create a template for more sprites that work in a "similar" manner, if needed. When adding, it'll ask if you want to scale the frames to match, depending on what it is, you would want to select for it to not match so it'll expand properly. Unless it does match, of course (may have to test variations out to be sure). On some clarifications in my post, when I tested my sprites before using this, I was testing animation in photoshop and using the actual rpg maker vx ace engine to test if the sprite would work correctly in it, which was time consuming and ineffecient in itself, since I have to go between programs. Also when I tried to import my "finished" sprite that was made beforehand, it shown me that the framing size wasn't correct (particularly in the middle column, thus cannot be imported properly, if at all), I had to correct it in photoshop by expanding it with the 32px grid sizing requirement to match the outer two columns. This program is best for those that either has a bunch of resources to import/work with or those who are creating their own templates, etc. Even if something isn't aligned right, it's not that hard to go in and make adjustments, just select the layer and make the adjustments. It's a slight learning curve, but not hard to work out. The other program I saw on Steam, cost over/around $100, so this is a great deal once you know how to work it.

Yes, it takes some time to learn what the hell you are doing.
Yes, you will crash and/or burn and/or explode midair many times.
Yes, it's a complex and powerful physics simulator and not a piece of story you can just eat up.
Yes, it still looks a bit "raw".
Yes, there is a ridiculously commited bunch of most helpful and very kerbal fans.
But, is it worth it? Yes, yes and another YES! Not only are there a million and one things to achieve, there are nearly infinite ways to do them. Build a sattelite? Sure! Shoot it into orbit on top of a tower of highly explosive rocket fuel? Go right ahead! Strap it into a spaceplane, shoot for the sky and burn into orbit? Right this way! Give it some engines, aim for the stars, miss, and hit the moon? Hell yeah! Slap wheels onto it, some batteries and solar cells and roam around in craters and canyons no living beeing has ever set foot on? There are the parts, do it! Send a Kerbal instead of a lifeless computer core? Damn, just do that then! Catch a passing asteroid, anchor a space station onto it and mine ores from it that you can turn into fuel so you can refill your ships that are stationed in orbit? Holy crap, thats an awesome idea, I'll steal it and I WILL DO THAT!
It is a learning experience and that is very much part of the fun. The game itself is filled with humor and crazyness and that is exactly the way its supposed to be played, even if you can also take it very seriously and, for example, mirror the race to the moon of the sixties.
There are three gameplay modes to choose from. In career mode, you will have to manage your space programs funds and reputation. You can do contracts to earn both, do milestone goals and break records to make you more noticable so you will get even more lucrative and complex contracts. At the very beginning there are just a few parts and an unexperienced crew to choose from and you are very limited in your construction. There are special science parts to do research with, which you can bring back or transmit and get research points for. These you can invest in the tech-tree to unlock more parts. Together with the upgrade system for your space center the game lets you progress your way to more and more complex builds. Your crew gains experience by doing new things, which will make them better at what they do and you can also hire more.
There is science mode, where you won't have to worry about funds, reputation or crew experience, but you still have to do research to unlock parts. It's a nice midway when you want to have progression, but not the limitations and liabilities of the career mode.
And then there is sandbox mode, where you can do whatever you want without limit and consequence. Everything is unlocked, upgraded and paid for.
Give it some time, do the tutorials, watch some videos about things that aren't clear by then. You will not regret it.
Kerbal Space Program also supports mods. This is true, but very much an understatement. You can enhance the core game whithout changing the gameplay in the slightest, or you can throw in things from your wildest sci-fi dreams. Want to build a fusion-powered plasma-driven mothership to visit exoplanets in other starsystems? There are mods for that. Want to play in our solar system with original russian and american rocket engines, fuel tanks, sattelite cores, command capsules and worry about life support, food, water and air? There are also mods for that. Just want to have your thrust-to-weight ratio and delta-v automatically calculated for the more and more complex rockets you will eventually build, an autopilot system that helps you with the long maneuvers late in the game, a calculator that plots your launch windows to other planets to maximise your efficiency and an alarm clock that reminds you when maneuvers and events are coming up when you eventually handle several missions simultaneously? These are the most popular right there. What about colonizing other planets, building ships in space, having parts to constuct complex folding vehicles or just guns for your version of the space shuttle? Stop asking for things that already exist!
Eventually "kerbal" will replace "astronaut" in your vocabulary. You will learn what periapse, apoapse, oberth effect and hohman transfers are and worry regulary about delta-v, TWR and ISP. You will be able to circularize an orbit, match planes, rendevouz and dock in your sleep. You will know the difference between aerocapture and aerobraking maneuvers and you will understand why the suicide burn very much earns its name. Then you will look back at the first time you strapped a capsule onto a solid rocket booster, pressed space to launch it into an uncontrollable spin, burn out, fall back to Kerbol and explode on high speed impact with the ground ... and smile. And you will never again forget fins and parachutes. And the struts. Yep. Never forget the struts.

People are complaining about microtransactions, but this is just a label games are tagged with without people really understanding what it means. You can buy chests that give you high-rarity gear, followers, follower add-ons etc. Now, I simply did 3 vendetta missions and got free chests that gave me a couple epic and a couple legendary followers. The same thing you can get from microtransactions.
Micros can be used to gain things faster than normal, perhaps for people that don't have a lot of time. Just because it's seen as a "money grab" doesn't mean the game isn't high quality. It's still Shadow Of Mordor, same as always with some much needed features, enemies, and utilities added. Without even paying mind to the "store" where these "dreaded" microtransactions take place...the game itself is beautiful and worthy of praise.
Stop focusing on what steps the company is making to gain some extra cash. Just don't support the microtransactions by not buying any, and then you can say you earned everything yourself, and enjoy a really good game without stressing yourself out about things that make you mad for virtually no reason. Whether people buy things or not, there are always going to be a large amount of people better than you. So just enjoy the game, and take it for what it is.
TLDR; Microtransactions aren't a big deal. Game is amazing in itself and stays true to the franchise. Don't judge it because of silly things.

The gameplay itself is pretty repetitive but smooth and fun.
It all revolves around light - flashlights, flares, flashbangs, electricity, lightbulbs etc. - that you need to use to make the Taken vulnerable to physical weapons / control the crowd / buy a few seconds to take a breath and reload. The gameplay quite stands out itself from other shooters.

Long story short ORION: Prelude (Competitive PvP) was the original game announced in 2010, a spiritual successor to the ORION: Source Beta. It was not able to release due to a series of events and we had to focus on a smaller scaled experience. This was called Dino Beatdown (Open World Co-Op). It was a disaster and so we continued to work on improving it using the revenue made and the next massive chunk was ORION: Dino Horde (Arena PvP, Duel).
With the success of Dino Horde we were finally were able to deliver the experience originally promised (Prelude) back in 2010. And then some - considering the original Prelude was to be strictly PvP and only have three game modes (CTF, Vital, Deathmatch) compared to it's modern day predecessor (15 game modes and a variety of play styles). Comparison:
Original Prelude / Modern Prelude
3 Modes / 15 Modes
5 Dinosaurs / 10 Dinosaurs (All Playable)
30 Weapons&Gear / 50 Weapons&Gear
5 Multiplayer Maps / 20+ Multiplayer Maps & SDK
It is now called ORION: Prelude because it *finally* is ORION: Prelude.

A puzzle/platformer with a surprising amount of depth to it. There's plenty of challenge here, in the mould of some of the older NES games - albeit not quite as tough - with the most fragile vampire outside of Twilight. Shuggy has a variety of tricks at his disposal to help negotiate through the levels, and these assists change depending on the level. Teleportation, rotating the level itself, ropes, multiple Shuggys and even time travel are options open to you throughout the game.
The genius of the game is that it challenges casual players, but is also designed around making life difficult for speedrunners. Many of the hazards seem to clog the optimal quickest route through a level, so if you want to replay levels and go for your best times, you'll appreciate the quality of the level design on display here. Throw in a very fun local co-op mode and a bunch of additional teleportation levels, and you have a game that can certainly keep you occupied.

Recommended for fans of puzzlers and platformers.
Beautiful cartoony 2-D graphics, with the main campaign consisting of 116 short levels. The story is simple, but is animated nicely through several comics. In addition to the story mode, there are dozens of co-op and extra teleporting levels for added challenge and fun.
Unlike many puzzlers, I found the difficulty curve for the main campaign fairly nice and not overly difficult, but still presenting a decent challenge. You do not have to complete all of the levels in a certain order -- you only have to unlock and beat the boss level in each of the five-ish rooms, as well as beating a certain amount of levels total. Of course, its more fun to beat them all. You can try levels again for a better time and to compete against players on a leaderboard, which for the most part doesn't seem hacked yet like many other games.
Most levels after the first few have some sort of "trick" and/or puzzle elements with switches you have to activate in a certain order. Some examples of the tricks are using a rope (sometimes with gears), getting little ball creatures to a certain point, rotating the whole or parts of the stage, and the enemies and a harmful version of you traveling back in time. Other tricks are infinite jumps and long jumps with a hover ability.
Try it out!

In almost every aspect attributable to a videogame, Alpha Protocol fails to impress. The graphics are ugly, the artstyle is generic, the gunplay is tripe and the AI borderline schizophrenic.
It is a testament, then, to Obisdian's writing staff that this game is merely mediocre.
The game has a solid RPG heritage and this shows, with the RPG elements arguably being the game's only true strength. There are some solid choice and consequences here and the leveling system is basic, but functional (operating on a hybrid of perks and number-based attribute upgrades). The story the game weaves between flashbacks is not in itself ground-breaking nor is it free from a number of tried and tested spy clichés, but the influence the game allows you to have on the story is commendable. There's no TW2-tier decision here, but characters will reflect on how you played a level and this will result in other characters reacting accordingly. For example, playing steathily throughout will mean characters that respect stealthy-operators are more likely to respect you and your methods, perhaps resulting in an allegiance several levels later. These are relatively minor touches, but they permeate the game's writing, with the game itself having a number of different endings depending on who you allied with and how friendly you were with them.
The gunplay is heavily influenced by the RPG mechanics of old, with the reticule taking some time to focus on weapons you are not trained for. However, even when your character is maxed out on a weapon's skill, the gunplay fails to feel anything better than floaty and ill-equipped. I ended up playing as a sneaky spy in an effort to avoid the gunplay.
Stealth in this game is hampered by the AI. It's laughably stupid in some cases and borderline psychic in others. The game gets around this in later levels by allowing your character to become invisible (with no in-game reasoning as to why) but this quickly becomes over-powered as your pour more points into stealth.
To be sure, I found Alpha Protocol a deeply unsatisfying experience, but I found myself constantly wanting to like it as I progressed, there's a distinct lack of good RPGs set in the spy mythos. This is a game that was clearly crafted with a small budget and unlike other budget games (such as DMC1) which inspire a certain cheap charm to them, you can't help but lament the lost potential with Alpha Protocol.

I wasn't really sold on the game until I had played through and failed, then took a closer look at the opening cinematic, and it dawned on me: This isn't just a tower defense game, this is taking control of an organic mutating monster hiding in the guise of a clean, isometric world.
From the beginning, all three dimensions are brilliantly used, with the travel path going over, under, and all around the map, leaving you to find the nooks and crannies to place you units, but it seems lacking and some of the very limited build spots are useless. The game truly comes alive as soon as you start using the trees to build off in dizzying directions. No place to put a unit? Cobble an insane hodgepodge of trees around to wherever you want it. Forget the ground, hang a dozen turrets right over the path and make them walk the gauntlet. With enough cleverness and cash you could win the game from a single build spot. I strongly prefer to use the 4-way trees instead of the 6-way for the surprising element of organic chaos they introduce.
No game will ever be "optimal" and no two games will ever feel the same, unless you consciously force it. So it was late i was bored and there was a steam sale, nothing seemed good intill i took a look at hotline Miami, so i siad simple Indie game; why not. As soon as i started playing i knew this game was legit everything about seemed to be just right, from the art style to the gameplay Hotline was very soild. then i finished it and i have to say Hotline Miami my be one of my favorite Indie games of all time, and all of this is because of the little things the game didn't turn a blind eye to. First of all there is the head rushing gameplay like a scene out of Super Meat Boy you will have one life and one hit will kill you, but one hit will kill almost everything else. This simple idea grew into hard, fast, and bloody levels in a 80's drug driven high, I spent hours runing through hotel floors smashing and bashing my way through crazy numbers of mobsters. I could run in with a automatic rifle and go nuts while all the mobsters dashed at me or i could sneak in with a knife and take them out room by room. This chocie which seemed so obvious was just as perfect as i thought, but the game also adds a fun perks system in it as well. Now you may be saying damm another perk system to learn and figure out, but actully its as simple as a mask. A slurry of colorful masks give you perks like your fists can be a one hit kill or guns are silent make finding all these masks worth while, and they also tie into the deep story of Hotline. You dont know your name or who you are but you do know one thing and that thing is to kill. You get orders from phone calls left on your anwering machine, but none of the measages mention killing. "i have a rat problem for you to deal with," or "i need you to do some babysitting," ring across the line and you don't know if your crazy or if you just like hurting people. then the end rolled around and from a lifetime playing games with big plot twists like Bioshock i was pretty impressed. All in all Hotlin Miami is a must have on any game system, it is fun and bloody romp through a deep and involving story and it is a must have.

A venerable entry in the Star Wars saga, Dark Forces set up the characters of Kyle Katarn and Jan Ors, while also introducing the Imperial Dark Troopers into the lore. Dark Forces went on to spawn a successful sequel, Jedi Knight, which then was followed by two more games featuring Katarn. Although the canon has been overwritten by the Disney acquisition, Katarn's daring capture of the Death Star plans and sabotage of the Dark Trooper program are still among fans' most beloved extended universe story arcs.
Released in the wake of the early/mid 90's DOOM craze, Dark Forces presents gameplay very similar to other shooters of that era: blast through waves of enemies, solve the puzzles, get the keys, open the doors, etc. In truth, there are very few discerning features, those being the familiar universe and music, voice acting, cut scenes, the ability to look up and down (albeit awkwardly), items and inventory management, and some other minor details.
What sets Dark Forces apart is really the sum of these unique features. It's a solid, old-school shooter in the Star Wars universe - that alone will draw fans. There is much greater variety than DOOM and it's many clones when it comes to missions and environments. One mission sees you skidding over ice, helpless until you slide your way into a pair of ice cleats. Another sees you captured by Jabba the Hutt, with your weapons taken away, trapped between a wall and huge monster that you will need to punch to death.
For Star Wars fans: Highly recommended. This is an important original story from the extended universe, and an enjoyable shooter.
For everyone else: Recommended, but far from essential. If you don't know much about Star Wars, it'll feel like a very well-polished DOOM clone.

My opinions after playing this game for a while (written during OB42):
-fix the hitboxes (at least, the body hitboxes. The head hitboxes are just fine.) It is one of the core mechanics of a shooting game. In paladins you can kill a person by entirely shooting the air around an enemy. With these giant hitboxes, the game does not feel smooth or polished AT ALL. This should be the number one thing Hi-Rez should be fixing right now.
-Increase character movement speed. I'm not a big fan of the "movement acceleration," since it doesn't allow you to strafe at all. This problem, in conjunction with the huge hitboxes, makes it feel like as if moving is pointless in this game. It is so easy to get hit by fast moving bullets (then again, it is really easy to aim at others too... which essentially means that in a 1v1 situation, the person who gets the first jump is almost garanteed to win).
-get rid of the horses. The maps are well designed aesthetically, but the fact that they don't have forward spawns are a pain. Pressing almost any button outside of the spawn room will kick you off your horse, and you have to painfully and slowly walk all the way to the point (in addition, The horses just simply feel weird and out of place). Increasing character movement speed and/or adding more spawn rooms should help solve this problem.
-Allow decimals for the sensitivity value! (it's not that hard!!!)
-Show if people are queueing together on the team menu (so people can see if we are against a five-man or a duo or whatever)
-one last thing I can possibly complain about is team voice chat. I'm sure it's being worked on, but considering it's already OB42, it's a bit late.

Life is Strange is one of my absolute favourite games ever and let me put out all my feelings out in here too ('cos why the hell not):
Details. This game had so many beautifully created moments such as the sunsets and the storms - everything was perfectly and very well detailed. It shows how much effort has been put on to this game.
Story. As much as I like to play games that don't really have a story behind them, I also enjoy playing games with a story backing up the choices that you can make while playing. Life is Strange was truly an eerie game, jumping from timeline to other and forming a new storyline here and there was done really well - as the output of it all could've been really messy too. The fact that the player can make some choices which will also show the consequences of it all is just brilliant. About that last sentence, I do have to add the fact that personally I think this game was also teaching that everything
has consequences, the choices we make in our daily lives have an impact on other people too. It was a heartbreaking story with a few happy moments here and there. A game that has a little bit of that powerful friendship, a lil' bit of that romantic side to it as well as that melancholic outcome with tearful moments? Yes please, give me all those feels.
It's also worth noting that I really loved the character developments. (And some of the developments happened because of the choices I made, but it was really nice noticing how it all just mattered).
I can truly recommend this game to everybody (though everybody has probably already played this lmao).

Long story short ORION: Prelude (Competitive PvP) was the original game announced in 2010, a spiritual successor to the ORION: Source Beta. It was not able to release due to a series of events and we had to focus on a smaller scaled experience. This was called Dino Beatdown (Open World Co-Op). It was a disaster and so we continued to work on improving it using the revenue made and the next massive chunk was ORION: Dino Horde (Arena PvP, Duel).
With the success of Dino Horde we were finally were able to deliver the experience originally promised (Prelude) back in 2010. And then some - considering the original Prelude was to be strictly PvP and only have three game modes (CTF, Vital, Deathmatch) compared to it's modern day predecessor (15 game modes and a variety of play styles). Comparison:
Original Prelude / Modern Prelude
3 Modes / 15 Modes
5 Dinosaurs / 10 Dinosaurs (All Playable)
30 Weapons&Gear / 50 Weapons&Gear
5 Multiplayer Maps / 20+ Multiplayer Maps & SDK
It is now called ORION: Prelude because it *finally* is ORION: Prelude.

Nuclear Throne! The wasteland twin stick shooter you've always wanted, but didn't know it.
STORY - There isn't much story to discover here outside of your own imagination and interpretation of the Text-less cutscenes you receive each time you reach the throne (ala Binding of Isaac) or loop a certain number of times, but the story is clearly not the focus in these type of games.
GAMEPLAY - The gameplay is all it's about and this game has it pretty solid, playing like a much quicker paced Binding of Isaac with a stockpile of unique and fun weapons with ever limited ammo, you race across a handful (4 for the most part then later on 7) of randomly generated levels with random enemy counts - the way the levels are designed to generically path themselves hardly creates something much different then the last time you ran through,
The only noticeable difference comes in where the enemy spawns. sometimes they could all be scattered about in every corner making the level longer or sometimes they will just spawn on top of or in front of the player - It feels in need of some work and doesn't quite live up to the remarkable feature other games have utilized.
But I don't expect it to be perfect as it is random. You have good runs, you have bad.
BADDIES: The guns are insanely fun and the enemies are interesting and frightening upon first sight, not know how they attack or move towards you.
You hardly ever see the same types on other levels. Which brings us to the BOSSES. Starting off there are 4 for every 3 stages of each location. Many are total pushovers except, the 3rd boss, Lil' Hunter who arguably is more difficult to fight than the main boss of the game and almost requires you have equip a melee to combat his endless reinforcements!
As you beat these enemies and defeat their leaders. You're thrown back to the start of 1-1 to continue your game through "Loops" with tougher enemies, higher counts and rarer weapons. Only problem with the game getting harder as you "Loop" is the poor level generation, resulting in instant deaths and unfair, unsafe spawns in the middle of the dozens of quick moving enemies, making the randomly dropped melee weapons A MUST by those levels.
MUSIC - I like the music, it really distinguished each of the environments adding it's own flair to every map.
Couldn't be better, unless there was more.
ART - The art is just above barebones and still leaves much to be desired for these interesting levels and Characters.
Controls - Are bindable, But CANNOT be overwritten, by this I mean, if you change "Space" for swap weapons to "E", "Space" will still swap weapons, but now so will "E", the main controls can't be swapped between the actions. only new ones added,
COOP - Terrible. It's ONLY playable through 2 Xbox controllers. Each player starts off with their chosen character, their own ammo and weapon equips, each player also has priority of the camera however the HEALTH is shared in a stupidly obtuse way. If one player dies, the health bar of the other is depleted each second until they're are dead and the game ends or they reach their partner and give half of their HP to save them and repeat. Kerbal is a great game. It's quirky, buggy, laggy; and fun. There has been a concerted efffort of the original devs to create a game that takes a cue from the best building scenes of the A Team and MacGuyver; Scrapheap challenge into space. It's flair and humor are incontestible. The challenge is simple. Here are some rocket parts. You've all seen movie clips of rockets going into space. Can you trial and error your rocket simulacra into orbit? If yes; add more parts and go further. Step by step taking it further through the Kerbin solar system.
The first time you reach orbit, or the first time you land on a moon or another planet will be an epic experience. A 4d puzzle where you find yourself always lacking in vital information and underqualified.
However the way the game was meant to be played by the devs, it's very capable of provoking interest in the history of contemporary space flight and science; this game allows the player to create the specific space flight experience they desire personally. The keyword here is: modding. There are loads and loads of excellent, creative and beautifully made mods.
But in the core it's a fun physics simulator that, via reddit and forum communities, youtube and imgur, allows you to get creative and share your creations. If you like building and flying things; and that specific combination, you're set.

First and formost, if you cannot code or configure your dosbox controls, you're gonna have a bade time.  If you do not know what dos box is, you're going to be unhappy with this game.
That said, this is a very old game with very old design choices. You are going to have to put yourself in the mindset of the mid 90's gamer and computer user to enjoy this game.
That said, its a blast to play.  There is a quality aesthetic to this game that was quite consistent in the rest of the Katarn games that made me enjoy it very much.  The Lucas-verse felt like a place, somewhere you were in, rather than just another level.  Sewer monsters, Gamorran guards, thermal detonators, blaster rifles, everything felt on point.'
That said, the only issues I have with it from a gaming perspective is that there is no save system, so you're going to wind up memorizing much of the levels to get through them healthy and in one piece.  The back half missions have boss battles that ....aren't bad, but aren't great as well.  The Corescant mission felt like I was fighting the AI more than anything.  The fuel depot mission was similarly confusing in that exactly how you were to accomplish the objectives was a pain that look my lateral thinking ability to solve.
But all in all, this was a fun game, I enjoyed blasting imperials.
If Disney were to put a new FPS out, I'd only ask for something between this and Dark Forces 2, but minus a certain type of weapon near the end.
But seriously, learn to configure your dosbox setting so you can have a proper resolution and control setup.

On the coattails of highly successful puzzle-platformer titles such as Super Meat Boy, Braid and VVVVVV comes the Adventures of Shuggy. This puzzler pits you as a young vampire who has just inherited his grandfather's problem riddled mansion and it is up to you to fix it.
The graphics of this game seem reasonably polished although there is not much that's animated besides the main character.
Unlike VVVVV with a driving soundtrack that kept you playing, the music feels like a bland set of fill tracks that do little for the ears.
I'd like a brief description of the gameplay but I can't get more specific than saying it's a puzzle-platformer because I feel this game suffers from the ADHD of gameplay. There are a lot of mechanics in this game, I mean a lot, and they vary per level and there doesn't seem to be much of a logical progression. More doesn't always mean better and in my opinion this game would be better if it focused on a limited number of mechanics and developed them better. The vast amount of mechanics in this game made the experience feel disjointed. It didn't seem like the levels were too carefully designed as many of them were unsatisfying and some even boring.
In a level in the third area I found an obvious bug that was very easily reproducable. This bug ended my time with this game.
This game does feature controller support and local coop with levels especially designed for two players.
If you are a huge fan of these types of games, and you've exhausted all your other options, you may derive some amusement from this. Otherwise I would not recommend getting this game

An exercise in frustration!!!  I REALLY wanted to love this game and bought it when it first came out, because I thought the story was intriguing and there were choices in dialog etc.  I love Deus Ex, so when I saw this game I thought yeah this is gonna be a great game with a different story line, different type of character and menu system.  I'm a completionist type player, and if you aren't a completionist then this review won't be any use to you.
Let me start with the hacking...  the tutorial at the beginning of the game is useless, and it took me several tries over the years to eventually get past it.  I'd try and then get annoyed then stop playing, then I picked up the game up again and give it another try, and so on.  Use google and read the endless amount of people who hate the hacking as much as I do.  One guy says look for the string that doesn't move, which does work! I can get the right string set, however I can't activate the left string EVER even when I find it because for some stupid reason the  key that the instructions on the bottom to set it doesn't work.  Each string uses a different key to set it the string for left and right.
Now after endless reading on what others have tried to make the hacking simpler, with the string hacks and some even say avoid hacking and move on.  Okay I could do that, skip hacking all together.  However if you are a completionist type player who's aim is to earn as much exp as possible to develop the character to the max this is going to be an irritating feeling of leaving things undone!
Also if you are a completionist aiming to get the most exp pts per mission/dialog etc the checkpoints are going to be an irritation as well.  For instance if you accidentally chose the wrong thing in dialog and lost a reputation point with someone too bad.  This happened to me during a dialog and my phone rang and well let's just say the game forces you to be chained to your chair and disregard what goes on in real life.  If this doesn't bother you, then no worries.. however I like the feeling of physical freedom.  When the dialog gets screwed up because I am addressing something in real life like answering the phone, it's like I'm being punished.  To me it's a design flaw in the game, and the devs didn't take any consideration to real life when the game is on.  True you could reload a checkpoint, yay you get to do the section all over again.. kinda like punishment. IMO there should not be a checkpoint save systems in this type of game, with dialog choices.
I play with a keyboard and mouse and I read on the forums that this game isn't too friendly with them.  Maybe that's my problem with the hacking, who knows?  I know the mouse and keyboard work fine with combat movement, and the combat is kinda ABC 123/no brainer.
I bought this game when it first came out over 3 years ago and then tried it again over 3 years later and I am still having issues.  I don't want to give it a thumbs down, but I feel I have to as not to confuse people because of the irritating features of the game.  The story  development I think I would like if I ever was able to play the game long enough to experience it.  However I've got a completionist type mentality, in any game I want to explore every area, I want to hone my choices to get the maximum expierience, if I don't then I feel like I'm missing parts of the game and have failed.  That's just me, I know there are plenty of people who are satisfied with not doing that.  Until I can change who I am, and lower my standards then I'll not be able to play the game to the end so I'm shelving it again.
If you don't think these things will bother you that I mentioned, then great.  I do suggest checking the forums on Steam and other sites to get a census of what experiences others had, before you buy.   I think the game would have had great potential as a series, irritating design mechanics aside. I guess there's a reason why there was never a follow up game to it, because maybe the hacking, and mach speed dialog chosing peaved too many people off.

A rather intriguing action roguelike that's sort of a cross between The Legend of Zelda, Smash TV, and Nethack. Odd as that matchup sounds, it actually works.
Like most rougelikes luck plays a significant factor whether you'll finish a playthrough or not, as everything (level layout, items, enemies, bosses, etc) but the character you play is randomized. There's enough of a skill requirement to make it challenging no matter how the chips fall. Various unlocks help make future playthroughs interesting (sometimes easier, sometimes not), so there's plenty of reasons to keep playing after you finally manage to eke out a win.
It can be very unfair and frustrating at times due to the luck factor, but it's definitely an excellent challenge and worth playing.

Imagine hightened reflexes, split-second reactions and fast paced shooting, those are your enemies.
Your character is sluggish and fairly imprecise so prepare to die very, very often.
Prepare for a video game that will make you hate it and love it all at the same time.
My experience can be summed up in a single sentence "a door opened and I swung a golf club at a dog, the club hit the door instead and the dog killed me"
The gameplay is a unique mixture of frustrating and satisfying, while you playthrough stages multiple times after dying multiple times there is a sense of satisfaction with certain kills or completing certain stages.
The music is nice and works well with the atmosphere.
The limited ammunition and availability of guns partnered with the fact that using them draws attention gives a challenge and makes having to make precise but often quick decisions a must, this isn't for the CoD players who run & gun their way through any situation, despite the fast pace this game does take some skill and patience.
The retro art style doesn't take away from the experience, if anything it enhances it and allows for a far more fun gameplay.
A huge advantage is that this game can also run on older model computers and ones that don't have enough RAM to operate NASA computers.
If you're looking for a fun game, that won't break the bank, your hard drive but might break your sanity, check out Hotline Miami.

Nuclear Throne is an amazing arcade-style top-down shooter with startling amounts of replayability. It's fast-paced and not once have I been bored in all of my playtime.
The characters are the most colorful and creative I have ever witnessed, which is extremely surprising, considering most of them are simple one-word concepts drawn up as people. Or gods. Or even fish. I don't know how it works, but it does.
The gameplay is perfectly designed; the mutations are really satisfying to pick, and get even more satisying as you get better at the game and actually know which mutations do what.
For those that are iffy on the difficulty of the game, I can say the difficulty is definitely high, but I consider it a large feature of the game. The goal is to reach the Nuclear Throne, and it's not expected of you to do it on your first try, but when you do, (took me 50-60 hours) you will feel so accomplished. Everything in your entire life will light up in stunning clarity, and just as you commence the final fight, ready to take your Nuclear Throne...
you die because you didn't know there was a sudden-death beam at the beginning.
But it was worth it, because then you knew it was possible, and you could do it again with an entirely different character, different levels, different guns, and all the same glorious feeling of killing everything in your sight.
It's fun. I promise.

Compared to the first game, it's sequel Shadow of War is incredibly boring.
On the surface the game seems to build upon the first one. The combat system is the same, it's a continution of the first storyline. You can command orcs to fight for you and the Nemesis system is in full effect.
The problem begins when you consider everything else. The new skill tree seems to intentionally limit you from getting overpowered as you did in the first game. I can't count the number of times I ran away from a group of low level  orcs in this game, which I never would have done in the first one. Dominating beasts is a chore and takes way too long in this game.
The platforming is imprecise, getting stuck on walls and ledges is a frequent occurnance at the worst of times especially when fighting warlords. The maps are huge but aside from the Gondorian city at the start, it all looks the same after the 10 hour mark. Fast travel markers are useful but there aren't enough of them and there rarely near a mission marker.
The two biggest problems with this game are the story and gameplay. The story is ridiculous, it feels artificially extended with a penchant for making every supporting character a female human hybrid for some weird reason. Shelob does not need to be a woman in a sexy nightgown. A tree person does not need wooden boobs. I like well written female characters, the problem starts when you can't just let a spider be a scary mf spider with a female voice.
The gameplay is fun at first but after 10 hours it just becomes a rinse and repeat situation. Go into an area, dominate a bunch of orcs, lay seige to a fortress, rinse and repeat. You do battle ringwraiths but those fights feel pointless.
On a side note the marketplace has better loot than you can find ingame. You can buy silver chests with ingame currency while gold chests requires a purchase with real money. As an example the bow I recieved from a 750  mithril chest was way better than a weapon found behind a ihtildrin door.
Not worth the legacy the first game established for itself. Just not worth it. I highly recommned Shadow of Mordor if you've never played the first one but Shadow of War is just that a Shadow of the first game pretending through repitition.

Invisible is a turn-based stealth strategy game. It has often been compared to XCOM, but really these games take entirely different approaches to squad-based tactics. Here, your spy agency has been raided by the dystopian megacorps and you're on the run. You've escaped with two agents, minimal gear, and your hacker AI that's on 72 hours of emergency power. That means you have three days to bust out more agents, steal new gear, and prepare for a decisive strike back at the corporations. Every agent is precious, and if you want to succeed you have to use every resource that you can get your hands on.
The game is essentially a roguelike strategy game. A run through the campaign takes about 5-6 hours, and win or lose you gain experience towards unlocking new starting options like additional agents or hacking programs. Each mission is a procedurally generated network of rooms filled with safes to crack, terminals to hack, and plenty of guards, robots, cameras, and other defenses. A straight fight with armed guards is out of the question, so you have to peek through doors and stealth around security as much as you can. The behaviors of the guards are simple but must be managed carefully to prevent situations getting out of control. Guards are normally stationary or on a two-point patrol path, but if they see something suspicious, they check it out (using scanners and other tools if they have them!). Fully alerted guards break from their patterns and search for you relentlessly, so stealth is ALWAYS the best option. You can knock out guards with tasers or darts, but when they come to they'll be on full alert. Killing is an option but an expensive one; lethal weapons are expensive, generally need ammunition, and advance the alarm tracker.
The alarm tracker, by the way, is a brilliant little feature that makes sure you don't take a million years waiting out guard patrols and extended hacks. When you start a mission, the corporations know SOMETHING is going on, but not WHAT. So every turn, the alarm tracker advances a step. Every 5 steps, the alarm level advances and a new security feature comes online. It might be more cameras, it might be tougher firewalls, or it might be additional guards. Certain actions you take can additionally advance the tracker, like being spotted by guards or tripping a hacking Daemon. Your strategy needs to be balanced between caution and speed, and riding that line makes every mission tense and challenging.
And that's just the basics! Robotic drones have their own properties and tactics, which ties into the whole hacking side of the game. Your AI can hack any of the networked features of the level to give you access to security cameras, safes, and even take over drones and turrets. This costs power, which you can hack out consoles, generate using your agent skills, or supply with programs purchased for your AI. And this is really the beauty of Invisible, that everything has so many solutions. Just with guards alone, you can create a natural distraction (opening a door) to stealth past them, you can stun them, you can kill them, you can set traps using special items, you can steal keys from them to open up alternate paths, you can hack turrets or drones to take them down with, or you can use special distraction programs to lure them away. Unlike XCOM, the random element isn't in whether or not a dice roll will make your strategy work, it's in what resources you will find to form a strategy around. You're not always going to find personal cloaks or AP-restoring stims, so you have to work with whatever you've got. It's guerrilla espionage, and it's thrilling when you make a plan work.
Missions will earn you credits to buy new gear and upgrade your agents' basic abilities (max AP, inventory slots, etc.), augments to give them new abilities, programs for hacking, and chances to free new agents (up to 4 total). Even the selection of missions is randomized, as well as the travel time between them, so your overarching strategy for each game is going to vary wildly. It's a game made to be played multiple times and the INCREDIBLE wealth of difficulty options ensure that you can play at a level you enjoy. Beginner difficulty lets you rewind up to 5 turns per mission and even restart the entire mission once, allowing you to learn and experiment as much as you want. Experienced loses the restart option and cuts your rewinds down to 3, forming a good middle-ground between Beginner and Expert, the "base" difficulty which only allows one rewind. There are additional modes like Endless where you survive as many days as you can and Time Attack where you only have 2 minutes to take your turn. You can even expand difficulty options in any mode to tailor specific features exactly how you want them.
Invisible has very quickly become the gold standard of strategy for me. The balance of stealth and strategy is perfect, there are tons of items and skills to work with, there are no unwinnable situations, and there's an amazing amount of replayability between the different modes and difficulties. The Klei art style is perfect for this as well, and it does the dark, slick oppression of megacorps really well as you skulk around. There is a story to the campaign but it's a very thin one and hardly the reason to dive deep into this game. It's consistently one of the most rewarding gaming experiences, and more people absolutely need to be playing it.

I'll give this an honest pros and cons:
Pros:
The graphics of the map are fantastic, they did a really tremendous job there. It looks beautiful. I really like how they did the fog of war with the illustration style renderings, it's very nice.
The district system seems interesting. Not sure if it's a good or bad thing, but I like some innovation there.
Cons:
Bugs, inconsistent text, random issues everywhere. This game is really not polished, needs a lot more work before it can be considered "done". Through my first playthrough, I had nothing but frustration. I know games can be rough on release, so I purposefuly stay away for that period, but now that the first expansion is officially announced, I figured it should be fixed up enough now to be playable without major issues, that's not the case.
Some bugs I encountered were:
-The music just randomly stopping. There were times I would be playing, and the music would just randomly stop, while in the middle of a song. No particular reason why, or any important events, just randomly stopped. While this doesn't break the game, it does break the atmosphere.
-Voice dialog repeating. Multiple times in the same first playthrough, I would achieve an advancement of some type, and the default voice acting would start playing, I would hit the button to close the window, and them it would just repeat the same voice line again. Really annoying, happened multiple times.
-Inconsistent text/ablitities. I built a district that said it gave "+2 G for each river tile connecting to it", when planning the location, I chose a spot that was in the middle of a Y split off two rivers, I was expecting a bunch of gold for the spot, only gave +2. While this in and of itself isn't a big deal, I would expect the text explaining the units/tiles/districts to be clear, so I can tell what is going on. But this one was just one of many examples of stuff like this.
Other cons include:
-The new movement system is simplistic, and frustating. While in Civ V, you were rewarded for creative movement, in this one, it feels like they removed a dimension of gameplay, and it's just boringly simple now. I was playing as rome and had a road between my two cities, but yet a worker could only walk two tiles each on them, the same speed as walking on plains? I really feel like they have over simplified this area.
-New leader animations are too cartoony and ugly, with unskippable dialogs that keep popping up over and over. Sure, I understand you're denouncing me, do I really have to see your ugly character animations over and over each time with no way to skip? It's just frustratingly bad.
I won't list all my other minor gripes. I honestly wanted to really like this game, but it's just hard for me to. I'm just going to stick to Civ V, you might want to too.

Alpha Protocol lets you take the role of Michael Thorton, a new agent of the top secret organisation Alpha Protocol. During the game you will solve a global missile crisis, expose traitors and do all that good spy stuff we know and love. The story behind the game is well done, with no plot holes I could find and believable, if slightly caricatured, characters. It will take you through several different missions in an order of your choice, with each mission influencing the other ones and demanding meaningful choices that not only warrant, but leave you encouraged for several playthroughs.
Gameplay is varied and easily customized to your liking; in fact, this is one of the very few games where both stealth and going in guns blazing is a valid choice in all situations, though some might favour one thing over the other. Combat is not your standard Third Person Shooter - Mike actually has to aim his weapons, which constantly affords you the choice of going for precise, slow shots or spraying and hoping for the best. This choice is by no means obvious; while precise shots are generally preferable, one kind of weapon (the SMGs) actually rewards spray and pray behaviour.
To me, the really interesting part was the dialogue system. Talking to people becomes a far more engaging experience than in other titles simply due to the fact that you are timed and the game actually progresses while you speak. Have a skill on cooldown? Keep the terrorist talking until you're good and ready to take him down. Filled to the brim with adrenaline and fuming at the mouth? Cut his speech short before you come down and your buff runs out. Not only that, but most of the conversations actually feel realistic and have a strong impact on the world around you. If you tell someone off, this will be represented in your later communications, and he might be more hesitant to help you or just not mention information, preferring not to go the extra mile for the idiot that insulted him. Ths makes the game world seem very alive and helps the characters become more than just cutouts with a "press button, get quest" mechanism.
Not only do you have a choice in the way you fight and the way you talk, you also have an rpg-like levelling system to shape Michael the way you want him to be. Not only are placing skill points and unlocking abilities, the world also changes you. Depending on your actions and the things that happen, you gain perks that can influence everything from hitpoints to skill cooldowns to equipment prices.
All in all I heartily recommend you pick up the game if you like spy thrillers and/or third person RPGs/shooters. This game has an awesome storyline and interesting customization options that easily rival games like Mass Effect. However, you should know that more than a few people have reported bugs, some of them game breaking, and while I personally have never encountered any be aware that you may have to fiddle a bit to make everything run smoothly.

It's been a long time since I've played this one. This is actually the first time I've completed it.
The coolest thing about Dark Forces is its atmosphere. It's genuine Star Wars, more than almost any other Star Wars related game I've seen. Everything is done right here - from interiors (all those shafts, white corridors, control panels - just like in the movies) to the sounds of doors opening. It's funny how subsequent Star Wars games couldn't make this as authentic, despite having all kinds of technological advantages.
Gameplay is very simple but still satisfying as hell. First few missions are little boring but then it gets better and better. My personal favorite is the one on Nar Shaddaa. The final mission was awesome too - very challenging and intense.
The graphics here are basically huge flickering pixels all over the screen. I've never had any serious issues with dated visuals but still I got to get used to these graphics for some time (it's been a while since I've played something that old). Even had a minor headache for the first 30-40 minutes - you got to strain your eyes sometimes because at first you can't even tell what's ahead of you in pixels. But once you get used to it, it feels totally fine. I must say, I still like this look better than early polygonal games which look unspeakably ugly.
The plot here is also really simple, but at least it's not something like Battle of Hoth or Death Star assault for the 100th time, it's its own thing. Yeah, back in pre-Disney Star Wars era we used to think it was Kyle Katarn, not the chick from The Theory of Everything, who stole the plans of Death Star and handed them to Leia.
I liked all that Dark Trooper Project thing. It's nothing that great, but it fits the universe and works fine for a little spin-off story.
Definitely try this if you're into Star Wars (and Doom) and not scared of 1995 graphics and archaic controls. Still entertaining.

After 20 years I can finally play Dark Forces. When I was a kid I've always been puzzled whether or not I should have played it but, you know, money wasn't mine and my father was very reluctant on spending too much money, we already had DooM and DooM 2, so... But now, with steam sales... MUAHUAHUAHAUHAU...
Star Wars Dark Forces was the first chapter of what later would become the Jedi Knight Saga. It's obviously set in the Star wars universe, around the first trilogy, between Episode IV (Kyle brings the death star plans to Mon Mothma) and VI (Kyle frees Crix Madine who explains the attack plan at the Moon of Endor). Our protagonist Kyle Katarn is a Mercenary hired by Mon Mothma and the Rebellion for various operations against th empire. During a mission Kyle and his partner Jan Ors will meet an odd advanced and deadly robotic trooper, and they will investigate this creation to find out a plan for mass production of these deadly "Dark Troopers".
So the game is essentially an FPS, one of the first as this came out after DooM, so the engine and the aspect is quite similar, hence there will be solid ambiences and 2d characters and items. But even though the engine looks pixellous as much as doom there are some very "solid" ad interesting news. There are Moving level parts, and I'm not talking about the classic elevators, but solid bridges or other parts that will slide or rotate according to their purpose. Besides there will be solid objects, or "entities" that will move, such as mechanic assembly arms, Tie Fighters, and that little black imperial Mini4wd that will run around rooms...
Besides the engine, the weaponry is quite impressive apart from the trooper's iconic blaster (imprecise by default, almost kind of justifying the HORRIBLE Stormtroopers' aim... XD), the Thermal detonator (used by Leia to threaten Jabba The Hutt, but despite the name, here's just a grenade exploding on impact) you can count on a very big arsenal, but the most interesting part are items: especially night vision goggles and the light are the most impressive to me, especially the latter influencing the lighting of the rooms.
Unfortunately (or luckily) this game is released as the original one running on DosBox. I was almost afraid to face another useless HORRIBLE release as seen with the original DooMs, BUT!!! It runs perfectly, with a good (X-axis only) mouselook integration and WASD movement setting. Unfortunately I wasn't able to find any key binding setup both ingame or in DosBox config (I know, there shouldn't be any, but you know, just in case) so I had to rely on some trial and error. I could have avoided that since there's a steam F.A.Q. with all the keys list and explains how to remap through a DosBox specific function. I also had to manually increase the cycles for the DosBox Emulator because the framerate was too low
What really surprised me is the level design. Apart from the Star Wars aspect, the game gets to the point of pushing you to the limit by forcing you to get to hidden points, shoot to remotely triggered buttons, Make tough jumps and go back and forth in a maze of doors and buttons. It wasn't that nightmare today, but for the time I believe it was a very tough game, I'm sure.
Music is made of classic Star Wars themes and original Star Wars oriented tracks... rendered in MIDI, obviously XD. The best part of this is something that was very original at the time: dynamic music. A Slow pace track during exploration and faster more intense tracks smoothly kick during more active and shooting situations. This gives a great effect, because of both the Star Wars nostalgia themes and for the kind of music that perfectly suits the situation.

This is one of those "where do I start" games for writing a review!! It's not much, but I'm going to start with my first game. The only way to describe it is epic!
The match started with me walking around HQ getting a feel for the looks of the game. And enjoying the elevator music... Anyhoo, I soon decided that it was time to start playing the RTS part of the game. I walked over to my computer and logged in. Soon I was on my way to building a base. I had all the basics set up:
Power plant
Refineries
Bot production
Everything was going good so far. I had a steady income. My warbots were being built. It was a good time to be a CEO.
Then the fire nation attacked...
I was on a large map with three other opponents, and one of my neighbors, Yellow, was attacking. They had sent of two tanks, and a couple bots. In retaliation, I sent all of my warbots over to help defend my iron mine.
This is where things got epic.
I took control of a bot, and what happened next was amazing. The bot wasn't some sort of super
machine capable of terminating the enemy. I was one in a group of 12. My companion bots were marching next to me in a rhythmic style. You could feel each step. Whoomp. Whoomp. Whoomp. Then we got close enough for the enemy to start firing upon us. They opened up in a blaze of fire. Bullets streaming across the map. My allies death cry's could be heard as they were being cut down. We didn't lose the fight if that's where you thought this was going. While they were
firing at us, we were returning the fire. My warbots, even though they were dying, were fighting
as hard as they could. Being down there with them made the hair on the back of my neck raise.
Yellow's bots were falling fast and hard. It was the tanks that caused us the most grief. One by
one my warbots were falling to the blasts of the enemy, but we prevailed and drove the enemy away.
For now.
Losing 9 of my warbots from the original group of 12, I knew that I needed better hardware. This
is when I started to research tanks, and getting better armor for my warbots. Within no time at
all, I had produced two tanks with Gatling guns, and some tougher warbots.
I was ready for war.
The new army that I made was on the march to attack Yellow because they attacked first. I was
halfway there when all of a sudden I saw a massive explosion from the yellow base.
Green had beaten me to them.
Depending on the ratings of this review, I will tell the fate of the three remaining groups:
Red
Green
Myself
Overall, I think this game is amazing. From my one game, there were a LOT of epic moments that
I feel are only there because I could go into a FPS mode. Basically, how many times have you
played an RTS where you wish you could be one of your troops in that massive battle? The feeling
of finally being able to do this was amazing!! Besides the FPS mode, this game has a lot to
offer. The research system is diverse. Your units are all customizable. Having to worry about the
insides of your buildings adds a new layer to the strategy.
This is one of those games that I hope has a very long life.
I HIGHLY recommend this game to everybody!!
Keep up the good work devs!!

Okay, I'm not even the review guy. I never write reviews. So here is my honest and objective opinion 13 hours in.
1. Loot Packs: Forget the loot packs, don't listen to the people crying about their existence. It's a single player game, and the loot packs can also be purchased with in game currency. Most of us will grind out the in game currency to buy loot packs, consider purchasing loot pack a "money cheat code" of the old days.
2. Story: The cinematics are beautiful, although some consider the occasional switch between CGI and game engine to be annoying, I don't really mind. This game does, however, completely♥♥♥♥♥♥on the LOTR, Hobbit, and Simillrion lore and literature. If that is going to bother you, this game is not for you. However, if you can treat the story as "fan fiction" with many blatant differences, you may make it through.
The story itself is weak as ♥♥♥♥. You and Cerebrimbor forge a new ring of power which is promptly turned over to a spider, shelob for Cerebrimbor's.... life? You then continue bargaining with her in exchange for visions, yet Talion never seems to act in a meaningful way as a result of the visions, and they all come to pass anyway. At the end you are betrayed by a general of Gondor who turns over a relic to the Nazgul like it's nothing. Oh, and the Nazgul are transparent ghosts who can move through walls and travel as clouds of dust at will, did I mention that? Anyway after the relic is turned over to the Nazgul by the traitor they do the obvious thing - slay him and head for shelob to get the ring of power. At this point a random character saves you with bright magic and you and her save shelob from the Nazgul. Shelob is so stoked that she gives you the ring of power back.... LOL! Go you!
That brings us to Act II which I've currently started, and hopefully is more interesting. With the ring back you can dominate orcs and you begin to build an army.
3. Gameplay: Gameplay is good, improved mechanics from the first game and the same old right click action we all love. The new loot system is very good, and fun.
My one complaint thus far, at least through the first act, was the Captain/Warchief system. In SOM, a captain encounter was pretty meaningful, and a warchief encounter was simply epic... remember? "PAH-DRUK, PAH-DRUK, PAH-DRUK!!" In SOW, they throw captains at you by the threes and you kill 3 warchiefs before act I is even over. The warchiefs don't feel that much stronger than the captains and the way they throw them at you just feels clunky. You'll see.
Other than most of that, it's a great game. It's worth $60 because of the quality of the graphics, audio, and amount of sheer content in the game, but I certainly would not pay for an edition or DLC.
TL;DR - I wrote a good and honest review, read it.

Game of the year.
No, seriously, I know it's trendy to hate on this game because of the whole lootbox thing, and I hate the fact they exist, but I tell you - they have no reason to. Buying lootboxes isn't just optional, it's the most useless thing you can do with your money, next to literally burning them. Orcs and gear from boxes have 0 advantages over the ones you find in game, it's just that you don't have to find them in game. And if you don't wanna look for them, why do you even play the game?
Now that this is out of the way, this is the perfect SoM sequel. We were promised SoM on steroids, and that is exactly what we got. Very little from SoM was cut, if anything, and the number of the new features is massive. 5 regions with strongholds, expanded Nemesis system, RPG elements, drakes and trolls - everything we've seen in trailers is here, and it's epic. I especially loved the Fighting Pits - little arenas where you can train your followers by making them duel against random enemies. If the follower wins, he levels up. If he dies - he dies, but you can instantly avenge him by killing or dominating his killer.
The game is quite a bit harder now - the orcs are smarter (now they can climb, for example), the more OP skills were removed, and the other ones now have their effect split into interchangeble "upgrades" (e.g. in SoM draining dominated the orc and gave Talion elf-shot, now it's either one of those, not both). But now you have 2 summoning skills - a beast summon and a follower summon, and those 2 skills are massively useful.
There are very little bugs for a 1.0 version, the game runs in stable 60fps for me, with no freezes or CTDs on high quality settings.
In short, do not listen to the haters if you are interested in the game, just give it a go. I really hope this is not the last game in series and I'd hate to see it crash and burn just because of WB's greed. Monolith and this game both deserve better.

In my humble opinion I consider this game one of the best RPGs that I have played in the most recent years.
This is mainly due to the choice & consequence prevalent throughout the entire title, what you do, how you talk and dress echoes and reverberates throughout the narrative and shapes your relationships with the generally varied cast of characters.
It's not a game with open environments, but rather a game that funnels players to key locations but then lets the player choose with what method obstacles will be approached, both on a macro- and micro-level (Do I go to Rome first? Do I equip myself with casual clothing for this mission? Should I respond with a snarky or professional comment? Do I sneak past or kill this guard?)
Alpha Protocol also boasts a strong amount of replayability purely to discover the various ways in which conversations and characters actions are altered by the player's choices.
However the game is not as polished when it comes to the actual missions and the combat in those, I feel there's a lack of depth in the stealth, bodies disappear almost immediately, enemies patrol almost like robots and for some reason bashing open locked doors immediately triggers an alarm, even if said door is just a rickety wooden one not visibly connected to anything.
The combat is functional, but not fantastical, assault rifles and SMGs feel neglected compared to the awe-stopping power of a shotgun and the critical-hit-with-blindfire pistol method.
Bossfights can be either annoying or terrible, depending on if you built your character around combat or stealth (and tech) respectively, this is simply due to the player being forced into combat even if the rest of the mission had been successfully approached with complete silence.
Overall I'd very much recommend it if you enjoy choice & consequence, character interactions and generally being a special ops man who may or may not shoot gun a lot, just remember to put at least some points into one type of firearm.

"There have been many RPGs that let you define your character's personality to a certain extent. Say you're given a quest to get a schoolgirl's cat down from a tree. On average, you'll be given three options: neutral, where you get the cat down and accept the schoolgirl's allowance as payment; good, where you waive the fee and fondly tousle the schoolgirl's hair as she scampers off; and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, where you set fire to the tree and jump up and down on the schoolgirl's face.
And speaking as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this offends me. There are so many wonderful ways to be a complete ponce that these games rarely cater for. Or get the cat down by throwing rocks at it so it breaks all its legs on the concrete and then still expect to be paid, with the infuriatingly infallible logic of a complete tosser? Why can't there be an RPG that covers the entire ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spectrum? Well, good news, ponce fans: now there is!
Alpha Protocol follows Mike Thorton, a member of a covert U.S. government agency with strong ties to a private military company that might as well rename itself Kitten Stranglers PLC. He gets betrayed, goes rogue, has to work alone to build a case against them, blahdee blahdee blah. But what's important is that however you play him Mike Thorton is the is the ponciest ponce that ever ponced past a poncing parlour.
The dialogue system lets you switch between three attitudes: a professional, by the book sort of ponce who wouldn't emote if the angel Gabriel blow off in his face; an aggressive ponce who sounds like he's five seconds away from snarlingly flipping the global crisis onto its front and pounding away at its netherhole with a Franchi SPAS-12; and the suave ponce, who might as well just save time and mace himself every time he opens his ♥♥♥♥ing mouth. Best of all, even if he only ever talked about his favorite breakfast cereal, he'd still sound like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥, because the voice actor delivers every line in the level, smug tones of a highbrow film critic archly dismissing the latest superhero blockbuster as he spoons himself another helping of baby seal.
Let's get the good over with quickly. For once, this is a game that claims that "every action has consequences" and actually means a consequence more significant than a character maybe wearing a different hat. For example, although the hub-based mission system lets you do the operations in any order, during the one I chose to do last an informant mentioned the previous operations I'd completed in conversation. "♥♥♥♥," I said, "this game's just showing off now." So I immediately became an aggressive ponce and slammed his head into a desk. After which, there was more security in my next mission because the informant went crying to his big brother or something.
The RPG action stuff reminded me of Deus Ex - in a good way. It's nice to see a game where your character has to work on their gun skills and can't expect to draw their pistol and immediately hit the on button on a tumble dryer from nine hundred years. And I was also impressed by the lockpicking and hacking minigames, which nicely balance skill and incremental difficulty, and I can't think of a joke for that sentence, so here's a picture of a dog in a hat.
The thing about Deus Ex, though, was that you could arguably specialize completely in combat or stealth or hacking or playing the cello and still beat the game. Even the final encounter had equal parts monsters, security systems, and incomplete string quartets to allow any approach. Alpha Protocol, on the other hand, is happy to let you sink all your points into learning to waltz only to find yourself stuck in an unavoidable freestyle disco competition. The skills you can upgrade are stealth, hand-to-hand combat, and then four kinds of guns, which I feel makes little sense. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would anyone specialise in shotguns when a shotgun is a situational weapon? What are you gonna do if there's an enemy more than ten feet away, throw your shoes at him?
The dialogue system gives you about one second to pick a conversational attitude that is summed up in one word, and it's often hard to decipher. You might be talking to a sexy lady, for e.g., when suddenly an option comes up reading, say, "Trousers." And there's no way of knowing if this means the poncemaster general will change the conversation to the subject of trousers or draw attention to a specific pair of trousers sneaking up behind them or whatever. So you select it out of panic, whereupon El Ponco promptly pulls his trousers down and slaps his bum while mooing like a lost calf, spoiling your reputation with the character somewhat.
Dialogue seems a bit buggy at times, too, which I guess is inevitable with conversation trees as labyrinthine as this. There was a moment when I was gabbing away with another sexy lady when the option came up to initiate a quick knobbing, which went down reasonably well. And nothing could pose a challenge after that, short of the invention of some kind of ponce-seeking missile.
All in all, Alpha Protocol is weak and poorly balanced, like a three-legged dog with an eating disorder. But I want to come back to the story for a bit. You know that extremely brief summary I gave about five paragraphs ago? That's literally the extent of the plot I understood.
