Before Alpha Protocol, I didn't know Obsidian Entertainment existed. I didn't know they developed Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II, I didn't know they made Fallout: New Vegas, and I didn't know they created the Neverwinter Nights series. Heck, it wasn't until my second playthrough of Alpha Protcol almost half a year later that I discovered how much I really, really like this game.
Obsidian Entertainment is best known for being the developer other developers hand their franchises to when they hit a creative rut. Bioware handed them Knights of the Old Republic, and Bethesda handed them Fallout. In both cases, Obsidian took those franchises and surpassed the original games.
Alpha Protocol, while technically released after Fallout: New Vegas, could be seen as Obsidian's first original IP since Neverwinter Nights, and boy is it an ambitious one. Alpha Protocol is an action-y/stealth-y/gadget-y/spy-y with aspirations to being everything that Mass Effect promised to be. It plays like a movie, emphasizes player choice, and offers a diverse number of playstyles.
It comes within micrometers of being one of my favorite games. It's so close to being perfect that I can almost smell it. With some tweaking, the stealth could be great, the shooting fun, and the storyline fascinating. Unfortunately, small things muck up the gameplay. Stealth is hampered by the lack of attention the boss battles pay to it, alongside inconsistent NPC fields of view. The story is... well, while it's very nicely presented, it tends to be an incomprehensible mess.
I didn't have much of an idea what was going on until my second playthrough.
But despite the flaws, Alpha Protocol is very, very good. For all its flaws, it's an ambitious game, and it earns an easy recommendation from me.

Sneaking steadily into the future, Invisible Inc. is sure to please fans of both stealth and turn-based strategy. A steep learning curve can make it difficult to warm up to, but impressive depth, customizability, and replayability easily make it worth the time.
The major highlight is the variety of abilities, both for your agents and hacking entity “Incognita”. They give the player a great degree of control and flexibility – essential for the high difficulty and occasionally unfair procedurally-generated maps. I also like the moody visual/audio presentation, which aptly depicts the oppressive corporate-dominated sci-fi world.
I have an issue with the length, though. The last mission in particular feels less like a finale and more like a turning point, after which I was expecting the story to begin a new arc. But...then the credits started rolling. It's a shame, because the way the game is designed would have made it easy to write a longer, more thought-provoking story. Thankfully, the replay value of the 5-hour campaign is very high; it's fun to play around with different abilities and character builds.
As it is, Invisible Inc. feels like second-tier turn-based strategy, behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Valkyria Chronicles. As a fan of stealth games, I love how unique it is, and how deep it can be at times, but I also feel that it could have been much better. No regrets picking it up, though.

Before Alpha Protocol, I didn't know Obsidian Entertainment existed. I didn't know they developed Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II, I didn't know they made Fallout: New Vegas, and I didn't know they created the Neverwinter Nights series. Heck, it wasn't until my second playthrough of Alpha Protcol almost half a year later that I discovered how much I really, really like this game.
Obsidian Entertainment is best known for being the developer other developers hand their franchises to when they hit a creative rut. Bioware handed them Knights of the Old Republic, and Bethesda handed them Fallout. In both cases, Obsidian took those franchises and surpassed the original games.
Alpha Protocol, while technically released after Fallout: New Vegas, could be seen as Obsidian's first original IP since Neverwinter Nights, and boy is it an ambitious one. Alpha Protocol is an action-y/stealth-y/gadget-y/spy-y with aspirations to being everything that Mass Effect promised to be. It plays like a movie, emphasizes player choice, and offers a diverse number of playstyles.
It comes within micrometers of being one of my favorite games. It's so close to being perfect that I can almost smell it. With some tweaking, the stealth could be great, the shooting fun, and the storyline fascinating. Unfortunately, small things muck up the gameplay. Stealth is hampered by the lack of attention the boss battles pay to it, alongside inconsistent NPC fields of view. The story is... well, while it's very nicely presented, it tends to be an incomprehensible mess.
I didn't have much of an idea what was going on until my second playthrough.
But despite the flaws, Alpha Protocol is very, very good. For all its flaws, it's an ambitious game, and it earns an easy recommendation from me.

Off of the high that was Civilization V, I was excited to get my hands on Civ VI. New features, unstacking cities, making wide play viable, it was looking promising. And then I played it.
At first it seemed okay, time would allow it to improve. But it didn't get better; it got worse. New "features" were added instead of fixing problems.
The AI is brutal: you need to jump through arbitrary hoops just to please them and check the boxes. Instead of ambitious leaders wanting to expand power we are left with toddlers that want to play a game with you. Follow their rules and they'll leave you alone. Let's just ignore leaders that have the drive to look out for their best interest and cause you trouble. Instead we need to pacify minor obstacles so we can do our thing alone.
Units are extremely thin on progression. You jump from an outdated unit to the greatest unit ever, which then becomes outdated soon enough. Not only do there need to be more units to fill the gap they need to be balanced better. Units shouldn't be specialized to the extreme they  all need to be dangerous. And Unique units, outside of War Carts are extremely forgettable. Add some danger.
And my biggest issue with the game is the only way to play well is to maximize your adjacency bonuses. Meaning that tactics, risky investments, unique playstles are all really punchless and the only way to succeed is to play your land. You don't design your city, you fit into what you're given. And if you didn't get that amazing spot for a Science District you don't have much you can do.
Not everything was better in Civ V and earlier, but when you have a game that just got more details right and then go to a game where they cared more about making history look the way they wanted rather than paying attention to balancing their own game.
Civ VI can be a great game but first they need to focus on the details.
It feels like watching a good American TV drama.

The game is highly unplayable for any length of time. There are just too many show-stopper bugs that are simply not being addressed.
* "Balanced" start position is not balanced.
* Barbarians are hopelessly overpowering in the early game.
* Start positioning was broken completely with the Fall "patch", so you have to start 20-30 games just to get one that has a reasonable position for your capital.
* The fog of war is terrible. They use the same colors for both currently not visible terrain and never-visited terrain.
* The icons for visted terrains with resources are all brown, rather than having at least the shading of the resource colors.
* In single-player mode, the game focuses on defeating the human far too much. Barbarians will bypass other civ or city-state units just to attack the human, even if it should be obvious that they need to attack the AI.
* Many options in the game were present in Civ V, but completely missing from VI. How do I turn off spying? You don't. How do I turn off barbarians, or make them tougher? You don't. How do you get the game to use a new random seed if you go back to a saved game? You don't. All of these and many more were in Civ V, but are not in VI. How can a game "upgrade" forget important features from previous versions?
* And many more.
Most of all, they seem to be completely oblivious to the major issues they have. They need to have a feedback mechanism that works. If only I could get some kind of response that says they realize how bad they did and want to make it better. But, they don't seem to care about their players, beyond advertising the next expansion.
There are a lot of really cool features (like eurekas, builders, districts, and more). But, not nearly enough to make up for the horrible gaffs.
Overall the game is not very good at all. Unless they make fixes (BEFORE the expansion), I will avoid buying more product from them completely. I'm not about to pay for them to fix their bugs.

I have been looking forward to Executive Assault for a long while now. It is still in early access and is a really great concept. However, it is not ready for any real gameplay. The visuals are ok but the game has a lot of work to be a truely great game.
Pros:
+ Cool art style allows for graphics to stay as is without any real issues, though is early 2000s looking.
+Decent RTS gameplay and ok FPS gameplay.
+Can enter buildings and build interior and exterior defences.
+Cannot spam defenses so it is possible to take an enemies base.
+Best elevator music ever.
Cons:
-Unit desync is a major issue. Connecting to another player is also an issue and is very sporatic. I had a 1v1 match and the other player could see exactly where I was, exactly where my single bot was, but said they had an army in my office, and I killed them all with one invulnerable bot. As far as I could tell, all his men were outside shooting my walls.
-Graphics are 2000s looking. Not a big deal, however there are loads of detail issues that need fixed, such as clipping and shots going through walls and not really being there.
-Damage is severely unbalanced. A tank destroys everything, but a group of bots destroys the world. Defence is useless. It is better to just invest in more bots with better weapons. They grind though doors like they dont exist, yes, forcefield, safety and security doors like tissue paper. Walls last only a few seconds longer. Your greatest defense is the long travel time of the elevator.
-Low tech weapons and ballistics in general are useless.
-No guides or tutorials.
-Air vehicles easy to shoot down but can destroy all your defences including interior defences while building.
-FPS mode rendered useless as unit ai is just too quick and does sooo much damage that there is no reason to use FPS mode. Sniping is possible, but you do so little damage that FPS mode only helps with late game fights. Strafing has little to no effect so why bother?
-Base building is more of a puzzle of placement more than anything. Once the enemy is inside your base it is game over unless you have spammed lots of hallways to have loads of turrets inside the base. More often than not, the game is over before you even build your first few handfulls of bots.
-There is no point to leaving your office ever as CEO. If you leave, your are dead. 1 shot kills you. Your pistol is a joke. If you leave and the enemy takes your office, you might as well surrender. You cannot do ANYTHING on foot as the CEO. Unless you have an ally or lots and lots of units on the ground, you are dead. You might as well just stay in the office and die ending the match.
In conclusion, the game is a great concept, works kinda , but has lots of bugs and balancing issues. Being in Early access, this could all be fixed, in which case the game would be a 9/10. Otherwise, it is currently a 5/10 as it is mostly unplayable for me.

♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC decisions aside (which have always been present), I think that the gameplay of Civ VI is a pretty strong improvement upon what came before.
The new District system feels completely organic and the way it's meant to be played. Gone are the days of building every improvment in your one new city as fast as possible, as now you can develop a city to complement its natural surroundings. This, in turn, places a higher importance on placing a city in the proper spot. Now, the beauty, resources, water access, and terrain all can factor into a successful or abyssmal city, while the civilation you chose might be able to squeeze the extra resources needed to make a poor tundra city into a sprawling scientific or religious sanctuary.
Great people now have purpose other than getting 400 of them to build observatories since you can't figure out anything else you want to do with them. They have distinct abilities which allow you to purchase or use them in a way that can benefit even other victories for your civilization.
If I have a sticking point, it has to be on the leader's aesthetics and map designs. I feel the cartoony version of characters they have created does not lend themselves to the epic historical tale they are trying to tell. It feels much more like a mobile game design than it does a AAA Strategy Turn-Based Game. Not to mention, the minimap no longer shows borders only on land, so water is now included for an abysmal mess of a map. While it seems like it would be strategically efficient, it ends up looking like a hexagonal mess rather than the nice and distinct map styles of Civ V. This is my main sticking point with the game, as I don't know how many times I make a proud archipelago country, only to realize that I look like a big block since half my tiles cover the ocean.
The AI can make some dumb decisions, however I have equally seen them make some brilliant moves that I just don't see coming. The lower difficulties can have you get caught in a loop where a leader plays right into your abilities, so you win super fast (I had Australia, and I kept having Civs that were classical level technology declare war on my atomic era nation; this gave me way better production and I basically got catapulted to my science ending). However the divide is distinct to the regular game mode, where it seems like win/loss is about 60/40 if you aren't min/maxing your cities and playing some odd statistical game.
Generally a title worthy of the Civilization name, however, some baffling design choices that just leave me wondering whether the "love of history" will remain long over the "love of simplicity for the sake ease".

Life is Strange, a game that buries some other story rich games with lots of additions.  A game that shows an example that goes beyond just a point and click.
The story revolves around a student named Max Caulfield who is a college student in photography and has the ability to reverse time. Which is the the crucial part about the game. However this is one game that I will always recommend above anything else because of the power to rewind time. The whole game takes place on Arcadia Bay, set in Oregon. The whole setting will take places from you own school or junkyards. The story itself is written above and beyond. There are lots of plot twists, multiple climaxes, and can feel like a real emotion roller coaster and can make you cry multiple times that you might end up with dry eyes after multiple flushes....well not really...but in general you will love the story and the cast of characters with different personalities.
Reversing time in this game is the key component of gameplay. When you make a decision in the game and you thought you made a bad one, you can always reverse and try choosing the other option and what you think, so you can get the best choice. Speaking of choices, you will have not to choose between two, but three or more in some parts of the story. However, there will be a few moments in the game that you will never be able to reverse time during critical moments in the story. And you cant rewind an entire episode just to fix something from 2 hours earlier. So it doesn't mean you're completely safe. Other story rich games like this don't give you the option to reverse completely and try something else. Unless you want to replay an entire episode that takes 1 hour just to say something different in one part of the story.
While time reversing will be very helpful in tough situations, it also plays a role in puzzles. Some puzzles in the game require you to be at a different place at an early time before something happens. Making it so there is someone to save or something bad to happen that is optional but can help along the way of the main plot.
Your character, Max, will also have an inventory with her. She carries a diary, photo album, cellphone, and charcater biographies. You will be using your cell phone and photo album for completeing puzzles and helping you progress through the story. However, when you mess with time, your phone and album can also change. So for example, you might have a enemy in the present but changing time can make that enemy, your ally, but it will negatively effect the closest characters in the game. The photo album is usefull for typing in passwords  or bypassing locks. Your diary will describe your history before and during the game, from the choices you made to what you have seen. Adn your character bios are, well you know, bios of the characters you meet and interacted with. Your cell phone will notify you about text messages from the characters you meet, messages will also change if you changed time so you might be suprised if your friends with your closest enemy.
But what makes this game better than other story rich games is its brain games. For example, since you have time powers you will use them to memorize things in the present and predict them in the past. Although you can rewind time to try again, it takes several attemps if you have bad memory skills.
Even though you will be doing point and clicks with other characters in the game, there will be times where you will have to control your charcters and do stealth sections when sneaking into somewhere, this makes the game less boring with
clicks and more like a mini metal gear solid game (still waiting for chapter 3 *hint* *hint*) and is a wonderful touch to the immersion of the game and I thank DONTNOD for adding this addition to the game.
Now while you can still rewind time backwards a couple of minutes from the present, you actually can travels years bacwards by focusing on photos. This matches with Max's love for photography and her powers at the same time. By playing a little mini game on a photograph, you will be able to travel years back for the start of the actual game. But heres the catch, you can't travel everywhere as there are walls that will block where you go so you have little room to explore and that its a limited time trip. However, there will be cutscenes where you will brough back to the start of the game but will some limits and changes.
During your adventure, you will have opportunities to get pictures of certain objects or people. Most of the pictures you will take are basically achievements that you earn but there will be times where you will be able to take pictures that can benefit you during your story.....or make it worse......depends on what you choose or believe.
The soundtrack to the game blends perfectly well with the game. Its not some retro, orchestra bs. The genres to the music goes from country, to rock, and simple acoustics and maybe a few snyths. It brings a nostalic feel of being a kid or being curious about everyting.
The graphics are simple and I like it that way. Its good for people who can't afford a beast pc and gives that old school cartoon feel, but with violence and real drama thrown in.....basically an upgrade from the walking dead graphics.
However, the only small thing that I found that was kinda weird in my 14 hour session was the lip syncing issues in the game. Although you will mostly pay attention to the subtitles and dialoge, you might come across lip syncing problems in a few parts of the story. Mostly the lip syncing would be working fine during the story but you might come across where your protagonist, Max, will talk without moving lips and it might look weird (and sometimes I think that shes talking to herself in her head, lol). I don't find it annoying or bothering since I don't really pay attention to it but a fix to this bug would be appreciated so it doesn't kill my crying mood, lol.
Ok, well I think I covered almost everything I've experienced in this game. My conclussion: IT IS TOTTALLY 100% WORTH A BUY, Even if it's not on sale. This is probably the best story rich experience I had ever since playing the walking dead.
Rating: 10/10
Note: 10/10 doesn't mean its perfect, but it means that this game is memorable and deserves to be in everyones library.

Klei is involved with some excellent games with roguelike elements,
(Darkest Dungeon, Necrodancer, Don't Starve) and Invisible is no exception.
The asking price is pretty steep, in my opinion, because roguelikes inherently reuse content. You only get the thrill of hearing the music, seeing the visuals, and watching the story unfold once. Things only become worth it because of the replayability.
It's pretty damn good, but don't expect a Shadowrun: Dragonfall without the magic. (Or any RPG elements)
Invisible feels very high stakes and is quite short. The roguelike-ness makes it a replayable puzzle,
like a game of chess played on a rubiks cube.
Buy it if you like hardcore challenge and strategy, or wait for a decent sale.
There is no praying to RNG here, only cold hard calculation.

A top down mega violent ultra stylish game with cool music and art. It's gritty and challenging as one mistake can see you PRESSING R TO RESTART and prepare to do it many times over the course of the game. It was short but for ten bucks I felt the length was appropriate; I'm just being selfish and wanting it to last longer. Unlockables consist of different masks that you can wear while "working" (DIE DIE DIE) and weapons of all types. My personal favorite are the throwing knives and standard shotgun. I haven't unlocked all the weapons as they're not all so different that I want to repeat any missions to unlock them.
Let's talk replay value. for me, it's relatively low; I wish there was more outside of the story to do. After you beat the game there isn't much to unlock that you haven't unlocked already. There's a healthy amount of achievement get if that's your poison but I feel like achievements are just padding for the game at times. Kill x amount of enemies with x, kill x amount of enemies, break this many windows; maybe I'm nut's but it really just doesn't do that much for me. I'd much rather have a set of challenge maps included that are stupid hard. Maybe they're waiting for me in the sequel.

Some people say this game is really weird. Well, the story is bizarre, but the game is fast paced and fun. I skip most of the story anyway, so it really doesn't matter. The game feels like a speed run; kind of like Super Meatboy, except the visuals are more of a top-down shooter, like SmashTV. The game doesn't play like those games though; it plays more like a stealth game, and, though you can play it like that, just going as fast as you can is more rewarding. Also, if you mess up, you start over right away, so you keep telling yourself "one more time".
The flaw I have with the game is the terribly mapped controls if playing via a controller. They have your main abilities mapped to the bumpers/triggers, instead of on the buttons, like a standard game. I couldn't find a way to remap the controls either. Most people say the game is good with a mouse and keyboard, but I am currently on a laptop, and do not have access to a mouse.
Overall, I'd say try this game out. It's really fun, but use a mouse and keyboard. If you can get used to the controls, try a controller, but I am sick of playing it with the controls as they are.

An excellent blend of extremely dark and depressing atmosphere with a psychotic sense of humor. The play value stays high, and in some ways increases each time you attempt to play through the game.

All in all this is a game that holds enough challenge to keep any player entertained, and a vast enough range of possible "power-up" combinations to keep you coming back to this long after you should have gone to bed. The over-the-top darkness is both disturbing and humorous so that the less mature players will laugh at poo-poo-jokes, while the more mature ones contemplate the more grim aspects of a child covered in excriment attempting to kill his half-aborted bretheren with nothing more than his own tears

If you are a fan of stealth games you should definitely try this one out.
To summarize this game, it's a 2D top down stealth/strategy game with a variety of characters to choose from. You start with 2 characters and you unlock more as you gain xp which can be done by completing the campaign or getting as far as you can. Each character has their own unique augments and items that offer a lot of options on how to progress through each level. The biggest draw for me is the fact that each level is randomly generated so there's no such thing as replaying the campaign and knowing exactly what to expect.
The game gets more challenging as you increase the difficulty which means every action you make and your positioning matters more than ever. Other game modes include time attack which gives you about 2 minutes to complete your turn and endless mode which gradually increases the difficulty everyday. You can even modify the settings of these modes very thoroughly. One more thing i should add is that the voice acting and sound effects are great.

There are some bugs that make gameplay a bit more difficult than it should be, however, nothing is gamebreaking and I never had to re-load the game because something bugged out to where I couldn't do something.  For me, I had a bit of a camera-jerkiness problem that was easily fixed in the Engine.ini file. Quite honestly, I'm not too sure what the big deal was about this game being so bad when it was released.  I experienced no game-breaking issues at all.  Now, for the good: this story is as interesting as you want to make it. The timed dialogue choices are awesome, and this game has ridiculous replay value.  I played as the "nice and professional" guy, which landed expected results, but there are three or even four other choices at times that will drastically change your experience.  You can go through the game at your own pace and to whichever place you want first - which also impacts your game.  (Unless you write down everything you do, I doubt you'll have a run that is EXACTLY the same.)  The story is neat, and what I liked most is that I never truly knew who to trust.  At times I thought a certain person had my back, just to find out they sold me out and then tried to kill me.  The twists were interesting and the game is quite good.  I played on Normal and it took me about 17 hours, exploring everywhere, experimenting with the Black Market, etc.  I would recommend you guys to get this guy as it's the only game like this that I know of.  Deus Ex is the general comparison, but this game is nothing like DE:HR, so it's not fair to compare it.  Next time it's on sale, be sure to grab it.

I highly recommend this game but this recommendation comes with a warning.
In short : the game is good, there is a bit of re-playability here. If you are looking for graphics and progressive and diverse game play this isn't it. This is immersive in it's style.
The story line is great. You wake up one morning as a guy who consistently gets phone calls telling him he needs to go to work. Thing is, the guy one day works as a handyman the next he's some sort of bar tender. Does it matter? No as you show up to the location ready to make your screen red.
The game play is addictive. I found though that this game was a hit for a few of my friends while others found it repetitive very quickly and boring as there wasn't anything major progressing. As you go through the missions, you unlock weapons as well as masks which give you special features (such as seeing further or being able to take a bullet). You may use a keyboard or a controller to play the game. Either way, the controls are made nice and feel really smooth. Once you get the hang of it, setting targets up and hitting the right guy (usually the guy with the gun) becomes natural. LT also let's the player see a little further ahead of themselves. Guns can be used, people can be knocked out, knives can be used, people can be choked out on the ground, people can be knocked out for a bit with doors, and you can be seen through windows and quickly get shot by a guy you neglected to see.
The graphics are as you see. They are decent and are fitting for the game. Again though, some of my friends thought the graphics sucked and walked away from the game without trying it.
I would recommend the game on sale.

Civilization VI lacks what made earlier versions of the game so fun to play.  This becomes apparent when you play at the most basic level (Settler).  In earlier games this level was sort of a beer and peanuts style level .. something to play quick and know you were going to easily beat the AI .. something where you go make all the mistake you wanted just having fun and still come home a winner.  Not Civ VI.  Even at the basic level you still have to carefully balance all the needs of your empire from where to build items, building of trade routes (otherwise you run out of gold fast).  Heck I was playing a recent game and on the last turns once I declared on the last enemy (pure dom game) my income went negative and I could not correct.  Even as I attacked the capital the game was deleting army units to pay down costs (without asking me what to delete) and I barely took the capital.  IN other words Civ VI is far more complex to play that prior versions.  The whole faith based religion system makes it easy to win with religon (how many replays have you seen on you tube where someone is close to a victory and loses to a religon based empire who with all those advantages keeps spamming out apostles) to the detriment of other styles of play.  The economy forces you to interact and trade with other empires as without that you won't have the needed gold.  Resource distribution is also so hit ans miss as it forces interaction with the other empires.  It's become more like a socialist view of the world game where you have to work with the others playing to get your resources and gold or fail, fail, fail (and in between trade deals you sit around singing kum-bai-yah).
It's superior to Mass Effect 3..... I'll stand by that.

I think the Telltale style adventure game was the future when TWD first came out. And in some ways I still think that's the case. But of course, this kind of game has also its problem: one of the major ones being the game endings, and how to let the player know that his choice actually matters. The first game (as in some other telltale titles) said "Ok, you get to choose who lives" but a lot of the times the characters will die further ahead (or the will be irrelevant to the plot).
This is a pretty big issue that comes with these games: you have to make the player feel like they have control over the story arc, but you also have to just make one game that anyone can play. In some ways I'm cool with some decisions the team made with this title and Wolf Among Us, by letting the player know their action at the end caused some sort of results (a character will not like what the protagonist did, and things like that), but again this was not a perfect solution since...Well, people want the game to be resolved and not to continue infinetely
So, as a conclusion for this strange review I just want to say this: I feel like the decision-making of this game is scarse and yet pretty solid, especially in the end. So I would recommend it, I think it will give you at least 8-9 hours of enjoyment

If you feel pressured into buying anything from the market, PLEASE wait until the end game. Only legendary gear can level up with you, and I have already replaced my lvl 5 epic sword (preorder bonus, game was 35% off) with a bog standard weapon dropped by a lvl 10 enemy.
With that out of the way, I am enjoying my time with the game, but there are just too many things that annoy me in order to reccomend it. This will likely be the game i play while watching youtube on my second monitor while i chase that 100% completion goal. I will not be engaged the entire time in any meaningfull way, so while i am perfectly happy with playing a game like this, well, not everyone likes mindless busy work. I know not everyone will be irked by the same things as me, so positives first.
Pros:
The new movement mechanics are fun to play with and the sprint is very much appreciated. The world is much larger and there is an increadible amount of variety. The vast ammount of collectibles discovered via climbable light houses can be a detractor for some people, but i've already discovered several areas that i wouldnt have found without the collectables so i like them. The lore of the items and world are very engaging, granted i have never read the books so please take it with a grain of salt.
Combat has also been rebalanced, focus recharges quicker and rather than using runes to change how your abilities work, the skill tree has three possible upgrades for nearly every ability. I eagerly await the end game to see which game i feel more powerful in. Enemy ranks also refill very quickly. In the first game i would regulaly have an empty nemesis tree because they repopulated so slowly. Im constantly fighting new war chiefs that make the world feel more lived in.
Cons:
The loot system feels increadibly unnecesary. I've stopped picking up loot until i can get the upgrade that does it for me. The 5-10 extra damage is just too small an improvement to be worth my time. This could have EASILY been a "bow does +20% damage" style of upgrade tree. There was no need to reinvent the wheel, and was only done to sell loot boxes. I'm saddened by the thought of what all of that extra work could have gone towards, especially when i see poor writing and a seveer lack of polish.
This game has more cliche's than should ever be associated with a professional work. The obvious bad guy who betrays you because they are bad, laughably poor dialogue and character development, and stopping in the middle of a warzone to dramatically ask someone their name. All of this is within the first hour of play, mind you. The poor writing also extends into the gameplay.
You start the game with the new ring of power but loose it quickly (another cliche...). Even during the time that you have it, it is NEVER displayed how or why it is so great. For all their love of cliches they could have at least given us a max lvl character so we could utterly destroy the few enemies we encounter before loosing it. This lack luster writing fails to drive home why it is so important to get back.
The game also lacks a LOT of polish. Clothing textures will clip through each other in PRE-RENDERED cutsceens, cutscenes don't show the armor i actually have equipped, hair textures have easily seen layers even on ultra (with dlc textures), Golum's mouth doesn't move in some in game cutsceens, NPC's don't grip weapons, and walking through puddles doesn't change or influence the environment at all (Is a ripple or stock splash effect too much to ask for?). Enemies on the map also repopulate the world VERY quickly. They give no XP so they are litterally only there to get in the way and waste time.
The new enemy types are appreciated and change the flow of combat, but i am unimpressed with the constant bombardment of combat cinematics that only give me time to see just how graphically unimpressive the game looks (even with HD texture pack). Is there even a way to turn off the combat slow down cinematics? Only two hours into the game and I've already grown tired of getting the same dull cinematic executions and attacks recycled from the first game. It breaks up the flow of the game and sucks me out of my immersion.
Also, despite spending 100+ hours playing the first game there is no recognition of this. I start with no bonuses to wealth, experience, or gear. Games like Borderlands and Mass Effect do this, so why can't this game?

80 minutes in and I have to say, this game is worth the 24c I payed. But I would be disappointed if I payed the 5USD asking price (6.24AUD for me currently). As a fun tower defense game, I can say there is nothing onscreen that isn't needed. After 5 minutes I turned off all Audio ingame as it is just a small set of annoying sounds, a stock robot voice and infuriatingly annoying music. The menu music is too loud for it's own right. But, I do enjoy this game. Tower Defense games are immensely fun, and this is no exception. I would get it while it is on sale, otherwise, I would hold your money and get another TD game. This feels like it should be in early access though, so be warned. It is rough around the edges, I am unable to get Multiplayer Co-Op working, and did I mention the horrible audio effects? Yes? Well, I will until they're changed.
The gun variety. This is something I would file as neutral instead of just good or bad. It has good variety, from the stock Laser turret (essentially a short burst machine gun turret) to the EMP turret which slows down enemies (but is not worth the money, keep away as it is faulted massively). I like the plama turrets. They are very nifty for when there is a distance to cover with a lot of power needed. I tend to put them near to the entry point.
The EMP turret is very bad. I thought it would be helpful but took me 10 rounds to realise the geo is only slowed down until it gets shot. Why would they chose this as a design decision? It is very strange in my opinion. But the other turrets do suffice in how well they work, just stay off of the EMP.
All in all, this game is fun and a good distraction, not the best TD game. Not the most well made game in general either. It's UI is about as bland as the UI from Bad Rats. And we all know how terrible that game was, dont we...
If you have some money to spare from maybe some steam trading cards, go for it, it's worth a buy then. But for the $5 marking price I personally wouldn't go for it. There are plenty of other TD games out there for such a low price with much higher content and a lot more well made than this one. But for a game which you can lose hours in , I don't regret ny purchase one bit.

Pros:
- Story. This is the main part of this game. If you like the story, you will like the game. It contains many themes: self-identification and coming of age, insecurities and bullying, time travel and consequences. These themes are very relevant in every age, so I can recommend this game not only to highschoolers and young adults, but to older peaople as well. In some moments it reminds me about 'Catcher in the Rye', which is a great book - read it if you like story in the game. Story has it flaws but I was into it from the start to finish. This game would be really good part of school program. If sometimes we see videogames as part of school program :)
- Level and charcters design. Each place in the game is very atmospheric and beliavable. Characters based on standard archetypes, but multidimensional and actually feel realistic and unpredictable.
- Music and sound. Music is on point and perfectly fits atmoshere. Sound is very good.
- Voice acting. One of the best i've heard in video games. Beliavable and polished.
- Gameplay. This is a light adventure game(e.g. "walking simulator") so gameplay is pretty simple. You looking at items at people and hear Max comments about them. Rewind mechanic is used to replay dialog and to solve simple puzzles. Though it is simple, gameplay is engaging and not boring. And Max's remarks about what she sees are hilarious sometimes. It does not irritate you with QTE(like Fahrenheit or Heavy Rain) or bores you to death with a long walks and expositions(like Firewatch or Uncharted climbing sections).
Cons:
- Facial animation. Characters barely move their lips and facial expressions are very stiff.
Verdict: 9/10, Play free first episode to see are you into the story or not. If yes, buy, even without discount.

This is a great game! I feel it's important to state up-front that this is a rogue-like game. Some people are calling it "rogue-lite" because there are options to allow single-turn rewinds and level replays, but expert mode (the intended mode) only gives you a single rewind per level and no level retries. This is only barely more forgiving than iron-man mode which is effectively full rogue-like mode with no rewinds. It is very well done if you like the genre.
Playing this game feels like a hybrid between FTL, Dungeon of the Endless (DotE), and Monaco. Upgrading your character with augmentations and items feels very much like FTL's ship upgrades (minus the energy requirement). Level play has similarities to DotE in that room control is important and you sometimes leave a man back a room or two to keep a guard occupied. You also find "merchants" within levels to upgrade rather than in between levels (mostly). Evading guards reminds me of Monaco's playstyle.
In other words, it's stealth X-COM in a rogue-like format. Amazing game. Very well done!

Disclosure: X-COM, which this game draws inspiration from, is one of my all time favorites, as is Klei's Mark of the Ninja. As a team, Klei Entertainment has made indies that are are both innovative and fun, and I respect that. However, I really wish this game could have been better...
My actual rating is: Mixed, but in absence of that option, it leans towards negative
Invisible Inc is a gameplay mechanic driven roguelike that holds a huge amount of promise, if only the game didn't feel like it was made entirely by the gameplay mechanics and graphics teams, two areas where the game shines. This is a game that was designed to be replayed a lot, and to remain challenging each time. Unfortunately, the weak story deprives the player of a lot of motivation to invest in that content. Let me elaborate:
The Pledge: A stealth driven random generated roguelike where confronting guards heads on is infeasible, the objective is to build the best team you can in 72 hours, like FTL. Excellent cutscene introduction sets expectations high for great visuals and great plot points. This game had one of the very best Pledges, setting my expectations really high given the slick execution of the first two hours
The Turn: Tense game of Cat and Mouse, with each action decidedly a calculated risk and the ever increasing security timer forcing an aggressive play style. Difficult to get new items, and soon PWR is a scarce resource to be rationed. New guard types (thankfully no dogs), viruses, and new goodies to buy keep moderately interested but lack of any story content during missions / barely any between missions is a gigantically big missed opportunity. Feels more like an elaborate puzzle than an actual strategy game due to the limited patrol areas of guards, and the extremely strange rule of sitting on top of guards as the only way to prevent them from waking up, while taking them out comes with strong penalties. Strategic decisions are related to which missions to pursue (each provides different boosts dependent on the type of mission), and where to invest your limited cash reserves (augmentations / gadgets / skill upgrades).
The Prestige: Where it all falls apart, only one ending, though the level map and specific enemies & locations are randomized. Due to a lack of context due to a dearth of story content, the ending feels both abrupt and all too sudden, with no fair visibility given on what will happen next in the series (beyond the very obvious). This was the point where I started questioning my purchase.
The Aftermath: Where the bulk of content is held, new agents, alternate agents (different abilities), and new abilties for your AI. Unfortunately, due to a lack of new story it came across as less appealing than it probably is, and I doubt I'll be investing a lot of time in it in the future.
For specific demographics:
Price sensitive: If you enjoy the Aftermath, it's worth the price, otherwise you're out of luck
Genre sensitive: Lots of throwaway cyberpunk joy, but never synthesized in any way that makes sense. Tons of tidbits but no overarching narrative that puts the pieces into context, major letdown
Strategy gamers: Frankly the game feels a lot like a puzzle but does have meaningful strategic choices, so it's worthwhile
Diversity seekers: Good premise, decent gameplay, fair variety in Aftermath. If you don't mind a weak story, go for it
Those with older systems: Game worked and ran beautifully and smoothly on my humble laptop, should run well anywhere
Art lovers: This, like Transistor, is a treat to the eyes
Final verdict: Great potential, if only it had invested more in story, this version feels incomplete. If you like mechanic driven games or particularly Turn Based games, go for it, it's a great product. For others, check out videos first and then take a call.
For more on the Pledge/Turn/Prestige/Aftermath Review structure, check out my blog, criticalh1t on Blogspot

"Mostly Positive" is a fair way to describe this game. The mechanics are superb, a great improvement over 5. City planning is a fun new aspect, and the inspirations make for a new and dynamic game every time you play as you take advantage of the situation you're given the best you can. Waging war is rewarded as well, unlike in its predecessor when having more cities crippled your infrastructure through unhappiness. And let's not forget an excellent presentation, including wonderful music, heartfelt narration, and utterly charming graphics and character design.
Several problems are worth bringing up, however.
The AI is terrible. Diplomacy is scarcely worth attempting, as the designers tried to balance the game by making computer players hate anyone that is doing well, and stamping tremendous relationship penalties for each city you take, even when at war with a third party and even when you are not the aggressor.
On top of that, CPU players don't understand combat at all, to a downright embarrassing degree. It's unclear how the designers could have screwed that part up so bad, as the combat isn't all that complicated.
There are also several interface issues, from unexplained mechanics like ranged unit obstructions, to combat predictions randomly displaying combat values in the tens of thousands. The Civilopedia is miserably incomplete and not always helpful, prompting excursions to the unofficial internet wiki to answer questions.
Then we have the more egregious issues.
Those who purchased the deluxe edition got ripped, plain and simple. On one hand, it's the own fault of consumers who threw their money at something without any concrete promise of what they were getting back, but on the other hand it took a very long time to get but a few extra leaders and Civs.
We've been promised cross-platform compatibility between Windows and Mac since launch. They still have no definite date set for this.
Patches have been slow to come and haven't fixed the major issues. Aspyr has, by all appearances, been very forthcoming about what they are hoping to achieve, but results have been consistently disappointing.
Ultimately, this is a very, very good game, but it's anything but "solid". For multiplayer, it's the best Civ game out there, and overall it's one of the best 4x games out there. But I still think you should wait for a good sale.

Buggy: I have 240 hours in this game and have yet to see 1 individule bugg. If any one says the game is buggy i do not mean to come off as rude but they could not be any more wrong.
What you should take away from this is that this game has very differnet game mechanics than any other civ game making it hard to start but once you learn the new mechanics it is an amazing game.

I've got mixed feelings when it comes to 'Alpha Protocol', the espionage-based RPG developed by Obsidian. I know it sounds pretty cool, right?  As far as RPGs go there are a lot of unique game play features in Alpha Protocol. There are plenty of stealth moments, tons of different guns and gadgets all with upgrades, and a branching storyline with many different twists and turns.
But, for every cool feature I listed above there is a negative to go with them.. Sure, there is indeed stealth and the stealth mechanic itself is pretty solid but if you set off ONE alarm you'll have to backtrack and MAKE SURE you turn it off. Otherwise guards will be alerted to your presence through out the WHOLE level, even if the alarm was set off 15minutes ago at the beggening part of the mission.
And yeah, there are a bunch of weapons to deck your main character out with and they are upgradeable, but the shooting mechanics are so spotty that it dosn't really matter. Its always more effective and reliable to simply go up and melee your enemies to death.
And then there is the story with many different player choices to be made, lots of different factions to ally with, and several paths and endings to be seen. Its just that....... The story only makes minimal sense to me and 90% of the time I was lost.. I got betrayed, chased people around that didnt even relate to me or the story, killed some people, and then received a generic ending... Yay?
Still..... I had some fun with the game, there is a little entertainment value here, and possibley after playing the game through several times and seeing different outcomes you might be able to grasp the 'whole' story and understand the things going on with the plot.. I'm just not convinced the game is good enough to warrant a second play through.

__Edit #2 (the only one worth reading)__
Having now played twenty hpurs of this game, I still stand by it. Shadow of War is an amazing game. Even my former complaints about captains being buffed to oblivion has more-or-less disappeared as I've gotten better. The gameplay is glorious and so is the story (both the actual campaign and the natural stories that unfold as part of the Nemisis System). YES, the loot boxes are a trashy addition (frankly the entire marketplace is), but it is not nearly enough to sour such an incredible game. Play the game as Monolith intended: sans loot boxes. Or whatever. Just play it -- it is so good.
__Edit__
Having played several more hours, I am having a harder time ignoring a few flaws. I still recommend the game, but qith some qualms. Monolith tried to improve upon SoM formula and in some areas it doesn't feel like the improvement was fleshed out enough. The best example if that of Captain (or higher) adaptation. The idea is that capatins will learn from your stategy if you don't mix it up enough; this is awesome, in theory. The problem, however, is that you often don't have enough tools at your disposal to battle a Captain who has adapted a lot. Some fights very quickly lose all ability to be done hand-to-hand and when hand-to-hand is the only option (such as fighting a Warlord) killing them becomes essentially impossible. Maybe if we had more options for combos or counters (or really just other ways to stun), this wouldn't be a problem. But when a Captain is immune to your stun strike ("E") and can't be vaulted over and is a shieldbearer or a savage (meaning they can't be struck from the front) and is immune to ranged.... what option do you have?
It is things like this that show the great intentions of Monolith, undone at least partially by a lack of development.
All that being said, I still love the game and highly recommend it.

Sharing my review.
Pros:
-Fluent FPS. I never had any lag at all throughout 70+ hours of gameplay, never froze, never crashed, no problems whatsoever. I don't know why people give a negative review, because you're either; crashing, lagging, low fps, freezing. It's the problem on your end, not the game's fault, so don't give a negative review just because your computer sucks, or you forgot to update your drivers.
-Good graphics. I don't know why people say that graphics are bad or not 'next gen.' There are two free dlcs that make your graphics a little better and more sharp, however it doesn't make much difference. In the end, the game looks beautiful and if you're not satisfied with the graphics then you can stick with Horizon Zero Dawn and keep moaning about how good it looks.
-Side quests are super fun and interesting. Well, at least Buz The Chopper one for me. I liked the orc, I liked his comedy, I liked his ambitions. Perhaps my most favourite orc of all time since I like comedy.
-Nemesis system. It's much improved since the last game. Much better. They took the system from the first one and built on it to create even better nemesis system than ever before. Orcs are interesting, many different orcs and huge variety of them and their personalities. You'll never get bored of listening to them. Sure, there are repetitive lines sometimes, but that's about it.
-Much bigger world. Maps. Gigantic compared to Shadow of Mordor. Lots to do.
Cons:
-The game's story is mediocore. You will yawn a lot during the cutscenes because nothing interesting is going on. There were a few parts that got me out of my chair and I was quite intrigued with the story in some moments. Side stories were more interesting than the main story line itself. All in all, it's as boring as Shadow of Mordor, but better. Not to mention they make you grind for the true ending. End game becomes mundane, repetitive and boring fast that you'll either watch the ending on youtube or cheat your way out. Not including the money whales that will actually buy lootboxes to get true ending.
-The combat. It's the same as Shadow of Mordor, they barely changed anything. Just added more skills to the pool. Same animations, most of the skills are the same, although that did not hinder my gameplay and enjoyment of the combat since they added a lot of new skills.
-Equipment. Armour and weapon sets were kind of repetitve. I'd say there's only like 10 sets of armours and weapons in general. Because most of them were re-colored. Same piece of armour, but different color. So there was no excitement at all whenever I got a piece of equipment from the orcs in late game. Once you get Armor of Vengeance legendary set, you will not part from it for awhile. End game legendary set you get for free is pretty much the same design as the set of Vengeance, just different colors. They could've made more armour sets with different designs or it's pretty limited. It's an improvement from the previous game though because Shadow of Mordor didn't have armours at all.
-Online conquests. Boring. Plain disappointment. It will become tedious after some time. I want to know how my fort was conquered. Able to know the weaknesses of your fort and cover them so it wouldn't happen again. Since I am competitive and perfectionist, it's hard when there's no info or data of my defeated fortress. I want to improve and not make the same mistakes so it would be harder for the players to conquer my fortress. The option to participate in defending your fortress would be sweet, just like Metal Gear Solid 5, where you could defend your base from invaders. The conquering itself is a bit better, but could be better. I like how armies clash against the armies, I like how I blow up the door and rush into the fortress that soon will be mine. Yet, I feel no sense of accomplishment even if I do conquer. What I do get? Lootbox. What a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reward. With ♥♥♥♥♥♥ items in it. Doesn't make me feel motivated to continue to conquer other players' fortresses. Could I at least steal other players' orcs? That's a better reward.
-The orcs relationships. Devs said we'll get to be friends with the orcs. Uhm. Where? I never encountered that in the game. Sure, some of the orcs saved me from the death a few times, but that was it. I felt no connection with my orcs whatsoever. Whenever I was walking through my conquered fortress I wanted to interact with my orcs in some way. All they did was stand there like statues or dolls. Won't even pay attention to my existence when I am near them either. So the world felt less immersive and I didn't see any 'friend' part they had mentioned before the release. 74-77 hours in and nothing. I might have missed something, but from my experience that was it. What I wanted is the option to talk with my orcs, have some kind of relationship meter. I know it's not a sim game, but that option would've been super nice. This game is mostly about the orcs, nemesis system and personal stories we create, right? It's what is this game is most well-known for besides being LOTR game. So add the feature.
-Non memorable soundtrack. The music was mediocore at best, but it was not bad. The main thing we remember about the game is their music, and it was generic.
-Bugs. I encountered game breaking bugs sometimes, where I fell off the map and lost, and had to restart 20 minutes back since I was conquering main-story fort. There were a few other minor bugs, but nothing major.
-What I hated a lot is the movement of the character, it didn't listen to me most of the time, because my character didn't want to heed my commands. Especially climbing walls, I got stuck a few times when I was rushing to save my warchief since he was dying. And I lost him because my character decided to bump into wall 10 times before deciding to climb onto it. It was annoying. Sometimes my character jumps on a completely different object that I did not intended to, and I was not even aiming at that object at all. It's like the object sucked me in. Execution skill is a bit lousy as well. I am like 20 metres away from the captain I DO NOT WANT TO ATTACK. And I aim at the grunt instead, but my character decides to attack captain that is far away rather than an uruk that is close. Talion starts to moonwalk all the way to the captain with execution. It's ridiculous.
-No orc customization. I wish we could create our own custom orcs, a lot of them look bland and there were so many times I've seen a cool looking orc but with generic armour. Let us create our own orc captains. That would be superb. However, don't get me wrong, I've seen A LOT of cool looking orcs I've recruited, but still would've been wonderful if I could customize.
-Microtransactions. As a lot of people say, there shouldn't be microtransactions in a single-player game. Lootboxes don't really affect the gameplay all that much, but they cut a portion of the game from singleplayer campaign and added into lootboxes, and I am very annoyed because of that. Some have reported that there are orcs in the lootboxes you can't get in the normal game, there are items, armour, and everything in the paid lootboxes that you won't find in singleplayer. Let me quote what the devs said 'what you get from lootboxes you can get in singleplayer.' Well, that sounded like a complete lie, because it's not true. They lied about 'lootboxes ads' as well not being in the game, but hey, they're there anyway. Conclusion would be. Lootboxes DOES AFFECT YOUR GAME, but not your gameplay and not in the way where you won't be able to finish the game because of it. Yes, there's a heavy grind at the end of the game, but you can always cheat to get to the ending, while the items that were supposed to be originally in singleplayer game are in the paid lootboxes and out of our reach. They took out the content from 60$ game and want us to pay for it to access it.
Final thoughts: 7/10.

In addition to having a wonderfully clever title, Invisible, Inc. is a fantastic stealth game through and through; though it is possible to play the game by taking down guards and hacking drones left and right, the real triumph comes from navigating each of the randomly-generated levels while alerting or knocking out as few guards as possible. Klei Entertainment already has a solid stealth game, Mark of the Ninja, under its belt, so continuing with another stealth title is no surprise, and a real treat. Each agent has his or her own unique abilities that allow for a variety of tools for and methods of reaching each objective, and the characterization and voicework help flesh out a lovely dystopian future. Advanced difficulty levels provide ruthless, but balanced, challenges, and the endless mode allows room for experimenting and learning. For a great turn-based, stealth-focused game, Invisible, Inc. hits all the marks.

A pretty incredible stealth game which has a very strong aura of "Chess" toward the latter half of missions when♥♥♥♥♥♥starts to hit the fan. You're thrown into missions which you choose from a limited handful each playthrough to build yourself up to a grand finale.
At the beginning of each mission, you're thrown into a facility with no idea where your goal or your exit is, and control up to four agents at a time to achieve it. With the clock ticking, things get crazy fast. Real fast. Often a step ahead of when you expect, which keeps things constantly exciting.
The story is very simple and wont single handedly hold you through more than your first playthrough, but that's to be expected. I've got mixed feelings when it comes to 'Alpha Protocol', the espionage-based RPG developed by Obsidian. I know it sounds pretty cool, right?  As far as RPGs go there are a lot of unique game play features in Alpha Protocol. There are plenty of stealth moments, tons of different guns and gadgets all with upgrades, and a branching storyline with many different twists and turns.
But, for every cool feature I listed above there is a negative to go with them.. Sure, there is indeed stealth and the stealth mechanic itself is pretty solid but if you set off ONE alarm you'll have to backtrack and MAKE SURE you turn it off. Otherwise guards will be alerted to your presence through out the WHOLE level, even if the alarm was set off 15minutes ago at the beggening part of the mission.
And yeah, there are a bunch of weapons to deck your main character out with and they are upgradeable, but the shooting mechanics are so spotty that it dosn't really matter. Its always more effective and reliable to simply go up and melee your enemies to death.
And then there is the story with many different player choices to be made, lots of different factions to ally with, and several paths and endings to be seen. Its just that....... The story only makes minimal sense to me and 90% of the time I was lost.. I got betrayed, chased people around that didnt even relate to me or the story, killed some people, and then received a generic ending... Yay?
Still..... I had some fun with the game, there is a little entertainment value here, and possibley after playing the game through several times and seeing different outcomes you might be able to grasp the 'whole' story and understand the things going on with the plot.. I'm just not convinced the game is good enough to warrant a second play through.

Invisible Inc is an amazing game. I've been playing it over the past 2 weeks, and the more I play, the more I like it. Currently have 45 or so hours clocked in the game, which is actually the second highest playtime of any game in my Steam library! It's also one of the most addictive games I have played in recent memory that keeps drawing you back for more. Those 45 hours were played in under 10 days.
Anyways, the gist of the game is that it is a punishing "rogue-lite" turn-based strategy game, with a heavy emphasis on stealth. It draws inspiration from XCOM Enemy Unknown and has got similar interface, but the core tactical gameplay is very different.
The game's campaign can be completed pretty quickly (on your first try on Beginner, you should do it in under 4 hours), but this game has been thoroughly designed with increasing difficulty levels in mind. From Beginner to Experienced, and then to Expert, you should get three complete runs at least, each offering a unique playing experience. Also, you will die a lot, particularly when you get to expert, so the game makes you learn from your mistakes to improve future runs.
I myself played the game on Beginner first, then after 15 or so tries I got through Expert, after which I played Expert Ironman and finally completed Endless 5/10 days in the same run.
The game's levels are always randomly generated. Initially, I didn't like this, cause sometimes you can be dealt an unfair hand and the level generated could be extremely difficult to traverse. But eventually, over time, you learn to deal with it.
There's an element of risk vs reward. Do you go slow, at the expense of your alarm tracker increasing quickly...or do you go faster, at the expense of being spotted by the enemy?
Even though I've played for 45 odd hours, there are so many unique combinations of augments, programs, items and weapons that the game has got an incredible room for experimentation. Since all of these are randomly obtained or bought along the way, you always have to adapt your playstyle, and as such, the game doesn't become boring or repetitive.
There are 4 different enemy corporations, each of them having a different unique threat, so that adds to keep the game fresh as well. There's also around 7 or 8 different mission types, and you have to make your choices count on which mission type to select, based on your needs.
When I played the game on Beginner at first, I liked it. Then moving on to Expert, I found it too frustrating to the point I was almost going to stop playing. However, once I cleared that hurdle and moved on to Ironman and Endless runs, I have grown to absolutely love the game.
Recommended if you like turb-based strategy like XCOM, and/or if you like stealth games, and/or if you like challenging games that punish and make you learn from your mistakes.

Alpha Protocol is a game not without flaws, some of which can be noticeable and frustrating. The gunplay is unpolished and for the most part not very enjoyable. Enemy AI can be inconsistent, especially when it comes to the stealth aspects of the game. Some of the in-game animations can be painful to watch (I get back pains just thinking about the sneak/crouch animation). It's also known to have its fair share of bugs and glitches.
Having said all that, Alpha Protocol is still a fantastic action-RPG that I absolutely adored. It all starts with the timed dialogue system which offers several choices and forces you to think fast and pay close attention to the characters on-screen. Just about every decision you make can have an impact on the game going forward and cause the story to branch off in noticably different directions. Combined with the ability to tackle levels in various orders (which in turn influences how the story unfolds), you could play the game multiple times and have each playthrough be unique. The amount of freedom you're given over the course of the game is huge and quite refreshing.
The writing and story-telling are also bright spots. The complex story is full of conspiracy, coverups and espionage. The numerous characters you'll encounter along the way are generally interesting and well-written, most of which have lengthy backstories that you might not be able to uncover in a single playthrough. It's the kind of quality work you'd expect from Obsidian.
And while the sneaking mechanics can be janky at times, going the stealth route is still a whole lot of fun. Executing non-lethal take-downs and maneuvering through levels quiety and undetected is a satisfying feeling. Focusing on stealth/pistol gameplay and playing the Sam Fisher role is the preferred way to go and helps improve the gameplay exponentially.
Given its flaws and inconsistencies, Alpha Protocol is (understandably) a game not everyone will enjoy. However, I feel that if you can look past its problems and appreciate the unique aspects of the game, you can really enjoy the product that Obsidian created. In my opinion it's one of the finer and most underrated RPGs of the last few years.

This game is one of the greatest games ever made. It is a work of art. A masterpiece. I love everything about it.
If you have not played this game, then you are missing out. I know my friend said it looks♥♥♥♥♥♥(probably because of the pixel art style) but it really, really is the complete and utter opposite. Sure it has its problems, everything does. It's frustrating as ♥♥♥♥, it's caused me to yell and scream and break things. But it's amazing. The key to the game is your strategy, your tactics and your reactions. You have to think ten steps ahead of what you are about to move. What you will do next and where to go after that. You need to scout your soroundings, see how many weapons there are, how many weapons, et cetera. You need to PLAN.
The pixel art style is amazing, working in awesome colaboration with the modern techno music from MOON, Sun Arraw and the likes, to make you realise that it's set in the 1980's, but is actually from present day. There are vibrant neon colours to match this theme too. The pixel art style is supposed to represent the golden era of video games and how they were all pixelly, yet has a better colour pallet making it appear more modern.
Also the checkpoint system is the same, with the game only saving at the end of each "chapter" but checkpoints at the beginning of each floor. So if you die, you have to do the whole floor again - but if you quit you have to do the whole level again. I'm on the fence about that. I liked it but sometimes it was annoying. Especially as bosses were classified as a floor of the chapter, not seperate - so if a boss made you rage quit, you had to do the whole level again.
The story is great, you follow "Jacket" (real name unknown) as he recieves mysterious calls on his answering machine asking for him to perform simple tasks such as "make a delivery" but when he gets there, he finds out it is a hideout full of mobsters, and he has to figure out how to take them all out without dying. Guns alert nearby mobsters, some have guns, some melee weapons - and they WILL attack you if they see you, and to an extent try and find you.
Overall, I love this game. The Art Style is amazing, the soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing gorgeous and the story is great. It's one of the best games I have ever played, and I can't recomend it enough.

Although I recommend this game, I'm rather split on some of the issues Civ VI currently has. While I have a lot of fun playing Civ VI as someone who enjoys playing the game casually more than anything else, tiny things nag at me every so often that stop me from simply showering praise on the game as a whole
To begin, let me list some pros and cons, as well as some things I'm personally a little mixed on
To summarise, Civ VI is great fun if you enjoy the aspect of planning your own empire bit by bit into a self-contained superpower, and can be great fun in multiplayer. The managing of your empire is fun but not overwhelming or micro-manage-y (if that's a word?), and there are tools to help you plan where to place things, such as Lenses and Pins (which you can add more of with the right mods!), and building a wonder is just so satisfying!
However, the AI is, for lack of better word, flawed, and isn't something that I don't a hardcore strategist would fully enjoy, as they can jump from stupid to just plain unfair in a heartbeat. For example, I'm currently in a game as Nubia where Prince difficulty France suddenly skyrocketed ahead into the Information Era despite all the other AI of the same level being in the Renaissance and me just reaching the Modern Era. I still have no idea how they did this, but they are currently in the process of declaring a joint war against me with a warmongering civ and doing nothing besides letting the warmongering civ do the work while they build a rocket to Mars.
In short, I recommend the game, but expect some weirdness here and there

Well. I saw this version of the old masterpiece at 50% reduction so I bought in. I think that for my 12€ or so it's a decent price. So, what are my impressions? I'll keep this short.
Firstly, the almost 5 hour download astonished me, considering that the disc version is installed and up and runnung in less than an hour. But fair enough, I don't expect the earth for that price.
When I'd tweaked the settings to the same as my disc version I took a Mooney Bravo up from Kai Tak, just for a quickie.
The first thing I noticed - has anyone else? - is the torque drag (prop plane pulling to one side gradually on the run up to take off). That's cool, because you do get some of this in most real single props.
The flight itself was nice and smooth, 50fps with no stutters, and no 3rd party performance booster. That's good. A lot of people want more fps than that but 50 works fine with me, whether I can get more or not - it also frees up resources to puch other settings a bit more. And I did. And it worked fine. Well done there.
I've only tried Kai Tak as yet, but the Kai Tak scenery... So-o-o-o-o empty!!! I've got the scenery addon disc on my disc FSX version and wow. I'm not only comparing but saying that Steam could have included some better scenery as a part of their tweaks of the disc version. Maybe in the pipeline?
I'd be interested to find out how to uninstall the military planes as I've no time in this life for such stuff. I don't shoot at people - even if it's a simulator.
Last thing, a question. Do freeware addons really install into Steam FSX? Maybe I could get my sceney discs installed into this version? Help?
And last but certainly not least, can I get my FSUIPC (paid) download into this program?
To summarise, then, I'll recommend this simulator (I wish Steam would stop calling it a game...) as I think with future updates initial issues will be ironed out and it will be a very good app indeed. I'll also keep my disc version though because I've got too much third-party stuff installed and I like flying around a full Manhattan scenery as opposed to the one that comes with Steam.
Yep, I recommend it. It's worth the 20-odd Euros, no problem.

Plain and simple, Alan Wake is a mediocre game but I can't help but think it would have made for a much better movie. The story isn't necessarily original but it is compelling and the game's only strength. Because of this the gameplay just feels tacked on; busy work to keep the player occupied in between the story's progression. The main character, Alan Wake, is a best-selling author who has hit writer's block for a year or so. This convinces his wife to book a vacation for the urbanites in Washington state. In short order it is revealed that Alan's wife Alice is a clinical nyctophob and it goes downhill from there. What's great is you will continuously ask yourself what the hell is going on and whether what is happening is real or a figment of Wake's mind.
Alan Wake is all about light and dark in the literal and philosophical senses. Wake is "safe" from enemies and healed when standing in the beams of light from lamps and street lights. When light is absent monsters, dark shadows, pursue him relentlessly and will kill him. Luckily you are equipped with a flashlight to assist in combating them. In order to actually kill a shadow you need to first break a protective barrier by shining a flashlight on them. Once it is broken shadows can be killed by normal weaponry. The novelty of this light/dark dynamic is great at first, and the idea sounds wonderful on paper, but it becomes tediousness quickly (not to mention all the generators you have to start up). Granted I'm sure the combat would be staler than it already is without it.
I guessed the ending incorrectly and for that alone I give Alan Wake kudos. I think gamers who are fans of true psychological thrillers and horrors games (Silent Hill, Deadly Premonition...etc.) can get past Alan Wake's gameplay and enjoy the story--because that's the selling point if there is one. Too bad it wasn't a movie, or at the very least a point-and-click adventure game to the likes of The Walking Dead.

This is a tough one to review. I'm going to try and assert what this game is trying to be, followed by what it actually is.
Alpha Protocol is advertised as espionage game with RPG elements, this may give potential buyers the idea that the level of sneaking involved is reminiscent to that of the elder Splinter Cell series, but unfortunately this is far from true. The mechanics in Alpha Protocol limit you to basic climbing, basic hand-to-hand combat and you should expect that most sneaking will consist of simply taking cover behind objects to break the line of sight, which is rather disappointing. However, the RPG elements in Alpha Protocol are nifty and interesting, they can greatly influence the game and the modifications you make will definitely be an asset to your personal skills and gameplay.
Lastly, spy thrillers usually involve conspiracies or dirty gritty stories, and Alpha Protocol does this in a somewhat decent way. Don't get me wrong there, the story is pretty interesting and involves the player traveling to diverse locations and meeting different people, but the presentation of the story is lacking.
With that in mind, my last important note and a lot of the justified criticism for this game can be mentioned shortly and firmly: this game should not have been released yet. Alpha Protocol is very buggy, feels unpolished and in overall these things killed what would have been a great experience. My verdict: only buy this if it's on sale, a price tag of  €5,- would be as far as I'd go. Of course, one might pay more if he or she is not annoyed by bad character animations, odd NPC behavior, graphics glitches and event triggers that do not work as intended. For reference, you can look up Voidhead's 'Alpha Protocol - bugs, glitches and annoyances' video on YouTube.
