Don't be confused by the pixel graphics: this is not a flash-game, and it's not a throw-back to 90's classics. This is a modern game that stands up on its own. It just chooses to use these graphics, and that may be a good thing. Many people would probably be horrified if they decided to use current generation realistic graphics. Not only one of the best indie games I've ever played, but in my top 10 games ever, period.
Story:
Hotline Miami places you in the shoes of a man losing his mind, leaving you just as confused as he is. Vivid hallucinations or dreams place him in the room of three masked characters, either screaming violent threats at him, being a consoling care giver, or asking the obvious, or painful questions about what is happening. Outside of this, he keeps receiving cryptic messages that order him to go to a random building in Miami and murder everyone in sight while wearing animal masks. Follow him as he descends farther into madness and violence. On the surface, it's just an excuse for needless violence. But the deeper you dig (which I highly recommend), the more complicated it becomes. It serves as something of an expression about the violence in media, our justifications and cravings for violence as people. Intentionally very vague to make you fill in the blanks yourself, but with enough clues and exposition for you to fill in (most) of the blanks yourself. But, if you don't feel like doing that, leave the critical thinking out of it and watch this guy lose his mind and murder everyone.
Gameplay:
One shot, one kill. That applies to everyone (outside of a few specific bosses and two enemy types.) One baseball bat swing will take a man's head and split it down the middle. A rifle bullet to the chest will drop them. But the same applies to you too. Enemies are quick and have no problem mowing you down if you're not paying attention to your surroundings. If you don't have a weapon, or the gun is empty, use your fists, doors, or simply chuck the weapon at them to knock them to the ground before brutally finishing them off. The only ones you can't do this on are bosses and "thugs," overweight bosses with Kevlar vests. Them, you have to blast with multiple bullets or a shotgun blast to drop. Guns are great at long range, but are loud and send everyone on the floor your way, Melees are quick and quit, if you can get the drop on them. Expect to get the "Karma" achievement (die 1000 times) pretty easily. Thankfully, respawns are instant with no consequence, other than having to start the floor over again. Just expect frustration across the board, until the relief sets in on the score tally screen, which adds plenty of incentive for replays. "Recklessness is rewarded."
Sound:
No voice acting, instead sprawling text across the bottom of the screen, next to the speaker's animated face. Every weapon is accented by a beautiful, disturbing sound. You can hear the whistle of the iron pipe if it swings past your target, or the sickening splat when it connects with their head. Guns are loud and will startle you if someone takes a shot from somewhere you weren't looking. Executions have particularly gruesome, depending on the method. Let's just say few will forget the sound of the power drill going through the side of the victim's head. And the soundtrack is pure awesome. A surreal elctronic mix that accents the adrenaline pumping in you while you clear floor after floor of enemies. Even as a die-hard rock fan (go Foo Fighters), I have downloaded the soundtrack myself and listen to it in my own free time. Even if it brings back unpleasant memories of all the people I killed.
Graphics:
Every thing in the game is bright and colorful, like a horrid drug trip that's escalated farther than it ever should. The top-down view lets you see only the enemies and their heads, which furthers the disconnection between the player and the violence. It's not until the level is cleared and you see all the bodies that it suddenly dawns on you what you did. It's then you notice how gory the game really is. Entrails everywhere from people who took a shotgun to the stomach, skulls with brain leaking out, faces blown off, torsos riddled with bullets, and lots of limbs pointing in unnatural directions. Not for the squeamish. And let's all be glad they chose the pixel graphics. If this was as graphic as Last of Us with the same level of brutality, nobody would have the stomach for this game.
Final Thoughts:
The best way to describe this is "creativity through violence." Use your preferred methods to kill everything in your path for a vague goal you don't understand while questioning your own sanity and what's happening around you. Just an utterly great game that just isn't for everyone. But for critical thinkers and adrenaline seeking gamers, enjoy.

Very rewarding turn-based stealth strategy game. I'm a huge fan of XCOM-like games and roguelikes like FTL, and this game makes me feel like I'm playing both of those games at once!
Invisible Inc. borrows heavily from the mission component of XCOM, as opposed to the base-building strategic layer; it borrows a few key concepts from roguelikes like FTL, and adds a stealth element that I don't recognize from other strategy games. The result is an absorbing game that scratches an itch I never knew I had, and there's enough replay value here to keep me playing for a good long while.
I bought this game while it was in Early Access, and I'm glad to say that investment paid off. When I bought it, it was a great game and well worth the asking price, and it has only gotten better since then.
Congrats to Klei on an excellent game!

Even though I've been playing Civ VI for a good many hours now, I still continue to feel let down by the direction they've taken with this rendition of the series. Had this been some other game or even just Civilization Revolutions 3, I might have felt very different about this, but this is Civilization - a game series Ive played since my childhood and through three decades.
There are some improvements - like the way workers/builders now function, the casus belli implementation and splitting up cultural and scientific progression. But the AI interaction (despite the supposed addition of complex motives) feels anaemic and the concept of traders being the (only) ones that construct roads is outright bizarre. Not to mention that progression seems way off, with the final ages passing by so fast you can scarcely mobilize the features they add before they've become technologically obsolete even on the slowest game speed.
But above anything else, what really disappointed me was that it has lost the -feel- of ruling a nation through history as it epically unfolds. Sure, Civilization was never truly realistic, but it could still immerse you into history like it was. And not the least did the game respect history, presenting cultures, wonders and achievements with reverence, often inspiring you to want to learn more.
Now it's all humorous, oversaturated. cartoonish visuals and the quotes you are presented are most often just goofy tongue in cheek remarks. And time and time again gameplay design completely ignore the call for conceivability that's fundamental to immersion, like the unfolding of the cities to spread them out across the entire country, with wonders that take up the same amount of land as the city centre itself, and science districts relying on being close to mountains (!). How many actual, real top universities would qualify for that bonus? Certainly it solves some gameplay balance issues of prior renditions, but there are better ways to do that (many Civ V mods could serve as excellent examples).
Of course I've been spoiled with the expansions and many mods for Civ V (I cannot recommend the Community Balance Patch enough), but what saddens me is that with the concerns listed above, Civ VI seems beyond saving. I just hope this rendition of the series will be a detour and Civ VII will get the series back on track.

I read the comics, watch the TV show and have played through the first season of The Walking Dead, and this season does not disappoint.
The story continues with Clementine, though there are characters from the first season who also appear.  Many of the choices you made in the first season will also affect the dialogue in this one, though not significantly.
The graphics and the HUD have greatly improved, and there is less wandering around looking for a way to continue to the next scene, giving the story a faster pace.
I also liked the characters a great deal, though the chaos of living in an apocalyptic world where survival is the main focus has done much to harden everyone. As a result, Clementine seems more detached from the new people she encounters compared to the first season.  She has basically grown up and now has to make the hard choices that were reserved for the older characters in the first season.
A lot of depressing and bleak situations occurred during the first season, but this season is much worse.  Rarely does Clementine get any respite from conflict, whether it stems from the Walkers or from the living.  The moral choices she has to make are much more difficult and there are moments when you can tell she is becoming numb to some of the behaviors that would have horrified her in the past.
However, this season seems to be more "on rails" than the first in that your choices don't appear to alter the main storyline significantly.  People might live a bit longer depending on what you choose, but generally not for long. The ending, however, offers several choices compared to the first season, and though it's uncertain how much the story will deviate until the third season comes out, what you decide will significantly alter the ending.
Like Season 1, this is more of an interactive story than a game becuase you won't find much in the way of difficult puzzles or quicktime events, but the story remains strong and I recommend it to those who love horror and the world of The Walking Dead.

Firstly, I'll get the obvious stuff out of the way...
It's from 2006, so graphically it's not great. The UI is typically Microsoft-Fugly. It doesn't have a great deal of charm. It is spectacularly reliant on community contribution, and while there's a lot of extra free content, it's a pain in the neck to install some of it. As in, unzip files into folders and then move them into other folders...
But if you're OK with the base scenery/planes then this isn't going to be a major issue.
Get a joystick or a controller (I use a controller. I'd love a joystick.) with as many buttons and levers as it is humanly possible to acquire, and it would be beneficial to run multiple screens, because, despite the drawbacks...
... if you want a non-combat flight-sim which doesn't cut corners, you're going to have a hell of a hard-time beating this one... and you may as well have all the kit.
This is a remarkably deep sim, allowing you to take off and fly around much of the world in a staggering variety of aircraft (though you'll have to install a fair few of those yourself if you really want to broaden your horizons)
There are missions to complete if you want to, or free-flight if you don't. If you live in a moderate population centre, you'll likely even find your local airfield is there... though if there's no specific scenery pack for it, you may find - as I did - that the basics are right - such as where the coast is - but the procedurally generated filler will just hazard a guess as to what your city or town actually looks like.
Where the game excels is how it allows you - as a sim enthusiast - to develop your own flight plans and actually FLY the plane from point-A to point-B, in real-time, using real-world weather taken from your local weather station, and with real light conditions based on your actual time of day.
You can do it using all the electronic gadgetry in anything from a modern Air New Zealand SAAB passenger jet, to the visual 'fly by the seat of your pants' Bleriot XI from 1905... assuming you bother to download them.  The point is that there are plenty of options.
For those of you who are interested, but are not really familiar with the Microsoft sim range... you don't get to shoot things. There are races and missions and training courses, but no enemies diving in from the sun.   There are airports and cities and landmarks, but no AAA or bombing runs.  There's a lot of button pushing (some of it quite obscure) and it depends on the aircraft you're using whether there's a virtual cockpit, or a static BMP one, or none at all.
You'll spend a lot of time watching the autopilot tell you how far away from your next waypoint you are... though you may be able to have a chat to other players or the control tower in multi-player games. It's not about the action.
But it REALLY hit the spot for me as far as flight-sims go, and I'm loving finding those rare downloadable aircraft online and flying them around.

Excellent game!
What I love about Invisible Inc is the constantly shifting power balance between the player characters and the enemies.  Guards behave in predictable ways and can even be manipulated to provide crucial openings.  But despite their stupidity, even the weakest guard can kill your agent in a single attack.  If you get caught out in the open, almost nothing can save you.  It always feels satisfying getting through a tricky level by being smart because failure is always a danger.
Another interesting gameplay aspect is the Alarm Level.  Every turn the security level increases by one, and player actions can increase it further (tripping alarms, being spotted, etc).  At thresholds, the alarm advances and security becomes tighter (more cameras, firewalls, and guards).  Similarly, guards have varying levels of alertness that increases as the game goes on.  This means that the game has a constant risk-reward of investing resources and moves to shave off turns.  Do I move through this laser grid or go around?  Is it worth knocking out this stationary guard and taking his credits, knowing he'll wake up and start hunting?  Can I afford to detour to loot a safe before security arrives?  Do I spend power to lower this forcefield or redirect the drone coming for me?
In a way, it's a triumph of design.  Any challenge can be overcome with basic starting gear, but with a prohibitive turn cost.  Using items and clever planning to rob the entire facility in seven turns feels amazing, as does pulling out a win after playing chicken with the alarm level.  And as appropriate for roguelikes, losing can feel pretty good too.
Aesthetic-wise the game is gorgeous.  All the characters look incredibly stylish, especially in their close-up portraits.  There's a stupid number of props, each of which are appropriately themed for the faction that owns them.  This is complemented by some top-notch voice acting, although only for three characters in the cast.

Don't be confused by the pixel graphics: this is not a flash-game, and it's not a throw-back to 90's classics. This is a modern game that stands up on its own. It just chooses to use these graphics, and that may be a good thing. Many people would probably be horrified if they decided to use current generation realistic graphics. Not only one of the best indie games I've ever played, but in my top 10 games ever, period.
Story:
Hotline Miami places you in the shoes of a man losing his mind, leaving you just as confused as he is. Vivid hallucinations or dreams place him in the room of three masked characters, either screaming violent threats at him, being a consoling care giver, or asking the obvious, or painful questions about what is happening. Outside of this, he keeps receiving cryptic messages that order him to go to a random building in Miami and murder everyone in sight while wearing animal masks. Follow him as he descends farther into madness and violence. On the surface, it's just an excuse for needless violence. But the deeper you dig (which I highly recommend), the more complicated it becomes. It serves as something of an expression about the violence in media, our justifications and cravings for violence as people. Intentionally very vague to make you fill in the blanks yourself, but with enough clues and exposition for you to fill in (most) of the blanks yourself. But, if you don't feel like doing that, leave the critical thinking out of it and watch this guy lose his mind and murder everyone.
Gameplay:
One shot, one kill. That applies to everyone (outside of a few specific bosses and two enemy types.) One baseball bat swing will take a man's head and split it down the middle. A rifle bullet to the chest will drop them. But the same applies to you too. Enemies are quick and have no problem mowing you down if you're not paying attention to your surroundings. If you don't have a weapon, or the gun is empty, use your fists, doors, or simply chuck the weapon at them to knock them to the ground before brutally finishing them off. The only ones you can't do this on are bosses and "thugs," overweight bosses with Kevlar vests. Them, you have to blast with multiple bullets or a shotgun blast to drop. Guns are great at long range, but are loud and send everyone on the floor your way, Melees are quick and quit, if you can get the drop on them. Expect to get the "Karma" achievement (die 1000 times) pretty easily. Thankfully, respawns are instant with no consequence, other than having to start the floor over again. Just expect frustration across the board, until the relief sets in on the score tally screen, which adds plenty of incentive for replays. "Recklessness is rewarded."
Sound:
No voice acting, instead sprawling text across the bottom of the screen, next to the speaker's animated face. Every weapon is accented by a beautiful, disturbing sound. You can hear the whistle of the iron pipe if it swings past your target, or the sickening splat when it connects with their head. Guns are loud and will startle you if someone takes a shot from somewhere you weren't looking. Executions have particularly gruesome, depending on the method. Let's just say few will forget the sound of the power drill going through the side of the victim's head. And the soundtrack is pure awesome. A surreal elctronic mix that accents the adrenaline pumping in you while you clear floor after floor of enemies. Even as a die-hard rock fan (go Foo Fighters), I have downloaded the soundtrack myself and listen to it in my own free time. Even if it brings back unpleasant memories of all the people I killed.
Graphics:
Every thing in the game is bright and colorful, like a horrid drug trip that's escalated farther than it ever should. The top-down view lets you see only the enemies and their heads, which furthers the disconnection between the player and the violence. It's not until the level is cleared and you see all the bodies that it suddenly dawns on you what you did. It's then you notice how gory the game really is. Entrails everywhere from people who took a shotgun to the stomach, skulls with brain leaking out, faces blown off, torsos riddled with bullets, and lots of limbs pointing in unnatural directions. Not for the squeamish. And let's all be glad they chose the pixel graphics. If this was as graphic as Last of Us with the same level of brutality, nobody would have the stomach for this game.
Final Thoughts:

Microsoft Flight Simulator X (X as the Roman Numeral 10) is as you expect, an aviation based simulator released in 2006 by, well, Microsoft Studios. The game has recently been released on VALVe’s Steam distribution by Dovetail Games, bringing modern compatibility to a game that was (ironically) incompatible with Windows 7 and 8. The game is equivalent to the Gold edition, meaning Flight Simulator X Deluxe with the Acceleration expansion.
Gameplay: The game plays as you expect, to simulate the characteristics of piloting aircraft of varying types from private propeller planes, passenger jets, stunt planes, gliders and even several helicopters. Either this can be done in freeflight where the player chooses their craft, starting location, weather, date and time or can take on missions, ranging from tutorial missions teaching the basics of aircraft to missions with specific objectives ranging from a simple navigation and landing at airports, rescue missions like landing a chopper at a burning oil rig to rescue the workers or running a Red Bull stunt course in the Extra 300S stunt plane. The Acceleration expansion pack adds three new craft, the Boeing F/A - 18 Hornet, the P-51 Mustang and the AgustaWestland EH-101 with new respective missions such as Mustang races or more military missions with the F/A - 18 such as directing air traffic away from a shuttle launch, chasing down a UFO or, with the EH-101, carrying cargo on the lift hook. Many, if not all, missions give themed rewards, completing the taxiing tutorial would reward you the “Rubber Wings”, for example. The player also has the ability to adjust in-game settings of realism such as the torque applied on propeller aircraft, turbulence effects, etc. (These apply to Free Flight only, missions force specific settings). This game either works as a straight-up game and simulator to a training aid that people aspiring to be pilots can use to get a grasp on piloting skills, the game is even used by real-world pilots to brush up on their skills while they’re not flying for real. Part of the appeal is being able to take off from locations close to home, for example I take off from Anoka County-Blaine Airport (ICAO: KANE) frequently, which is 2 nm from my house.
Graphics: For a game from 2006, this game holds up well by today’s standards, especially since addons can be installed to enhance the graphical capabilities. They say gameplay needs focus over graphics but this is a simulator, it’s really not a crime to add graphical effects and detail into a game like this to give the potential to explore famous locations and in manners not legal or safe in real-life (such as flying in the Grand Canyon in an F/A - 18). As far as I know, the game’s optimized for nVidia cards and it seems to show. The effects can be adjusted to suit one’s taste and/or computer performance, aircraft detail, scenery density, water effects and weather effects. The camera view can either be a 2D cockpit overlay with buttons to bring up specific panels, a 3D virtual cockpit with movement effects and interactable switches, an outside “spot” view that allows viewing of the aircraft from any angle, specific outside views like from the perspective of landing gear shown in movies and a top-down view.
Sound & Music: The sounds, are, amazing. The point in all simulators is to give a player a sense of feeling and feedback and one of the best ways to do this is through sound. Either the noise of propeller planes, the blasting woosh of jets along with other effects such as the electric motors moving flaps or retracting landing gear. Of course their are also environmental effects such as rain, wind and even thunder. The developers tried their best to emulate the real sounds these aircraft make such as the iconic ringing noise in Bell produced helicopters such as the Jet Ranger. The soundtrack is only present on the menus but the main theme has a very adventurous feel, the second is dramatic, the third is a slow peaceful theme while the rest are varying techno songs, each can be selected or if desired, third-party music can be imported to play on the main menu. The voicework is also well done, the tutorial speaker’s very nice sounding, giving various real aviation trivia and letting you know what to do when needed and giving fair warning of like, say, going too fast and stressing the aircraft. The pilot’s voice is very spliced to give out callsigns like FSX2006 as “Foxtrot-Sierra-Xray-Two-Zero-Zero-Six” but it would make sense to speak slowly and robotically in a real situation to ensure your callsign is loud-and-clear.
Difficulty: The difficulty is extremely subjective but this game does carry a steep learning-curve to those new to the series or wanting to learn flying. It’s easy to take-off and fly but landing can be a challenge at first when learning the correct speeds and approach patterns. This only gets worse with helicopters that are extremely sensitive and require the utmost care when moving. The realism (and by extension, the difficulty) can be adjusted as stated before, trainees are recommended to keep options such as unlimited fuel, automatic management of fuel/air mixture, etc.
The Goods: A very fun if relaxing game with a lot of possibility. Either to set up scenarios for oneself like performing cargo runs or flying passenger jets. At least in Free Flight, things like traffic rules and ATC communication are completely optional, allowing very casual play without the requirement of flight plans.
The Bads: Early on, the game had a lot of optimization and performance issues but with the Steam edition, that doesn’t seem to be the case anymore. The game has a steep learning curve that can put of a grand majority of players.
Overall: Aviation enthusiasts, trainees and even real pilots are recommended to try this game out. Not only is it great as a game but also as a training tool (do keep in mind this is not a stand-in for real world training).

I remember in 2010 when Alan Wake first came out on the XBOX to much graphical fanfare.  At that time the publisher was refusing to release a PC version which irked me a bit, but I got over it.  Well, here it is and was it worth all the hoopla?  Not really.  I do like the idea of an action/suspense game based on the writings of a popular novelist.  The primary setting, a small backwoods town on the pacific coast somewhere, is a bit cliche'd.  The characters are also cookie cutter.  The primary action mechanic, using a light source to stun your foes then blasting them a weapon, is fresh but overused.  Since there are no "unlocks" to make action sequences more interesting, the game simply reuses the same mechanic but llimits resources to create a challenge.  Yawn.  The story starts off with gusto but loses steam in the later chapters.  Graphically the game is nice looking; I liked the attention to detail in some of the set pieces.  I would recommend getting this on sale for less than $5 and giving it a whirl... but you will probably get bored around Chapter 4.

The music choices were top-notch as they compliment the melancholic theme of the game. As an amateur photographer, I also enjoyed the high level of detail the developers have implemented in the game about art and photography. The character depth and development were also outstanding. I truly felt sorry for Chloe's tragic character and was inspired by Max's character development.
Ultimately, I believe this game is for people who enjoy quality storylines over intense graphics or gameplay.  After finishing this game, it's strong emotional impact will leave you in tears and feeling empty.

Life is Strange is one of many games that claims to be an interactive fiction where choices matter, however, I believe they completely fail at this. The following blacked out text will be an example. If you haven't played the game and still wish to do so, don't read:

So, now the spoilers are out of the way, I'm going to explain why I am not recommending this game. To put it simply, this game is false advertising. You can not make a game where "choices matter" if by the end of the game, the last decision renders every other choice completely pointless. The plot is emotional and forces players to think, but there are pointless subplots and many choice points which are just completely unneccessary.
In the end, I do not recommend this game based on the constant use of filler content and choices that DON'T matter.

Civ 6 is by far the worst entry in the entire Civilization series, taking all of the elements that were fun and enjoyable from previous games and eliminating them completely. The options also allow you to extend/reduce the fixed duration of the game or to turn it into an "endless" game ... it's not really endless, the enemies just get harder and harder and eventually you fail to complete too many missions or your team is all captured/killed. Ther random nature of the missions, equipment you can find/buy and the abilities you can find for your pet AI can make some of the games harder/trickier than other sessions but overall it is enjoyable. This game is spectacular. It is a turn-based single-player strategy game. First off, the premise of the game. You have 72 hours to prepare your agents for the final mission. Each place you go to has a different amount of time to get there, and different rewards. It is up to you, the operator, to choose the missions and guide the agents through said levels. This is not a game for those who want an easy game that you can put down at any time; you really need to finish the run in one go. But it is an extremely well coded game. More specifically-
1) The difficulty curve is perfect. Within each difficulty setting, there is a curve as you go through the 72 hour time frame which is very well balanced. And if it is too hard, or too easy, you can make a custom game with specialized settings to adjust to your taste.
2) The animation is beautiful. It just works.
3) The characters are incredibly well balanced. No character is better than the last- the one you use depends on your playing style. And there are just enough characters to satisfy everybody's needs, while not making a list that takes an hour to scroll through.
This is one of the best games I have ever played, PC or Console. I would highly recommend this to anybody looking for a great game to lose many hours to.

Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a game in which you have your very own space agency. This agency is run by little green creatures known as Kerbals. (all of which are totally qualified for the job and totally not randomly plucked form the streets). Your goals is to design and build spacecraft to help the kerbal species explore their solar system. You will need to earn money by fulfilling contracts, which are constantly being offered by a plethora of kerbal companies. You can do a lot of easy jobs to make a profit, but the big money is of course earned through the more challenging contracts. Money is not the only thing you have to worry about though, as you will also have to advance your scientific progress by unlocking new tech in the tech tree. These techs are unlocked with science data you can collect thoughout the solar system. Of course, the hard-to-reach places like the outer planets provide much more science than, say, the moon. When playing KSP, you will face frustration (when your rockets keep exploding), great joy (when you actually manage to land on the moon), and endless dispair (when you realise you don't have enough fuel to get home).
-Very educational, teaches a lot about how spacecraft work in real life.
-Great sense of accompishment if things actually work (eventually they will, really...)
-Very flexible and fun Physics engine to play around with.
-Funny theming (subjective) -I just love the descriptions of the rocket parts and the exaggerated kerbal emotions.
-Good modding support and very healthy modding community.
-Some aspects of the game feel a bit underdeveloped (i.e. space stations and ground-based colonies do not serve a lot of purpose other than being cool).
-The physics engine can get a little glitchy sometimes. Things exploding randomly is not an uncommon occurrence.
While this game may not be entirely realistic on all fronts, it offers a great deal of depth on how orbital mechanics work. For people who don't know a thing about rockets, this game will teach you a lot - and make you have fun while doing it.
While it can be frustrating to spend a long time building a new spacecraft just to watch it explode on the launchpad, these is a great sense of accomplishment when you build that enormous mothership or awesome spaceplane. Until you see the creations of people who are far better at the game...
I strongly recommend this game to anyone who wishes to know more about space exploration or wants to test their creative ability by designing the most amazing spacecraft. Or anyone who just likes to watch things go boom I guess.

Sid Meier's Civilization VI
Fantastic Games Edition
Months ago I began to watch one of my friends playing Sid Meier's Civilization Revolution on their Xbox. It looked interesting, so I thought I’d see what’s available for the PC. I noticed that the latest Civilization for PC was VI, so I set my sights on it, I eventually got the Digital Deluxe Edition for half price.
During this time Civ3 became free, so I thought getting a free Civilization game would be a good way to play the game and decide if I wanted to buy it. However, Civ3 offered no tutorial, so I was lost. However, I realized that Civ6 is the first of the series to offer a tutorial. Luckily, I found out that the game also has a free demo.
So, I tried out the demo. I started with the tutorial, but ran into a few problems. One of the worst things about the tutorial is that you cannot save your game. So, you either have to keep playing or lose your progress. I also thought I ran into a glitch, but I found my way around it. My next problem was that the amount of turns in the game was running out. This happens at 2050, but the game didn’t end. It continued and I built a massive force and thought I took over my opponent, but the game continued. I may not have completed the final objective (a Domination Victory) in time.
If you’re not familiar with the game series, Civilization is a turn based strategy game. The game focuses on managing a civilization, kind of like Sim City. There are many ways to play and thus many ways to win. You can work towards amassing an army, conquering other nations, and achieving a Domination Victory. You can also work towards science and eventually launch into space achieving a Science Victory. You can also work towards religion, including getting into religious wars, and achieving a Religious Victory. You can also work towards culture, generating tourism, and achieving a Culture Victory. The final way to win is with a Score Victory, when no other victory has been achieved and thus victory depends on who has the highest score.
The game reflects real world civilizations including modern and historic. There are many to play, each with their unique bonuses. I find the real world modern and historical aspects of the game to be extremely appealing.
There are a variety of ways to manage your civilization. The AI provides some suggestions, including an adviser. Each turn you research civics, like policies, and science, technologies. You can trigger eureka moments which boost research. This is done by completing certain conditions, for instance killing an enemy with a Slinger boosts the research towards Archer. When that’s complete, you can pay in-game gold to upgrade the unit or build new ones. Units also receive experience and get promotions, which includes offensive and defensive bonus trees.
I’ve only barely scratched the surface of things here, this game is deep. There is a bit of a learning curve for new players, but it's fun. While it doesn’t cover everything, it helps you get started. You will learn a lot as you play and the game includes Civilopedia, basically the game’s detailed manual. However, I’ve found an excellent “Tutorial for Complete Beginners” on YouTube
.

I'm propably the only old school Civ player writing a review, because I simply do not understand why this game gets such good reviews. I'm betting they are all pretty new to Civ.
I've played Civilization for over 20 years, ever since the first game was released. I was hooked from the start. Civ 2, I loved it even more. Civ 3 was such an amazing development for the game and Civ 4 was simply the best! Then came Civ 5, wich never really felt like a compleate game. productivity was harder and the size of my army was never really the same. Plus the religion was in my opinion just a waste of production. Now after 300 hours of Civ 6, I must say: I am bitterly disapointed. The game has progressed little since Civ 5. Now I have even less production and everything feels like in slow motion. Religion has moslty been copy-paste from Civ 5. And the ai is terrible. The only online games I've played have all been over in the middle age at the latest.
Gone are the big armies and world domination plots, instead we have endless turns of waiting for things to get built. The best way to get production, gold or science is to send emisaries to city states or through trade routes. Workers are now compleatly under your control and you must micromanage them the entire game. The only Civ that has any productivity are the germans and in my opinion the only usable civ.
By the time you reach renaissance the game becomes just to much micromanage to enjoy a bigger picture game. And if ever your army gets viped, then you are done for. No chance to rebuild after a war. If you get ravaged by war then you can pack it in.
The balance of Civ 4 is in the past, where you could chose from a variety of ways to play the game and have a multiple fun ways to win and losing a war and half your territories did not mean you were down and out. Now when I reach industrial age I just soldier through the turns and go for the space race victory. Anything else just takes to long, mostly because you have to micromanage everything the entire game.
As big of a disapointment Civ 5 was for me, Civ 6 is even bigger. And how the ai can be worse and worse is beyond me.
If you want to play a game of Civilization, buy Civ 4. I give Civ 4 a 10/10, Civ 6 I give 3/10 and that's only for the first three ages. There is absolutely nothing new and exciting to be found here, the introduction of districts was cool when I first played it but now I see it just adds on to the micromanage of the game which is to much of to begin with.
Do not buy this, unless you like to spend alot of time micromanaging and planning the same thing over and over and over and over. And then if you do, try not to expand to much or the game will just start to feel like a job that you cant wait to finish.
In Civ 4 I had empires with over 100 cities and I could reduce the micromange by automating units and cities. Now the thought of controlling 25 city's is a micromanage hell.
I find it really sad that my favorite game for so many years has been reduced to this.

So I finally decided to put down Civ 4 after playing it to death and finally bite the bullet and try 6.  TLDR is at the bottom:
The hex style movement and 1UPT never really appealed and I was somewhat put off by it, but after playing a game and a half it's not been as bad as I thought. Gets a little tedius sometimes having to micro units all over the place.
The districts seem ok enough for most other people. Me personally I'm not overally excited by them.
The technology tree again compared to Civ 4 feels alot more condensed. I would have hoped to have seen more techs and really expanding further into the future as well. Reseaching tech based on your surroundings is cool enough, not enough though that I feel that my civ has developed a unique sense of tech advancement, because in the end I would still have to research older techs in order to advance. I
n Civ 4 I would almost never research Archery or Horseback riding, wouldn't bother researching Drama and Literiture and for the longest time ignored some of the thelogical techs, whilst still being able to advance.
Diplomacy
So in my games so far it seems that diplomacy is pretty lackluster. The constant civ's telling me my faith is poor, my navy is poor, my city expansion is poor is extemely annoying and unrealistic I think. And then to top it off, they denounce you for it. It would be like the USA to denounce the UK for having such a small country, and then declaring War on them later because of it.
Secondly I have so far found trades largely pointless. Is there a point to Open Borders? I can still send my trade carts without them. As for trading resources, it so far seems that the player always has to pay more. Why this arbituary extra cost? Even as allies, the player still has to be pay just that little more. I'd rather not bother.
Thirdly, it seems Wars are so infrequent. Now it might have been just the few games I've played but even on a large map with several AI's, up until the Industrial era there had been only 1 war, initated by myself to stop the Khmer from plopping a settler down. It was a surprise war and wasn't aiming to go to war but decided to do it and took his capital. Since then, no further wars.
Further that, I've not felt a need to go to war, theres nothing to gain except huge warmongering penalties. Granted I don't  know enough about these penalties but when it says the penalty is severe and ergorgious, I'm really not inclined to do so. Which kind of makes the game very bland. I want the world to have some wars going on. I loved it in Civ 4 when wars would be going on all over the world.
Barbarians
This is quite possibly a deal breaker for me. I understand that to almost everyone they love the challenge of having your civilisation being potentiall wiped out by barbs from the very beginning. I do not. Barbarians are fine, and were fine in Civ 4. I would say they were quite managable. In Civ 6, as soon as that scout spots your city, they rush back to that encampment and immediatly start spawning Spearman, Horseman, Horse Archers and they very quickly march to your city.
Now perhaps in a Standard game, on a Standard Map on Standard Speed its manageable as you can get your units out fast enough. I like to play on Huge Maps with Marathon speeds, so to find barbs have already got an encampment and a horse archer and horseman within around 10- 15 turns whilst my very first Slinger is still being produced with 10 or so turns left to make, it's hugely frustrating.
So I'm either forced to have to turn them off which ruins the immersion for me, or spend the whole of the ancient era spamming out units just to fend off then endless hordes of barbarians.
TLDR:
o Tech tree feels limited, Tech research based on surroundeds is cool but not overly exciting
- Diplomacy is lackluster.
- War feels somewhat pointless and few and far betweena
- Barbarian difficulty can be hugely frustrating depending on your play style
- Wish I hadn't spent £70 on this. Should have put it towards saving for the house depost instead.

Alpha Protocol. The game that got killed by the "professional" reviewers that never bothered to get past the tutorial, in most cases. Most of them admited years later their mistake. Behind its roughness, AP has, probably, the best choices and consequences system that you will ever encounter in a video game, with only The Witcher series and Fallout 1/2 being on par or better.
Marketing did not help this game, either. Sega presented this puppy as an adventure/shooter game. But AP is an RPG. You have skills and abilities that will affect combat and gameplay. You want better shooting/aiming/etc, you will have to invest in the respective skills.
But this game is so much more than an action RPG. What you are saying in the conversation matters. The attitude matters. The skills you take. The background you get for your character.
I've played my DVD to hell an back, as the game offers a lot of replayability. Got it on Steam as a backup solution. My most satisfying walkthrough was me playing as a plain spy. No armor, stealth, hand to hand combat that is incapacitating the enemy (the usual crawl and subdue), playing with words and guessing the right answers for the people you will encounter, transforming enemies into allies. At the end of the playthrough i had behind me a small army ready to help. From zero to hero. That was something and took me a couple of playthroughs to get that result.
The graphics are still standing. The sound, well, you will encounter some glitches but just check the Obsidian forums for some working fixes. The hacking mini-game is bad, but it can be bearable after applying some fixes available on the aforementioned forum. The worst bug of the game: saving when you are crouching in cover and discovering on loading that you are fully exposed.
If i would recommend it?! In a hearbeat! But keep in mind: this is an RPG not a shooter. And if you want for your weapon to work as intended, you need to invest points in that weapon. But as a wise man said: a spy that needs to draw a weapon means that he made a mistake somewhere down the road. Your name is not Rambo, nor Bond. Think more like Michael Westen from Burn Notice.

It's 10:10pm, 9 miles out of Sydney. I've been flying IFR from Adelaide, in RT. 737. My RT weather add-on throws up storms, heavy turbulence. My scenery add-on shows a beautiful Sydney in the distance, glimpsed through the heavy cloud. The take-off was simple, the AP locked on GPS track and the job is nearly done. I've been descending for a while, saving fuel... you know how it goes.
I'm loving it. Calm. Controlled. Content.
Out of the misty depth of somewhere between 9000 and 10000 I'm asked to turn left on 300 and descend and maintain 6000. I dial it in, acknowledge.  Easier to disengage AP now. We're nearly home.
Suddenly. "TRAFFIC ALERT". An A320 is 12.00 o'clock 4 miles at 10000. Can I see him? No. Where?
Sorry tower, no sight. No. Look, there he is. Flying above me. Phew. Sorted.
Sorry. Were you talking to me? Turn left on 340, descend and maintain 4000? OK. Doing it now....
(This turbulence. It's killing me.  Maybe I should go back on AP?)
Sorry tower. Climb and maintain 6000?! What? Oh wait. I thought you said 4000? Oh... That wasn't me. I'm Sierra TANGO, not Sierra ROMEO. Ahhh... Climbing back to 6000, trying to smooth out the heading.
Sorry. What was that? TRAFFIC ALERT. Again!! What sort of ATC are you?! 3 o'clock, 2 miles, 4500. Altitude check. 4500. Oh Oh! Collision course.... My life starts flashing before my eyes then I realise it was the Piper's strobe as he flies just feet in front of me. Phew.
Sorry. Sierra TANGO. (Hey that\s me). I'm 500 below my assigned. Ahh.. What?? That's right. I'm supposed to be 6000. Check heading. 270?? I'm heading to Perth. Dammit. I need to sort the heading too!
Climbing.... Turning..... Climbing.....
WHAT'S THAT DAMN NOISE!!! Sink rate? What sink rate?!! GS is below 120. Head wind? Oh. Oh..... I drop the nose instinctively as I grab the throttle and ram them home. 130, 150, 170..... I knew I watched those airplane movies for a reason.
Sorry tower. What? I'm 3000 below assigned. Yeah. Too bad. I'm busy.
Pull up. Pull up. Pull u..........................
It was then I realised that commercial heavy pilots don't get paid for 100% of their time. They get paid for that 1%.... just before they hit the ground.......gently.
9/10
You must use add-ons though.
FUN.

I grew up playing the best shooters from the 90s like the Doom, Quake, Wolfenstein, Duke Nukem, Blood and Redneck Rampage games, but I only recently had the chance to try out this gem. 20 years after it was originally released Dark Forces is still one of the best shooters ever made, and definitely one of the finest Star Wars game out there.
Its graphics are the usual retro pixelated stuff with sprite objects and simplistic 3d environment. Though, it is not as shiny as nowadays action pieces, still the style and detail it presents is immersive and nice to look at. The story is good enough for a shooter, telling various information before every mission and showing cutscenes which are similar those seen in old LucasArts adventure titles, so the quality standard is high. The gameplay is fast-paced and refined making progression through the levels fun. There is a set of well-designed maps which are filled with shortcuts and secret areas allowing and rewarding exploration and adding replay value. The whole game feels good to play with all its mechanics, and never feels clunky as most older games do.
Overall, everyone who are interested in retro shooters should try DF along with Jedi Outcast and Jedi Academy. There is no way that these games could disappoint anyone.

I highly recommend this game for those who liked Super Meat Boy. A boy and his mother that wants to kill him, and he is forced to escape to the basement and fight against his mother's other children. It is surprisingly addicting, and it is possible to run through the whole game in 15-20 mins. Lots of replayability here since everything is randomized each time you play through the game; or after you die and start over. Expect to die a lot, and get better stuff each time. Also think of it as Legend of Zelda's twisted clone. Except in this game you can sign pacts with the Devil using your heart containers as payment; find tarot cards and pills as power ups. Items are unique in that there is a large random factor and you just have to find them to figure out how they work. Not to mention items such as a coat hanger which affect the character himself. The affects all stack together for some interesting combinations.

So here we are, Hotline Miami 2 was finally released, it's time for an evaluation for the first one XD
Hotline Miami, violent, a story, a really good fiction, a gameplay that was different from the others and make you remember the good all beat'em all arcade games being "gory" and trash.

Why did I like the game ? I love bash'em all like Hotline Miami and the genre has been dead for quite too long, the last I had played was from 1998 and the name has faded in my memory, the controls are a bit hard at first but you get used to them quickly, it's a do or die condition :P
The mess you leave behind you is quite realistic though enemies are dumb in their own ways, you'll find the particularities of these enemies really soon, eyes in the back of their head, insensible to some weapons, etc...
The story is well written, the line of events, awesome, 5 parts, each of them giving more sense or the contrary x)

In the end, yeah, I liked this game, I'm a good public anyway. :D

I like them both but cannot run xplane anywhere near maxed;Fsx is near maxed graphics wise on same desktop computer.

Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a game in which you have your very own space agency. This agency is run by little green creatures known as Kerbals. (all of which are totally qualified for the job and totally not randomly plucked form the streets). Your goals is to design and build spacecraft to help the kerbal species explore their solar system. You will need to earn money by fulfilling contracts, which are constantly being offered by a plethora of kerbal companies. You can do a lot of easy jobs to make a profit, but the big money is of course earned through the more challenging contracts. Money is not the only thing you have to worry about though, as you will also have to advance your scientific progress by unlocking new tech in the tech tree. These techs are unlocked with science data you can collect thoughout the solar system. Of course, the hard-to-reach places like the outer planets provide much more science than, say, the moon. When playing KSP, you will face frustration (when your rockets keep exploding), great joy (when you actually manage to land on the moon), and endless dispair (when you realise you don't have enough fuel to get home).
-Very educational, teaches a lot about how spacecraft work in real life.
-Great sense of accompishment if things actually work (eventually they will, really...)
-Very flexible and fun Physics engine to play around with.
-Funny theming (subjective) -I just love the descriptions of the rocket parts and the exaggerated kerbal emotions.
-Good modding support and very healthy modding community.
-Some aspects of the game feel a bit underdeveloped (i.e. space stations and ground-based colonies do not serve a lot of purpose other than being cool).
-The physics engine can get a little glitchy sometimes. Things exploding randomly is not an uncommon occurrence.
While this game may not be entirely realistic on all fronts, it offers a great deal of depth on how orbital mechanics work. For people who don't know a thing about rockets, this game will teach you a lot - and make you have fun while doing it.
While it can be frustrating to spend a long time building a new spacecraft just to watch it explode on the launchpad, these is a great sense of accomplishment when you build that enormous mothership or awesome spaceplane. Until you see the creations of people who are far better at the game...
I strongly recommend this game to anyone who wishes to know more about space exploration or wants to test their creative ability by designing the most amazing spacecraft. Or anyone who just likes to watch things go boom I guess.

Alan Wake is one of the most incredibly unique games I've experienced. You play as Alan Wake (go figure), a famous author who is on vacation with his wife Alice. To say anything more about the plot would spoil the journey. Primarily, the game is focused on linear gameplay "go from here to here" while shooting enemies in between. As dull as it sounds, it's the intrigue and mystery surrounding the plot which keeps you wanting to push forward.
What this game does perfectly is immerse you in the story. Alan narrates the thoughts running through his head and the events transpiring, so you feel like you're experiencing a Stephen King story. A lot of the game is set in the dark, but it's NOT a horror game, more of a chiller (if such a genre for games exists). Knowing what lurks in the night, there is danger around every corner and sometimes it's best to just run as fast as you can towards the next safe zone.
Taking roughly 8-10 hours to complete, it's worth the time you invest. A great story and tense moments make this game a worthwhile experience.

An awesome stealth/spy Roguelike.
For the main game, you get a limited amount of time to perform as many ops as you can, making the most of stealth and hacking to get through stages. Steal from the corps, get clues on where to go, free other agents to join your team. All of this prepares you for the final showdown.
There is also the option for an endless mode, where you simply see how long you can run missions before something goes horribly wrong.
The mechanics are solid and the stealth system is very well done. Peek through keyholes and around corners to get an idea of what's coming. Observe guards to figure out where they're patrolling. Hack into cameras to make them work for you. Use blind spots to get the jump on enemies, or more often simply to get around them.
This isn't a combat game. While there is knockouts and some lethal weapons, the majority of this game is based on getting through a stage with as little attention as possible.
A hell of a lot of fun, and full of replay value. A must have.

This is the best parts of FTL, XCOM, Frozen Synapse, and Netrunner. Turn-based, strategic, square-grid, isometric, cyberpunk, stealth roguelike puzzler.
Like FTL, you can be utterly screwed by the random generation of the levels, and can spend hours getting to the end fight, only to lose horribly because you just couldn't get enough of the right equipment, or the mission targets were impossibly placed. Other times, you can approach it like a puzzle game, where there *has* to be a solution if you just think about it hard enough. Or like chess, perhaps? And then other times you find yourself roleplaying the agents and their different strengths and personalities.
FTL's biggest drawback was the limited campaign length, where just about the time you felt that you had gotten things under control, you had the boss fight, and were either prepared or not. And then the game ended either way. XCOM had a limited campaign length, but ended right before you got tired of it. Invisible, however, offers you an "endless" mode, once you've gotten the hang of the campaign mode. It has custom options for all of the cool bits, so you can make it as difficult or easy as you'd like.
I highly recommend this one. It's good value for your money.

There are issues - many of them - with Telltale's follow up to one of their most successful titles. Relationships between characters galvanise in tepid fashion regardless of one's choices. Some choices fail to bear the tantalising payoffs that they tease. The supporting cast is no way as endearing enough to care about as their predecessors. Worst of all is the whole pacing of Season Two. But never before has a video game so unapologetically demanded the player to mold a young child in the palm of nightmare. The perennial choice here is define an optimist or a realist of this growing heroine and what type of survivor she will become in a world gone to ruin. Telltale makes an emotional bedrock out of this one particular character portrayal. Yes, guiding sweet Clementine onwards from her tearful ending in Season One is excessively cruel and often heartwrenching, ensuring that by its conclusion the innocence we all desperately wanted to save will be gone forever.

Invisible Inc is such an awesome game! I played during early access and was really quite interested in it, It's great to see how far the game has come and the things that has changed. Highly recommend getting it if you're interested in turn-based strategy-ish games, and who doesn't like secret agents?. Just don't expect it to be easy ;)
The basic storyline is that Invisible Inc. HQ was overthrown by a surprise attack, which resulted in the company fleeing the building. Central, the owner of the company managed to retrieve the special program "Incognita" before leaving, but the program can only run on backup power for another 72 hours.
It's a turn-based stealth game where you take control of a handful of secret agents (2 to begin with, but can increase to a maximum of 4) which break into big corporation buildings. Your agents move silently (while not running) but with guard patrols you have to plan your moves carefully so they don't get seen, which involves hiding behind cover.
Your agents have weapons such as the Neural Disruptors which temporarily disable guards for a few turns, while an agent is on top of them they will pin them down and the guard won't be able to get back up. You can also steal money and key-cards from guards to get through locked doors. Once a weapon is used, most have some sort of cooldown. There are also weapons that can kill guards, but killing guards will set off their heart monitors which raises the alarm level.
"Incognita" is a special program which Invisible Inc. owns, it allows them to hack cameras, safes, turrets, and other objects to take control of them. You need power to hack objects, which is gained from consoles around the map. If an agent is seen by a camera it will start recording them and guards will be alerted to their location. If a guard finds them, it will enter overwatch and will shoot during the players turn if the agent being targeted moves into an open area. The agent must either find cover (behind a object in the room 1 square away), use a cloaking rig to turn invisible, or the guard has to be taken out.
With a limited timer in the main game (72 hours (not real hours), though there is also a endless mode) you have to choose places which are near, and determine which buildings are best to visit first. For example, some places such as the bank vaults (money!!) require special access cards gained from other levels to get into the high security vaults (aka: extra room with lots o' money). Also look out for detention centers which hold another agent which can join your team if you manage to rescue them.
Also, graphics are great, cutscenes are beautiful. I just love the high-tech look of it all, even the menus are pretty. <3

Alpha Protocol is best, and perhaps most favorably described as different. It is the standard cover based third person shooter stealth game mixed in with a dialog system and storytelling mechanics that would put any RPG to shame.
The variety of choices and options in this game, and how they effect everything from the storyline to stat bonuses is truly inspired. It is one of the few games that can honestly claim that every game will play different and deliver on that promise.
The gameplay is fairly generic however and it is marred by seemingly unending wave of bugs that can turn an otherwise entertaining game into a frustrating exercise in teeth-grinding within minutes.
Despite it's obvious problems Alpha Protocol should be applauded for integrating choice and consequence into the gameplay in a way Bioware can only dream of. The mediocre gameplay and exorbitant amount of bugs however means this will never be the classic it was meant to be. Such a shame.

After numerous bad experiences with ostensibly-well-reviewed flight simulators, I was beginning to think the genre wasn't for me any more, that maybe it was now inaccessible to anyone who didn't either have a real world pilot's license or Job-like patience.  I fondly remember spending hours trying to land my Cessna in the original Microsoft Flight Simulator, and the joy I felt when I finally got it right, but I just don't have that sort of time any more.
I am glad to say Flight Simulator X brought that joy back.  It is not perfect by any means - the shell is a little unstable, alt-tabbing (on my installation of Windows 7 at least) means kissing your session goodbye, and the scenery is often somewhat lacklustre.  But it is accessible, and that counts for a lot.
You get a wide variety of aircraft to play with, the game simulates the /entire world/, and you can choose the skill level that's right for you.  FSX ~wants to let you into its tree fort to play, and has very well done tutorial missions to get you up and running.  (A lot of simulators forget the importance of good tutorial missions.  If the tutorial missions aren't done well, the new user experience is likely to be limited to those missions and the 'Delete all local content' menu option on Steam.)
How far you want to take it is up to you, and you don't have to take it all as one lump - you can, for example, ignore the radio and navigation entirely if you so choose, and concentrate on learning to fly by the seat of your pants.  If you want to land on a carrier in oatmeal-thick fog on one engine, FSX will let you do that, too: enough real world pilots seem to play FSX that it doesn't seem likely it's been overly diluted.
FSX is, in other words, easy to learn but hard to master.  My advice for newbies is to take the ultralight, tune down the realism settings, and just enjoy flying around the photogenic city of your choice for a while.  Land on a scenic landmark or two, watch the AI traffic come in and out, then maybe try a short intercity hop or two.

It's been a long time since I've put as much time into a game as I have with Nuclear Throne. It's a game that captures the sinking lows and heart-pumping highs of an arcade game extremely well. Nuclear Throne just FEELS fun to play. With many other games, I find myself having to think hard to justify why the game is fun or worth my time. With Nuclear Throne, it's very simple. Playing this game is fun as hell. This game wants you dead, and picking it up always feels like a fresh challenge; you vs the game. This game WILL kill you eventually, but you're always given a fun, challenging opportunity to go down swinging.
Nuclear Throne is a game that balances chaos and elegance near-perfectly. The characters, weapons, enemies, and upgrades appear very simple at first. An upgrade that gives you +4 HP, so what? But as you progress in your skill and your runs, these simple elements get mixed together at larger scales, and you'll be presented with a unique set of challenges based on your skill and the choices you've made in the run. As you get further in your run, you're given harder enemies, uniquely challenging bosses, and more traps. But you're also given bigger, deadlier guns, and that +4 HP will be your best friend when it saves you from death after you mess up a tight dodge. As the game scales upward and the chaos ramps up, the strength of the simple designs really shines, and when you finally die, it rarely feels cheap, and it's very difficult to not say "alright, one more run".

I played the hell out of Civ V, so I naturally was looking forward to Civ VI. Unfortunately, Civ VI turned out to be a buggy mess of unrefined gameplay and AI.
There are some fantastic ideas here. If you boil the game down to its core mechanics, it's objectevly an improvement over Civ V. Everyone agrees the new district mechanic is a pretty great idea as you can build cities that are really good at focusing on one or two resources instead of depending only on the terrain.
However, it's very obvious that the game was pushed out the door. The game runs at a snail's pace in the late game, with load times inbetween turns taking 2-3 min on larger maps. The AI is really weird and unatural. The game crashes quite often, at least once every 5 hours. Numerous scripting issues that are especially odd because of how easy patching them would be. Still no production queue. Unbalanced Civs with the same ones always coming out on top every time. The game's pacing is clunky and some periods are either way too short-lived or last too long. Unbalanced strategies, with religion being near useless and money being universal. Very unblanced buildings and districts, industrial district is basically useless. Wonders have been powered way down, they are pretty situational and most aren't very impactful.
I could go on and on, my point is, Civ VI was rushed. I don't know for sure who's fault it could be, whether the publisher's or the developer's, but it's crystal clear they gave us an unfinished product so they could start pumping out dlc's. The game has been out for over a year now and it seems like they barely worked to fix some of the glaring bugs. But they still have time to release more Civ and Scenario packs!
"PRE-Order the NEW $30 DLC with BRAND NEW MECHANICS and 8 NEW CIVS, WOW!"
That's all they care about, your money. They don't care if the players get an unfinished product, they know we're stupid enough to pay full price and buy all the DLC. They make these flashy expensive looking trailers with explosions and cool transitions and this loud amazing music, but they release these tiny monthly patches that fix one or two bugs.
The worst part is, there are a lot of people who really do try and enjoy the game. These people are true gamers, all they want is to have fun playing their favorite strategy franchise. They've created an active healthy community with people of all ages. They share strategies and screenshots of their empires, give tips to new players, talk about their favoite civs and strategies to play. They put up with all the bugs and poor design because underneath them, there is a pretty fun time to be had. These people are seen as exploitable consumers who'll buy an unfinished product and all the DLCs by whomever is at fault here.
These people deserve a complete and clean experience. We deserve a game that lives up to the Civilization name, not a game that uses it to sell more $4.99 Civ and Scenario packs!

The story in Alan Wake is quite exceptional comparing to other video games in the genre. Too bad the rest of the game can't match up to the well-written storytelling.
The game kicks off interestingly where we meet our protagonist, who is struggling with writing crisis and a "little bit" of insanity. Soon we find ourselves fighting with shadowy creatures named 'The Taken' controlled by a mysterious force.
The fighting mechanics based on the power of light are unique. While this newish fighting scheme is fun at first it lacks deepness, so it becomes repetitive. Unfortunately nothing good can be said about the controls, which is one of the most discouraging features of the game: awkward movements, slow reaction times, super sensitive mouse controls
One of the high points of the game is the voice acting. It phenomenally supports the great story, which pushes the player for resolution...that may or may not exists in the end. The end of the story will leave many with questions and bad taste, but the open nature of the conclusion is not necessarily a bad thing at all. However, the special chapters (The Signal and The Writer) will help put a proper end to this tale.
After 6 chapters it is hard to think of any reasons why anyone, who is not a fan of Alan would start this game all over again. The replay value of the game is very low thanks to its linear nature. Other than some collectibles there's no point to return. Alan Wake is one of those games that would've been enjoyable on a big screen rather than with a controller in a hand.
Rating: 65/100; Replay Value: 1/5; To Beat: 14-16 hours (incl. the specials); Played on: normal.
